metadata.Initiative / Programme: EU AI Act (Reg. (EU) 2024/1689), incl. Art. 4 AI literacy
metadata.Description: Horizontal EU regulation on AI; Art. 4 requires providers and deployers to take measures to ensure/support AI literacy of staff; certain education uses are classified high-risk (Annex III).

summary: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (the EU AI Act) is a binding, EU-wide framework governing artificial intelligence systems. Article 4 requires AI providers and deployers to take measures to support sufficient AI literacy among staff and others operating or using AI on their behalf, taking account of their knowledge, experience, education or training, the context of use, and the people affected by the systems. The Act does not prescribe a curriculum, teaching method, or delivery technology.
pedagogicalSummary: The inspected regulation establishes an AI-literacy obligation but does not prescribe a teaching method or learning design. Article 4 requires providers and deployers to take measures to support sufficient AI literacy among staff and others operating or using AI systems on their behalf, with the measures suited to factors such as their knowledge, experience, education or training, and the context of use. This indicates context-sensitive support, but the text inspected does not specify whether learning should be formal or informal, individual or collaborative, theoretical or hands-on, or how it should be assessed. The missing detail should not be read as evidence that no particular approaches are used in practice. Source: https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1689/oj#art_4
prioritySummary: The regulation’s AI-literacy emphasis is on enabling people involved in providing, deploying, operating, or using AI systems to have a level of understanding suited to their role and context. Article 4 specifically places responsibility on providers and deployers to take measures for their staff and other people dealing with system operation and use on their behalf; it also requires attention to the people or groups affected by the systems. The regulation’s recitals describe informed decisions about AI deployment and awareness of opportunities, risks, and possible harms as relevant aims. The inspected text therefore supports a practical, role- and context-oriented priority, rather than a narrowly defined workforce-training curriculum or an explicit individual well-being programme. Source: https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1689/oj
educationalTechnologySummary: The inspected regulation does not identify a learning platform, software, hardware, or other educational technology developed or used to deliver AI-literacy learning. It is a legal instrument that requires providers and deployers to take measures supporting AI literacy, without specifying the delivery tools or materials for those measures. The Act’s provisions about AI systems, including systems used in education, concern the regulation of AI; they do not by themselves establish that the Act or its institutions use those systems as educational technologies for AI-literacy instruction. Accordingly, no educational technology can be named from the inspected evidence. This is a limit of what the regulation specifies, not evidence that organizations implementing it use no tools. Source: https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1689/oj

inclusion.reason: This initiative qualifies for inclusion under the 'Issued by a national or sub-national government' route (specifically, a supranational intergovernmental body - the EU). The regulation is directly applicable law issued by the European Union institutions. It includes explicit AI literacy requirements in Article 4, mandating that providers and deployers implement measures to ensure/support AI literacy of staff, which satisfies the mandatory AI-literacy requirement.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: EC–OECD AI Literacy Framework (AILit) "Empowering Learners for the Age of AI"
metadata.Description: Joint European Commission–OECD framework defining AI literacy competences across four domains (Engage with, Create with, Manage and Design/Shape AI), with learning scenarios; basis for PISA 2029 MAIL.

summary: The European Commission–OECD AI Literacy Framework (AILit) is a competency framework focused primarily on helping primary- and secondary-school learners engage with AI critically, creatively and responsibly. It organises knowledge, skills and attitudes into four domains—Engage with AI, Create with AI, Manage AI and Shape AI—with expectations progressing from basic to advanced. An interactive framework lets educators explore competencies and classroom scenarios across contexts and subjects; examples include activities on training data and bias and on evaluating generative-AI outputs. The framework is intended to inform teaching and wider education initiatives, and is linked to PISA 2029’s Machine-AI Learning Literacy assessment.
pedagogicalSummary: The initiative offers a competency framework rather than prescribing a single teaching method. Learning is organised across four domains—Engage with AI, Create with AI, Manage AI and Shape AI—with competencies progressing from basic through intermediate to advanced expectations. Each combines knowledge, skills and attitudes with learner expectations and classroom learning scenarios, and the interactive framework lets educators filter competencies by context and subject area. The exemplars indicate practical activities, including a primary-level game about training data and bias and a lesson in which students use generative AI to communicate science while evaluating and verifying outputs. This supports staged, applied and critical learning, but the inspected pages do not establish one required pedagogy. Sources: https://ailiteracyframework.org/; https://ailiteracyframework.org/frameworks/; https://ailiteracyframework.org/ai-for-oceans/; https://ailiteracyframework.org/ai-for-science-communication/
prioritySummary: The framework’s principal emphasis is preparing primary- and secondary-school learners to understand and engage with AI with critical judgement, creativity and agency. It aims to help students assess AI’s opportunities, risks, ethical implications and effects on people and society, while learning when and how to use AI responsibly. Its audience also includes teachers, education leaders, policymakers, learning designers and families: the framework is intended to inform classroom materials, standards and wider education initiatives, and to support educators in integrating AI literacy across subjects. The site also connects the initiative to inclusive digital education and the PISA 2029 assessment; these are institutional and system goals alongside, rather than substitutes for, the learner-facing emphasis. Sources: https://ailiteracyframework.org/; https://ailiteracyframework.org/about/
educationalTechnologySummary: The inspected pages identify an online Interactive AILit Framework that allows educators to filter and explore competencies, their progression, classroom scenarios and associated knowledge, skills and attitudes; it is a framework-navigation resource, not evidence of a particular student learning platform. The site also presents AI for Oceans as a web-app learning game for young learners, introducing how AI systems are trained and how training data can introduce bias and errors. A separate science-communication exemplar has students use generative AI to develop communication while practising prompting, output evaluation and accuracy checking, but no particular AI product is named. The pages do not establish that the initiative developed these exemplars or any named AI tool; they describe them as educational resources/examples. Sources: https://ailiteracyframework.org/frameworks/; https://ailiteracyframework.org/ai-for-oceans/; https://ailiteracyframework.org/ai-for-science-communication/

inclusion.reason: This initiative qualifies for inclusion because it is formally endorsed by the European Commission (a national/sub-national government body) and the OECD (an intergovernmental body). It also includes explicit AI-literacy content through its defined competency domains and learning scenarios. The involvement of CodeAI and an international expert group further supports its credibility and reach.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: Digital Education Action Plan 2021–2027
metadata.Description: Commission policy initiative with two priorities (high-performing digital education ecosystem; digital skills), incl. actions on AI and data in education.

summary: The European Commission’s Digital Education Action Plan 2021–2027 is an EU-wide policy framework to help education and training systems adapt to the digital age. Its priorities are developing a high-performing digital education ecosystem and strengthening digital skills and competences. It addresses learners, teachers and trainers, institutions and policy communities through actions including digital education content, blended-learning approaches, competence frameworks, and practical guidance on ethical AI for primary and secondary teachers. It is a broad policy agenda rather than a course with a prescribed teaching method; AI and data are components of its wider digital education focus.
pedagogicalSummary: The inspected pages present the Digital Education Action Plan as a policy framework rather than a programme with a defined teaching method or sequence of lessons. It supports learning indirectly through actions such as practical AI guidance for primary and secondary teachers, digital education content, and blended-learning approaches. The policy-background page describes digital education broadly as using digital tools and content to support teaching, learning and assessment, but this is not evidence of one prescribed pedagogy. The accessible pages do not explain how the AI guidance is taught or how learners engage with it, so a more specific pedagogical approach cannot be established from this inspection. Sources: https://education.ec.europa.eu/focus-topics/digital-education/actions/plan and https://education.ec.europa.eu/focus-topics/digital-education/actions
prioritySummary: The initiative’s stated emphasis is improving Europe’s digital education capacity through two linked priorities: fostering a high-performing digital education ecosystem and enhancing digital skills and competences for the digital transition. It aims to help national education and training systems adapt to the digital age, while advancing quality, inclusive and accessible learning. Its intended beneficiaries and participants include learners, teachers and trainers, education institutions, and policy and other stakeholder communities; the action overview includes teacher-facing AI guidance and broader digital-skills measures. AI and data in education appear as components of this wider policy agenda, not as the initiative’s sole or clearly dominant objective. Sources: https://education.ec.europa.eu/focus-topics/digital-education/actions/plan and https://education.ec.europa.eu/focus-topics/digital-education/actions
educationalTechnologySummary: The pages identify SELFIE, SELFIE for Teachers and SELFIE for work-based learning as free self-reflection tools on digital competences, available in EU official languages. They support schools in reviewing their use of technology for teaching and learning, teachers in reflecting on and developing their digital competence, and vocational education and training settings in considering work-based learning. The digital education page also identifies the European Digital Education Hub as an online collaborative community, but the inspected material does not describe it as a teaching platform. The Action Plan overview mentions digital education content and AI guidance, but does not name a particular AI teaching system, software or hardware, nor establish that the Action Plan itself developed the SELFIE tools. Sources: https://education.ec.europa.eu/focus-topics/digital-education/tools-for-schools-and-educators and https://education.ec.europa.eu/focus-topics/digital-education

inclusion.reason: Initiative qualifies via the first inclusion route as it is issued by the European Commission (an intergovernmental body), and includes specific actions addressing AI in education, satisfying the AI-literacy requirement.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: Ethical guidelines on the use of AI and data in teaching and learning for educators (2022; updated)
metadata.Description: Commission guidelines (DEAP Action 6) helping educators understand AI and data use and address misconceptions, with ethical considerations and guiding questions.

summary: The European Commission’s Ethical Guidelines on the Use of AI and Data in Teaching and Learning support educators, particularly in primary and secondary education, in understanding AI and making informed decisions about its use in educational settings. The resource combines explanations of key terms and relevant legal context with guiding questions, scenarios, and examples to help educators weigh potential benefits and risks, address misconceptions, and apply ethical and responsible data practices. It emphasizes reflective, context-based professional decision-making rather than a formal course or specific AI tool.
pedagogicalSummary: The initiative offers practical guidance rather than a described course or formal teaching sequence. It supports educators’ learning through guiding questions, scenarios, and examples for classroom and school settings, alongside explanations of key terms, principles, and legal context. This suggests an emphasis on reflective, context-based decision-making and applying ethical considerations to professional practice; the page does not specify a particular instructional method, schedule, or assessment approach. The guidelines are intended to help educators build understanding and confidence, including by considering AI’s benefits and risks. Evidence is limited to the overview page, so further pedagogical detail may be present in the guidelines themselves. (https://education.ec.europa.eu/focus-topics/digital-education/actions/plan/ethical-guidelines-for-educators-on-using-artificial-intelligence)
prioritySummary: The principal emphasis is helping teachers and educational staff—particularly those working in primary and secondary education—understand and engage with ethical AI and data use in teaching and learning. The page highlights building educators’ confidence to make informed, context-based decisions, strengthening their ability to use AI’s benefits while recognising and managing risks, and increasing awareness of ethical data practices. It also situates this support amid growing AI use in education and the need to attend to relevant regulation, including the AI Act and GDPR. The stated focus is educator capacity and responsible educational practice; the page does not establish a separate priority hierarchy beyond these aims. (https://education.ec.europa.eu/focus-topics/digital-education/actions/plan/ethical-guidelines-for-educators-on-using-artificial-intelligence)
educationalTechnologySummary: The inspected page identifies no particular educational technology, platform, software, or hardware developed or used by the initiative to deliver AI-literacy learning. Its named resource is a set of guidelines, including practical scenarios and examples, guiding questions, a glossary, and background material; these are learning-support materials, not identified technology products. AI is discussed as a subject and as something educators may encounter in teaching and learning, but the page does not say that the initiative uses a specific AI tool for instruction. It mentions a video about potential benefits and risks, but gives no details about its platform or role beyond “watch and learn.” This summary is limited to the overview page and does not establish what the full guidelines may contain. (https://education.ec.europa.eu/focus-topics/digital-education/actions/plan/ethical-guidelines-for-educators-on-using-artificial-intelligence)

metadata.Initiative / Programme: DigComp – European Digital Competence Framework for Citizens (2.2 / 3.0)
metadata.Description: JRC framework describing digital competences; DigComp 2.2 added AI examples, DigComp 3.0 integrates AI across competences.

summary: DigComp is the European Commission Joint Research Centre’s non-prescriptive framework for citizens’ digital competences, intended to inform education, assessment, learning recognition and employment contexts. It organises competences into five areas and 21 competences, with learning outcomes spanning four proficiency levels from basic to highly advanced. DigComp 3.0 integrates AI-related knowledge, skills and attitudes across the competences, while treating AI as one part of broader digital competence. It provides a reference for users such as educators, policymakers, researchers, employers and learners, rather than a course or prescribed teaching method.
pedagogicalSummary: DigComp is a non-prescriptive reference framework, not a prescribed teaching method or course. It organises learning content hierarchically into competence areas, competences and learning outcomes, with four proficiency levels from Basic to Highly advanced. The learning outcomes state what a person knows, understands and can do, and are intended to help users develop or revise curricula and courses and recognise formal, non-formal and informal learning. The pages do not specify classroom activities, instructional sequences or a particular pedagogy, so these should not be inferred. AI-related knowledge, skills and attitudes appear across all 21 competences in DigComp 3.0. (https://joint-research-centre.ec.europa.eu/scientific-activities/key-competences-lifelong-learning/digital-competence-framework-digcomp_en; https://joint-research-centre.ec.europa.eu/scientific-activities/key-competences-lifelong-learning/digital-competence-framework-digcomp/digcomp-30_en)
prioritySummary: DigComp’s central purpose is to support development and shared understanding of digital competence among people of all ages, across basic to highly advanced levels. It serves individuals as well as policymakers, employers, researchers, educators and other organisations, and can inform education and training, assessment, learning recognition and employment profiles. DigComp 3.0 specifically integrates AI competence throughout the framework, covering knowledge, skills and attitudes relevant to understanding AI and using it safely and ethically, while treating AI as one digital technology among others. The stated rationale spans participation in everyday life, learning, work and society; the inspected pages do not establish a single narrower priority over these. (https://joint-research-centre.ec.europa.eu/scientific-activities/key-competences-lifelong-learning/digital-competence-framework-digcomp_en; https://joint-research-centre.ec.europa.eu/scientific-activities/key-competences-lifelong-learning/digital-competence-framework-digcomp/digcomp-30_en)
educationalTechnologySummary: The inspected pages identify DigComp as a technology-neutral framework, not as a learning platform or software product. DigComp 3.0 is made available in PDF, editable and structured-data formats, with learning outcomes also available through a data collection in spreadsheet and linked-open-data formats; these resources support users in interpreting, adapting and applying the framework, rather than delivering instruction themselves. The main page also links to DigComp-based assessment and monitoring tools, but their details were not available in the pages inspected, so no specific tool or platform can be named here. No hardware or AI learning application developed or used by the initiative is identified in the accessible evidence. (https://joint-research-centre.ec.europa.eu/scientific-activities/key-competences-lifelong-learning/digital-competence-framework-digcomp_en; https://joint-research-centre.ec.europa.eu/scientific-activities/key-competences-lifelong-learning/digital-competence-framework-digcomp/digcomp-30_en)

metadata.Initiative / Programme: DigCompEdu – European Framework for the Digital Competence of Educators
metadata.Description: JRC framework describing 22 digital competences for educators organised in six areas.

summary: DigCompEdu is a European Commission Joint Research Centre framework describing 22 digital competences for educators across six areas. It is intended for educators in varied education and training settings, from early childhood and schools to higher, adult and non-formal education, and offers a shared reference for developing digital practice rather than a single course or delivery programme. Its guidance emphasizes adapting digital resources and teaching methods to learners and goals, inclusion, collaboration and reflective professional development. A 2026 draft update integrates AI literacy, including understanding system outputs and limitations and exercising professional judgement; the final update is scheduled for 2027. SELFIEforTEACHERS is identified as a self-reflection tool for school educators, available in 24 EU official languages.
pedagogicalSummary: DigCompEdu is a competence framework, not a described course or single teaching programme, so the inspected pages do not establish a delivery model. Its pedagogical orientation is nevertheless visible in the competences it sets out: educators are expected to reflect on and develop their practice, collaborate with colleagues, and use digital resources to support guidance, collaborative and self-regulated learning, assessment, learner inclusion and active engagement. The framework encourages adapting resources and methods to learning goals, context and learners, rather than focusing on technical skills alone. The website says AI literacy is integrated throughout the draft 2026 update, including understanding system outputs and limitations and exercising professional judgement; this is a draft, with the final update scheduled for 2027. Sources: https://joint-research-centre.ec.europa.eu/scientific-activities/key-competences-lifelong-learning/digcompedu_en and https://joint-research-centre.ec.europa.eu/scientific-activities/key-competences-lifelong-learning/digcompedu/digcompedu-framework_en
prioritySummary: The initiative principally aims to give educators across education levels and settings a shared reference for developing digital competence, so they can use digital technologies to enhance and innovate education and training. Its intended beneficiaries include educators from early childhood through higher and adult education, as well as general, vocational, special-needs and non-formal learning contexts; learners benefit through the framework’s emphasis on inclusion, engagement and support for their digital competence. The site also describes AI literacy as a cross-cutting element of the draft update, alongside professional judgement, and identifies digital well-being and sustainability as draft themes. These are framework priorities, not evidence of a separate AI course or a ranked set of goals. Sources: https://joint-research-centre.ec.europa.eu/scientific-activities/key-competences-lifelong-learning/digcompedu_en and https://joint-research-centre.ec.europa.eu/scientific-activities/key-competences-lifelong-learning/digcompedu/digcompedu-framework_en
educationalTechnologySummary: The pages identify SELFIEforTEACHERS as a self-reflection tool available for school education in 24 EU official languages; it supports educators’ reflection on their digital competence. The inspected material does not describe its features or establish whether the initiative developed it. DigCompEdu itself is a framework, not an educational technology, and the pages do not name particular AI systems, learning platforms, software or hardware used to teach AI literacy. They describe digital technologies broadly as resources educators may select, create and use in teaching, learning, assessment and professional development, but that is guidance about technology use rather than evidence of specific tools deployed by the initiative. The draft update discusses AI literacy but does not identify an AI learning product. Sources: https://joint-research-centre.ec.europa.eu/scientific-activities/key-competences-lifelong-learning/digcompedu_en and https://joint-research-centre.ec.europa.eu/scientific-activities/key-competences-lifelong-learning/digcompedu/digcompedu-framework_en

metadata.Initiative / Programme: Digital Omnibus on AI (amending the AI Act)
metadata.Description: Commission package simplifying digital rules; amends AI Act incl. Art. 4 (from "ensure" to "support" AI literacy) and the timeline for high-risk rules.

summary: The Digital Omnibus on AI is a European Commission proposal to simplify selected provisions of the EU AI Act and support their timely, proportionate implementation. It proposes changes including adjusting Article 4’s AI-literacy wording from “ensure” to “support” and extending timelines for certain high-risk rules. The proposal is relevant to policymakers, regulators, and organizations developing or deploying AI systems, but the inspected materials describe a legislative measure rather than a learning programme or instructional offering.
pedagogicalSummary: The inspected material presents the Digital Omnibus on AI as a policy and legislative proposal, not a learning programme: it proposes targeted simplification to support timely, smooth and proportionate implementation of parts of the AI Act. It describes no teaching activities, instructional sequence, learner support, or pedagogy. This is a lack of pedagogical evidence in the inspected pages, rather than evidence that the broader AI Act has no literacy-related provisions. Sources: https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/library/digital-omnibus-ai-regulation-proposal and https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/regulatory-framework-ai.
prioritySummary: The proposal’s stated priority is simplifying selected AI Act provisions to make their implementation timely, smooth and proportionate. The related AI Act overview frames the wider regulatory effort around trustworthy AI, safety and fundamental rights, while setting rules for AI developers and deployers. The inspected proposal page does not specify which groups benefit from each proposed change or identify AI literacy as a principal objective; accordingly, a more specific beneficiary priority cannot be established from these pages. Sources: https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/library/digital-omnibus-ai-regulation-proposal and https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/regulatory-framework-ai.
educationalTechnologySummary: The inspected pages identify no educational technology developed or used by the Digital Omnibus on AI to teach AI literacy. The initiative is presented as a legislative proposal; the proposal page offers access to the proposal and annexes in EU official languages, but those documents are policy materials, not evidence of a learning platform, software, or teaching tool. The AI Act overview mentions a Single Information platform and Service Desk for information and implementation support, but does not describe them as educational technologies for AI-literacy learning. This conclusion is limited to the pages inspected. Sources: https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/library/digital-omnibus-ai-regulation-proposal and https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/regulatory-framework-ai.

inclusion.reason: This initiative qualifies for inclusion because: (1) it is formally issued by the European Commission (an intergovernmental body), satisfying the inclusion route for intergovernmental bodies; and (2) the summary explicitly states that the initiative includes a substantive change to the AI Act regarding Article 4, shifting the mandate from 'ensure' to 'support' AI literacy. This constitutes an educational element and guidance about how the EU approaches AI literacy as a public good, meeting the core requirement of including AI literacy content.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: General Data Protection Regulation (Reg. (EU) 2016/679)
metadata.Description: EU data protection law applying to processing of learner/staff data incl. by AI tools.

summary: The General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), Regulation (EU) 2016/679, is a binding EU-wide law governing the processing of personal data by organisations, including when data is processed through AI tools. It sets requirements for controllers and processors and establishes rights for people whose data is processed, with an emphasis on protecting fundamental rights and enabling the free movement of personal data within the EU. It is a legal framework, not a teaching programme; the available evidence identifies no instructional approach or educational technology.
pedagogicalSummary: The inspected page presents Regulation (EU) 2016/679 as a legal instrument, not a teaching programme. It describes rules for processing personal data rather than learning activities, instruction, or learner support, so no pedagogical approach is evidenced on this page. This is a lack of teaching evidence in the inspected material, not evidence that related educational activities do not exist elsewhere. Source: https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2016/679/oj
prioritySummary: The regulation’s stated emphasis is protecting natural persons’ fundamental rights and freedoms in relation to personal-data processing, particularly their right to data protection, while also supporting the free movement of personal data within the EU. Its beneficiaries are people whose data is processed; the page does not frame the measure as an AI-literacy initiative or identify learners or educators as its particular audience. The inspected text establishes a general legal priority, not a specific workforce or educational objective. Source: https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2016/679/oj
educationalTechnologySummary: The inspected page identifies no educational technology developed or used to support AI-literacy learning. It is the text of a data-protection regulation, not a description of a learning platform, software, or hardware. The regulation addresses personal-data processing, including processing carried out wholly or partly by automated means, but that scope does not establish that it uses or develops educational technology. No such technology could be identified in the inspected page. Source: https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2016/679/oj

inclusion.reason: The GDPR is directly applicable in all EU Member States and is issued by the European Union (an intergovernmental body). It includes provisions relevant to AI tools used for educational purposes (e.g., automated decision-making, transparency requirements), thus satisfying the AI-literacy requirement as it provides legal guidance on how AI systems should process personal data. The inclusion route 'Issued by an intergovernmental body' applies.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: AI Office Living Repository of AI literacy practices
metadata.Description: Living repository run by the EU AI Office collecting AI literacy practices from AI Pact participants to support Art. 4 implementation.

summary: The EU AI Office’s Living Repository of AI Literacy Practices collects examples from AI Pact participants and other organisations to support learning and exchange among providers and deployers of AI systems. It focuses on organisational approaches to fostering AI literacy among staff and people using systems on their behalf, in support of Article 4 of the EU AI Act. The repository is a reference and practice-sharing resource, rather than a prescribed course or curriculum; the available description does not specify teaching methods or assessment.
pedagogicalSummary: The initiative supports learning mainly through the collection and exchange of examples: the EU AI Office gathers ongoing AI-literacy practices from AI Pact participants and other organisations in a “living repository” intended to help providers and deployers learn from one another. The inspected page does not describe a prescribed curriculum, teaching sequence, learner assessment, or specific instructional method, so the repository is best evidenced as a practice-sharing resource rather than a direct teaching programme. It also cautions that copying a practice does not itself establish compliance with Article 4. Details of the practices in the linked compilation were not available in the inspected page. (https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/library/living-repository-foster-learning-and-exchange-ai-literacy)
prioritySummary: The initiative’s stated emphasis is to foster AI literacy by sharing examples of organisational practices, while supporting implementation of Article 4 of the AI Act. That provision requires AI-system providers and deployers to take measures to support AI literacy among their staff and people using systems on their behalf. The repository is intended to encourage learning and exchange among providers and deployers, and to contribute examples for the Commission’s future compliance information. The page also places it within the AI Office’s broader effort to support AI literacy, skills, and talent development. It does not specify a more narrowly targeted beneficiary or rank these aims. (https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/library/living-repository-foster-learning-and-exchange-ai-literacy)
educationalTechnologySummary: The inspected page identifies a living repository of AI-literacy practices and a downloadable compilation titled “Compilation AI Literacy Practices - April 2025 update.” These are presented as shared reference materials for discovering and exchanging organisational practices, not as named learning software or a teaching platform. The page does not identify any specific digital learning system, AI tool, or hardware used or developed to deliver instruction. Although the repository is accessible online, the available evidence does not establish that it is an educational technology beyond serving as a collection of learning-related examples. The compilation’s contents and any technologies described within it were not accessible in the inspected page, so conclusions about tools used in those practices are limited. (https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/library/living-repository-foster-learning-and-exchange-ai-literacy)

inclusion.reason: The initiative is issued and managed by the EU AI Office (a formal statutory body of the European Commission), satisfying the 'Issued by a national or sub-national government or intergovernmental body' inclusion route. It includes educational content in the form of a living repository that provides examples of AI literacy practices, thereby meeting the AI-literacy requirement. The initiative serves providers and deployers of AI systems across the EU.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: European Digital Education Hub (EDEH)
metadata.Description: Commission community of practice on digital education; squads produce reports (e.g. AI in education, ethical AI in practice).

summary: The European Digital Education Hub (EDEH), managed by the European Commission’s Directorate-General for Education, Youth, Sport and Culture, is a community of practice connecting educators, policymakers, researchers and other digital-education stakeholders in Europe and beyond. It supports knowledge exchange and collaboration through webinars, workshops, working groups and publications. Its wider focus is digital education policy, research and practice; AI-related work includes reports on AI in education and activities concerning ethical AI. The Hub is not described as a formal course or curriculum.
pedagogicalSummary: The accessible pages describe a community-of-practice model rather than a formal course or curriculum. Members can learn from experts through webinars and take part in hands-on workshops and working groups where they collaborate and co-create ideas and solutions; a members’ reading corner supports further exploration. These activities suggest peer exchange, expert input and collaborative learning. The pages do not specify a sequence of instruction, assessment, or a distinct pedagogy for AI literacy, so evidence is limited to the Hub’s broader digital-education activities. Sources: https://education.ec.europa.eu/focus-topics/digital-education/hub and https://education.ec.europa.eu/focus-topics/digital-education
prioritySummary: The Hub’s stated emphasis is to reduce fragmentation in digital education by strengthening cooperation and dialogue among stakeholders, and by connecting policy, research and implementation practices at European level. Its intended participants and beneficiaries include educators, policymakers, experts and other digital-education stakeholders in Europe and beyond. The wider context also frames digital education as a means to enhance citizens’ competences and skills for the digital transition, but the inspected Hub page presents collaboration and knowledge exchange as its central purpose. The pages do not establish workforce upskilling or individual well-being as a more specific or dominant Hub priority. Sources: https://education.ec.europa.eu/focus-topics/digital-education/hub and https://education.ec.europa.eu/focus-topics/digital-education
educationalTechnologySummary: The inspected pages identify no specific learning platform, software product, hardware, or AI tool developed or used by the Hub. They describe it as an online community with member access, a reading corner, webinars, workshops and working groups; these are ways of accessing and organising learning and collaboration, but the pages do not name the underlying platform or describe a bespoke educational technology. The Hub’s publication and knowledge-sharing activities may address AI in education, but that does not establish use of an AI product as a learning technology. This summary is limited to the Hub and digital-education pages inspected; it cannot confirm whether members use additional tools within activities. Sources: https://education.ec.europa.eu/focus-topics/digital-education/hub and https://education.ec.europa.eu/focus-topics/digital-education

metadata.Initiative / Programme: European Commission AI literacy Q&A (guidance on Art. 4 AI Act)
metadata.Description: Commission Q&A explaining how organisations can comply with the AI literacy provision of Art. 4 AI Act.

summary: The European Commission’s AI Literacy Questions and Answers page provides guidance on Article 4 of the EU AI Act, which requires providers and deployers to support AI literacy among staff and others operating or using AI on their behalf. It addresses context-sensitive compliance, training and literacy activities, and points readers to related Commission resources, including a repository of AI literacy practices. The initiative is regulatory guidance rather than a course or teaching programme; the available evidence does not establish a prescribed instructional method or delivery technology.
pedagogicalSummary: The initiative is principally regulatory guidance, not a teaching programme: the Q&A page explains Article 4 and raises questions about training formats, programme content and whether other literacy activities can be used, but the rendered page inspected lists these questions without their answers. The linked Commission policy page says measures should take account of staff and other learners’ technical knowledge, experience, education, training and the context in which AI is used; it also describes a repository intended to encourage learning and exchange through examples of existing practices. This supports a context-sensitive and practice-sharing approach, but the inspected pages do not establish a prescribed instructional method or a specific course design. Evidence: https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/faqs/ai-literacy-questions-answers and https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/ai-talent-skills-and-literacy
prioritySummary: The Q&A’s main emphasis is helping providers and deployers of AI systems understand and act on their Article 4 responsibility to support AI literacy among staff and other people operating or using AI on their behalf. The linked policy page describes the obligation as context-sensitive and says the Commission and Member States should support providers’ and deployers’ efforts, particularly those of SMEs. It also situates this work within broader aims: expanding the pool of AI experts, improving workers’ AI skills, and increasing AI understanding among the general population. The inspected material therefore indicates both organisational compliance support and wider skills and awareness goals, without establishing that one broader goal takes precedence over the Q&A’s Article 4 focus. Evidence: https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/faqs/ai-literacy-questions-answers and https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/ai-talent-skills-and-literacy
educationalTechnologySummary: The inspected Q&A does not identify a learning platform, software or hardware used to deliver instruction; its mention of ChatGPT appears only in a question about workplace use, not as an educational tool provided by the initiative. The linked Commission policy page does identify a digital repository of AI literacy practices, with more than 40 examples, launched to support learning and exchange among providers, deployers and the wider public. This is a resource for discovering and sharing practices, rather than evidence of a course-delivery system or interactive teaching technology. No other educational technologies developed or used by the initiative were identified in the limited pages inspected. Evidence: https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/faqs/ai-literacy-questions-answers and https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/ai-talent-skills-and-literacy

inclusion.reason: The initiative qualifies for inclusion because it is issued by an intergovernmental body (the European Commission) under the EU AI Act. It directly addresses the AI literacy requirement by explaining how to achieve compliance with Art. 4 of the AI Act and discussing educational elements such as training initiatives, competence frameworks for citizens/teachers/students, and guidance on resources and courses. The inclusion route is met via its status as a document from an intergovernmental body.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: Guidelines for teachers and educators on tackling disinformation and promoting digital literacy (2022; updated)
metadata.Description: Commission guidelines with practical tips and activity plans for teachers to counter disinformation and build digital literacy (Oct 2022; updated).

summary: The European Commission’s 2022, updated guidelines support primary and secondary teachers in tackling disinformation and strengthening students’ digital literacy. The resource offers practical tips and activity plans, including work on fact-checking, critical thinking, recognizing deepfakes, and assessing digital-literacy competences. It also addresses generative AI and large language models, including their societal, ethical, and safety implications. The approach emphasizes practical, teacher-supported learning rather than a specified lesson sequence or technology platform.
pedagogicalSummary: The page presents the guidelines as practical support for teachers rather than specifying a complete teaching model. It says they include hands-on tips and activity plans for primary and secondary educators, including those without specialist digital-education knowledge. The suggested learning aims include fact-checking and critical thinking, understanding ethical and economic dimensions of disinformation, recognizing deepfakes, and assessing students’ digital-literacy competences. This supports describing the approach as practical, teacher-supported learning with attention to competence assessment; the inspected page does not establish a particular lesson sequence, classroom format, or assessment method. (https://education.ec.europa.eu/news/guidelines-for-teachers-and-educators-on-tackling-disinformation-and-promoting-digital-literacy-through-education-and-training)
prioritySummary: The initiative’s stated emphasis is to help educators tackle disinformation and strengthen learners’ digital literacy through education and training. Its direct beneficiaries are primary and secondary teachers and educators, whom the guidelines aim to equip with usable advice; the intended learner benefit is that young people become more critical and confident users who can assess information and use digital technologies responsibly. The page identifies this resource as a deliverable of the Digital Education Action Plan, but the inspected evidence does not present workforce upskilling or individual well-being as its focus. (https://education.ec.europa.eu/news/guidelines-for-teachers-and-educators-on-tackling-disinformation-and-promoting-digital-literacy-through-education-and-training)
educationalTechnologySummary: The inspected page does not identify a named platform, software application, device, or other educational technology that the initiative develops or uses to deliver learning. It refers generally to responsible use of digital technologies and includes identifying deepfakes among the topics teachers may address; these are learning aims, not evidence of a particular tool being provided. The guidelines themselves are described as a resource containing tips and activity plans, rather than as an educational technology. Because the full guidelines were not accessible in the inspected page text, this finding is limited to the public page and does not establish whether the document contains specific tool recommendations. (https://education.ec.europa.eu/news/guidelines-for-teachers-and-educators-on-tackling-disinformation-and-promoting-digital-literacy-through-education-and-training)

inclusion.reason:
AI-literacy requirement: The guidelines include educational content and practical guidance on how to use AI (generative models, large language models) and understand their implications for society, ethics, and safety. This satisfies the literacy element.
Inclusion route: It is issued by the European Commission, an EU-level statutory body that represents member states; therefore it qualifies under the intergovernmental/official government endorsement rule. The page URL (https://education.ec.europa.eu/news/guidelines-for-teachers-and-educators-on-tackling-disinformation-and-promoting-digital-literacy-through-education-and-training) confirms this.

metadata.Description: Commission communication (2025) on basic, digital and AI skills, incl. further action on AI in education and training.

summary: The European Commission’s 2025 Union of Skills communication sets out an EU-wide strategy for strengthening basic, digital, STEM and AI skills through education, vocational training, lifelong learning, and worker upskilling and reskilling. It addresses learners from early education through adulthood, workers, employers, and education and training institutions, with emphasis on skills shortages, employability, and adapting to economic and digital change. AI is one component of the broader skills agenda; the inspected description does not specify teaching methods, learning materials, or educational technologies.
pedagogicalSummary: The inspected page frames the Union of Skills as a strategy spanning education, training, lifelong learning, and regular upskilling and reskilling—from early-years education to adult learning. It identifies initiatives in basic skills, STEM, vocational education and training, and worker reskilling, but does not describe teaching methods, lesson formats, or how learners are taught or assessed. The accessible evidence therefore supports a broad, continuing-learning orientation, not a specific pedagogical approach; details of pedagogy may be set out in the individual initiatives, which were not examined here. (https://employment-social-affairs.ec.europa.eu/policies-and-activities/skills-and-qualifications/union-skills_en)
prioritySummary: The Union of Skills principally aims to address skills shortages and mismatches, helping people gain or update skills for quality jobs while supporting businesses’ access to talent and Europe’s competitiveness. The page also emphasizes people’s ability to navigate changes in work and life, portability of skills across the EU, and attracting and retaining talent. It identifies students, adults, workers, employers, education and training institutions, and the wider EU as beneficiaries or participants; it does not establish a single priority that overrides the others. Digital and green transitions, basic skills, STEM participation, and inclusion are among its stated concerns. (https://employment-social-affairs.ec.europa.eu/policies-and-activities/skills-and-qualifications/union-skills_en)
educationalTechnologySummary: The inspected page does not identify any specific educational technology, learning platform, software, or hardware that the Union of Skills develops or uses to support learning. It mentions digital skills and upskilling for the digital transition as areas of focus, but these are learning aims, not evidence of particular educational technologies. The page describes a policy strategy and lists education, training, and skills initiatives, without explaining technology-mediated teaching or learning. This is a limit of the inspected page, not confirmation that no technology is used across the Union of Skills or its component initiatives. (https://employment-social-affairs.ec.europa.eu/policies-and-activities/skills-and-qualifications/union-skills_en)

inclusion.reason: This initiative is issued by the European Commission, which qualifies as an intergovernmental body, satisfying the inclusion criteria. The page explicitly describes the Union of Skills as including 'further action on AI in education and training,' confirming it contains educational content and guidance about using AI, thus meeting the AI-literacy requirement.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: Erasmus+ (digital transformation priority)
metadata.Description: EU programme for education, training, youth and sport; digital transformation is a horizontal priority.

summary: Erasmus+ is an EU programme supporting education, training, youth and sport through learning mobility, cooperation projects and opportunities for individuals and organisations. Its 2021–2027 priorities include digital transformation, encouraging digital skills, meaningful use of technology, stronger institutional capacity, and online or blended learning. The programme spans school, higher, adult and other education contexts, but the available evidence does not establish a programme-wide AI-literacy curriculum, teaching method or dedicated AI-learning technology.
pedagogicalSummary: The inspected pages describe Erasmus+ as supporting learning through mobility, exchanges, staff training, and cooperation between education organisations, rather than prescribing one teaching method. Its digital-transformation priority encourages digital tools and methods, blended and online learning, and activities that develop digital literacy and confidence using technology. Organisations may also develop, transfer, or implement innovative practices through partnerships. These are broad forms of learning support, not evidence of a single programme-wide pedagogy or a specific approach to teaching AI literacy. The pages inspected do not describe an AI-literacy curriculum, lesson model, or assessment method, so the approach to AI-literacy teaching remains unclear. (https://erasmus-plus.ec.europa.eu/about-erasmus/programme-priorities; https://erasmus-plus.ec.europa.eu/opportunities/organisations; https://erasmus-plus.ec.europa.eu/opportunities/individuals)
prioritySummary: Erasmus+ is a broad EU programme for education, training, youth, and sport, with opportunities for learners, staff, and organisations. Digital transformation is one of four horizontal priorities for 2021–2027, not the programme’s sole or explicitly highest-ranked aim. Under this priority, the programme encourages digital skills for learning, teaching, and work; meaningful use of technology; stronger digital capacity in education and training institutions; and efforts to address the digital divide. The wider programme also emphasizes inclusion, environmental sustainability, and participation in democratic life. The inspected pages establish these broad goals but do not identify AI literacy as a specific programme-wide priority or specify one primary beneficiary group for it. (https://erasmus-plus.ec.europa.eu/about-erasmus; https://erasmus-plus.ec.europa.eu/about-erasmus/programme-priorities)
educationalTechnologySummary: The inspected pages identify some digital resources, but do not establish an AI-literacy technology developed or used by Erasmus+. Online Language Support (OLS) provides language assessments, personalised learning pathways, and interactive online language courses for programme participants; its stated purpose is language learning, not AI literacy. The opportunities page also points teachers to eTwinning for connecting with colleagues and starting projects, and to SELFIE for Teachers for developing digital skills, without detailing these tools or linking them specifically to AI learning. The digital-priority page endorses digital tools and online or blended learning generally but names no platform for AI-literacy instruction. Thus, the available evidence shows adjacent learning tools, not a confirmed AI-literacy technology. (https://erasmus-plus.ec.europa.eu/resources-and-tools/online-language-support; https://erasmus-plus.ec.europa.eu/opportunities/individuals; https://erasmus-plus.ec.europa.eu/about-erasmus/programme-priorities)

inclusion.reason: The Erasmus+ initiative satisfies the inclusion criteria because it is issued, funded, and mandated by the European Union (an intergovernmental body). The website explicitly identifies digital transformation as a priority and offers educational content, resources, and guidance on how to use the tools and participate in Erasmus+ actions (including e-learning courses, mobility agreements, and training platforms). This provides the required AI literacy/educational component about using AI tools for education. The inclusion is based on the government/intergovernmental body route and the presence of educational/digital-content guidance.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: Digital Decade 2030 – Digital Compass & Digital Decade Policy Programme
metadata.Description: EU targets for 2030 incl. 80% of adults with basic digital skills and 20 million ICT specialists.

summary: The EU Digital Decade 2030 is a policy and governance framework for coordinating Europe’s digital transformation through shared objectives, annual progress monitoring, and cooperation between the European Commission and Member States. Its four priority areas are digital skills and specialists, digital infrastructure, business digitalisation, and digital public services, with goals including basic digital skills for 80% of adults and 20 million ICT specialists by 2030. It emphasizes inclusive, human-centred digital progress; the available evidence describes policy targets rather than a teaching programme or specific learning methods.
pedagogicalSummary: The inspected pages describe the Digital Decade as a policy and governance framework, not a teaching programme. They establish shared objectives and targets, annual progress monitoring, and cooperation between the Commission and Member States; they do not describe lessons, learning activities, instructional methods, or learner support. Digital skills are a policy target, but that alone does not establish a pedagogical approach. Thus, teaching approaches were not identifiable in the accessible evidence, rather than confirmed absent across every activity associated with the initiative. Sources: https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/europes-digital-decade and https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/digital-decade-policy-programme
prioritySummary: The initiative’s main emphasis is coordinating Europe’s digital transformation toward common 2030 objectives, with a stated human-centric and sustainable vision intended to benefit citizens and businesses. Its four priority areas include a digitally skilled population and highly skilled digital professionals, alongside digital infrastructure, business transformation, and public services. The pages also stress inclusion—ensuring people are not left behind and can participate in digital opportunities—and improving businesses’ ability to use technologies. The evidence supports several linked priorities rather than a single narrow beneficiary or an explicit hierarchy among them. Sources: https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/europes-digital-decade and https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/digital-decade-policy-programme
educationalTechnologySummary: The inspected pages do not identify an educational technology, learning platform, software, or hardware developed or used to teach AI or digital literacy. They mention digital technologies—including cloud, data analytics, and artificial intelligence—as subjects of business-adoption objectives, not as learning tools. The policy page describes key performance indicators and a DESI visualisation tool for tracking digital-transformation progress; this is presented as monitoring infrastructure, not as technology supporting instruction or learner practice. Accordingly, no educational technology can be identified from this limited inspection; this is a lack of evidence on the inspected policy pages, not proof that no related tools exist elsewhere. Sources: https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/digital-decade-policy-programme and https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/europes-digital-decade

inclusion.reason: The initiative includes clear AI literacy elements through its chatbot tool, educational resources for the public and professionals, and structured engagement mechanisms like the AI Board and Advisory Forum. It is issued by a sub-national government body (the European Union/Commission), satisfying the inclusion route for governmental endorsement. The AI Office actively promotes awareness of AI risks, rights, and responsibilities, fulfilling the requirement for educational content about how to use AI or its implications.

metadata.Description: Report by the European Digital Education Hub squad covering XAI concepts, legal aspects (AI Act/GDPR), trust and educator competences.

summary: The European Digital Education Hub squad’s report, “Explainable AI in education: Fostering human oversight and shared responsibility,” is a resource for educators and other education stakeholders. It explains core XAI concepts, discusses trust, human oversight and shared responsibility, and covers relevant legal frameworks, including the EU AI Act and GDPR. The report also addresses educator competences and offers guidance on applying explainability in educational contexts; the available evidence does not establish a specific teaching format or learning technology.
pedagogicalSummary: The accessible PDF preview identifies this as a report titled “Explainable AI in education: Fostering human oversight and shared responsibility,” but does not show evidence of lessons, teaching activities, or a particular way of organising learning. The inspected material is therefore insufficient to identify a pedagogical approach; this is missing evidence, not confirmation that the report contains no pedagogical recommendations. The PDF’s extracted text was too large to inspect in full. Source: https://www.daad-brussels.eu/files/2025/06/EDEH_XAI-Report-1.pdf
prioritySummary: The report’s title indicates an emphasis on explainable AI in education, specifically fostering human oversight and shared responsibility. This points to an aim of keeping human oversight and responsibility central in educational contexts involving AI. The accessible preview does not establish which groups are the intended beneficiaries or whether the report gives these aims a priority beyond what its title states. The full report could not be inspected, so further priorities remain uncertain. Source: https://www.daad-brussels.eu/files/2025/06/EDEH_XAI-Report-1.pdf

metadata.Initiative / Programme: HERMMES framework (digital & media education)
metadata.Description: Erasmus+ project (2022-2025) providing guidelines and training for age-appropriate, development-oriented ICT and media education for teachers, parents and schools.

summary: HERMMES is an EU-funded Erasmus+ project (2022–2025) offering age-sensitive digital and media education guidance, curriculum materials and online learning for teachers, parents and schools. Its curriculum supports children’s digital and media maturity through topics including safety, well-being, information and data literacy, computational thinking, communication and empathy, balancing skill development with reflection on risks and media use. Adult learning journeys use reflection and practice-based activities, with self-directed online study and opportunities for group discussion. AI is not a central focus of the initiative.
pedagogicalSummary: HERMMES combines a developmental, age-sensitive curriculum with reflective and practice-connected adult learning. Its curriculum is organised by learner age and learning area, with learning aims, teaching strategies and practice examples intended for use in existing or new school subjects. For teachers and parents, online learning journeys connect background knowledge to participants’ own situations through questions, reflection and observation tasks; learners can work independently and asynchronously or use the materials in group sessions, supported by peer learning and practice research. The community guidance uses questions to prompt discussion and change across school and home settings. The inspected pages describe these approaches but do not establish that HERMMES has a distinct AI-teaching pedagogy; its overall focus is holistic digital and media education. (https://hermmes.eu/curriculum/; https://hermmes.eu/the-hermmes-learning-journeys/; https://hermmes.eu/community-and-culture/)
prioritySummary: HERMMES principally aims to support children and young people in developing age-appropriate digital and media maturity, resilience, well-being and the ability to make conscious, critical choices about media use. Its stated desired outcome is that pupils can use analogue and digital media for learning, civic participation and work, while deciding for themselves how much to use digital tools and for what purposes. The initiative supports this through guidance and training for teachers, parents and caregivers, treating schools, families and the wider community as relevant settings for children’s development. It balances risk mitigation with skill development, including safety, problem-solving, content creation, information literacy, communication and empathy; the inspected pages do not indicate that workforce upskilling is its central end goal. (https://hermmes.eu/about-us/; https://hermmes.eu/guidelines/; https://hermmes.eu/curriculum/)
educationalTechnologySummary: The inspected pages identify the Elewa (E-Learning Waldorf) platform as the host for HERMMES online training and learning journeys. The courses are available for self-directed, asynchronous study, with materials in text, audio, image and video-interview formats; online meetings and webinars also support exchange, and some webinars are recorded for later access. These are technologies and formats used to deliver adult learning, not evidence that HERMMES develops an educational software product or hardware. The curriculum discusses digital technology and the resources page lists AI-competency framework documents, but the inspected material does not identify AI tools as technologies used or developed by HERMMES for teaching. This account is limited to the pages inspected. (https://hermmes.eu/the-hermmes-learning-journeys/; https://hermmes.eu/the-hermmes-parents-training-2/; https://hermmes.eu/resources/)

inclusion.reason: The initiative includes explicit AI-literacy elements: it provides educational content (guidelines, curriculum, training) about how digital media and technology work and how to use them, covering computational thinking, data literacy, and critical information skills. It also includes learning objectives mapped to DigComp. As an Erasmus+ project funded by the EU (a sub-national/international governmental body), it qualifies under the inclusion route for government funding and endorsement.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: SELFIE & SELFIE for Teachers
metadata.Description: Free Commission self-reflection tools for schools and teachers on digital capacity and competence.

summary: SELFIE and SELFIE for Teachers are free European Commission online tools that support reflection on digital capacity and competence. SELFIE brings students, teachers and school leaders together to answer customisable questions about technology use and review an aggregated school report to set priorities and plan improvements; a work-based-learning module also serves VET providers and participating companies. SELFIE for Teachers supports educators’ reflection on their digital competence and professional learning. Guidance and planning resources complement the tools. The emphasis is on organisational and professional digital development, rather than AI literacy specifically.
pedagogicalSummary: SELFIE is not presented as a course or a prescribed teaching method. Its learning-support approach is structured, collective self-reflection: students, teachers and school leaders answer short, anonymised questions about technology use, then review the school’s aggregated report, discuss priorities and formulate an action plan. Schools can customise questions and repeat the exercise to track progress, making the process diagnostic and iterative rather than a sequence of lessons. The resources page adds a SELFIE Pedagogical Innovation Assistant Toolkit with step-by-step guidance and templates for planning, implementing and evaluating an action plan. These features support organisational learning about teaching and learning with digital technologies; the inspected pages do not establish a specific classroom pedagogy or describe SELFIE for Teachers’ learning process in detail. (https://education.ec.europa.eu/selfie/get-started; https://education.ec.europa.eu/selfie/resources; https://education.ec.europa.eu/selfie/news)
prioritySummary: The initiative principally aims to help education organisations understand and improve how digital technologies support teaching, learning, assessment and training. SELFIE involves school leaders, teachers and students in school-wide reflection and provides evidence they can use to set priorities, decide where training or funding may be useful, and plan improvements. Its work-based-learning module extends this emphasis to vocational education and training schools and participating companies. The intended beneficiaries are therefore education communities and organisations, including VET providers and employers, rather than only individual teachers. The pages frame digital transition and digital capacity as central goals; they do not present a distinct AI-literacy objective. Although the news page identifies SELFIE for Teachers as part of the wider set of tools, the inspected material gives little detail about its specific goals or beneficiaries beyond that. (https://education.ec.europa.eu/selfie/introduction; https://education.ec.europa.eu/selfie/introduction/why-selfie; https://education.ec.europa.eu/selfie/selfie-for-work-based-learning; https://education.ec.europa.eu/selfie/news)
educationalTechnologySummary: The main identified educational technology is SELFIE, a free, online self-reflection platform developed for schools, with a work-based-learning module adapted for VET schools and companies. It presents customisable questions and statements to participants and generates a visual, interactive report of aggregated responses, which schools can use to guide discussion and planning. The platform is the tool being developed and used; the pages do not identify particular hardware or third-party learning software. The resources page also lists downloadable planning guidance and the SELFIE Pedagogical Innovation Assistant Toolkit, plus an external self-paced online course for digital action planning, but these are supporting materials or a separate course, not components shown to be built into SELFIE. The news page names SELFIE for Teachers but does not describe its underlying technology, so its specific platform features could not be established from the inspected pages. (https://education.ec.europa.eu/selfie/introduction; https://education.ec.europa.eu/selfie/get-started; https://education.ec.europa.eu/selfie/resources; https://education.ec.europa.eu/selfie/selfie-for-work-based-learning; https://education.ec.europa.eu/selfie/news)

Additionally, SELFIE for Teachers is mentioned, indicating specific guidance for educators. This qualifies under the 'Issued by a national or sub-national government or statutory body' route since it is from the European Commission (EU-level government), which is an intergovernmental body per the inclusion criteria.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: ADMIT – Guide of ethical use of LLM/GenAI in higher education (Erasmus+)
metadata.Description: Erasmus+ project producing a practical guide and an eight-dimension ethics taxonomy for responsible adoption of LLMs and generative AI across European universities.

summary: ADMIT is an Erasmus+ project focused on responsible, ethical, and inclusive use of large language models and generative AI in European higher education. It offers educators a free, English-language, 20-hour online course covering GenAI, ethics, learning design, teaching competencies, assessment, and institutional preparedness, with a practical focus on integrating GenAI into learning activities. The project also develops role-specific ethical guidance, an institutional self-assessment tool, research-based frameworks, and policy recommendations for educators, students, institutional leaders, and policymakers.
pedagogicalSummary: ADMIT supports learning through a free, beginner-level, 20-hour course for higher-education educators, organised around introductory GenAI and ethics, learning design, teaching competencies, and institutional preparedness. Its stated outcomes include designing learning goals, activities, and assessments that integrate GenAI, and adapting materials for inclusion and personalisation. This indicates a practical, design-oriented approach, although the inspected course description does not specify teaching methods such as facilitated discussion, exercises, or assessment formats. The project also describes a modular course developed collaboratively from research and project outcomes, alongside CPD sessions and open-licensed educator resources. Evidence is available at https://admit.eadtu.eu/genai-in-education, https://admit.eadtu.eu/outcomes, and https://admit.eadtu.eu/timeline.
prioritySummary: ADMIT principally aims to support the ethical, effective, and inclusive integration of large language models and generative AI in European higher education. Its intended beneficiaries include educators and institutional leaders, who are offered professional learning and guidance, as well as students, whose learning, rights, and equitable access are among the concerns addressed. The project combines practical capacity-building with institutional and policy-level work: it develops a course, role-specific guidance, ethical frameworks, self-assessment resources, and policy recommendations. It also seeks to strengthen teaching and learning while safeguarding academic integrity, inclusion, and responsible innovation; the inspected pages do not establish a single priority that overrides these related aims. Sources: https://admit.eadtu.eu/ and https://admit.eadtu.eu/outcomes.
educationalTechnologySummary: ADMIT identifies an online course hosted on the AI Campus Moodle platform, offered free in English and described as a 20-hour course for higher-education educators. It uses this learning platform to deliver professional development on GenAI, learning design, assessment, ethics, and institutional preparedness; access to the course link led to a login page, so its specific learning materials and features could not be inspected. ADMIT also reports developing a web-based institutional self-assessment tool: ethical-taxonomy indicators are presented through three role-specific questionnaires with tailored feedback for students, educators, and institutional leaders. The inspected descriptions do not identify specific GenAI products as learning technologies used by ADMIT. Sources: https://admit.eadtu.eu/genai-in-education and https://admit.eadtu.eu/outcomes.

inclusion.reason: The initiative has clear AI-literacy content: its course covers generative AI and its ethical considerations and sets learning objectives for responsible use; its recommendations explicitly address AI literacy. The project states it is EU-funded, meeting the government-funding inclusion route. Sources: https://admit.eadtu.eu/ ; https://admit.eadtu.eu/genai-in-education ; https://admit.eadtu.eu/outcomes. The pages do not establish the extent of course uptake.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: AI Pact
metadata.Description: Voluntary Commission initiative encouraging organisations to prepare early for AI Act implementation, incl. AI literacy pledges.

summary: The AI Pact is a voluntary European Commission initiative that brings together organisations across business, research, civil society, public administration and education to prepare for implementing the EU AI Act. Its pledges encourage actions such as developing governance approaches, identifying potentially high-risk AI systems, and promoting AI literacy and awareness among staff. The initiative supports information-sharing through webinars and workshops on the Act and its implementation, including exchanges of practices. Learning is informational and professional in focus; the available descriptions do not specify a formal curriculum or assessment.
pedagogicalSummary: The AI Pact supports learning through recurring webinars that explain the AI Act and its implementation, alongside opportunities for participants to exchange experience and best practices. The events page describes webinars that may include expert presentations, dialogue and Q&A; a session on AI literacy also introduced signatories’ shared practices. Pillar II adds workshops for signatories, tailored to specific regulatory topics, while Pillar I is open to a broad stakeholder community. These are knowledge-sharing and informational activities rather than evidence of a formal curriculum or specified teaching method. The inspected pages do not describe assessment or structured learner progression. (https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/ai-pact; https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/ai-pact-events)
prioritySummary: The initiative’s central emphasis is helping organisations prepare early for implementing the AI Act, rather than providing AI literacy as a stand-alone educational programme. It engages a wide range of stakeholders—including companies, non-profits, academics and civil servants—through information-sharing, while its voluntary pledges specifically invite AI providers and deployers to plan compliance actions. Pledges include developing governance strategies, identifying potentially high-risk systems, and promoting AI awareness and literacy among staff. The Commission also presents knowledge-sharing and preparation as ways to support trustworthy AI and build trust. The pages describe these aims together, without establishing a separate hierarchy among the supporting benefits. (https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/ai-pact; https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/ai-pact-events)
educationalTechnologySummary: The inspected pages identify no named software, learning platform, or hardware developed or used by the AI Pact. They describe webinars and workshops as learning and exchange formats, but do not specify the technology used to deliver them. The AI Pact page says that shared best practices may be published on a platform for information about AI Act implementation, and the events page notes a repository of practices shared by signatories in an AI-literacy webinar.
