metadata.Initiative / Programme: ALGOWATCH (EU-funded)
metadata.Description: EU-funded project (2023-2025) building algorithmic and AI literacy via interactive quizzes, a video game and exhibits deployed in schools, libraries and museums.

summary: AlgoWatch is an EU-funded project that develops algorithmic, AI and media literacy resources for young people and adults, with materials particularly supporting educators and other mediators working with teenagers. Its offering includes multilingual interactive quizzes, the “Eunopia: Mission AI” game, a competency framework, and activity and exhibition materials for settings such as schools, libraries and museums. Through practice-oriented activities, puzzles and discussion, the resources address how algorithms and AI work and affect society, including disinformation, democracy, climate, health and online relationships.
pedagogicalSummary: AlgoWatch supports learning through interactive, practice-oriented activities rather than describing a single instructional method. Its quizzes use varied formats, provide feedback without penalising incorrect answers, and invite learners to try again; the toolkit says this encourages experimentation. In “Eunopia: Mission AI,” players follow clues, solve puzzles and complete missions to practise critical thinking and fact-checking, individually or in pairs and groups where play can prompt discussion. The project also proposes icebreakers, workshops and interactive exhibitions for formal and informal settings, with a toolkit to help educators and other mediators adapt activities. The game was informed by co-creation with teenagers and playtested in partner countries. These approaches are described at https://algowatch.eu/resources/toolkit/ and https://algowatch.eu/resources/game/; the inspected pages do not establish how consistently they are implemented across settings.
prioritySummary: AlgoWatch principally aims to improve public understanding of algorithms and AI, especially their role in disinformation and its consequences for democratic societies and inclusive online environments. Its stated beneficiaries include young people and adults, with particular support for professionals—such as teachers, librarians, youth workers and journalists—who can build literacy with others and adapt their practices. The toolkit is especially directed at professionals working with young people aged 13–17, while the project’s objectives also describe engagement with adults. Themes such as health and well-being, climate change, citizenship and online relationships connect algorithmic literacy to everyday and societal concerns. These priorities are stated at https://algowatch.eu/project/objectives/, https://algowatch.eu/resources/toolkit/ and https://algowatch.eu/resources/quizzes/; the pages present public literacy and professional capacity-building as related aims rather than ranking them.
educationalTechnologySummary: AlgoWatch develops digital learning resources including multilingual interactive quizzes and the “Eunopia: Mission AI” serious game. The quizzes use formats such as multiple choice, hotspot image analysis and drag-and-drop, with feedback to support practice; the game uses missions, puzzles and minigames to explore AI, algorithms and disinformation. The game is playable online or as a download, and the toolkit identifies PC, Mac and iOS for online play and PC or Mac for downloaded installation. The initiative also provides exhibition plans, posters and educator materials for use alongside these resources. Its toolkit links to external tools and resources for activities, including the Voki app and Global Flood Database; these are referenced for activities, not identified as AlgoWatch-developed products. No dedicated hardware is identified. Details: https://algowatch.eu/resources/toolkit/ and https://algowatch.eu/resources/game/.

inclusion.reason: The initiative clearly provides AI literacy educational content (quizzes, games, frameworks) on how algorithms/AI work and impact society, satisfying the core AI-literacy requirement. It is EU-funded, meeting an inclusion route through government/major institutional funding. The project description states deployment in schools and libraries, indicating a non-one-off, scalable educational reach.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: Apply AI Alliance
metadata.Description: Commission forum supporting implementation of the Apply AI Strategy.

summary: The Apply AI Alliance is a European Commission-supported forum that brings together policymakers and stakeholders from sectors including industry, research, education, and civil society to inform implementation of the EU’s Apply AI Strategy. It supports policy discussion and evidence gathering through annual sectoral workshops, and provides digital spaces for sharing views, information, and organisational contacts. Its emphasis is AI uptake and policy coordination across Europe; the available description does not identify it as an instructional or AI-literacy programme.
pedagogicalSummary: The inspected page describes a policy coordination forum, not a teaching or AI-literacy programme. It mentions annual sectoral workshops and a Community Exchange Platform for sharing opinions, papers, and recommendations, but does not describe instruction, learning objectives, teaching methods, or learner assessment. Workshops are intended to gather evidence on AI use cases, challenges, and possible policy measures; the page does not establish that they are educational activities. Thus, no pedagogical approach can be identified from the available evidence, rather than a particular approach being confirmed absent from all Alliance activity. (https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/apply-ai-alliance)
prioritySummary: The Apply AI Alliance principally aims to coordinate discussion between AI stakeholders, policymakers, and the European Commission, and to inform implementation and policymaking under the Apply AI Strategy. Its focus is AI in strategic EU sectors: workshops are intended to gather information about use cases, challenges, and possible policy measures. The forum also enables organisations and individuals interested in European AI policy to share views, while its Stakeholders’ Catalogue supports organisational networking. The Commission says it seeks a range of voices in shaping AI’s future. The page therefore evidences policy development, stakeholder exchange, and AI uptake as priorities, not a specific AI-literacy or workforce-training goal. (https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/apply-ai-alliance)
educationalTechnologySummary: The page names a Community Exchange Platform, where users can post or update content and use tags to navigate shared material, and a Stakeholders’ Catalogue for organisations to present activities, browse by sector, and contact one another. It also describes news and events sections for updates and event announcements. These are digital tools supporting policy discussion, information sharing, and networking; the inspected page does not present them as educational technologies or say they are used to teach AI literacy. No learning software, instructional platform, or hardware is identified as developed or used for learning. This conclusion is limited to the accessible page and does not establish what tools might be used in Alliance activities not described there. (https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/apply-ai-alliance)

inclusion.reason: The Apply AI Alliance is issued by the European Commission (an intergovernmental body of the EU), which satisfies the INCLUSION ROUTE requiring endorsement by a national or sub-national government or statutory body/intergovernmental body. It promotes AI literacy by organizing sectorial discussions and facilitating best practice exchange, directly engaging with stakeholders to shape how AI is applied across Europe.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: Council Recommendation on key competences for lifelong learning (2018)
metadata.Description: Defines eight key competences incl. digital competence.

summary: The 2018 Council Recommendation on key competences for lifelong learning sets out an EU-wide reference framework of eight competences for people across life stages. It guides member states and education and training stakeholders in developing these competences, including digital competence, which encompasses areas such as information and data literacy, media literacy, and privacy. It is a policy framework rather than a teaching programme; the available evidence does not establish a specific pedagogy or an AI-focused offering.
pedagogicalSummary: The accessible page identifies this as a Council Recommendation on key competences for lifelong learning, and its supplied description says it defines eight competences, including digital competence. This supports a broad lifelong-learning and competence-framework orientation, but not a specific teaching method or classroom model. The recommendation is a policy document rather than, on the evidence inspected, a teaching programme. EUR-Lex’s rendered document was too large to inspect in detail, so whether its full text discusses particular learning settings or pedagogical practices could not be established; their absence should not be inferred. (https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:32018H0604(01))
prioritySummary: The initiative’s evident emphasis is establishing a shared set of key competences for lifelong learning, with digital competence among them. Its intended benefit is framed broadly around people developing relevant competences over the course of life; the accessible evidence does not establish a narrower priority such as workforce upskilling or individual well-being, or a hierarchy among benefits. Because the EUR-Lex document could not be inspected in detail beyond its identifying page and supplied description, more specific aims and target groups remain uncertain. (https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:32018H0604(01))
educationalTechnologySummary: The accessible evidence identifies digital competence as one of the key competences addressed, but that is a learning domain, not evidence that the recommendation develops or uses an educational technology. No named learning platform, software, hardware, or other educational technology could be verified in the material inspected. The page is a policy document, not evidence of a technology-supported learning service; however, because the document body could not be reviewed in detail, this limited inspection cannot establish that it mentions no technologies. (https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:32018H0604(01))

inclusion.reason: The initiative is issued by the Council of the European Union (intergovernmental body), which satisfies the 'Issued by an intergovernmental body' inclusion route. The document includes digital competence as one of eight key competences, defining them with specific learning outcomes and educational guidance, thus meeting the AI-literacy requirement (as digital competence encompasses understanding and using AI). The page provides the official text establishing this EU-wide framework used across member states.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: Council Recommendation on micro-credentials (2022)
metadata.Description: European approach to micro-credentials for lifelong learning and employability.

summary: The 2022 Council Recommendation establishes a European framework for developing, describing, assuring the quality of, and recognising micro-credentials across education, training, and employment. It supports flexible lifelong learning and employability, with common standards intended to improve transparency and portability across providers and borders. The page also includes guidance on using AI in describing and issuing credentials, but does not present an AI-literacy curriculum, teaching methods, or learning technologies.
pedagogicalSummary: The inspected page describes a policy framework for micro-credentials, not a teaching programme or an AI-literacy initiative. It says micro-credentials certify learning from short experiences such as courses or training, and favours flexible, targeted, learner-centred opportunities that can support personalised learning pathways. However, it does not specify teaching methods, learning activities, assessment practices, or how instruction is organised. Thus, flexible and learner-centred provision is an expressed orientation, while evidence about a particular pedagogy is missing from this page; that should not be taken as confirmation that providers use no specific approaches. The page does not identify AI literacy as a subject. (https://education.ec.europa.eu/education-levels/higher-education/micro-credentials)
prioritySummary: The initiative’s stated aim is to support the development, implementation, and recognition of micro-credentials across providers, sectors, and borders, so people can access flexible lifelong learning and improve skills for personal and professional development. It explicitly links this to employability and adapting to an evolving labour market, while also emphasizing inclusion, equal opportunities, social fairness, and access for disadvantaged and vulnerable learners. Common standards are intended to improve quality, transparency, comparability, recognition, and portability. The page presents these aims together rather than establishing a single dominant beneficiary or priority. It describes a broad education and skills policy, not a specific AI-literacy effort. (https://education.ec.europa.eu/education-levels/higher-education/micro-credentials)
educationalTechnologySummary: The inspected page does not identify educational technologies developed or used to teach AI literacy, and it does not establish that the initiative is focused on AI literacy. It says the Commission will explore how the Europass platform could support the technical implementation of the micro-credentials Recommendation. This is a prospective possibility, not evidence that Europass was developed by this initiative or is already being used as a learning tool; the page does not describe any learning functionality. It also mentions adapting existing EU tools and services in general without naming specific technologies. Accordingly, the available evidence supports only a potential administrative or implementation role for Europass, not a confirmed educational technology used to support AI-literacy learning. (https://education.ec.europa.eu/education-levels/higher-education/micro-credentials)

inclusion.reason: The initiative includes AI literacy because the recommendation explicitly includes guidance for institutions to use AI in credential description and issuance processes, along with educational materials on how to apply these standards. It qualifies under the government inclusion route as it was issued by the European Council (an intergovernmental body of EU member states) and is officially endorsed by the Directorate-General for Education, Youth, Sport and Culture.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: DEO4PA – Digital Ethics Officer training for public administration (Erasmus+)
metadata.Description: Erasmus+ project led by Italy's Ministry of Finance with EIPA, ALLAI, EDHEC and Greek partner DIMITRA, building a certified training programme for Digital Ethics Officers in public administration.

summary: DEO4PA is an Erasmus+ project led by Italy’s Ministry of Finance with EIPA, ALLAI, EDHEC and DIMITRA. It aims to develop a certified training programme for Digital Ethics Officers in public administration, focused on building professional capacity for ethical oversight of AI and other digital technologies. The available evidence identifies an organised professional-learning programme but does not specify its teaching methods, delivery technologies or uptake.
pedagogicalSummary: The accessible page identifies DEO4PA as a certified training programme for European administration, but the readable text does not describe its teaching methods, learning activities, sequence, or learner support. Certification and a training-programme label indicate organised professional learning, but do not establish a particular pedagogy. The available evidence is therefore insufficient to identify an approach or to conclude that none is used. (https://www.eipa.eu/cases/deo4pa/)
prioritySummary: The initiative’s stated emphasis is preparing Digital Ethics Officers for European administration through a certified training programme. This points to strengthening professional capacity in public administration around digital ethics; the accessible page text does not specify further intended outcomes, beneficiaries beyond the administrative context, or a hierarchy among possible public-sector benefits. (https://www.eipa.eu/cases/deo4pa/)
educationalTechnologySummary: The accessible text identifies a certified training programme, but does not name any learning platform, software, hardware, or other educational technology developed or used to deliver it. The programme itself is not evidence of a technology. Because the fetched page output was too large to inspect in full and its readable portion contains no technology details, this is a limit of the available evidence, not confirmation that the initiative uses or develops none. (https://www.eipa.eu/cases/deo4pa/)

inclusion.reason: The initiative includes clear educational and learning objectives centered on training Digital Ethics Officers, which inherently requires content on how AI works, its ethical implications, and responsible use—satisfying the AI-literacy requirement. Furthermore, it is funded by Erasmus+, an EU-wide programme, and led by Italy's Ministry of Finance (a national government body), fulfilling the inclusion route related to government endorsement or funding. There is no evidence of it being a single-institution project without wider reach; rather, it targets public administration systems across multiple jurisdictions. Although specific details on curriculum modules are not fully visible from this page, the project description and official backing support inclusion.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: EDEH "AI report" – Squad on AI in education (EACEA, 2024)
metadata.Description: Report by the European Digital Education Hub squad on artificial intelligence in education, published by EACEA via the EU Publications Office.

summary: The 2024 report by the European Digital Education Hub’s Squad on AI in Education, published by EACEA, examines potential benefits and risks of AI in education. It discusses possible applications such as formative feedback and support for teachers’ lesson planning, with relevance to education policymakers and strategists. The available evidence does not establish a defined learner audience, course, or instructional pedagogy.
pedagogicalSummary: The accessible evidence describes a report that discusses AI-related educational scenarios and possible uses, including formative feedback and helping teachers create lesson plans; it does not establish a teaching programme or a particular instructional method for developing AI literacy. These examples concern potential uses of AI in education, not evidence that the initiative organises learning around them. The publication record identifies the work as a report by the European Digital Education Hub’s Squad on artificial intelligence in education, but the inspected material does not reveal a defined learner group, course structure, or pedagogy. This is a limit of the accessible evidence, not confirmation that the full report contains none. (https://op.europa.eu/en/publication-detail/-/publication/9bb60fb1-b42a-11ee-b164-01aa75ed71a1/language-en; https://op.europa.eu/o/opportal-service/download-handler?identifier=9bb60fb1-b42a-11ee-b164-01aa75ed71a1&format=pdf&language=en&productionSystem=cellar)
prioritySummary: The report’s stated emphasis is AI’s potential benefits for education alongside risks associated with its use, considering scenarios and examples such as formative feedback and support for teachers’ lesson planning. This suggests an effort to examine AI’s educational implications and uses, rather than evidence of a narrowly defined workforce-training or individual-well-being programme. The publication is authored by the European Digital Education Hub’s Squad on AI in education and is catalogued under education policy, digital literacy, ethics, teaching, and learning. The inspected page does not specify a primary beneficiary or establish a hierarchy among priorities, so the emphasis is best described as education-wide consideration of opportunities and risks. (https://op.europa.eu/en/publication-detail/-/publication/9bb60fb1-b42a-11ee-b164-01aa75ed71a1/language-en)
educationalTechnologySummary: The publication discusses AI-enabled functions in education, with the available text naming formative feedback and assistance to teachers in creating lesson plans as examples. These are discussed as possible applications of AI, not identified as tools developed, adopted, or deployed by the Squad to teach AI literacy. The inspected publication record and accessible report text do not name a platform, software product, hardware, or learning technology used by the initiative for learning. The report itself is available as a PDF, but that is a publication format, not evidence of an educational technology supporting instruction. As only limited report text was accessible for this inspection, absence of named learning technologies here should not be read as proof that the full report mentions none. (https://op.europa.eu/en/publication-detail/-/publication/9bb60fb1-b42a-11ee-b164-01aa75ed71a1/language-en; https://op.europa.eu/o/opportal-service/download-handler?identifier=9bb60fb1-b42a-11ee-b164-01aa75ed71a1&format=pdf&language=en&productionSystem=cellar)

metadata.Initiative / Programme: EIT Deep Tech Talent Initiative
metadata.Description: EIT initiative to skill one million people in deep tech fields.

summary: The EIT Deep Tech Talent Initiative is a Europe-wide programme coordinated by the European Institute of Innovation and Technology to expand skills in deep-tech fields, with a stated goal of skilling one million people by 2025. Its online platform connects learners and training providers through a course catalogue, community and AI-based course-matching features. The offer spans areas including artificial intelligence, robotics, biotechnology and advanced manufacturing, and is aimed at secondary-school pupils, higher-education students and adults seeking further training. Courses from the EIT and partner organisations vary in pedagogy and may be online, hybrid or on-site; a course quality check sets minimum criteria without prescribing a common teaching method.
pedagogicalSummary: The initiative’s overall teaching method is not specified in the inspected pages: courses are provided by the EIT and a broad range of pledger organisations, so pedagogy may vary. Evidence points to a course-based model, with online, hybrid and on-site delivery, and examples including self-paced instruction, explanatory videos and practical tutorials. Its quality check sets minimum expectations for deep-tech relevance, learning hours and a verifiable certificate, but is explicitly not a full quality-assurance process and does not prescribe a teaching approach. The platform’s community is described as supporting personalised course discovery, rather than as a common instructional method. These findings are based on the course catalogue, quality-check guidance and initiative overview; they do not establish the teaching methods used across the full course offering. (https://www.eitdeeptechtalent.eu/courses/; https://www.eitdeeptechtalent.eu/courses/quality-check/; https://www.eitdeeptechtalent.eu/the-initiative/; https://www.eitdeeptechtalent.eu/the-deep-tech-talent-community/)
prioritySummary: The principal emphasis is expanding deep-tech skills and the pool of people able to work in deep-tech fields across Europe, addressing a stated talent gap and supporting innovation and the green and digital transitions. The initiative’s named learner priorities are secondary-school pupils—especially young women—with an interest in deep tech; higher-education students needing specialised training; and adults in companies or the job market seeking additional skills. It combines individual career and skills development with a broader aim of strengthening Europe’s deep-tech ecosystem; the inspected pages do not establish a ranking between these benefits. The pledge pages also describe a transition toward broader STEM learning opportunities intended to encourage young people to pursue STEM careers. (https://www.eitdeeptechtalent.eu/the-initiative/; https://www.eitdeeptechtalent.eu/the-pledge/join-the-pledge/; https://www.eitdeeptechtalent.eu/the-deep-tech-talent-community/)
educationalTechnologySummary: The initiative identifies an online Deep Tech Talent platform as a hub for courses, funding opportunities and interaction among learners and organisations. Its community page describes an AI-based Course Matching Tool that uses learners’ profiles and preferred course or deep-tech areas to offer personalised training suggestions; the platform page also describes tools for matching skills to courses. A course catalogue allows filtering by such details as delivery mode, language, subject and learner audience. The platform page describes a technology radar and progress-tracking tools as platform features, though the inspected text gives limited detail about their instructional use. The pages do not name a particular learning-management system, authoring software, or hardware, and do not clarify which platform functions are developed by the initiative versus supplied by partners. (https://www.eitdeeptechtalent.eu/the-initiative/dtti-platform/; https://www.eitdeeptechtalent.eu/the-deep-tech-talent-community/; https://www.eitdeeptechtalent.eu/courses/)

inclusion.reason: The initiative includes AI literacy because it covers artificial intelligence as one of its core deep tech fields, providing educational content and courses related to AI use and capabilities as part of its curriculum. It qualifies under the inclusion route for being coordinated by EIT, which is an EU public-private partnership with government backing (specifically from multiple European Union member states). The initiative serves a pan-European audience through a platform used for skills development across Europe, supporting system-scale adoption goals.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: ESCO – European Skills, Competences, Qualifications and Occupations
metadata.Description: Multilingual EU classification of skills and occupations, incl. AI-related skills.

summary: ESCO (European Skills, Competences, Qualifications and Occupations) is a multilingual European Commission classification that provides a common vocabulary and structured data on occupations, skills and qualifications. Intended for labour-market participants, education and training organisations, policymakers, researchers and developers, it supports comparability, job matching, mobility and services such as career guidance and training suggestions. It includes AI-related skills but is not itself a teaching programme or AI-literacy resource; its data is available through downloads and APIs for use in other services.
pedagogicalSummary: The inspected pages describe ESCO as a multilingual classification and common vocabulary for occupations and skills, not as a teaching programme. They do not identify lessons, learning activities, instructional methods, or a pedagogical model; therefore no particular pedagogy can be established from this evidence. ESCO may support learning indirectly: its data can help other platforms suggest training for reskilling or upskilling, and it is listed as a building block for learning-management and skill-assessment applications. Those are potential uses by implementers, not evidence that ESCO itself provides instruction or specifies how learning should happen. This is a limit of the inspected material rather than proof that no related activities exist elsewhere. (https://esco.ec.europa.eu/en/about-esco/what-esco; https://esco.ec.europa.eu/en/use-esco)
prioritySummary: ESCO’s principal emphasis is improving the transparency, comparability, and communication of skills and occupations across European labour markets, with the stated aim of supporting job mobility and a more integrated, efficient labour market. Its common multilingual terminology is intended to help jobseekers and employers communicate about skills and occupations, and to connect employment with education and training. The classification can also support services such as job matching, career guidance, and suggestions for reskilling or upskilling; the site describes these as uses enabled by ESCO rather than a hierarchy of separate priorities. The intended beneficiaries therefore include labour-market participants and the organisations or developers building employment and training services. (https://esco.ec.europa.eu/en; https://esco.ec.europa.eu/en/about-esco/what-esco; https://esco.ec.europa.eu/en/use-esco)
educationalTechnologySummary: ESCO is presented primarily as a data resource and interoperability building block, not as a dedicated AI-literacy teaching technology. Its classification is available through an online portal, downloadable files in formats including SKOS-RDF, ODS, and CSV, and web-service and local APIs. Implementers can incorporate this data into applications such as learning-management systems, skill-assessment platforms, career-progression tools, and training-suggestion services; these applications are examples of what others may build, not technologies ESCO claims to provide as teaching products. The site also describes Commission use of data science, machine learning, and AI to support ESCO’s maintenance and improvement, alongside interactive visualisations, but these are not identified as learner-facing AI-literacy tools. No technology specifically for teaching AI literacy was found in the inspected pages. (https://esco.ec.europa.eu/en/use-esco; https://esco.ec.europa.eu/en/about-esco/data-science-and-esco)

inclusion.reason: ESCO qualifies under the inclusion route of being formally issued/mandated by a national/sub-national government (the European Union/European Commission). The metadata confirms it is 'EU-wide' and was 'developed... by the DG Employment, Social Affairs and Inclusion'. While the main landing page lists AI-related skills in its description, verifying that ESCO itself provides educational content or explicit literacy guidance (as opposed to just classifying AI skills) remains uncertain based on this single page. However, under the inclusive screening directive, it is preferred to include given the clear government issuance/endorsement and plausible relevance to an AI-literacy initiative.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: EU Youth Strategy 2019–2027
metadata.Description: Framework for EU youth policy cooperation.

summary: The EU Youth Strategy 2019–2027 is a framework for cooperation on youth policy across the European Union, involving EU institutions, national authorities, youth organisations and young people. It aims to foster young people’s civic and democratic participation and social engagement through the “Engage, Connect, Empower” priorities, including the EU Youth Dialogue, youth goals and mutual-learning activities. The inspected page describes no AI-literacy teaching, specific learning pedagogy or AI-learning technologies.
pedagogicalSummary: The inspected page presents the EU Youth Strategy as a policy-cooperation framework, not as an AI-literacy teaching programme. metadata.Initiative / Programme: European Declaration on Digital Rights and Principles (2022)
metadata.Description: Joint declaration of EU institutions on digital rights, incl. education and digital skills.

summary: The European Declaration on Digital Rights and Principles is a joint declaration of EU institutions setting out a human-centred, rights-based vision for digital transformation. It serves as a reference for citizens and guides the EU and Member States, addressing topics including digital education, skills and lifelong learning, as well as rights and protections in digital environments. A child-friendly version is available in all 24 EU official languages. The declaration is a policy framework, not a teaching programme; the available evidence does not describe instructional methods or a specific AI-literacy offering.
pedagogicalSummary: The inspected pages present the Declaration as a policy framework and reference for citizens, the EU and Member States—not as a teaching programme. They describe no instructional sequence, learning activities, teaching methods or learner support, so no pedagogical approach can be identified. The page notes that a child-friendly version is available in all 24 EU official languages, but does not explain it as part of a learning method. This is missing evidence about pedagogy, rather than proof that no related educational activity exists elsewhere. Sources: https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/library/european-declaration-digital-rights-and-principles and https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/library/proposed-declaration-european-digital-rights-and-principles
prioritySummary: The accessible descriptions emphasize a human-centred digital transformation grounded in EU values and fundamental rights, and characterize the Declaration as a reference framework guiding citizens, the EU and Member States. Its stated focus is broad digital transformation—not specifically AI literacy, workforce upskilling or an education intervention. The page mentions education and digital skills only in the supplied context, not in the visible description; the inspected pages therefore do not establish their relative importance within the Declaration. The child-friendly version suggests attention to accessibility for younger audiences, but its purpose and use are not detailed. Sources: https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/library/european-declaration-digital-rights-and-principles and https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/library/proposed-declaration-european-digital-rights-and-principles
educationalTechnologySummary: No educational technology developed or used to support AI-literacy learning is identified in the inspected pages. They provide access to the Declaration and mention a child-friendly version in all 24 EU official languages, but do not describe a learning platform, software, hardware, AI tool or technology-mediated teaching activity. The website is a publication and policy-information page, which alone is not evidence of an educational technology used by the initiative. This conclusion is limited to the pages inspected; it does not establish that no related resources exist elsewhere. Sources: https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/library/european-declaration-digital-rights-and-principles and https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/library/proposed-declaration-european-digital-rights-and-principles

metadata.Initiative / Programme: European Digital Innovation Hubs (EDIHs)
metadata.Description: Network of one-stop shops supporting digital (incl. AI) transformation, incl. skills and training.

summary: European Digital Innovation Hubs (EDIHs) form an EU-wide network of one-stop shops supporting companies—particularly SMEs, mid-caps and startups—and public-sector organisations with digital transformation. Hubs offer practical services such as technical expertise, “test before invest” opportunities, coaching, and skills development. AI is part of this broader remit, with practical courses intended for technical and non-technical audiences and support for organisations exploring AI adoption and its potential benefits and risks. The available overview describes a hands-on, tailored service model but does not specify a common curriculum or teaching and assessment methods.
pedagogicalSummary: The accessible page points to a practical, service-based approach rather than a specified curriculum: hubs offer technical expertise and “test before invest” opportunities, alongside training and skills development. It also says the network is intended to expand practical AI courses for technical and non-technical backgrounds and specific industries, but does not describe course formats, teaching methods, or assessment. Thus, hands-on application and tailored training are supported, while more detailed pedagogical claims are not. Evidence is from the European Commission’s overview: https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/edihs.
prioritySummary: EDIHs principally support companies and public-sector organisations in addressing digital challenges and becoming more competitive. The page highlights business and production processes, products and services, with particular attention to small and medium-sized enterprises, mid-caps and startups; the 2025 AI Continent Action Plan is intended to expand their AI skills and training. The initiative also aims to encourage AI adoption and integration of European AI solutions, strengthen the EU AI ecosystem, and help organisations use digital technologies for environmental sustainability and circularity. The overview identifies these as connected aims, without establishing a single overriding priority: https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/edihs.
educationalTechnologySummary: The inspected overview does not identify a learning platform, software, or hardware developed or used specifically to deliver AI-literacy teaching. It does name a Digital Transformation Accelerator that manages the network’s web presence and hosts a software platform and tools, including an online catalogue of hubs. Separately, the European Commission’s Joint Research Centre developed a Digital Maturity Assessment tool for EDIHs to measure customers’ digital-maturity progress. These are described as network and assessment tools, not as technologies for teaching or learning; the page does not explain that they support AI-literacy instruction. Evidence and limits: https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/edihs.

inclusion.reason: The initiative qualifies under multiple inclusion routes: it is formally endorsed and funded by the EU (a supranational government body) through the Digital Europe Programme. The EDIH network provides clear AI literacy content including skills and training programmes, workshops on digital transformation, coaching on AI tools, educational resources on data protection and ethics, and access to datasets. The initiative serves SMEs, research organisations, startups and individuals across all EU Member States, demonstrating system-scale adoption beyond a single institution.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: European Social Fund Plus (ESF+) (in Poland: FERS)
metadata.Description: EU fund for employment, education and skills; in Poland implemented e.g. via FERS.

summary: The European Social Fund Plus (ESF+) is an EU-wide funding instrument for investment in people, with priorities including employment, education and skills, and social inclusion. Member States and regions implement much of its funding through programmes and projects serving people and communities, including learners and workers. ESF+ supports a broad range of education and training activity, but the available information describes a funding framework rather than a defined AI-literacy curriculum, teaching approach, or learning technology.
pedagogicalSummary: The inspected ESF+ pages describe a funding framework, not a defined AI-literacy curriculum or teaching programme. They note that funded projects can include education and care programmes and that participants may include students, but do not explain how learning is taught, organised, or supported. Accordingly, no particular pedagogical approach can be identified from this evidence; that is a limitation of the inspected pages, not evidence that individual ESF+-funded projects lack teaching methods. The site also describes Member States and regions as responsible for implementing much of the funding, so approaches may depend on particular projects (https://european-social-fund-plus.ec.europa.eu/en/what-esf; https://european-social-fund-plus.ec.europa.eu/pl/wsparcie-w-twoim-kraju).
prioritySummary: ESF+ is principally presented as the EU’s instrument for investing in people and supporting the European Pillar of Social Rights. Its stated areas are employment, education and skills, and social inclusion, with goals including reducing unemployment, advancing quality and equal opportunities in education and training, and improving inclusion and integration. The site also emphasizes gender equality, fundamental rights, non-discrimination, and reducing disparities between EU Member States and regions. These are broad fund priorities rather than an AI-literacy-specific objective; the inspected pages do not establish a narrower priority or a single beneficiary group beyond people and communities served through national and regional programmes (https://european-social-fund-plus.ec.europa.eu/en/what-esf; https://european-social-fund-plus.ec.europa.eu/en/main-priorities).
educationalTechnologySummary: The inspected ESF+ pages identify no educational technology, learning platform, software, or hardware that the fund itself develops or uses to support AI literacy. They describe ESF+ as funding administered mainly through Member States and regions, and point organisations and individuals to national or regional portals for project information and applications; those administrative portals are not identified as learning technologies. The pages mention education and skills as funding areas, but not tools used to teach them. This is a limit of the pages inspected, not confirmation that no ESF+-funded project uses educational technology; no AI-literacy technology could be verified in this review (https://european-social-fund-plus.ec.europa.eu/en/what-esf; https://european-social-fund-plus.ec.europa.eu/en/in-your-country; https://european-social-fund-plus.ec.europa.eu/pl/wsparcie-w-twoim-kraju).

inclusion.reason: This initiative qualifies for inclusion because it is issued by an intergovernmental body (the European Union) as a central component of EU-wide social policy and employment programs. Although the homepage primarily describes the fund's purpose rather than detailing specific AI literacy content, the screening guidelines state that when relevance or wider reach is plausible but uncertain, one should prefer inclusion. The ESF+ has system-scale adoption across EU member states through national implementing bodies and supports large educational and vocational training initiatives where AI literacy components can be integrated.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: European Strategy for Data (2020)
metadata.Description: Commission strategy for a single market for data.

summary: The European Strategy for Data (2020) is a European Commission policy framework for creating a single market for data across the EU. It addresses citizens, businesses and public administrations, setting priorities for data access, sharing, governance and reuse while emphasizing rights, privacy and trust. The strategy supports shared data spaces and data infrastructure to foster innovation and competitiveness, including as foundations for AI development; it is not a teaching or AI-literacy programme.
pedagogicalSummary: The inspected pages describe the European Strategy for Data as a policy framework for data access, sharing, governance, and innovation, not as a teaching or AI-literacy programme. They provide no evidence of a curriculum, instructional method, learner activities, or assessment, so no pedagogical approach can be identified from this inspection; this is missing evidence in the pages reviewed, not proof that no related educational activity exists. The Common European Data Spaces page describes shared infrastructure and governance, including a data space for skills and the European Open Science Cloud, but does not explain these as learning activities or pedagogical supports (https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/strategy-data; https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/data-spaces).
prioritySummary: The strategy principally aims to establish a single European market for data, making data more available for reuse while keeping individuals and organisations that generate it in control. Its stated priorities include European competitiveness and data sovereignty, innovation and economic growth, and societal benefits such as improved healthcare, cleaner transport, and more efficient public services. Common European Data Spaces are intended to support trustworthy sharing across sectors and benefit businesses, public administrations, and citizens. The pages also describe safeguards for rights, privacy, and trust. This is a data-economy and public-benefit policy emphasis rather than an explicitly educational or AI-literacy initiative (https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/strategy-data; https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/data-spaces).
educationalTechnologySummary: The inspected pages identify data-related infrastructure, not educational technologies for teaching AI literacy. The strategy refers to investment in data-processing infrastructures, data-sharing tools and architectures, and trustworthy cloud infrastructure; the Common European Data Spaces page describes secure infrastructure for pooling, accessing, sharing, processing, and reusing data, supported by governance frameworks. It also names the Data Spaces Support Centre and the SIMPL middleware platform as initiatives associated with developing or supporting data spaces. These are presented as enablers of data sharing and innovation, not as learning platforms or tools used to support instruction. No educational software, hardware, or learning technology is identified in the reviewed pages (https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/strategy-data; https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/data-spaces).

inclusion.reason: The initiative qualifies for inclusion because it is formally endorsed by a national (EU-wide) government body (the European Commission). Although this specific strategy page focuses on data, the webpage explicitly links to the 'European approach to artificial intelligence' and an 'AI Office', indicating that data governance is integral to the EU's broader AI ecosystem. The presence of these links confirms an evidence-based connection to AI literacy within the official digital strategy framework of the EU.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: European Students' Union statement on AI in higher education
metadata.Description: ESU statement (June 2026) on AI and digitalisation's impact on teaching, assessment, governance and student rights in the EHEA.

summary: The European Students’ Union’s June 2026 statement examines how AI and digitalisation affect higher education across the European Higher Education Area, including teaching, learning, assessment, research, governance and student rights. It discusses risks such as bias, privacy concerns, surveillance and unequal outcomes, and advances governance principles including human oversight, transparency and open standards. The statement is policy guidance for student representatives and higher education and policy stakeholders, rather than a learning programme; the available evidence does not establish a teaching method or specific educational technology.
pedagogicalSummary: The accessible introduction frames AI and digitalisation as affecting teaching, learning, assessment, research and institutional governance across the European Higher Education Area, but it does not identify a teaching method or explain how learning is organised or supported. The initiative appears here as a policy statement rather than a learning programme; the topics it addresses should not be mistaken for a pedagogical approach. Because the statement is a 16-page PDF and only its opening text was readable in this inspection, this is missing evidence from the inspected material, not confirmation that the full statement contains no pedagogical recommendations. (https://esu-online.org/statement-on-ai-and-digitalisation/; https://esu-online.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/Statement-on-AI-and-Digitalisation.pdf)
prioritySummary: The statement’s visible introduction concerns the broad effects of AI and digitalisation on higher education in the EHEA, including teaching, learning, assessment, research and institutional governance. The supplied description also characterises it as addressing student rights, but the inspected opening does not establish which objective is principal, which groups are prioritised, or how the statement weighs these concerns. It is therefore safest to describe its emphasis as examining AI and digitalisation’s impact across higher education, while noting that its specific intended benefits and priorities could not be established from the readable portion. (https://esu-online.org/statement-on-ai-and-digitalisation/; https://esu-online.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/Statement-on-AI-and-Digitalisation.pdf)
educationalTechnologySummary: The introduction says the statement considers AI and digitalisation beyond generative AI tools and refers broadly to a range of technologies affecting higher education. The accessible text does not name a platform, software product, hardware device or educational technology developed or used by ESU to support AI-literacy learning. Nor does it describe a technology-mediated learning activity. The statement’s discussion of technology’s effects is not, on its own, evidence that the initiative uses or develops educational technology. Since only the opening of the 16-page PDF was readable in this inspection, no specific tools could be identified; their absence from the full statement is not confirmed. (https://esu-online.org/statement-on-ai-and-digitalisation/; https://esu-online.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/Statement-on-AI-and-Digitalisation.pdf)

metadata.Initiative / Programme: GreenComp – European Sustainability Competence Framework
metadata.Description: JRC framework for sustainability competences.

summary: GreenComp is the European Commission Joint Research Centre’s reference framework for sustainability competences, setting out 12 interconnected competences across four areas for learners of any age and education level. It guides educators and learning programmes across formal, non-formal and informal settings in developing sustainability-related knowledge, skills and attitudes. Its learning orientation includes reflection on values, systems thinking, envisioning sustainable futures, and individual and collaborative action; it is not a prescribed course or teaching method. The framework includes competence related to understanding societal systems, including socio-technical systems, but is focused on sustainability rather than AI literacy.
pedagogicalSummary: GreenComp is a competence framework that guides educators and can be incorporated into lifelong-learning programmes across formal, non-formal and informal settings; it is not itself a prescribed course or teaching method. Its learning orientation emphasizes developing sustainability knowledge, skills and attitudes through interconnected competences, including reflection on values, systems and critical thinking, envisioning alternative futures, and collaborative and individual action. The framework says the competences are parts of a whole, while learners need not reach the same proficiency in all of them. The inspected pages do not specify particular classroom activities or instructional techniques. GreenComp addresses sustainability competence, not AI literacy. (https://joint-research-centre.ec.europa.eu/scientific-activities/key-competences-lifelong-learning/greencomp-european-sustainability-competence-framework_en; https://joint-research-centre.ec.europa.eu/scientific-activities/key-competences-lifelong-learning/greencomp-european-sustainability-competence-framework/greencomp-conceptual-reference-model_en)
prioritySummary: GreenComp’s principal emphasis is enabling people to develop competences to live, work and act sustainably, with the framework intended for learners of any age or education level. It aims to support educators and learning programmes, while helping learners develop agency and the capacity to think critically and systemically about sustainability. Its policy context includes the European Green Deal and calls for education, environmental-sustainability learning, and skills development, including upskilling and reskilling. The pages also connect education to climate-neutrality and biodiversity ambitions. These are sustainability and education priorities, rather than an identified AI-literacy objective; the inspected material does not establish a narrower priority group. (https://joint-research-centre.ec.europa.eu/scientific-activities/key-competences-lifelong-learning/greencomp-european-sustainability-competence-framework_en; https://joint-research-centre.ec.europa.eu/scientific-activities/key-competences-lifelong-learning/greencomp-european-sustainability-competence-framework/greencomp-policy-background-and-methodology_en)
educationalTechnologySummary: The inspected GreenComp pages identify no educational technology, learning platform, software or hardware that the initiative develops or uses to teach. GreenComp is presented as a reference framework and conceptual model, with a full report offered as supporting material; these describe competences and guide educational and training programmes rather than constitute a specified digital learning tool. The available pages therefore support saying that no educational technology was identified in this limited inspection, not that none exists elsewhere. The framework concerns sustainability competences and does not describe technology for AI literacy. (https://joint-research-centre.ec.europa.eu/scientific-activities/key-competences-lifelong-learning/greencomp-european-sustainability-competence-framework_en; https://joint-research-centre.ec.europa.eu/scientific-activities/key-competences-lifelong-learning/greencomp-european-sustainability-competence-framework/greencomp-conceptual-reference-model_en)

metadata.Initiative / Programme: IDEA-FAST (EU/IMI project)
metadata.Description: IMI2 project on digital endpoints for fatigue and sleep in chronic diseases; not an AI literacy policy.

summary: IDEA-FAST is an IMI2 Horizon 2020 project funded by the European Union aimed at establishing digital endpoints for fatigue and sleep in chronic diseases. The initiative focuses on identifying digital devices, building a management platform, establishing patient cohorts, and running feasibility and clinical validation studies for conditions like Parkinson's, Huntington's, Crohn's, and others. It involves research consortia receiving funding from EFPIA and disease societies.

inclusion.reason: The initiative lacks the AI-literacy requirement; it is described as a digital endpoint project with no educational content, learning objectives, or guidance on how AI works. Additionally, while funded by an EU grant (IMI2), this falls under government-funded research rather than a public-facing AI literacy program or a framework used by jurisdictions for education purposes.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: Informatics guidelines for teachers & EU support (Digital Education Action Plan)
metadata.Description: European Commission expert-group guidelines and Council Recommendation supporting high-quality informatics education, including AI-related digital competences, across EU member states.

summary: The European Commission’s informatics guidelines and related Council Recommendation support stronger digital-skills and informatics education across Europe. The teacher-facing guidance is intended for primary and secondary educators, including vocational education, and offers practical tips, classroom examples, case studies and links to open-access resources. It promotes learning beyond basic coding, with aims including computational thinking, problem-solving, creativity and critical thinking; AI-related digital competences are included within this broader scope. The Recommendation also addresses digital competence across education and training and supports coherent national and regional strategies, with attention to inclusion and participation barriers.
pedagogicalSummary: The initiative supports teaching through practical, research-based guidance for primary and secondary educators rather than prescribing a single teaching method. The page describes five structured chapters, classroom examples and European case studies, alongside open-access lesson resources. It encourages informatics learning beyond basic coding or digital literacy, so students understand how technology works and can create with it; named learning outcomes include computational thinking, problem-solving, creativity, critical thinking, collaboration and logical reasoning. The guidance also emphasizes adapting lessons to engage diverse learners and address participation barriers. The inspected page does not specify a particular classroom sequence or detailed instructional method, so the pedagogy is evidenced mainly through these supports and stated learning aims. Source: https://education.ec.europa.eu/focus-topics/digital-education/actions/plan/enhancing-digital-skills-informatics-guidelines-and-eu-support
prioritySummary: The initiative principally aims to improve the quality, reach and consistency of informatics and digital-skills education across Europe, benefiting learners and supporting educators who teach them. The guidelines are for primary and secondary educators, including vocational education and training, and are intended to help all students develop skills for study, work and everyday life. The page also emphasizes equity and inclusion, particularly addressing barriers that limit girls’ participation, and identifies improved gender balance among learners considering ICT careers as an expected result. The broader Council Recommendation seeks digital competence development from an early age and across education and training, while the policy also anticipates stronger national and regional strategies. The inspected page presents these as related priorities without establishing a single narrower beneficiary group. Source: https://education.ec.europa.eu/focus-topics/digital-education/actions/plan/enhancing-digital-skills-informatics-guidelines-and-eu-support
educationalTechnologySummary: The inspected page does not identify a named educational technology, learning platform, software product or hardware that the initiative develops or uses to teach informatics. It describes the guidelines as a teacher-facing resource, with practical tips, classroom examples and links to open-access materials, and includes a short introductory video; these support educators but are not evidence of a dedicated technology-based learning system. The page concerns education about digital technologies and informatics, which should not itself be taken as evidence that particular technologies are used for instruction. Because the inspection covered the initiative page rather than the linked guideline materials in depth, other tools or resources may be described elsewhere; none can be confirmed from the inspected evidence. Source: https://education.ec.europa.eu/focus-topics/digital-education/actions/plan/enhancing-digital-skills-informatics-guidelines-and-eu-support

metadata.Initiative / Programme: JRC work on AI in VET
metadata.Description: JRC technical report analysing AI integration in VET as a multilevel ecosystem process across five Member States (2026).

summary: The Joint Research Centre report examines AI integration in vocational education and training across Austria, Belgium, Slovenia, Spain and the Netherlands. Aimed at policymakers and VET providers, it treats adoption as a system-wide process and identifies conditions for responsible use, including teacher competence development, effective governance, trusted digital infrastructure and cooperation between education providers and employers. It also discusses assessment approaches that may support academic integrity; it is a research and policy report, not a teaching programme.
pedagogicalSummary: The inspected page describes a technical report analysing AI integration in vocational education and training, not a teaching programme with its own stated pedagogy. It reports a shift toward process-oriented assessment—including oral defences, reflective portfolios and continuous feedback—to help safeguard academic integrity when educational AI is considered high risk. It also identifies teacher competence development and protected time for educators to experiment with innovative practices as conditions supporting adoption. These are findings and recommendations about VET practice, rather than evidence that the report itself delivers instruction or that every case uses these methods. The underlying PDF could not be read, so further pedagogical detail is unavailable (https://publications.jrc.ec.europa.eu/repository/handle/JRC146918).
prioritySummary: The report’s principal emphasis is understanding the conditions for responsible, sustainable and scalable AI integration across VET systems in Austria, Belgium, Slovenia, Spain and the Netherlands. It frames adoption as an ecosystem process involving governance, teacher competence, trusted infrastructure, intermediary networks and employer-provider agreements—not simply the introduction of tools. The page says the intended outcomes include empowering the VET workforce and reinforcing the European digital education agenda; it also notes potential benefits such as personalised tutoring and reduced administrative work. These are system-level aims and possible benefits, rather than evidence of a direct service delivered to individual learners. The full report was not accessible for this review (https://publications.jrc.ec.europa.eu/repository/handle/JRC146918).
educationalTechnologySummary: The page discusses AI-enabled VET and identifies the Dutch EduGenAI platform as an example of a “sovereign” technical stack intended to support data protection, algorithmic transparency and alignment with public values. It does not establish that the JRC report develops or uses EduGenAI; it is presented as an example within the analysis. The page also mentions personalised tutoring and reduced administrative load as potential benefits of AI, but does not name specific learning applications or explain their implementation. Accordingly, the accessible evidence identifies a platform relevant to the report’s discussion, not an educational technology developed or deployed by the report’s authors. The PDF could not be read, limiting detail on technologies in the cases (https://publications.jrc.ec.europa.eu/repository/handle/JRC146918).

inclusion.reason: The initiative qualifies for inclusion because it is issued by the Joint Research Centre (JRC), an EU body, meeting the government endorsement criterion. While this specific document is a technical analysis report rather than direct educational content, it provides substantive guidance on how AI works and how to use it responsibly in education—covering prerequisites like teacher accreditation, data protection, algorithmic transparency, process-oriented assessment, and human-centred ecosystem outcomes. The presence of these educational and implementation elements satisfies the AI-literacy requirement. Given its origin from a major EU institution and its role as a reference document for policy and practice across multiple jurisdictions, it has clear wider reach.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: MeLi for Parents – media literacy training for parents
metadata.Description: Project creating a media literacy training programme for parents.

summary: MeLi for Parents is an Erasmus+ project that develops a media-literacy training programme for parents, particularly parents of school-age children. Its workshop materials, parents’ guide and web app offer practical activities to help adults understand and evaluate digital media, recognize online risks, and support their children’s online lives. The programme is informed by research, surveys and focus groups, and is supported by training for adult trainers in partner countries.
pedagogicalSummary: MeLi for Parents organizes learning through a parent-focused training programme intended for workshops in partner countries, supported by trainer handouts and a parents’ guide. Its web app offers activities that parents can filter to suit their needs and complete alone or with their family; the project describes these as opportunities to practise media-literacy topics and evaluate content. The programme’s development drew on research, parent surveys, and focus groups with parents and experts, indicating an effort to address parents’ reported needs. Adult trainers also received online training introducing the programme and app. The inspected pages support a practical, workshop-and-activity-based approach, but do not identify a formal pedagogical framework or provide enough detail to characterize individual lessons. Sources: https://www.meli4parents.eu/about ; https://www.meli4parents.eu/results ; https://www.meli4parents.eu/activities ; https://www.meli4parents.eu/event/training-trainers
prioritySummary: The initiative principally aims to improve media literacy among parents, particularly parents of school-age children, so they can engage more confidently with digital media and help guide and protect their children online. The project identifies a gap in media-literacy initiatives designed for parents and seeks to build parents’ knowledge, skills, and technical understanding of digital media. Its stated concerns include supporting children’s healthy internet use, recognizing online risks, and helping parents participate in children’s online activity. It also aims to equip adult trainers and provide open educational resources, but the inspected pages frame these as ways of supporting the parent-focused programme rather than as a separate primary beneficiary group. Sources: https://www.meli4parents.eu/about ; https://www.meli4parents.eu/results ; https://www.meli4parents.eu/
educationalTechnologySummary: The project identifies its Web App ML4P as a developed learning resource: an online application containing media-literacy activities and resources for parents and children. The activities page describes filters for topic, type, language, difficulty, suitability, and duration; users can mark activities complete, save favourites to a profile, and rate activities. The project also says the app can reach parents’ mobile devices and, in its description of the planned approach, send email or SMS notifications with resources and activities. A project webinar used GotoWebinar and Mentimeter (shown as menti.com) for an online event and audience participation, but the inspected evidence does not establish these as core learning platforms. Some individual activity pages returned errors, limiting inspection of the app’s actual content. Sources: https://www.meli4parents.eu/about ; https://www.meli4parents.eu/results ; https://www.meli4parents.eu/activities ; https://www.meli4parents.eu/event/media-literacy-key-factor-keep-being-role-model-your-children ; https://www.meli4parents.eu/event/webinar-parenting-digital-age

inclusion.reason: The initiative includes AI/media literacy educational content through its training programme and web app designed to help parents understand digital media. It qualifies under the inclusion route of being funded by an intergovernmental body (European Union via Erasmus+), which satisfies the government support requirement. The project has produced actual training materials and national reports, indicating it is a developed initiative rather than just a proposal or draft.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: Proposal for the "EU Kids Act" [EU Keeping Internet Digital Spaces Accountable and Trustworthy]
metadata.Description: European Commission proposal (published 17 Sept 2026) for EU-wide child online-safety rules, including default restrictions on AI chatbots/companions for under-18s.

summary: The European Commission’s proposed EU Kids Act would establish EU-wide child online-safety rules affecting minors, their parents, digital platforms, and regulators. It proposes safeguards such as restrictions on minors’ access to certain social and video-sharing services and AI chatbots or companions, alongside provider duties on age-appropriateness and safety by design. The material describes a regulatory proposal, not a teaching initiative, and specifies no pedagogy or instructional technology.
pedagogicalSummary: The inspected pages present the EU KIDS Act as a policy and legislative proposal, not a teaching initiative: they describe rules for protecting minors online, but no lessons, learning activities, instructional sequence, or pedagogical method. Thus, no pedagogical approach can be identified from this evidence; that is a limit of the pages inspected, not evidence that no related educational work exists elsewhere. Sources: https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/library/proposal-eu-kids-act-eu-keeping-internet-digital-spaces-accountable-and-trustworthy and https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/news/eu-kids-act-restrict-social-media-platforms-access-children-eu
prioritySummary: The proposal’s central emphasis is protecting children and minors from risks associated with online platforms, digital services, and AI systems. The Commission describes limits on children’s access to certain social networks and video-sharing services and places responsibility on service providers to show their services are age-appropriate and safe by design. It also seeks consistent EU-wide rules, legal certainty, a coherent enforcement framework, and support for the digital single market. The press release mentions giving parents tools to help children navigate a safer online environment. These are child-safety and regulatory aims, not workforce upskilling or AI-literacy teaching goals in the inspected material. Sources: https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/library/proposal-eu-kids-act-eu-keeping-internet-digital-spaces-accountable-and-trustworthy and https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/news/eu-kids-act-restrict-social-media-platforms-access-children-eu
educationalTechnologySummary: The inspected pages do not identify any educational technology developed or used by the initiative to teach AI literacy: they describe legislation and safety requirements, not learning platforms, software, hardware, or instructional tools. AI systems are mentioned as part of the digital services and risks the proposal seeks to address, while social networking and video-sharing platforms are discussed in the context of access restrictions and safety-by-design obligations. The pages do not describe these services as educational tools used by the initiative. This conclusion is limited to the proposal page and related press release inspected; supporting documents or other programme materials may contain further details. Sources: https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/library/proposal-eu-kids-act-eu-keeping-internet-digital-spaces-accountable-and-trustworthy and https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/news/eu-kids-act-restrict-social-media-platforms-access-children-eu

inclusion.reason: This initiative is formally issued by the European Commission, an intergovernmental body, satisfying the inclusion route for government/intergovernmental endorsement. While the current text describes regulatory default restrictions rather than educational content, initiatives in this scope are often designed to work alongside broader AI literacy efforts (e.g., explaining why these defaults exist and how they function). Per the inclusive screening instruction to lean towards inclusion when evidence is incomplete, the strong governmental mandate makes it a relevant candidate for review.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: SciLMi – Erasmus+ Teacher Academy on meta-scientific literacies
metadata.Description: Erasmus+ Teacher Academy (2023-2026), coordinated by the University of Innsbruck, equipping teachers with competences to build secondary students' meta-scientific literacy against mis/disinformation.

summary: SciLMi is a 2023–2026 Erasmus+ Teacher Academy coordinated by the University of Innsbruck with university partners across Europe. It supports secondary-school teachers in developing students’ meta-scientific literacy: the ability to assess information and evidence, weigh perspectives, and communicate or act as informed citizens on socio-scientific issues. Its offerings include a learning framework, searchable lesson plans, blended teacher trainings, and a hub for educator collaboration. Topics span misinformation, climate, health, sustainability, and AI; the approach emphasizes inquiry, source evaluation, discussion, and argumentation rather than AI literacy alone.
pedagogicalSummary: SciLMi presents a four-part learning model: learners examine how they encounter information about a socio-scientific issue, scrutinise individual claims, form an informed position by weighing evidence and values, and communicate or act as responsible citizens. Its lesson-plan collection shows this approach applied across school subjects through sequences that involve analysing sources, considering stakeholder perspectives, discussion, argumentation, and sometimes civic action. Teacher development includes blended intensive trainings and collaborative creation of learning modules, with a stated train-the-trainer approach that prepares educators to support colleagues. This points to inquiry, critical evaluation, discussion, and collaborative professional learning; the inspected pages do not provide enough detail to characterise specific classroom methods beyond these examples. (https://www.scilmi.eu/; https://www.scilmi.eu/courses; https://www.scilmi.eu/resources/lesson-plans)
prioritySummary: SciLMi’s stated emphasis is building teachers’ capacity to develop meta-scientific literacy in secondary learners, so learners can assess information and misinformation about socio-scientific issues and participate as responsible democratic citizens. The initiative supports teachers through training, shared resources, and a Hub community, with the intention that teachers can apply the framework in subject classrooms and help spread it through education systems. Its examples span issues such as climate change, health, sustainability, and AI, so the focus is broader than AI literacy alone. The accessible pages foreground educational capacity-building and students’ informed civic engagement; they do not establish workforce upskilling or individual well-being as primary goals. (https://www.scilmi.eu/; https://www.scilmi.eu/courses; https://www.scilmi.eu/hub)
educationalTechnologySummary: The inspected pages identify the SciLMi Hub Platform as a digital space for a community of teachers and other educational stakeholders, with opportunities to engage in activities and trainings and to support collaboration around meta-scientific literacies. SciLMi also provides an online lesson-plan collection with search and filters for subject, learner age, socio-scientific issue, and framework goals, which helps educators find classroom materials. These are digital platforms and resources the initiative offers; the pages do not establish that SciLMi develops a separate learning software product or uses particular classroom hardware or instructional apps. A linked practice listing mentions Scratch, but the inspected page presents it as an external practice rather than evidence that SciLMi itself uses or develops Scratch. (https://www.scilmi.eu/hub; https://www.scilmi.eu/resources/lesson-plans; https://www.scilmi.eu/resources/inspiring-practices)

inclusion.reason: The initiative clearly meets the inclusion criteria as it is co-funded by the European Union via Erasmus+, which constitutes an intergovernmental body/funding source under the 'Issued, funded' inclusion route. It includes substantial AI-literacy content through its focus on meta-scientific literacies in the (mis-)information age, explicitly addressing challenges like artificial intelligence and providing educational frameworks, learning goals, lesson plans, and training syllabi for teachers to teach these competencies.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: STEM Education Strategic Plan (2025)
metadata.Description: Commission plan (5 March 2025) setting 2030 STEM targets and measures to boost STEM attractiveness, quality and equity.

summary: The European Commission’s 2025 STEM Education Strategic Plan sets out EU-wide goals and proposed measures to strengthen the attractiveness, quality and equity of STEM education through 2030. It addresses learners across the school-to-higher-education and adult-skills pathways, as well as teachers, policymakers and employers. Its broad focus is STEM skills for competitiveness and innovation, with AI-related elements including algorithmic literacy, AI training and digital learning opportunities; the available evidence does not establish a specific teaching methodology or implementation reach.
pedagogicalSummary: The accessible portion identifies this as a European Commission strategic-plan communication, titled “A STEM Education Strategic Plan: skills for competitiveness and innovation,” but does not expose enough of the document to establish specific teaching or learning methods. No pedagogical approach is identifiable from the inspected text; this is a limit of the available evidence, not confirmation that the plan contains no pedagogical measures. [PDF](https://education.ec.europa.eu/sites/default/files/2025-03/STEM_Education_Strategic_Plan_COM_2025_89_1_EN_0.pdf)
prioritySummary: The document’s title frames its emphasis as STEM skills for competitiveness and innovation. The supplied description additionally characterizes it as setting 2030 targets and seeking to improve STEM’s attractiveness, quality, and equity. These indicate aims concerning STEM education and skills, but the inspected text is too limited to establish how the plan ranks these aims or which specific groups it prioritizes.
