metadata.Initiative / Programme: Council of Europe Recommendation CM/Rec(2026)12 on AI literacy
metadata.Description: Committee of Ministers recommendation (2026) setting 22 guiding principles for AI literacy across education systems and society.

summary: The Council of Europe’s Recommendation CM/Rec(2026)12 provides a policy framework for AI literacy across member states. It sets out 22 guiding principles organized around human, technological and practical dimensions, with emphasis on understanding AI, human rights and dignity, democracy and the rule of law, and social agency and critical thinking. Seven recommendations address governance, curricula, teaching and assessment, professional development, higher education and research, and public awareness. The intended audience includes learners and educators across education systems as well as the wider public; the recommendation guides policy rather than prescribing specific classroom methods or technologies.
pedagogicalSummary: The inspected announcement describes a policy framework rather than a specific teaching programme or classroom method. It organizes AI literacy around a three-dimensional model—human, technological and practical—and four themes: foundational understanding of AI; human rights and dignity; democracy and the rule of law; and social agency and critical thinking. Its seven recommendations address governance, curricula, teaching and assessment, professional development, higher education and research, and public awareness, indicating where member states are encouraged to embed learning. The evidence supports a broad, rights-based and critical approach, but does not specify instructional techniques, lesson formats or how learning is assessed in practice. (https://www.coe.int/en/web/education/-/council-of-europe-adopts-recommendation-cm/rec-2026-12-on-artificial-intelligence-literacy-education-at-the-heart-of-europe-s-response-to-artificial-intelligence)
prioritySummary: The Recommendation principally aims to help people understand AI, use it responsibly and recognize risks to human rights, democracy and the rule of law. Its intended beneficiaries are broad: pupils, students, teachers, parents, workers and citizens of all ages, while member states are the audience for the policy framework and its implementation. The emphasis extends beyond technical competence to AI’s social effects, human dignity, privacy, autonomy, equity, non-discrimination, well-being, social justice, sustainable development and the environment. The Council of Europe frames education as part of democratic infrastructure and says it will support member states in translating the principles into policy and practice. These aims are stated together; the inspected pages do not establish a narrower single priority or beneficiary group. (https://www.coe.int/en/web/education/-/council-of-europe-adopts-recommendation-cm/rec-2026-12-on-artificial-intelligence-literacy-education-at-the-heart-of-europe-s-response-to-artificial-intelligence)
educationalTechnologySummary: The inspected pages do not identify a named educational technology, platform, software product or hardware that this AI-literacy initiative develops or uses to deliver learning. The Recommendation discusses AI as a subject of literacy and addresses how AI systems may affect education; that does not establish that the initiative uses those systems as teaching tools. A related Council of Europe page describes personalized learning pathways, real-time feedback and innovative teaching as potential roles for AI in education, while also emphasizing privacy, transparency and bias concerns; it presents these as possibilities, not as technologies adopted by this initiative. The announcement says the Education Department will build on existing work and develop practical tools for policymakers and educators, but does not specify them. (https://www.coe.int/en/web/education/-/council-of-europe-adopts-recommendation-cm/rec-2026-12-on-artificial-intelligence-literacy-education-at-the-heart-of-europe-s-response-to-artificial-intelligence; https://www.coe.int/en/web/education/artificial-intelligence)

metadata.Initiative / Programme: Council of Europe Digital Citizenship Education (DCE)
metadata.Description: CoE programme on digital citizenship education (10 domains), incl. DCE handbooks and curriculum framework.

summary: The Council of Europe’s Digital Citizenship Education initiative helps children and young people participate responsibly in digital society, with resources also for educators, parents and carers, and policymakers. Its competence-based, cross-curricular framework covers 10 domains; the DCE Planner organizes 320 exemplar learning outcomes by age and domain for educators to select and adapt. Handbooks, lesson plans, online courses, and videos with accompanying activities support teaching and curriculum planning. The programme includes an Artificial Intelligence and Education section, but its overall focus is broader digital citizenship, including rights, well-being, media literacy, and online participation.
pedagogicalSummary: The initiative describes a competence-based, cross-curricular approach: digital citizenship can be integrated across the curriculum rather than treated as dependent on learners’ technical know-how. The DCE Planner organizes 320 exemplar learning outcomes by age group and domain; educators select and adapt outcomes to create learning experiences, while the handbook provides learning goals and activities. Resources also include lesson plans and online courses. The Digi-Nauts videos are paired with activities, exercises, an Activity Book and a Teachers’ Guide, supporting classroom discussion and practice. These materials point to flexible curriculum planning and guided activities, though the inspected pages do not establish one single teaching method used everywhere. Sources: https://www.coe.int/en/web/education/dce-for-educators and https://www.coe.int/en/web/education/dce-planner
prioritySummary: The central aim is to equip children and young people to participate fully and responsibly in a digitised society: developing the values, attitudes, skills and knowledge to benefit from online opportunities while navigating risks. The programme links this individual learning to democratic and societal participation, including rights and responsibilities, ethical conduct, and participation in online and offline communities. It also addresses children’s well-being and supports parents and educators, while the DCE Planner and 2025 European Year materials seek to help education professionals and member states integrate the framework into curricula and policy. The inspected evidence presents these as connected aims rather than establishing a strict hierarchy. This is a broader digital citizenship initiative, not specifically an AI-literacy programme. Sources: https://www.coe.int/en/web/education/digital-citizenship-education, https://www.coe.int/en/web/education/dce-for-parents-and-carers and https://www.coe.int/en/web/education/european-year-of-digital-citizenship-education-2025
educationalTechnologySummary: The inspected pages identify educational media and an online curriculum-planning resource, but no AI-based learning technology. The DCE Planner is available for interactive online use or download; its age- and domain-organized learning outcomes help educators plan or adapt curriculum and professional development. The Council of Europe explicitly describes Digi-Nauts as a video series it developed for children, parents and educators; accompanying exercises, an Activity Book and a Teachers’ Guide connect the videos to DCE themes and classroom use. The educator page also lists online courses developed in collaboration with the European Wergeland Centre, but the inspected material does not identify their platform or software. These are resources supporting digital citizenship education, not evidence that the initiative uses AI tools to teach AI literacy. Sources: https://www.coe.int/en/web/education/dce-planner, https://www.coe.int/en/web/education/dce-for-educators and https://www.coe.int/en/web/education/dce-for-parents-and-carers

inclusion.reason: The page is hosted by the Council of Europe, an intergovernmental body, which satisfies the inclusion route for 'intergovernmental bodies.' Although specific learning objectives are not fully detailed on this landing page, the existence of this section within a formal DCE program that includes handbooks and curriculum frameworks implies educational guidance is available, meeting the AI-literacy requirement.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: Council of Europe Framework Convention on AI and Human Rights, Democracy and the Rule of Law (2024)
metadata.Description: First legally binding international treaty on AI; Art. 20 on digital literacy and skills.

summary: The Council of Europe Framework Convention on Artificial Intelligence (2024) is a legally binding international treaty setting requirements for AI-related activities to protect human rights, democracy and the rule of law. It addresses public authorities and private actors through principles and safeguards including transparency, accountability and risk assessment. Article 20 identifies digital literacy and skills as a cross-cutting theme, calling for efforts to build understanding of AI, its benefits, risks, opportunities, challenges, principles and applications across society. The Convention is a governance instrument rather than a teaching programme; the available evidence does not detail how its literacy provisions are implemented or specify a pedagogy or learning technology.
pedagogicalSummary: The Convention is a legally binding policy instrument, not a teaching programme, and its overview does not describe a pedagogy for AI literacy. A related Council of Europe activity, the HUDERIA Academy, does specify a hands-on format: participants spend two days applying and discussing risk-assessment stages through a model use case. This supports experiential, case-based learning for applying the HUDERIA process, but the inspected pages do not establish that it is a teaching component of the Convention itself or describe its connection to Article 20 on digital literacy and skills. (https://www.coe.int/en/web/artificial-intelligence/the-framework-convention-on-artificial-intelligence; https://www.coe.int/en/web/artificial-intelligence/huderia-academy)
prioritySummary: The Convention principally aims to ensure that AI-system activities throughout their lifecycle are consistent with human rights, democracy and the rule of law, while remaining conducive to technological progress and innovation. Its stated principles and requirements focus on protecting people affected by AI through safeguards, transparency, accountability, risk assessment and opportunities to challenge consequential decisions. The Convention covers use by public authorities and private actors, so its benefits are framed broadly rather than around a single learner or workforce group. The inspected overview does not detail how Article 20 on digital literacy and skills is implemented; the priority evidenced here is the treaty’s rights-based governance purpose. (https://www.coe.int/en/web/artificial-intelligence/the-framework-convention-on-artificial-intelligence; https://www.coe.int/en/web/artificial-intelligence/home)
educationalTechnologySummary: The inspected Convention overview identifies no educational technology, learning platform, software or hardware that it develops or uses; it is technology-neutral and sets legal obligations rather than describing instructional tools. A related Council of Europe resource, HUDERIA, comprises a methodology and the COBRA model, which supports systematic collection and mapping of information about an AI system’s context, design and deployment to identify risks and mitigation measures. The site presents these as guidance and supporting materials for risk management, not as educational software. The HUDERIA Academy applies the process to a model use case, but its page names no digital platform or other learning technology. The linked resources should not be mistaken for technology developed specifically for AI-literacy teaching. (https://www.coe.int/en/web/artificial-intelligence/the-framework-convention-on-artificial-intelligence; https://www.coe.int/en/web/artificial-intelligence/huderia-risk-and-impact-assessment-of-ai-systems; https://www.coe.int/en/web/artificial-intelligence/huderia-academy)

inclusion.reason: The initiative qualifies for inclusion because it is issued by an intergovernmental body (the Council of Europe). It clearly includes AI literacy through Article 20, which explicitly mandates 'Digital literacy' as a cross-cutting theme. The purpose of this article is to contribute to the understanding of AI and its benefits, risks, opportunities, challenges, principles and applications among all individuals and groups in society. Therefore, it meets both the core AI-literacy requirement and the inclusion route of being an intergovernmental initiative.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: Council of Europe HELP course on AI and Human Rights
metadata.Description: HELP online course on AI and human rights.

summary: The Council of Europe’s HELP programme offers an online course on AI and Human Rights for legal and justice professionals, addressing human-rights issues arising in the use of AI. The course is available through the HELP e-learning platform; HELP generally provides self-study and tutor-facilitated formats, though course-specific teaching activities are not detailed in the available evidence. The initiative is professionally focused, with no established audience or adoption figures for this course.
pedagogicalSummary: HELP describes a flexible, professionally tailored approach rather than a single classroom format. Its courses can be taken independently at the learner’s pace or in tutored groups, and may be delivered through distance or blended learning. The general methodology uses interactive course modules, learning objectives, practical assignments and case studies; national tutors adapt model curricula to local law and participants’ professional roles. Mandatory and optional resources accommodate differing levels of prior knowledge, and feedback and assessment inform course revisions. The available pages describe HELP’s general method, not the specific teaching activities or module structure of the AI and Human Rights course, so its application to that course cannot be confirmed. Sources: https://www.coe.int/en/web/help/training and https://www.coe.int/en/web/help/courses.
prioritySummary: HELP’s principal emphasis is building the capacity of judges, lawyers and prosecutors—and, increasingly, other justice-related professionals—to apply European human-rights standards in their work. Its stated purpose is to support effective national implementation of those standards and, in turn, the protection of human rights. The homepage identifies an AI and Human Rights course and reports its launch with justice professionals, but the inspected pages do not provide enough course-specific detail to establish a separate AI-related priority or rank objectives for that course. HELP also supports cross-border professional training and cooperation, particularly in the EU. Sources: https://www.coe.int/en/web/help/about-help, https://www.coe.int/en/web/help/courses and https://www.coe.int/en/web/help/home.
educationalTechnologySummary: HELP uses its Council of Europe HELP e-learning platform to host free online courses; users create an account to enrol. The courses are available as self-study resources, which learners can pause and resume, and as tutored courses moderated by certified tutors. HELP describes its course materials as interactive, visual and practical, and its general methodology includes developing interactive tools and assignments. The pages identify the platform and online learning formats, but do not name particular software or hardware beyond the platform, nor do they establish that the AI and Human Rights course uses AI-enabled educational tools. The inspected material concerns HELP’s general provision and does not show the specific technology or activities within that course. Sources: https://www.coe.int/en/web/help/about-help, https://www.coe.int/en/web/help/courses and https://www.coe.int/en/web/help/training.

inclusion.reason: The site confirms an educational offering specifically about AI (an 'AI and Human Rights' course), satisfying the AI-literacy requirement because it is an instructional module. It meets an inclusion route by being run by the Council of Europe, which is an intergovernmental body. Adoption evidence would strengthen the case but is not strictly necessary for inclusion under this route.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: Council of Europe Policy Toolbox for AI and Education
metadata.Description: Toolbox covering governance, education and AI literacy to guide policymakers and educators on teaching with and about AI.

summary: The Council of Europe’s Policy Toolbox for AI and Education is a policy-support initiative intended to help policymakers and education communities integrate AI into education systems. Its planned roadmap and tools cover governance, competences and education, including teaching and learning with and about AI. The initiative addresses school, higher and lifelong learning contexts and frames AI integration around human rights, democracy and learners’ interests. It is not described as a classroom teaching programme, and no specific pedagogy or instructional technology is established.
pedagogicalSummary: The accessible pages describe a policy-support initiative, not a teaching programme with a specified classroom pedagogy. The toolbox is intended to facilitate teaching and learning “with and about” AI, and its planned domains are governance, competences and education; the announcement also describes expert collaboration and stakeholder workshops as part of developing and consulting on the toolbox. These are design and consultation processes, not evidence of a particular learner-facing method such as project-based or direct instruction. The pages do not explain how the tools organise lessons or support learning in practice, so the pedagogy remains unspecified in this inspection (https://www.coe.int/en/web/education/-/council-of-europe-s-new-policy-toolbox-aims-to-support-education-systems-to-integrate-artificial-intelligence; https://www.coe.int/en/web/education/artificial-intelligence).
prioritySummary: The initiative principally aims to help education systems and policy developers integrate AI into education, including through a roadmap and tools spanning governance, competences and education. It is also concerned with enabling teaching and learning about and with AI. The wider AI-and-education page emphasizes accessible, inclusive and equitable education and aligning AI adoption with human rights, democracy, the rule of law and learner dignity, while identifying privacy, transparency and bias as issues to address. The pages therefore indicate both system-level support and learner-protective, inclusive aims, but do not establish a more specific beneficiary group or rank these priorities (https://www.coe.int/en/web/education/-/council-of-europe-s-new-policy-toolbox-aims-to-support-education-systems-to-integrate-artificial-intelligence; https://www.coe.int/en/web/education/artificial-intelligence).
educationalTechnologySummary: The inspected pages do not identify a named educational platform, software product, device or hardware developed or used by the initiative to teach AI literacy. They describe a policy toolbox and roadmap, which are guidance resources rather than evidence of an instructional technology. The AI-and-education page discusses AI systems in education in general, including possible personalized learning pathways and real-time feedback, but does not say the Council of Europe deploys these systems as part of this initiative. The pages provide no further detail about the toolbox’s format or any digital learning tools accompanying it, so whether such tools are used or developed cannot be established from this inspection (https://www.coe.int/en/web/education/-/council-of-europe-s-new-policy-toolbox-aims-to-support-education-systems-to-integrate-artificial-intelligence; https://www.coe.int/en/web/education/artificial-intelligence).

inclusion.reason: The initiative includes specific educational content related to AI literacy, offering guidance for teaching with and about AI as described on the page. Additionally, the Council of Europe is an intergovernmental body, which qualifies under the inclusion routes for intergovernmental bodies. The page indicates that this is a formal policy tool aimed at systemic integration rather than a single-institution or one-off event.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: UNESCO AI Competency Framework for Teachers (2024)
metadata.Description: Defines 15 competencies across 5 dimensions (human-centred mindset, ethics of AI, AI foundations & applications, AI pedagogy, AI for professional learning).

summary: The UNESCO AI Competency Framework for Teachers sets out 15 competencies across five dimensions: human-centred mindset, AI ethics, AI foundations and applications, AI pedagogy, and AI for professional learning. Organized into three progression levels—Acquire, Deepen, and Create—it guides teachers’ understanding and use of AI and is intended as a global reference for countries developing teacher training, competency frameworks, and assessment parameters. It is a framework rather than a prescribed course or teaching programme; the available description does not specify delivery methods or classroom activities.
pedagogicalSummary: The accessible UNESCO page presents a competency framework, not a detailed teaching programme or a prescribed classroom method. It organizes teacher competencies across five dimensions—human-centred mindset, AI ethics, AI foundations and applications, AI pedagogy, and AI for professional learning—and three progression levels: Acquire, Deepen, and Create. The framework is intended to inform teacher training programmes and assessment parameters, and to guide teachers in building AI knowledge and applying ethical principles. These features indicate staged competency development and support for professional learning, but the inspected page does not specify instructional activities, delivery formats, or assessment methods. (https://www.unesco.org/en/articles/ai-competency-framework-teachers)
prioritySummary: The initiative principally aims to define the knowledge, skills, and values teachers need in an AI-shaped educational environment, addressing the stated gap that few countries had defined these competencies or created national teacher-training programmes. Its direct beneficiaries are teachers and, through guidance for national frameworks and training, education systems developing support for them. The page also emphasizes protecting teachers’ rights, enhancing human agency, and promoting sustainability; it does not establish a single priority among these principles. The framework is positioned as a global reference for training and assessment, rather than as a specific AI product or course. (https://www.unesco.org/en/articles/ai-competency-framework-teachers)
educationalTechnologySummary: The inspected page identifies no specific educational technology, platform, software, or hardware that UNESCO develops or uses to deliver learning. AI is the subject of the competencies, including AI foundations and applications and AI pedagogy, but that does not establish that a particular AI tool is used for instruction. The framework itself is a publication intended to guide national competency frameworks, teacher training, and assessment; the page does not describe it as a digital learning technology or explain any technology-mediated learning activities. Accordingly, the accessible evidence supports describing a framework for developing teacher capability, but not naming an educational technology used or developed by the initiative. (https://www.unesco.org/en/articles/ai-competency-framework-teachers)

inclusion.reason: The initiative includes AI literacy by explicitly defining knowledge, skills, and values teachers must master regarding AI, including its foundations, applications, ethics, and pedagogical use. It qualifies under the inclusion route for being issued by UNESCO, an intergovernmental body.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: UNESCO AI Competency Framework for Students (2024)
metadata.Description: Defines 12 competencies across 4 dimensions (human-centred mindset, ethics of AI, AI techniques & applications, AI system design).

summary: UNESCO’s AI Competency Framework for Students (2024) guides educators in integrating AI learning objectives into school curricula. It organizes 12 competencies across four dimensions—human-centred mindset, AI ethics, AI techniques and applications, and AI system design—with progression through “Understand,” “Apply,” and “Create.” The framework aims to help students engage with AI safely and meaningfully and become responsible users and creative contributors. It also outlines domain-specific pedagogical methodologies, though the available description does not specify classroom activities or assessment methods.
pedagogicalSummary: The initiative presents a curriculum-oriented framework for educators to integrate AI learning objectives into official school curricula. It organizes student learning around 12 competencies in four dimensions—human-centred mindset, AI ethics, AI techniques and applications, and AI system design—and describes progression through “Understand,” “Apply,” and “Create” levels. UNESCO says the framework includes domain-specific pedagogical methodologies, but the inspected page does not describe particular teaching practices, classroom activities, or assessment methods. The evidence therefore supports a structured, staged approach to curriculum planning, but not a more specific characterization of how instruction is delivered. (https://www.unesco.org/en/articles/ai-competency-framework-students)
prioritySummary: The framework’s principal aim is to help educators incorporate AI learning objectives into school curricula so students can engage with AI safely and meaningfully. It seeks to prepare students as responsible users, creative citizens, and co-creators of AI, emphasizing critical judgment of AI solutions, citizenship responsibilities, and foundational knowledge for lifelong learning. It also highlights inclusive and sustainable AI design. The page frames these aims for students globally and does not identify a narrower priority such as workforce upskilling or individual well-being. It does not provide evidence about implementation, reach, or which of these educational goals takes precedence over the others. (https://www.unesco.org/en/articles/ai-competency-framework-students)
educationalTechnologySummary: The inspected page identifies the AI competency framework as a publication intended to guide curriculum integration; it does not name a learning platform, software, hardware, or other educational technology developed or used to deliver instruction. AI techniques and applications are among the topics students are expected to learn, but that is not evidence that the initiative uses an AI product as a teaching tool. The framework itself supports educators by setting out competencies, learning progression levels, curricular goals, and domain-specific pedagogical methodologies. The page does not explain whether digital tools accompany the framework or how any such tools support learning, so no specific educational technology can be identified from the inspected evidence. (https://www.unesco.org/en/articles/ai-competency-framework-students)

inclusion.reason: The initiative includes AI literacy content by explicitly defining competencies related to how AI works (techniques), ethical use (ethics), and human-AI interaction (mindset/design). It qualifies for inclusion because UNESCO is an intergovernmental body, meeting the 'intergovernmental body' inclusion route. The framework offers clear educational guidance for curricula integration rather than just providing a generic tool.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: UNESCO Guidance for Generative AI in Education and Research (2023)
metadata.Description: First global guidance on GenAI in education, incl. regulation steps, age limit recommendation and capacity building.

summary: UNESCO’s 2023 Guidance for Generative AI in Education and Research is an international policy resource for countries, policymakers, and education and research institutions. It explains generative AI and its implications, and recommends human-centred measures for regulation, privacy, age-appropriate use, ethical validation, and capacity building. It also considers creative applications in curriculum design, teaching, learning, and research, but does not prescribe a specific teaching programme or classroom model.
pedagogicalSummary: The inspected page presents policy guidance, not a described teaching programme or a specific instructional model. It says the guidance considers creative uses of generative AI in curriculum design, teaching, learning and research, and calls for human-centred, age-appropriate ethical validation and pedagogical design. These points indicate principles for designing and evaluating educational uses, but the page does not specify lesson formats, learner activities, assessment methods or how learning is organised in practice. Thus, evidence supports a proposed design orientation, not a confirmed classroom pedagogy. (https://www.unesco.org/en/articles/guidance-generative-ai-education-and-research)
prioritySummary: The guidance principally aims to help countries respond to generative AI in education and research through immediate action, longer-term policy and human-capacity development. Its stated emphasis is a human-centred approach: protecting user data, considering age limits for independent conversations with AI, and enabling ethical, safe, equitable and meaningful use. It also addresses educational institutions’ preparedness to assess tools and considers implications for education and research. The page frames these as priorities for countries and education and research systems, rather than describing a programme focused on individual learners’ workforce preparation or well-being. (https://www.unesco.org/en/articles/guidance-generative-ai-education-and-research)
educationalTechnologySummary: The page discusses generative AI technologies and models as the subject of the guidance and considers possible uses in curriculum design, teaching, learning and research. It does not identify a particular platform, software product, hardware device or educational technology developed or deployed by UNESCO for learners. Nor does it describe a technology-supported learning activity. The guidance instead proposes regulatory and design considerations for the use of GenAI tools, including privacy protection, age-appropriate use and ethical validation. On the inspected page, therefore, specific educational technologies used or developed by the initiative cannot be established; this is a limit of the available evidence, not proof that none are discussed in the full publication. (https://www.unesco.org/en/articles/guidance-generative-ai-education-and-research)

inclusion.reason: The initiative meets the inclusion criteria as it is issued by UNESCO, an intergovernmental body. It satisfies the AI-literacy requirement by explicitly explaining 'what GenAI is and how it works,' addressing ethical issues, policy frameworks, and practical applications for curriculum design and teaching/learning. The guidance supports countries to implement actions and develop human capacity, fulfilling educational objectives about using AI in education.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: PISA 2029 Media & Artificial Intelligence Literacy (MAIL) assessment
metadata.Description: OECD's innovative domain for PISA 2029 assessing students' media and AI literacy.

summary: PISA 2029 Media and Artificial Intelligence Literacy (MAIL) is an OECD assessment initiative for school-aged students, developed within the PISA programme and linked to the EC-OECD AI Literacy Framework. Rather than providing instruction, it is intended to assess students’ opportunities to learn and their ability to engage critically and effectively with media and AI, including evaluating digital content, understanding AI systems, and acting ethically and responsibly. The planned assessment combines conventional questions with simulated online, social-media, and AI environments; it also considers communication and collaboration.
pedagogicalSummary: The inspected page presents PISA 2029 MAIL primarily as an assessment, not as a teaching programme, and does not specify a pedagogy, lesson format, or instructional sequence. It says the assessment will help determine whether students have had opportunities to learn and to engage critically and proactively with media and AI; it also identifies communication and collaboration as competencies to assess. The page mentions collaborative learning among the broader opportunities digital tools can enable, but does not describe this as an approach used by MAIL. Thus, evidence of a particular pedagogy is missing from the inspected page, rather than evidence that no pedagogy exists elsewhere. (https://www.oecd.org/en/about/projects/pisa-2029-media-and-artificial-intelligence-literacy.html)
prioritySummary: PISA 2029 MAIL is principally intended to assess students’ media and AI literacy and help monitor educational interventions, rather than provide direct instruction. The OECD says it will assess whether students have opportunities to learn and how well they can understand media platforms and AI, evaluate digital content, and act effectively, ethically, and responsibly. The stated benefits include enabling students to participate responsibly in society and giving insight into the effectiveness of efforts to develop these competencies. The page therefore emphasizes student capability and informed societal participation, while also supporting evaluation of education initiatives; it does not identify a workforce-upskilling priority. (https://www.oecd.org/en/about/projects/pisa-2029-media-and-artificial-intelligence-literacy.html)
educationalTechnologySummary: The page identifies planned assessment tools, not learning technologies developed or used to teach AI literacy. PISA 2029 MAIL is described as combining traditional questions with simulated environments, using functional tools accessible to students, such as realistic simulations of the internet, social media, and AI tools, to gather evidence of competencies. These are presented as components of the assessment, not as named commercial platforms or instructional software. The page does not identify specific products, hardware, or technologies that learners use for instruction, nor does it establish that the initiative develops educational technology. Accordingly, the evidence supports describing assessment simulations, while use of learning technologies beyond these assessment instruments cannot be determined from the inspected page. (https://www.oecd.org/en/about/projects/pisa-2029-media-and-artificial-intelligence-literacy.html)

inclusion.reason: This initiative meets the inclusion criteria under multiple routes: (1) it is issued by an intergovernmental body (the OECD); (2) it is linked to the EC-OECD AI Literacy Framework, which is a joint governmental/intergovernmental effort; and (3) it clearly includes AI literacy educational content by defining specific competencies students need to learn regarding how media and AI systems work. It is not merely using AI to deliver education but explicitly provides AI-literacy learning objectives and guidance about AI function and ethical use. Therefore, it qualifies for inclusion in an AI-literacy initiative review.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: UNESCO Recommendation on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence (2021)
metadata.Description: Global normative instrument on AI ethics adopted by 193 Member States, incl. policy area on education and research.

summary: UNESCO’s 2021 Recommendation on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence is a global, human-rights-centred framework adopted by 193 Member States to guide ethical AI development, deployment, and governance. Its policy recommendations cover areas including education and research, and call for public understanding of AI and data through accessible education, civic engagement, digital skills, AI ethics training, and media and information literacy. It is a normative instrument rather than a teaching programme; the inspected evidence does not describe implemented instruction or specific educational technologies.
pedagogicalSummary: The inspected page presents the Recommendation as a global normative instrument with policy actions, not as a teaching programme. It calls for public understanding of AI and data to be promoted through open, accessible education, civic engagement, digital skills, AI ethics training, and media and information literacy, but does not explain how these activities are taught or organized. Thus, the page supports these as recommended educational approaches, not as confirmed pedagogy implemented by the initiative. Further teaching materials or implementation evidence were not inspected. (https://www.unesco.org/en/artificial-intelligence/recommendation-ethics)
prioritySummary: The Recommendation principally seeks to guide ethical development, deployment, and governance of AI through a shared, human-rights-centred framework and concrete policy recommendations for Member States. Its stated values encompass human dignity and rights, inclusive and just societies, diversity, and environmental flourishing. It also identifies public AI and data literacy as a policy priority, to be advanced through education, civic engagement, digital skills, ethics training, and media and information literacy. The intended beneficiaries are broad—individuals, societies, and the environment—while the page identifies policymakers and other stakeholders as users of UNESCO’s related Observatory. The inspected page does not establish a narrower priority or hierarchy. (https://www.unesco.org/en/artificial-intelligence/recommendation-ethics)
educationalTechnologySummary: The inspected page does not identify any specific educational technology, platform, software, or hardware that the Recommendation develops or uses to teach AI literacy. It recommends education, digital skills, and AI ethics training, but those are activities or policy aims rather than named technologies. The page also describes UNESCO’s Global AI Ethics and Governance Observatory as a resource for policymakers, regulators, academics, the private sector, and civil society, including information on countries’ readiness for ethical AI; it is not described there as a learning platform or teaching tool. The website itself is not evidence of an educational technology used by the initiative. This summary is limited to the inspected landing page. (https://www.unesco.org/en/artificial-intelligence/recommendation-ethics)

inclusion.reason: The initiative is issued by an intergovernmental body (UNESCO) with adoption across UN Member States. It explicitly includes AI literacy through its education and research pillars, including curricular development, public understanding of AI, and critical engagement training—meeting both the AI-literacy requirement and the intergovernmental inclusion route.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: International Baccalaureate guidance on (generative) AI
metadata.Description: IB statements and guidance on AI tools, academic integrity and assessment.

summary: The International Baccalaureate’s AI guidance and learning resources serve students, educators, schools, and the wider IB community across its educational programmes. They address ethical and effective use of generative AI, academic integrity, and assessment, encouraging learners to critically evaluate AI outputs for bias and gaps, acknowledge AI contributions, and use AI to support rather than replace their own thinking. Suggested classroom approaches include critiquing AI-generated examples, refining prompts, and reflecting on AI use, with teachers providing human guidance. The IB also offers educator learning resources and is developing broader principles and practical support for responsible AI in education.
pedagogicalSummary: The accessible guidance supports inquiry-led, learner-centred pedagogy rather than a single prescribed teaching method. It emphasizes active participation, critical thinking, creativity, and students’ ability to evaluate AI output for bias, gaps, and assumptions. Suggested classroom approaches include examining and critiquing AI-generated examples, refining prompts, comparing AI responses with course materials and discussion, and reflecting on how AI was used. The IB also highlights teacher modelling and human guidance: students’ work can be discussed through regular check-ins, while AI-generated material must be acknowledged. An IB-published school example describes formative feedback and student-led revision, but does not establish a universal IB practice. These approaches are described at https://www.ibo.org/programmes/artificial-intelligence-ai-in-learning-teaching-and-assessment/ and https://www.ibo.org/news/news-about-the-ib/artificial-intelligence-in-ib-assessment-and-education-a-crisis-or-an-opportunity2/.
prioritySummary: The initiative’s emphasis is on helping IB learners, educators, schools, and the wider IB community adopt AI ethically and in ways that support learning, while retaining human agency and academic integrity. The guidance pairs AI literacy—such as recognizing bias, reviewing outputs, and crediting AI-generated material—with adapting educational programmes and assessment to AI’s presence. More recent work broadens this to values-led, community-informed support: the IB is co-creating principles and practical tools, with educator AI literacy, school policy and governance, student participation, safeguarding, equity, and human and planetary flourishing among the concerns raised. The accessible pages do not establish one priority hierarchy; they present student learning and responsible ecosystem-wide adoption as linked aims. Sources: https://www.ibo.org/news/news-about-the-ib/statement-from-the-ib-about-chatgpt-and-artificial-intelligence-in-assessment-and-education/ and https://www.ibo.org/news/news-about-the-ib/updated-ai-design-principles/.
educationalTechnologySummary: The inspected pages identify no named, IB-developed AI platform already in use for student instruction. The IB does offer programme-specific AI e-learning resources; the accessible DP resource introduces classroom applications, though its linked interactive content was not inspected (https://www.ibo.org/professional-development/free-learning/dp-pd-learning-resources/dp-ai-e-learning-resource/). In March 2026, the IB described a PRC Chatbot as under development, so it is a planned example rather than a confirmed available learning tool (https://www.ibo.org/news/news-about-the-ib/ib-ai-principles/). The guidance discusses generative AI tools generally and names ChatGPT as an example; a school-practice article published by the IB describes Gemini and NotebookLM for feedback, source-based study, and learning scaffolds, but does not show that the IB itself provides or requires them (https://www.ibo.org/news/how-ai-is-reshaping-our-classrooms/). The IB also reports using AI to transcribe and synthesize input during its co-creation work.

inclusion.reason: The initiative includes explicit AI literacy content in the form of educational guidance on AI tools, academic integrity, and assessment; it is issued by a global education organization with adoption across 6,000+ schools in 160+ countries, satisfying the inclusion routes for non-government work with system-scale adoption and a clear AI-literacy element.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: OECD Digital Education Outlook 2026
metadata.Description: Flagship OECD report, 2026 edition on effective uses of generative AI in education.

summary: The OECD Digital Education Outlook 2026 is an international research report that synthesizes evidence on generative AI in education and offers recommendations for education stakeholders. It examines effects on learning, teaching and education systems, including impacts on lower-secondary learning, and emphasizes purposeful use that supports genuine learning while preserving student effort, teacher agency and human relationships. The report discusses approaches such as AI tutoring, collaborative learning and teacher co-design, and considers risks including academic integrity and weakened learning; these are topics and recommendations, not activities delivered by the OECD.
pedagogicalSummary: The inspected page presents the Outlook as a research synthesis and set of recommendations, not as a teaching programme. Its pedagogical emphasis is that generative AI supports learning when used with clear teaching principles and intentional educational purpose; simply outsourcing tasks can improve outputs without producing learning gains. It highlights AI as a tutor, partner or assistant and describes collaborative learning, questioning and nudging by digital tutors, and teacher involvement in co-design as potentially useful approaches. It recommends purposeful use that preserves cognitive effort, teacher agency and human relationships. The page does not specify a course structure or a pedagogy implemented by the OECD itself, so these are approaches discussed or advocated in the report, not confirmed OECD-delivered activities (https://www.oecd.org/en/publications/oecd-digital-education-outlook-2026_062a7394-en.html).
prioritySummary: The Outlook principally examines how generative AI can be used effectively in education to support genuine learning, rather than merely improve task performance. It emphasizes developing students’ knowledge and human skills—including independent thinking and foundational skills—and identifies critical thinking, creativity and collaboration as skills that educational uses may foster. It also considers benefits for teachers, such as improving tutoring and teaching capacity while preserving their agency, and for education systems through research and streamlined institutional work. The page frames these aims alongside concerns about disengagement, academic integrity and weakening human relationships. It does not establish a single beneficiary or rank these aims; its stated emphasis is on human-centred, purposeful educational use (https://www.oecd.org/en/publications/oecd-digital-education-outlook-2026_062a7394-en.html).
educationalTechnologySummary: The page discusses generative AI tools as technologies that may support education, including educational GenAI tools and GenAI-powered Intelligent Tutoring Systems (ITS). It describes ITS as potentially becoming dialogue-based pedagogical agents that can question learners, offer nudges and adapt strategies; it also notes general-purpose chatbots, while warning that performance gains from these do not necessarily translate into learning. These are technologies examined or described by the Outlook, not evidence that the OECD itself develops or deploys them. The inspected page names no specific software product, platform or hardware used by the initiative, and gives no implementation details; whether the full report identifies further examples cannot be determined from this page alone (https://www.oecd.org/en/publications/oecd-digital-education-outlook-2026_062a7394-en.html).

inclusion.reason: This initiative includes substantial AI literacy content by synthesizing evidence on how GenAI impacts learning, distinguishing between performance enhancements and genuine skill acquisition, and outlining design criteria for educational tools; it qualifies under the inclusion route for initiatives issued by an intergovernmental body (OECD).

metadata.Initiative / Programme: OECD Recommendation of the Council on AI (OECD AI Principles)
metadata.Description: First intergovernmental standard on AI (2019, revised 2024), incl. building human capacity.

summary: The OECD AI Principles are an international intergovernmental standard, first issued in 2019 and revised in 2024, offering values-based principles and policy recommendations for governments and other AI actors. They address trustworthy AI, including human rights, fairness, transparency, safety, and accountability, alongside research, governance, and international cooperation. Building human capacity through education and training, and preparing for labour-market transitions, is one policy recommendation; the inspected materials describe no particular teaching programme or pedagogy.
pedagogicalSummary: The inspected pages present the OECD AI Principles as an intergovernmental policy standard, not as a teaching or training programme. They provide no evidence of a particular pedagogy, such as courses, exercises, or facilitated learning. The overview lists “building human capacity and preparing for labour market transition” among recommendations for policymakers, but does not explain how learning is organised or supported. This is missing evidence about educational practice, not confirmation that no related learning activities exist elsewhere. (https://oecd.ai/en/ai-principles; https://legalinstruments.oecd.org/en/instruments/OECD-LEGAL-0449)
prioritySummary: The initiative’s stated emphasis is guiding AI actors and policymakers toward AI that is innovative and trustworthy and respects human rights and democratic values. Its principles encompass inclusive growth, sustainable development and well-being, fairness and privacy, transparency, safety, and accountability; its policy recommendations include research investment, an inclusive AI-enabling ecosystem, governance, international cooperation, and building human capacity while preparing for labour-market transition. The overview describes countries using the principles to shape policies and risk frameworks and support interoperability. Thus, the evidenced priority is broad public-policy guidance for trustworthy AI, with human capacity and workforce transition as one component rather than the sole focus. (https://oecd.ai/en/ai-principles)
educationalTechnologySummary: The inspected overview and linked OECD legal-instrument page describe principles and policy recommendations, including building human capacity, but do not identify an educational technology developed or used to support AI-literacy learning. They name no learning platform, software, hardware, or instructional tool. The OECD.AI page is a source of information about the principles, but the inspected evidence does not establish that the website itself is an educational technology used by the initiative. inclusion.reason: The initiative includes AI literacy elements via its dedicated chapter on building human capacity (education, training). metadata.Initiative / Programme: UNESCO-UNEVOC "Integrating AI in TVET: A practical guide for institutions" (2026)
metadata.Description: Guide (July 2026) helping TVET institutions integrate AI across teaching, governance and operations while centring equity and human agency.

summary: UNESCO-UNEVOC’s *Integrating AI in TVET: A Practical Guide for Institutions* is a guide for TVET policymakers, institutional leaders, educators, and other professionals. It supports institution-wide planning for AI integration across governance, curriculum, teaching and training, assessment, and operations, with attention to changing occupational skills and safety-critical work. The guide emphasizes educational purpose, human agency, equity, and responsible use; the available description does not specify particular classroom methods or learning technologies.
pedagogicalSummary: The accessible page describes an institution-wide guide that includes pedagogy and training delivery, assessment, curriculum development, and competency development among the areas for AI integration. It frames integration around educational purpose, human agency, equity, and safety, but does not explain specific teaching methods, learning activities, or how learning is organised in practice. Thus, it supports identifying a broad institutional and responsible-integration approach, not a particular classroom pedagogy; further detail may be in the guide itself. (https://www.unesco.org/en/articles/integrating-ai-tvet-practical-guide-institutions)
prioritySummary: The guide’s main emphasis is helping TVET institutions make coherent, responsible decisions about integrating AI across education and institutional practice. It is intended for policymakers, institutional leaders, educators, and other TVET professionals, while also aiming to prepare learners for changing occupational tasks and skill demands. The page highlights educational quality and relevance, human agency, equity, safety, and the risks and limitations of AI; it presents these as connected aims rather than establishing a single priority hierarchy. The intended contribution is to support successful and just transitions through informed institutional planning and implementation. (https://www.unesco.org/en/articles/integrating-ai-tvet-practical-guide-institutions)
educationalTechnologySummary: The inspected page identifies no specific educational technology, platform, software, or hardware that UNESCO-UNEVOC develops or uses to support AI-literacy learning. It discusses AI integration in TVET, including teaching, assessment, governance, and institutional operations, but AI as the topic or object of integration is not itself evidence of a particular learning technology. The page describes the publication as a practical guide for institutions, but does not specify digital delivery tools or technologies used in learning. Further details may be in the guide, which the accessible page summary does not elaborate. (https://www.unesco.org/en/articles/integrating-ai-tvet-practical-guide-institutions)

inclusion.reason: The initiative includes clear AI-literacy content, offering principles for ethical AI use and guidance on integrating AI across teaching, governance, and operations. It is issued by UNESCO-UNEVOC, an intergovernmental body (United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization), which satisfies the inclusion route requiring endorsement by an international/intergovernmental organization. The page explicitly targets TVET institutions with educational principles rather than being merely a tool for delivering education.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: AI Assessment Scale (AIAS)
metadata.Description: Five-level scale (Perkins, Furze, Roe, MacVaugh) defining permitted AI use in assessment.

summary: The AI Assessment Scale (AIAS), developed by Mike Perkins, Jasper Roe, Leon Furze and Jason MacVaugh, is a five-level framework that helps educators and institutions define AI’s role in assessment and align tasks, evidence and marking with learning outcomes. Its guidance and resources address higher education, K–12, TVET and EFL/EAP, with materials for communicating expectations, implementation, equity and assessment redesign. Downloads, editable templates and an AI advisor support its use; the framework is intended primarily for educators rather than as a sequenced AI-literacy course for learners.
pedagogicalSummary: The AIAS takes an assessment-design approach rather than prescribing a single classroom teaching method. Educators begin with learning outcomes and the evidence a task should generate, choose the intended role of AI, redesign the task and evidence accordingly, and align the marking rubric. The five levels range from independent work without AI to creative AI exploration; at collaborative levels, assessment can include how students evaluate, adapt and integrate AI outputs. The implementation guidance also recommends building evidence over time, communicating expectations clearly and considering equity. Level 5 tasks may be co-designed by students and instructors. The pages inspected describe support for educators and assessment design, not a separate AI-literacy course or sequenced learner curriculum (https://aiassessmentscale.com/; https://aiassessmentscale.com/implementation-guide/).
prioritySummary: The initiative principally aims to help educators and institutions redesign assessment for generative AI so that tasks, learning outcomes, evidence and marking remain aligned and grades retain validity. It also seeks to give students clearer, fairer expectations about whether and how AI may be used, while supporting academic integrity. The site explicitly presents integrity as relevant but says the framework’s main job is assessment redesign, not enforcement or detection. Its five levels allow AI to be excluded, used in planning or collaboration, expected, or explored creatively depending on the task’s purpose. The inspected material emphasizes assessment and learning in educational settings; it does not establish workforce upskilling or individual well-being as priorities (https://aiassessmentscale.com/; https://aiassessmentscale.com/implementation-guide/).
educationalTechnologySummary: The initiative provides the AIAS framework as downloadable diagrams and PDF and PowerPoint materials, plus an editable Canva template for adapting the scale; these communicate AI expectations and support educators’ assessment planning. Its AIAS Advisor, maintained by Learning Innovation Practice, is offered as a ChatGPT plugin and through Poe, guiding educators through level selection, task briefs, evidence planning and rubric alignment. The site also describes integrations rather than claiming ownership of the host platforms: Perusall lets instructors select and display an AIAS level in assignment setup, while Studiosity Validate includes level selection in an LMS workflow alongside student support and authorship-validation features. AI Disclose is identified as a third-party tool built on the AIAS, not as an initiative-developed product (https://aiassessmentscale.com/resources/; https://aiassessmentscale.com/integrations/).

metadata.Initiative / Programme: OECD.AI Policy Observatory
metadata.Description: Online platform with AI policies, data and analysis from countries worldwide.

summary: The OECD.AI Policy Observatory is an online resource for policymakers, researchers, businesses, and civil society to explore AI policies, data, analysis, and tools from around the world. It presents the OECD AI Principles and explanatory material on AI concepts, governance, human rights, privacy, transparency, and risk. Its dashboards and interactive AI Policy Toolkit support exploration of trends and structured policy planning, including comparisons with international examples. The platform is primarily a policy information and decision-support resource rather than a formal teaching programme.
pedagogicalSummary: OECD.AI is primarily a policy information and decision-support resource, not a teaching programme. The inspected pages describe no curriculum, courses, or formal instructional method. Its AI Policy Toolkit does, however, support structured, applied exploration: users map a country’s policy landscape through a modular questionnaire, identify priorities, and then examine relevant international examples. Pillars can be completed independently by different ministries and combined, supporting collaborative, context-specific inquiry rather than a fixed lesson sequence. Videos, publications, dashboards, and explanatory materials also let users explore topics at their own pace. These are forms of guided information access, not evidence of a broader educational pedagogy. Sources: https://oecd.ai/en/ai-toolkit/get-started; https://oecd.ai/en/ai-policy-toolkit-faq; https://oecd.ai/en/videos.
prioritySummary: OECD.AI’s central emphasis is enabling trustworthy, human-centric AI through better-informed governance and policy. The platform supplies policymakers, researchers, businesses, and civil society with international policy information, data, analysis, and tools; its AI Policy Toolkit is specifically tailored to government staff and stakeholders who need to map national policy, set priorities, and find examples for policy design and implementation. The stated aims include transparency, international cooperation, evidence-based decisions, and AI that benefits society while mitigating risks and respecting human rights. The evidence therefore points to institutional and societal governance benefits, rather than a primary focus on individual AI skills training or personal well-being. Sources: https://oecd.ai/en/about-oecd-ai; https://oecd.ai/en/ai-toolkit/get-started; https://oecd.ai/en/ai-principles.
educationalTechnologySummary: The clearest learning-support technology is the OECD-developed AI Policy Toolkit, an interactive online questionnaire and decision-support platform that helps government users map policy priorities and retrieve relevant examples. Its AI component uses existing OpenAI model APIs powered by Microsoft Azure with retrieval-augmented generation; OECD says it does not train or fine-tune a separate model. It generates document-grounded summaries, with source citations and side-by-side verification to support review. OECD.AI also provides interactive live-data visualisations for exploring AI trends. The separate Catalogue of Tools & Metrics is a searchable directory that includes educational tools, but those are contributed by originating authors and are not necessarily OECD-developed or endorsed. No dedicated teaching hardware or learning-management system was identified. Sources: https://oecd.ai/en/ai-policy-toolkit-faq; https://oecd.ai/en/data; https://oecd.ai/en/catalogue/overview.

inclusion.reason: The initiative qualifies for inclusion based on multiple criteria. First, it is issued by an intergovernmental body (the OECD), which satisfies a primary inclusion route under the guidelines. Second, it contains clear AI literacy elements: it explicitly provides 'AI terms & concepts' explaining how AI systems work and defining key terminology, along with extensive guidance on human rights, data privacy, transparency, and risk management. Third, the initiative has evidenced system-scale adoption as a global policy framework used by 47 member countries to adhere to its principles.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: UNESCO Media and Information Literacy (incl. in the age of GenAI)
metadata.Description: UNESCO programme on media and information literacy, incl. MIL Alliance and work on generative AI.

summary: UNESCO’s Media and Information Literacy (MIL) initiative supports the public, educators, learners, content creators, youth organizations and Member States in critically engaging with information and navigating digital environments. It offers curricula, guides, handbooks, toolkits, videos and online courses, while also supporting national MIL policies and initiatives. Its AI-related materials address understanding and using AI, evaluating AI-generated content, and considering AI’s societal effects, limitations, ethics and risks. Resources use varied formats, including self-paced courses, discussion, reflection and practical activities; these approaches are documented for particular materials rather than uniformly across the initiative.
pedagogicalSummary: The inspected evidence points to a resource- and activity-based approach rather than one uniform teaching method. UNESCO’s AI companion guide combines conceptual explanations with discussion questions, practical activities and examples educators can adapt to different contexts. Its MOOC offerings include self-paced learning; one interactive media-literacy course uses the Libre framework, which includes reflection, discussion, inquiry, storytelling, simulations and games. Another audio-MOOC follows UNESCO’s curriculum and provides pedagogical suggestions for educators and learners. These are documented features of particular resources, not necessarily every part of the initiative. The accessible pages describe materials and course formats but do not establish how consistently they are implemented in classrooms or how learning outcomes are assessed. (https://www.unesco.org/en/articles/ai-answers-you-decide-unesco-launches-new-media-and-information-literacy-curriculum; https://www.unesco.org/en/media-information-literacy/moocs)
prioritySummary: The initiative’s stated emphasis is to equip people broadly with media and information literacy and digital competencies so they can engage critically with information, navigate online environments safely and contribute to trust in information ecosystems and digital technologies. The site highlights responses to misinformation, disinformation and hate speech, as well as declining trust and challenges associated with AI. Its intended beneficiaries include the public across ages, with specific resources for educators, learners, adult educators, content creators and youth organizations; it also supports Member States developing MIL policies and strategies. The AI curriculum resource emphasizes critical assessment of AI’s effects on information and society, rather than technical AI skills alone. The pages present these as related priorities and do not establish a single dominant beneficiary or a clear hierarchy among goals. (https://www.unesco.org/en/media-information-literacy; https://www.unesco.org/en/articles/ai-answers-you-decide-unesco-launches-new-media-and-information-literacy-curriculum; https://www.unesco.org/en/media-information-literacy/moocs)
educationalTechnologySummary: The accessible pages identify online courses as learning formats supported by UNESCO and partners: these include self-paced MOOCs, an interactive self-directed course and an audio-MOOC. Course descriptions indicate that they deliver learning resources and activities, including material on evaluating online information, misinformation and generative AI. The pages do not name a specific learning-management platform or describe proprietary software or hardware developed by UNESCO. The main initiative page also lists FactiCITÉ as leveraging gaming for media and information literacy, but the linked resource could not be read during this inspection, so its game technology and use cannot be described further. AI is discussed as a subject learners should understand and evaluate; the available evidence does not establish that AI products themselves are used as teaching technology by the initiative. (https://www.unesco.org/en/media-information-literacy; https://www.unesco.org/en/media-information-literacy/moocs; https://www.unesco.org/en/articles/ai-answers-you-decide-unesco-launches-new-media-and-information-literacy-curriculum)

inclusion.reason: The page demonstrates AI literacy through dedicated sections like 'Advancing Media and Information Literacy in the Age of Artificial Intelligence' and a specific curriculum/news item on it, alongside multiple resources addressing generative AI risks; this satisfies the AI-literacy requirement. It qualifies for inclusion via the intergovernmental body route (UNESCO).

metadata.Description: Outcome of the International Conference on AI and Education with recommendations on AI in education.

summary: The Beijing Consensus on Artificial Intelligence and Education is a 2019 UNESCO conference outcome setting out recommendations on AI in education. It is intended for education policymakers and other stakeholders involved in planning and policy, with an international focus. The document is listed in six languages. The available evidence does not establish specific teaching approaches, technologies, or implementation activities.
pedagogicalSummary: The accessible UNESCO record identifies this as a 2019 conference document, but does not expose the consensus text or describe teaching and learning activities. The conference title refers to planning education in the AI era; that alone does not establish a pedagogical approach. Accordingly, no approach to organising or supporting learning can be identified from the inspected page, and this is a limit of accessible evidence rather than confirmation that the document contains no pedagogical recommendations. https://unesdoc.unesco.org/ark:/48223/pf0000368303
prioritySummary: The record establishes a broad emphasis on artificial intelligence and education: it names the document the “Beijing Consensus on Artificial Intelligence and Education” and links it to a conference titled “Planning Education in the AI Era: Lead the Leap.” It does not render the consensus recommendations, so its specific aims, intended beneficiaries, or relative priorities—such as workforce development or societal benefit—cannot be determined from the inspected evidence. https://unesdoc.unesco.org/ark:/48223/pf0000368303
educationalTechnologySummary: The inspected record identifies a UNESCO conference document about artificial intelligence and education, but provides no accessible detail about educational technologies developed or used by the initiative. It names no learning platform, software, hardware, or AI tool, nor describes any technology supporting learning. The digital library page is a catalogue record, not evidence that the initiative uses it as an educational technology. Because the consensus text is not available in the rendered page, absence of named tools here should be understood as an evidence limitation, not proof that the document discusses none. https://unesdoc.unesco.org/ark:/48223/pf0000368303

inclusion.reason: Included via the 'intergovernmental body' inclusion route: UNESCO is a UN specialized agency/intergovernmental organization that issued this consensus document. The document addresses AI in education at an international scale, and while the current page only shows metadata without rendering the full text content, the intergovernmental status alone satisfies one of the required inclusion routes. Per screening guidelines, when evidence for AI literacy is incomplete but relevance is plausible from context (international conference on AI and Education), lean toward inclusion rather than rejection.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: DQ Institute – Global Standards for Digital Intelligence (IEEE 3527.1)
metadata.Description: DQ framework adopted as IEEE standard for digital literacy, skills and readiness.

summary: The DQ Institute develops the DQ Global Standards for Digital Literacy, Skills, and Readiness, adopted as IEEE Standard 3527.1, alongside a youth-focused AI readiness initiative. Its AI literacy work aims to help young people use AI safely and wisely while strengthening critical and creative thinking and preserving human agency. Powered by DQ supports education providers with adaptable tools and resources to build programs, while an AI Readiness Challenge and assessment are intended to engage learners and identify needs. The Institute also addresses educators, families, workforce learners, industry, and policy audiences through its broader digital skills framework. The available descriptions outline program-building and progress-tracking supports but do not specify a detailed teaching method.
pedagogicalSummary: The accessible pages describe an educator-enabled, program-building approach rather than a detailed prescribed teaching method. Powered by DQ supports education providers in creating AI-literacy initiatives, with steps to assess community needs, adapt tools and resources, run education or training and awareness activities, and track progress. Young people are also invited to take an AI Readiness Challenge, discuss what they learn with friends, family, and teachers, and encourage peers to participate. The stated learning aim is for youth to use AI wisely and safely to amplify critical and creative thinking while retaining human values and agency. The pages do not specify lesson plans, instructional sequences, or a particular pedagogy, so those details remain unclear. (https://www.dqinstitute.org/ai-readiness/)
prioritySummary: The initiative’s clearest current emphasis is rapidly expanding AI literacy and readiness among young people by enabling education providers to build and scale programs. Its stated mission is to help youth use AI safely, wisely, and effectively to strengthen critical and creative thinking, with human values and agency. The initiative also emphasizes preparing teachers, families, and schools, including educator capacity, family support, and school leadership and policies. Equity is another stated concern: the page describes matching each learner reached with one from an underprivileged community and calls for investment in underserved communities. More broadly, DQ Institute frames its work around digital skills, safety, wellbeing, and closing the digital skills gap; the inspected pages do not establish that these broader goals supersede the youth AI-literacy focus. (https://www.dqinstitute.org/ai-readiness/; https://www.dqinstitute.org/about/)
educationalTechnologySummary: The AI Readiness page names the Powered by DQ platform as a means for education providers to design AI-literacy programs, and says it provides adaptable tools, templates, and resources for education, training, or awareness activities. It also describes an AI Readiness Challenge and an AI Readiness Assessment for individuals or communities, plus AI Readiness for Youth Index benchmarks for tracking program progress; the page labels the Index as forthcoming, so its availability is not confirmed by this inspection. These are described as program-building, assessment, or tracking supports, not as specific AI software used for instruction. The DQ Global Standards are a competency framework, not themselves an educational technology. The inspected pages do not identify particular learning software, hardware, or detailed platform features. (https://www.dqinstitute.org/ai-readiness/; https://www.dqinstitute.org/about/)

inclusion.reason: The initiative includes clear AI literacy elements as described in the provided text: educational content about how AI works, learning objectives (digital intelligence), and guidance for use via the Powered by DQ platform. The inclusion criterion of being an intergovernmental body or having widespread adoption is not definitively met here; however, the initiative is a non-government work with a recognized international standard (IEEE) and a specific educational mission to 'inspire cross-sectoral AI literacy,' which satisfies the inclusive screening guidance when specific government endorsement evidence is absent but relevant educational reach is described.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: ITU AI Skills Coalition
metadata.Description: ITU-led coalition offering AI skills training (AI for Good).

summary: The ITU AI Skills Coalition is an international, partner-led initiative that aims to expand access to AI skills and capacity-building. It connects learners with courses ranging from beginner to advanced levels across AI fundamentals, technical skills, practical applications and societal topics, alongside a Digital AI Skills Library of reports, videos and other resources. Offerings are listed in self-paced or synchronous formats and may be delivered online, in person or in hybrid settings. The stated audiences span professionals across sectors, including policymakers, researchers, educators and students, with priorities including learners in developing and Least Developed Countries, women and girls, and delivery in local languages and accessible formats. The available evidence describes a varied course-and-resource approach, not a single shared curriculum or assessment model.
pedagogicalSummary: The accessible pages describe a broad, partner-led learning offer rather than one defined teaching method. The course portfolio spans beginner to advanced levels, varied professional audiences and AI topics; listed formats include self-paced and synchronous training, delivered online, in person or in hybrid form. The Coalition also describes scalable learning pathways, localized delivery, and training in local languages and accessible formats. Its Digital AI Skills Library is presented as curated reports, videos and other educational resources. These details support a flexible, resource- and course-based approach, but the inspected pages do not establish a common curriculum, assessment model, or particular classroom pedagogy across partner offerings. (https://aiforgood.itu.int/ai-skills-coalition/; https://aiforgood.itu.int/ai-skills-coalition/ai-courses-portfolio/)
prioritySummary: The Coalition principally aims to expand access to AI skills and capacity-building globally, bridge the AI skills gap and support use of AI for sustainable development and good policy. It addresses professionals across sectors—including business leaders, policymakers, academics, researchers, students and educators—and says priority is given to learners in developing and Least Developed Countries, with an emphasis on women and girls. The stated inclusion goals also mention youth, marginalized groups, local languages and accessible formats. The pages additionally frame partnerships among industry, governments and academia as a means to strengthen skills development. These are stated priorities; the inspected material does not show how they are ranked against one another in practice. (https://aiforgood.itu.int/ai-skills-coalition/)
educationalTechnologySummary: The Coalition page points learners to a partner-network course portfolio and a Digital AI Skills Library of curated reports, videos and other resources. The portfolio lists courses in online, in-person and hybrid formats, with options including self-paced and synchronous study; the courses are described as offered by AI for Good and partner institutions. This supports access to learning materials and training, but the inspected pages do not name a particular learning-management system, software product, hardware, or AI tool developed by the Coalition, nor specify the platforms partners use to deliver courses. The website itself is a directory and access point, not evidence of a distinct educational technology. Further partner and course details were not inspected. (https://aiforgood.itu.int/ai-skills-coalition/; https://aiforgood.itu.int/ai-skills-coalition/ai-courses-portfolio/)

inclusion.reason: The ITU is a United Nations specialized agency (intergovernmental body), satisfying the intergovernmental inclusion route. This is not a single-institution or company-only project; it has international reach under a UN framework.
