metadata.Initiative / Programme: OECD "Developing vocational education and training with AI"
metadata.Description: OECD report (June 2026) on how AI can support curriculum, qualifications and occupational standards development in VET across 25 countries.

summary: The OECD’s June 2026 report, *Developing Vocational Education and Training with Artificial Intelligence*, examines how AI can support the development and updating of vocational education and training (VET) curricula, qualifications and occupational standards. Drawing on analysis across 25 countries and country examples, it discusses uses such as skills analysis, competency mapping, drafting and validation, and offers principles and policy recommendations emphasizing human judgement, stakeholder collaboration, and safeguards. It is aimed chiefly at policymakers, VET practitioners and other organizations involved in qualification and standards development; it is system-level guidance rather than a learner-facing AI-literacy course.
pedagogicalSummary: The inspected OECD page describes a policy report and does not present a teaching programme, learner activities, or a specific pedagogy for AI literacy. It says VET curriculum and qualification development typically involves collaboration and stakeholder engagement; that is a governance and development process, not evidence of a learning method. The report recommends co-created AI guidelines and targeted capacity-building for practitioners, but the page does not specify how that training is taught or organised. Thus, a pedagogical approach cannot be identified from the inspected material; this is a limit of the available evidence, not confirmation that no such activities exist elsewhere. (https://www.oecd.org/en/publications/developing-vocational-education-and-training-with-artificial-intelligence_e9f76b4e-en.html)
prioritySummary: The report’s principal emphasis is improving how VET curricula, qualifications, and occupational standards are developed and updated, so they can respond more efficiently and reliably to changing labour-market skill needs. It presents AI as a potential support for analysis, competency mapping, consultation, drafting, and validation, while stressing human judgement, stakeholder collaboration, and safeguards. The intended beneficiaries are VET systems and the practitioners, agencies, social partners, and industries involved in development; learners and employers may benefit indirectly through more relevant and timely qualifications. The page frames this as a system-level policy and capacity challenge, rather than primarily as individual AI-literacy education or workforce training in AI. (https://www.oecd.org/en/publications/developing-vocational-education-and-training-with-artificial-intelligence_e9f76b4e-en.html)
educationalTechnologySummary: The inspected page does not identify an educational technology developed or used by the OECD initiative to teach AI literacy. Instead, it reports examples of AI tools used in VET development: England’s SkillsCompass, the Netherlands’ SBB-Chat, occupation-specific custom GPT models in Switzerland’s ICT sector, and a secure Dutch platform integrating AI tools. The page associates these with tasks such as analysing skills needs, drafting qualifications, and supporting curriculum design—not with teaching learners about AI. It also notes that many tools are general-purpose or customised platforms. These are examples discussed by the report, not evidence that the OECD itself develops or deploys them as learning technologies. (https://www.oecd.org/en/publications/developing-vocational-education-and-training-with-artificial-intelligence_e9f76b4e-en.html)

inclusion.reason: The initiative includes AI literacy as it provides a framework/guidance on how to use AI in VET (supporting curriculum, qualifications, and standards). It qualifies for inclusion because the OECD is an intergovernmental body, satisfying the 'Issued by an intergovernmental body' inclusion route. The report was issued by this intergovernmental organization which has members from across the world.

metadata.Description: OECD report on policies for young children's digital lives.

summary: The OECD’s 2023 report *Empowering Young Children in the Digital Age* draws on a two-year policy review of 30 countries and jurisdictions to guide policymakers on digitalisation in early childhood education and care (ECEC). It considers how young children can explore technology’s benefits for play, creativity and self-expression while addressing risks, unequal access and skills, and the needs of ECEC professionals. Examples include robotic kits and unplugged puzzles, but the publication is policy guidance rather than a teaching programme or AI-specific curriculum.
pedagogicalSummary: The inspected OECD page describes policy recommendations for early childhood education and care (ECEC), rather than a specific teaching programme. It presents early digital learning as helping young children understand technology’s risks and benefits and explore how it can support play, creativity and self-expression. Learning need not require screen exposure: the page gives robotic kits and unplugged puzzles and cards as examples. It also stresses the role of ECEC professionals, but does not set out a particular lesson sequence or teaching method. These are approaches discussed in the report’s policy overview, not evidence that the OECD itself delivers instruction. The summary is based on the publication page; the full report was not inspected (https://www.oecd.org/en/publications/empowering-young-children-in-the-digital-age_50967622-en.html).
prioritySummary: The report’s central emphasis is helping young children thrive in a digital society through ECEC policy that balances opportunities with risks. It calls for children to be safe and prepared to understand digital technologies, while addressing concerns such as privacy, physical and social-emotional harms, and unequal access and skills. The page also identifies reducing digital divides—particularly for girls and disadvantaged children—as a policy priority, and highlights supporting ECEC staff and improving services as part of the response. The intended beneficiaries therefore include young children broadly, with attention to those at risk of exclusion, as well as ECEC professionals and services. The page summarizes a policy review, not a direct service or literacy intervention (https://www.oecd.org/en/publications/empowering-young-children-in-the-digital-age_50967622-en.html).
educationalTechnologySummary: The inspected page names no educational technology developed by the OECD initiative. It discusses technologies and resources that ECEC settings might use: digital learning materials and environments, and robotic kits or unplugged puzzles and cards for introducing ideas without direct screen exposure. It also notes that many countries offer staff development through online platforms, while digital mentoring or coaching tools are less common; these are described as country-level opportunities, not as OECD products. The report additionally discusses digital technologies for communication with families, without naming a platform. Thus, the page provides examples and policy context but does not identify a specific software, device, platform, or hardware product used or developed by the initiative. This summary is limited to the publication page, not the full report (https://www.oecd.org/en/publications/empowering-young-children-in-the-digital-age_50967622-en.html).

inclusion.reason: The initiative qualifies for inclusion under the AI-literacy screening criteria because it is issued by the OECD, an intergovernmental body. The document focuses on digital age education for young children, implying relevant educational guidance about using digital technologies including AI, which satisfies the AI-literacy requirement of providing educational content or guidance. No exclusion criteria apply as it is not a single-institution project but rather an international policy publication with broad applicability across jurisdictions.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: OECD "Opportunities, guidelines and guardrails for effective and equitable use of AI in education" (2023)
metadata.Description: OECD paper (Digital Education Outlook 2023 chapter) on principles for AI in education.

summary: The OECD’s 2023 Digital Education Outlook includes a chapter offering policy guidance for countries and jurisdictions considering whether and how to integrate generative AI into education. It addresses effective, equitable and responsible use, including concerns such as bias, privacy and stereotypes, and emphasizes dialogue with teachers and their continuing role in guiding learning. The chapter discusses potential benefits such as more personalized support, but is a policy and research resource rather than a course or direct AI-literacy teaching programme.
pedagogicalSummary: The inspected pages present a policy framework, not a course or teaching programme: they do not describe a sequence of lessons, learner activities, or a specific instructional method. The report discusses how generative AI might support personalised learning, while stressing that teachers should remain central in guiding learning and that digital transformation should improve teaching and learning rather than merely reproduce traditional methods. These are principles and potential uses, not evidence of a pedagogy implemented by the OECD initiative. The accessible pages therefore do not establish how AI-literacy learning itself is organised. (https://www.oecd.org/en/publications/oecd-digital-education-outlook-2023_c74f03de-en/full-report.html)
prioritySummary: The initiative’s stated emphasis is to help countries and jurisdictions decide whether and how to integrate generative AI into education effectively and equitably. It seeks responsible and ethical use, with attention to risks such as biased content, privacy breaches, and reinforcing stereotypes, and calls for dialogue between education authorities and teaching professionals so teachers retain a guiding role. The intended beneficiaries include education systems, teachers, and students; the report also identifies the potential for AI to offer learners more tailored support. The inspected material frames these as policy guidance and goals, rather than a programme focused on workforce training or direct AI-literacy instruction. (https://www.oecd.org/en/publications/oecd-digital-education-outlook-2023_c74f03de-en/full-report.html)
educationalTechnologySummary: The inspected pages identify generative AI and AI tools as technologies whose use in education the guidance addresses, including their potential to provide personalised learning support. However, they do not name a particular AI product, learning platform, software, or hardware developed or adopted by this initiative to teach AI literacy. The broader report discusses digital education infrastructure and tools, including learning-management and student-information systems, but this does not establish that the OECD initiative itself uses or develops them for instruction. Thus, the available evidence supports describing AI as the subject and potential application of the guidance, not a specific educational technology deployed by the initiative; further details may appear in materials not inspected. (https://www.oecd.org/en/publications/oecd-digital-education-outlook-2023_c74f03de-en/full-report.html)

inclusion.reason: The initiative includes clear AI literacy elements through its focus on guiding effective use of AI, which implies educational content about how to use AI responsibly and what considerations are needed. It qualifies for inclusion because the OECD is an intergovernmental body, satisfying the intergovernmental inclusion route. The page confirms it is a published report rather than a draft or one-off event.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: OECD AI and the Future of Skills
metadata.Description: OECD project assessing AI capabilities relative to human skills.

summary: The OECD AI and the Future of Skills project examines how AI and robotics capabilities compare with human skills and tasks, and what their development may mean for work, education and training. Aimed primarily at policymakers, it offers research and policy analysis, including OECD AI Capability Indicators, an AI Exposure Measure and associated dataset, reports and recommendations on preparing education systems and skills for future changes. Its focus is analytical and policy-oriented rather than on delivering instruction; the available evidence does not describe specific teaching methods or learner-facing activities.
pedagogicalSummary: The inspected project page describes research and policy analysis, not a teaching programme: it assesses AI and robotics capabilities and considers implications for education and training. metadata.Initiative / Programme: OECD Future of Education and Skills 2030 (Learning Compass)
metadata.Description: OECD project and Learning Compass 2030 framework for curriculum design.

summary: The OECD Future of Education and Skills 2030 project develops the Learning Compass and related frameworks to help shape curricula around the knowledge, skills, attitudes and values students need for the future. It engages students, teachers, researchers, school leaders and policymakers in international dialogue, and supports country curriculum analysis and peer learning. Its emphasis includes student agency, well-being and responsible action; AI appears in some commissioned work on education and teacher competencies, but is not presented as the project’s central focus or as a specific AI-literacy teaching method.
pedagogicalSummary: The inspected page presents the OECD Learning Compass as a broad, evolving learning framework rather than a prescribed classroom method. Its metaphor emphasizes students developing agency to navigate unfamiliar situations and find meaningful, responsible directions instead of merely receiving fixed instructions. The project supports a global dialogue involving students, teachers, researchers, school leaders and policymakers to co-create learning and teaching frameworks. In its curriculum-analysis strand, participating countries compare experiences, reflect on their own approaches and engage in peer learning about curriculum change. The page does not specify a particular teaching routine or AI-literacy pedagogy; that is missing evidence, not proof that none exists. (https://www.oecd.org/en/about/projects/future-of-education-and-skills-2030.html)
prioritySummary: The project principally seeks a shared understanding of the knowledge, skills, attitudes and values students need to thrive in the future, while helping countries adapt education systems through curriculum design, implementation and evaluation. Its stated beneficiaries include students and teachers, and its work engages education stakeholders and supports country-specific curriculum analysis. The Learning Compass links this preparation to student agency and well-being, as well as individual and collective well-being; the page also emphasizes responsible action and sustainability. Although it lists commissioned papers addressing teachers and AI, the inspected page does not present AI literacy as the project’s principal priority. (https://www.oecd.org/en/about/projects/future-of-education-and-skills-2030.html)
educationalTechnologySummary: The inspected page identifies no educational technology, platform, software or hardware that the project develops or uses to support AI literacy. It describes the Learning Compass and Teaching Compass as conceptual frameworks, not as digital learning tools, and references videos, papers and other resources without specifying a technology-mediated learning activity. AI appears among topics of some commissioned papers, including papers about AI in education and teacher competencies, but the page does not say that the project deploys AI products or uses them for instruction. This is a limit of the inspected evidence; it does not establish that no such tools appear elsewhere in the project’s materials. (https://www.oecd.org/en/about/projects/future-of-education-and-skills-2030.html)

inclusion.reason: This initiative qualifies under inclusion route 2 as it is issued by an intergovernmental body (OECD). While the specific AI literacy content within the Learning Compass 2030 framework needs further verification, the project includes a dedicated artificial intelligence topic area and appears to offer educational materials related to AI in education contexts. Given the inclusive screening approach, the initiative is included with the understanding that comprehensive evidence of AI literacy content may require examining additional OECD publications or resources linked from this site.

metadata.Description: Goal to ensure inclusive, equitable quality education and lifelong learning.

summary: UN Sustainable Development Goal 4 is part of the UN’s 2030 Agenda and calls for inclusive, equitable quality education and lifelong learning for all. It provides a global policy framework for governments and education stakeholders, with targets, indicators, and information on progress, financing, and related UN resources. The goal spans schooling, higher education, and lifelong learning, but the reviewed page does not describe a specific teaching programme, pedagogy, educational technology, or AI-literacy offering.
pedagogicalSummary: The inspected page presents SDG 4 as a global goal—to ensure inclusive and equitable quality education and promote lifelong learning opportunities for all—not as a teaching programme with a described instructional method. It gives no evidence about lesson formats, learner activities, teacher support, or how learning is organised. Lifelong learning is an intended educational outcome, not, on the evidence available, a specified pedagogy. Accordingly, no pedagogical approach can be identified from the inspected page; this is missing evidence in the page reviewed, not confirmation that related work under SDG 4 never uses particular approaches. The page also does not identify an AI-literacy curriculum or activity. Source: https://sdgs.un.org/goals/goal4
prioritySummary: The page’s stated emphasis is securing inclusive and equitable quality education and promoting lifelong learning opportunities for all. Its beneficiary is framed universally rather than as a particular workforce, age group, or sector, and the page does not set out a narrower priority or rank sub-goals. This is a broad sustainable-development goal and policy framing, not evidence of a discrete AI-literacy initiative or specific intervention. The accessible page supports describing the central aim as expanding access to quality education and learning across people generally; it does not provide enough detail here to identify which groups, delivery mechanisms, or individual benefits receive special priority. Source: https://sdgs.un.org/goals/goal4
educationalTechnologySummary: The inspected Goal 4 page does not identify educational technologies that the initiative develops or uses to support learning. It names no learning platform, software, device, or AI tool, and the presence of a website or an infographic reference does not establish an educational technology used for instruction. The page is a goal overview, not a description of a technology-supported learning programme. Thus, no relevant educational technology could be identified in the inspected evidence; this is a limit of the pages reviewed, not confirmation that no technology-related work exists across all activities associated with SDG 4. The page also does not specifically describe support for AI literacy. Source: https://sdgs.un.org/goals/goal4

inclusion.reason: The initiative qualifies for inclusion because it is issued by an intergovernmental body (the United Nations), which satisfies the inclusion route of being mandated or endorsed by a global intergovernmental organization. While this specific page serves as a high-level overview rather than a direct educational product with learning objectives, it functions as part of the UN's broader official framework for advancing SDG 4 globally. The website links to numerous educational resources, policy documents, and capacity-building initiatives that collectively provide AI literacy–compatible content if integrated with AI tools or curricula. Moreover, SDG 4 itself is a widely adopted international agenda item used across governments, schools, and institutions worldwide, satisfying the 'framework actually used by several jurisdictions' criterion. There is no evidence of exclusion; instead, there is strong institutional backing and global reach.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: UNESCO Digital Learning Week – ministers' call for education as common good in the age of AI
metadata.Description: Article on education ministers' call during Digital Learning Week.

summary: UNESCO Digital Learning Week’s ministerial statement calls for education to remain a human right and common good as AI is integrated into education. It addresses policymakers, education systems, AI providers, teachers and learners, emphasizing learner rights and safety, equity, public accountability, data protection and teacher agency. It also calls for teacher preparation and AI competencies for teachers and students. The article mentions UNESCO seminars on its AI Competency Frameworks and support for countries developing curricula and training, but describes no specific course, teaching sequence or educational technology.
pedagogicalSummary: The inspected article describes a ministerial policy statement, not a course or teaching programme, so it does not establish a specific instructional method or learning sequence. It does point to learning principles: AI should prompt learners to reason and do cognitive work rather than replace it, and its use should preserve human support and teacher judgment. UNESCO also reports awareness seminars about its AI Competency Frameworks and support for countries developing digital or AI competency curricula and training, but gives no details here about their teaching methods. Thus, evidence supports an emphasis on critical understanding, teacher preparation and professional development, not a particular classroom pedagogy. (https://www.unesco.org/en/articles/education-ministers-call-education-remain-common-good-age-ai-unescos-digital-learning-week)
prioritySummary: The central priority is to ensure education remains a human right and common good as AI enters education, with integration governed in the public interest and accountable to learners and teachers. The statement emphasizes learner rights and safety, critical understanding, teacher agency, equity and inclusion, protection of educational data, and public oversight of AI systems. It also calls for investment in teacher preparation and AI competencies for teachers and students, and for support to education systems with less governance capacity. The article presents these as shared priorities, without ranking them; the intended benefit is to protect the quality, rights and public purposes of education across education systems, rather than to advance a single workforce or personal-wellbeing goal. (https://www.unesco.org/en/articles/education-ministers-call-education-remain-common-good-age-ai-unescos-digital-learning-week)
educationalTechnologySummary: The article names no particular educational software, platform, or hardware developed or used by the initiative to deliver AI-literacy learning. It refers to AI systems in education in general and calls for systems that support reasoning, are explainable and auditable, and do not substitute for human relationships or teacher judgment; it does not identify a system that UNESCO or the ministerial initiative deploys. UNESCO’s AI Competency Frameworks, seminars, and support for countries developing curricula and training are described as learning and capacity-building resources, not as educational technologies. On the inspected page, therefore, no specific technology can be attributed to this initiative; further details about tools, if any, are not established. (https://www.unesco.org/en/articles/education-ministers-call-education-remain-common-good-age-ai-unescos-digital-learning-week)

inclusion.reason: The initiative qualifies for inclusion because it is officially issued by UNESCO, an intergovernmental body (Inclusion Route: Intergovernmental body). While the summary primarily addresses a high-level call to action rather than detailed pedagogical instructions, the context of 'Digital Learning Week' and UNESCO's core mandate implies the dissemination of literacy concepts as part of this global initiative. The screening follows the inclusive principle that does not reject potential relevance due to incomplete detail on a single news page.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: UNESCO Global Education Coalition – Digital Transformation Collaborative (6 pillars)
metadata.Description: UNESCO-led framework of six pillars (leadership, capacity, cost, content, connectivity, data) for system-wide digital transformation of education.

summary: The UNESCO Global Education Coalition’s Digital Transformation Collaborative presents a six-pillar framework to guide equitable, inclusive, and sustainable digital transformation across education systems. Aimed chiefly at decision-makers and education stakeholders, it covers leadership and coordination, capacity and culture, costs and sustainability, content and solutions, connectivity and infrastructure, and data and evidence. It recommends developing learners’ digital skills and educators’ digital and pedagogical competencies, alongside context-appropriate digital and blended learning. Ethical AI use is addressed within the data pillar, but the framework is not a dedicated AI-literacy programme and does not specify delivered courses or tools.
pedagogicalSummary: The inspected page presents a system-level framework, not a specific teaching programme or sequence of learner activities, so it does not establish a single implemented pedagogy. Its capacity-and-culture pillar calls for developing learners’ digital skills and educators’ digital and pedagogical competencies, integrating digital competencies into curricula, and supporting professional development and peer learning. The content-and-solutions pillar refers to digital and blended pedagogical models, personalised learning, and assessment systems that guide structured learning pathways. These are recommended components of digital transformation rather than evidence of particular courses or instructional practices being delivered by the initiative. The page does not describe AI-literacy teaching activities specifically (https://www.unesco.org/en/dtc-financing-toolkit/six-pillars).
prioritySummary: The framework’s stated emphasis is equitable and inclusive, system-wide digital transformation of education, supported by whole-of-government and whole-of-society cooperation. It addresses decision-makers’ coordination, governance, financing, infrastructure, content, and data responsibilities, while also identifying benefits and capacity needs for learners, educators, parents, caregivers, and communities. The page stresses human-centred educational goals, education’s role as a public good, and sustainable, accountable technology investment; it also calls for digital skills for learners and stronger educator competencies. These are presented as connected priorities, not as a ranked agenda. AI appears within the data pillar as something to leverage ethically to improve education processes, rather than as the framework’s sole or central objective (https://www.unesco.org/en/dtc-financing-toolkit/six-pillars).
educationalTechnologySummary: The page identifies categories of educational technology relevant to system planning, including learning platforms, application software, digital learning content, hardware and devices, system software and services, and online–offline or mobile and low-tech options. It describes desired qualities and roles—for example, platforms to deliver and manage content, secure and user-friendly services, and alternatives for low-connectivity settings—but does not name a particular product or platform that UNESCO or the Collaborative develops or uses to teach AI literacy. The framework is explicitly technology-agnostic and guides decision-makers in selecting tools suited to local learning contexts. It mentions ethical use of AI in education processes, but does not specify an AI educational technology or learning tool (https://www.unesco.org/en/dtc-financing-toolkit/six-pillars).

inclusion.reason: The initiative includes explicit AI literacy elements within the 'data and evidence' pillar by emphasizing ethical use of AI and includes an inclusion route via its status as a framework issued and promoted by UNESCO, an intergovernmental body.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: UNESCO work on AI in education
metadata.Description: UNESCO programme area on AI in education (guidance, competency frameworks, policy support).

summary: UNESCO’s work on AI in education provides international policy guidance and competency frameworks for education systems, policymakers, teachers, and students. Its resources include the Beijing Consensus, guidance for policymakers on readiness for AI, and frameworks to help teachers and students understand AI’s opportunities, challenges, and risks. The initiative emphasizes inclusive, equitable, human-centred use of AI in support of education, while the overview does not establish a formal course or teaching model.
pedagogicalSummary: The inspected overview does not set out a formal teaching method, course structure, or learning activities, so the initiative’s pedagogy cannot be fully established from this page. It does report a “Teacher to teacher” discussion in which teachers help students treat AI as a thought partner rather than a shortcut, while emphasizing creativity and critical thinking. metadata.Initiative / Programme: UNICEF Policy Guidance on AI for Children
metadata.Description: Guidance with requirements for child-centred AI (2021, updated 2025).

summary: UNICEF Innocenti’s Policy Guidance on AI for Children, issued in 2021 and updated in 2025, sets out a child-rights framework for developing, deploying and governing AI. Aimed principally at policymakers, businesses and other responsible actors, it addresses children’s safety, privacy, fairness, inclusion, best interests and well-being, and calls for preparing children for AI. Supporting resources include a checklist, guides for teens and parents, a policymaker roadmap, a development canvas and a poster. The initiative is policy-focused rather than a structured teaching programme.
pedagogicalSummary: The initiative is primarily policy guidance, not a described teaching programme. The page identifies a requirement to prepare and skill children for present and future AI developments, and notes practical implementation resources including an AI guide for teens, an AI guide for parents, a policymaker roadmap and an AI-for-children development canvas. These suggest support for awareness and implementation, but the inspected page does not explain a teaching method, learning sequence, or how the guides are used in instruction. UNICEF also consulted children and other stakeholders while updating the guidance; this is evidence of participatory development, not by itself a pedagogical approach. (https://www.unicef.org/innocenti/reports/policy-guidance-ai-children)
prioritySummary: The central emphasis is advancing children’s rights in AI policies and systems, principally for children’s benefit and to guide governments, businesses and other actors responsible for AI. The guidance sets out requirements concerning safety, privacy, fairness, transparency, inclusion, children’s best interests, development and well-being, alongside preparing children for AI. It also seeks to raise awareness of how AI can uphold or undermine children’s rights. Learning and accessibility are noted as possible benefits of AI, but the page presents the broader priority as child-centred rights protection and responsible AI governance, rather than workforce upskilling or a standalone education programme. (https://www.unicef.org/innocenti/reports/policy-guidance-ai-children)
educationalTechnologySummary: The inspected page does not identify a learning platform, software, hardware, or AI tool developed or used by UNICEF to deliver AI-literacy teaching. It describes AI systems as the subject of the guidance and mentions potential uses of AI to support learning and accessibility, but these are not presented as technologies used by the initiative. UNICEF reports developing practical implementation materials—a guide for teens, a guide for parents, a policymaker roadmap and a development canvas—along with a checklist, poster and policy guidance. These are documents or resources, not evidence of an educational technology platform. The page does not specify their formats beyond downloadable publications or describe technology-mediated learning activities. (https://www.unicef.org/innocenti/reports/policy-guidance-ai-children)

inclusion.reason: The initiative satisfies the AI-literacy requirement as it provides 'policy guidance' with requirements for 'child-centred AI', which inherently includes educational content and frameworks on how to use and govern AI. It qualifies for inclusion under the intergovernmental body route: UNICEF Innocenti is a mandate of the United Nations General Assembly, making this an officially endorsed initiative of an intergovernmental body.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: ASEAN Guide on AI Governance and Ethics (2024) & expanded GenAI guide (2025)
metadata.Description: ASEAN guidance on responsible AI; expanded guide covers generative AI.

summary: The ASEAN Guide on AI Governance and Ethics is a practical resource from the ASEAN Secretariat for organisations designing, developing, and deploying AI, alongside recommendations for governments at national and regional levels. It focuses on responsible AI and alignment and interoperability across ASEAN frameworks; an expanded 2025 guide addresses generative AI. The available evidence describes governance guidance, not a structured learning programme or teaching method.
pedagogicalSummary: The inspected page presents the ASEAN Guide as a practical guide for organisations designing, developing, and deploying AI, but it does not describe teaching activities, learner groups, or a method for organising or supporting learning. Its purpose is governance guidance rather than an evidenced educational programme, so no pedagogical approach can be identified from this page; that is a limit of the accessible evidence, not proof that no related learning activities exist. Source: https://asean.org/book/asean-guide-on-ai-governance-and-ethics/
prioritySummary: The page identifies the guide’s main emphasis as supporting responsible design, development, and deployment of traditional AI in commercial and non-military or dual-use applications. It is intended for organisations in the region and also aims to encourage alignment within ASEAN and interoperability among AI frameworks across jurisdictions. The guide includes recommendations for governments to consider at national and regional levels. These stated aims indicate a regional governance and responsible-use priority; the page does not specify a workforce, individual well-being, or other learner-centered priority. Source: https://asean.org/book/asean-guide-on-ai-governance-and-ethics/
educationalTechnologySummary: The inspected page identifies no educational technology, learning platform, software, or hardware developed or used by the initiative. It describes a downloadable governance guide, not a technology for supporting AI-literacy instruction, and discusses AI technologies as the subject of responsible design and deployment rather than as learning tools. The page’s download link is not exposed as an accessible resource in the inspected content, and no teaching or technology details are provided; therefore, the available evidence does not establish whether other related materials use educational technologies. Source: https://asean.org/book/asean-guide-on-ai-governance-and-ethics/

inclusion.reason: The initiative qualifies under the inclusion route 'Issued by an intergovernmental body' as it is issued by the ASEAN Secretariat, an intergovernmental organization comprising ten Southeast Asian nations. The document explicitly addresses AI governance and ethics with recommendations on national and regional initiatives for responsible AI deployment, satisfying the AI-literacy requirement through educational guidance on how to use AI responsibly within an organizational context.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: AI Ready ASEAN
metadata.Description: ASEAN Foundation programme building AI literacy of youth, educators and parents.

summary: AI Ready ASEAN is a 2024–2028 ASEAN Foundation programme that builds AI literacy among youth, educators, parents, and underserved communities across 13 Southeast Asian countries. It combines locally adapted curricula and practical training for K–12 teachers and tertiary students and faculty with short, modular online courses on AI concepts, practical use, and responsible use. A cascade model trains Master Trainers and educators to extend learning in classrooms and communities. The programme also supports research, regional exchange, and policy development; its platform is described as having a multiplier reach of over 1.7 million learners.
pedagogicalSummary: AI Ready ASEAN combines locally adapted learning with practical training and a cascade model: Master Trainers and trained educators extend AI literacy to wider communities and classrooms. The programme describes applied skills for teaching, learning, research, and everyday use; community stories also mention hands-on activities and playful, interactive examples. Its regional digital platform offers short, modular courses and e-learning, while local partners tailor delivery to national education contexts. These features indicate practical, contextualised learning supported by both online and locally delivered instruction, rather than a single uniform teaching method. The inspected pages do not provide enough detail to assess specific lesson sequences or evaluation methods; a course page redirected to login. (https://aseanfoundation.org/programme/ai_ready_asean; https://www.aiclassasean.org/; https://www.aiclassasean.org/about)
prioritySummary: The initiative’s central emphasis is broadening access to AI literacy across ASEAN, with particular attention to youth, educators, parents, and underserved communities. It aims to build knowledge, confidence, and practical ability to use AI safely and responsibly, while reducing gaps in access to digital learning. The current phase gives added focus to K–12 teachers, tertiary students, and faculty, equipping them for AI use in teaching, learning, research, and future work; training educators is also intended to extend learning to more students. The programme additionally seeks stronger local capacity and better-informed AI education policy through partnerships, research, and regional exchange. The inspected material presents these as connected priorities, not a single exclusive beneficiary or goal. (https://aseanfoundation.org/programme/ai_ready_asean; https://www.aiclassasean.org/about)
educationalTechnologySummary: The clearest identified educational technology is AI Class ASEAN, a regional digital learning platform run by the ASEAN Foundation. It provides AI-literacy courses for groups including youth, parents, educators, and Master Trainers; the listed courses are short and divided into modules, covering foundational AI, practical use, and responsible use. The platform also identifies an AI-powered chatbot for course or platform questions, an interactive discussion forum, and multilingual support, which are presented as learning and learner-support features. The initiative’s main page also describes e-learning, but the inspected sources do not name other dedicated software or hardware used in its training. AI tools and interactive games appear in participant stories as examples, but no specific products are identified as programme-developed technologies. (https://www.aiclassasean.org/; https://www.aiclassasean.org/about; https://aseanfoundation.org/programme/ai_ready_asean)

inclusion.reason: AI literacy: the initiative explicitly aims to build knowledge, skills, and confidence to understand and use AI safely, responsibly, and meaningfully; provides locally adapted curricula, applied training, and platform-based learning for educators and learners. Inclusion route: formally endorsed and launched by the ASEAN Foundation (the statutory development arm of ASEAN, a sub-national intergovernmental body) and co-funded/co-implemented with international partners (Google.org, AI Opportunity Fund, Asian Development Bank), operating across multiple ASEAN member states with collaboration with ministries of education and Local Implementing Partners. The scale and multi-country implementation satisfy the system-scale adoption criterion.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: African Union Continental AI Strategy (2024)
metadata.Description: AU strategy for AI development incl. human capital, skills and education.

summary: The African Union Continental Artificial Intelligence Strategy (2024) is an Africa-focused policy framework developed by the African Union Commission and endorsed by the AU Executive Council. It calls for coordinated national approaches and regional and global cooperation to support ethical, responsible, equitable AI and its contribution to development, innovation, jobs, and African culture. It addresses policy makers and other stakeholders across sectors, including education, and identifies human capital, skills, and education as priorities. The available page describes a strategy rather than a teaching programme and does not specify instructional methods or educational technologies.
pedagogicalSummary: The inspected African Union page presents the Continental AI Strategy as a policy framework, not as a teaching or training programme. It does not describe lessons, learning activities, instructional methods, or how learners are supported. Although education is named as one of the sectors affected by AI, that alone does not establish a pedagogical approach. The strategy document is linked from the page, but its contents were not available in the inspected page text, so this is a limit of the accessible evidence rather than confirmation that the full strategy contains no learning activities. (https://au.int/en/documents/20240809/continental-artificial-intelligence-strategy)
prioritySummary: The page characterises the strategy as an Africa-centred, development-focused approach to AI. It presents AI as a means to advance Agenda 2063 and the Sustainable Development Goals, foster innovation and new industries, create high-value jobs, and preserve and advance African culture and integration. It also emphasizes ethical, responsible, equitable, and inclusive AI, alongside unified approaches by AU Member States and stronger regional and global cooperation. These are stated priorities for Africa and its Member States; the page does not identify a narrower primary beneficiary or rank the goals. (https://au.int/en/documents/20240809/continental-artificial-intelligence-strategy)
educationalTechnologySummary: The inspected page identifies no educational technology developed or used by the initiative to support AI-literacy learning. It describes AI as a transformative technology affecting sectors including education, but does not name a learning platform, software, device, or other tool, nor explain how any technology supports instruction. The page links to the strategy document, whose contents were not available in the inspected page text; accordingly, no tools could be identified from this limited inspection. This is not evidence that the full strategy contains no relevant technologies. (https://au.int/en/documents/20240809/continental-artificial-intelligence-strategy)

inclusion.reason: This initiative qualifies for inclusion because it is formally issued by the African Union (an intergovernmental body) as stated in the document title and metadata. The strategy explicitly includes 'human capital, skills and education' components, satisfying the AI literacy requirement with educational content and guidance on how to use AI and develop related competencies. As an intergovernmental strategy endorsed by member states, it meets the inclusion route for being issued by an intergovernmental body.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: African Union Continental TVET Strategy 2025–2034
metadata.Description: AU strategy with four pillars incl. institutional and technology innovation in TVET.

summary: The African Union Continental TVET Strategy 2025–2034 is a continent-wide policy framework published by the African Union Commission, with English and French versions. metadata.Initiative / Programme: African Union Digital Education Strategy (2023–2028)
metadata.Description: AU strategy under CESA prioritising digital technology adoption, digital literacy and skills, and infrastructure.

summary: The African Union Digital Education Strategy and Implementation Plan (2023–2028), aligned with the Continental Education Strategy for Africa, provides a framework for Member States to expand digital technology across teaching, learning, research, assessment and administration. Its priorities are digital literacy and skills—particularly for teachers and students—and digital infrastructure such as networks and devices, with the broader aim of supporting digitally empowered citizens. It is a continental policy framework rather than a specified teaching programme, and the available description emphasizes digital education broadly rather than AI-specific learning or pedagogy.
pedagogicalSummary: The accessible strategy page describes a continental framework for accelerating digital technology adoption in education, but does not explain a teaching method, learning sequence, or how instruction is organised or supported. It identifies teaching, learning, research, assessment, and administration as areas where digital technologies may be adopted; these are intended application areas, not evidence of a particular pedagogy. The page also does not specify AI-literacy teaching activities. Thus, a pedagogical approach cannot be established from the inspected evidence; this is a limit of the page, not confirmation that the full strategy contains no pedagogical detail. (https://au.int/en/documents/20221125/digital-education-strategyand-implementation-plan)
prioritySummary: The African Union Digital Education Strategy and Implementation Plan (2023–2028) aims to accelerate digital technology adoption across education, strengthen digital literacy and skills for all—especially teachers and students—and build Member States’ capacity in digital infrastructure, including networks and devices. The page links these priorities to digitally empowered citizens and participation in the digital economy and society, while aligning the framework with the Continental Education Strategy for Africa. It presents these as three focus areas, without evidence on this page that one takes precedence over the others. The stated emphasis is broad digital education, rather than specifically AI literacy. (https://au.int/en/documents/20221125/digital-education-strategyand-implementation-plan)
educationalTechnologySummary: The strategy page supports broad adoption of digital technologies for teaching, learning, research, assessment, and administration, and identifies networks and devices as digital-education infrastructure whose capacity Member States should build. It does not name particular platforms, software, hardware products, or learning technologies, nor establish whether the initiative itself develops or deploys them. The page is therefore evidence of a technology-adoption and infrastructure priority, but not of a specific educational technology used to support AI-literacy learning. The inspected page also does not identify AI-focused learning tools. (https://au.int/en/documents/20221125/digital-education-strategyand-implementation-plan)

inclusion.reason: The initiative explicitly includes AI-literacy-aligned educational content (focus area 2: 'education in digital technology for digitally empowered citizens') and qualifies under the inclusion route of being issued by an intergovernmental body (the African Union).

metadata.Initiative / Programme: Albania Digital (Agenda for) Education Action Plan 2025–2030
metadata.Description: Ministry of Education and Sports plan for smart labs, teacher devices, curricula and connectivity to 2030.

summary: Albania’s Ministry of Education and Sports proposed the 2025–2030 Digital Education Action Plan through a public consultation. The national policy plan focuses on digital-competence standards and proposes measures including smart labs, teacher devices, curriculum development and connectivity. It addresses education broadly, including teaching, research and specialist development, but the available description does not specify a teaching method or implementation details, or explicitly identify AI literacy as a focus.
pedagogicalSummary: The inspected page presents the initiative as a government action plan for digital education and digital-competence standards, but does not describe a specific teaching method or learning design. It broadly says knowledge is to be created, developed and protected through teaching, scientific research, and the formation of specialists and young scientists. This supports describing instruction, research and specialist formation as intended channels, but not assigning approaches such as project-based, blended or experiential learning. The page does not explain how learning is organised, assessed, or supported in practice, and it does not explicitly frame the plan as AI-literacy teaching. These details may be in the linked plan documents, whose contents were not available in the rendered page inspected: https://arsimi.gov.al/single-konsultimi/?id=856
prioritySummary: The initiative is principally presented as a national public-policy effort to develop digital education and establish standards for achieving digital competence. The Ministry’s description frames education as a fundamental right and public responsibility, and links it to knowledge development through teaching and research, preparation of specialists and young scientists, national development priorities, and stronger democratic standards. The page therefore indicates several intended beneficiaries and goals—learners and the wider public, education and research, and the country’s development—without establishing a hierarchy among them. It does not specify an AI-literacy priority or provide enough detail on the plan’s implementation targets to identify a narrower emphasis. Source: https://arsimi.gov.al/single-konsultimi/?id=856
educationalTechnologySummary: The rendered consultation page identifies the proposal as a Digital Education Action Plan for 2025–2030 with digital-competence standards, but does not name any educational software, platform, hardware, or learning technology developed or used by the initiative. Nor does it describe how technology supports instruction. The linked plan and supporting documents may provide such information, but their contents were not accessible in the inspected page text; consequently, this is a limit of the available evidence, not confirmation that the initiative uses or develops no educational technologies. The page describes a policy proposal rather than an educational technology product, and does not explicitly identify AI as a technology or learning topic. Source: https://arsimi.gov.al/single-konsultimi/?id=856

inclusion.reason: Government inclusion route: issued/mandated by a national ministry (MA), satisfying the government endorsement/funding criterion. The page announces a consultation on curricula among other digital‑education elements; AI‑literacy content is not detailed on this single page but is plausible given the plan’s focus on curricula and teacher training, so evidence for AI literacy remains to be confirmed.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: ASCAP guide for the use of AI (Albania)
metadata.Description: Guide by Albania's Agency for Quality Assurance in Pre-university Education on use of AI.

summary: ASCAP, Albania’s Agency for Quality Assurance in Pre-university Education, publishes a guide on using artificial intelligence in schools. Intended for teachers and educational institutions, it also addresses AI use by students across school subjects. The guide covers practical applications and tools, teacher development, and responsible use, including ethics, privacy, inclusion, assessment, academic integrity, and critical verification of information. The available evidence describes a broad guidance resource but does not establish a specific teaching method or its uptake.
pedagogicalSummary: The inspected page presents an AI-use guide published by Albania’s Agency for Quality Assurance in Pre-university Education, and links to a 187-page PDF. The accessible page and PDF preview do not reveal how learning is organised, what teaching methods are recommended, or whether the guide includes activities, training, or classroom examples. Therefore, a pedagogical approach cannot be established from the inspected evidence; this is a limit of the available text, not confirmation that the guide contains no pedagogical guidance. Sources: https://www.ascap.edu.al/udhezuesi-per-perdorimin-e-inteligjences-artificiale and https://www.ascap.edu.al/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Udhezuesi-per-perdorimin-e-Inteligjences-Artificiale.pdf
prioritySummary: The initiative’s stated focus is guidance on the use of artificial intelligence, in the context of Albania’s pre-university education quality-assurance agency. The inspected page identifies the publication as an AI-use guide and provides a download link, but does not expose its purpose, intended readership, or recommendations in enough detail to establish a more specific priority or rank potential beneficiaries. The agency context supports describing the subject area as pre-university education, but not inferring whether the guide principally aims to support teachers, students, school leaders, or broader societal outcomes. The PDF preview shows an introduction and a section titled “Purpose of the guide,” but not their contents. Sources: https://www.ascap.edu.al/udhezuesi-per-perdorimin-e-inteligjences-artificiale and https://www.ascap.edu.al/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Udhezuesi-per-perdorimin-e-Inteligjences-Artificiale.pdf
educationalTechnologySummary: The inspected material identifies a downloadable PDF guide about using artificial intelligence, but does not name any AI systems, software, platforms, or hardware that the initiative develops or uses to support learning. The guide itself is an information resource, not evidence that a particular educational technology is deployed. The website page provides access to the document, but a website and download link alone do not establish use of an educational technology. Because the PDF’s extracted text was too large to inspect beyond its contents-page preview, specific tools or technology-supported learning activities may be present in the full document but could not be verified. Sources: https://www.ascap.edu.al/udhezuesi-per-perdorimin-e-inteligjences-artificiale and https://www.ascap.edu.al/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Udhezuesi-per-perdorimin-e-Inteligjences-Artificiale.pdf

inclusion.reason: This initiative meets the inclusion criteria because it is issued by a national government body (the Agency for Quality Assurance in Pre-university Education). It satisfies the AI-literacy requirement as it provides explicit educational content and guidance on how to use AI, rather than just using AI as a delivery tool. The page indicates the document is available for download as a PDF, confirming its status as an official publication.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: National Education Strategy 2021–2026 (Albania)
metadata.Description: Albania's education strategy from pre-school to higher education, prioritising inclusion, quality and digitalisation.

summary: Albania’s National Education Strategy 2021–2026 is a government framework and implementation action plan for the education sector, described as covering preschool through higher education. Its stated priorities include inclusion, quality and digitalisation, with AI and digital literacy also identified as goals. The accessible evidence confirms the strategy’s official approval but provides little detail on specific AI provisions or teaching methods.
pedagogicalSummary: The inspected page presents the National Education Strategy 2021–2026 as a government strategy and implementation action plan, approved by a Council of Ministers decision; it does not describe lessons, learning activities, or instructional methods. No pedagogical approach can therefore be identified from the accessible evidence, which is too limited to establish whether the strategy itself contains one. The page also lists a later Digital Education Agenda, but that is a separate plan and does not provide evidence about this strategy’s pedagogy. Source: https://arsimi.gov.al/akte/draft-strategjia-kombetare-e-arsimit-2021-2026/
prioritySummary: The accessible page identifies the initiative as Albania’s National Education Strategy 2021–2026 and says its implementation action plan was approved by government decision. It also lists a separate 2025–2030 Digital Education Agenda, which should not be taken as evidence of this strategy’s specific priorities. metadata.Initiative / Programme: Australian Framework for Generative AI in Schools (2023; reviewed)
metadata.Description: Approved 5 Oct 2023 by Education Ministers; six principles and 25 guiding statements on responsible generative AI use, implemented from Term 1 2024, subject to periodic review.

summary: The Australian Framework for Generative AI in Schools is a national government resource approved by Education Ministers in 2023 to guide responsible and ethical use of generative AI in Australian schools. It sets out six principles and 25 guiding statements for students, educators, school leaders, support staff, families, service providers and policymakers, and was designed for implementation from Term 1 2024. A 2024 review was endorsed by Education Ministers in June 2025. The resource is guidance rather than a specified teaching programme; the available evidence does not detail instructional methods or adoption.
pedagogicalSummary: The inspected page presents the Framework as guidance for responsible and ethical use of generative AI in schools, rather than describing a teaching programme or a particular way of organising learning. It identifies school leaders, teachers, support staff, providers, families, students and policymakers as people it supports, but does not specify instructional methods, learner activities, or professional-development formats. The page links to the Framework and a resource poster, but their contents were not inspected here; therefore, no specific pedagogy can be established from the accessible evidence, which is not proof that the full materials contain none. (https://www.education.gov.au/schooling/resources/australian-framework-generative-artificial-intelligence-ai-schools)
prioritySummary: The stated emphasis is guiding responsible and ethical use of generative AI in Australian schools, with the intended benefit extending to students, schools and society. The Framework is described as supporting a broad school-education community—including students, educators, school leaders, families, service providers and policymakers—rather than focusing solely on workforce upskilling or an individual learner group. The landing page also notes a 2024 review endorsed by Education Ministers in June 2025. It does not provide enough detail to rank the beneficiaries or identify a more specific priority beyond responsible, ethical use and those stated benefits. (https://www.education.gov.au/schooling/resources/australian-framework-generative-artificial-intelligence-ai-schools)
educationalTechnologySummary: The page concerns generative AI tools as the subject of guidance, but does not name particular AI products, learning platforms, software or hardware that the initiative develops or uses to support AI-literacy learning. It provides downloadable Framework documents in PDF and DOCX formats and a resource poster; these are informational materials, not evidence of an educational technology platform or tool. Because the linked materials were not inspected, this summary is limited to the landing page: no specific educational technology is identified there, rather than confirmed absent from the initiative as a whole. (https://www.education.gov.au/schooling/resources/australian-framework-generative-artificial-intelligence-ai-schools)

inclusion.reason: The initiative qualifies for inclusion because it is formally issued by a national government body (the Australian Government) through Education Ministers, satisfying the 'Issued by a national or sub-national government' inclusion route. The framework contains explicit educational content on responsible AI use, specifically 'six principles and 25 guiding statements,' which constitutes AI literacy guidance for schools. No exclusion criteria are met.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: AIM AT 2030 – Artificial Intelligence Mission Austria 2030
metadata.Description: Austrian federal AI strategy incl. education and skills.

summary: AIM AT 2030 is Austria’s federal strategy for artificial intelligence, led by the Federal Chancellery and the responsible federal ministry. It sets national priorities for AI adoption, research and innovation, economic competitiveness, and the responsible use of AI, including attention to rights, safety and skills. Education-related activities include an AI ethics course for public-administration staff, a practical AI competition for students aged 14–19, and funded projects developing digital-skills and programming modules in higher education. These examples serve learners across school, university and workplace settings, but the strategy is not a single teaching programme and does not establish a common curriculum or learning technology.
pedagogicalSummary: AIM AT 2030 is a national strategy rather than a single teaching programme, and the inspected pages offer only snapshots of learning activities. They describe a dedicated course for public-administration staff on digitalisation and AI ethics, covering topics such as AI bias, platform economies, privacy and law; the pages do not specify its teaching format or assessment. A youth AI competition provides a practical, challenge-based example: student teams develop and present AI-related project ideas. Separately, university-funded projects have developed digital-skills and programming modules and experimented with virtual teaching. These examples indicate professional learning, applied student projects and higher-education course development, but not a common pedagogy across the initiative. (https://www.ki-strategie.at/erfolgsgeschichten/digitalisierung-und-ethik-wie-man-ethische-grundsaetze-in-einer-digitalisierten-verwaltung-anwendet/; https://www.ki-strategie.at/erfolgsgeschichten/schuelerinnen-und-schueler-fuer-die-ki-von-morgen-bundeswettbewerb-kuenstliche-intelligenz-bwki/; https://www.ki-strategie.at/erfolgsgeschichten/ausschreibung-vorhaben-zur-digitalen-und-sozialen-transformation-in-der-hochschulbildung/)
prioritySummary: The initiative’s central emphasis is to enable broad, responsible AI use in Austria while reducing risks, strengthening the country’s research and innovation position, and sustaining the competitiveness of its technology and economy. It also identifies skills and education as a strategy action area. The examples show attention to several beneficiaries: public employees learning to apply AI ethically, young people encouraged to engage with AI and potentially become future experts, and university communities developing digital and AI-relevant skills. The 2024 implementation plan also names an AI-literacy emphasis within the Digital Competence Offensive. The inspected material supports these combined priorities, but does not establish one educational or workforce priority as overriding the strategy’s wider national aims. (https://www.ki-strategie.at/ki-strategie/; https://www.ki-strategie.at/umsetzungsplan-2024/; https://www.ki-strategie.at/erfolgsgeschichten/)
educationalTechnologySummary: The inspected pages do not identify a named educational software platform, learning management system, or dedicated AI-literacy hardware developed by AIM AT 2030. They do describe university-funded projects that developed digital-skills or programming modules and experimented with virtual teaching and learning-analytics methods; some used machine-learning methods to analyse student data. These are reported as activities within a broader higher-education digital-transformation funding programme, not as a particular technology created by the national strategy. The youth competition involved student AI projects, but the inspected description does not name tools used to teach or support participants. Thus, evidence points to some technology-enabled educational activity, but specific products, platforms, and their learning functions are not documented in the inspected pages. (https://www.ki-strategie.at/erfolgsgeschichten/ausschreibung-vorhaben-zur-digitalen-und-sozialen-transformation-in-der-hochschulbildung/; https://www.ki-strategie.at/erfolgsgeschichten/schuelerinnen-und-schueler-fuer-die-ki-von-morgen-bundeswettbewerb-kuenstliche-intelligenz-bwki/)

metadata.Initiative / Programme: Digitale Kompetenzoffensive (Digital Skills Initiative Austria)
metadata.Description: Federal initiative (BMF, BMAW, BMBWF et al.) launched 2022 to raise basic digital competencies of the population by 2030.

summary: Digitale Kompetenzoffensive (DKO) is an Austrian federal initiative launched in 2022 to strengthen digital skills across the population by 2030. Its broad audience includes digital beginners, learners, older people, workers, businesses, educators, and public administration. Offerings include free practical workshops, trainer development through self-paced and blended learning, and the DigComp 3.0 AT framework for shaping and assessing learning outcomes. AI is included in selected workshops, trainer modules, and framework outcomes, alongside wider topics such as online safety, e-government, and data literacy; the initiative also aims to strengthen IT skills and representation of women in IT.
pedagogicalSummary: The inspected pages describe practical, audience-tailored learning rather than a single prescribed teaching method. The Digital Everywhere programme offers free workshops for digital beginners, delivered across Austria by adult and continuing-education providers; topics include AI alongside online safety, e-government, and digital life. Its Train-the-Trainer offer supports educators to adapt teaching to learners’ needs, reflect on their practice, and use practical applications. It provides flexible self-paced modules, online learning pathways, and a supported blended-learning course. The DigComp 3.0 AT framework supplies learning outcomes and proficiency levels that can help shape curricula and training, but is a reference framework rather than a pedagogy. These details come from a limited set of accessible pages, so they may not represent every DKO activity. (https://www.digitalaustria.gv.at/en/digital-skills/digital-everywhere.html; https://www.digitalaustria.gv.at/kompetenzen/train-the-trainer.html; https://www.digitalaustria.gv.at/en/digital-skills/austrian-model-for-digital-competence.html)
prioritySummary: The initiative’s central emphasis is broad-based digital inclusion: raising basic digital skills among people across Austria, with a stated 2030 goal of at least 80% of the population having digital skills. Free, accessible workshops are aimed especially at digital beginners, and the initiative identifies seniors, citizens, learners, workers, businesses, and public administration among the groups and settings it serves. Its priorities also extend beyond general participation: the DKO aims to increase IT-specialist skills and representation of women in IT, support digital skills in the economy, and strengthen public-sector capability. The inspected pages present these as connected goals, without establishing a clear hierarchy beyond the broad population-wide skills objective. The summaries reflect a limited page inspection. (https://www.digitalaustria.gv.at/en/digital-skills/digital-skills-initiative-austria.html; https://www.digitalaustria.gv.at/en/digital-skills/digital-everywhere.html; https://www.digitalaustria.gv.at/kompetenzen/strategien.html)
educationalTechnologySummary: The inspected pages identify digital learning formats, but do not name a particular software platform or hardware used to teach AI literacy. The Train-the-Trainer page describes DISKIT KI as a free, self-paced online learning programme for people who teach digital skills, with updated modules on AI; DISKIT Pro KI is a supported blended-learning certificate course that includes AI competencies and AI didactics. NRDK online learning pathways guide trainers through applying the national competence framework. These are described as online or blended learning offerings, but the pages do not specify the underlying learning-management system or other technology. DigComp 3.0 AT is a competence framework with AI-related learning outcomes, not itself an educational technology. The finding is limited to the pages inspected. (https://www.digitalaustria.gv.at/kompetenzen/train-the-trainer.html; https://www.digitalaustria.gv.at/en/digital-skills/austrian-model-for-digital-competence.html)

inclusion.reason: The initiative meets the AI-literacy requirement through its explicit 'KI-Übersicht' (AI Overview) section, which provides content about artificial intelligence. Additionally, it qualifies under the inclusion route for being a government-led federal initiative issued and funded by Austrian ministries, serving as a national digital skills strategy.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: Aktionsplan KI-Kompetenzen
metadata.Description: 2026 national action plan with a three-level AI competence model spanning schools, further education, business and society.

summary: Aktionsplan KI-Kompetenzen is an Austrian federal action plan that sets out a three-level AI competence model and learning objectives for schools, further education, business and society. It provides a national framework to guide AI competence-building and implementation rather than a single teaching programme. Associated Digital Skills Offensive offerings include practical workshops and online or blended training for educators, though these formats are not established as features of every action in the plan.
pedagogicalSummary: The action plan is presented as a national framework rather than a single teaching programme; the accessible material does not reveal enough of the PDF’s contents to identify its specific teaching methods. The associated Digital Skills Offensive describes learning opportunities that include practical workshops and, for adult educators, flexible self-paced modules, online learning tracks, and a mentored blended-learning course. The educator training emphasizes real teaching and learning situations, application in practice, and reflection, but these features should not be assumed to characterize every action in the plan. Evidence: [action plan PDF](https://www.digitalaustria.gv.at/dam/jcr:ef733e94-4fe7-4511-8184-7a01e491f9ff/aktionsplan_ki-kompetenzen-final2026-bf.pdf); [competence overview](https://www.digitalaustria.gv.at/kompetenzen.html); [Train the Trainer](https://www.digitalaustria.gv.at/kompetenzen/train-the-trainer.html).
prioritySummary: The available evidence points to broad AI-competence building across schools, further education, business, and society, rather than a sole focus on one occupation or age group. The plan’s accessible title and description identify a national action plan and a three-level competence model across these settings, although the PDF text could not be inspected in full. The wider Digital Skills Offensive aims to strengthen capabilities across generations and regions, support participation in everyday life, work, and education, and develop more IT professionals. Its competence overview also sets a goal of expanding digital skills among the population and fostering innovation and competitiveness. These sources suggest several connected priorities; they do not establish a clear ranking among them. Evidence: [action plan PDF](https://www.digitalaustria.gv.at/dam/jcr:ef733e94-4fe7-4511-8184-7a01e491f9ff/aktionsplan_ki-kompetenzen-final2026-bf.pdf); [competence overview](https://www.digitalaustria.gv.at/kompetenzen.html).
educationalTechnologySummary: The accessible pages identify online learning formats, but do not establish that the action plan itself develops or deploys a dedicated AI-learning platform, AI product, or hardware. In the associated Train the Trainer offer, DISKIT KI is described as a free, self-paced online learning programme for people who teach digital skills, with modules intended to help them understand and teach AI competencies. DISKIT Pro KI is a mentored blended-learning course combining digital learning with supported instruction; NRDK online learning tracks guide educators in applying the digital-competence framework. These are learning programmes and formats, not evidence that the initiative uses AI tools as classroom technology. The plan PDF could not be fully inspected, so other technologies may not be captured here. Evidence: [Train the Trainer](https://www.digitalaustria.gv.at/kompetenzen/train-the-trainer.html); [action plan PDF](https://www.digitalaustria.gv.at/dam/jcr:ef733e94-4fe7-4511-8184-7a01e491f9ff/aktionsplan_ki-kompetenzen-final2026-bf.pdf).

inclusion.reason: Includes clear AI literacy through its three-level competence model with defined learning objectives. Qualifies via government endorsement as 'Digital Austria' is the Austrian federal ministry responsible for digitalization, making this an officially endorsed national initiative.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: Curriculum "Informatik und Künstliche Intelligenz"
metadata.Description: From school year 2027/28, Austria's upper-secondary computer science subject becomes "Informatik und Künstliche Intelligenz" with an added lesson hour.

summary: Austria’s planned upper-secondary subject “Informatik und Künstliche Intelligenz” is scheduled to begin in the 2027/28 school year, adding a lesson hour to computer science. It integrates AI with informatics foundations, data understanding, practical application, critical evaluation, and reflection on AI’s social effects and responsible use. The announcement presents the age-appropriate Austrian AI Basic Curriculum as a competency framework, including understanding AI, evaluating AI-supported information, creating with generative AI, and reflecting on AI-driven decisions; it does not specify classroom methods or teaching technologies.
pedagogicalSummary: The inspected announcement describes an integrated, competency-oriented approach rather than a specific classroom method: AI is to be taught alongside computer-science foundations, data understanding, reflection, social responsibility, and practical application, not as an isolated topic. It says the Austrian AI Basic Curriculum provides an age-appropriate, life-related framework and lists seven learning areas, including understanding AI, evaluating AI-supported information, creating with generative AI, and reflecting on AI-driven decisions. These are stated curricular aims and framework elements; the page does not describe lesson formats, teaching materials, or assessment practices. (https://www.bmb.gv.at/Ministerium/presse/20260714.html)
prioritySummary: The announcement principally emphasizes building broad AI competence among young people through school education: students should understand AI, assess it critically, use it effectively and responsibly, and develop digital autonomy. It also connects these aims to preparing students for AI’s growing role in everyday life, work, society, and democracy. The wider Austrian action plan is described as extending competence-building beyond schools to adult education, businesses, public administration, science, and society, but the inspected page does not establish a hierarchy among all those audiences. (https://www.bmb.gv.at/Ministerium/presse/20260714.html)
educationalTechnologySummary: The inspected page does not identify a particular educational platform, software product, device, or AI tool developed or deployed to support instruction. It refers to AI applications, digital tools, and generative AI as things learners should understand, evaluate, or use creatively, but does not specify which products or how they are used in teaching. The AI Basic Curriculum is presented as a competency framework, not as technology. An AI Skills Dashboard is named as part of the broader national action plan for transparency, coordination, and impact measurement; the page does not describe it as a learning tool. Further details about classroom technologies are not available in the inspected source. (https://www.bmb.gv.at/Ministerium/presse/20260714.html)

inclusion.reason: The initiative is officially issued and announced by the Austrian Federal Ministry for Digital and Economic Affairs (a national government body), satisfying the inclusion route regarding government issuance. It includes explicit AI literacy elements such as 'application competence' (Anwendungskompetenz), 'critical judgment' (kritische Urteilsfähigkeit), and 'reflective use of digital tools' (reflektierter Umgang mit digitalen Werkzeuges) within the new curriculum subject. Therefore, it qualifies for inclusion based on both government issuance and the presence of AI literacy educational content.
