metadata.Initiative / Programme: FH Vorarlberg – AI courses and responsible AI principles
metadata.Description: University of applied sciences resources referenced by respondent (courses, principles for responsible AI).

summary: FH Vorarlberg’s resource presents an eight-principle framework and a freely accessible checklist for responsible use of generative AI in university research, teaching, and theses. Aimed at researchers, lecturers, and students, it addresses topics including transparency, data protection, scientific integrity, energy use, and effects on work processes. The checklist supports documenting AI contributions and independent work; the principles were developed through a multi-stage Delphi process. The inspected page describes guidance rather than a course or sequenced teaching method.
pedagogicalSummary: The inspected article describes a framework and freely accessible checklist intended to guide AI use in research, teaching, and theses, rather than a course or defined teaching method. The checklist can support learners and researchers to document where AI contributed and where independent work was done; the article does not specify instructional activities, sequencing, or assessment beyond that documentation. The principles were developed through a multi-stage Delphi consensus process, which is how the framework was created, not a described pedagogy. Evidence is limited to this article, so other FHV teaching approaches may not be represented. (https://www.fhv.at/en/magazine/eight-principles-for-responsible-ai-in-research-and-universities-34724)
prioritySummary: The article’s principal emphasis is enabling responsible, transparent, and scientifically careful use of generative AI in university research and related teaching and student theses. It highlights data protection, transparency, energy consumption, scientific integrity, and effects on work processes, and presents disclosure as a way to strengthen trust in research and science. The guidance is intended for researchers, lecturers, and students, with students able to document AI support alongside their work. The inspected page does not establish a broader workforce-upskilling or general public-benefit priority, nor does it provide enough evidence to characterize the full range of FHV’s AI initiatives. (https://www.fhv.at/en/magazine/eight-principles-for-responsible-ai-in-research-and-universities-34724)
educationalTechnologySummary: The inspected page names generative AI, including ChatGPT, as technology already used in research for literature searches, writing, and analysis of large datasets; it does not say FHV develops or provides these systems as learning technologies. The initiative’s identified practical resource is a freely accessible checklist for courses or theses, used to document where AI was used and where independent work was performed. The page does not identify a learning platform, educational software, or hardware, and the checklist is not described as a digital product. Thus, evidence supports a documentation resource and discussion of AI use, but not a specific educational technology developed or deployed by FHV. (https://www.fhv.at/en/magazine/eight-principles-for-responsible-ai-in-research-and-universities-34724)

inclusion.reason: AI-literacy element: The page provides a list of eight principles for responsible AI use in research and universities and links to detailed explanations of each principle. This constitutes guidance about how to use AI responsibly, which satisfies the AI-literacy requirement. Inclusion route: While FHV is a university (not a government body), the initiative has clear educational value for researchers and university staff, and the content itself is structured as an educational resource with learning objectives (guidance on responsible use). It is not merely a product or tool but an educational framework.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: KI-Basiscurriculum
metadata.Description: A seven-field reference curriculum for AI basic competencies, developed under Austria's Digital Skills Initiative (DKO).

summary: KI-Basiscurriculum is a seven-field reference curriculum commissioned by OeAD within Austria’s Digital Skills Initiative. It sets out foundational AI competencies and learning outcomes for AI literacy, including understanding AI, communicating and creating with generative AI, critically evaluating AI outputs, and considering societal impacts, ethics, privacy and security. The broader initiative serves learners across generations, though the supplied evidence does not specify this curriculum’s target audience, teaching approach or adoption.
pedagogicalSummary: The accessible PDF identifies the KI-Basiscurriculum as a final report commissioned by OeAD within Austria’s Digital Skills Initiative, but its cover does not establish how learning is taught or supported (https://www.digitalaustria.gv.at/dam/jcr:5c61bd4d-cea0-46d9-b737-12603795e6db/KI_Basiscurriculum.pdf). The broader Digital Austria competencies page describes free workshops and trainer-development offers, including online learning, but does not show that these are methods prescribed by this AI curriculum (https://www.digitalaustria.gv.at/kompetenzen.html). Thus, the inspected evidence supports a curriculum/reference function, not a specific teaching approach; the report’s detailed pedagogical content could not be assessed from the available PDF extraction.
prioritySummary: The report’s cover places the KI-Basiscurriculum within the Digital Skills Initiative but does not, in the accessible text, specify its intended learners or a hierarchy of aims (https://www.digitalaustria.gv.at/dam/jcr:5c61bd4d-cea0-46d9-b737-12603795e6db/KI_Basiscurriculum.pdf). The broader initiative emphasizes building digital competencies across generations and regions, supporting opportunities in everyday life, work, and education, and increasing the supply of IT professionals. It also frames foundational skills as important for social participation and for Austria’s competitiveness (https://www.digitalaustria.gv.at/kompetenzen.html). These are parent-initiative priorities; the inspected pages do not establish which are specifically foregrounded by the AI curriculum.
educationalTechnologySummary: The inspected curriculum PDF is a report/reference document, not evidence that the initiative develops or uses a learning platform, software, hardware, or AI tool to teach AI literacy (https://www.digitalaustria.gv.at/dam/jcr:5c61bd4d-cea0-46d9-b737-12603795e6db/KI_Basiscurriculum.pdf). The broader competencies page mentions online learning programs and workshop/trainer offers, but does not identify them as tools used by the KI-Basiscurriculum or describe their use for AI learning (https://www.digitalaustria.gv.at/kompetenzen.html). Accordingly, no educational technology specific to this initiative can be identified from the inspected evidence. This is a limit of the accessible pages and PDF extraction, not confirmation that no such technology exists.

inclusion.reason: The initiative is included because it provides explicit AI literacy educational content with defined learning outcomes (LE) explaining how AI works, distinguishing AI from traditional software, discussing environmental impacts, and addressing safety and ethics. It meets the inclusion route as it was developed under a government Digital Skills Initiative (DKO) in Austria, implying endorsement or funding by a national statutory body.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: Ministry of Education AI pilot schools, guidance and teacher training
metadata.Description: Austria's education ministry package designating 100 AI pilot schools with project budgets, evaluation by University of Graz, and teacher training incl. a MOOC.

summary: Austria’s Ministry of Education sets out a national framework for responsible and pedagogically useful AI use across schools. It addresses students, teachers, school administrators and education leaders through strategic guidance, FAQs and handouts, alongside ongoing teacher professional development. The approach emphasizes understanding AI’s capabilities and limits, critically checking its outputs, and balancing AI-supported learning with AI-free work that builds and demonstrates foundational skills. The roadmap also describes planned pilots for a virtual AI learning space and an expanded marketplace of quality-assured tools.
pedagogicalSummary: The strategy describes a pedagogical approach rather than a specific course: learners should build understanding of AI’s capabilities and limits, critically check its outputs, and decide when its use is appropriate. Learning is to alternate deliberately between phases without AI and with AI: foundational skills and evidence of independent learning remain AI-free, while AI may support learning without replacing essential thinking and work. Teachers may use it for lesson preparation, differentiated tasks, and feedback when the use is pedagogically justified and their professional judgment remains decisive. The pages also emphasize ongoing teacher professional development. The inspected material is primarily strategic guidance; it does not establish a single teaching method or detailed program of lessons. Sources: https://www.bmb.gv.at/Themen/schule/zrp/ki.html ; https://www.bmb.gv.at/Themen/schule/zrp/ki/faq.html
prioritySummary: The initiative principally aims to guide and strengthen the responsible, pedagogically useful use of AI across Austrian schools and education administration. Its stated priorities include developing AI-related competencies among students, teachers, and administrators; improving teaching and learning while safeguarding independent foundational skills; and easing pedagogical and routine administrative work. It also seeks to help all learners benefit from AI opportunities and to prevent unequal educational opportunities from worsening. The strategy is framed as shared work involving schools, teacher-training institutions, administration, families, and others, rather than as a workforce-only or individual well-being initiative. The inspected pages describe these aims but do not establish the reported AI pilot-school budgets or evaluation as part of this strategy page. Source: https://www.bmb.gv.at/Themen/schule/zrp/ki.html
educationalTechnologySummary: The inspected pages do not name a particular AI platform, software product, or hardware that the initiative currently develops or deploys for instruction. They describe AI tools generically as possible supports for lesson preparation, differentiated learning, and feedback, and say that the education administration should use approved applications for tasks such as summarizing, translation, and plain-language information. Two planned supports are more specific: a virtual “KI-Sandbox” for learning about and experimenting with AI, with a pilot planned for Q1 2027, and an expansion of the “Marktplatz Lernapps” to include quality-assured AI tools for lesson preparation and design, with piloting planned from summer semester 2027. The pages do not identify the sandbox’s underlying technology or specific marketplace tools. Source: https://www.bmb.gv.at/Themen/schule/zrp/ki.html

inclusion.reason: The page is issued by Austria's national Ministry of Education (BMB), satisfying the inclusion route of being a government-endorsed initiative. The initiative includes AI literacy via teacher training, a MOOC, public strategy guides, FAQs on pedagogical use, and an AI sandbox for learning about AI. Scope uncertainty: full details of the MOOC content are not fully rendered on this landing page, but the existence of these elements and their educational nature is indicated; per the inclusive screening instruction, incomplete evidence on literacy specifics does not warrant exclusion.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: Pflichtfach "Digitale Grundbildung" (years 5–8)
metadata.Description: Compulsory subject on basic digital education since 2022/23.

summary: Digitale Grundbildung is Austria’s compulsory digital education subject for students in grades 5–8, taught for at least one fixed lesson per week. Its curriculum uses the Frankfurt Triangle to consider digital technologies, including AI, through technological, societal and interaction perspectives. Learning is organised across five competency areas: orientation, information, communication, production and action, and is intended to prepare students for later informatics education. The ministry lists supporting resources such as interactive Eduthek materials, videos, Saferinternet exercises and a micro:bit textbook; these are supplementary rather than specified as required course tools.
pedagogicalSummary: The subject is organised as a compulsory, competency-focused course: students in grades 5–8 receive at least one fixed weekly lesson, and its content is grouped into orientation, information, communication, production and action. The curriculum uses the Frankfurt Triangle to consider digital technologies from technological, societal and interaction perspectives, linking how technologies work with their effects and students’ possible responses. This supports a broad, reflective approach, but the inspected page does not specify classroom methods such as project-based or collaborative learning for grades 5–8. Its mention of playful engagement with technology and problem-solving applies to primary education, not necessarily this subject. The course is described as preparation for later informatics education. (https://www.bmb.gv.at/Themen/schule/zrp/dibi/dgb.html)
prioritySummary: The initiative’s main emphasis is establishing foundational digital competence for lower-secondary pupils through a compulsory subject in Austrian middle schools and lower-secondary academic schools. The curriculum aims to help students understand digital technologies, consider their societal effects, and identify their own interaction and action options; its five competency areas span orientation, information, communication, production and action. The ministry also presents the subject as preparation for informatics in grade 9 and further informatics subjects. The page establishes a school-learning priority, but does not identify workforce upskilling or individual well-being as primary aims. (https://www.bmb.gv.at/Themen/schule/zrp/dibi/dgb.html)
educationalTechnologySummary: The subject page lists supplementary teaching resources, including multimedia and interactive materials in Eduthek, videos and documentaries on Edutube, Saferinternet classroom exercises, and a free textbook on computational thinking with the BBC micro:bit. These are identified as materials that can support digital education, but the page does not establish that they are required, routinely used in the compulsory subject, or developed by the initiative. It does not name a specific learning-management platform, software, or hardware required for grades 5–8. The broader ministry page on Digital School discusses digital infrastructure and learning-management and communication systems at the school-system level, but does not tie a particular system to this subject. (https://www.bmb.gv.at/Themen/schule/zrp/dibi/dgb.html; https://www.bmb.gv.at/Themen/schule/zrp/dibi.html)

The page confirms it is a compulsory subject across multiple public school systems in Austria, indicating system-scale adoption. URL: https://www.bmb.gv.at/Themen/schule/zrp/dibi/dgb.html

metadata.Initiative / Programme: KU Leuven guidance on (generative) AI
metadata.Description: KU Leuven guidelines on responsible use of GenAI for students, teachers and researchers.

summary: KU Leuven provides institutional guidance on responsible generative AI use for its students, teaching staff, researchers and other employees. The resources set out principles including transparency, critical evaluation and protection of personal and confidential data; identify tools such as Microsoft Copilot; and offer role-specific advice. In education, they connect permitted use to course learning goals and fair assessment of students’ knowledge and skills. Staff can access an AI bootcamp, and the university also points to the Elements of AI course for foundational learning. The guidance addresses topics including bias, copyright, academic integrity and environmental impact, while offering limited detail on specific teaching methods.
pedagogicalSummary: The accessible pages describe guidance and staff training, but provide limited detail about teaching methods. KU Leuven’s AI bootcamp is presented as a general foundation for staff, with participants expected to apply what they learn to their own work; the linked bootcamp page could not be inspected because it redirected to a login page. The university also points to the free online Elements of AI course for foundational learning about AI and how it can be developed. In education, guidance connects permitted GenAI use to course learning goals and asks that assignments allow students’ acquired knowledge and skills to be assessed; teaching staff are expected to explain whether use is allowed. The pages do not establish a more specific instructional method. (https://www.kuleuven.be/english/genai; https://www.kuleuven.be/english/education/student/educational-tools/responsible-use-of-generative-artificial-intelligence; https://www.kuleuven.be/english/education/leuvenlearninglab/support/genai; https://www.elementsofai.be/)
prioritySummary: The initiative principally aims to enable responsible and critical use of generative AI across KU Leuven, serving students, teaching staff, researchers and other university staff. It emphasizes understanding the technology while maintaining academic standards, individual responsibility and ownership of work, transparency, and protection of personal data and copyright. For education, guidance links AI use to course learning goals and fair assessment of student competences. A staff AI bootcamp offers a general foundation intended to be applicable across different roles, while the university also promotes foundational AI learning through Elements of AI. The pages additionally stress ethical concerns, bias and sustainability, but do not present these as a single ranked priority. (https://www.kuleuven.be/english/genai; https://www.kuleuven.be/english/education/student/educational-tools/responsible-use-of-generative-artificial-intelligence; https://www.kuleuven.be/english/education/leuvenlearninglab/support/genai)
educationalTechnologySummary: The pages identify Microsoft Copilot, accessed with a KU Leuven account, as KU Leuven’s preferred GenAI tool, particularly for confidential information; students are also directed to M365 Copilot Chat. These are AI tools users may apply in their work or learning, not technologies the pages say KU Leuven developed for instruction. KU Leuven and VAIA jointly offer the free online Elements of AI course, an identified learning resource about what AI is, its capabilities and how AI methods can be developed. The AI bootcamp is another named training offer, but its linked details page redirected to login during inspection, so its platform and any learning technologies could not be verified. The university describes developing on-premise AI infrastructure for specific use cases and sensitive data, but does not identify it as an educational technology. (https://www.kuleuven.be/english/genai; https://www.kuleuven.be/english/education/student/educational-tools/responsible-use-of-generative-artificial-intelligence; https://www.elementsofai.be/)

inclusion.reason: The initiative includes significant AI literacy elements through its dedicated 'AI Literacy' landing page, references to educational frameworks like 'Elements of AI', descriptions of an internal AI bootcamp aimed at boosting team literacy, and guidelines explaining critical thinking and transparency principles. It qualifies for inclusion under the Inclusion Route for government-funded institutions or organizations with national-level reach (KU Leuven is a major Belgian university system), as it represents institutional policy and educational guidance rather than a mere company product. Although the page describes internal usage, the structured educational content and training components satisfy the requirement that the initiative itself includes AI literacy guidance.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: National Convergence Plan for the Development of AI (Belgium)
metadata.Description: Belgian federal AI strategy (2022, updated 2026) structured around nine pillars including ethical AI and lifelong learning.

summary: Belgium’s federal National Convergence Plan for the Development of AI sets a cross-sector agenda for AI, spanning trustworthy use, competitiveness, data infrastructure, research and applications in areas such as health, mobility and public services. It also identifies education and lifelong learning as priorities, including integrating AI into training. The plan is strategic rather than a structured teaching programme; related AI4Belgium activities include events, workshops, public-service training and a coached hackathon, with no specified curriculum or learning assessment.
pedagogicalSummary: The inspected pages describe several supported, mostly collaborative ways of building AI understanding, rather than a single formal teaching model. AI4Belgium runs or contributes to events including EU AI Week, which offers lectures, workshops, research perspectives and public debates for experts and non-experts. Its AI4GOV page also mentions workshops, seminars and training for public servants. A 2024 three-day AI hackathon brought teams together to address public-sector challenges, with support from experienced coaches—evidence of practical, coached learning. The coalition’s thematic working groups are intended to share experience among stakeholders. The pages do not specify a structured curriculum or learning assessment. (https://bosa.d8.pr.belgium.be/nl/AI4Belgium; https://bosa.belgium.be/nl/AI4Belgium/AI4GOV)
prioritySummary: The plan presents AI development as a national, cross-sector priority: it aims to make Belgium a “#SmartAINation” and lists trustworthy AI, competitiveness, data infrastructure, health, mobility, the environment, lifelong training, and better citizen services and protection among its nine objectives. The pages therefore support multiple emphases, not a single dominant beneficiary group. For learning specifically, “better lifelong training” is an explicit objective, while AI4GOV describes more efficient public administration and more personalized services for citizens. AI4Belgium also seeks to connect public, private, academic and civil-society actors and strengthen the Belgian AI ecosystem. (https://bosa.d8.pr.belgium.be/en/themes/digital-administration/digital-strategy-and-policy/national-convergence-plan-development; https://bosa.belgium.be/nl/AI4Belgium/AI4GOV; https://bosa.d8.pr.belgium.be/nl/AI4Belgium)
educationalTechnologySummary: The inspected pages do not identify a learning platform, educational software, or hardware developed or used specifically to teach AI literacy. They do describe digital resources related to the AI ecosystem: an AI and new digital technologies observatory that maps Belgian actors and projects, and an AI-project mapping tool for the public sector. These are presented as information and monitoring resources, not as teaching technologies. The AI4Belgium page also mentions an AI expertise centre and lab developing AI and distributed-ledger solutions, but does not describe them as educational tools. AI4GOV refers to workshops, seminars, training and a coached hackathon without naming a supporting learning technology. This conclusion is limited to the pages inspected. (https://bosa.d8.pr.belgium.be/en/themes/digital-administration/artificial-intelligence-and-emerging-technologies; https://bosa.belgium.be/nl/AI4Belgium/AI4GOV; https://bosa.d8.pr.belgium.be/nl/AI4Belgium)

inclusion.reason: This initiative is issued by the Belgian federal government (confirmed by metadata stating 'Belgian federal AI strategy' and page content referencing 'the federal government'), satisfying the inclusion route for government endorsement. It includes explicit AI-literacy elements: Objective 3 focuses on lifelong learning and education, while other objectives emphasize training, mastering AI use, integrating AI into training courses, and providing guidance to institutional and private clients. The initiative outlines concrete educational and literacy components rather than merely using AI as a delivery tool. No exclusion criteria apply.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: Kenniscentrum Digisprong (Flanders)
metadata.Description: Flemish knowledge centre supporting schools' digitalisation, incl. AI guidance for schools.

summary: Kenniscentrum Digisprong is a Flemish Government knowledge centre supporting digitalisation in schools. Its AI-related guidance serves school leaders, teachers, and other education professionals, as well as supporting pupils’ AI literacy. Resources address responsible AI use in school policy, classroom practice, and educators’ work, alongside pupils’ AI knowledge, skills, and critical judgement. The centre also offers professional learning through webinars and peer networks; its guidance encourages integrating AI competencies into existing subjects rather than prescribing a single teaching method.
pedagogicalSummary: The inspected pages show a mix of teacher professional learning and guidance for classroom practice, rather than a single prescribed teaching method. Digisprong supports educators with online webinars featuring practitioner and researcher presentations, questions, and—where available—recordings and slides; the sessions share examples and reflect on how AI might be used for teaching, feedback, and learner support. It also describes learning networks as regular peer exchanges in which participants contribute topics and learn from one another. For pupils, its AI-literacy guidance recommends building knowledge, skills, and attitudes, integrating competencies into existing subjects, and developing critical and responsible use. The pages do not establish one required classroom pedagogy. Sources: https://www.vlaanderen.be/kenniscentrum-digisprong/themas/innovatie/artificiele-intelligentie/ai-geletterdheid-duidelijke-competenties-die-je-je-leerlingen-het-best-kunt-aanleren-om-ai-te-gebruiken ; https://www.vlaanderen.be/kenniscentrum-digisprong/themas/innovatie/artificiele-intelligentie/ai-gebruiken-als-onderwijsprofessional/tussen-prompt-en-praktijk-ai-inspiratie-voor-het-onderwijs ; https://www.vlaanderen.be/kenniscentrum-digisprong/themas/professionalisering
prioritySummary: Digisprong’s stated institutional purpose is to help school leaders, teachers, and ICT coordinators across Flemish schools use educational technology to strengthen competencies, teaching and learning processes, and school organisation. Its AI-related work supports responsible use in schools and the development of pupils’ AI knowledge, skills, and attitudes. The site emphasizes ensuring that all pupils—not only those who gain knowledge of AI at home or through social media—can understand and use AI critically, participate in society, and develop for professional life. It also highlights teachers’ professional capacity and practical classroom support, including differentiated learning and multilingual-class support. The inspected evidence therefore points to connected school, learner, and teacher benefits, without establishing a narrower single priority. Sources: https://www.vlaanderen.be/kenniscentrum-digisprong/over-ons ; https://www.vlaanderen.be/kenniscentrum-digisprong/themas/innovatie/artificiele-intelligentie/ai-geletterdheid-duidelijke-competenties-die-je-je-leerlingen-het-best-kunt-aanleren-om-ai-te-gebruiken
educationalTechnologySummary: The inspected pages identify learning resources and delivery platforms, but do not identify an AI-literacy software product developed by Digisprong. Its AI webinar series is delivered online with VAIA; the series page specifies Zoom participation and provides recordings and slides when available. Digisprong also describes an interactive DigCompEdu resource with e-learning, videos, and reflection materials for teachers’ broader digital professional learning, and KlasCement as a network for sharing educational materials, including AI-related resources. Digisnap, developed by the centre, is a self-reflection tool for teachers’ ICT competencies linked to training resources; it supports general digital professional development rather than AI literacy specifically. The site discusses or showcases AI tools and adaptive platforms, but does not indicate that these are Digisprong-developed products. Sources: https://www.vlaanderen.be/kenniscentrum-digisprong/themas/innovatie/artificiele-intelligentie/ai-gebruiken-als-onderwijsprofessional/tussen-prompt-en-praktijk-ai-inspiratie-voor-het-onderwijs ; https://www.vlaanderen.be/kenniscentrum-digisprong/themas/professionalisering ; https://www.vlaanderen.be/kenniscentrum-digisprong/tools/digisnap

metadata.Initiative / Programme: Flemish minimum goals/attainment targets for digital competence (incl. AI)
metadata.Description: Flemish minimum learning goals covering digital competence (computational thinking, information/media literacy), updated September 2025.

summary: The Flemish Government’s education-goals framework sets learning outcomes for schools across education levels, including goals for digital competence such as computational thinking and information and media literacy, with AI included in the framework. It guides educators and informs education policy; the goals are standards rather than a standalone AI-literacy programme or teaching method. The framework is available through a searchable online repository, with implementation support described for schools, including a knowledge-rich curriculum approach for new primary-school goals.
pedagogicalSummary: The inspected pages describe curriculum goals and implementation support, rather than a specific teaching method for AI or digital literacy. For the new primary-school minimum goals, the stated approach is a “knowledge-rich curriculum,” intended to build pupils’ knowledge clearly and systematically; selected inspiration schools are expected to translate the goals into classroom practice and share expertise. Schools are to develop a considered, phased implementation, with support materials and professional support identified. These are curriculum and implementation principles, not evidence of a particular classroom pedagogy for AI literacy. The accessible pages do not establish whether the digital-competence goals use project-based, inquiry-based, or other specific methods. (https://www.vlaanderen.be/onderwijsprofessionals/lesgeven-en-begeleiden/opleidingsinhouden/opleidingsinhouden-basisonderwijs/nieuwe-minimumdoelen-basisonderwijs; https://onderwijsdoelen.be/)
prioritySummary: The initiative is a government repository of official learning goals across multiple education levels, not an AI-literacy programme with a clearly stated, discrete AI priority in the pages inspected. The related primary-school minimum-goals policy emphasizes updating goals, strengthening learning outcomes through a knowledge-rich curriculum, and addressing disparities in pupil achievement; the page also links quality education with social mobility, equal opportunity, personal development, and participation in society. These priorities concern education broadly, and the inspected material does not show which, if any, is the principal purpose of the digital-competence or AI-related goals. The repository itself serves educators and others seeking the goals; it does not identify a narrower beneficiary group for AI literacy. (https://onderwijsdoelen.be/; https://www.vlaanderen.be/onderwijsprofessionals/lesgeven-en-begeleiden/opleidingsinhouden/opleidingsinhouden-basisonderwijs/nieuwe-minimumdoelen-basisonderwijs)
educationalTechnologySummary: The inspected pages identify no AI-learning software, devices, or instructional platform developed or used to teach learners. The initiative’s website, https://onderwijsdoelen.be/, is a digital repository for finding official education goals; the government page also points users to a search function and downloadable documents. These support access to and consultation of curriculum requirements, but the available evidence does not establish that the portal is used as an educational technology in lessons or that it teaches AI literacy. The related primary-goals page lists implementation support and professional-support organizations, but does not name a particular AI teaching technology. Thus, evidence supports a web-based curriculum-access tool, not a learner-facing educational technology; what schools may use in practice is not established by the inspected pages. metadata.Initiative / Programme: Flemish AI strategy for education (2026, €10m)
metadata.Description: Flemish government funding (€10m) for Flemish universities to develop a structured AI-in-education strategy and classroom AI rules.

summary: The Flemish government is funding five universities to develop a coordinated AI-in-education strategy for Flanders. The planned work spans schools and higher education, aiming to help students and education staff use AI critically and responsibly, support teaching and learning, and establish common safety, privacy and governance principles. Universities are expected to identify applications to test and involve schools and teachers; the source does not specify a curriculum, training format or named AI tools.
pedagogicalSummary: The inspected report describes a planned education strategy, not a specified teaching programme or classroom method. Its pedagogical aims include teaching young people and teachers to use AI critically and responsibly, and ensuring AI contributes to stronger learning and teaching. Universities are to decide which applications to test and how to involve schools and teachers, suggesting planned evaluation and stakeholder participation, but the article gives no details of lesson formats, training methods, or a curriculum. These aims should therefore be distinguished from evidence of an established pedagogy, which is not provided in the inspected source. Source: https://www.vrt.be/vrtnws/nl/2026/06/11/vlaamse-universiteiten-krijgen-10-miljoen-euro-om-ai-beleid-voor/
prioritySummary: The initiative’s central emphasis is a coordinated, safe and responsible approach to AI across Flemish education, rather than leaving schools and institutions to develop separate rules and practices. The report identifies several intended beneficiaries and aims: students should learn to use AI critically and safely; teachers and lecturers should receive organisational support; education should prepare learners for the future labour market; and schools, institutions and policymakers should be able to learn more quickly what works. It also stresses a secure common basis, clear agreements and human oversight. The article presents these as connected priorities and does not establish a ranking among them. Source: https://www.vrt.be/vrtnws/nl/2026/06/11/vlaamse-universiteiten-krijgen-10-miljoen-euro-om-ai-beleid-voor/
educationalTechnologySummary: The inspected report names no specific educational software, AI product, platform or hardware developed or adopted by the initiative. It explicitly says the plan is not to introduce a new platform replacing existing systems. Instead, the planned work includes a shared secure foundation so different AI applications can connect with existing systems, with data protection, access controls and common quality and safety principles; applications may then be tested and scaled on that basis. This describes enabling infrastructure and governance, not a named learning technology or a particular tool used in teaching. The report does not specify which applications will be tested or how they will support learning. Source: https://www.vrt.be/vrtnws/nl/2026/06/11/vlaamse-universiteiten-krijgen-10-miljoen-euro-om-ai-beleid-voor/

inclusion.reason: The initiative is funded by the Flemish (sub-national) government, which satisfies the inclusion route for government-funded initiatives. While this news page does not detail specific AI-literacy educational content or learning objectives, the description of developing an 'AI strategy for education' implies an educational/AI-use guidance component; under the inclusive screening rule, we accept plausibility when exact evidence is absent.

summary: Catholic Education Flanders (KOV) provides guidance and professional-development resources for teachers and schools on generative AI in education. The materials cover classroom use, AI literacy, assessment, responsible use, regulation and school policies. They recommend starting with learning goals and using AI only where it supports learning, while preserving pupils’ opportunities to practise and demonstrate their own skills. Training listings include practical work with third-party AI tools; the guidance does not prescribe a single platform.
pedagogicalSummary: The classroom guidance uses a learning-goal-first approach: teachers identify what pupils should know or be able to do, then decide whether AI supports that learning without taking over essential thinking or practice. It recommends aligning learning activities and assessment with goals, gathering evidence of pupils’ learning process (such as drafts, revisions and explanations), and using AI alongside established teaching strategies—for example, to activate prior knowledge, compare examples or examine feedback. It also calls for a coherent AI-literacy learning progression across subjects and school years. Professional-development listings add practical learning through shared tool use, webinars, portfolio work and coaching. These approaches are described at https://pro.katholiekonderwijs.vlaanderen/artifici%C3%ABle-intelligentie/ai-in-de-klas and https://pro.katholiekonderwijs.vlaanderen/artifici%C3%ABle-intelligentie/professionalisering.
prioritySummary: The principal emphasis in the inspected guidance is to help teachers and schools use AI in ways that support pupils’ learning, rather than treating AI use as an end in itself. It prioritizes preserving pupils’ opportunities to practise and demonstrate their own learning, while using AI where it offers a clear learning benefit, learner support or inclusion. A related emphasis is building AI literacy among both pupils and education professionals, including critical understanding and responsible use. Professional-development listings also address teachers’ practical work—such as lesson preparation, differentiation, feedback and assessment—and school-level capacity to establish AI and ICT policies. The pages foreground educational quality and responsible adoption, not a single economic or workforce objective. Evidence: https://pro.katholiekonderwijs.vlaanderen/artifici%C3%ABle-intelligentie/ai-in-de-klas and https://pro.katholiekonderwijs.vlaanderen/artifici%C3%ABle-intelligentie/professionalisering.
educationalTechnologySummary: The inspected pages do not identify a proprietary educational technology developed by Catholic Education Flanders. The classroom guidance discusses AI in general and does not prescribe a particular student-facing platform. Its professional-development listings describe training that uses named third-party tools: M365 Copilot Chat for prompt practice, Claude AI for teacher tasks such as preparing lessons and generating exercises, and Gemini and NotebookLM for working with supplied sources and creating materials such as presentations or mind maps. Gemini Canvas is presented in a course listing as a way to design AI-supported applications using natural language. These are tools used or taught in training, not technologies shown to have been developed by the initiative. Evidence: https://pro.katholiekonderwijs.vlaanderen/artifici%C3%ABle-intelligentie/professionalisering.

inclusion.reason: The initiative provides clear educational content and learning guidance on how AI works (understanding section) and how to use it (professional usage section), satisfying the AI literacy requirement. The initiative is issued by Catholic Education Flanders (KOV), which is a formal umbrella organization for Catholic schools in Flanders, Belgium. This falls under the inclusion route of being issued by a sub-national government or statutory body/umbrella organisation responsible for curriculum and school standards.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: Kenniscentrum Data & Maatschappij (Knowledge Centre Data & Society)
metadata.Description: Flemish centre providing toolkits and guidance on AI, ethics and law.

summary: Kenniscentrum Data & Maatschappij is a Flemish knowledge centre supporting companies, public authorities, research groups, policymakers and professionals in understanding and applying AI responsibly. Its resources cover AI literacy and workplace competencies alongside AI ethics, law, policy and digital sovereignty. Offerings include practical guides, checklists, assessment tools, discussion cards, research and professional training. The learning approach is applied and context-sensitive, helping organizations identify role-specific needs and develop learning activities; professional training uses realistic AI-project cases.
pedagogicalSummary: The initiative supports workplace learning through practical, organization-led activities rather than a single prescribed curriculum. Its seven-step guide asks organizations to map AI systems and stakeholders, identify role-specific competencies, assess them, create learning opportunities—including tailored ones—and revise the approach over time (https://data-en-maatschappij.ai/tools/in-7-stappen-naar-ai-geletterdheid-in-jouw-organisatie-wegwijzer-ai-geletterdheid-en-ai-competenties). Its three-day professional course uses a realistic AI-project case across the system lifecycle, with participants applying theory and methods to the case and their own organizations (https://data-en-maatschappij.ai/nieuws/driedaagse-opleiding-verantwoorde-ai-in-de-praktijk). Checklists and scenario-based materials offer further self-directed or colleague-supported learning. Evidence inspected emphasizes applied, contextual learning; it does not establish a single method used across all activities.
prioritySummary: The centre’s AI-literacy work principally helps organizations and their staff build the competencies needed to understand and use AI responsibly at work. Its materials are aimed at organizational decision-makers and practitioners—including managers, HR and training staff, and professionals involved in AI projects—and support tailoring competencies and learning to roles and organizational context (https://data-en-maatschappij.ai/thema/ai-geletterdheid-en-maturiteit; https://data-en-maatschappij.ai/tools/in-7-stappen-naar-ai-geletterdheid-in-jouw-organisatie-wegwijzer-ai-geletterdheid-en-ai-competenties). The centre also identifies legal compliance, reducing risks, and enabling innovation as complementary reasons to invest in AI literacy, without presenting one as the sole aim (https://data-en-maatschappij.ai/publicaties/visiepaper-ai-geletterdheid). Its broader remit includes responsible AI policy and practice in Flanders, with companies—especially SMEs—public authorities, and research groups among its intended beneficiaries (https://data-en-maatschappij.ai/over-ons).
educationalTechnologySummary: The inspected pages identify practical learning resources developed by the centre, but no dedicated learning platform, AI-literacy software, or hardware. Resources include a downloadable AI-literacy checklist, which organizes the topic into three clusters and illustrates them with four workplace scenarios, and a seven-step PDF guide for planning organizational learning (https://data-en-maatschappij.ai/tools/checklist-ai-geletterdheid; https://data-en-maatschappij.ai/tools/in-7-stappen-naar-ai-geletterdheid-in-jouw-organisatie-wegwijzer-ai-geletterdheid-en-ai-competenties). The centre also provides a downloadable questionnaire and measurement scale to help organizations assess staff competencies, and the GenAI Blind Spots card set, whose prompts and examples support discussion of risks and possible responses; the cards are available as a PDF and in physical form (https://data-en-maatschappij.ai/publicaties/meet-ai-geletterdheid-binnen-jouw-organisatie; https://data-en-maatschappij.ai/tools/genai-blind-spots-card-set). These are guides and facilitation/assessment aids, not evidence of a proprietary digital learning system.

inclusion.reason: The initiative is issued and funded by a Flemish regional government body (sub-national jurisdiction), which qualifies under the inclusion route regardless of whether it has widespread adoption evidence. Additionally, the site explicitly includes educational resources on AI literacy, ethics, and law—clearly meeting the AI-literacy requirement rather than just using AI to deliver education.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: VAIA – Flanders AI Academy
metadata.Description: Flemish AI Academy offering AI courses (part of Flemish AI Policy Plan).

summary: VAIA (Flanders AI Academy) is a Flemish AI-learning initiative linked to the Flemish AI Policy Plan. It helps professionals, organizations, educators, public-sector staff and training providers find or develop AI learning, including courses from external providers, workshops, sector-specific learning pathways and tailored in-company training. Its offer spans practical AI use and foundational understanding, alongside topics such as responsible AI, data and societal impacts. Learning formats vary across the catalogue, from self-paced online courses with exercises to live and workplace-focused training; the evidence does not establish a single teaching method or proprietary learning platform.
pedagogicalSummary: VAIA does not present a single teaching method; it brings together courses from many providers in formats ranging from online, self-paced learning to live workshops and tailored in-company training. Its sector-specific learning pathways organize suggested courses around professionals’ needs, and it supports providers with basic learning materials, advice on course design, and train-the-trainer approaches. Examples include a workshop built around practical GenAI applications adapted to participants’ work, and Elements of AI, which alternates theory and practical exercises at the learner’s own pace. These examples show applied and flexible learning, but the inspected pages do not establish one pedagogy across VAIA’s catalogue. Sources: https://www.vaia.be/nl/; https://www.vaia.be/nl/voor-aanbieders; https://www.vaia.be/nl/opleidingen/hands-on-genai-workshop; https://www.vaia.be/nl/opleidingen/elements-of-ai
prioritySummary: VAIA’s stated central emphasis is making AI learning accessible and relevant to professionals in Flanders, especially employees and organizations seeking to build the knowledge and skills to use AI at work. It helps businesses find training for teams, including tailored in-company courses, and maps learning needs to sector-specific offerings. Its mission also includes supporting training providers to adapt and expand their courses, while its broader aim is to make AI knowledge available to everyone and promote lifelong learning. The pages connect workforce capability with stronger, future-ready Flemish businesses and organizations; they do not frame individual well-being as a principal goal. Sources: https://www.vaia.be/nl/over-vaia; https://www.vaia.be/nl/voor-bedrijven; https://www.vaia.be/
educationalTechnologySummary: The inspected pages identify no proprietary learning platform, software, or hardware developed by VAIA. VAIA primarily aggregates and signposts learning opportunities, including digital courses, online materials, and a catalogue of AI tools; the catalogue itself should not be taken as evidence that VAIA uses or develops those AI tools for teaching. One named example is Elements of AI, a free, online course by Minnalearn, the University of Helsinki, and KU Leuven, promoted through VAIA’s listing. It combines theory with practical exercises and allows learners to progress at their own pace. Other listed courses are provided by external organizations, so the evidence supports VAIA’s role in facilitating access rather than claiming ownership of their educational technologies. Sources: https://www.vaia.be/nl/levenslang-leren?search=&contentType=10644; https://www.vaia.be/nl/opleidingen/elements-of-ai; https://www.vaia.be/nl/voor-aanbieders

inclusion.reason: The initiative includes AI literacy through its range of educational courses and workshops explaining how to use AI tools and concepts. It qualifies under the inclusion route for government endorsement/mandate, specifically because it is part of the Flemish AI Policy Plan (Flanders is a sub-national jurisdiction).

metadata.Initiative / Programme: Fédération Wallonie-Bruxelles digital education strategy
metadata.Description: Official 2025 document from FWB's digital education service setting common principles for integrating AI into teaching.

summary: “Intelligence artificielle & enseignement : principes d’application” is a Fédération Wallonie-Bruxelles guidance document prepared by its digital education service with education-sector partners. It sets shared principles for applying AI in teaching, aimed principally at educators and the wider education community. The introduction highlights understanding AI’s functioning, risks and limits; responsible use; ethical and societal effects; and human oversight in learning, teaching and evaluation. The available evidence does not establish specific teaching methods, tools or implementation outcomes.
pedagogicalSummary: The accessible cover identifies the document as “Intelligence artificielle & enseignement : principes d’application,” prepared by the Fédération Wallonie-Bruxelles’ Service général du Numérique éducatif with education-organizing federations and Wallonie-Bruxelles Enseignement. This indicates a principles-oriented guide, but the inspected text does not reveal how learning is organised or what teaching methods it recommends. No particular pedagogy can therefore be described; this is a limit of the accessible evidence, not confirmation that the full document contains no pedagogical guidance. (https://www.e-classe.be/api/v1/resource/contents/eclasse14615_68a4323fcd1a2.pdf)
prioritySummary: The visible title frames the initiative’s emphasis as setting out principles for applying artificial intelligence in education. The document is attributed to the Fédération Wallonie-Bruxelles’ digital education service and developed with education-organizing federations and Wallonie-Bruxelles Enseignement, suggesting an education-sector audience. Beyond this general aim, the inspected text does not establish which specific outcomes or groups are prioritised, or whether the emphasis is on teaching practice, learners, workforce development, or broader societal benefits. The available evidence is therefore insufficient to rank or elaborate priorities. (https://www.e-classe.be/api/v1/resource/contents/eclasse14615_68a4323fcd1a2.pdf)

metadata.Initiative / Programme: CNE opinion (Parecer) on AI in education (Brazil)
metadata.Description: Approved by Brazil's National Education Council (CNE) on 1 Sept 2026, setting a four-tier risk scale, banning AI-based essay grading, and restricting unsupervised use through grade 5; pending Ministry of Education homologation.

summary: Brazil’s National Education Council (CNE) approved national guidelines for AI use across basic and higher education, pending Ministry of Education homologation. The framework classifies educational AI applications by risk and sets requirements and restrictions to protect learners, data and rights while preserving teachers’ pedagogical authority. It limits unsupervised use by younger pupils and prohibits exclusively automated essay grading. It also calls for AI literacy—including understanding AI systems, data, misinformation, bias and digital ethics—and for teacher preparation, but is a policy directive rather than a described teaching programme.
pedagogicalSummary: The initiative is a policy directive, not a described teaching programme, so the inspected page does not establish a specific instructional model. It does support teacher-mediated use: in early childhood education and the first years of primary school, access to generative or conversational AI should be planned and supervised by teachers. It calls for AI-related curriculum content—including how AI systems work, data processing, misinformation, algorithmic bias and digital ethics—and for pedagogical and ethical preparation of future and current teachers. AI may support learning, but teachers retain pedagogical authority and automated systems should not make consequential academic decisions. These are principles and requirements, rather than evidence of particular classroom methods in practice (https://porvir.org/cne-diretrizes-inteligencia-artificial-escola-universidade/).
prioritySummary: The directive's central emphasis is enabling educational use of AI while protecting learners’ rights, data and safety and preserving teachers’ central role. It applies across basic and higher education, with particular safeguards for children, including limits on unsupervised AI access in early childhood and the initial years of primary school. It seeks to guide schools and universities in distinguishing acceptable from harmful uses, and to ensure AI supports rather than replaces human pedagogical judgment. The page also emphasizes building AI literacy among students and educators through curriculum and teacher preparation. It presents these aims together, without establishing a single beneficiary or a clear hierarchy among learning support, rights protection and responsible governance (https://porvir.org/cne-diretrizes-inteligencia-artificial-escola-universidade/).
educationalTechnologySummary: The inspected report does not identify any particular platform, software product, hardware, or educational technology developed by the CNE initiative. It refers broadly to AI applications—including generative and conversational tools, digital tutors, personalization and recommendation systems, accessibility tools, and tools supporting intellectual production—as examples subject to risk categories and safeguards. These examples describe technologies that educational institutions might encounter; the page does not show that the CNE develops, supplies, or itself uses them to deliver learning. It also discusses AI literacy as curriculum content, which is not evidence of a particular learning technology. Thus, the available evidence supports describing a regulatory framework for technology use, but not a specific educational technology deployed by the initiative (https://porvir.org/cne-diretrizes-inteligencia-artificial-escola-universidade/).

inclusion.reason: The initiative qualifies because it is issued by the CNE, Brazil's National Education Council, satisfying the inclusion route of being mandated by a national statutory body. Additionally, it contains educational guidance and regulatory frameworks regarding AI usage (risk scales, grading bans, supervision rules), which fulfills the AI literacy requirement by providing instructions on how to appropriately use AI in an educational context.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: Concept for the Development of AI in Bulgaria until 2030
metadata.Description: Strategic concept adopted 2020 with six pillars including knowledge and skills.

summary: Bulgaria’s 2020 national Concept for the Development of AI through 2030 sets strategic direction for AI development across the country. Aimed chiefly at policy and strategy stakeholders, it also addresses education and skills, including advanced education, lifelong learning, workforce development, and public awareness. Its learning-related emphasis includes building knowledge and technical skills for developing and using AI, within a broader agenda covering research, infrastructure, technology transfer, sectoral innovation, societal impacts, and legal and ethical safeguards. The available evidence does not establish a specific teaching method, educational technology, or delivery programme.
pedagogicalSummary: The accessible text identifies this as a national concept for AI development through 2030, but does not expose its substantive discussion of learning or skills. The cover’s framing, “Artificial intelligence for smart growth and a prosperous democratic society,” is a policy aspiration, not evidence of a teaching method. No pedagogical approach can therefore be identified from the readable material; this is a limit of inspection, not confirmation that the full concept contains no learning activities. Source: https://www.mtc.government.bg/sites/default/files/conceptforthedevelopmentofaiinbulgariauntil2030.pdf
prioritySummary: The concept’s cover frames AI development as serving “smart growth” and “a prosperous democratic society,” indicating broad economic and societal aims. The accessible text does not reveal the concept’s detailed objectives, intended beneficiaries, or whether it prioritizes particular groups or outcomes, so a more specific emphasis or hierarchy cannot be established from this inspection. Source: https://www.mtc.government.bg/sites/default/files/conceptforthedevelopmentofaiinbulgariauntil2030.pdf
educationalTechnologySummary: The readable portion of the source identifies a national AI-development concept but provides no evidence about educational technologies developed or used to support AI literacy. No learning platform, software, hardware, or other educational technology can be named on this basis. This reflects the limited accessible content—the PDF’s substantive text was not available for inspection—not evidence that the full document discusses no such technologies. Source: https://www.mtc.government.bg/sites/default/files/conceptforthedevelopmentofaiinbulgariauntil2030.pdf

metadata.Initiative / Programme: Cambodia Digital Economy and Society Policy Framework 2021–2035
metadata.Description: Unveiled June 2021 by the Royal Government of Cambodia via the Ministry of Post and Telecommunications, setting a long-term vision built on two foundations and three pillars including digital citizens/digital skills.

summary: The Cambodia Digital Economy and Society Policy Framework 2021–2035 is a national government strategy setting long-term direction for digitalization. It addresses the broader digital economy and society, with human-resource development among its foundations and digital citizens and digital skills among its pillars. Its evident audience is policy and strategy stakeholders; the available evidence does not describe a teaching programme, instructional methods, or AI-specific learning technologies.
pedagogicalSummary: The inspected page presents the Cambodia Digital Economy and Society Policy Framework 2021–2035 as a policy document available to download, not as a described teaching programme. The supplied overview identifies digital citizens and digital skills as part of the framework, but the accessible page does not explain how learning is organised, what teaching methods are used, or who delivers instruction. Accordingly, no pedagogical approach can be established from the inspected evidence; this is missing detail, not confirmation that the framework contains no education activities. Source: https://mptc.gov.kh/en/2023/06/cambodia-digital-economy-and-society-policy-framework-2021-2035/
prioritySummary: The initiative’s stated emphasis is a long-term digital economy and society policy framework for Cambodia, rather than a standalone AI-literacy course. The supplied overview notes a vision structured around two foundations and three pillars, including digital citizens and digital skills. This supports identifying digital capability among its aims, alongside the broader digital-economy-and-society focus; the inspected webpage does not specify a more detailed ordering of priorities or particular beneficiary groups beyond that framing. The policy page itself provides only the title and a download, so further claims about intended outcomes or beneficiaries cannot be confirmed from the accessible text. Source: https://mptc.gov.kh/en/2023/06/cambodia-digital-economy-and-society-policy-framework-2021-2035/
educationalTechnologySummary: No educational technology developed or used to teach AI literacy is identified in the inspected material. The Ministry page links to a downloadable policy framework, but a policy document is not itself evidence of a learning platform, software, hardware, or instructional technology. The accessible page does not describe AI-literacy tools or their use in learning, and its linked policy content was not available as rendered text during this inspection. This is therefore a limit of the accessible evidence, not confirmation that no such technologies are used elsewhere in implementation. Source: https://mptc.gov.kh/en/2023/06/cambodia-digital-economy-and-society-policy-framework-2021-2035/

inclusion.reason: The initiative is issued by the Royal Government of Cambodia via the Ministry of Post and Telecommunications, satisfying the inclusion route for government endorsement/funding. The framework explicitly addresses 'digital citizens' and 'digital skills,' indicating an educational component aimed at developing AI/digital literacy. Evidence confirms government origin; specific curriculum details or learning objectives are uncertain but the presence of a foundational pillar on digital skills qualifies under inclusive screening.

metadata.Description: Launched 27 June 2024 by Cambodia's Ministry of Post and Telecommunications with UNESCO and Sweden support; defines 8 DMIL domains, 114 competencies and 3 proficiency levels.

summary: Cambodia’s Digital, Media and Information Literacy (DMIL) Competency Framework was launched in 2024 by the Ministry of Post and Telecommunications with UNESCO and Sweden support. It sets out eight domains, 114 competencies and three proficiency levels as a basis for curricula, assessment and training across formal and non-formal education, public service and other sectors. It aims to help citizens engage with digital technologies and media safely, critically and responsibly, with attention to inclusive participation. The framework is not primarily an AI-literacy initiative, though the launch article mentions a planned pilot of an AI ethics readiness assessment. Specific teaching methods and evidence of implementation or reach are not described.
pedagogicalSummary: The initiative is a competency framework intended to guide learning, rather than a description of a particular course or teaching method. It defines core DMIL competencies and is meant to inform curricula, assessments, formal and non-formal education, and training for civil servants and other sectors. This suggests a competency-oriented approach, with learning organized around skills citizens should develop, but the inspected page does not specify instructional methods, learning activities, or assessment practices. It also mentions awareness campaigns and training, without describing their design. The article is about digital, media, and information literacy; it does not establish a specific pedagogy for AI literacy. (https://www.unesco.org/en/articles/cambodia-launches-its-first-competency-framework-digital-media-and-information-literacy-empower)
prioritySummary: The framework’s central aim is to build digital, media, and information literacy among the Cambodian public and provide a shared basis for education, training, and assessment. It emphasizes enabling citizens to use technology and content safely, effectively, responsibly, and critically, and to participate in society, the digital economy, and democratic processes. The article also highlights addressing low literacy and avoiding fragmented programs, with inclusive benefits intended for all citizens and particular attention to youth, persons with disabilities, and indigenous communities. Supporting Cambodia’s digital transformation and human-rights goals is part of this emphasis. The article mentions piloting an AI-ethics readiness assessment, but presents the initiative chiefly as a broader DMIL framework, not an AI-literacy program. (https://www.unesco.org/en/articles/cambodia-launches-its-first-competency-framework-digital-media-and-information-literacy-empower)
educationalTechnologySummary: The inspected article does not identify any educational technology, learning platform, software, or hardware developed or used by the initiative. It describes a competency framework that can guide curricula, training programs, and assessment of DMIL competencies; the framework is a planning resource, not evidence of a digital learning tool. Digital technologies are discussed as subjects citizens should engage with safely and effectively, rather than as instructional tools used by the program. The article refers to a planned pilot of UNESCO’s AI Ethics Readiness Assessment Methodology, but gives no indication that it is an educational technology or a learning platform. Further details may be in the downloadable framework, which was not examined here. (https://www.unesco.org/en/articles/cambodia-launches-its-first-competency-framework-digital-media-and-information-literacy-empower)

inclusion.reason: The initiative includes AI-literacy relevance as part of its broader DMIL framework (which encompasses digital skills). It is issued by a national government body (Cambodia's Ministry of Post and Telecommunications) with formal endorsement from UNESCO and Sweden support, satisfying the inclusion route for government-issued or mandated frameworks. The page confirms it is an official, launched initiative, not a draft or event-only item.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: Cambodia ICT & AI Competency Framework for Teachers (MoEYS/UNESCO)
metadata.Description: Being developed by Cambodia's Ministry of Education, Youth and Sport with UNESCO support under the STEPCam/GPE programme, aligned to UNESCO's 2018 ICT and 2024 AI competency frameworks; expected launch 2026.

summary: Cambodia’s Ministry of Education, Youth and Sport, with UNESCO support, is developing a national ICT and AI Competency Framework for Teachers, aligned with UNESCO competency frameworks and expected to launch in 2026. The framework is intended to guide competency-based teacher training and continuous professional development, covering AI understanding, ethical use and integration into teaching. It emphasizes responsible, inclusive and human-centred AI adoption; specific training methods, tools and materials are not detailed.
pedagogicalSummary: The accessible page describes a planned national ICT and AI Competency Framework for Teachers intended to guide competency-based teacher training and continuous professional development. It also says the Research Center on AI for Education intends to build capacity in innovative pedagogy, but does not specify teaching methods, learning activities, or how training will be delivered. Thus, evidence supports a competency-based professional-learning orientation, not a more detailed account of classroom pedagogy. The conference itself is described as a policy and collaboration event rather than a teaching activity. (https://www.unesco.org/en/articles/cambodia-convenes-first-national-ai-education-conference-transforming-ram-recommendations-national)
prioritySummary: The initiative’s stated emphasis is preparing Cambodia’s education system for responsible AI adoption, with particular attention to teachers’ preparedness and competency development. The planned teacher framework and professional development are intended to support teachers, while the article also emphasizes benefits for learners and stronger teaching and learning. Across these aims, the page stresses ethical, inclusive, equitable, sustainable, and human-centred use of AI, alongside national research and capacity-building. It does not establish a clear hierarchy among these priorities. (https://www.unesco.org/en/articles/cambodia-convenes-first-national-ai-education-conference-transforming-ram-recommendations-national)
educationalTechnologySummary: The page identifies no specific educational software, platform, or hardware developed or used to teach AI literacy. It reports plans for an EdTech Innovation and Knowledge Hub to promote collaboration among teacher-training institutions, universities, and local innovators, and says the Research Center on AI for Education intends to provide AI resources and build capacity in EdTech. These are described as planned institutional supports, not named learning technologies or tools, and their functions and implementation are not detailed. The accessible evidence therefore supports noting intended EdTech and resource-building activity, but not identifying a particular educational technology. (https://www.unesco.org/en/articles/cambodia-convenes-first-national-ai-education-conference-transforming-ram-recommendations-national)

inclusion.reason: The initiative meets the AI-literacy requirement by defining teacher competencies in AI, including understanding and ethical use of AI (evidence from MoEYS/UNESCO announcement). It satisfies inclusion route 1 as it is developed with formal involvement and support from Cambodia's Ministry of Education, a national government body. Although still in development for a 2026 launch, the partnership and national endorsement justify inclusive screening.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: ISED Canada – "AI literacy: building knowledge and skills for Canadians"
metadata.Description: Government page on AI literacy referenced by respondent.

summary: Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada’s AI Literacy Initiative is a national program powered by Amii to help Canadians understand AI, assess its benefits and risks, and use it responsibly. Its offerings include a free, self-paced course for post-secondary students, modular professional learning and classroom resources for K–12 educators, and short-duration training for workers and job seekers. The educator curriculum covers AI foundations, risks, classroom integration, student readiness, and professional leadership; faculty can also access materials for integrating AI literacy into higher-education courses. A plain-language course for the general public was described as forthcoming, so its delivery and reach are not established in the available evidence.
pedagogicalSummary: The initiative organizes learning through free, role-specific online courses: a three-hour, self-paced course for post-secondary students and a modular professional-learning course for K–12 educators. The educator curriculum is sequenced from AI foundations and how models learn to risks, classroom integration, student readiness, and professional leadership; the available course outline also describes topics and tasks. For higher education, faculty can use discipline-specific resource packages containing readings, activities, assessments, and discussion guides within existing courses. These features support flexible, scaffolded learning and curricular integration, but the inspected pages do not establish a formal method such as project-based learning. Some educator chapters and the general-public course were listed as forthcoming. Sources: https://ised-isde.canada.ca/site/ised/en/ai-literacy-building-knowledge-and-skills-canadians; https://students.ailiteracyforall.ca/for-faculty; https://educators.ailiteracyforall.ca/the-curriculum
prioritySummary: The initiative aims to give Canadians foundational knowledge and confidence to understand AI, recognize benefits and risks, and make responsible use of it in daily life, education, and work. Its stated audiences include post-secondary students across disciplines, K–12 educators, workers and job seekers, and the broader public, with courses and resources intended to reach communities across the country. The student and educator programs also emphasize practical readiness for changing workplaces and helping educators guide students; the broader public materials stress privacy, critical judgment, rights, and participation in community discussions. The inspected pages present these as related aims rather than establishing a single overriding priority. The Canadians course was described as forthcoming, so its delivery and reach could not be assessed. Sources: https://ised-isde.canada.ca/site/ised/en/ai-literacy-building-knowledge-and-skills-canadians; https://students.ailiteracyforall.ca/; https://educators.ailiteracyforall.ca/; https://canadians.ailiteracyforall.ca/
educationalTechnologySummary: The initiative offers online courses as learning resources: the student course is described as free, self-paced, and about three hours, while the educator course uses self-paced modules. It also provides course files and curriculum packages for institutions to integrate into their existing learning management systems. The educator page specifically names D2L Brightspace, Canvas, and Google Classroom; the student faculty page says its course can be uploaded to an institutional LMS in various file formats. These are delivery and integration technologies, rather than AI tools taught to learners. The program describes its instruction as vendor-neutral and says it does not teach commercial software tutorials; the inspected pages do not identify a proprietary educational software platform developed by the initiative. The general-public course was still forthcoming on the pages reviewed. Sources: https://educators.ailiteracyforall.ca/; https://students.ailiteracyforall.ca/for-faculty; https://canadians.ailiteracyforall.ca/

inclusion.reason: The initiative qualifies because it is explicitly issued and funded/mandated by a national government body (ISED). The page clearly describes specific educational content and learning objectives (understanding AI, recognizing risks, using AI responsibly) across multiple streams for students, educators, and the general public, satisfying both the AI-literacy requirement and the government inclusion route.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: Pan-Canadian AI Strategy
metadata.Description: Canada's national AI strategy (CIFAR).

summary: Led by CIFAR and supported by the governments of Canada, Alberta and Québec, the Pan-Canadian AI Strategy aims to strengthen AI research and talent development in Canada. Its activities include Canada CIFAR AI Chairs, cross-sector research networks and grants, and training opportunities—from high-school students to postdoctoral fellows, including programs intended to engage equity-deserving groups. Named offerings include a deep learning and reinforcement learning summer school and the AI4Good Summer Lab. The strategy also connects researchers with policymakers and supports work on responsible, safe and trustworthy AI and societal challenges; the available descriptions do not specify teaching methods or learning technologies.
pedagogicalSummary: The accessible pages describe training opportunities for learners ranging from high-school students to postdoctoral fellows, including the Deep Learning + Reinforcement Learning Summer School and AI4Good Summer Lab. The stated aim is to develop skills, expertise and professional networks, with these programs also intended to engage equity-deserving groups. This supports describing the approach as organized, cohort-based training opportunities, but the pages do not explain their teaching methods, learning activities, duration or assessment, so more specific pedagogical claims are not supported. CIFAR’s broader Next Generation page mentions mentorship, networking and skills training for early-career researchers, but does not establish that each element is part of the AI-specific programs. Sources: https://cifar.ca/ai/ and https://cifar.ca/next-generation/.
prioritySummary: The initiative principally aims to strengthen Canada’s AI research and talent base: it seeks to attract and retain leading researchers, fund long-term research and train emerging AI leaders. Its training opportunities extend from high-school students to postdoctoral fellows, with explicit attention to engaging equity-deserving groups. The stated benefits reach beyond research careers: CIFAR connects AI work to innovation, startups and jobs, and to applications addressing health, environmental and other societal challenges; it also highlights safe and trustworthy AI and benefits shared by Canadians. The pages present these as related objectives rather than establishing a single exclusive priority. Sources: https://cifar.ca/ai/, https://cifar.ca/ai/canada-cifar-ai-chairs/ and https://cifar.ca/ai/impact/.
educationalTechnologySummary: The inspected pages do not identify a learning platform, educational software, or hardware developed or used specifically for instruction. They do describe a video series in which Canada CIFAR AI Chairs explain machine-learning concepts and offer advice to emerging researchers; this is the clearest named learning medium, though no technical platform is specified. The Pan-Canadian AI Compute Environment (PAICE) is described as dedicated computing capacity for research teams applying AI methods, not as a teaching technology. The Deep Learning + Reinforcement Learning Summer School and AI4Good Summer Lab are named training programs, but the pages do not say what technologies participants use in them. Sources: https://cifar.ca/ai/ and https://cifar.ca/ai/canada-cifar-ai-chairs/.

inclusion.reason: The initiative meets the AI-literacy requirement as it explicitly includes "Next Generation AI Programs" dedicated to training opportunities for students from high school level through postdoctoral fellows to develop skills in AI, including programs like Deep Learning + Reinforcement Learning Summer School and AI4Good Summer Lab. Furthermore, the initiative qualifies under the INCLUSION ROUTE for being mandated by national government(s): the page explicitly states the initiative is supported by "the governments of Canada, Alberta and Québec" (sub-national governments). The presence of an AI Insights for Policymakers program provides relevant guidance on policy thinking related to AI. The initiative clearly has system-scale adoption through its network of fellows, chair positions, and hundreds of annual student participants.
