metadata.Initiative / Programme: CLAiRE project
metadata.Description: Project referenced by respondent.

summary: CLAiRE (Constraints-Led AI Redesign for Education) is a project supporting higher-education educators and institutions in integrating AI into curricula through the Constraints-Led Approach, which considers interactions among learners, tasks, and environments. It aims to develop students’ AI literacy alongside disciplinary and professional knowledge, encouraging critical and ethical use through authentic AI-enabled activities. Educator resources include planning worksheets and workshop materials, while the CLAiRE beta app supports learning-activity and assessment design and curriculum mapping. Available evidence describes the intended approach and resources but provides limited detail on implementation and outcomes.
pedagogicalSummary: CLAiRE frames its pedagogy around the Constraints-Led Approach (CLA): learning is treated as emerging from interactions among learner, task, and environment. Educators act as coaches, progressively adjusting factors such as AI access, task complexity, and ethical or institutional conditions. Students engage in authentic, AI-enabled activities intended to reflect disciplinary practice, with AI literacy developing alongside subject expertise. The project emphasizes applying this approach to whole-programme curriculum design, and its resources page offers teaching materials and planning worksheets for educators. These descriptions indicate an adaptive, practice-oriented approach, rather than simply teaching about AI tools. The accessible pages describe the intended model but provide limited detail about specific classroom implementations or evaluated outcomes (https://constraintsledai.org/; https://constraintsledai.org/resources/).
prioritySummary: The initiative principally aims to help higher-education educators and institutions redesign curricula for a context in which AI is part of learning and work. It seeks to build students’ AI literacy alongside disciplinary and professional knowledge, standards, and values, and describes AI use as critical and ethical rather than banned or added as an afterthought. The project says it works with educators, students, and professional bodies, and its research page identifies students, educators, and administrators as perspectives in exploring AI’s possibilities and challenges. The available evidence therefore points to curriculum and educational practice as the central emphasis, with benefits intended for students and the higher-education community; it does not establish a separate workforce-training or individual-well-being priority (https://constraintsledai.org/; https://constraintsledai.org/research/).
educationalTechnologySummary: The project offers the CLAiRE App, described on its site as a live beta, as a digital aid for educators. Its interface offers learning-activity design informed by CLA, assessment design using CLA and named approaches, curriculum mapping, and a question-and-answer option about CLA and AI in assessment. The app says its suggestions are informed by educational research and should be reviewed and adapted to context. The project also links educator resources, including planning worksheets and a guide to building a custom CLAiRE app. These pages identify the app and materials but do not specify the software or AI model behind the app, nor provide enough detail to establish how the custom assistants are implemented. The website itself is not treated here as a learning technology (https://constraintsledai.org/claire-app/; https://claireapp.constraintsledai.org/; https://constraintsledai.org/resources/).

inclusion.reason: The initiative includes explicit AI-literacy guidance: it teaches educators and students how to use AI by applying the Constraints-Led AI (CLA) framework—a pedagogical approach that explains how to design and build AI tools with human-centered constraints. This satisfies the AI-literacy requirement as it offers learning content about using and understanding AI, not just delivering education via AI. Regarding inclusion routes, the initiative shows evidence of wider reach beyond a single institution, including cross-disciplinary applications in nursing, medicine, and law mentioned on its resources page, and it provides open educational materials (toolkit, guides, workshop resources) that suggest system-scale or multi-institution adoption. While specific government endorsement is not explicitly detailed on the homepage, the initiative’s open toolkit format, cross-institutional references, and structured pedagogical framework align with non-government work demonstrating plausible wider reach rather than a single-institution project, thus qualifying under inclusion.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: ETF DARYA project – SCAFFOLD guide
metadata.Description: European Training Foundation project on skills and VET in Central Asia.

summary: DARYA is an EU-funded European Training Foundation project supporting education and training systems in five Central Asian countries, with a focus on vocational education, skills development and young people’s transitions to work. It works with educators and other system stakeholders through teacher training, peer learning and teaching resources. Its SCAFFOLD card deck supports educators in planning and testing inclusive, flexible and collaborative approaches, including project-, problem- and work-based learning. The broader skills agenda also covers digital, green and entrepreneurial competencies; the supplied evidence does not describe AI-specific learning content.
pedagogicalSummary: The inspected pages describe a competence-focused VET approach, not an AI-literacy curriculum. DARYA’s teaching-and-learning module promotes inclusive, flexible and outcome-oriented learning, including project- and problem-based collaborative and authentic learning, work-based learning, and continuous professional development for teachers. It supports this through teacher training, adapted teaching materials, and networks for sharing methods. SCAFFOLD is used as a coaching and teaching-practice resource: educators receive training, explore its card deck, and develop and test lesson plans, with peer-learning opportunities to exchange practices. The pages do not establish that these activities teach AI literacy specifically. (https://www.etf.europa.eu/en/what-we-do/darya-dialogue-and-action-resourceful-youth-central-asia/module-3; https://www.etf.europa.eu/en/media-centre/events/darya-scaffold-national-training-trainers-kazakhstan; https://www.etf.europa.eu/en/media-centre/newsroom/scaffold-pedagogical-practices-competition-first-winners-announced)
prioritySummary: DARYA principally aims to strengthen education, training and employment systems in five Central Asian countries so young people can gain inclusive, adaptable, labour-market-relevant skills and better employment prospects. Its emphasis includes improving VET teaching and qualifications, anticipating skills needs, and supporting transitions from education to work. It also seeks system capacity and cooperation among national authorities, educators and other stakeholders, while addressing inclusion and gender-sensitive guidance. The pages frame digital, green and entrepreneurial competencies as parts of a broader skills agenda; they do not identify AI literacy as a specific priority. (https://www.etf.europa.eu/en/what-we-do/darya-dialogue-and-action-resourceful-youth-central-asia; https://www.etf.europa.eu/en/what-we-do/darya-dialogue-and-action-resourceful-youth-central-asia/module-3; https://www.etf.europa.eu/en/what-we-do/darya-dialogue-and-action-resourceful-youth-central-asia/thematic-modules/evidence-skills)
educationalTechnologySummary: The inspected material identifies no AI educational technology or AI product used or developed by DARYA. For broader teaching support, it describes SCAFFOLD as a card deck used by educators to plan teaching practices and as a coaching resource; the pages document its use and training, but do not clearly establish who originally developed the deck. The teaching module also says DARYA will adapt the ETF’s SELFIE self-assessment tool to monitor digital, green and entrepreneurial approaches to learning. Separately, the skills module identifies an online Skills Anticipation and Matching e-Toolkit, described as a training programme for skills anticipation and labour-market intelligence. These support VET teaching and skills planning, not AI-literacy learning specifically. (https://www.etf.europa.eu/en/media-centre/events/darya-scaffold-forum-webinar-1-peer-learning; https://www.etf.europa.eu/en/what-we-do/darya-dialogue-and-action-resourceful-youth-central-asia/module-3; https://www.etf.europa.eu/en/what-we-do/darya-dialogue-and-action-resourceful-youth-central-asia/thematic-modules/evidence-skills)

inclusion.reason: The initiative is funded by the European Union via the European Training Foundation, which qualifies under the inclusion route of being funded/endorsed by a supranational governmental body (the EU). The project focuses on skills development and VET but there is no specific mention of AI literacy content, educational materials about AI, or learning objectives regarding AI in the description. However, given the inclusion criteria allow for government funding alone to qualify for this route alongside AI literacy requirements, we must determine if AI literacy is present. Since no AI-specific elements are mentioned in the available information, and the requirement explicitly states the initiative must include AI literacy (educational content, learning objectives, or guidance about how AI works or how to use it), and no such content is evident on this project page, the AI-literacy requirement appears absent. The inclusion route through EU funding does not substitute for missing AI literacy content. Therefore, despite being government-funded (EU), without evidence of AI literacy components, this initiative should be excluded as it fails the core AI-literacy requirement necessary for inclusion in an AI-literacy initiative review.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: China "AI + Education" action plan
metadata.Description: Joint notice issued 10 April 2026 by the Ministry of Education and four other bodies mandating AI integration across all education stages by 2030.

summary: China’s “AI + Education” Action Plan is a national policy initiative, issued by the Ministry of Education and other government bodies, to integrate AI across education by 2030. It addresses learners from early education through higher, vocational and continuing education, as well as teachers, education managers and industry partners. Its directions include developing AI literacy and specialist skills, curricula and digital resources, and training teachers. It also proposes interdisciplinary, project-based and experiential learning, personalized AI-supported study and teaching, and measures addressing ethics, safety and access. These are policy goals and proposed approaches; the documents do not establish their implementation or uptake.
pedagogicalSummary: The plan supports structured AI education across school, university, vocational and lifelong-learning settings, with stage-specific courses and curricula. It encourages interdisciplinary teaching and combines technology education with humanities, aiming to develop AI understanding, creativity, critical thinking and complex problem-solving. It also proposes practical and experiential learning through research visits, project- and inquiry-based activities, vocational practice bases, and virtual simulation experiments. Learning is intended to be personalized: student profiles and learning records can inform dynamic learning pathways, while AI tools may support independent study and feedback. Teachers are to receive role-specific training and use AI-supported preparation, instruction, assessment and professional development. These are policy directions and proposed approaches, not evidence that they are already implemented everywhere. Sources: http://www.moe.gov.cn/srcsite/A16/s3342/202604/t20260410_1433240.html ; http://www.moe.gov.cn/jyb_xwfb/s271/202604/t20260410_1433232.html
prioritySummary: The initiative’s central emphasis is broad integration of AI into education and the development of AI literacy and talent across the life course. It targets school pupils, university and vocational students, teachers, and wider groups of social learners, seeking both general AI understanding and specialist or job-relevant skills. The plan also aims to improve teaching and learning, cultivate high-quality talent for the intelligent era, and support research and education-system modernization. It highlights more individualized learning, teacher workload reduction, and improved access and inclusion, including support for rural and remote communities and learners with special educational needs. The documents present these aims together rather than establishing a single beneficiary or a clear hierarchy among them. Sources: http://www.moe.gov.cn/srcsite/A16/s3342/202604/t20260410_1433240.html ; http://www.moe.gov.cn/jyb_xwfb/s271/202604/t20260410_1433232.html
educationalTechnologySummary: The plan proposes developing and deploying several educational technologies; the inspected documents describe intended actions, not proof of widespread implementation. Named tools include intelligent learning companions for students, intelligent teaching systems to assist teachers before, during and after lessons, AI-supported assessment and feedback, and interactive virtual-simulation experiments. It also calls for education-specific large models, intelligent agents, digital learning resources, smart online courses, digital textbooks and intelligent terminals. A national education computing-service platform and upgraded national digital education platform are intended to provide infrastructure, resources and AI-enabled services. The stated learning functions include personalized resource recommendations and pathways, self-study support, simulated practice, and assistance with lesson preparation and tutoring. The documents do not identify specific commercial software or hardware products. Sources: http://www.moe.gov.cn/srcsite/A16/s3342/202604/t20260410_1433240.html ; http://www.moe.gov.cn/jyb_xwfb/s271/202604/t20260410_1433232.html

inclusion.reason: The initiative is issued by the Chinese Ministry of Education (a national government ministry), satisfying the 'Issued...by a national or sub-national government' inclusion route. It explicitly contains AI literacy requirements, including goals to cultivate comprehensive AI literacy in students to understand basic principles, technical evolution, and ethical issues; it mandates training teachers in AI knowledge and digital literacy; and it requires the development of teaching materials focused on AI applications and literacy across all education levels.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: CARNET BrAIn project
metadata.Description: CARNET-led ESF+ project (2023–2029) developing AI curricula, teacher training and an AI learning-recommendation system.

summary: CARNET BrAIn is a Croatian ESF+ project running from 2023 to 2029 that aims to strengthen digital competencies among students and teachers in secondary and higher education. Its planned work includes developing AI curricula, educational content and teacher training, alongside a smart recommendation system to support personalized learning. The project also proposes research into digital technologies’ effects on education and systems to support the security and availability of digital educational services; implementation details and current uptake are not specified.
pedagogicalSummary: The project describes a personalized approach to learning and teaching, supported by curriculum development and digital educational content in emerging digital technologies. It also proposes ongoing research to monitor how digital technologies affect education and to strengthen students’ and teachers’ digital competencies. The page does not specify classroom activities, teaching methods, or how the curricula and content will be delivered, so the evidence supports these broad design aims but not a more detailed pedagogical model. (https://www.carnet.hr/en/projekt/brain/)
prioritySummary: BrAIn principally aims to improve the quality and duration of students’ educational experiences through digital technologies, while developing students’ and teachers’ digital competencies. A further stated priority is more personalized student development, using a recommendation system intended to provide better insight into student achievement. The project also addresses the availability and sustainable management of digitized educational services, including network and cybersecurity systems. The page identifies these as objectives but does not establish a hierarchy among them. (https://www.carnet.hr/en/projekt/brain/)
educationalTechnologySummary: The project page identifies a smart recommendation system as a technology to be developed: it is intended to give better insight into students’ achievements and support a personalized approach to each student’s development. It also describes an automated monitoring and management system for network and cybersecurity, intended to help maintain the availability of digitized educational services; this is infrastructure support rather than a specified teaching tool. The inspected page names no learning platform, software product, hardware, or AI tool used in instruction, and does not provide implementation details or indicate that the proposed systems are already in use. (https://www.carnet.hr/en/projekt/brain/)

inclusion.reason: The website confirms the initiative is explicitly funded under ESF+ by Croatian authorities (national-level public funding), satisfying the government-inclusion route. The project’s stated outputs—curricula and teacher training focused on AI—are clearly educational content addressing how to use AI and build AI skills, meeting the AI-literacy requirement.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: Cyprus National AI Strategy
metadata.Description: 2026 government strategy with eight strategic objectives incl. AI skills and talent development.

summary: Cyprus’s National AI Strategy 2032 is a government roadmap for developing national AI capability and guiding adoption across public services and business. Its eight strategic objectives include AI skills and talent development, with an ambition to raise digital and AI skills nationally. In education, reported plans include school-readiness assessments, teacher training and a supervised pilot before any wider classroom rollout; the available descriptions do not specify a curriculum or teaching method. The strategy also addresses workforce development, responsible AI use and public-sector capacity.
pedagogicalSummary: The inspected pages do not describe a specific teaching method or curriculum for AI literacy. They do indicate that classroom AI adoption would be preceded by school-readiness assessments and teacher training, and tested in a supervised 12-month school pilot before decisions about wider rollout or pedagogical validation. Existing education bodies are to provide pedagogical oversight. These are preparation and evaluation arrangements, not evidence of a particular classroom pedagogy; details of what or how pupils would learn are not provided. (https://www.kiprinform.com/en/news/cyprus-approves-national-ai-strategy-2032-but-funding-amounts-and-delivery-timelines-remain-undefined/)
prioritySummary: The strategy’s broad emphasis is to build Cyprus’s national AI capability and sovereignty while using AI to improve public services and strengthen economic competitiveness, with the ambition of becoming a trusted Eastern Mediterranean AI hub. For AI literacy specifically, the reported target is to place Cyprus among Europe’s top ten countries for digital and AI skills by 2032. The pages also describe teacher training for possible classroom rollout and staff training to help businesses—especially smaller firms—adopt AI. Benefits are therefore presented for the public sector, businesses and the wider population, though the inspected coverage does not explain the skills programme’s content or establish a more specific beneficiary hierarchy. (https://www.kiprinform.com/en/news/cyprus-unveils-national-ai-strategy-2032/; https://www.kiprinform.com/en/news/cyprus-approves-national-ai-strategy-2032-but-funding-amounts-and-delivery-timelines-remain-undefined/)
educationalTechnologySummary: The inspected pages name no dedicated educational platform, learning software, or hardware developed or used by the initiative. The approved strategy is reported to support open-source AI models and platforms for public-sector and mission-critical use, but the article does not identify these as educational tools. It describes possible AI use in classrooms only at a general level, alongside school-readiness checks, teacher training, and a supervised pilot; it gives no product names or account of how AI would support learning. Multilingual AI assistants are also proposed for public services, not identified as learning technologies. These limits reflect the accessible reporting, rather than confirmation that no education technology is specified elsewhere in the strategy. (https://www.kiprinform.com/en/news/cyprus-approves-national-ai-strategy-2032-but-funding-amounts-and-delivery-timelines-remain-undefined/; https://www.kiprinform.com/en/news/cyprus-unveils-national-ai-strategy-2032/)

inclusion.reason: The initiative qualifies for inclusion because it is issued and supported by the national government of Cyprus (a sub-national jurisdiction equivalent to a state/province), meeting the inclusion route for government endorsement. The strategy explicitly includes objectives related to AI skills and talent development, which provides the required educational component on how to use AI or develop AI literacy. The URL indicates this is an official government announcement rather than a single-institution project.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: "Jak na AI ve škole" methodological guidance
metadata.Description: National Pedagogical Institute recommendations and AI resource hub for teachers on responsible use of AI in schools.

summary: “Jak na AI ve škole” is guidance from the Czech National Pedagogical Institute for using AI in primary and secondary schools. It offers practical recommendations for school leaders, teachers, pupils, and parents, emphasizing purposeful, responsible use rather than blanket adoption or prohibition. It encourages students to experiment with AI while checking outputs against reliable sources, and addresses privacy, children’s rights, fairness, misinformation, and assessment. For teachers, it recommends professional learning and considering AI for individualized learning and teaching. The guidance favors discussion and learner activity but does not prescribe a detailed curriculum; an editable template supports local adaptation.
pedagogicalSummary: The guidance favors exploratory, learner-active approaches: students are encouraged to experiment with AI tools, formulate questions, use AI to clarify or extend learning, and check its answers against sources. Teachers are urged to develop critical evaluation, source verification, and responsible use, and to consider AI for individualized tasks and assessment, including inclusive learning. Learning is also supported through open discussion, shared rule-setting, and professional development such as workshops, training, and peer mentoring. These are recommendations rather than a detailed curriculum or prescribed teaching sequence. This summary is based on the inspected guidance PDF; no linked teaching materials were available there to clarify implementation (https://digitalizace.rvp.cz/files/ai-doporuceni-online-a4.pdf).
prioritySummary: The initiative’s central emphasis is helping primary and secondary schools integrate AI purposefully and responsibly, for the benefit of students, teachers, and the wider school community. It presents AI literacy and effective learning as important goals, including using AI to support individualized learning and students’ development while preparing them for a changing future. It also emphasizes equitable access and inclusion, teacher capacity, student agency, privacy and children’s rights, and accountability for AI-assisted work. The document advocates neither blanket adoption nor prohibition, but informed use balanced with essential human skills and well-being. These priorities come from the inspected recommendations; the PDF does not establish a more specific implementation hierarchy (https://digitalizace.rvp.cz/files/ai-doporuceni-online-a4.pdf).
educationalTechnologySummary: The guidance discusses AI tools in general, including generative tools that produce text, images, video, and music, and identifies large language models as a common form of AI. It suggests that students experiment with such tools for learning, such as asking questions or seeking explanations, while teachers may consider AI for tailored activities, materials, tasks, or assessment. However, the inspected document names no particular platform, software product, or hardware, and does not establish that the initiative itself develops or deploys an educational technology. It mentions an editable template for adapting the recommendations, but this is a document resource, not evidence of a learning technology. metadata.Initiative / Programme: National AI Strategy of the Czech Republic 2030
metadata.Description: Government strategy (July 2024) with 7 priority areas incl. "Education and expertise in AI", with annual action plans.

summary: The National AI Strategy of the Czech Republic 2030 is a government policy framework coordinated by the Ministry of Industry and Trade. It sets priorities for national AI development and use across areas including research and innovation, industry, public services, governance, and education and expertise in AI. Intended for policymakers and stakeholders across government, business, and society, it is supported by annually evaluated action plans. Education and workforce skills are part of the wider agenda; the available evidence does not specify teaching methods, learning formats, or educational technologies.
pedagogicalSummary: The initiative is a national strategy rather than a described teaching programme. The Ministry’s overview identifies “AI Education and Expertise” and “AI Skills and the Impact of AI on the Labour Market” as two of seven connected areas, but does not explain teaching methods, learning formats, or how learning is organised or supported. The strategy therefore signals education and skills development as policy concerns, not a particular pedagogy. The overview says detailed activities are set out in an annually evaluated Action Plan, but those plans were not examined here; the accessible evidence does not establish whether they specify instructional approaches. Sources: https://mpo.gov.cz/en/business/digital-economy/artificial-intelligence/ and https://mpo.gov.cz/assets/cz/podnikani/digitalni-ekonomika/umela-inteligence/2024/7/Narodni-strategie-umele-inteligence-2030.pdf
prioritySummary: The strategy’s stated emphasis is to develop the Czech AI ecosystem and use AI’s potential while addressing its challenges. The Ministry overview identifies three intended outcomes: stronger economic competitiveness, greater efficiency of the state, and increased societal preparedness and resilience. Its seven areas span research and innovation, education and expertise, labour-market skills, legal and ethical and security matters, industry and business, and public administration and services. The stated benefits therefore extend to the Czech economy, government, and society; the overview does not establish one of these as overriding the others. Education and workforce skills are components of this wider national agenda, rather than the sole purpose. Sources: https://mpo.gov.cz/en/business/digital-economy/artificial-intelligence/ and https://mpo.gov.cz/assets/cz/podnikani/digitalni-ekonomika/umela-inteligence/2024/7/Narodni-strategie-umele-inteligence-2030.pdf
educationalTechnologySummary: The inspected Ministry overview presents the National AI Strategy as a framework for activities and says that detailed initiatives appear in a follow-up Action Plan, evaluated and updated annually. It does not identify a learning platform, software, hardware, or other educational technology that the initiative develops or uses to support AI-literacy learning. AI is discussed as the subject of the strategy and as a technology for the economy and society, but that alone does not show its use as an educational tool. The strategy PDF was supplied, but its full extracted text was too large to inspect in detail; therefore, the absence of named educational technologies here reflects limited accessible evidence, not confirmation that none appear in implementation plans. Sources: https://mpo.gov.cz/en/business/digital-economy/artificial-intelligence/ and https://mpo.gov.cz/assets/cz/podnikani/digitalni-ekonomika/umela-inteligence/2024/7/Narodni-strategie-umele-inteligence-2030.pdf

inclusion.reason: The initiative is issued by a national government body (Czech Ministry of Industry and Trade). It includes an 'Education and expertise in AI' priority area with learning objectives and guidance, satisfying the AI-literacy requirement. The document was developed through a whole-of-government approach with stakeholder participation, indicating formal government endorsement and support, thus qualifying under the inclusion route for government-mandated initiatives.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: Revised Framework Educational Programmes (RVP)
metadata.Description: 2021 revision introducing "Informatika" and digital competence as a key competence, phased in 2023–2024.

summary: The Revised Framework Educational Programmes (RVP) is the Czech Republic’s national framework for basic education. Its 2021 revision adds Informatika and establishes digital competence as a key competence to be developed across subjects, aiming to help pupils use digital technologies safely, critically, confidently and creatively while building computational-thinking and data skills. The framework is being phased into school programmes from 2023–24; linked support offers teachers courses, consultations, workshops and classroom materials, including resources on AI. It is a broad digital-competence curriculum rather than a dedicated AI programme, and the available evidence does not establish a prescribed teaching method or a specific platform developed by the initiative.
pedagogicalSummary: The revised RVP is a curriculum framework rather than a single teaching programme, so the inspected pages do not identify one prescribed pedagogy. They do support a cross-curricular approach: digital competence is to be developed across subjects, alongside the dedicated Informatika area. Linked guidance supports teachers with courses, consultations, workshops and classroom materials; AI teaching resources include a curriculum with a learning-progression map and practical materials. This indicates structured, applied learning and teacher support, but the inspected summaries do not establish a specific method such as project-based or inquiry learning. prioritySummary: The revised RVP’s stated emphasis is modernising primary education for the needs of the 21st century, particularly by adding Informatika and making digital competence a key competence. Its principal beneficiaries are pupils: the framework aims to help them use digital technologies safely, critically, confidently and creatively in learning, work, leisure and civic life. Digital competence is presented as extending across subjects, not as a goal limited to producing IT specialists. The linked support also helps teachers and schools implement the changes, and AI resources address responsible use while preserving human thinking, creativity and critical judgement. The original framework’s stated aims are at https://edu.gov.cz/dokumenty/rvp-ramcove-vzdelavaci-programy/rvp-zv-ramcovy-vzdelavaci-program-pro-zakladni-vzdelavani/; digital competence and AI teaching priorities are at https://digitalizace.rvp.cz/co-se-meni/digitalni-kompetence and https://digitalizace.rvp.cz/napric-predmety/ai/materialy.
educationalTechnologySummary: The inspected framework page establishes curricular changes, not a technology platform developed by the RVP initiative. Its linked AI guidance identifies school-use technologies: Google Workspace for Education and Microsoft 365 Education, including Google Gemini and Microsoft Copilot in school-oriented configurations. The page advises schools to use school accounts and tools that do not use pupils’ data to train models, and describes privacy, student-safety and administrative controls; these are presented as options for schools, not as tools developed by the RVP. The linked materials page also offers downloadable teaching PDFs and AI curriculum materials, but these are resources rather than identified learning software. Evidence is limited to the pages inspected. Sources: https://digitalizace.rvp.cz/napric-predmety/ai/nastroje and https://digitalizace.rvp.cz/napric-predmety/ai/materialy.

The content focuses on diplomatic relations, cooperation frameworks, and high-level political commitments between the EU and its Southern neighbours.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: AI4T – Artificial Intelligence for and by Teachers (Erasmus+)
metadata.Description: Erasmus+ project on training teachers to use AI in education (incl. open textbook/MOOC).

summary: AI4T (Artificial Intelligence for and by Teachers) is an Erasmus+ project supporting secondary-school teachers and school leaders in understanding and using AI in education. Its professional learning offer centres on a four-module MOOC and an open textbook, with texts, videos, activities and practical exercises. The training covers AI and data in educational resources, and helps teachers assess tools’ relevance, risks and usefulness in context. It also explores using school data and learning traces to support differentiated learning and assessment while keeping decisions with people. The project adapted its training to participating countries and tested AI-enabled educational resources.
pedagogicalSummary: AI4T organises teacher learning through a four-module MOOC using varied formats—texts, videos, activities and practical exercises—to build understanding of AI and its challenges in education. The project also describes experimentation with AI-enabled educational resources and a method for analysing such tools, supporting a practical and critical approach: teachers consider their context, acceptability, relevance and usefulness rather than treating AI use as automatic. The training was adapted from the IAI Class’Code MOOC to participating countries’ needs and experiences. The inspected pages do not specify a more detailed teaching sequence or assessment approach. (https://www.ai4t.eu/teacher-training/; https://www.ai4t.eu/about/; https://www.ai4t.eu/resources/)
prioritySummary: AI4T principally aims to strengthen teachers’ and school leaders’ capacity to understand and use AI in education thoughtfully. It seeks to help teachers identify AI in educational resources, explain to students what AI and data are used for, and judge tools’ relevance and risks in their teaching context. The project also emphasizes using school data and learning traces to support differentiated learning, training and assessment, while explicitly retaining human decision-making rather than leaving decisions to AI. Students are beneficiaries through these improved teaching practices, but the inspected pages frame professional learning and teacher agency as the direct focus. (https://www.ai4t.eu/about/; https://www.ai4t.eu/teacher-training/)
educationalTechnologySummary: AI4T identifies its MOOC as the central resource for teacher training. The site describes a four-module course with texts, videos, activities and practical exercises; it does not name the MOOC’s hosting platform. The project also offers an open textbook in online, EPUB and PDF formats and multiple languages. For hands-on exploration, teachers experimented with digital educational resources containing AI, including the French application KWYK, which the site says was made available free to French teachers undertaking the MOOC. These are learning resources or tools used in training; the inspected pages do not establish that AI4T developed the underlying AI products. (https://www.ai4t.eu/teacher-training/; https://www.ai4t.eu/textbook/; https://www.ai4t.eu/about/; https://www.ai4t.eu/resources/)

inclusion.reason: AI4T qualifies for inclusion because it is an Erasmus+ funded project, which constitutes government funding (European Commission). This satisfies the INCLUSION ROUTE regarding government funding. The initiative includes specific educational content with explicit AI literacy: teaching teachers how to use AI tools, analyse their own educational resources including AI elements they may not be aware of, understand data and natures of AI, and improve pedagogical diagnosis and assessment using these tools (as described in the 'Why AI4T?' and 'AI4T, how?' sections).

metadata.Initiative / Programme: Egypt MOETE/MCIT & UNESCO consultation on AI Competency Framework for Teachers (2025)
metadata.Description: UNESCO and Egypt's Ministry of Education and Technical Education, with MCIT, ran a national consultation (Oct 2025) and officially launched the contextualized teacher AI competency framework in 2026.

summary: Egypt’s Ministry of Education and Technical Education and Ministry of Communications and Information Technology, with UNESCO, developed and launched a national AI competency framework for teachers, informed by a 2025 consultation. Adapted to Egypt’s educational context, it guides teachers in understanding, evaluating and using AI responsibly, emphasizing ethics, inclusion, human agency and critical thinking. The framework is intended to inform teacher training, professional development and education policy; planned support includes online and face-to-face training, master trainers and Arabic learning resources, though specific training methods and implementation details are not described.
pedagogicalSummary: The inspected article describes a teacher-competency framework, not a detailed teaching method. It says the framework supports teachers in learning about, understanding, evaluating and responsibly using AI, with emphasis on ethics, inclusion, human agency and critical thinking. Its development involved surveys, focus groups, interviews and stakeholder consultations; these are participatory design methods rather than evidence of classroom pedagogy. Implementation is described as a next step, with planned online and face-to-face training, preparation of master trainers, Arabic learning resources and teacher-training hubs intended to support interactive professional development. The article does not specify instructional sequences or activities within these trainings. Evidence: https://www.unesco.org/en/articles/national-artificial-intelligence-competency-framework-teachers-launched-egypt
prioritySummary: The initiative principally aims to build teachers’ capacity to engage confidently and responsibly with AI in teaching and learning, while providing Egypt with a contextualized reference for teacher training, professional development, educational planning and curriculum reform. The article presents AI as a means to support and empower teachers—not replace them—and highlights ethical, inclusive and human-centered use. It also connects the framework to broader aims of improving teaching and learning, including efficiency, creativity and personalized learning, and to access, inclusion and quality basic education. The inspected page does not establish a more specific ranking among these aims. Evidence: https://www.unesco.org/en/articles/national-artificial-intelligence-competency-framework-teachers-launched-egypt
educationalTechnologySummary: The article identifies no specific software, platform, device or AI product developed or used for instruction, and does not describe the framework itself as a digital learning technology. It says the framework will serve as a capacity-building tool and policy reference. Online and face-to-face training programmes, Arabic learning resources, master-trainer preparation and innovative teacher-training hubs are described as planned capacity-building initiatives; the page gives no platform names or technical details, so it is unclear what technologies the online training or hubs will use. The article also refers generally to digital infrastructure, connectivity and technology-enabled learning, without identifying particular systems. Evidence: https://www.unesco.org/en/articles/national-artificial-intelligence-competency-framework-teachers-launched-egypt

inclusion.reason: The initiative includes AI literacy content (a competency framework for teachers), is issued by the Egyptian government (MOETE/MCIT) in collaboration with UNESCO (an intergovernmental body), and involves national-level endorsement. The inclusion route for governmental support applies here. Uncertainty: No specific learning modules are detailed on the page, but a framework for teacher AI competencies generally implies educational guidance; thus we lean toward inclusion when unsure.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: AI Leap (TI-Hüpe)
metadata.Description: Estonian programme giving students and teachers access to AI tools combined with AI literacy training.

summary: AI Leap (TI-Hüpe) is an Estonian national education initiative serving students, teachers, and education leaders. It combines AI-literacy training and student workshops with teacher development, subject-specific materials, and school-based professional learning communities. Its ITI learning app, built with OpenAI and Estonian researchers, uses explanations, hints, and feedback to guide students’ own problem-solving; the program also provides teachers access to existing AI tools such as ChatGPT or Gemini. The initiative emphasizes responsible use, equitable access, and adapting teaching to AI in Estonia’s language and cultural context, alongside research and evaluation of its educational effects.
pedagogicalSummary: AI Leap combines teacher development with learning activities for students. Teachers are supported through training, subject-specific materials, and school-based professional learning communities where they can share practice and rethink teaching. For students, the initiative describes interactive AI-literacy workshops and practical activities such as hackathons, co-creation sprints, debates, and creative workshops. Its ITI learning app uses a scaffolded tutoring approach: students request explanations, try problems themselves, receive feedback, and reflect on their understanding rather than being given finished answers. Teachers decide when the app fits their instruction. These approaches are described on the [home page](https://tihupe.ee/en/) and [learning-application page](https://tihupe.ee/en/learning-application/); the inspection does not establish how consistently each activity is delivered across schools.
prioritySummary: AI Leap principally aims to help Estonian schools use AI in ways that support learning rather than replace students’ thinking. Its stated priorities include developing students’ thinking and learning skills, advancing responsible AI literacy among teachers and students, and providing equitable access to AI tools so benefits are not limited to better-resourced schools. It also emphasizes supporting teachers and schools to adapt instruction, while creating learning-supportive tools suited to Estonian language and cultural context. The program is therefore focused on educational benefit across students and educators, alongside a broader goal of helping Estonia’s education system respond to AI; the inspected pages do not present workforce upskilling or individual well-being as its primary purpose. Sources: [effectiveness goals](https://tihupe.ee/en/tulemuslikkuse-mootmine/) and [About AI Leap](https://tihupe.ee/en/organisatsioon-ja-osapooled/).
educationalTechnologySummary: AI Leap develops ITI, a learning app made with OpenAI and Estonian researchers and built on ChatGPT. The app is designed to support learning through explanations, guiding questions, hints, and feedback that prompt students to solve problems, review mistakes, and reflect, rather than simply receive answers. The initiative also provides teachers access to paid versions of ChatGPT or Google Gemini; these are existing tools made available through the program, not described as AI Leap products. Its effectiveness page also reports a teacher-facing AI Leap Moodle environment, though the inspected material gives limited detail about its learning functions. No hardware is identified in the pages reviewed. Sources: [learning application](https://tihupe.ee/en/learning-application/), [home page](https://tihupe.ee/en/), and [measuring effectiveness](https://tihupe.ee/en/tulemuslikkuse-mootmine/).

inclusion.reason: The initiative qualifies for inclusion because: 1) It provides clear AI literacy educational content (training for teachers, responsible use guidance) meeting the mandatory AI-literacy requirement. 2) It is officially issued and endorsed by a national government body—the Ministry of Education and Research—as evidenced on the homepage describing it as an Estonian national programme. This satisfies the government endorsement inclusion route per the screening criteria.

metadata.Description: Ministry guidance for schools on AI literacy and AI tools.

summary: The Estonian Ministry of Education and Research’s 2024 guidance helps school leaders, teachers, and learners use AI purposefully in education. It introduces key AI concepts and offers practical recommendations for trying tools such as chatbots, checking their outputs, protecting privacy, and addressing attribution and academic integrity. It encourages teachers and students to discuss when AI supports learning and when it may undermine intended skill development, while keeping learning outcomes central. The document is advisory rather than a structured course and does not prescribe a platform or teaching sequence.
pedagogicalSummary: The guidance recommends learning through purposeful experimentation with AI applications, including trying different prompts and comparing chatbot responses. Teachers are encouraged to discuss with learners when AI use supports a task and when it may prevent development of the intended skill, and to foster critical checking of outputs against learning materials and reliable sources. Shared agreements between teachers and students, followed by dialogue and reflection about AI use, are also recommended. AI may support teachers’ lesson planning, differentiated materials, and feedback, but the document emphasizes that use should serve learning outcomes. These are recommendations rather than a prescribed course or formal teaching model; the inspected guidance does not set out a structured sequence of lessons. (https://www.hm.ee/sites/default/files/documents/2024-03/Tehisaru%20juhend%202024.pdf)
prioritySummary: The guidance principally aims to help schools integrate AI purposefully into education while keeping learner development and learning outcomes central. It identifies equitable development of students’ digital competence and equal future opportunities as reasons to use technology, and describes the broader aim of helping young people become capable of adapting to change and using competitive knowledge and skills. It also seeks to help teachers and school leaders explore AI applications, potentially reducing routine work so they can devote more time to activities requiring human input. Responsible, ethical, and critical use—including attention to privacy, accuracy, and learners’ own contribution—is a recurring emphasis. The document addresses school leaders, teachers, and learners; it does not establish a single priority hierarchy among these aims. (https://www.hm.ee/sites/default/files/documents/2024-03/Tehisaru%20juhend%202024.pdf)
educationalTechnologySummary: The document recommends that schools and educators try AI applications, but does not identify a required platform or describe a technology developed by the Ministry. It discusses text robots/chatbots as tools learners can use for ideas and teachers can use to support lesson planning, differentiated worksheets, tests, and feedback; learners are also encouraged to experiment with prompts. ChatGPT is named in an example citation for chatbot use, and Canva is named as an example source for a generated image. These are examples, not evidence that the initiative develops or formally provides those products. The guidance also points to HARNO training and webinars about AI, but the inspected pages do not specify a dedicated learning platform or hardware. (https://www.hm.ee/sites/default/files/documents/2024-03/Tehisaru%20juhend%202024.pdf)

metadata.Initiative / Programme: Estonian digital competence model for general education
metadata.Description: Estonia's digital competence framework for students and teachers, aligned with EU DigComp 2.1, structures skills across five dimensions.

summary: The Estonian digital competence model for general education is a national framework issued by the Estonian Education and Youth Board for students and teachers. Aligned with EU DigComp 2.1, it organizes competence across five dimensions, with stage-specific criteria and AI-use skills included as part of broader digital competence. Supporting resources include e-courses, self-assessment tools, teacher guidance, webinars, and adaptable lesson scenarios that integrate digital skills into subject teaching.
pedagogicalSummary: The initiative supports competency-based learning through national digital-competence models, stage-specific assessment criteria, and teacher-created lesson scenarios that integrate digital skills into subject teaching rather than treating technology as an end in itself. Its Digiõpilood are downloadable, adaptable teaching scenarios for supporting subject knowledge through digital technology. E-courses for grades 6–9 combine learning materials, tasks, and teacher-facing methodological guidance; they can be used as complete courses or incorporated by topic into informatics or other subjects. Assessment support includes student self-assessment questionnaires, while early-years criteria are developed through discussion and play. These indicate structured, integrated, and reflective learning, but the inspected pages do not establish one single pedagogy for every resource. (https://digipadevus.ee/digiopilood/; https://digipadevus.ee/oppija-digipadevusmudel/e-kursus/; https://digipadevus.ee/oppija-digipadevusmudel/enesehindamise-kusimustik/; https://digipadevus.ee/oppija-digipadevusmudel/hindamiskriteeriumid/)
prioritySummary: The principal emphasis is building students’ digital competence for learning and everyday participation, while giving teachers frameworks and resources to develop that competence through subject teaching. The student model spans information and data literacy, communication and collaboration, digital content creation, safety, and problem-solving; the site says AI-use skills have also been added to the Estonian models. The initiative also supports teachers’ professional digital competence, assessment, and purposeful selection of digital solutions that serve subject learning. Its pages describe educational aims rather than a narrow workforce or commercial goal. AI literacy appears as one component of a broader digital-competence effort, not as the initiative’s sole or clearly dominant priority. (https://digipadevus.ee/oppija-digipadevusmudel/; https://digipadevus.ee/digipadevus-ja-digipadevusmudel/; https://digipadevus.ee/digital-competence/)
educationalTechnologySummary: The initiative develops digital learning resources rather than identifying a dedicated AI-learning product. Its grade 6 and 9 e-courses were created in Moodle, with mostly original materials and H5P activities; the page says they support teaching the model’s assessment criteria and can be used whole or integrated into subjects. The initiative also provides student and teacher self-assessment questionnaires in Google Forms, LimeSurvey, Microsoft Excel, and, for some versions, TAO, allowing schools to configure them in a suitable environment. GeoGebra and school platforms such as eKool and Stuudium appear as course topics, but the inspected pages do not establish that the initiative develops or centrally provides them. AI is listed as a course topic, but no specific AI tool or platform is named. (https://digipadevus.ee/oppija-digipadevusmudel/e-kursus/; https://digipadevus.ee/oppija-digipadevusmudel/enesehindamise-kusimustik/; https://digipadevus.ee/opetaja-digipadevusmudel/enesehindamise-kusimustik/)

inclusion.reason: The initiative is issued by a national statutory body (Haridus- ja Noorteamet), satisfying the inclusion route of government endorsement/funding. It provides explicit AI/digital literacy educational content (skills across five dimensions, models, and guidance) rather than merely using AI to deliver education. There is evidence of system-scale adoption in Estonia’s general education system. The site offers learning materials, self-assessment tools, and teacher training resources that explain how to develop digital/AI competence.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: European Schools – documents on educational use of generative AI (2025)
metadata.Description: Guidance of the European Schools system on use of generative AI.

summary: The European Schools system has issued a framework and legal and pedagogical guidelines for the educational use of generative AI in its nursery, primary, and secondary schools. The documents provide system-level guidance for school education; available evidence does not establish specific teaching methods, tools, or classroom activities.
pedagogicalSummary: The accessible evidence identifies this as a framework and guidance initiative, not a described course or teaching programme: the English basic-texts page lists both a “Framework for the educational use of Generative Artificial Intelligence” and “Legal and pedagogical guidelines for the educational use of generative artificial intelligence” (https://www.eursc.eu/en/office/official-texts/basic-texts/en/). The titles indicate that pedagogical considerations accompany rules for educational use, but the documents themselves could not be read in this inspection. No specific teaching method, learning sequence, or classroom activity is therefore established by the accessible pages. This is missing evidence about the guidance’s recommendations, not confirmation that the documents contain no pedagogical approach.
prioritySummary: The initiative’s stated emphasis is setting a framework for the educational use of generative AI within the European Schools system, rather than a separately evidenced workforce, personal-well-being, or societal-benefit programme. The basic-texts page lists a general framework and legal and pedagogical guidelines on that subject (https://www.eursc.eu/en/office/official-texts/basic-texts/en/). The home page describes the European Schools as providing multilingual and multicultural education for children at nursery, primary, and secondary levels (https://www.eursc.eu/en/). Together these pages place the guidance in a school-education context, but do not reveal its detailed aims, intended user groups within schools, or the relative weight given to different benefits; the underlying guidance documents were not accessible for review.
educationalTechnologySummary: The accessible pages identify generative artificial intelligence as the technology addressed by the initiative, listing a “Framework for the educational use of Generative Artificial Intelligence” and “Legal and pedagogical guidelines for the educational use of generative artificial intelligence” (https://www.eursc.eu/en/office/official-texts/basic-texts/en/). They do not identify any particular AI product, software, platform, or hardware, nor establish that the European Schools develop or deploy a specific educational technology. The documents’ titles indicate guidance about educational use, rather than evidence of a learning tool supplied by the initiative. Because the listed documents could not be read, it is not possible to determine whether they recommend particular tools or describe their use in learning.

inclusion.reason: The initiative qualifies under the inclusion route for government bodies as it is issued by the European Schools (a body of the European Union). metadata.Initiative / Programme: European Schools – Digital Competence Framework (2020)
metadata.Description: Digital competence framework of the intergovernmental European Schools system.

summary: The European Schools Digital Competence Framework (2020) is an official system-level document for the intergovernmental European Schools, which provides multilingual and multicultural education from nursery through secondary school. It sets out a digital-competence framework for the school system, with pupils the best-supported intended audience; the available evidence does not establish its specific competencies, teaching methods, or use of educational technologies, nor whether it addresses AI explicitly.
pedagogicalSummary: The accessible pages describe a structured, age- and stage-based school curriculum, with syllabi organised by education level and subject and an effort to harmonise learning outcomes and assessment standards. They list the Digital Competence Framework as an official system document, but the framework itself was not readable in this inspection. The pages therefore do not establish how digital-competence learning is taught—for example, whether it uses projects, direct instruction, or other methods. The general curriculum description supports an account of structured curricular organisation, not a specific pedagogy for the framework. Sources: https://www.eursc.eu/en/european-schools/studies/syllabuses/ and https://www.eursc.eu/en/office/official-texts/basic-texts/en/
prioritySummary: The initiative’s stated focus, as evidenced by the official listing of the 2020 Digital Competence Framework, is digital competence within the European Schools system. The system serves pupils from nursery through secondary education and describes its broader mission as providing multilingual and multicultural education; the inspected pages do not explain the framework’s specific objectives or identify a more detailed priority, such as employment readiness or personal well-being. The best-supported beneficiary is therefore the system’s pupils, while the precise competencies and intended outcomes remain uncertain because the framework document itself was not accessible in this inspection. Sources: https://www.eursc.eu/en/office/official-texts/basic-texts/en/ and https://www.eursc.eu/en/european-schools/studies/studies-organisation/
educationalTechnologySummary: The inspected pages identify no particular educational technology, platform, software, or hardware developed or used to teach digital competence. They list the Digital Competence Framework as an official document and list Information and Communication Technology (ICT) as a subject in several secondary-school stages, but neither fact establishes which tools, if any, support learning. The school website is an information source, not evidence of an instructional platform. Because the framework document itself could not be read and the syllabus page provides course listings rather than descriptions of classroom tools, the available evidence is insufficient to say whether the initiative uses or develops educational technologies. Sources: https://www.eursc.eu/en/office/official-texts/basic-texts/en/ and https://www.eursc.eu/en/european-schools/studies/syllabuses/

inclusion.reason: This initiative qualifies for inclusion under the 'intergovernmental body' inclusion route. The European Schools are an intergovernmental organization managed by their own administration, making this framework a formally issued document of an intergovernmental entity. metadata.Initiative / Programme: "AI in education – legislation and recommendations" (OKM/OPH, 2025)
metadata.Description: Finland's Ministry of Education/Culture and National Agency for Education published 2025 recommendations on AI covering legal obligations under the EU AI Act.

summary: Finland’s Ministry of Education and Culture and National Agency for Education published national recommendations on AI for early childhood education, schools, upper-secondary and vocational education, and liberal adult education. The guidance is aimed primarily at education providers and staff, helping them build understanding of AI and set rules for its safe, responsible, and lawful use. It addresses legal responsibilities, including under the EU AI Act and data-protection and copyright rules, and practical issues such as assessing work involving AI. The package includes background material; it is guidance rather than a defined teaching programme or technology platform.
pedagogicalSummary: The inspected ministry announcement describes a national recommendations package, not a defined teaching programme. It says AI may diversify ways of learning and notes that core skills such as reading, arithmetic, and subject concepts remain important, but it does not specify teaching methods, learning activities, or how learning is organised. metadata.Initiative / Programme: Framework for citizens' AI competence (Kansalaisten tekoälyosaamisen viitekehys)
metadata.Description: Finland's Ministry of Education and Culture published a national framework defining citizens' AI competence needs, based on EU DigComp 3.0.

summary: Finland’s Ministry of Education and Culture has published a national framework, based on EU DigComp 3.0, describing AI competence for citizens across four levels and three areas: understanding AI, assessing its effects, and using and applying it. Intended to inform competence development in everyday life, work, and society, it offers recommendations for education and training across life stages, including curriculum integration, teacher development, and support through libraries and adult education. It is a competence framework rather than a specified course or teaching programme; the announcement does not detail learning activities or assessment methods.
pedagogicalSummary: The initiative is a competence framework and set of recommendations, rather than a described course or teaching programme. It organizes citizens’ AI competence into four levels and three areas: understanding AI, assessing its effects, and using and applying it. The announcement recommends strengthening competence across life stages through measures including curriculum integration, teacher development, and libraries and liberal adult education as basic digital support. It does not specify classroom methods, learning activities, or assessment practices, so a particular pedagogy cannot be identified from the inspected announcement. These points are described at https://okm.fi/-/okm-julkaisi-kansallisen-viitekehyksen-kansalaisten-tekoalyosaamiselle.
prioritySummary: The framework aims to define and strengthen the AI competence citizens need in everyday life, working life, and participation in society. Its recommendations address several groups, including children and young people, students and working-age adults, people outside education, teachers, and decision-makers; the announcement does not establish a single group as the overriding beneficiary. The stated broader aims are to support individual agency, build trust, and promote a sustainable and equitable society in the AI era. The framework is also intended to guide competence descriptions, curriculum and training design, organizational development, and policy measures. This account is based on the ministry’s announcement: https://okm.fi/-/okm-julkaisi-kansallisen-viitekehyksen-kansalaisten-tekoalyosaamiselle.
educationalTechnologySummary: The inspected announcement does not identify a specific educational technology, platform, software, or hardware that the initiative has developed or is currently using. It proposes developing a national AI-competence portal and self-assessment tools, which could support access to information and reflection on one’s own competence, but presents these as future measures rather than existing resources. The framework itself is a competence structure, not an educational technology. The announcement also mentions using AI in higher education and research, without naming tools or explaining their use as AI-literacy learning technologies. These limits reflect the inspected page, not confirmation that no further tools are described elsewhere: https://okm.fi/-/okm-julkaisi-kansallisen-viitekehyksen-kansalaisten-tekoalyosaamiselle.

inclusion.reason: The initiative is issued by a national government body (Finland’s Ministry of Education and Culture), satisfying the inclusion route requiring government endorsement. Although the detailed content of the framework document was not fully read, the definition of 'citizens' AI competence needs' based on EU DigComp 3.0 inherently implies inclusion of educational content or learning objectives related to AI literacy, which is a required element per the screening criteria.

metadata.Description: Finnish National Agency for Education core curricula.

summary: Finland’s National Agency for Education sets the national core curriculum for primary and lower-secondary basic education, providing shared objectives and subject content that municipalities and schools use to develop local curricula. It covers the wider learning and school framework, including transversal ICT competence, and supports learner participation, active learning and varied assessment. The curriculum references AI in learning and teaching and critical engagement with technology and information, but the inspected materials do not describe AI-specific teaching methods or tools, or present AI literacy as a distinct priority.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: Finland's Digital Compass
metadata.Description: A 2022 Finnish government strategic roadmap to 2030 setting digital-transformation targets across four areas including skills.

summary: Finland’s Digital Compass is a national government roadmap setting direction and targets for the country’s digital transformation through 2030. It covers digital skills, infrastructure, business digitalisation and public services, with citizens, businesses and public-sector stakeholders among those addressed. Skills development is one priority, including diverse skills for citizens and stronger digital capacity for small and medium-sized enterprises; the available evidence describes a strategic framework rather than a teaching programme or specific learning methods.
pedagogicalSummary: The inspected page presents Finland’s Digital Compass as a national strategic roadmap, not as a teaching programme. It says citizens should develop diverse skills and identifies skills as one of four priorities, but does not describe lessons, learning activities, instructional methods, or how learning is supported. Thus, no pedagogical approach can be identified from this page; this is a limit of the available evidence, not confirmation that the full strategy contains no learning activities. Source: https://valtioneuvosto.fi/en/-/10623/government-report-on-the-digital-compass-sets-the-course-for-finland-s-digital-transformation
prioritySummary: The initiative’s central aim is to guide Finland’s digital transformation through 2030, with targets spanning skills, secure and sustainable digital infrastructure, business digitalisation, and digital public services. The page highlights benefits for people, communities, and companies, and specifically calls for diverse skills among citizens and stronger digital capacity in small and medium-sized enterprises. It also frames skills, research, development, innovation, and investment as important to addressing workforce shortages and enabling Finland’s competitiveness. The inspected page establishes these as connected priorities but does not indicate that one beneficiary group or goal outranks the others. Source: https://valtioneuvosto.fi/en/-/10623/government-report-on-the-digital-compass-sets-the-course-for-finland-s-digital-transformation
educationalTechnologySummary: The inspected page does not identify any educational technology, learning platform, software, or hardware developed or used to support AI literacy. It discusses digital systems, communication networks, data, and digital services as elements of Finland’s broader digital transformation, but does not present them as tools for teaching or learning. Nor does it describe specific AI-literacy materials or technologies. Because the source is a press release summarising a national roadmap rather than a detailed account of learning provision, this is a limit of the inspected evidence and does not establish that none are mentioned elsewhere in the strategy. Source: https://valtioneuvosto.fi/en/-/10623/government-report-on-the-digital-compass-sets-the-course-for-finland-s-digital-transformation

metadata.Initiative / Programme: Generation AI (Finland)
metadata.Description: Research project on AI literacy for children and young people.

summary: Generation AI is a Finnish university-led research project developing AI literacy for children and young people, with resources also aimed at teachers and the wider public. It offers free, browser-based tools and classroom materials, including lesson units in which learners train or test AI systems and explore recommendation algorithms, data, privacy and AI’s social effects. Its research-based, hands-on and collaborative approach emphasizes how AI works, how data and design choices shape its outputs, and how to engage critically with its opportunities and risks; the project also conducts school pilots and teacher training.
pedagogicalSummary: The initiative describes a research-based, practical pedagogy built around learning by doing: pupils train or test AI systems, often using their own data, and examine how data and design choices shape results. Its browser-based activities are paired with ready-made multi-lesson units, including a six-lesson unit in which learners make a machine-learning app and a five-lesson unit on social algorithms and privacy. The project also emphasizes learning together, critical questioning, and developing understanding without requiring coding; materials are co-designed with teachers and students and piloted in schools. These details support a hands-on, collaborative and inquiry-oriented approach, rather than merely teaching AI as a topic. Evidence: https://generation-ai-stn.fi/en/for-teachers/; https://generation-ai-stn.fi/en/materials/; https://generation-ai-stn.fi/en/activities/.
prioritySummary: Generation AI principally aims to strengthen children’s and young people’s AI literacy and agency: helping them understand AI’s workings, opportunities, limitations, risks and effects on society. Its stated concerns include digital inequality and skills gaps, children’s rights and privacy, and how algorithmic environments can affect safety and trust. The project seeks to benefit learners directly through school education and free resources, while supporting teachers and contributing research and policy engagement. The pages present these as connected aims; they do not establish a single overriding priority among them. The initiative also makes materials accessible to the wider public, but its educational focus is especially on pre-primary and primary learners and young people. Evidence: https://generation-ai-stn.fi/en/; https://generation-ai-stn.fi/en/research/; https://generation-ai-stn.fi/en/activities/.
educationalTechnologySummary: The project develops free, browser-based learning applications, described as usable without registration or programming skills. These include Teachable Machine, for training image, sound or pose models and making simple apps; Social Media Machine, a social-feed and recommendation simulator; Small Language Machine, for exploring next-word prediction; Breakable Machine, for testing AI vulnerabilities; and Profiling Game, for examining what data can reveal. Manipulation Game is also listed, but the inspected pages mark it as coming soon. The tools are paired with lesson materials; the Teachable Machine page explains that learners train classifiers with their own data and observe how training data affects outcomes. The pages distinguish these project-developed tools from general AI products; they do not identify external platforms as required learning technologies. Evidence: https://generation-ai-stn.fi/en/materials/; https://generation-ai-stn.fi/en/for-teachers/; https://www.gen-ai.fi/en/tools/tm.

inclusion.reason: The initiative provides clear AI-literacy educational content including lesson plans, guides, and tools that explain how AI works. It has national platform access via Finland’s Gen-ai.fi. The project includes a dedicated funding/programme section (SHIELD programme) indicating government or statutory body support.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: Media Literacy in Finland – national media education policy (2019)
metadata.Description: Finland's Ministry of Education and Culture, with KAVI, published this 2019 national policy for systematic media literacy education for all ages.

summary: Media Literacy in Finland is a national policy published in 2019 by Finland’s Ministry of Education and Culture with KAVI. It sets objectives and proposed measures to support systematic, high-quality media education and improve opportunities for people of all ages to develop media literacy. It is intended to guide the organisations and practitioners involved in planning and delivering media education, with attention to ethical and sustainable practice, equality and human rights. The available announcement describes a policy framework rather than a specific course or teaching method and does not identify a distinct AI-literacy component.
pedagogicalSummary: The inspected page describes a national media-education policy, not a specific teaching programme or AI-literacy course. It calls for media education that is comprehensive, high-quality, systematic, goal-oriented, ethical and sustainable, with different organisations collaborating to design, deliver and develop activities. The policy is intended to support planning, but the page does not specify instructional methods, learning formats, or how learners participate. These are therefore gaps in the accessible evidence, not confirmation that the wider policy materials contain no such detail. The announcement does not identify a distinct AI-literacy pedagogy. (https://okm.fi/en/-/uudet-suuntaviivat-medialukutaidolle-julkistettu)
prioritySummary: The policy’s central priority is improving everyone’s opportunity in Finland to develop media literacy through comprehensive, high-quality and systematic media education. It presents media literacy as both a capability that can support a meaningful, good life and a civic skill belonging to all. The intended beneficiaries are therefore broad rather than limited to a particular age group or workforce: the policy’s target audience also includes people and organisations that promote, support, research or implement media education across society. The announcement additionally links quality media education to human rights, equality, non-discrimination and sustainable development, without establishing these as a ranked set of priorities. (https://okm.fi/en/-/uudet-suuntaviivat-medialukutaidolle-julkistettu)
educationalTechnologySummary: The inspected announcement does not identify any educational technology, platform, software or hardware that the initiative develops or uses to support learning. It refers generally to social, cultural and technological trends affecting media education, but that is not evidence of a technology deployed as an educational tool. The page describes a policy that supports the planning and development of media-education activities, rather than a technology-based learning intervention. No AI-specific educational technology is mentioned. This conclusion is limited to the accessible announcement; the policy document itself is not presented in the inspected page text, so its possible technology examples could not be assessed. (https://okm.fi/en/-/uudet-suuntaviivat-medialukutaidolle-julkistettu)

inclusion.reason: The initiative satisfies the inclusion requirement via government endorsement: it is issued and funded by Finland’s Ministry of Education and Culture, a national government ministry. Although this specific URL does not yet detail AI literacy content, the policy is framed as a broad media-literacy framework; under inclusive screening, we prefer inclusion when evidence on wider reach or support is plausible but uncertain. Further review of the full guidelines would be needed to confirm explicit AI-literacy educational components, but current evidence supports inclusion based on government mandate and national scope.
