metadata.Initiative / Programme: Osaava DigiOpe
metadata.Description: A Finnish Ministry of Education and Culture project developing national digital (incl. AI) competence descriptions to guide teacher continuing education.

summary: Osaava DigiOpe is a Finnish Ministry of Education and Culture project developing national digital and digital-pedagogical competence descriptions for early-childhood and basic-education staff. The descriptions are intended to guide educators’ continuing professional development and clarify the skills needed to use digital tools, learning environments, materials, and AI in support of teaching and learning. The project also addresses responsible technology use, critical media literacy, and cyber risks. It defines a framework for competence development rather than specifying courses or a particular teaching method.
pedagogicalSummary: The inspected project page describes a working group developing digital-competence descriptions for early-childhood and basic-education staff, including digital-pedagogical skills. These descriptions are intended to clarify the understanding and skills staff need to use digital tools, learning environments, materials, and AI in support of teaching goals and learners’ skills. The page does not describe courses, classroom activities, or a specific teaching method; it presents a framework to guide competence development rather than detailing how that learning is delivered. Thus, evidence supports a focus on defining and supporting professional learning needs, but not a particular pedagogy or training format (https://okm.fi/hanke?tunnus=OKM048:00/2025).
prioritySummary: The project’s stated emphasis is strengthening and reducing disparities in the digital competence of early-childhood and school education staff, particularly in preschool and basic education. It aims to help staff guide pupils’ learning and participation in a digital society, including responsible technology use, critical media literacy, and understanding of AI. The page also identifies benefits for learners—narrowing differences in their skills—and for staff, including smoother work, workload management, and continued professional development. These aims are presented together; the inspected page does not establish a single priority above the others (https://okm.fi/hanke?tunnus=OKM048:00/2025).
educationalTechnologySummary: The page says the competence descriptions will address skills for using digital tools, learning environments, learning materials, and AI in education, but it does not name any specific platform, software, device, or AI system. The project’s identified output is competence descriptions, not an educational technology product. The page therefore supports that technologies are among the subjects staff are expected to learn to use, but it does not establish which technologies the initiative itself uses or develops to support learning. This summary is limited to the project page inspected (https://okm.fi/hanke?tunnus=OKM048:00/2025).

inclusion.reason: The initiative includes AI literacy as it specifically develops competence descriptions covering AI for educators, which provides educational guidance on how to understand and use AI. This meets the AI-literacy requirement under the 'Issued, funded, mandated, or formally endorsed by a national or sub-national government' inclusion route, as it is a project of the Finnish Ministry of Education and Culture.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: University of Helsinki guidelines on responsible AI in research
metadata.Description: University guidelines referenced by respondent.

summary: Published in 2024, the University of Helsinki’s guidelines support researchers using generative AI in research. They set out expectations for transparent and accountable use, including verifying outputs, reporting and justifying AI use, and considering research integrity, privacy, confidentiality, intellectual property, fairness, and safety. The guidelines are practical guidance rather than a teaching programme and supplement the university’s general AI principles.
pedagogicalSummary: The inspected page describes research-use guidelines, not a teaching programme: it gives principles and practical expectations for researchers, including checking AI outputs against reliable sources and reporting and justifying AI use. It does not describe lessons, learning activities, assessment, or a method for teaching AI literacy, so a pedagogical approach cannot be established from this evidence. The article says the research guidelines supplement the University’s general AI principles, but those principles are linked to an intranet page requiring login and were not inspected. Source: https://www.helsinki.fi/en/news/university/university-helsinki-guidelines-support-researchers-responsible-use-ai
prioritySummary: The initiative’s stated emphasis is supporting researchers in the responsible use of generative AI in research. The guidelines focus on researcher accountability and research integrity, alongside transparency, privacy, confidentiality, intellectual property, and AI ethics. They also call attention to fairness, security, safety, and avoiding discrimination and bias, and advise verification and disclosure of AI use. The page frames these as safeguards for research practice; it does not identify a broader workforce-upskilling or societal-benefit programme, so such priorities should not be inferred. Source: https://www.helsinki.fi/en/news/university/university-helsinki-guidelines-support-researchers-responsible-use-ai
educationalTechnologySummary: The page refers generally to generative AI and AI tools used in research, and says researchers should verify their outputs and report and justify their use. It names no particular platform, software, or hardware, and does not describe any technology developed or deployed specifically to support learning or AI literacy. The tools are discussed as instruments used in research, not as educational technologies. The article also refers to the University’s general AI principles on an intranet page that requires login, which was not accessible for this inspection; therefore, this summary is limited to the public article. Source: https://www.helsinki.fi/en/news/university/university-helsinki-guidelines-support-researchers-responsible-use-ai

inclusion.reason: The initiative includes clear AI literacy elements: it explains how researchers should use AI responsibly (verification, transparency, ethical considerations) and offers practical guidance for research contexts. Although issued by a university, it is supported by a Finnish statutory body—TENK (Finnish National Board on Research Integrity), as indicated by the involvement of Simo Kyllönen, a TENK member—and aligns with European Research Area guidelines, suggesting broader framework use beyond a single institution. This satisfies inclusion via governmental/statutory support and plausible wider reach through alignment with supra-national standards.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: Pix – AI pathway (Pix IA)
metadata.Description: French public platform for assessing and certifying digital skills; includes AI pathway for secondary pupils.

summary: Pix IA is an AI-literacy offer from Pix, a French state-initiated public service for digital skills. It provides two AI pathways mandatory since March 2026 for pupils in 4e, 2de and first-year CAP, with related awareness activities available to higher-education students and professionals. On Pix’s online platform, a diagnostic recommends short, interactive modules with immediate feedback; teachers and trainers can assign pathways and follow learner progress through Pix Orga. Topics include how AI works, practical prompting, generative AI’s limits, misinformation, bias, copyright and environmental and social impacts, with an emphasis on critical and responsible use. The pathways were tested with more than 10,000 pupils, 300 teachers and 140 schools.
pedagogicalSummary: Pix IA uses an active, learner-centred approach built around experimentation: learners begin with a short diagnostic, then receive recommended learning modules tailored to their results and level. The modules are described as short, interactive and progressive, with immediate feedback and an emphasis on trying, making mistakes and developing autonomy. Learners can work at their own pace; teachers can incorporate assigned pathways into lessons or group projects, complementing rather than replacing teacher support. The content includes practical prompting alongside exploration of how AI works and its limitations and social and environmental effects. The initiative reports that its AI content was designed by instructional designers with research expertise in AI, cognition and education. These approaches are described on https://pix.fr/intelligence-artificielle; the inspected pages do not detail individual lesson plans.
prioritySummary: Pix IA principally aims to equip learners to understand AI and use it effectively, critically and responsibly, rather than focusing only on technical operation or workforce preparation. Its materials address how AI works, generative AI’s strengths and limitations, prompting, misinformation and deepfakes, bias, copyright and environmental impact. For school pupils, the pathways are complementary to teaching and intended to support critical thinking and sound digital skills; the site says two AI pathways have been mandatory since March 2026 for pupils in 4e, 2de and first-year CAP. The wider Pix offer also serves professionals and students through guided awareness activities, so the initiative is not exclusively for school pupils. Evidence for these aims and audiences appears at https://pix.fr/intelligence-artificielle and https://pix.fr/enseignement-scolaire.
educationalTechnologySummary: The initiative identifies its Pix online platform as the setting for AI learning pathways, and Pix Orga as the educator-facing service through which schools can find and assign those pathways and follow learner activity and results. The pathways combine an initial diagnostic with recommended short, interactive learning modules; the AI page describes modules of roughly 7–10 minutes, adjusted to learner level and supported by immediate feedback. Pix’s broader challenge format also includes interactive exercises and, for some tasks, an embedded simulator, though the inspected pages do not establish which simulations appear in the AI pathway. ChatGPT, LeChat and DeepSeek are named as examples of public generative AI discussed in the curriculum, not as tools Pix says it uses to deliver instruction. Details: https://pix.fr/intelligence-artificielle and https://pix.fr/enseignement-scolaire.

inclusion.reason: The initiative includes AI literacy content aimed at teaching students how AI works and how to use it responsibly. It qualifies for inclusion because it is issued and mandated by the French national government (Ministry of National Education) and is a public service, satisfying the government mandate/inclusion route.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: Cadre d'usage de l'IA en éducation (Ministère de l'Éducation nationale, 2025)
metadata.Description: National framework for AI use in schools (graduated by school level, human-centred, data protection).

summary: France’s Ministry of National Education’s 2025 framework sets national guidance for AI use across primary and secondary education and for education professionals. It recommends progressively developing pupils’ understanding and critical use of AI, with classroom use becoming more autonomous by school level under teacher-defined conditions. The guidance addresses learning and assessment, teachers’ work, human oversight, data protection, transparency, ethics and environmental responsibility; it is a policy framework rather than a course or dedicated technology platform.
pedagogicalSummary: The framework sets guidance rather than prescribing a single teaching method or course. It recommends building AI knowledge and critical use progressively from primary school, grounded in scientific, cultural, and linguistic knowledge. Primary pupils are to learn basic concepts without directly manipulating generative AI; from year 9 (4e), classroom use may be limited, explained, and supervised by a teacher; at lycée, students may use it more autonomously within a teacher-defined learning framework. It also recommends emphasizing reasoning and problem-solving, checking AI outputs against other sources, and adapting assignments and assessment. These are policy recommendations, not evidence of a particular implemented pedagogy (https://www.education.gouv.fr/cadre-d-usage-de-l-ia-en-education-450647).
prioritySummary: The initiative’s central purpose is to establish ethical and legal guardrails for AI use in education while enabling use that serves learning and education professionals’ work. It aims to help pupils understand AI, weigh its opportunities and limits, and use it critically as learners and future citizens; for some, it also supports orientation toward AI studies and careers. The framework additionally addresses teachers’ work, such as lesson preparation and assessment, and stresses personal-data protection, transparency, and environmental responsibility. The page presents these as connected aims and does not establish a more specific priority hierarchy (https://www.education.gouv.fr/cadre-d-usage-de-l-ia-en-education-450647).
educationalTechnologySummary: The inspected framework page does not identify a named platform, software product, device, or educational technology developed by the initiative. It discusses AI generically, distinguishing predictive and generative AI, and notes that pupils and staff already use public-facing AI services for activities such as revision, lesson preparation, and adapting content. These examples describe possible uses, not a tool provided or developed by the initiative. The page advises against entering personal or confidential data into public services, says pupils should not be required to create personal accounts with them, and recommends preferring open solutions when they allow greater control over data and processing. The accessible evidence does not establish which specific technologies, if any, the framework itself deploys (https://www.education.gouv.fr/cadre-d-usage-de-l-ia-en-education-450647).

inclusion.reason: This initiative qualifies for inclusion under the 'Issued by a national government' route, as it is officially produced by France's Ministry of National Education. It satisfies the AI-literacy requirement because it functions as an educational guidance document, providing pedagogical directions, implementation guidelines, and principles (human-centered approach) specifically for teachers and students on how to use AI in education.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: CNIL guidance on AI
metadata.Description: French data protection authority's recommendations on AI and data protection.

summary: The CNIL, France’s data protection authority, provides public-facing information about AI and its implications for personal data, privacy, and individual rights, alongside practical recommendations for professionals and organisations developing or using AI. Its online resources explain AI and related risks, offer precautions for everyday use, and address data-protection compliance; topic-focused webinars provide expert presentations and discussion. The offering supports self-directed learning and professional guidance, with a principal emphasis on applying data-protection principles rather than a structured AI course.
pedagogicalSummary: The inspected pages present an informational and practice-oriented approach, not a defined AI course or classroom curriculum. For the public, CNIL offers accessible explanatory materials and a curated selection of books, films, and online resources to help people understand AI and its personal-data implications. For professionals, it provides recommendations and topic-focused webinars: these are approximately 45-minute presentations by CNIL staff, followed by questions and discussion. This supports learning through self-directed reading and expert explanation with opportunities for interaction; the pages do not establish a broader teaching sequence or assessment for AI literacy. Evidence: https://www.cnil.fr/fr/particulier-intelligence-artificielle-ia and https://www.cnil.fr/fr/les-webinaires-de-la-cnil. This summary reflects the limited pages inspected.
prioritySummary: The initiative chiefly aims to help people understand AI’s implications for personal data and to protect privacy and individual rights as AI is used and developed. Public-facing guidance explains everyday risks and precautions, including data use by conversational AI. Professional-facing recommendations address applying data-protection rules to AI development and supporting deployment that respects people’s rights, while the CNIL’s wider framing includes reconciling innovation with those protections. The pages address both public awareness and professional practice; they do not establish a single priority hierarchy beyond this shared emphasis on data protection and rights. Evidence: https://www.cnil.fr/fr/particulier-intelligence-artificielle-ia and https://www.cnil.fr/fr/intelligence-artificielle?page=2. This reading is based on a limited inspection of the site.
educationalTechnologySummary: The inspected pages do not identify a dedicated AI-literacy learning platform, software, or hardware developed or adopted by CNIL. They point to online informational resources and webinars, but these are delivery formats rather than a named educational technology. The AI topic listing also describes a CNIL demonstrator for exploring the genealogy of open-source AI models; its stated purpose is model traceability, not instruction, so the inspected evidence does not establish it as an educational technology. The public-facing AI page mentions LINC resources for understanding AI, but does not specify a learning platform or technology supporting them. Evidence: https://www.cnil.fr/fr/particulier-intelligence-artificielle-ia and https://www.cnil.fr/fr/intelligence-artificielle. This conclusion is limited to the pages inspected and does not confirm that no other tools exist.

inclusion.reason: AI literacy element: The page offers educational content explaining how AI works, its applications, associated risks, and user rights in relation to AI. Inclusion route: Issued by a national statutory body (the CNIL), which serves as France's data protection authority. This meets the government-endorsed inclusion criteria.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: Pix+ Édu (incl. AI) – teacher digital competence
metadata.Description: Pix+ Édu programme for teachers' professional digital competences.

summary: Pix+ Édu is a French public-service programme for developing and recognizing the professional digital competencies of practicing teachers, education staff, and students in teacher-training programmes. Aligned with the CRCN-Édu framework, it uses Pix learning pathways for assessment and skill development, including an AI pathway with diagnostic and personalized, interactive modules. The AI content covers practical use and limitations of generative AI, as well as topics such as data, bias, misinformation, deepfakes, ethics, and environmental impacts. Continuing professional development is supported through Magistère access, tutorials, webinars, and training from partner education organizations; related Pix pathways for pupils are part of the wider Pix offer.
pedagogicalSummary: Pix+ Édu organises teacher learning through an initial discovery phase followed by themed Pix learning pathways designed to deepen professional digital skills. Its AI pathway uses a diagnostic to identify strengths and gaps, then recommends personalized, short, interactive and progressive learning modules. The AI materials describe an active, experimentation-based approach, with immediate feedback, a secure setting for interaction, and encouragement to learn through trial and error. The wider Pix+ Édu offer also points to tutorials, webinars and training provided by teacher-training institutes and education organisations. These are learning and support methods, distinct from the digital platforms that deliver them. The inspected pages provide a broad outline rather than detailed lesson plans (https://pix.fr/edu; https://pix.fr/intelligence-artificielle).
prioritySummary: Pix+ Édu principally aims to develop and recognize the professional digital competencies of teachers and education personnel, from initial preparation through their careers. Its AI pathway addresses educators’ competencies in a context of continuing professional development; the wider AI offer also seeks to help users understand AI and use it effectively, critically and responsibly. The stated beneficiaries include students in teacher-training programmes and practicing teachers and education staff. The pages also describe AI learning pathways for school pupils, intended to support critical thinking and informed use, but this is a related, broader Pix activity rather than the central purpose of Pix+ Édu. The inspected pages do not establish a more specific hierarchy among teacher-development goals (https://pix.fr/edu; https://pix.fr/intelligence-artificielle).
educationalTechnologySummary: Pix develops and delivers its learning pathways through its Pix platform. For AI literacy, the platform offers diagnostic activities and personalized, interactive learning modules; its AI page describes short modules on topics such as prompting, hallucinations and deepfakes, with immediate feedback. For teachers and education personnel in continuing training, access to Pix+ Édu pathways is through a dedicated Magistère space; the page identifies Magistère as the access route, not as a Pix-developed product. Pix+ Édu also incorporates tutorials and webinars, including resources produced by Réseau Canopé, and training offered by partner institutions. The pages name generative AI products as learning topics, not as educational technologies used by Pix+ Édu. No specific hardware is identified (https://pix.fr/edu; https://pix.fr/intelligence-artificielle).

inclusion.reason: Pix+ Édu qualifies because it (1) is issued by a French government body (DRANE/Ministry of Education context), satisfying the national government inclusion route; (2) includes specific AI literacy educational content under its 'Intelligence artificielle' theme and broader digital competency curriculum; and (3) serves scale across the entire French education system with international reach, rather than being a single-institution project.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: Réseau Canopé
metadata.Description: Public operator for teacher professional development and resources.

summary: Réseau Canopé is a French public operator supporting professional development for teachers and other education personnel, with resources also serving pupils and local authorities. It offers online and in-person training, including self-paced modules, videos, webinars, workshops and classroom-ready activities. Its AI-related offer includes resources and training on generative AI, classroom practice, assessment, responsible use and critical thinking; some activities help pupils examine AI and digital practices. The wider programme also covers digital and media literacy, inclusion and other educational topics.
pedagogicalSummary: Réseau Canopé supports teachers’ professional learning through a mix of in-person and online training, including self-paced modules, short videos, webinars, conferences and workshops, with opportunities for exchange among participants. Its AI-focused offer includes a structured series of videos and webinars, practical sessions such as creating quizzes, and guidance on active pedagogy, responsible use and critical thinking. For students, some resources propose analyzing familiar digital practices or using unplugged activities to understand AI. The evidence therefore points to flexible, practice-oriented professional development alongside classroom activities, rather than one single teaching method. The formats are described on the [home page](https://www.reseau-canope.fr/) and [CanoTech](https://www.canotech.fr/qui-sommes-nous); AI activities appear in the [AI education series](https://www.canotech.fr/serie/lintelligence-artificielle-au-service-de-leducation) and [digital education resources](https://www.reseau-canope.fr/numerique-en-education).
prioritySummary: The initiative’s central emphasis is continuing professional development for teachers and other education personnel, helping them adapt teaching methods and respond to students’ needs. Its AI-related offer extends this goal: it aims to help educators understand generative AI’s principles, risks and educational opportunities, use it thoughtfully in practice, and guide students toward critical, responsible and ethical use. The inspected resources also connect digital literacy with student citizenship, prevention of online harms, inclusion and support for diverse learners; these are presented as related aims, not as a clearly ranked set of priorities. Réseau Canopé describes its continuing-training mission and adapting teaching to each learner on its [about page](https://www.reseau-canope.fr/qui-sommes-nous.html); AI goals are outlined in its [AI education series](https://www.canotech.fr/serie/lintelligence-artificielle-au-service-de-leducation) and [digital education page](https://www.reseau-canope.fr/numerique-en-education).
educationalTechnologySummary: CanoTech is identified as a Réseau Canopé online professional-learning platform, offering short videos, modular courses and webinars; its AI series organizes videos and sessions on generative AI, classroom practice, assessment and ethical use. The initiative also presents Quizinière as an assessment tool: one webinar proposes combining it with an AI tool to create quizzes and give feedback on students’ answers. The AI tool itself is not named, and the inspected pages do not establish that Réseau Canopé develops or provides a particular AI system for learners. Magistère and e-INSPÉ are also referenced as routes to training, but their role in the specific AI offer is not detailed. Sources: [CanoTech](https://www.canotech.fr/qui-sommes-nous), the [AI series](https://www.canotech.fr/serie/lintelligence-artificielle-au-service-de-leducation), and [digital education resources](https://www.reseau-canope.fr/numerique-en-education).

inclusion.reason: The initiative is issued by a national public operator (Réseau Canopé) that falls under the category of a government/statutory body (public operator for teacher professional development), which qualifies under the inclusion route for 'Issued, funded, mandated, or formally endorsed by a national or sub-national government or statutory body'. While the homepage itself does not explicitly describe AI literacy content, the presence of a dedicated 'Numérique en éducation' (Digital in Education) section and various other educational topics suggests that the platform likely includes resources on digital tools and AI usage. The inclusion criteria are met due to the strong government/public operator status, even though specific AI-literacy details require further exploration of sub-pages to confirm.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: University of Orléans charter on AI use
metadata.Description: Charter on the use of AI at the University of Orléans (2024).

summary: The University of Orléans’ 2024, board-approved charter sets an institutional framework for AI use in its higher-education community, including students and staff. The supplied description says it covers acceptable generative AI use, ethics, academic integrity, how AI systems work and their limitations, and citation of AI-generated content. It is a policy and guidance document rather than a documented course or teaching programme; the accessible evidence does not establish specific learning activities or technologies.
pedagogicalSummary: The accessible portion of the document identifies it as the University of Orléans’ charter on AI use, approved by its Board of Directors, but does not show teaching or learning activities. It therefore supports describing the initiative as a university-level charter rather than identifying a pedagogical approach. The available evidence is only the document’s cover, so it does not establish whether the charter discusses teaching practices elsewhere. (https://www.univ-orleans.fr/upload/public/2025-01/2024_10_18_Charte%20sur%20l%27utilisation%20de%20l%27IA%20au%20sein%20de%20l%27UO.pdf)
prioritySummary: The document is titled as a charter governing the use of artificial intelligence within the University of Orléans and is marked as approved by the university’s Board of Directors. This indicates an institutional focus on setting a framework for AI use at the university, but the accessible cover does not specify the charter’s substantive priorities, intended beneficiaries, or any hierarchy among goals. The PDF’s remaining contents could not be inspected in the available text, so more specific aims cannot be established. (https://www.univ-orleans.fr/upload/public/2025-01/2024_10_18_Charte%20sur%20l%27utilisation%20de%20l%27IA%20au%20sein%20de%20l%27UO.pdf)
educationalTechnologySummary: The accessible cover names artificial intelligence as the subject of the University of Orléans’ charter, but identifies no educational technology, learning platform, software, or hardware developed or used by the initiative. The charter itself is a policy document, not evidence that a particular AI product supports learning. Because the PDF’s substantive text was not accessible for inspection, it is not possible to determine whether it names technologies elsewhere; their absence from the inspected evidence should not be taken as confirmed absence from the charter. (https://www.univ-orleans.fr/upload/public/2025-01/2024_10_18_Charte%20sur%20l%27utilisation%20de%20l%27IA%20au%20sein%20de%20l%27UO.pdf)

inclusion.reason: The initiative clearly includes AI literacy: it provides educational content explaining how generative AI functions statistically, describes concepts like hallucinations, and gives guidance on ethics, usage limits, and proper citation. It qualifies via the inclusion route of being issued by a sub-national government entity (the University of Orléans is part of France’s public higher education system) and serves a large institutional audience.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: KMK strategy "Bildung in der digitalen Welt" (2016/2021) & Handlungsempfehlung KI (2024)
metadata.Description: KMK strategy on digital education and 2024 recommendation on handling AI in school education.

summary: The KMK’s “Bildung in der digitalen Welt” strategy provides a shared framework for digital education across Germany’s Länder, aiming to develop students’ competencies for participation in everyday life, work and society. It covers school and vocational education and teacher education; a 2024 recommendation addresses the use of AI in school education, while AI is also identified as an area for further development of the broader strategy. The KMK page lists coordinated projects and tools for digital learning, assessment, adaptive support and teacher development, but does not specify a common teaching method or classroom sequence.
pedagogicalSummary: The inspected KMK page describes a policy framework for developing students’ competencies through school and classroom learning, but it does not specify a particular teaching method or classroom sequence. It lists cross-state projects grouped around teaching with digital materials and tools, online diagnostics and assessment, adaptive learning, and teacher professional development and collaboration. These suggest forms of instructional support and individualized learning, but the page provides too little detail to establish how they are used pedagogically or whether they specifically teach AI literacy. Thus, a defined pedagogy was not identifiable in the inspected material; this is a limit of the available evidence, not proof that participating schools use no particular approach. (https://www.kmk.org/bildungsministerkonferenz/bildungsthemen/bildung-in-der-digitalen-welt.html; https://www.kmk.org/en/bildungsministerkonferenz/bildungsthemen/bildung-in-der-digitalen-welt.html)
prioritySummary: The KMK strategy’s stated emphasis is preparing students in Germany for digitalization across all areas of life, enabling them to develop competencies for a self-determined life and to participate in shaping the future in school, work, and society. The page also identifies digital education across all education sectors, including general and vocational schools and teacher education, and highlights coordinated implementation by the Länder. Its stated aims therefore include individual capability as well as readiness for working life and participation in society; the page does not establish one as more important than the others. AI is described as an area for which the strategy is being expanded, rather than as its sole priority. (https://www.kmk.org/bildungsministerkonferenz/bildungsthemen/bildung-in-der-digitalen-welt.html; https://www.kmk.org/en/bildungsministerkonferenz/bildungsthemen/bildung-in-der-digitalen-welt.html)
educationalTechnologySummary: The KMK page lists cross-state digital education projects and infrastructures, but does not explain which are specifically used to teach AI literacy. Named examples include the School-Cloud, the itslearning development project, and a media database with AI-powered services for providing and assessing educational media. For learning diagnostics and support, it lists technology-based assessment and feedback portals, an Adaptive Intelligent System, and adaptive tools for German as a second language and primary education. These are presented as platforms or tools supporting access to materials, assessment, and adaptive learning; the page does not detail their functions or classroom adoption. It also names a “KI-gestützter Bedienassistent” (AI-supported operating assistant) without describing its learning role. (https://www.kmk.org/bildungsministerkonferenz/bildungsthemen/bildung-in-der-digitalen-welt.html; https://www.kmk.org/en/bildungsministerkonferenz/bildungsthemen/bildung-in-der-digitalen-welt.html)

inclusion.reason: This initiative includes explicit AI literacy content (educational objectives, usage guidance, ethical frameworks) and is issued by the KMK, which is the statutory intergovernmental coordinating body of Germany's 16 state education ministries. Route: intergovernmental/sub-national government endorsement and formal policy status.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: Wissenschaftsrat – paper on AI and "intellectual sovereignty" (2026)
metadata.Description: The German Science and Humanities Council's July 2026 paper recommends fostering "intellectual sovereignty" in higher education amid generative AI.

summary: The German Science and Humanities Council’s 2026 recommendations address how higher education can respond to generative AI, with “intellectual sovereignty”—independent thought, judgment, and action—as a guiding principle. Intended for universities and their staff and students, the paper calls for developing AI competence alongside disciplinary knowledge, preserving opportunities to work without AI, and adapting teaching and assessment. It also discusses ethical and social consequences, accessibility, academic exchange, and shared AI infrastructure. These are policy recommendations rather than a delivered curriculum or implementation programme.
pedagogicalSummary: This is a set of recommendations for higher education, not a teaching programme with its own delivered curriculum. It advocates building AI competencies alongside disciplinary knowledge, while reserving AI-free parts of study for practicing independent thought. It also recommends adapting assessment to recognize students’ own work, fostering trust rather than relying mainly on detailed usage rules, and strengthening personal guidance and opportunities for social and subject-based exchange. These proposals suggest a combination of explicit competency development, independent practice, and supported collaborative learning; the pages inspected do not describe a specific teaching method or implementation. Sources: https://www.wissenschaftsrat.de/SharedDocs/Pressemitteilungen/DE/PM_2026/PM_1526 and https://www.wissenschaftsrat.de/download/2026/3319-26?__blob=publicationFile&v=12
prioritySummary: The central aim is to make “intellectual sovereignty”—autonomous thinking, judgment, and action—a guiding principle for higher education as generative AI becomes more prevalent. The recommendations are for universities and the people within them, especially students and teaching staff: develop AI competence while preserving subject expertise, independent judgment, and the capacity to work through difficult tasks without AI. They also emphasize social and academic exchange, inclusion and accessibility as potential benefits of AI, and attention to ethical, social, and ecological consequences. The document further calls for dependable shared AI infrastructure and clearer legal and financial conditions. The inspected material presents these as connected concerns, without establishing a separate workforce-training priority. Sources: https://www.wissenschaftsrat.de/SharedDocs/Pressemitteilungen/DE/PM_2026/PM_1526 and https://www.wissenschaftsrat.de/download/2026/3319-26
educationalTechnologySummary: Generative AI is discussed as technology that could support higher-education learning: the Council identifies potential for improved access to knowledge, personalized learning support, new feedback, creative teaching materials, and greater accessibility and inclusion. These are described as possibilities, not as evidence that the Council itself operates or deploys a particular educational tool. No named platform, software product, or hardware is identified in the inspected pages. The recommendations do call for developing powerful, sovereign, networked AI infrastructure for higher education, but this is a proposed enabling infrastructure, not an educational technology shown to have been developed or put into use by the initiative. The full 113-page paper was not examined in depth, so additional examples may be absent from this summary. Sources: https://www.wissenschaftsrat.de/SharedDocs/Pressemitteilungen/DE/PM_2026/PM_1526 and https://www.wissenschaftsrat.de/download/2026/3319-26

inclusion.reason: The document contains explicit educational content about how to use generative AI responsibly (critical thinking, intellectual independence, handling uncertainty) and provides guidance on AI literacy for higher education, satisfying the AI-literacy requirement. It is issued by a national statutory body (the Wissenschaftsrat), fulfilling the inclusion route of endorsement by a national government/statutory body.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: DigitalPakt Schule
metadata.Description: Federal-Länder programme funding digital infrastructure in schools (DigitalPakt 2.0 follow-up).

summary: DigitalPakt Schule is a German federal–state funding programme that supports digital infrastructure and development in schools. Its beneficiaries include schools and pupils, with support also for teachers and education authorities through equipment, educational software, technical support, and teacher qualification. DigitalPakt 2.0 broadens this work to school and teaching development and practice-oriented research. The programme emphasizes linking technology investments to pedagogical concepts and integrating digital learning across subjects; AI is mentioned among its focus topics, but the available evidence does not establish a distinct AI-literacy curriculum or teaching method.
pedagogicalSummary: The inspected pages do not describe an AI-literacy teaching method or a single prescribed classroom pedagogy. They do state that digital education should follow the “primacy of pedagogy”: funding should be tied to pedagogical concepts and teacher qualification, and digital learning is intended to be integrated systematically across subjects, guided by a competency framework. The follow-up programme also describes practice-oriented research to develop digital teaching approaches with educators. Separately, transfer events share implementation examples and bring education and administrative stakeholders into dialogue; these are knowledge exchange activities, not a stated classroom method. This evidence supports a pedagogy-first and cross-curricular orientation, but not a specific AI-literacy approach. Sources: https://www.digitalpaktschule.de/de/was-ist-der-digitalpakt-schule-1701.html and https://www.digitalpaktschule.de/de/digitalpakt-2-0-startet-funf-milliarden-euro-fur-die-digitale-zukunft-der-schulen-1874.html and https://www.digitalpaktschule.de/de/transfer-veranstaltungsreihe-digitalpakt-schule-nachhaltig-wirksam-transfer-ermoglichen-1881.html
prioritySummary: DigitalPakt Schule principally aims to improve schools’ digital educational infrastructure so that schools can teach the digital competencies learners need. Its stated beneficiaries are schools and their pupils, with teachers and school providers also supported through infrastructure investment, teacher qualification, and technical support. The follow-up DigitalPakt 2.0 broadens the emphasis: alongside infrastructure, it includes digital school and teaching development, education software, and practice-oriented research and teacher development. The site also highlights cross-state cooperation and transferring implementation experience. These are documented priorities of a digital-education programme; the pages inspected do not identify AI literacy as a distinct central objective. Sources: https://www.digitalpaktschule.de/de/was-ist-der-digitalpakt-schule-1701.html and https://www.digitalpaktschule.de/de/digitalpakt-2-0-startet-funf-milliarden-euro-fur-die-digitale-zukunft-der-schulen-1874.html and https://www.digitalpaktschule.de/de/transfer-veranstaltungsreihe-digitalpakt-schule-nachhaltig-wirksam-transfer-ermoglichen-1881.html
educationalTechnologySummary: The initiative is a funding programme rather than a documented developer of a named educational-technology product. The inspected pages describe support for school digital infrastructure; the DigitalPakt 2.0 page specifically lists technology, tools, educational software, digital applications, and professional technical-support structures. It also mentions infrastructure for providing and assessing digital educational media and for online-based diagnostics and assessment in cross-state projects. The earlier programme page uses whiteboards and laptops as examples of equipment, while stressing that equipment alone does not ensure educational quality. No specific platform, software product, or AI tool is identified in the inspected material, and the website itself is an information portal rather than evidence of a learning technology used in teaching. Sources: https://www.digitalpaktschule.de/de/digitalpakt-2-0-startet-funf-milliarden-euro-fur-die-digitale-zukunft-der-schulen-1874.html and https://www.digitalpaktschule.de/de/digitalpakt-schule-landerubergreifende-vorhaben-1848.html and https://www.digitalpaktschule.de/de/was-ist-der-digitalpakt-schule-1701.html

inclusion.reason: The initiative is officially issued and funded by the German federal government (Federal Ministry of Education and Research) and sub-national state governments (Länder), satisfying the 'government funding' inclusion route. It also explicitly includes AI literacy elements: the 'DigitalPakt Schule' website mentions AI as one of the priority topics ('KI – Künstliche Intelligenz') under the 'Im Fokus' section, indicating that the programme provides educational content and support for understanding and using AI in schools. This confirms that the initiative meets both the inclusion route (government-funded) and the AI-literacy requirement.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: Bavarian Ministry – guide "KI in der pädagogischen Praxis" & AI tools via ByCS
metadata.Description: The Bavarian education ministry issued a guide on AI in pedagogical practice and rolled out AI tools (ByCS, AIS.chat) to all schools.

summary: The Bavarian State Ministry of Education’s AI-in-schools initiative combines guidance, professional learning, classroom materials, and school-oriented AI tools. Its guide and implementation checklist support school leaders and teachers in assessing, selecting, and integrating AI, while training develops foundational, pedagogical, and legal understanding. Student resources, including the KI-Kompass for grades 5–8, promote understanding and responsible use of AI. Through BayernCloud Schule (ByCS), schools can access AI functions such as chat and text, image, and audio generation; AIS.chat offers a browser-based chatbot for guided classroom use. The initiative emphasizes evaluating AI outputs, recognizing limitations, and considering ethical and safe use alongside practical applications in teaching and learning.
pedagogicalSummary: The initiative combines teacher professional learning with classroom-oriented guidance rather than prescribing one teaching method. Teachers can use a self-paced course for foundational knowledge, further practice-focused training, and regional or school-based sessions where skills are deepened through professional exchange. The guidance calls for teachers to understand AI’s operation and limits, assess the subject and pedagogical quality of outputs, and reflect on effects and ethical issues. For students, materials such as the KI-Kompass for grades 5–8 support learning to understand, evaluate, and use AI responsibly; the school chatbot is also described as suitable for guided introductory classroom dialogue. The inspected pages give this broad picture but do not detail a complete sequence of lessons (https://www.km.bayern.de/gestalten/digitalisierung/kuenstliche-intelligenz; https://www.bycs.de/ki-systeme/index.html; https://klickpunktschule.bycs.de/digitalkompass/startseite/ki-kompass/ki-kompass-5-8-uebersicht).
prioritySummary: The initiative focuses on helping Bavarian schools integrate AI competently and responsibly, with support directed to school leaders, teachers, and students. For educators and school leaders, it emphasizes building AI skills, choosing tools suited to local pedagogical needs, and introducing them through school development with transparency, feedback, and review. For students, the stated aims include developing foundational AI understanding and awareness of opportunities and limits, so they can use AI safely and navigate a digital working world. The ministry also identifies potential benefits such as more individualized learning and reduced teacher workload, alongside improved access to information. The inspected pages present these as complementary aims rather than establishing a single dominant benefit (https://www.km.bayern.de/meldung/kuenstliche-intelligenz-in-der-paedagogischen-praxis; https://www.km.bayern.de/gestalten/digitalisierung/kuenstliche-intelligenz; https://www.bycs.de/ki-systeme/index.html).
educationalTechnologySummary: The initiative provides AI functions in the BayernCloud Schule (ByCS) learning platform and the school chatbot AIS.chat. ByCS platform functions include a chatbot and tools for generating text, images, and audio within course spaces; teachers can use them for differentiated tasks, feedback suggestions, and adapting materials, while students can use them during assignments and to obtain feedback. A control centre allows schools or teachers to manage functions, timing, model selection, and access for classes or learners. AIS.chat, developed by FWU on behalf of the German states, is a browser-based, school-oriented chatbot for guided introductory use; students access it through a teacher-provided link or QR code, without installing software. The pages describe these tools as available through ByCS; they do not identify underlying AI models (https://www.bycs.de/ki-systeme/index.html; https://www.bycs.de/ki-systeme/ais-chat-der-ki-chatbot-fuer-schulen/index.html).

inclusion.reason: This initiative qualifies for inclusion because it is formally issued by the Bavarian State Ministry of Education (a sub-national government entity), providing AI literacy guidance through an official guide on "AI in Pedagogical Practice". The tools were deployed to all schools in Bavaria, indicating system-scale adoption across a school system. This meets both the AI-literacy requirement and the inclusion route for government-endorsed initiatives at the sub-national level.

summary: The Bavarian State Institute for School Quality (ISB) provides a teacher-facing handout and supplementary materials through the mebis learning platform to support the grade 13 Gymnasium computer science curriculum’s AI unit. The resources cover foundational AI subject matter and offer teaching concepts and materials for teachers of standard and advanced computer science, including late-starting standard courses. The initiative emphasizes curriculum-linked teacher support; students benefit through classroom implementation, but specific teaching methods and platform functions are not established in the available description.
pedagogicalSummary: The initiative supports teaching through a teacher-facing handout that presents foundational AI subject matter, concrete teaching concepts, and a range of instructional materials for the grade 13 curriculum. This indicates curriculum-linked lesson planning and provision of ready-to-use or adaptable resources; the accessible description does not specify particular classroom methods, such as project-based learning, discussion, or student collaboration. The stated purpose is to help teachers implement the curriculum, rather than to prescribe a detailed teaching model. These limits reflect the information available on the inspected page, not evidence that the full handout contains no further pedagogical guidance. The materials are intended for teachers of both standard and advanced-level computer science, as well as late-starting computer science at the standard level. The direct beneficiaries are therefore teachers receiving curricular and instructional support, with students in those courses benefiting through implementation of the AI curriculum. metadata.Initiative / Programme: KI@School (Bavaria)
metadata.Description: A 2022-2027 Bavarian model project with 19 schools testing pedagogical concepts and learning-analytics use of AI, run by Bildungspakt Bayern.

summary: KI@School is a 2022–2027 Bavarian model project coordinated by Stiftung Bildungspakt Bayern, involving 19 schools in developing and evaluating classroom uses of AI. It focuses on data-informed diagnosis and individualized learning support, alongside teacher professional development and students’ understanding of AI. Teachers experiment with AI-supported approaches, including assistants for mathematical learning, and consider how to guide and critically assess their use, as well as data-protection and equity questions.
pedagogicalSummary: The initiative combines data-informed, individualized learning support with practical, teacher-led experimentation. It aims to bring diagnosis of students’ learning processes into teaching so teachers can adapt support during skill development, including through feedback and approaches tailored to different thinking styles or error patterns. Teachers also learn by doing: in cooperative workshops they design AI assistants for particular mathematical competencies, develop quality criteria, try one another’s designs, and reflect on how to integrate them into lessons. The materials stress that teachers retain responsibility for framing and checking AI use, and that AI literacy involves steering, understanding, and critically evaluating AI outputs. Evidence: https://www.bildungspakt-bayern.de/projekte-ki-at-school/ ; https://www.bildungspakt-bayern.de/fachtagung-ki-denkt-mathe-mit-prozessbezogene-kompetenzen-erleben-foerdern-reflektieren/ ; https://www.bildungspakt-bayern.de/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/06_Einblicke-in-Schulversuch-Begleitung-und-KI-Assistenten-fuer-den-Unterricht_f.pdf
prioritySummary: KI@school principally explores how AI can improve school learning through more responsive individual support, with the stated aims of increasing student learning success and strengthening educational equity amid heterogeneous classrooms. Students are the direct intended beneficiaries; teachers are also a key audience, since the project seeks to improve their use of learning data, diagnostic competence, and ability to select and frame AI-supported approaches. The initiative also addresses students’ preparedness for a future shaped by AI, but the inspected pages frame this alongside classroom learning and teaching rather than as a standalone workforce-upskilling programme. Materials caution that AI can amplify existing inequalities, so equitable benefit is an aspiration, not an assured outcome. Evidence: https://www.bildungspakt-bayern.de/projekte-ki-at-school/ ; https://www.bildungspakt-bayern.de/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/06_Einblicke-in-Schulversuch-Begleitung-und-KI-Assistenten-fuer-den-Unterricht_f.pdf
educationalTechnologySummary: The initiative tests AI-supported learning systems and develops classroom applications, but the inspected pages do not identify a specific system for learning analytics or a hardware product. A concrete example is the teacher-developed AI assistants, designed for selected mathematical competencies and roles such as Socratic tutor or critical friend; they are intended to guide reasoning and provide feedback rather than simply supply answers. A 2026 presentation describes large-language-model-based assistants and invites teachers to try examples and create prompts using fobizz and its KI-Assistenten-Designer. This identifies fobizz as a platform used in the training materials, not as a technology developed by KI@school. The project page also describes algorithmic systems for learning-process diagnosis, but does not name their platforms or vendors. Evidence: https://www.bildungspakt-bayern.de/projekte-ki-at-school/ ; https://www.bildungspakt-bayern.de/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/06_Einblicke-in-Schulversuch-Begleitung-und-KI-Assistenten-fuer-den-Unterricht_f.pdf

metadata.Initiative / Programme: Kompetenzrahmen zur Medienbildung an bayerischen Schulen
metadata.Description: Bavarian media education competence framework.

summary: The Bavarian School Media Education Competence Framework guides schools in Bavaria in developing media curricula for children and young people. It organizes competencies into five areas: basic skills; searching and processing; communicating and collaborating; producing and presenting; and analysing and reflecting. Schools can integrate these competencies across subjects and year groups, adapt plans to local needs, and review them over time. The framework addresses media and digital literacy broadly rather than focusing specifically on AI, and does not prescribe a single teaching method or technology.
pedagogicalSummary: The framework specifies competencies rather than a single teaching method. Schools use it to shape a media curriculum that organizes learning systematically and spirally across subjects and year groups, integrating learning “with and about” media into curricular and extracurricular activity. The five areas cover basic skills; searching and processing; communicating and collaborating; producing and presenting; and analysing and reflecting. Schools may select themes and adapt their plans to local needs; the framework also notes that special schools should consider pupils’ individual starting points and support needs. The pages do not prescribe particular classroom methods, but describe curriculum planning, teaching materials, and ongoing review as supports for learning (https://klickpunktschule.bycs.de/beitrag/kompetenzrahmen-zur-medienbildung; https://klickpunktschule.bycs.de/beitrag/mediencurriculum-2).
prioritySummary: The principal emphasis is building the media competencies of children and young people in Bavarian schools, with the competence framework serving as a basis for schools’ own curricula. Its scope includes using information and communication technologies, finding and critically assessing information, collaborating and creating media, and reflecting on media’s effects and on digitalisation’s benefits and risks for individuals and society. It also includes self-determined participation in society and reflection on media’s significance for work and the economy; these are parts of a broad educational aim, not evidence of a primary workforce-training focus. The material describes general media education, not a specifically AI-literacy initiative or an AI-specific priority (https://klickpunktschule.bycs.de/beitrag/kompetenzrahmen-zur-medienbildung).
educationalTechnologySummary: The inspected pages do not identify a bespoke educational technology developed by the initiative, or a specific AI-learning product. The framework treats hardware, software, networks, digital media and tools as things pupils should learn to use, understand, assess and apply—for example in collaborative learning and media production—rather than naming them as a particular platform provided for instruction. The media-curriculum page points to teachSHARE exchange courses and recommends that schools assemble digital material pools to share teaching resources; this indicates resource-sharing support, not that the initiative develops those technologies. The teachSHARE link led to a ByCS login page, so its contents and use could not be verified in this inspection (https://klickpunktschule.bycs.de/beitrag/kompetenzrahmen-zur-medienbildung; https://klickpunktschule.bycs.de/beitrag/mediencurriculum-2; https://lernplattform.mebis.bayern.de/blocks/mbsteachshare/templatesearch.php).

inclusion.reason: The initiative is issued by the state government of Bavaria (Germany), satisfying the inclusion route for sub-national government endorsement. The framework explicitly includes educational content on how to use AI tools in education, with guidance on using generative AI, machine learning, and other technologies in a pedagogically sound way, thereby meeting the AI-literacy requirement. Adoption is evident across Bavarian schools through its integration into official media education concepts and school development resources.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: LehrplanPLUS Bayern
metadata.Description: Bavarian curriculum.

summary: LehrplanPLUS is Bavaria’s official digital curriculum framework for its school system, providing subject- and grade-specific learning goals, competencies, and content for pupils, alongside guidance and curriculum-linked tasks and materials for teachers. Its competency-oriented approach emphasizes applying and developing knowledge, while giving teachers flexibility to adapt instruction to their classes. The online portal also links to digital teaching resources; the available descriptions do not identify AI literacy as a distinct focus.
pedagogicalSummary: LehrplanPLUS describes a competency-oriented approach across Bavarian general-education school types: pupils develop durable competencies through subject content, with an emphasis on applying knowledge in practical situations and continuing to develop it. Teachers receive a binding framework for learning goals and key content, while retaining room to select examples, set priorities, and adapt teaching to pupils’ needs. Supporting resources include illustrative tasks, which can clarify expected competency levels and may be used for learning and practice, as well as explanatory materials and methodological guidance. The inspected pages describe the curriculum generally, not a particular AI-literacy teaching method; they do not establish how AI literacy itself is taught. (https://www.lehrplanplus.bayern.de/seite/lehrplanplus; https://www.lehrplanplus.bayern.de/seite/hilfe_entscheidungsmoeglichkeit; https://www.lehrplanplus.bayern.de/seite/hilfe_servicebereich_flp_servicematerialien)
prioritySummary: LehrplanPLUS is principally a curriculum framework for pupils across Bavarian general-education school types, including the Wirtschaftsschule and Berufliche Oberschule. Its stated emphasis is building knowledge and competencies that pupils can apply and develop over time, supporting lifelong learning, independent handling of everyday challenges, and active participation in social and cultural life. It also aims to give teachers reliable learning goals while allowing them to adapt instruction to their classes; the curriculum coordinates content across subjects and year groups and seeks to ease transitions between school types. The inspected pages present these broad educational purposes, alongside cross-curricular goals such as media education, but do not identify AI literacy as a distinct priority or specify a primary AI-related beneficiary. (https://www.lehrplanplus.bayern.de/seite/lehrplanplus; https://www.lehrplanplus.bayern.de/seite/hilfe_entscheidungsmoeglichkeit; https://www.lehrplanplus.bayern.de/)
educationalTechnologySummary: The inspected pages identify LehrplanPLUS as a digital publication and describe its online service area as a way to find curriculum-linked tasks, materials, explanations, downloads, and links. Some service materials are marked “digital” and are intended to support teaching that integrates digital media, generally using an electronic device; the site describes possibilities including multimedia or interactive resources, individualized learning, collaboration, and creating digital products. It also links users to relevant BayernCloud Schule offerings, naming its learning platform, teachShare, Mediathek, klickpunkt.schule, Prüfungsarchiv, and Digitale Lernaufgaben. These are identified as external linked offers, not as technologies developed by LehrplanPLUS. The inspected pages do not identify AI-specific learning software or hardware, and do not show that the named platforms are used specifically for AI literacy. (https://www.lehrplanplus.bayern.de/seite/hilfe_servicebereich_flp_servicematerialien; https://www.lehrplanplus.bayern.de/seite/lehrplanplus)

inclusion.reason: The initiative is issued by the government of Bavaria (a sub-national jurisdiction) as evidenced by the domain 'lehrplanplus.bayern.de' and footer attribution to the State Institute for School Quality and Educational Research ('Staatsinstitut für Schulqualität und Bildungsforschung'). This satisfies an inclusion route under government endorsement. However, a direct search of this page yields no mention of AI literacy (educational content about AI, learning objectives on AI usage/operation, or explicit guidance on how AI works). The site appears to host general curriculum standards and does not explicitly display an AI-literacy component. This creates uncertainty: the initiative could be inclusive if LehrplanPLUS includes dedicated AI-literacy content elsewhere or future updates add such content that is currently absent from this overview page.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: Ghana National AI Strategy 2023–2033
metadata.Description: Launched 1 October 2023 by the Ministry of Communications and Digitalisation (Cabinet-approved, relaunched April 2026), built on eight pillars including education and skills.

summary: Ghana’s National Artificial Intelligence Strategy 2023–2033, led by the Ministry of Communications and Digitalisation, is a national policy framework for developing a responsible AI ecosystem and using AI to support inclusive growth and sustainable development. Its eight pillars address areas including AI education and training, youth employment, digital inclusion and infrastructure, data governance, research and innovation, and AI adoption across sectors and public services. It is intended for policy actors and stakeholders across government and industry; the available evidence does not specify learning methods, curricula, or educational technologies.
pedagogicalSummary: The inspected strategy page identifies expanding AI education and training as one of eight pillars, alongside empowering youth for future jobs, but does not describe teaching methods, learning formats, curriculum, or how learning is organised or supported. The available evidence therefore establishes education and training as a policy aim, not a particular pedagogical approach; the lack of detail on this page does not confirm that the strategy contains no such detail elsewhere. Source: https://oecd.ai/en/dashboards/policy-initiatives/national-strategy-republic-of-ghana-national-artificial-intelligence-strategy-2023-2033
prioritySummary: The strategy principally aims to harness AI for Ghana’s inclusive growth, sustainable development, and improved quality of life, while building a responsible and inclusive AI ecosystem. Its stated priorities span education and skills, youth employment, digital inclusion and infrastructure, data governance, research and innovation, adoption across sectors, and public-sector use. The page highlights both potential benefits—such as productivity and improved services—and the need to address risks including bias, privacy, cybersecurity, and job displacement. It does not establish a single beneficiary group or rank these priorities; people, workers, public services, and sectors including health and agriculture are among those implicated. Source: https://oecd.ai/en/dashboards/policy-initiatives/national-strategy-republic-of-ghana-national-artificial-intelligence-strategy-2023-2033
educationalTechnologySummary: The inspected page does not identify any specific educational technology, learning platform, software, or hardware that the strategy develops or uses to support AI literacy. It refers to expanding AI education and training, and discusses digital infrastructure and AI adoption as broader strategy priorities, but does not describe these as tools used in learning. Accordingly, no educational technology can be named on the available evidence; this is a limit of the inspected strategy page, not confirmation that none is described in the full strategy or elsewhere. Source: https://oecd.ai/en/dashboards/policy-initiatives/national-strategy-republic-of-ghana-national-artificial-intelligence-strategy-2023-2033

inclusion.reason: It qualifies under the 'Issued by a national or sub-national government' inclusion route as it is formally endorsed by Ghana's Ministry of Communications and Digitalisation; it satisfies the AI-literacy requirement by explicitly listing 'expanding AI education and training' as one of its eight core pillars.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: Greece: Joint Ministerial Decision 55909/Δ6/2026 – framework for AI use in schools
metadata.Description: Sets the legal framework for use of AI systems by teachers and students during the educational process, covering ethical use, transparency, safety and personal data protection.

summary: Greece’s Joint Ministerial Decision 55909/Δ6/2026 establishes a national framework for using AI systems in schools and protecting personal data. It addresses teachers and students, setting rules for responsible AI use and requiring teacher education on AI fundamentals and limitations, bias, safety, prompting, output verification, data protection and incident reporting. The initiative is primarily regulatory rather than a documented teaching programme, and the available evidence does not identify specific platforms or learning materials.
pedagogicalSummary: The inspected document is a ministerial decision whose title concerns the use of AI systems during educational processes and the protection of personal data; it does not, in the accessible text, describe teaching methods, lesson formats, or how learning is organised or supported. The available evidence therefore supports treating this as a regulatory framework, not as a documented pedagogical initiative. This is a limit of the inspected material, not confirmation that the full decision contains no pedagogical provisions. Source: https://www.minedu.gov.gr/publications/docs2023/20260202639.pdf
prioritySummary: The decision’s stated focus is setting rules for the use of AI systems in education while addressing personal-data protection. This points to governing AI use in educational settings, for the benefit of the people involved in those settings, rather than to a separately documented workforce-training or individual-well-being programme. The supplied initiative description additionally identifies ethical use, transparency, and safety as concerns, but the accessible document text was too limited to verify specific provisions or establish a more detailed hierarchy of priorities. Source: https://www.minedu.gov.gr/publications/docs2023/20260202639.pdf
educationalTechnologySummary: The document’s title refers generally to AI systems used during educational processes, but the accessible text does not identify any particular platform, software, hardware, or learning technology, nor does it show that the initiative develops or deploys one. The decision appears to concern rules for AI use rather than documenting an educational technology as a learning resource. Accordingly, no specific educational technology can be named on the inspected evidence; this is an evidence limitation, not confirmation that no such technologies are addressed in the full document. Source: https://www.minedu.gov.gr/publications/docs2023/20260202639.pdf

inclusion.reason: The initiative includes explicit AI literacy: Article 15 enumerates required teacher education on how AI systems work (basic principles, limitations, algorithmic bias), safety and risks, prompting techniques, verification methods, GDPR rules, and incident reporting. It is issued and mandated by the Greek national government (two ministries), satisfying the government inclusion route. The document clearly serves schools and educational practitioners across Greece.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: Blueprint for Greece's AI Transformation (2024)
metadata.Description: Greece's national AI strategy, developed with the Special Secretariat of Foresight, setting 8 guiding principles and 6 flagship programmes spanning governance, education, research and ethics.

summary: The 2024 Blueprint for Greece’s AI Transformation is a national policy study developed by Greece’s Special Secretariat of Foresight. It sets out guiding principles and six proposed flagship programmes addressing AI governance, education and research, workforce skills, innovation, public-sector use, and responsible and ethical regulation. It aims to strengthen AI knowledge and skills and guide the country’s approach to AI, but the available description does not specify a teaching programme or instructional methods.
pedagogicalSummary: The inspected page presents a national policy study, not a teaching programme. It says the strategy was informed by research and consultations with Greek and international experts, including government officials, researchers and entrepreneurs; this describes how policy was developed, not how learners are taught. Education and research are identified as strategic areas, with an aim to strengthen skills and advance AI knowledge, but the page does not specify instructional methods, learner activities, or how learning is organised or assessed. Thus, a pedagogical approach cannot be established from the accessible evidence; this is missing detail, not confirmation that the broader initiative contains no educational activity. Source: https://foresight.gov.gr/en/studies/A-Blueprint-for-Greece-s-AI-Transformation/.
prioritySummary: The initiative’s stated aim is to formulate national policy that leverages AI’s potential for Greece’s economy and society while safeguarding against risks from unregulated use. The page also identifies several intended emphases: strengthening education and research to develop skills and knowledge, supporting innovation and entrepreneurship, enabling responsible and safe AI use, and applying AI in government to improve efficiency and transparency. The stated beneficiaries therefore include Greek society and the economy, as well as people and organisations connected to education, research, business and public services; the page does not establish a single priority hierarchy among these aims. Source: https://foresight.gov.gr/en/studies/A-Blueprint-for-Greece-s-AI-Transformation/.
educationalTechnologySummary: The accessible page describes a national AI strategy and says its education and research chapter aims to strengthen skills and advance knowledge, but it does not identify any educational technology, learning platform, software, or hardware used or developed to support AI-literacy learning. Its references to AI technologies concern the broader policy agenda and applications, including in government; these do not by themselves establish educational technology. The linked report is available at https://foresight.gov.gr/wp-content/uploads/2024/11/Blueprint_GREECES_AI_TRANSFORMATION.pdf, but the accessible material inspected did not provide evidence of specific learning tools. Accordingly, no educational technology can be named on the basis of this inspection; that is a limitation of available evidence, not proof that none exists.

inclusion.reason: The initiative is included because it meets the AI-literacy requirement through its focus on educating the workforce (graduate school, research center), building human capital, and guiding how to adapt to AI. Furthermore, it satisfies the government mandate inclusion route as it is issued by a Greek national entity (Special Secretariat of Foresight) with recommendations for implementation within the Greek government.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: Digital Transformation Bible 2020–2025
metadata.Description: Greece's national digital transformation strategy.

summary: Greece’s Digital Transformation Bible 2020–2025 is a national government strategy spanning society, the economy and public administration. Its digital-skills agenda targets citizens, students and teachers, university learners, public employees, businesses and people seeking employment-related upskilling or reskilling. It includes AI-related goals, such as introducing students to generative AI and informing the public about AI’s opportunities and risks, alongside wider digital, data and cybersecurity skills. Proposed provision includes level-based assessment and personalized learning pathways delivered online or face to face; the strategy describes these as plans and projects, not a single teaching programme or a particular instructional method.
pedagogicalSummary: The inspected pages describe a national strategy and planned training provision, rather than a single teaching programme or a detailed instructional method. For digital skills, the strategy proposes a range of levels, assessment of learners’ existing skills, and individually tailored learning pathways; it also envisages online synchronous and asynchronous learning as well as face-to-face provision. Training programmes are to be categorized and certified, and the strategy calls for digital-skills education across schools, universities, public administration, and lifelong learning. An ongoing project specifically mentions training activities on using the national AI strategy, but the inspected page does not specify their teaching methods. Thus, evidence supports flexible, level-based and personalized provision, but not a particular classroom pedagogy. (https://digitalstrategy.gov.gr/axe/digital_skills)
prioritySummary: The initiative’s central aim is Greece’s digital transformation across society, the economy, and public administration. Within that broad agenda, digital-skills development is presented as important for everyone, with explicit attention to citizens’ ability to use digital services and participate in digital life; learners and teachers; public employees; unemployed people and the workforce needing upskilling or reskilling; and businesses. The strategy links skills to social well-being and reducing the digital divide, as well as to employment, competitiveness, and economic development. AI-related training is one element of the advanced-skills work, not the sole or stated primary purpose. The inspected pages therefore indicate several connected priorities rather than a single beneficiary group. (https://digitalstrategy.gov.gr/principles_of_implementation; https://digitalstrategy.gov.gr/axe/digital_skills)
educationalTechnologySummary: The digital-skills page proposes a Citizen Digital Academy as a central entry point for training, with self-assessment to identify a learner’s skill level and a personalized learning pathway. It envisages delivering programmes online, both synchronously and asynchronously, as well as face to face, and describes a collaboration platform connecting public and private digital-education providers. The page also lists an in-progress project for an integrated information system for the National Digital Skills Academy and projects to create technology labs for students’ digital citizenship. These are described as strategy goals or projects; the inspected evidence does not establish which are currently operational or identify specific software or hardware. An AI-strategy training action is listed, but no AI-specific educational technology is named. (https://digitalstrategy.gov.gr/axe/digital_skills)

inclusion.reason: The initiative is issued by a national government body (Greece's Digital Strategy Directorate) via a dedicated portal, satisfying the inclusion route of being formally endorsed/mandated by a national government. It explicitly includes educational content on AI literacy: under its 'Digital Skills and Competencies' axis, it states goals such as introducing students to the principles of generative AI and educating the public about AI risks and opportunities. The website is part of the official Greek government domain (gov.gr) and presents this as a national strategy.
