metadata.Initiative / Programme: IEP "Artificial Intelligence: New horizons in teaching and learning" (2026)
metadata.Description: Online seminar co-organised by the Institute of Educational Policy and the Epirus Regional Education Directorate on pedagogically sound, responsible use of AI in teaching and learning.

summary: “Artificial Intelligence: New Horizons in Teaching and Learning” is a 20-hour online professional-development seminar co-organised by Greece’s Institute of Educational Policy and the Epirus Regional Education Directorate. It is intended for primary and secondary teachers and education-support professionals. Across a two-month programme, it combines foundational AI concepts, practical applications for lesson planning, differentiated teaching and educational-material creation, and discussion of AI’s social, pedagogical and ethical implications. Sessions include presentations and a round-table discussion; participants receive a certificate of attendance.
pedagogicalSummary: The seminar uses a professional-development approach that combines theoretical understanding of AI with practical applications, authentic examples from educational practice, and learning scenarios. Its published programme also includes presentations and a round-table discussion, offering opportunities to consider pedagogical and ethical questions; it does not specify hands-on exercises or how participants’ learning is assessed. The stated focus is on educators’ pedagogically meaningful and responsible use of AI in teaching and learning, rather than on a detailed teaching method for students. The announcement and programme provide the available evidence, but do not describe the sessions’ activities in depth (https://www.iep.edu.gr/techniti-noimosyni-neoi-orizontes-sti-didaskalia-kai-sti-mathisi/; https://www.iep.edu.gr/wp-content/uploads/2026/02/2026-02-13_%CE%A0%CE%A1%CE%9F%CE%93%CE%A1%CE%91%CE%9C%CE%9C%CE%91.pdf).
prioritySummary: The initiative principally aims to help school educators understand and responsibly apply AI in teaching and learning. The announcement highlights familiarisation with basic AI concepts and applications that may support lesson design, differentiated teaching, and creation of digital educational materials. It also emphasizes reflection on AI’s social, pedagogical, and ethical implications in school settings. The intended participants include primary and secondary teachers across subjects and levels, as well as specified specialist and support education staff; the seminar is not presented as workforce training outside education or as an initiative primarily targeting students directly. These priorities are described in the seminar announcement and programme (https://www.iep.edu.gr/techniti-noimosyni-neoi-orizontes-sti-didaskalia-kai-sti-mathisi/; https://www.iep.edu.gr/wp-content/uploads/2026/02/2026-02-13_%CE%A0%CE%A1%CE%9F%CE%93%CE%A1%CE%91%CE%9C%CE%9C%CE%91.pdf).
educationalTechnologySummary: The announcement refers generally to digital AI tools and applications that educators may explore for lesson planning, differentiated teaching, and creating digital educational materials, but it does not name particular products, platforms, or hardware, nor establish that the organisers developed them. The programme includes a session on the pedagogical and ethical framework for developing an educational chatbot; this indicates a topic for discussion, not evidence that the initiative itself develops or deploys a chatbot. The seminar is delivered remotely, but the inspected pages do not identify the conferencing platform or describe it as a learning technology beyond enabling online attendance. Thus, specific technologies used or developed to support participants’ learning could not be established from the available pages (https://www.iep.edu.gr/techniti-noimosyni-neoi-orizontes-sti-didaskalia-kai-sti-mathisi/; https://www.iep.edu.gr/wp-content/uploads/2026/02/2026-02-13_%CE%A0%CE%A1%CE%9F%CE%93%CE%A1%CE%91%CE%9C%CE%9C%CE%91.pdf).

inclusion.reason: The initiative qualifies for inclusion because it is issued/endorsed by a Greek government statutory body (the Institute of Educational Policy). It explicitly includes AI literacy through its focus on 'pedagogically sound, responsible use of AI', which indicates educational content about using AI in teaching and learning. The seminar description confirms it addresses AI usage rather than just employing AI tools.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: "GenAI Empowered Educators" programme (2025)
metadata.Description: Free distance-learning programme by The Tipping Point and IEP training Greek teachers on responsible generative-AI use in class, expanding from 535 educators in 2024-25 to 1,000 in 2025-26.

summary: “GenAI Empowered Educators” is a free, 50-hour distance-learning programme in Greece for active primary and secondary teachers, run by The Tipping Point with stated involvement from the Institute of Educational Policy. It combines instructional videos, asynchronous and live online learning, and practical activities using GenAI tools and the wiserwork platform. The programme focuses on understanding and using generative AI effectively and responsibly in teaching, including evaluating its limitations and guiding students’ use. It offers a completion certificate and has expanded across successive cohorts, with reported participation of more than 1,500 educators and planned cohorts of up to 1,000.
pedagogicalSummary: The program combines theoretical study with practical learning by doing. Its stated activities include instructional videos introducing generative AI concepts and tools, asynchronous and live online training, hands-on activities, and real-world examples; participants also practise applying their knowledge through the wiserwork platform. The stated focus includes building educators’ skills in communicating with GenAI tools, while participant accounts and reported outcomes point to critical evaluation and practical classroom use. The site describes a 50-hour distance-learning program but gives limited detail about the content of all three listed training topics or the design of particular activities. (https://www.genaieducation.gr/home-en; https://www.genaieducation.gr/home)
prioritySummary: The central emphasis is to equip active primary and secondary teachers in Greece to use generative AI effectively and responsibly in their educational work. The program aims to strengthen educators’ skills and professional role, help them navigate the opportunities and challenges of GenAI, and enable them to guide students toward a healthy relationship with the technology. The site also describes wider intended benefits: teachers sharing knowledge and innovation within school communities, improved educational experiences, and a contribution to local communities and future generations. These are presented alongside teacher development rather than as evidence of a separate primary beneficiary. (https://www.genaieducation.gr/home-en; https://www.genaieducation.gr/home)
educationalTechnologySummary: The site identifies the wiserwork platform as a technology used for practical application of learning; it describes the platform as combining GenAI capabilities with human experience and knowledge. It also says educators watch instructional videos and learn about main GenAI tools that may be used in teaching, learning, and related work, but does not name those tools or establish that the initiative develops them. The program uses distance-learning formats, including asynchronous and live online training, although the specific learning-management or video-conferencing software is not identified. The inspected pages therefore support a named platform and video-based learning, but provide limited detail about their technical features or other educational technologies. (https://www.genaieducation.gr/home-en; https://www.genaieducation.gr/home)

inclusion.reason: The initiative clearly contains AI literacy: its learning objectives include understanding capabilities/limitations of GenAI, responsible use, avoiding inaccuracies, integrating 21st-century skills, and practical instruction in using AI tools. It has strong inclusion evidence via national scale adoption across Greek schools (over 1,500 educators and ~40,000 students), and is explicitly framed as a national program for the Greek educational community, indicating endorsement and involvement of the Greek state.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: 13 Innovation Centres (one per Regional Directorate of Education)
metadata.Description: Ministry of Education initiative establishing 13 Innovation Centres, one per Regional Education Directorate, operating from school year 2025-2026 and integrating AI, robotics, XR and STEM.

summary: Greece’s Ministry of Education is establishing a network of 13 Innovation Centres, one for each Regional Directorate of Education, announced to begin operating in the 2025–2026 school year. The centres are designed to offer primary and secondary students curriculum-connected, hands-on programmes and to support teachers through training and teaching resources. Their broad focus spans STEM and digital literacy, including AI and machine learning, robotics, programming, and extended reality, using equipment such as robots, sensors, 3D printers, and VR/AR devices. The programme framework emphasizes inquiry-based, experiential and collaborative learning, with activities, worksheets and assessment suggestions; online resources and a virtual centre are also described, including planned remote access for schools.
pedagogicalSummary: The initiative organizes age-appropriate, informal educational programs around visits to its Innovation Centres, with learning connected to primary and secondary school curricula. Programs use a common structure: clear learning objectives, suggested activities before, during and after a visit, worksheets, assessment suggestions and supporting materials. The initiative explicitly identifies inquiry-based, experiential and collaborative learning, alongside creativity, problem-solving and interdisciplinary connections. Its broader framework also describes learning through investigation, practical engagement with technology and interaction with experts beyond the classroom. These approaches are the pedagogy; AI, robotics and XR are topics and tools used within it. The inspected pages describe the intended design, but do not establish how consistently every Centre implements it (https://ic.cti.gr/el/psifiako-yliko/ekpaideftika-programmata.html; https://ic.cti.gr/el/about/epistimoniko-plaisio.html).
prioritySummary: The initiative principally aims to give primary and secondary students learning opportunities in STEM, digital literacy and emerging technologies, while also supporting teachers through training and teaching resources. It emphasizes creativity, 21st-century skills, scientific inquiry and preparation for participation in a digitally changing society; its stated longer-term aims include encouraging further STEM study and strengthening the country’s science and technology workforce. The network is also presented as a way to improve educational equality and access to technology learning, including through virtual provision for remote and hard-to-reach schools. It connects schools with universities, research institutions, local communities and businesses. The pages present these priorities together rather than establishing a single dominant outcome (https://www.minedu.gov.gr/site/62046-07-07-25-idrysi-13-kentron-kainotomias-mia-stratigiki-ependysi-sto-mellon-tis-ekpaidefsis; https://ic.cti.gr/el/about/ta-kentra-kainotomias.html).
educationalTechnologySummary: The initiative equips physical Centres with learning technologies and develops educational programs and materials to use them. Identified equipment includes VR headsets such as Meta Quest 3, Magic Leap 2 augmented-reality glasses, robotic arms and programmable robots, Arduino and Raspberry Pi boards, sensors, 3D printers, laser cutters, laptops and tablets. These support activities in AI, machine learning, robotics, IoT, XR, programming, experimentation and digital fabrication; the pages also name Scratch and Python for programming. Digital infrastructure includes a Virtual Innovation Centre with a tour, a digital repository and a collaboration platform. The site says the virtual centre currently provides access to these resources and plans future virtual access to Centres for remote schools. The inspected pages do not identify a proprietary AI-learning application (https://ic.cti.gr/el/about/xoroi-mathisis.html; https://ic.cti.gr/el/about/diathesimos-eksoplismos/ektetameni-pragmatikotita-xr.html; https://ic.cti.gr/el/about/diathesimos-eksoplismos/robotics.html; https://ic.cti.gr/el/).

inclusion.reason: The initiative qualifies for inclusion based on two criteria: it is formally endorsed and funded by a national government body (the Ministry of Education of Greece), satisfying the 'Issued, funded, mandated, or formally endorsed by a national or sub-national government' route. Additionally, the summary confirms the presence of AI literacy elements as the centres are explicitly tasked with integrating AI into education, implying educational content regarding its use. The initiative targets the entire national system (13 Regional Directorates), indicating system-scale adoption rather than a single-institution project.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: Pilot programme "Introduction of AI in Schools" (incl. ChatGPT Edu)
metadata.Description: Ministry pilot introducing the ChatGPT Edu platform in 20 Greek lyceums (14 model/experimental and 6 Onassis schools), with teacher training in Oct-Nov 2025 and student access from Dec 2025.

summary: The Greek Ministry of Education’s pilot is designed to introduce ChatGPT Edu in 20 lyceums, serving teachers and upper-secondary students. Its staged approach includes teacher training, ongoing support and self-paced materials to help educators design subject-specific activities and customized GPTs, with students’ use intended to be gradual and teacher-guided. The programme emphasizes responsible use, critical thinking and creativity, alongside privacy, safety, copyright and plagiarism concerns. Materials describe planned supports and stages; they do not establish how consistently these were delivered or their outcomes.
pedagogicalSummary: The initiative describes a staged, teacher-led approach rather than a single teaching method. Selected school “GenAI Ambassadors” receive an introductory session, followed by teacher training, continuing support, practical activities, subject-specific examples and self-paced video modules. Teachers are then supported to design classroom activities and, in a later stage, guide students’ individual assignments and projects using tailored tools. The stated learning aims include critical thinking, creativity, collaboration and responsible use; the document proposes gradual, supervised integration into teaching, not simply access to an AI tool. Student participation and teacher participation are described as voluntary. The public materials outline the stages and intended supports but do not establish how consistently they were delivered in practice. (https://edugpt.sch.gr/docs/guidesAIedu.pdf; https://edugpt.sch.gr/features.php)
prioritySummary: The initiative’s central emphasis is building educators’ capacity to introduce generative AI into secondary-school teaching and learning, with students as a further intended beneficiary. It aims to help teachers use AI responsibly and effectively for lesson preparation, individualized learning, new teaching approaches and some administrative tasks, and to support students’ gradual use of AI for learning. The programme also stresses ethical, creative and pedagogically useful use, including attention to privacy, digital safety, minors’ mental health, copyright and plagiarism. It is a pilot in 20 listed schools, and its materials frame teachers as agents of change. The documents describe aims and planned stages, rather than evidence of measured outcomes or relative priority among these goals. (https://edugpt.sch.gr/features.php; https://edugpt.sch.gr/docs/guidesAIedu.pdf; https://edugpt.sch.gr/schools.php)
educationalTechnologySummary: The specifically identified learning platform is ChatGPT Edu, which the programme says it will introduce in participating schools. Teachers are to learn to use it and create subject- or task-tailored Custom GPTs as learning tools; the later student-focused stage describes controlled access to teacher-supported Custom GPTs for individual work and projects. The plan also identifies asynchronous video modules and digital supporting materials, such as examples and activity templates, for teacher learning and classroom design. These materials distinguish the platform used from the customized tools teachers are expected to create. The documents do not identify other learning software or hardware, and the website itself is primarily an information and participation portal, not evidence of an educational technology used for instruction. Student access is described as planned, with some details subject to later assessment. (https://edugpt.sch.gr/docs/guidesAIedu.pdf; https://edugpt.sch.gr/docs.php)

inclusion.reason: The initiative includes AI literacy through the provision of educational guidance (e.g., 'guides for responsible use'), official documentation on data privacy, and structured teacher training sessions. It qualifies under the INCLUSION ROUTE of being issued and formally mandated by a national government (the Greek Ministry of Education), with explicit participation across multiple public schools and published official decrees (FEK).

metadata.Initiative / Programme: Skills Labs (Εργαστήρια Δεξιοτήτων) & IEP curriculum modernisation
metadata.Description: Skills Labs cross-curricular programme and new curricula by the Institute of Educational Policy.

summary: The Institute of Educational Policy (IEP), an educational research institution supporting Greece’s Ministry of Education, develops school curricula and supports teacher training. Its Skills Labs provide a cross-curricular framework for skills-development programmes and related educational materials, while its curriculum-modernisation work makes new programmes of study and guidance available to educators. School-age learners are the intended beneficiaries, with teachers supporting delivery. The inspected descriptions do not establish a specific teaching method, AI-literacy emphasis, or AI tool used in instruction.
pedagogicalSummary: The inspected pages do not provide enough detail to identify a specific teaching method for the Skills Labs or the new curricula. The Skills Labs page says that educational materials called Skills Cultivation Programmes may be submitted for approval for use in the labs, and provides a guide and application materials; it does not explain classroom activities, sequencing, or how learning is assessed. The new-curricula page lists curriculum materials and presentation videos but gives no account of their pedagogy in the accessible text. Thus, the evidence confirms a curriculum-and-materials framework, but not a particular instructional approach; this is a limit of the pages inspected, not evidence that no approach exists. Sources: https://www.iep.edu.gr/ergastiria-dexiotiton/ and https://www.iep.edu.gr/nea-programmata-spoudon/
prioritySummary: IEP describes its central institutional purpose as supporting Greece’s Ministry of Education and supervised bodies on primary and secondary education, teacher training, transitions between education levels, and addressing educational inequalities, student dropout, and early school leaving, with the stated aim of safeguarding every child’s right to education. The site also presents Skills Labs and new curricula as parts of its education-facing work: the Skills Labs page concerns educational programmes for use in the labs, while the curricula page provides access to new curriculum materials. The accessible evidence therefore points to broad school-system and learner benefit, alongside support for educators; it does not establish a narrower AI-literacy priority or rank these aims. Sources: https://www.iep.edu.gr/ and https://www.iep.edu.gr/ergastiria-dexiotiton/
educationalTechnologySummary: The inspected Skills Labs page describes approved educational materials and an online proposal-submission process, but does not identify a learning platform, software, device, or AI tool used by students or teachers in the labs. The new-curricula page offers access to curriculum materials and presentation videos, without showing that these technologies are themselves used to teach AI literacy. IEP’s homepage separately mentions a digital supplementary Informatics textbook and a digital platform for comments on textbooks, but the inspected evidence does not connect either to Skills Labs or to AI-literacy instruction. Accordingly, no educational technology supporting AI literacy can be identified from these pages; that is an evidence gap, not confirmation that none is used. Sources: https://www.iep.edu.gr/ergastiria-dexiotiton/, https://www.iep.edu.gr/nea-programmata-spoudon/, and https://www.iep.edu.gr/

inclusion.reason: Inclusion via government connection (IEP supports the Greek Ministry); plausible cross-curricular reach; AI-literacy content status uncertain due to truncated homepage text but screened as included per inclusive criteria.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: Hungary AI Strategy (2025)
metadata.Description: Renewed government AI strategy with pillars incl. regulation, infrastructure and education/skills development.

summary: Hungary’s 2025–2030 national AI strategy sets objectives for AI regulation, safety, infrastructure, applications and education and skills development. Its education agenda spans school-age learners (including responsible-use learning from grade 5), teachers and other education workers, higher education, and workforce and public AI education; the strategy aims to involve 2.5 million citizens in AI education. It also addresses AI adoption in business and public services and the protection of rights and personal data. The available evidence describes strategic goals, not specific teaching methods or learning materials.
pedagogicalSummary: The accessible PDF text identifies the document as Hungary’s AI Strategy for 2025–2030 and begins a contents page, but the inspected text does not reveal teaching activities or how learning is organized. Therefore, no particular pedagogical approach can be established; this is a limit of the available inspection, not evidence that the strategy contains no learning activities. Source: https://cdn.kormany.hu/uploads/document/c/c0/c0d/c0dfdbd37cfa520ae37361a168d244c85e7295af.pdf
prioritySummary: The document title establishes that this is a national AI strategy for 2025–2030. The supplied initiative description identifies regulation, infrastructure, and education/skills development as pillars, suggesting a broad national strategy rather than a single learner-focused intervention; the inspected PDF text did not expose enough detail to establish a hierarchy among these priorities or specify whose benefit is emphasized. Source: https://cdn.kormany.hu/uploads/document/c/c0/c0d/c0dfdbd37cfa520ae37361a168d244c85e7295af.pdf
educationalTechnologySummary: The inspected PDF text does not identify educational technologies, platforms, software, or hardware used or developed to support AI literacy. Its title and the visible start of its contents are insufficient to determine whether the strategy discusses such tools or learning infrastructure, so none can be named on this evidence; this is an evidence gap, not confirmation that none are used or developed. Source: https://cdn.kormany.hu/uploads/document/c/c0/c0d/c0dfdbd37cfa520ae37361a168d244c85e7295af.pdf

inclusion.reason: This initiative qualifies for inclusion because it is officially issued by the Hungarian national government (government domain, official state document). The metadata confirms it includes an education/skills development pillar alongside AI literacy components as stated. Under INCLUSION ROUTE #1, being issued by a national government is sufficient for inclusion regardless of whether I can see all educational content in detail from this partial PDF reading.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: IndiaAI Mission
metadata.Description: Government programme to build India's AI ecosystem incl. skills (IndiaAI FutureSkills).

summary: IndiaAI Mission is a Government of India programme to develop the country’s AI ecosystem across areas including skills, compute infrastructure, innovation, applications, and responsible AI. Its FutureSkills pillar serves students from undergraduate to doctoral levels and people preparing for AI careers through courses, fellowships, industry-aligned certification, and planned Data and AI Labs in Tier 2 and Tier 3 cities. The labs are intended to support hands-on experimentation with AI tools and datasets, problem-solving, and collaboration. The portal also offers AI learning resources and policy material, while platforms such as AIKosh provide access to datasets, models, and toolkits for experimentation and development.
pedagogicalSummary: The accessible description supports a mix of formal study, skills training, and practical learning, rather than a single stated teaching method. FutureSkills backs undergraduate through doctoral study with fellowships, and plans foundational courses through local Data and AI Labs in Tier 2 and Tier 3 cities. The labs are explicitly intended to provide hands-on exposure to tools and datasets, problem-solving, experimentation, and collaborative learning. The pillar also describes industry-aligned, NCVET-recognized certification courses for entry-level skills, with future modular and stackable pathways for different learners and domains. These are stated formats and learning supports; the inspected pages do not explain detailed lesson design, assessment, or how courses are taught. (https://indiaai.gov.in/hub/indiaai-futureskills)
prioritySummary: The initiative’s stated emphasis is building India’s AI talent pipeline while widening access to AI education. FutureSkills targets learners from undergraduate to doctoral levels, supports advanced study and research through fellowships, and aims to prepare people for entry-level AI careers through skills courses. Establishing Data and AI Labs in Tier 2 and Tier 3 cities is presented as a way to democratize access beyond major urban centres. The broader IndiaAI Mission frames these efforts within an inclusive AI ecosystem and socio-economic development, while the portal also offers resources and career insights for students, entrepreneurs, professionals, and executives. The inspected material therefore indicates both workforce and research-capacity development and broader access; it does not establish a more specific hierarchy among these priorities. (https://indiaai.gov.in/hub/indiaai-futureskills; https://indiaai.gov.in/; https://indiaai.gov.in/about-us)
educationalTechnologySummary: The clearest learning-related technologies identified are the planned Data and AI Labs, which FutureSkills says will give learners hands-on access to tools, datasets, and problem-solving environments; the page does not name specific lab hardware or software. The IndiaAI site also presents a Learning collection of AI courses and lists “Yuva AI for All” as a course, but the inspected pages do not establish which learning platform or software delivers it. AIKosh is a named digital platform for discovering and accessing datasets, models, and toolkits, designed to support experimentation and collaboration in AI development; it is described primarily as ecosystem/research infrastructure, not as a teaching platform. Thus, some digital and physical resources are identified, but details of instructional technology use remain limited. (https://indiaai.gov.in/hub/indiaai-futureskills; https://indiaai.gov.in/learning; https://indiaai.gov.in/hub/aikosh-platform)

inclusion.reason: The initiative is issued and funded by the Government of India (National-level government), which satisfies the INCLUSION ROUTE for government endorsement/funding. The portal includes an explicit 'Learning' section offering curated AI courses and resources, fulfilling the AI-literacy requirement with educational content about how to use AI tools and models.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: ISTE Standards
metadata.Description: ISTE standards for students, educators and leaders.

summary: The ISTE Standards, developed by the nonprofit International Society for Technology in Education, provide a framework for using technology in learning, teaching, coaching and educational leadership. They define competencies for students, educators, coaches, school leaders and higher-education faculty, emphasizing learner agency, digital citizenship, collaboration, problem-solving, computational thinking and equitable technology use. ISTE provides implementation guidance and professional-learning resources, including courses, ebooks and videos. The framework addresses educational technology broadly rather than focusing specifically on AI literacy.
pedagogicalSummary: The ISTE Standards are a framework for guiding learning and teaching, not a single prescribed course or method. The student standards support learner agency: students set or pursue goals, use feedback, investigate and evaluate information, design solutions, create, and collaborate. Educators are encouraged to design authentic, learner-driven activities, accommodate learner differences, facilitate student ownership, and use assessment data to guide progress. The framework also emphasizes peer collaboration and ongoing professional learning supported by coaches. These are recommended practices rather than evidence that every adopting school uses them. The inspected pages describe standards and implementation supports, but do not establish a specific pedagogy for AI literacy; the standards address technology broadly. (https://iste.org/standards/students; https://iste.org/standards/educators; https://iste.org/standards/coaches)
prioritySummary: The initiative’s central emphasis is to guide effective use of technology in education so that learning experiences are impactful and equitable, and students can develop skills to participate and thrive in a changing, connected world. It addresses students directly while also supporting educators, instructional coaches, school leaders, and higher-education faculty through competencies for teaching, professional growth, leadership, and system-level implementation. The pages also stress access, digital citizenship, student agency, and sustained improvement; the faculty standards mention preparing students for workforce demands, but the inspected evidence does not make workforce preparation the overarching priority. These standards are a broad technology-in-education framework, not demonstrably an AI-literacy initiative specifically. (https://iste.org/standards; https://iste.org/standards/education-leaders; https://iste.org/standards/faculty; https://iste.org/adopting-the-standards)
educationalTechnologySummary: The inspected standards pages do not name a particular app, device, AI system, or learning-management platform developed or used by ISTE. Instead, they describe technology generically: students may use digital tools and platforms to research, create, communicate, collaborate, and solve problems, while educators may use collaborative tools, technology-enabled assessments, and course-management systems. ISTE offers supporting learning materials, including online courses on the student and educator standards, ebooks, videos, and posters, but the pages inspected do not identify their delivery software or detail the course technology. The Learning Library lists AI-related articles and school case studies, not a named AI product used by ISTE for instruction. Thus, evidence supports broad guidance on educational technology and some digital learning resources, but not a specific technology stack. (https://iste.org/standards/students; https://iste.org/standards/educators; https://iste.org/learning-library)

inclusion.reason: The initiative includes explicit AI-related competencies (e.g., Computational Thinking under Student Standard 1.5) and offers educational content on using technologies and solving problems with digital tools, fulfilling the AI-literacy requirement. Additionally, ISTE is a non-government organization with evidence of system-scale adoption: its standards are used across thousands of schools worldwide, adopted into national curricula, and endorsed by many education systems (e.g., US, Europe). The site provides structured learning objectives and guidance on using technology/AI appropriately, satisfying the inclusion criteria through demonstrated widespread adoption.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: Guidance on Artificial Intelligence in Schools (Dept. of Education and Youth, 2025)
metadata.Description: Department guidance on safe, ethical, responsible use of AI in schools ("4P" approach).

summary: Guidance on Artificial Intelligence in Schools (2025) is an Irish Department of Education and Youth framework to help school leaders and teachers plan and govern AI use in teaching, learning, and school leadership. Its 4P approach emphasizes purposeful, planned, policy-aware and pedagogically appropriate use, while addressing AI benefits and risks, human oversight, transparency, bias, privacy, age restrictions, and student wellbeing. The guidance is supported by Oide resources, including an introductory online course, explainer videos, and examples of practice; it does not prescribe a student-facing curriculum or particular AI tool.
pedagogicalSummary: The initiative is principally school guidance rather than a prescribed classroom teaching programme: it offers a framework for schools to plan and govern AI use. Its 4P approach asks schools to establish a purpose, plan in alignment with existing school plans, review policies, and set expectations for practice. Practice should be curriculum-aligned, support learning, protect student wellbeing, and retain the teacher’s central role. Oide’s associated materials support educators through a short introductory online course, explainer videos, and examples of classroom practice. The inspected pages do not establish a particular student-facing pedagogy or a required teaching method; they emphasize responsible planning and teacher understanding instead. Sources: https://assets.gov.ie/static/documents/dee23cad/Guidance_on_Artificial_Intelligence_in_Schools_2025.pdf and https://www.oidetechnologyineducation.ie/ai-hub/guidance-on-artificial-intelligence-in-schools/ and https://www.oidetechnologyineducation.ie/onlinecourses/ai-for-schools/.
prioritySummary: The main emphasis is helping school leaders and teachers understand relevant considerations and make responsible decisions about AI in teaching, learning, and school leadership. The guidance recognizes potential benefits while addressing ethical and compliance challenges, and its 4P framework supports purposeful, planned, policy-aware implementation. It also emphasizes safeguarding student wellbeing and maintaining teachers’ central role. The companion introductory course is aimed at teachers and school leadership teams and covers what AI is, relevant policy documents, and ethical considerations. The inspected evidence therefore points chiefly to supporting schools and their staff, with student learning and wellbeing as important considerations; it does not identify workforce upskilling beyond the school-education context as a separate objective. Sources: https://www.oidetechnologyineducation.ie/ai-hub/guidance-on-artificial-intelligence-in-schools/ and https://www.oidetechnologyineducation.ie/onlinecourses/ai-for-schools/.
educationalTechnologySummary: The inspected materials identify digital learning resources, not a particular AI product required for classroom use. Oide’s AI in Schools Hub provides an introductory online course for teachers and school leaders, three short animated explainer videos about AI, generative AI, and algorithms, and links to examples of practice and the Department’s guidance. These resources support educator understanding and planning; the guidance itself is a PDF document. The course page also links to Slido and Padlet privacy information in its requirements, indicating possible use of these platforms in the course, though the inspected text does not explain their precise role. No specific AI software or hardware is identified as developed or used by the initiative to support student AI-literacy learning. Sources: https://www.oidetechnologyineducation.ie/ai-hub/ and https://www.oidetechnologyineducation.ie/ai-hub/ai-explainer-videos-for-teachers/ and https://www.oidetechnologyineducation.ie/onlinecourses/ai-for-schools/.

inclusion.reason: The initiative clearly includes AI literacy educational content by providing guidance on how to use AI safely and ethically in schools, covering topics like prompt engineering, bias detection, GDPR compliance, age restrictions, and pedagogical integration. The document is issued by a national government statutory body (Ireland's Department of Education and Youth) which satisfies the government inclusion route.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: National AI Strategy "AI – Here for Good" (2021; Refresh 2024)
metadata.Description: Ireland's national AI strategy incl. skills and education strands.

summary: Ireland’s National AI Strategy, “AI – Here for Good,” is a government policy framework published in 2021 and refreshed in 2024. It sets out a people-centred, ethical approach to developing and adopting AI for economic and societal benefit, addressing policymakers, businesses and SMEs, workers, and public services. Its skills and education strand focuses on AI talent and workforce upskilling and reskilling, with the refresh also proposing a safe space for public servants to experiment with AI tools. The strategy does not specify a teaching method, curriculum, or dedicated learning technology.
pedagogicalSummary: The inspected strategy pages describe a national policy and skills agenda rather than a teaching programme, and do not specify a teaching method, curriculum, or learning sequence. The 2024 refresh calls for updating research on AI skills and expanding digital upskilling and reskilling through initiatives including Skillnet Ireland, Springboard+, and apprenticeships, but gives no detail on how those activities teach AI literacy. It also proposes a safe space for civil and public servants to experiment with AI tools; this suggests practical exploration, though the page does not present it as a defined pedagogical model. These are limited signs of learning support, not evidence of a particular pedagogy. (https://enterprise.gov.ie/en/publications/national-ai-strategy-refresh-2024.html; https://enterprise.gov.ie/en/publications/national-ai-strategy.html)
prioritySummary: The strategy aims to help Ireland use and develop AI for economic and societal benefit through a people-centred, ethical approach. The 2024 refresh highlights productivity, business and public-service adoption, addressing societal challenges, and building Ireland’s position in AI, while also emphasizing trust and proportionate regulation. Its skills-related priorities include developing AI talent, updating evidence on workforce skills, and expanding upskilling and reskilling opportunities. SMEs, workers, civil and public servants, businesses, public services, and people more broadly are among the intended beneficiaries. The inspected pages present these aims together and do not establish a single overriding priority among them. (https://enterprise.gov.ie/en/publications/national-ai-strategy.html; https://enterprise.gov.ie/en/publications/national-ai-strategy-refresh-2024.html)
educationalTechnologySummary: The inspected pages do not identify a named platform, software product, or hardware developed or used specifically to support AI-literacy learning. The 2024 refresh proposes creating a safe space for civil and public servants to experiment with AI tools, but names no tools and describes this as workplace experimentation, not a defined educational technology or learning platform. Skillnet Ireland, Springboard+, and apprenticeships are identified as routes for digital upskilling and reskilling, not as technologies. Accordingly, the pages provide evidence of intended skills initiatives and some AI-tool experimentation, but not enough to identify educational technologies or explain how any technology supports AI-literacy instruction. (https://enterprise.gov.ie/en/publications/national-ai-strategy-refresh-2024.html)

inclusion.reason: This initiative qualifies for inclusion because it is issued by a national government (Department of Enterprise, Tourism and Employment in Ireland), which satisfies the first inclusion route (government endorsement). The strategy explicitly includes 'skills and education strands' addressing AI literacy requirements as educational content and guidance about how AI works. While the full PDF document could not be accessed to verify specific learning objectives, the presence of a dedicated skills/education strand on an official government strategy page indicates AI literacy components. Government origin alone provides sufficient inclusion basis per the screening criteria.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: Digital Strategy for Schools to 2027
metadata.Description: Framework guiding integration of digital technologies in primary/post-primary teaching, learning and assessment to 2027.

summary: Ireland’s Department of Education’s Digital Strategy for Schools to 2027 sets a system-wide direction for integrating digital technologies into primary and post-primary teaching, learning and assessment. Its three-pillar framework and implementation plan aim to build learners’ digital skills and support teachers and school leadership in using technology effectively. The publication page also links to separate 2025 guidance for schools covering AI, generative AI, and their benefits and risks; the available evidence does not establish that this guidance is formally part of the strategy.
pedagogicalSummary: The accessible overview describes a system-wide strategy to embed digital technologies in teaching, learning and assessment, but does not set out a specific classroom pedagogy or explain how instruction should be organised. It identifies high-level objectives under three pillars and links to a separate strategy and implementation plan; the overview alone does not provide enough detail to identify approaches such as project-based, collaborative or inquiry-led learning. This is a limit of the inspected evidence, not confirmation that the full strategy contains no pedagogical guidance. (https://www.gov.ie/en/department-of-education/publications/digital-strategy-for-schools-to-2027/; https://assets.gov.ie/static/documents/digital-strategy-for-schools-to-2027.pdf)
prioritySummary: The strategy principally aims to support the school system so that all learners can gain the knowledge and skills needed to navigate an evolving digital world. Its emphasis is therefore on learner capability and on integrating digital technologies into school teaching, learning and assessment, rather than on a narrowly specified workforce or individual well-being objective. The publication also includes an implementation plan and links to guidance on artificial intelligence in schools, but the inspected overview does not establish a more specific hierarchy of priorities or identify particular beneficiary groups beyond learners and the school system. (https://www.gov.ie/en/department-of-education/publications/digital-strategy-for-schools-to-2027/; https://assets.gov.ie/static/documents/digital-strategy-implementation-plan.pdf)
educationalTechnologySummary: The strategy identifies digital technologies broadly as something to be embedded in teaching, learning and assessment, but the accessible overview does not name a particular platform, software product, device or educational technology developed or used by the initiative. It links to AI-in-schools guidance and to external resources and tools, including Scoilnet and the SELFIE tool; those links alone do not show that the strategy itself deploys or develops them as learning technologies. The evidence inspected therefore supports a general technology-integration aim, but not claims about specific tools or how they support learning in practice. (https://www.gov.ie/en/department-of-education/publications/digital-strategy-for-schools-to-2027/; https://assets.gov.ie/static/documents/digital-strategy-for-schools-to-2027.pdf)

inclusion.reason: The linked AI guidance includes sections on what AI is, generative AI, and its benefits and risks, providing AI-literacy content. The guidance is listed on the strategy page, though the page does not clarify whether it is formally part of the strategy. metadata.Initiative / Programme: QQI / National Academic Integrity Network (NAIN) – guidance on generative AI
metadata.Description: NAIN (hosted by QQI) guidelines and principles on GenAI and academic integrity.

summary: The National Academic Integrity Network (NAIN), established by Ireland’s QQI, is a peer-collaborative network serving further and higher education and training. It develops and shares resources and supports collaboration among institutions, educators, learners and other sector stakeholders to foster academic integrity. Its resources include GenAI guidelines for educators addressing AI capabilities and limitations, ethical use, assessment and integrity, and privacy, alongside broader academic-integrity principles and frameworks. The available evidence describes resource-sharing and peer exchange but does not specify a particular teaching method or how the guidelines are used.
pedagogicalSummary: The inspected page describes NAIN as a peer collaborative network, not a teaching programme with a specified instructional method. It supports learning and practice indirectly by empowering members to foster academic integrity, sharing resources for stakeholders, and facilitating engagement and collaboration among members and external experts. The page lists “GenAI guidelines for educators” and other guidance, but does not explain their learning activities, format, or how educators or learners work through them. Thus, peer exchange and resource-sharing are evidenced as ways of supporting the network; a more specific pedagogy cannot be established from this page. (https://www.qqi.ie/national-academic-integrity-network)
prioritySummary: NAIN’s stated emphasis is fostering and upholding academic integrity across further and higher education and training. Its goals include empowering members to build a culture of integrity, providing leadership and stewardship, developing and disseminating resources for sector stakeholders, and strengthening collaboration with relevant European and international agencies and experts. The network includes education providers, institutions, agencies, organisations, and learners, including student-union representatives, so its work is directed toward a broad education-sector community rather than a single learner group. The page names GenAI guidance for educators among its resources, but does not establish that generative AI is the network’s sole or principal priority. (https://www.qqi.ie/national-academic-integrity-network)
educationalTechnologySummary: The inspected page names “GenAI guidelines for educators” as a NAIN resource, but does not describe any educational technology that NAIN develops or uses to support AI-literacy learning. It identifies no learning platform, software, hardware, or specific generative-AI product, and provides no account on this page of how the guidelines are delivered or used. The guidance itself is a resource about GenAI, not evidence that NAIN uses a particular AI tool as an educational technology. Consequently, no specific educational technology can be identified from the accessible page; this is a limit of the inspected evidence, not confirmation that none exists elsewhere. (https://www.qqi.ie/national-academic-integrity-network)

inclusion.reason: The guidelines support AI literacy by helping readers understand what generative AI can and cannot do and by providing guidance on its use. The NAIN page says the network was established by QQI, and QQI’s role page identifies it as a public body established by legislation, supporting the government/statutory-body inclusion route. metadata.Initiative / Programme: Digital Ireland – national digital and AI strategy (2026)
metadata.Description: Government's February 2026 strategy with 20 objectives and 90 deliverables covering digital and AI adoption, skills and public services.

summary: Digital Ireland is Ireland’s government-wide national digital and AI strategy, setting 20 objectives and 90 deliverables toward 2030. It aims to advance digital and AI adoption across enterprise and public services while developing skills and supporting participation in a digital society. Its commitments include digital, AI and media literacy across curricula, workforce upskilling and reskilling, a planned online AI-skilling platform and campaign, and staged support for businesses to explore, pilot and implement AI. The strategy also emphasizes responsible adoption, public trust, safety, privacy and rights; detailed instructional methods and the platform’s implementation are not established in the available evidence.
pedagogicalSummary: Digital Ireland is a government strategy rather than a described course or teaching programme, so the inspected pages do not establish a detailed instructional method. They do outline several ways learning and capability-building are intended to happen: a nationwide digital and AI skills campaign, an online AI skilling platform, basic digital, AI and media literacy across curricula, and accessible upskilling and reskilling. For businesses, the Department describes phased support moving from awareness to opportunities to experiment and pilot AI, planning, capacity-building and implementation. The 2024 AI Strategy Refresh also proposes a safe space for civil and public servants to experiment with AI tools. These point to awareness-raising, curriculum integration, skills development and experiential opportunities, but details such as lesson formats, assessment or learner activities are not available in the inspected summaries. Sources: https://www.gov.ie/en/department-of-the-taoiseach/publications/empower-skills-talent-for-a-digital-society-economy/ ; https://www.gov.ie/en/department-of-enterprise-tourism-and-employment/policy-information/digital-and-ai-strategy/ ; https://www.gov.ie/en/department-of-enterprise-tourism-and-employment/publications/national-ai-strategy-refresh-2024/
prioritySummary: The strategy has several stated priorities rather than a single learning objective. Digital Ireland aims to use digital technologies and AI to support Ireland’s competitiveness, productivity and economic growth, modernise public services, and enable people to thrive in a digital society. It also emphasizes enterprise adoption, domestic capabilities and Ireland’s position as a hub for applied AI and investment. For people and workers, it commits to broad digital and AI literacy, future-relevant workforce skills, support with potential job displacement, and public trust and engagement. Responsible adoption, safety, privacy and rights are also explicit concerns. The available evidence presents these as mutually reinforcing ambitions, without establishing a hierarchy among all benefits; the enterprise chapter particularly foregrounds competitiveness and adoption, while the skills chapter emphasizes inclusive participation and workforce readiness. Sources: https://www.gov.ie/en/department-of-the-taoiseach/campaigns/digital-ireland-connecting-our-people-securing-our-future/ ; https://www.gov.ie/en/department-of-the-taoiseach/publications/grow-a-digital-innovative-competitive-enterprise-sector/ ; https://www.gov.ie/en/department-of-the-taoiseach/publications/empower-skills-talent-for-a-digital-society-economy/
educationalTechnologySummary: The inspected strategy summaries identify a planned “new online AI Skilling Platform” intended to enhance awareness of available opportunities, alongside a nationwide Digital & AI skilling campaign. The pages do not describe the platform’s functions, content, audience-specific features or implementation status, so it is best understood from this evidence as a planned learning-support technology, not a confirmed operational product. They also mention opportunities for businesses and public servants to experiment with or pilot AI tools, but do not name particular software, platforms or hardware, and do not establish these tools as educational technologies developed by the initiative. The government’s strategy documents and gov.ie pages communicate the initiative but are not themselves evidence of a learning technology. Further technical details could not be established from the limited pages inspected. Sources: https://www.gov.ie/en/department-of-the-taoiseach/publications/empower-skills-talent-for-a-digital-society-economy/ ; https://www.gov.ie/en/department-of-enterprise-tourism-and-employment/policy-information/digital-and-ai-strategy/ ; https://www.gov.ie/en/department-of-enterprise-tourism-and-employment/publications/national-ai-strategy-refresh-2024/

metadata.Initiative / Programme: AI Advisory Council – Advice paper "AI and Education" (Feb 2025)
metadata.Description: Advice from Ireland's AI Advisory Council to government on AI and education.

summary: Ireland’s AI Advisory Council’s February 2025 “AI and Education” paper advises the Irish Government on generative AI in education. It addresses guidance for educational use, educator AI literacy and professional development, AI’s capabilities and limitations, ethical and equitable use, privacy and security, and effects on teaching, learning, and assessment, including academic integrity. Its primary audience is policymakers, with educators and the education community as relevant beneficiaries of its recommendations.
pedagogicalSummary: The accessible page identifies the “AI and Education” paper as an advice paper from an independent council, but does not describe teaching or learning activities, instructional methods, or how learning is supported. It therefore provides no evidence of a pedagogical approach; this is a limit of the inspected page, not confirmation that the paper itself contains no pedagogical discussion. https://enterprise.gov.ie/en/publications/ai-advisory-council-advice-papers.html
prioritySummary: The stated purpose of the AI Advisory Council is to provide expert advice to the Irish Government on artificial intelligence, and the listed “AI and Education” paper indicates that education is one topic of that advice. The page does not specify the paper’s recommendations, intended beneficiaries, or whether its emphasis is on learners, educators, workforce skills, or wider societal outcomes. The clearest supported priority is informing government consideration of AI in education; a more specific priority cannot be established from the accessible page. https://enterprise.gov.ie/en/publications/ai-advisory-council-advice-papers.html
educationalTechnologySummary: The accessible page lists an “AI and Education” advice paper but does not identify any educational technology, learning platform, software, or hardware developed or used by the Council to support AI literacy. The page itself is a publication listing, not evidence that its website is an educational technology. The linked paper’s contents were not accessible in the inspected material, so it is not possible to determine whether it names specific tools or technologies. https://enterprise.gov.ie/en/publications/ai-advisory-council-advice-papers.html

inclusion.reason: The initiative qualifies for inclusion because it is issued by a formally appointed body (the AI Advisory Council) that provides advice directly to the Irish national government, satisfying the government endorsement route. The document addresses the intersection of AI and education, which inherently involves providing guidance on how AI should be understood and utilized in educational contexts, thereby meeting the AI literacy requirement.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: AI in Schools External Advisory Taskforce (2026)
metadata.Description: Department of Education taskforce (announced 2026) of unions, school leaders and experts examining AI's implications for teaching, learning and assessment.

summary: Ireland’s Department of Education is establishing the AI in Schools External Advisory Taskforce to advise on AI’s implications for schools and inform future policy, guidance and supports. Through engagement with teachers, school leaders, unions, agencies and experts, it will consider ethical and appropriate AI use, initially prioritising assessment—including summative and state-certified assessment—while also addressing teaching, learning and formative assessment. Its remit includes supporting teachers’ confidence in pedagogical AI use and students’ digital and AI literacy; it is an advisory body, not a classroom teaching programme.
pedagogicalSummary: The taskforce is an advisory and policy-development body, not a teaching programme, so the announcement does not establish a classroom pedagogy. Its stated approach is structured engagement with teachers, school leaders, unions, agencies and experts, using evidence and practical experience to shape advice and supports; initial work prioritises assessment while also addressing teaching, learning and formative assessment. A related but distinct EU-funded project describes workshops, exchanges, webinars, and co-design and testing of toolkits and professional-development modules with teachers and school leaders. These are collaborative development and professional-learning activities, not evidence that the taskforce itself delivers instruction. Further details on its work programme were not yet available in the inspected pages. (https://www.gov.ie/en/department-of-education/press-releases/ai-in-schools-external-advisory-taskforce-to-be-established/; https://www.oidetechnologyineducation.ie/projects-initiatives/european-tsi-project-for-safe-ethical-and-meaningful-use-of-ai-in-schools/)
prioritySummary: The taskforce’s main purpose is to help Ireland’s Department of Education and Youth respond to AI’s implications for schools through policy, guidance and practical supports. Its initial emphasis is assessment, including summative and state-certified assessment, alongside work on teaching, learning and formative assessment. The announcement particularly stresses equipping teachers with confidence and competence for pedagogical use of AI, while supporting students’ digital and AI literacy and safeguarding the integrity of learning and assessment. It also frames benefits for students as fair, safe and inclusive, and describes engagement across the school system rather than a workforce-only or individual-focused initiative. The relative weight of these aims may evolve as the taskforce’s phased work programme is developed. (https://www.gov.ie/en/department-of-education/press-releases/ai-in-schools-external-advisory-taskforce-to-be-established/)
educationalTechnologySummary: The announcement does not identify a specific AI application, classroom platform, software product or hardware that the taskforce itself develops or uses. It points to Oide Technology in Education’s AI in Schools Hub as a support for teachers and school leaders; that online resource hub offers an introductory AI for Schools course, explainer videos, FAQs and curated resources. The course is described as a short online course for teachers and school leaders covering AI, policy documents and ethical considerations. Separately, the related EU-funded project proposes toolkits, a CPD module and proposals for integrating AI into existing digital learning platforms, but the inspected page names no platforms and describes these as project outputs, not established taskforce technologies. Thus the evidence identifies digital learning resources available to educators, but not a taskforce-developed educational technology. (https://www.gov.ie/en/department-of-education/press-releases/ai-in-schools-external-advisory-taskforce-to-be-established/; https://www.oidetechnologyineducation.ie/ai-hub/; https://www.oidetechnologyineducation.ie/onlinecourses/ai-for-schools/; https://www.oidetechnologyineducation.ie/projects-initiatives/european-tsi-project-for-safe-ethical-and-meaningful-use-of-ai-in-schools/)

inclusion.reason: The initiative qualifies for inclusion under the 'Issued by a national government' inclusion route: it is formally endorsed by Ireland’s Department of Education, with explicit links to existing AI literacy-focused resources (e.g., Guidance on Artificial Intelligence in Schools and EU-supported projects). The taskforce’s mandate to examine ethical AI use in education directly supports AI literacy goals. Uncertainty remains only around the specific deliverables or timeline for the taskforce's work, but these do not affect its current eligibility for inclusion based on established criteria.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: Guidelines for the Responsible Use of AI in the Public Service (2025)
metadata.Description: Government guidelines for public service AI use.

summary: Ireland’s Department of Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation has issued guidelines and practical resources to help public servants and public-service organisations assess, plan, develop and use AI responsibly in policy and service delivery. The materials address responsible-use principles, risk assessment, EU AI Act roles and obligations, and the AI project lifecycle, with a Decision Framework, Responsible AI Canvas and lifecycle guidance. An online tutorial, learning materials and bespoke training support applied professional learning, though details of their format and reach are limited.
pedagogicalSummary: The initiative supports public servants through learning and development materials, an Institute of Public Administration tutorial, and bespoke training intended to help participants apply the guidelines in their workplaces. Its practical resources also structure application: a Decision Framework helps evaluate possible AI uses, a Responsible AI Canvas is for the planning stage, and AI Lifecycle Guidance supports consideration from development through deployment and review or decommissioning. This suggests applied, work-related professional learning rather than evidence of a particular classroom method or learning theory. Human oversight and responsible-use principles inform the guidance, but are not themselves teaching methods. The inspected pages provide only limited detail about the tutorial’s format or the training activities. Sources: https://www.gov.ie/en/department-of-public-expenditure-infrastructure-public-service-reform-and-digitalisation/publications/artificial-intelligence-resources/ ; https://www.gov.ie/en/department-of-public-expenditure-infrastructure-public-service-reform-and-digitalisation/publications/guidelines-for-the-responsible-use-of-ai-in-the-public-service/
prioritySummary: The central emphasis is enabling Irish public servants and public-service organisations to use AI responsibly in developing and delivering improved policy and services. The stated rationale combines public-service transformation and innovation with human involvement, public trust, and protection of people’s rights; the listed principles also include fairness, privacy, safety, accountability, and societal and environmental well-being. Government describes digitally enabled, seamless and inclusive services and using technology to address societal challenges as broader aims. The pages therefore identify both organisational/service improvement and safeguards for the people affected by public-sector AI, without establishing a single exclusive priority among them. The materials are directed particularly to public servants and public-service organisations, rather than to general AI literacy for the whole population. Sources: https://www.gov.ie/en/department-of-public-expenditure-infrastructure-public-service-reform-and-digitalisation/publications/artificial-intelligence-resources/ ; https://www.gov.ie/en/department-of-public-expenditure-infrastructure-public-service-reform-and-digitalisation/publications/guidelines-for-the-responsible-use-of-ai-in-the-public-service/
educationalTechnologySummary: The inspected pages identify no dedicated learning platform, educational software, or hardware developed or used for this initiative. They do describe an online tutorial and training offered through the Institute of Public Administration, but the page provides no details about the tutorial’s delivery technology; its embedded content was not accessible in the inspection. Government-developed learning and practice supports include the Responsible AI Canvas, Decision Framework, and AI Lifecycle Guidance, available as linked documents or guidance. These can support planning and structured consideration of AI projects, but the evidence does not establish that they are software or digital learning technologies, so they should not be equated with an educational platform. AI itself is the subject of the guidelines, not evidence of an AI teaching product used by the initiative. Sources: https://www.gov.ie/en/department-of-public-expenditure-infrastructure-public-service-reform-and-digitalisation/publications/artificial-intelligence-resources/ ; https://www.gov.ie/en/department-of-public-expenditure-infrastructure-public-service-reform-and-digitalisation/publications/guidelines-for-the-responsible-use-of-ai-in-the-public-service/

inclusion.reason: The initiative includes explicit AI literacy through its educational content: it explains the roles of providers and deployers under the EU AI Act, outlines responsible use principles, provides step-by-step guidance on implementing AI, and offers real-world examples. It is issued by a national government department (Ireland’s Department of Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation), satisfying the inclusion route for government-issued mandates. The document serves as authoritative guidance for public servants across Ireland, confirming widespread institutional adoption and relevance to AI literacy in the public sector.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: HEA / National Forum – Generative AI in HE Teaching & Learning Policy Framework
metadata.Description: HEA/National Forum framework (Dec 2025) guiding responsible adoption of generative AI in Irish higher education teaching, learning and assessment.

summary: The Higher Education Authority, in collaboration with the National Forum for the Enhancement of Teaching and Learning in Higher Education, published a national framework to guide Irish higher education institutions in adopting generative AI in teaching, learning and assessment. It offers values-based guidance for institutional leaders, educators and support staff while recognizing students’ interests and institutional autonomy. Its emphasis includes AI literacy, critical engagement, human oversight, equity, academic integrity, privacy and AI-resilient assessment. Supporting resources address areas such as AI literacy training, assessment, regulation and procurement; the framework sets direction rather than prescribing a specific teaching method or technology for delivering instruction.
pedagogicalSummary: The initiative is a policy framework, not a teaching programme, so the inspected pages do not establish a specific instructional method or structure for learner activities. Its pedagogical direction is to support deliberate, values-based decisions about generative AI in teaching and learning, with principles including critical engagement, human oversight, AI literacy, and sustainable pedagogy. It also identifies AI-resilient assessment practices and AI literacy training as supporting instruments, but the inspected pages do not describe their learning activities or delivery in enough detail to characterize a pedagogy. The framework calls for staff, students, leadership, and support units to share responsibility for pedagogically sound adoption. (https://hea.ie/2025/12/22/hea-publishes-national-policy-framework-on-generative-ai-in-teaching-and-learning/; https://hub.teachingandlearning.ie/genai/policy-framework/)
prioritySummary: The framework principally aims to guide responsible, values-based adoption of generative AI in teaching, learning, and assessment across Irish higher education. Its immediate audience is higher education institutions and the educators, academic leaders, and professional staff making decisions about practice and policy; students and the wider public mission of higher education are also considered through principles such as equity, inclusion, academic integrity, and safeguarding higher education’s values. It seeks a coordinated national reference point while preserving institutional autonomy, academic freedom, and disciplinary judgment, rather than prescribing uncritical adoption or rejection. The inspected pages describe sector-wide guidance and support, not a primary focus on workforce upskilling or individual well-being. (https://hea.ie/2025/12/22/hea-publishes-national-policy-framework-on-generative-ai-in-teaching-and-learning/; https://hub.teachingandlearning.ie/genai/policy-framework/)
educationalTechnologySummary: The inspected framework pages identify no educational technology platform, software, or hardware developed or used by the initiative to deliver learning. They mention generative AI, particularly large language models such as ChatGPT, as the technology whose use in higher-education teaching and learning the policy addresses; this does not establish that the initiative itself deploys ChatGPT or another AI tool for instruction. The National Resource Hub provides access to policy documents and supporting resources, including an AI literacy training instrument, but the inspected framework page does not specify a technology used to deliver that training. Accordingly, the evidence supports describing the initiative as guidance about technology use, not as a technology-based learning intervention; details of any training delivery tools remain unclear. (https://hea.ie/2025/12/22/hea-publishes-national-policy-framework-on-generative-ai-in-teaching-and-learning/; https://hub.teachingandlearning.ie/genai/policy-framework/; https://hub.teachingandlearning.ie/genai/)

inclusion.reason: This initiative is clearly issued by a national government body (the HEA) and formally endorsed through its partnership with the National Forum. This satisfies the 'Government Body' inclusion route. Additionally, it explicitly includes AI literacy components through specific educational guidance for students on understanding how AI works, evaluating its outputs, and developing critical engagement skills. The framework is designed to be adopted across Irish higher education institutions, providing system-scale guidance rather than being a single-institution project.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: Literacy, Numeracy and Digital Literacy Strategy 2024–2033
metadata.Description: Joint Dept of Education/Dept of Children strategy to improve literacy, numeracy and digital literacy from birth to young adulthood.

summary: Ireland’s Literacy, Numeracy and Digital Literacy Strategy 2024–2033 is a joint national strategy of the Departments of Education and Children, covering early learning and care through post-primary education and young adulthood. It aims to strengthen learners’ literacy, numeracy and digital literacy, alongside educators’ professional practice, through coordinated action on curriculum, pedagogy, assessment and support from families and communities. It highlights equity and the needs of diverse learners; the evidence describes broad strategic directions rather than a specific teaching method or technology.
pedagogicalSummary: The strategy frames pedagogy as one part of a wider, coordinated approach: one of its five pillars is to improve learners’ experience through curriculum, pedagogy and assessment. It spans early learning and care through post-primary school and also aims to strengthen educators’ professional practice and leadership, while enabling parents and communities to support learning. The launch account describes attention to different learners’ strengths and needs, including tailored support for disability and disadvantage. These are strategic directions rather than a specified teaching method; the accessible pages do not establish a single classroom model or detailed sequence of learning activities. Sources: https://www.gov.ie/en/department-of-education/publications/literacy-numeracy-and-digital-literacy-strategy/ and https://www.gov.ie/en/department-of-education/press-releases/ministers-foley-and-minister-ogorman-launch-irelands-literacy-numeracy-and-digital-literacy-strategy-2024-2033/
prioritySummary: The initiative principally seeks to develop literacy, numeracy and digital literacy for every learner from birth to young adulthood, across early learning and care and school settings. It presents these capabilities as supporting learners’ individual flourishing and participation in society, including navigating an evolving digital world. The strategy also emphasizes the people and institutions supporting learners—families, communities, educators and school leaders—and identifies support for diverse learners and improved equity as priorities. The evidence describes a broad national education strategy, not a program focused solely on workforce upskilling or on AI literacy; digital literacy is one of its wider learning aims. Sources: https://www.gov.ie/en/department-of-education/publications/literacy-numeracy-and-digital-literacy-strategy/ and https://www.gov.ie/en/department-of-education/press-releases/ministers-foley-and-minister-ogorman-launch-irelands-literacy-numeracy-and-digital-literacy-strategy-2024-2033/
educationalTechnologySummary: The accessible pages describe digital literacy as a learning goal, including the ability to navigate an evolving digital world, but do not identify a named educational technology, learning platform, software product or hardware developed or used by the strategy. The launch account mentions screening and diagnostic tests for early literacy and numeracy and a STEM micro-credential initiative, but does not describe these as digital tools or explain their technologies. Accordingly, the inspected evidence does not establish a technology-mediated teaching approach; this is a limit of the accessible descriptions, not evidence that no technologies are used in implementation. The linked strategy PDF was supplied, but its full extracted text was not available in the inspection. Sources: https://www.gov.ie/en/department-of-education/publications/literacy-numeracy-and-digital-literacy-strategy/ and https://www.gov.ie/en/department-of-education/press-releases/ministers-foley-and-minister-ogorman-launch-irelands-literacy-numeracy-and-digital-literacy-strategy-2024-2033/

inclusion.reason: The initiative qualifies under both the government endorsement route (issued by two Irish statutory ministries) and the AI-literacy requirement. The document explicitly addresses 'digital literacy' as a key component of the strategy, proposing improvements in digital skills for learners across all stages from birth to young adulthood and emphasising high-quality professional learning for educators in this area. This meets the definition of AI literacy (educational guidance on how to use digital tools/AI) even though it does not exclusively focus on generative AI. Uncertainty remains only regarding the specific granularity of AI-focused content, but the inclusive screening guidance directs towards inclusion when evidence is incomplete and there is clear government mandate.
