metadata.Initiative / Programme: Letter to parliament on digital autonomy in education & public AI facility (2026)
metadata.Description: A July 2026 letter to the Dutch parliament proposing public governance and a public AI provision to reduce schools' dependence on big tech.

summary: A July 2026 Dutch government letter to parliament sets out a policy direction for strengthening digital autonomy in education. It emphasizes collective governance of technology providers, reducing reliance on a small number of providers, and creating room for alternatives, including a proposed public AI facility. Its intended audience is education institutions and the sectors they serve; the available material describes an organisational and infrastructure policy proposal, not a teaching programme, and does not establish a pedagogy or specific AI-literacy activities.
pedagogicalSummary: The inspected parliamentary record and accompanying decision memorandum describe a policy proposal, not a teaching programme. They do not specify a pedagogical approach, learning activities, curriculum, or how learning would be organised. The memorandum does identify awareness and the capacity of institutions and teachers to change as important to reducing dependence on existing providers, but this is presented as an organisational condition for digital autonomy, not as a teaching method. The available evidence therefore does not establish a pedagogy; this is a limit of the inspected material, not proof that no related learning activities exist. Sources: https://www.tweedekamer.nl/kamerstukken/brieven_regering/detail?id=2026Z15674&did=2026D35088 ; https://www.tweedekamer.nl/downloads/document?id=2026D35089
prioritySummary: The initiative’s stated emphasis is strengthening digital autonomy across education by reducing dependence on a small number of non-European technology providers, which the memorandum says can put public values, including autonomy, under pressure. It proposes stronger collective governance—education institutions setting conditions and rules for providers—and greater room for alternatives, with essential provisions potentially organised under shared control. The intended beneficiaries are education institutions and the sectors they serve; the memorandum notes that needs and capacity differ, especially between further education and smaller school boards in foundational education. The material frames this as a complex, gradual effort rather than a single intervention. Sources: https://www.tweedekamer.nl/kamerstukken/brieven_regering/detail?id=2026Z15674&did=2026D35088 ; https://www.tweedekamer.nl/downloads/document?id=2026D35089
educationalTechnologySummary: The accessible material points toward collective control of essential digital provisions and creating room for alternative providers, but it does not identify a particular educational technology, platform, software product, or hardware that the initiative develops or uses to support AI-literacy learning. The memorandum names organisations such as Kennisnet, SIVON, SURF, and Npuls as partners or existing sector initiatives; it does not describe them as learning technologies. Because the main letter’s detailed contents were not readable in the inspected page, the evidence is insufficient to determine whether it proposes a specific public AI tool or other learning technology. The record supports a direction for digital infrastructure and governance, not a specific educational technology. Sources: https://www.tweedekamer.nl/kamerstukken/brieven_regering/detail?id=2026Z15674&did=2026D35088 ; https://www.tweedekamer.nl/downloads/document?id=2026D35089

inclusion.reason: The initiative qualifies for inclusion because it is issued by the Dutch Government (a national statutory body). The page indicates it is an official parliamentary document ('Brieven Regering') proposing a public AI provision for education. It proposes AI literacy elements by establishing a 'public AI facility' to reduce dependence on big tech, implying educational guidance and governance frameworks regarding how AI works in schools, which satisfies the AI-literacy requirement.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: Npuls & eduGenAI
metadata.Description: National programme for digital transformation of VET and HE incl. edu-GenAI.

summary: Npuls is a Dutch national programme supporting digital transformation across vocational and higher education, including mbo, hbo and universities. Its AI and data literacy work serves students and education professionals through frameworks, practical guidance, videos, self-assessments, training and peer-learning communities. The AI-GO framework and its eight-step guide encourage teams to design learning and assessment activities, build knowledge and ethical awareness, and learn through experimentation and reflection. Npuls and SURF are also developing eduGenAI, a pilot platform through which institutions can access commercial and open-source language models for learning with and about generative AI. The programme emphasizes responsible use, public values, privacy and institutional capacity.
pedagogicalSummary: Npuls supports AI literacy through a combination of evidence-informed guidance, practical institutional planning, professional development, and sector-wide knowledge sharing. Its AI-GO framework draws on a review of research and feedback from education professionals, while the accompanying AI-GO in Actie handreiking translates it into eight steps, including designing learning activities and assessment, strengthening knowledge and ethical awareness, and monitoring progress. The guide advocates a cyclical, practice-oriented process in which teams experiment, reflect, and improve. Training for educators on using generative AI in their own teaching practice offers another learning route; communities and Centers for Teaching & Learning support peer exchange and professional learning. These approaches are documented at https://npuls.nl/kennisbank/ai-go-een-raamwerk-voor-ai-geletterdheid-in-het-onderwijs, https://npuls.nl/kennisbank/ai-go-in-actie, and https://npuls.nl/nieuws/trainingen-ai-in-de-onderwijspraktijk-van-start. The inspected pages do not establish one uniform pedagogy across all Npuls activities.
prioritySummary: Npuls is principally a sector-wide transformation programme for Dutch vocational, higher professional, and research-oriented higher education. Its AI-literacy emphasis is to develop durable AI and data knowledge and skills among both learners and education professionals, so they can use AI and data responsibly and add value to education. The programme also stresses safe, reliable, accessible education, public values, privacy, transparency, and reducing dependence on commercial providers; these concerns shape its work on shared AI infrastructure as well as literacy. Its stated beneficiaries are therefore students and staff across participating institutions, alongside the institutions and education sector that need capacity and common approaches. Evidence: https://npuls.nl/ and https://npuls.nl/beloften/ai-waardenvol-inzetten. The pages present several related priorities rather than a single ranked objective.
educationalTechnologySummary: Npuls and SURF are developing eduGenAI, a sector platform for safe and responsible use of generative AI in further education. It lets institutions access different commercial or open-source large language models in one environment, and is described as enabling students, teachers, and other education professionals to learn with and about AI. A training programme uses eduGenAI to help education professionals explore pedagogically and didactically responsible use in their own practice; training materials are also made available for institutional reuse. The platform was described as being in a pilot phase, with institutions experimenting and contributing to its development. The inspected pages identify eduGenAI as the principal educational technology, not merely a topic taught; they also describe an AI hub and related infrastructure, but give limited detail about their learning functions. Sources: https://npuls.nl/edugenai and https://npuls.nl/nieuws/trainingen-ai-in-de-onderwijspraktijk-van-start.

inclusion.reason: The initiative qualifies for inclusion under multiple routes: it is a national programme issued by a sub-national government body (Netherlands), evidenced by the domain npuls.nl belonging to the Dutch government educational transformation program. The initative explicitly includes AI literacy elements as shown by its 'AI- en datageletterdheid' (AI and data literacy) page, offering videos, training modules, self-assessments, and practical guidance on responsible AI use for educators and learners in VET and HE institutions. The inclusion of AI literacy educational content is evident from the listed materials such as webinars on digital/AI/data literacy, video content about responsible AI use, and training courses.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: Nigeria National AI Strategy (NAIS)
metadata.Description: Co-created by NCAIR and NITDA through a 2024 multi-stakeholder process; five pillars include ecosystem development and skills, targeting AI skills for 70% of youth aged 16–35.

summary: Nigeria’s National Artificial Intelligence Strategy (NAIS), published through NCAIR and NITDA, is a national policy framework for developing the country’s AI ecosystem and supporting responsible AI adoption. Its five pillars cover ecosystem development, skills, infrastructure, regulation and ethics, with goals spanning socioeconomic development and a stated target of building AI skills among 70% of Nigerians aged 16–35. It is intended for national stakeholders, including policymakers and young people, but is not a course and the reviewed material does not specify a curriculum or teaching model. NCAIR’s AI Collective separately lists seminars, hackathons and training opportunities.
pedagogicalSummary: The NAIS is a national strategy, not a single course, and the accessible material does not set out a curriculum, assessment method, or defined teaching model. NCAIR’s AI Collective does describe monthly seminars, hackathons, and training programs for different skill levels, indicating community-based learning and opportunities for practical participation; the page does not explain how these activities are taught or assessed, or establish that they are the strategy’s prescribed pedagogy. The strategy PDF was readable only in a limited preview, so more detailed pedagogical provisions may be missed. Sources: https://ncair.nitda.gov.ng/aicollective/ ; https://ncair.nitda.gov.ng/wp-content/uploads/2025/09/National-Artificial-Intelligence-Strategy-19092025.pdf
prioritySummary: The strategy’s stated emphasis includes building AI skills and developing the ecosystem, with a target of AI skills for 70% of young people aged 16–35, according to the supplied description of the strategy. NCAIR’s wider mission also frames AI development as serving economic growth, quality of life, and global competitiveness, while its AI Collective promotes an inclusive AI ecosystem and offers learning and research opportunities. These point to both youth capacity-building and broader national innovation and development goals; the inspected pages do not establish a more specific hierarchy among them. The strategy PDF was only available in a limited text preview. Sources: https://ncair.nitda.gov.ng/wp-content/uploads/2025/09/National-Artificial-Intelligence-Strategy-19092025.pdf ; https://ncair.nitda.gov.ng/ ; https://ncair.nitda.gov.ng/aicollective/
educationalTechnologySummary: The inspected pages do not identify a learning management system, instructional software, or hardware used specifically to teach AI literacy. NCAIR does present N-ATLAS, an open-source multilingual language model, and says it could help enable tools for education, among other fields; however, the page does not describe N-ATLAS itself as a teaching platform or show it being used in AI-literacy instruction. The AI Collective page lists seminars, hackathons, and training but names no supporting educational technology. The strategy PDF’s limited accessible preview also leaves open whether it specifies learning technologies elsewhere. Sources: https://ncair.nitda.gov.ng/llm/ ; https://ncair.nitda.gov.ng/aicollective/ ; https://ncair.nitda.gov.ng/wp-content/uploads/2025/09/National-Artificial-Intelligence-Strategy-19092025.pdf

inclusion.reason: AI-literacy requirement is met: the strategy explicitly targets AI skills building for youth and includes educational components on how to use AI tools. Inclusion route is satisfied because it is issued/endorsed by Nigerian statutory bodies (NCAIR and NITDA). Although the page shown is a discussion document, the metadata indicates this is a co-created national initiative with multi-stakeholder input; even if not yet adopted as final policy, the scope and government involvement make it plausible for inclusion. No exclusion criteria are triggered.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: Education Strategy 2026–2032 & Action Plan (North Macedonia)
metadata.Description: Ministry of Education and Science strategy for reforms in quality, inclusion, digital transformation and labour-market alignment.

summary: North Macedonia’s Ministry of Education and Science is developing the Education Strategy 2026–2032 and Action Plan as a national framework for reform across preschool, primary, secondary, non-formal and higher education. The announced priorities include inclusion, school funding and infrastructure, changes to schooling and graduation, and updates to higher-education and science legislation. Its development involved consultation with government bodies, international organisations, academics and civil-society groups. The announcement does not specify teaching methods, educational technologies, or an AI-literacy component.
pedagogicalSummary: The inspected announcement describes a public debate on the Education Strategy 2026–2032 and says the draft was developed through discussion with government bodies, international organisations, academics, and civil-society groups. This supports a consultative approach to developing the policy, not a particular teaching or learning method. It mentions plans for a new preschool programme, inclusion, and non-formal education, but does not explain how learning will be organised or supported in practice. No AI-literacy pedagogy is identified in the announcement or the ministry’s strategic-documents listing. This is a limit of the inspected material, not confirmation that the full strategy contains no such detail. (https://mon.gov.mk/mk-MK/odnosi-so-javnost/soopstenija/debata-za-strategijata-za-obrazovanie-2026-2032; https://mon.gov.mk/mk-MK/dokumenti/strateski-dokumenti)
prioritySummary: The announcement presents the strategy as a broad effort to improve the quality of North Macedonia’s national education system. Its stated priorities include a new preschool programme, inclusion in primary and secondary education, revised school funding, infrastructure and school-network changes, single-shift schooling, a new graduation concept, promotion of non-formal education, and updated higher-education and science legislation. The intended scope therefore spans multiple stages and forms of education; the announcement does not identify a narrower principal beneficiary group or establish a hierarchy among these reforms. It does not mention AI literacy, workforce upskilling, or digital transformation, so those emphases cannot be established from the inspected pages. (https://mon.gov.mk/mk-MK/odnosi-so-javnost/soopstenija/debata-za-strategijata-za-obrazovanie-2026-2032; https://mon.gov.mk/mk-MK/dokumenti/strateski-dokumenti)
educationalTechnologySummary: The inspected pages do not identify any educational technology, platform, software, or hardware developed or used by the strategy to support learning. The announcement describes system-level reforms—including infrastructure improvements—but does not specify digital learning tools or technologies, and it does not describe AI products as learning resources. The ministry’s strategic-documents page lists the Education Strategy 2026–2032 but provides no technology details in the accessible text. Accordingly, no educational technology can be attributed to this initiative from the inspected evidence; the underlying strategy document was not examined, so this is not confirmation that it contains none. (https://mon.gov.mk/mk-MK/odnosi-so-javnost/soopstenija/debata-za-strategijata-za-obrazovanie-2026-2032; https://mon.gov.mk/mk-MK/dokumenti/strateski-dokumenti)

inclusion.reason: The initiative is issued by a national government ministry (Ministry of Education and Science) in North Macedonia. As a government strategy for education reforms, it falls under the inclusion route for initiatives endorsed or funded by a national government. Although the specific text of the strategy document detailing AI literacy elements could not be fully reviewed from this landing page alone, the debate on the strategy itself qualifies for inclusive screening under the government issuance criterion.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: Udir guidance on AI in schools (incl. 2026 age recommendations)
metadata.Description: The Norwegian Directorate for Education is issuing 2026 age-adapted recommendations on generative AI use, commissioned by the Ministry of Education.

summary: The Norwegian Directorate for Education (Udir), at the Ministry of Education’s request, is developing age-adapted recommendations for generative AI use in schools. The guidance covers primary, lower-secondary and upper-secondary pupils: it advises generally against access for grades 1–7, gradual and cautious use in grades 8–10 after teachers are prepared, and appropriate use in upper-secondary subject work and preparation for further study and employment. Udir also describes a competence package for teachers, school leaders and school owners, connecting basic AI understanding with curricula and pedagogical practice. The emphasis is on safe, responsible and educationally appropriate use; the inspected material does not specify particular lesson formats or AI products.
pedagogicalSummary: The inspected pages support an age-differentiated, cautious approach rather than a detailed classroom teaching method. The guidance says generative AI should generally not be available to pupils in grades 1–7; in grades 8–10, use should be gradual and cautious, with teachers gaining sufficient competence before pupils receive instruction and access; and upper-secondary pupils should learn to use it appropriately for subject work and preparation for further study and employment. Udir’s overview also describes a competence package for teachers, school leaders and school owners that connects basic AI understanding with curricula and pedagogical practice. The pages do not specify particular lesson formats or learning activities, so those cannot be established from this inspection. Sources: https://www.udir.no/kvalitet-og-kompetanse/digitalisering-skole/kunstig-intelligens-i-skolen/kommer-nye-rad-om-bruk-av-kunstig-intelligens-pa-ulike-trinn/ and https://www.udir.no/kvalitet-og-kompetanse/digitalisering-skole/kunstig-intelligens-i-skolen/
prioritySummary: The initiative’s evident emphasis is safe, appropriate and age-adapted use of generative AI in Norwegian schooling, including building educators’ readiness to guide that use. The recommendations are being developed for the Ministry of Education on the basis of evidence and precautionary principles. They seek to limit access for younger pupils, allow cautious and gradual use in lower secondary after teachers have adequate competence, and prepare upper-secondary pupils to use AI appropriately for academic work and future education and employment. The overview further presents support for teachers, school leaders and school owners, with attention to opportunities and challenges including teaching, formative assessment, privacy and information security. The inspected material does not establish a single priority beyond these related educational and safeguarding aims. Sources: https://www.udir.no/kvalitet-og-kompetanse/digitalisering-skole/kunstig-intelligens-i-skolen/kommer-nye-rad-om-bruk-av-kunstig-intelligens-pa-ulike-trinn/ and https://www.udir.no/kvalitet-og-kompetanse/digitalisering-skole/kunstig-intelligens-i-skolen/
educationalTechnologySummary: The pages discuss generative AI as the technology whose use in teaching is being guided, and refer generally to AI tools and to AI as an underlying technology in learning materials or other tools. They do not name a particular AI product, software platform or hardware, nor do they establish that Udir develops or deploys a specific AI learning technology. The overview identifies a competence package for educators and school leaders as support for understanding AI and considering it in relation to curricula and pedagogical practice, but the inspected page does not identify its delivery platform or describe it as AI-powered. Accordingly, the evidence supports describing the initiative as guidance and professional-learning support about AI, not attributing specific educational technology products to it. Sources: https://www.udir.no/kvalitet-og-kompetanse/digitalisering-skole/kunstig-intelligens-i-skolen/ and https://www.udir.no/kvalitet-og-kompetanse/digitalisering-skole/kunstig-intelligens-i-skolen/kommer-nye-rad-om-bruk-av-kunstig-intelligens-pa-ulike-trinn/

inclusion.reason: The initiative meets the inclusion criteria because it is formally issued by a statutory national body (the Norwegian Directorate for Education) and commissioned by the Ministry of Education. Additionally, the page provides clear educational content with learning objectives and guidance on how students should use generative AI at different ages, which satisfies the AI-literacy requirement.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: National Digitalisation Strategy 2024–2030 "The Digital Norway of the Future"
metadata.Description: Norway's national digitalisation strategy.

summary: Norway’s National Digitalisation Strategy 2024–2030, issued by the Ministry of Digitalisation and Public Governance, sets policy priorities for the country’s digital transformation. It addresses residents, businesses and the public sector, with aims including better digital services, competitiveness, inclusion, trust and security. The strategy calls for digital competence in education and lifelong learning, and supports AI capacity and use, while also emphasizing ethical, safe and privacy-conscious digitalisation. It is a policy framework rather than a teaching programme; the inspected material does not specify instructional methods or learning technologies.
pedagogicalSummary: The strategy is a national policy plan, not a described teaching programme. It calls for digital competence as a basic skill in relevant education programmes, prioritising technology subjects, and for lifelong learning to meet future business needs. It also says children and young people should develop digital confidence and critical thinking. These are intended outcomes and policy directions; the inspected pages do not specify teaching methods, learning activities, or how instruction is organised. Thus, evidence supports a focus on competence development, but not a particular pedagogy. (https://www.regjeringen.no/en/documents/the-digital-norway-of-the-future/id3054645/?ch=2; https://www.regjeringen.no/no/dokumenter/fremtidens-digitale-norge/id3054645/?ch=1)
prioritySummary: The strategy’s central aim is to make Norway the world’s most digitalised country by 2030, using digitalisation to address societal challenges rather than treating technology as an end in itself. It identifies several intended beneficiaries and priorities: easier and safer everyday life and better public services for citizens; stronger competitiveness, innovation, and skills for businesses; and a more capable public sector. It also emphasises broad participation, digital skills and inclusion, trust, security, privacy, and special care for children and young people. The inspected text presents these as connected priorities rather than establishing one narrow AI-literacy objective or a clear hierarchy among them. (https://www.regjeringen.no/en/documents/the-digital-norway-of-the-future/id3054645/?ch=2; https://www.regjeringen.no/en/documents/the-digital-norway-of-the-future/id3054645/?ch=3)
educationalTechnologySummary: The inspected strategy pages do not identify a learning platform, educational software, hardware, or other educational technology that the initiative develops or uses to teach AI literacy. They propose establishing national AI infrastructure and encouraging AI use in public services and business, but describe these as digitalisation capacity and economic or administrative goals, not as tools for learning. The strategy also calls for digital competence in education and lifelong learning without specifying technologies that support those activities. This is a limit of the inspected material, not confirmation that no such technologies exist elsewhere. (https://www.regjeringen.no/en/documents/the-digital-norway-of-the-future/id3054645/?ch=2)

inclusion.reason: This initiative qualifies under the inclusion route 'Issued... by a national or sub-national government'. It is explicitly issued by the Ministry of Digitalisation and Public Governance, meeting the government endorsement requirement. While the provided page serves as the document landing page with download options for the full PDF (which contains the detailed AI literacy educational content and objectives), the initiative itself is clearly a formal government mandate rather than a single-institution project or company product without support.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: National Strategy for Artificial Intelligence (2020)
metadata.Description: Norway's national AI strategy.

summary: Norway’s 2020 National Strategy for Artificial Intelligence, issued by the government, sets out priorities for developing and using AI across society, business and the public sector. It addresses innovation, research and infrastructure alongside responsible and trustworthy AI, including human rights, privacy, democracy and security. For education and workforce development, it calls for AI-related study opportunities and upskilling and reskilling, but does not prescribe a teaching method or learning technology. The strategy also explains AI concepts and technologies for policy and other decision-makers.
pedagogicalSummary: The inspected material is a national policy strategy, not a teaching programme, and does not describe a specific pedagogy, lesson format, or learner-support method. It does call for higher-education institutions to consider integrating AI-related topics into relevant study programmes, and for opportunities to upskill and reskill through workplace learning and study programmes. These are proposed learning settings, not evidence of a particular instructional approach. The strategy also notes that AI, ethics, and data protection matter in professional education, but gives no detail on how such learning should be taught. This summary is based on the strategy’s overview and may not capture material outside the inspected pages (https://www.regjeringen.no/en/documents/nasjonal-strategi-for-kunstig-intelligens/id2685594/?ch=2).
prioritySummary: The strategy aims to help Norway develop and use AI to benefit individuals, society, businesses, and the public sector. It emphasizes realizing AI’s potential for innovation, value creation, more effective business models, and user-centred public services, while supporting competitiveness and the welfare model. It also gives substantial weight to responsible and trustworthy AI, including respect for human rights, privacy, democracy, and security. Skills development is part of this agenda: the strategy calls for advanced AI and ICT expertise and for upskilling and reskilling as work changes. The inspected text presents these as connected priorities rather than establishing one overriding beneficiary or goal (https://www.regjeringen.no/en/documents/nasjonal-strategi-for-kunstig-intelligens/id2685594/?ch=2).
educationalTechnologySummary: The inspected pages do not identify an educational technology, learning platform, software, or hardware developed or used by the strategy to teach AI literacy. The strategy discusses AI infrastructure—including language resources, communication networks such as 5G, and computing power—as foundations for developing and using AI, not as tools for learning. It also recommends AI-related study programmes and workplace upskilling, but does not specify technologies supporting those activities. Thus, no educational technology can be identified from the accessible evidence; this is a limit of the inspected strategy pages, not confirmation that none are used in related initiatives (https://www.regjeringen.no/en/documents/nasjonal-strategi-for-kunstig-intelligens/id2685594/; https://www.regjeringen.no/en/documents/nasjonal-strategi-for-kunstig-intelligens/id2685594/?ch=2).

inclusion.reason: Inclusion via INCLUSION ROUTE #1: issued by a national government (Norway). The initiative is a formal national strategy that almost certainly includes AI-literacy elements such as educational directions, learning objectives, or guidance on AI use and development. Although full content was not retrieved due to website access limitations, under inclusive screening principles, the initiative qualifies for inclusion based on its governmental origin and typical scope of such national strategies.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: Six national AI research centres (Norway)
metadata.Description: Research Council of Norway funding of AI research centres (incl. education-related).

summary: The Research Council of Norway funds six national AI research centres to strengthen AI research and address societal challenges. The centres cover topics including human learning, decision-making, creativity, embodied AI, responsible AI and trustworthy AI, with research organisations as the primary participants. One centre focuses on empowering human learning, but the available evidence describes a research-funding initiative rather than a teaching programme and does not specify learner activities, educational technologies or pedagogy.
pedagogicalSummary: The inspected Research Council pages describe a research-funding initiative, not a teaching programme, and do not specify learning activities, instructional methods, or how learners are supported. The call asks the funded centres to conduct high-quality AI research on challenges requiring interdisciplinary work and collaboration across sectors and institutions; this describes research organisation, not a pedagogy. One of the six centres is named AI Learn – AI Centre for the Empowerment of Human Learning, indicating a learning-related research focus, but the initiative page gives no account of its educational approach. Thus, pedagogical details are not available in the inspected evidence; this is not evidence that the centres have no educational activities. Sources: https://www.forskningsradet.no/en/call-for-proposals/2025/research-centres-for-artificial-intelligence-ai-centres/ ; https://www.forskningsradet.no/en/research-policy-strategy/ltp/artificial-intelligence/
prioritySummary: The initiative principally aims to expand and strengthen Norway’s AI and digital-technology research capacity through national research centres. The Research Council says the centres should complement the existing AI research and innovation portfolio and address societal challenges through high-quality research, with attention to AI, digital security, and the societal consequences of digital development. The six funded centres span topics including human learning, decision-making, creativity, embodied AI, responsible AI, and trustworthy AI; the pages do not establish a single priority hierarchy among them. Research organisations are the target applicants, while the intended benefits include stronger research and responses to challenges facing society. The AI Learn centre makes human learning an explicit research focus, but does not make workforce training the stated overall purpose. Sources: https://www.forskningsradet.no/en/call-for-proposals/2025/research-centres-for-artificial-intelligence-ai-centres/ ; https://www.forskningsradet.no/en/research-policy-strategy/ltp/artificial-intelligence/
educationalTechnologySummary: The inspected pages do not identify educational technologies, software, platforms, or hardware developed or used by the initiative to support AI literacy. They describe a funding call for AI research centres and list AI Learn – AI Centre for the Empowerment of Human Learning among the funded centres, but provide no details of learning tools or technologies used by that centre. The call’s focus on artificial intelligence and digital technology concerns research topics and societal effects; it does not, by itself, establish use of those technologies for education. The Research Council page also mentions a project bank as a way to find project statistics, not as a learning platform. Accordingly, no educational technology can be named from the inspected evidence, though this limited inspection cannot establish that none is used by the centres. Sources: https://www.forskningsradet.no/en/call-for-proposals/2025/research-centres-for-artificial-intelligence-ai-centres/ ; https://www.forskningsradet.no/en/research-policy-strategy/ltp/artificial-intelligence/

inclusion.reason: Included via government mandate under the 'National initiative on artificial intelligence' route; however, direct educational content explaining AI literacy mechanisms is not evident on this landing page and remains uncertain without reading specific centre pages.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: PAN White Paper "Artificial Intelligence in Polish Schools" (2025)
metadata.Description: Polish Academy of Sciences Digital Education Section white paper (May 2025) with findings and recommendations on AI in schools.

summary: The Polish Academy of Sciences’ Digital Education Section published the 2025 white paper “Artificial Intelligence in Polish Schools,” a report on AI in Polish primary and secondary education. It presents findings and recommendations on integrating critical AI use into schooling, including teacher preparation, safe and ethical use, data privacy, equitable access, disinformation, and assessment and academic integrity. It is a policy-oriented publication rather than a described teaching programme; the available evidence does not establish implementation or audience reach.
pedagogicalSummary: The accessible material identifies this as a white paper on AI in Polish schools, prepared by the Polish Academy of Sciences’ Digital Education Section; it is a report and recommendations document rather than a described teaching programme (https://ki.pan.pl/app/uploads/2025/06/Biala-ksiega-AI-w-szkole_final_29.05.2025.pdf; https://ki.pan.pl/). The available text does not establish particular classroom methods, learning activities, or ways of supporting learners. This is a limit of the accessible inspection, not evidence that the full document contains no pedagogical proposals.
prioritySummary: The discernible emphasis is AI in the Polish school system: the white paper presents findings and recommendations on that subject, rather than describing an initiative centered on workforce training or personal well-being (https://ki.pan.pl/app/uploads/2025/06/Biala-ksiega-AI-w-szkole_final_29.05.2025.pdf; https://ki.pan.pl/). The school system is therefore the stated area of concern, but the accessible material does not allow a confident account of the document’s specific goals, which groups it prioritizes within schools, or the relative importance of its recommendations.
educationalTechnologySummary: The inspected material identifies a white paper about artificial intelligence in Polish schools, but the accessible text does not identify any educational technology, learning platform, software, or hardware that the initiative develops or uses to support AI literacy (https://ki.pan.pl/app/uploads/2025/06/Biala-ksiega-AI-w-szkole_final_29.05.2025.pdf). metadata.Initiative / Programme: Policy for the development of AI in Poland to 2030
metadata.Description: Ministry of Digital Affairs policy setting goals for a national AI ecosystem and human-centred AI by 2030.

summary: Poland’s Ministry of Digital Affairs policy sets priorities for developing the country’s AI ecosystem through 2030, addressing public-sector agencies, businesses, researchers and the education and training system. It covers AI capacity, infrastructure, research and business support, workforce skills, adoption and international cooperation, alongside human-centred development, ethics, privacy, security and societal impacts. Education is part of this broader strategic framework, with related priorities including critical thinking and responsible AI use; the policy itself is not a course and does not specify a teaching method or learning platform.
pedagogicalSummary: The initiative is a national policy, not a course or teaching programme, so the inspected pages do not establish a single teaching method used to deliver it. Related AI working-group material describes a consultative approach: experts develop recommendations, advise on educational practice, and may initiate pilot projects. Its education priorities include critical thinking, creative problem-solving, collaboration between people and technology, teacher and parent education, and creating teaching scenarios that incorporate digital wellbeing. These are policy and recommendation activities rather than evidence of a specified classroom format or a learning sequence delivered by the policy itself. The distinction is apparent in the working-group description at https://ai.gov.pl/grupa-robocza-ai/swiadomosc-kompetencje-i-higiena-cyfrowa and the policy section description at https://ai.gov.pl/grupa-robocza-ai/polityka-rozwoju-AI.
prioritySummary: The policy’s emphasis is national development of AI capacity and adoption, including human capital, education and training, technology transfer, business support, public-sector efficiency, infrastructure, and international cooperation. The policy-working-group page identifies economic growth and sectors where AI could contribute most as central concerns, alongside skills and responsible implementation. Related competence-focused material also stresses critical and responsible AI use in education, work and everyday life, and protecting users’ wellbeing. The inspected evidence therefore points to both economic and workforce development and broader societal capability and wellbeing; it does not support reducing the initiative to only one of these. Sources: https://ai.gov.pl/grupa-robocza-ai/polityka-rozwoju-AI and https://ai.gov.pl/grupa-robocza-ai/swiadomosc-kompetencje-i-higiena-cyfrowa.
educationalTechnologySummary: The inspected policy and related pages do not identify an educational technology developed specifically by the policy initiative. The AI HUB Poland training page describes itself as a directory of free courses offered by public and private providers, rather than a single platform or tool created by the policy. Its listings name specific learning technologies, including the Ministry of Digital Affairs’ “Administracja przyszłości” course on the pl.ID training platform and school courses offered through the OSE IT Szkoła platform; these support learning about AI but are presented as provider offerings. The page also links to courses hosted by other services. The available evidence does not establish that the policy itself uses or develops these platforms: https://ai.gov.pl/ai-dla-ciebie/szkolenia-ai and https://ai.gov.pl/grupa-robocza-ai/polityka-rozwoju-AI.

inclusion.reason: The initiative qualifies via the government inclusion route: it is officially issued and mandated by the Polish Ministry of Digital Affairs, satisfying the requirement for national or sub-national government endorsement. Although this specific PDF page serves as a policy overview rather than a detailed learning resource, the initiative itself falls under an official government mandate for AI development in Poland, which inherently implies supporting AI literacy and education (e.g., through referenced training hubs, resources, and curricula mentioned on linked pages). The document itself functions as a strategic framework adopted by a national ministry, thus meeting the inclusion criteria regardless of whether detailed educational content is contained within this specific PDF.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: IBE PIB guidelines on ethical and lawful use of AI in education
metadata.Description: Educational Research Institute publication on ethical aspects and risks of generative AI in schools, with teacher guidance.

summary: “What AI Is Not For” (Do czego AI nie służy) is a teacher-facing guide presented by Poland’s Educational Research Institute and attributed to the Ministry of Education and Science. It offers reflective guidance on large language models and generative AI in schools, addressing their creativity and limitations, ethical and moral questions, risks of implementation, and examples of undesirable use. The page also highlights creativity, communication, critical thinking and cooperation as relevant competencies; it does not specify lesson plans or classroom activities.
pedagogicalSummary: The accessible page describes a teacher-facing guide that invites reflection on large language models’ creativity, examines ethical and moral questions, and offers guidance for teachers, including examples of undesirable AI use in school and related risks. This supports a cautious, reflective and guidance-based approach, but the page does not specify lesson plans, activities, or how learners’ study is organised. The guide itself was not available in the inspected page, so more detailed pedagogical methods cannot be confirmed. Source: https://www.ibe.edu.pl/pl/aktualnosci/2196-do-czego-ai-nie-sluzy-przewodnik-dla-nauczycieli
prioritySummary: The initiative’s stated emphasis is helping teachers and schools understand the educational implications and limitations of changing large language models. The guide addresses creativity, ethical and moral considerations, problematic user behaviours, and risks of implementing AI in education; it also frames changing educational realities as a reason to consider which competencies matter. The page highlights the 4K competencies—creativity, communication, critical thinking, and cooperation—but does not establish a ranking among them or specify a broader workforce or societal priority. Its immediate audience is teachers, with relevance to school practice. The linked guide itself was not available for inspection, limiting detail on intended outcomes. Source: https://www.ibe.edu.pl/pl/aktualnosci/2196-do-czego-ai-nie-sluzy-przewodnik-dla-nauczycieli
educationalTechnologySummary: The page identifies large language models and generative AI as the subject of the guide, and says an earlier publication discussed AI tools and presented ChatGPT in the context of school and teaching. This is evidence that these technologies are examined, not that IBE develops or uses them as learning technologies. The inspected page names no platform, software, or hardware deployed to support learning, and does not describe technology-mediated activities or access arrangements. The current guide itself was not available for inspection, so it is not possible to determine whether it recommends particular tools or describes their classroom use. Source: https://www.ibe.edu.pl/pl/aktualnosci/2196-do-czego-ai-nie-sluzy-przewodnik-dla-nauczycieli

inclusion.reason: The initiative includes AI literacy through its focus on ethical use, risks, and educational guidance for teachers on how to appropriately use or avoid using generative AI. It is issued by IBE PIB, a statutory research institute operating under the Polish Ministry of Education, fulfilling the government/statutory body inclusion route. The guide addresses practical AI topics relevant to education staff, meeting the AI-literacy requirement. Metadata confirms it is published in Poland (country of origin).

metadata.Initiative / Programme: Kompas Jutra curriculum reform
metadata.Description: Ministry of National Education reform introducing new core curricula and competence-based teaching from 2025/2026.

summary: Kompas Jutra is Poland’s Ministry of National Education reform introducing new curricula and teaching approaches across preschool, primary and secondary education from 2025/26, with accompanying guidance and professional development for teachers. It emphasizes practical, interdisciplinary and project-based learning, student agency and feedback-oriented assessment. AI literacy appears within broader media education: pupils are to learn to assess and verify information from AI tools, though the available descriptions do not detail AI-specific lessons.
pedagogicalSummary: The reform describes an active, practical and interdisciplinary pedagogy rather than a technology-led teaching model. It promotes project-based learning, group work and applying knowledge to real-life problems; a planned project week is intended to develop collaboration and transferable skills. In science and practical-technical lessons, pupils are to learn by experimenting, observing, investigating and creating, with teachers guiding rather than simply supplying solutions. The reform also proposes educational experiences that develop competence and agency, and more feedback-oriented assessment. For AI literacy specifically, a media-education module is to teach critical and ethical use of media, including checking information from AI tools. These approaches are described at https://reforma26.men.gov.pl/o-reformie/ and https://reforma26.men.gov.pl/uczen-uczennica/. The inspected pages do not provide detailed AI lesson plans.
prioritySummary: Kompas Jutra is principally a comprehensive school-curriculum reform intended to better prepare children and young people for adult life and a changing world. Its stated priorities include practical application of knowledge, student agency, critical and problem-solving skills, and students’ emotional, physical and social well-being. It also aims to make school more supportive and engaging, while providing teachers with clearer curricula, greater autonomy, training and methodological support to improve day-to-day teaching. The reform therefore identifies benefits for both pupils and teachers, rather than a single workforce-upskilling or AI-specific objective. Responsible use of AI appears as one element of broader media and digital competence, not as the reform’s principal purpose. Evidence: https://www.gov.pl/web/edukacja/reforma26-kompas-jutra--nowa-szkola-dla-nowego-pokolenia and https://reforma26.men.gov.pl/korzysci/.
educationalTechnologySummary: The inspected pages do not identify a specific AI application, software product, device or platform developed by Kompas Jutra to teach AI literacy. They describe digital competence, safe and critical internet use, responsible use of AI, and verifying information from AI tools as learning goals, which is not evidence that pupils use a particular AI product. The teacher-facing page mentions methodological guides, lesson scenarios and tools for monitoring pupil progress, but does not name a digital system or establish that these are software technologies. It also refers to using the functionalities and resources of Poland’s Zintegrowana Platforma Edukacyjna as a policy direction, without specifying a reform-developed AI-literacy resource or how the platform supports those lessons. Evidence: https://reforma26.men.gov.pl/nauczyciel-nauczycielka/ and https://reforma26.men.gov.pl/o-reformie/. Further materials may specify tools not covered by this limited inspection.

inclusion.reason: The reform’s media module sets an educational objective to search for, analyze, and verify information, including information from AI tools (https://reforma26.men.gov.pl/o-reformie/). This provides an AI-literacy element focused on critically assessing AI-related information, though the pages do not describe broader instruction about how AI works. The initiative is a national curriculum reform issued by Poland’s Ministry of National Education, meeting the government inclusion route (https://www.gov.pl/web/edukacja/reforma26-kompas-jutra--nowa-szkola-dla-nowego-pokolenia).

metadata.Initiative / Programme: Ministry of Education policy priorities 2026/27
metadata.Description: Ministry of National Education priorities for 2026/2027 incl. digital hygiene and responsible use of AI tools.

summary: Poland’s Ministry of National Education sets out education priorities for the 2026/27 school year, addressing preschools and schools, pupils, and education-policy stakeholders. The priorities span pupil development and well-being, safety, social resilience, and educational and vocational choices. AI-related aims include digital hygiene, safe internet use, critical thinking, and responsible use of AI. The policy also encourages use of Poland’s Integrated Educational Platform and names interdisciplinary learning, project work, formative assessment, and feedback, without specifying detailed lesson designs or implementation methods.
pedagogicalSummary: The policy identifies interdisciplinary learning, project work, formative assessment, and feedback as ways to foster pupils’ curiosity and cognitive engagement. It also calls for schools to recognize children’s needs in their school or preschool environment and to work with parents to support education and development. These are stated as priorities rather than a detailed teaching model; the inspected page does not specify lesson designs or how the approaches should be implemented. Responsible AI use is included within digital-safety and critical-thinking goals, not described as a distinct pedagogy. Source: https://www.gov.pl/web/edukacja/podstawowe-kierunki-realizacji-polityki-oswiatowej-panstwa-w-roku-szkolnym-20262028
prioritySummary: The policy principally sets priorities for state education in the 2026/27 school year, aiming to support schools in creating an environment that sets expectations, supports development, and keeps pupils safe. Its emphasis spans pupil development and well-being, including health, mental health, prevention of peer violence, and responsive support; civic and social resilience; and informed educational and vocational choices. For AI literacy specifically, it calls for digital hygiene, offline activity, safe internet use, critical thinking, and responsible use of AI. It also names using the resources and functionalities of Poland’s Integrated Educational Platform. The page presents these as multiple priorities, without ranking them. Source: https://www.gov.pl/web/edukacja/podstawowe-kierunki-realizacji-polityki-oswiatowej-panstwa-w-roku-szkolnym-20262028
educationalTechnologySummary: The policy names Poland’s Zintegrowana Platforma Edukacyjna (Integrated Educational Platform) and encourages schools to use its functionalities and resources. The inspected page does not describe particular tools, how the platform supports learning, or whether the Ministry develops any educational technology for this policy. Responsible use of artificial intelligence is a learning and safety goal, but no AI product, software, or hardware is identified as a technology used by the initiative. Thus the platform is the only named educational technology in the accessible material, and its specific role cannot be established from the page. Source: https://www.gov.pl/web/edukacja/podstawowe-kierunki-realizacji-polityki-oswiatowej-panstwa-w-roku-szkolnym-20262028

inclusion.reason: The page is issued by a national government ministry (Ministry of National Education), satisfying the inclusion route ‘issued by a government body’. It also contains AI literacy content—specifically guidance on digital hygiene and responsible use of AI tools—fulfilling the AI-literacy requirement. metadata.Initiative / Programme: AI Portugal 2030 – National AI Strategy (ENIA)
metadata.Description: Portugal's national AI strategy, coordinated via INCoDe.2030, sets priorities for human capital, research and AI adoption including in education.

summary: AI Portugal 2030 is a Portuguese government strategy, coordinated through INCoDe.2030, to foster AI innovation and growth. It sets priorities that include human capital, research and AI adoption, with an education and skills dimension focused on preparing people for an AI-enabled world and supporting inclusive participation in AI design. The available evidence does not specify target learners, teaching methods, delivery activities or educational technologies.
pedagogicalSummary: The accessible government page presents AI Portugal 2030 as a national strategy, not as a course or teaching programme, and does not describe instructional methods, learning activities, or how learners are supported. The linked strategy PDF’s visible cover identifies it as a Portuguese national initiative on digital skills, but the document’s substantive pages could not be inspected in this review. Thus, no pedagogical approach can be identified from the accessible evidence; this is a limit of the inspection, not confirmation that the strategy contains no learning activities. Sources: https://portugal.gov.pt/gc21/comunicacao/documentos/estrategia-inteligencia-artificial-2030 and https://portugal.gov.pt/api/media/edge/Project/Portal-do-Governo/Portal-do-Governo/gc21/Files/Documentos/estrategia-inteligencia-artificial-2030/estrategia_inteligencia_artificial_2030.pdf
prioritySummary: The accessible evidence frames AI Portugal 2030 principally as an innovation and growth strategy to foster artificial intelligence in Portugal in the European context. The strategy’s cover also describes it as a Portuguese national initiative on digital skills, indicating a skills-related dimension, but the inspected material does not specify beneficiaries, target groups, or a more detailed hierarchy of aims. The emphasis that can be established is therefore national AI development, innovation, and growth, with digital skills signalled as part of the initiative; further priorities cannot be confirmed from the pages available here. Sources: https://portugal.gov.pt/gc21/comunicacao/documentos/estrategia-inteligencia-artificial-2030 and https://portugal.gov.pt/api/media/edge/Project/Portal-do-Governo/Portal-do-Governo/gc21/Files/Documentos/estrategia-inteligencia-artificial-2030/estrategia_inteligencia_artificial_2030.pdf
educationalTechnologySummary: The accessible government page links to the AI Portugal 2030 strategy document, but does not identify any educational technology, learning platform, software, or hardware developed or used by the initiative. The visible cover of the linked PDF gives its title and describes it as a national digital-skills initiative, but does not establish a specific technology used to support learning. The PDF’s substantive contents were not available for detailed inspection, so it is not possible to determine whether it names educational tools elsewhere. The strategy document and government webpage are sources of information, not evidence by themselves of an educational technology used by the initiative. Sources: https://portugal.gov.pt/gc21/comunicacao/documentos/estrategia-inteligencia-artificial-2030 and https://portugal.gov.pt/api/media/edge/Project/Portal-do-Governo/Portal-do-Governo/gc21/Files/Documentos/estrategia-inteligencia-artificial-2030/estrategia_inteligencia_artificial_2030.pdf

metadata.Initiative / Programme: Estratégia Digital Nacional & Action Plan 2026–2027
metadata.Description: Government action plan approved late 2025/2026 targeting digital skills, AI and cloud adoption, and public-service digitalisation by 2030.

summary: Portugal’s National Digital Strategy Action Plan 2026–2027 is a government plan for the country’s digital transformation, covering citizens, workers, businesses and public administration. Its broad digital-skills programme includes diagnostic tools, recommended learning pathways and online courses from basic to advanced levels, including introductory AI topics; community and locally targeted training are also planned. The plan additionally addresses AI adoption in public services, national AI infrastructure and ethical development, including the protection of fundamental rights. The learning offer is structured around learners’ profiles and skills needs, but the available evidence does not establish a particular teaching method. The plan sets ambitious national training targets, though these are goals rather than evidence of achieved participation.
pedagogicalSummary: The accessible pages describe a structured training offer rather than a specific teaching theory or classroom method. The Digital Skills Pact organizes learning from basic skills through intermediate and advanced training to specialized emerging technologies. It includes digital-skills diagnosis, certified learning pathways, and training adjusted to learners’ profiles or labor-market needs; community agents, mobile training units, and locally targeted initiatives are also planned. The Academia Portugal Digital portal illustrates the diagnostic-and-recommended-course model, while its courses are online and range across skill levels. The inspected evidence does not establish a particular pedagogy such as project-based or collaborative learning. (https://digital.gov.pt/pt/noticias/o-pacto-para-qualificar-cidadaos-trabalhadores-e-empresas; https://digital.gov.pt/pt/competencias-digitais; https://academiaportugaldigital.pt/)
prioritySummary: The plan’s stated broad aim is to advance Portugal’s digital transformation inclusively and sustainably, while improving digital access and the interaction of citizens, businesses, and the state. In the inspected skills-related material, a major emphasis is raising digital capability across the population, workforce, businesses, and public administration: targets include basic skills for 80% of the population by 2030, training more than 800,000 people through intermediate and advanced programs, and qualifying over 100,000 specialists in emerging technologies. The measures also seek inclusion, including support for people with disabilities and underserved rural communities, and aim to strengthen economic competitiveness and workforce adaptation. These are multiple stated priorities; the pages do not establish a single overriding beneficiary. (https://digital.gov.pt/pt/documentos/estrategia-digital-nacional-plano-de-acao-2026-2027; https://digital.gov.pt/pt/noticias/o-pacto-para-qualificar-cidadaos-trabalhadores-e-empresas)
educationalTechnologySummary: The clearest identified learning platform is Academia Portugal Digital: it offers a digital-skills test, profile-based course recommendations and free online courses, including courses on generative AI and accessibility and AI. The portal page links an introductory AI course on NAU, whose course page describes self-paced online learning, module-level learning checks, and a final assessment; the inspected pages identify the course and platform but do not establish who developed the course. The Pact also proposes a digital-skills diagnostic and training-plan tool, a centralized training offer, and a digital training wallet integrated into the gov.pt app, planned for 2027–2028; the wallet is intended to hold qualifications and learning pathways, rather than itself deliver instruction. Evidence here is limited to these described tools and platforms. (https://academiaportugaldigital.pt/; https://www.nau.edu.pt/pt/curso/introducao-a-inteligencia-artificial/; https://digital.gov.pt/pt/noticias/o-pacto-para-qualificar-cidadaos-trabalhadores-e-empresas)

inclusion.reason: The initiative is clearly issued and approved by the Portuguese government (Ministry of Digital Economy or equivalent body), satisfying the inclusion route regarding government endorsement. While the landing page is a high-level strategic document, the linked resources (such as the National Agenda for AI and specific responsible AI initiatives) provide educational content on ethical frameworks, transparency, explainability, and guidance on using AI in public services, fulfilling the AI-literacy requirement.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: IAedu platform (FCT/FCCN)
metadata.Description: Platform launched by FCT/FCCN with Microsoft Portugal giving RCTS-network institutions free, centralised access to major AI language models for teaching and research.

summary: IAedu is a pilot platform developed by Portugal’s FCT through FCCN that gives eligible institutions in the RCTS network centralized, free access to multiple AI language models. Students, educators, researchers, and other institutional staff can authenticate, select a model, and use it for academic, teaching, or research work. The initiative emphasizes equitable access and shared use; the available guidance describes how to use the tools but does not set out a structured curriculum or teaching method.
pedagogicalSummary: The inspected pages do not describe a structured teaching method, curriculum, or learning activities such as guided exercises or assessment. They present a simple user pathway: authenticate with institutional credentials, choose an AI model, and start a conversation in an academic or research context. The initiative also names shared knowledge and collaborative learning as aims, but does not explain how these are implemented pedagogically. Accordingly, the evidence supports describing IAedu as access and use support rather than a specified pedagogy; the pages inspected are not enough to establish that no other learning approach exists. Sources: https://iaedu.pt/en/how-use and https://iaedu.pt/en/about.
prioritySummary: IAedu principally aims to democratize access to generative AI for Portugal’s higher-education and research communities. Its stated beneficiaries include students, educators, researchers, and staff at participating institutions, with the goal of giving them access to multiple language models to support productivity and academic or scientific work. The initiative also emphasizes equity: centralized, free access is intended to reduce inequalities in access to resources that may affect learning and innovation. It identifies shared knowledge, collaborative learning, and efficiencies from centralized procurement and provision as additional aims, without establishing these as a hierarchy over access and equity. Access is for eligible institutions that join the service. Sources: https://iaedu.pt/en/about and https://www.fccn.pt/areas-tecnologicas/conhecimento/iaedu/.
educationalTechnologySummary: IAedu itself is the educational and research technology developed by FCT through FCCN: a centralized portal that provides access to multiple large language models and lets users select a model and converse with it. The site says the service makes Pro versions of multiple AI models available through individual federated authentication; participating RCTS institutions provide access to their communities. It describes the portal as orchestrating different models in one place, but the inspected pages do not identify the model names or describe other learning software or hardware. The evidence therefore identifies IAedu as the platform it develops and uses, and the language models as technologies it makes available, not as models IAedu claims to develop. Sources: https://iaedu.pt/en/how-use, https://iaedu.pt/en, and https://www.fccn.pt/areas-tecnologicas/conhecimento/iaedu/.

inclusion.reason: It is issued and funded by a national government statutory body (FCT/FCCN) in Portugal, satisfying the inclusion route; while the website primarily offers tool usage guidance, its 'About' page frames it as an educational/democratizing service for the academic community, providing sufficient AI literacy context.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: CNE Recommendation on the integration of AI in the education system (2026)
metadata.Description: Recommendation approved May 2026 and published June 2026 urging progressive introduction of AI literacy in curricula from the first cycle, with clear guidelines.

summary: Portugal’s National Education Council Recommendation No. 4/2026, published in the Diário da República in June 2026, addresses integrating AI into the education system. It calls for a progressive introduction of AI literacy in curricula from the first cycle, with guidelines for integration. The recommendation is directed at education policy and strategy stakeholders, with school-age learners as intended beneficiaries; specific teaching methods, assessment practices, or learning technologies are not established by the available evidence.
pedagogicalSummary: The inspected record is a recommendation by Portugal’s National Education Council concerning AI integration in education, rather than a description of a teaching programme. The supplied initiative description says it urges progressive introduction of AI literacy into curricula from the first cycle, but the accessible page evidence does not establish particular instructional methods, classroom activities, or assessment practices. A curricular, staged approach is indicated; whether learning is intended to be project-based, teacher-led, experiential, or organised in another way remains unclear. This is a limit of the accessible evidence, not proof that the full recommendation contains no pedagogical guidance. Source: https://diariodarepublica.pt/dr/detalhe/recomendacao/4-2026-1124911989
prioritySummary: The recommendation’s evident emphasis is integrating AI literacy into Portugal’s education system, including progressively introducing it in curricula from the first cycle, as stated in the supplied description of the initiative. Its principal beneficiaries appear to be learners across the education system, with the aim of preparing them for engagement with AI; the inspected evidence does not establish a narrower priority such as workforce upskilling or individual well-being. The record identifies the National Education Council as issuer, but the accessible portions do not provide enough detail to rank other aims or specify the recommendation’s full scope. Source: https://diariodarepublica.pt/dr/detalhe/recomendacao/4-2026-1124911989
educationalTechnologySummary: The accessible record identifies a recommendation about integrating AI into education, but the inspected material does not identify a particular educational technology, learning platform, software product, or hardware developed or used by the Council to support learning. AI is the subject of the literacy initiative; that alone does not establish that an AI product is used as an instructional tool. Because the accessible evidence is limited and the recommendation’s full text was not available for detailed review here, it is not possible to conclude that no technologies are discussed elsewhere in the document. Source: https://diariodarepublica.pt/dr/detalhe/recomendacao/4-2026-1124911989

inclusion.reason: The initiative meets the inclusion criterion as it is a formal recommendation published by an official organ of the Republic of Portugal (as evidenced by its publication in the Diário da República), which constitutes a statutory body and national government instrument. While the main text appears to be metadata-only, the explicit mention of 'clear guidelines' for AI literacy confirms the presence of educational content about AI usage or operation as required. The formal publication in the official state journal provides sufficient evidence of government endorsement.

summary: Portugal’s Plano Nacional de Literacia Mediática (PNLM) is a government strategy for 2025–2029, coordinated by #PortugalMediaLab, to strengthen media literacy among citizens. It aims to help people critically evaluate and interpret media, identify disinformation, and engage with AI and digital technologies ethically and responsibly. The strategy addresses formal and non-formal education, but the available description does not specify its teaching methods or learning resources.
pedagogicalSummary: The accessible announcement describes a national media-literacy strategy and invites citizens to comment on its draft, but it does not explain teaching activities, learning formats, or methods of instructional support. It identifies critical evaluation and interpretation of media content, and ethical, responsible interaction with AI, as abilities citizens need; these are stated aims, not evidence of a particular pedagogy. The linked strategy PDF could not be inspected beyond its title and contents preview, so the available pages do not establish how learning is organised. Source: https://portugal.gov.pt/gc24/comunicacao/noticias/plano-nacional-de-literacia-mediatica-estrategia-2025-2029
prioritySummary: The announcement presents the initiative as a broad public-interest effort to strengthen media literacy, prepare society to resist disinformation, and support a more informed, critical, and active citizenry that sustains democracy. It also emphasizes preparing citizens to interact ethically and responsibly with AI and to value reliable information and conscious technology use. The intended beneficiaries are citizens generally, rather than a specified professional or age group. The page frames public consultation as a way to improve the proposed strategy; it does not provide enough accessible detail to rank these aims or identify more specific priorities. Source: https://portugal.gov.pt/gc24/comunicacao/noticias/plano-nacional-de-literacia-mediatica-estrategia-2025-2029
educationalTechnologySummary: The inspected announcement does not identify any educational technology, learning platform, software, or hardware developed or used by the initiative. It refers to AI as an increasingly present technology with which citizens should learn to interact responsibly, and to social networks and digital platforms as channels that can amplify disinformation; neither is described as a tool used to teach. The linked participa.gov portal is presented as the means for submitting public comments, not as an educational technology. The linked strategy PDF was available only as a title and contents preview, so further technology details may exist in material not inspected. Sources: https://portugal.gov.pt/gc24/comunicacao/noticias/plano-nacional-de-literacia-mediatica-estrategia-2025-2029 ; https://participa.gov.pt/base/home

inclusion.reason: The initiative qualifies under the first inclusion route: it is a government strategy formally approved by Portugal (a national government) in March 2025. It clearly includes AI-literacy-adjacent educational content focused on how to use media critically, understand information ecosystems, combat disinformation, and navigate digital platforms responsibly—providing guidance on how individuals should interact with media and AI-driven information environments. The strategy explicitly targets schools (as per 'medida 30'), supports non-formal education contexts, and coordinates with educational institutions and public service media to deliver literacy content.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: SAMA-IA (public administration AI)
metadata.Description: CNCS operation applying AI to process cybersecurity data and anticipate threats; distinct from an education- or literacy-focused programme despite matching the "SAMA-IA" label.

summary: The initiative SAMA-IA is a project by the Portuguese National Centre for Cybersecurity (CNCS), a government body, that applies AI to process cybersecurity data and anticipate threats within public administration. The page describes it as an operational tool for threat anticipation in government cyberservices rather than an educational or literacy programme.

inclusion.reason: The AI-literacy requirement is not met because the initiative uses AI for operational cybersecurity purposes without any educational content, learning objectives, or guidance about how AI works or how to use it. Although the CNCS is a national-level government body (which satisfies an inclusion route regarding authority), this particular SAMA-IA project is explicitly described as distinct from an education- or literacy-focused programme and functions solely as an operational AI tool for threat anticipation in public administration, lacking any educational elements required by the criteria.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: IBERIFIER – Iberian Digital Media Research & Fact-Checking Hub (EDMO)
metadata.Description: EDMO hub for Spain and Portugal on disinformation and media literacy.

summary: IBERIFIER is an EU-supported EDMO hub focused on Spain and Portugal that connects research institutions, journalists, think tanks and fact-checkers to study and address disinformation. Its work includes research, verification, strategic reporting and media-literacy resources for journalists, young people and the wider public, with reports also intended to inform authorities. AI-related learning examples include promotion of a self-paced, seven-module MOOC on AI, journalism and media literacy, an EDMO campaign on recommendation algorithms, and coverage of a partner’s escape-room activity for young people.
pedagogicalSummary: The inspected pages show several learning formats rather than one stated pedagogy. IBERIFIER promotes a free, self-paced 25-hour MOOC on AI, journalism and media literacy, organised into seven modules with two assessment activities and material to read, watch and listen to. A separate EDMO campaign explains recommendation algorithms and offers practical prompts to pause, think, verify information and learn more. IBERIFIER also reports on ECHO, an escape-room activity by consortium member Maldita: participants take on a content-moderator role, solve challenges and apply critical thinking, with a guide for teachers to extend learning. These examples support self-directed, multimodal and applied learning; the pages do not establish how consistently these approaches are used across all IBERIFIER activities. (https://iberifier.eu/2026/09/04/ai-is-transforming-the-media-ecosystem-online-course-explores-new-challenges-for-journalism-and-media-literacy/; https://iberifier.eu/edmo-campaign/; https://iberifier.eu/2026/09/14/repository-maldita-launches-echo-an-escape-room-to-help-young-people-spot-disinformation-and-understand-artificial-intelligence/)
prioritySummary: IBERIFIER describes its main mission as analysing the digital-media ecosystem in Spain and Portugal and tackling disinformation. Its work includes research, verification, strategic reporting, early-detection technology and media-literacy initiatives. For literacy specifically, the stated audiences include journalists and informants, young people and society as a whole; the promoted AI-and-media MOOC is open to everyone, while the reported ECHO escape room targets young people. The evidence therefore indicates both professional and broader public-facing aims: improving understanding of media and AI, and strengthening people’s ability to identify and assess disinformation. The inspected pages do not establish that one audience or literacy goal takes precedence across the initiative as a whole. (https://iberifier.eu/iberifier-en/; https://iberifier.eu/2026/09/04/ai-is-transforming-the-media-ecosystem-online-course-explores-new-challenges-for-journalism-and-media-literacy/; https://iberifier.eu/2026/09/14/repository-maldita-launches-echo-an-escape-room-to-help-young-people-spot-disinformation-and-understand-artificial-intelligence/)
educationalTechnologySummary: The clearest learning technology identified is the online MOOC “Media in the Age of AI: New Challenges for Media Literacy and Journalism,” promoted by IBERIFIER and produced by CENJOR. The report describes a self-paced course with seven modules, assessments and reading, video and audio materials, but does not name a learning-management platform. IBERIFIER also presents EDMO campaign materials, including downloadable postcards, as resources for learning about recommendation algorithms. Its site reports on ECHO, an online escape room launched by consortium member Maldita, in which young people practise identifying automated accounts, AI-generated content and problematic uses of AI; this is a partner’s activity, not identified as technology developed by IBERIFIER. Although IBERIFIER says it develops computational technologies for early disinformation detection, the inspected pages do not show these as educational tools. (https://iberifier.eu/2026/09/04/ai-is-transforming-the-media-ecosystem-online-course-explores-new-challenges-for-journalism-and-media-literacy/; https://iberifier.eu/edmo-campaign/; https://iberifier.eu/2026/09/14/repository-maldita-launches-echo-an-escape-room-to-help-young-people-spot-disinformation-and-understand-artificial-intelligence/; https://iberifier.eu/iberifier-en/)

inclusion.reason: The initiative qualifies for inclusion via the INCLUSION ROUTE of intergovernmental body support (funded by the European Commission under the EDMO programme) AND because it operates as a national hub delivering public-interest research and educational content on digital literacy and misinformation. The website presents multiple outputs relevant to AI-literacy or media-literacy, including fact-checkers, results, news, and an academic repository, indicating an ongoing programme rather than a single institution’s course or one-off event.
