metadata.Initiative / Programme: Romania National Strategy for AI 2024–2027
metadata.Description: Government-approved strategic framework for AI adoption covering research, skills and governance.

summary: Romania’s National Strategy for Artificial Intelligence 2024–2027 is a national, cross-sector framework for developing and adopting AI. Its objectives include research and development, AI education and skills, infrastructure and datasets, technology transfer, wider adoption, and governance, with an emphasis on trustworthy AI and human rights. It is intended to benefit people and organisations across sectors, including education, research, industry, and public administration. The available profile identifies AI education and skills as goals but does not specify curricula, teaching methods, or educational technologies; smart labs are listed as a related initiative, not established as part of this strategy.
pedagogicalSummary: The OECD profile identifies support for education in research and development and training in AI-specific skills as a strategic objective, but does not describe teaching activities, curricula, or a particular instructional approach. The evidence therefore supports an education and skills goal, not a claim about how learning is pedagogically organised. The profile also lists “Smart labs” among related initiatives, describing personalised learning with AI, but does not establish those labs as part of this strategy. The linked official legislation page could not be read during inspection, so further pedagogical detail may be missing. Source: https://oecd.ai/en/dashboards/policy-initiatives/romanias-national-ai-strategy-3795
prioritySummary: The strategy’s stated emphasis is broad development of Romania’s AI ecosystem, rather than a single target group or outcome. Its objectives include AI education and skills, research and development, infrastructure and reusable datasets, technology transfer, adoption of AI in society, and governance and regulation. The profile presents these as a set of objectives without ranking them. Its stated framing is excellence and trust in AI, with respect for human rights and alignment with OECD principles and EU requirements. The intended beneficiaries are correspondingly broad: people and organisations across sectors, including education, research, industry, public governance, and society. The linked official legislation page was inaccessible during inspection, limiting verification of further priorities. Source: https://oecd.ai/en/dashboards/policy-initiatives/romanias-national-ai-strategy-3795
educationalTechnologySummary: The inspected strategy profile does not identify a specific educational platform, software, hardware, or AI learning tool developed or used by the strategy. It mentions goals concerning AI education and skills, and separately lists smart labs as a related Romanian initiative; those labs are described as enabling personalised learning with AI, but the profile does not say they are technologies delivered by this strategy. The strategy’s broader references to infrastructure and datasets are not specified as educational technologies. Accordingly, no educational technology can be attributed to the strategy from the accessible evidence; this is a limit of the inspected profile, not confirmation that none exists. The linked official legislation page could not be read. Source: https://oecd.ai/en/dashboards/policy-initiatives/romanias-national-ai-strategy-3795

inclusion.reason: The initiative qualifies for inclusion because it is issued by a national government body (Romania) through formal strategic frameworks endorsed by the Ministry of Education and aligned with EU-wide digital plans. It explicitly includes AI literacy through high school 'smart labs' that teach personalized learning and reflection on the learning process using AI, fulfilling the educational content requirement. Additionally, the strategy is linked to the National Recovery and Resilience Plan (NRRP), confirming government funding and formal endorsement.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: "Ghid AI pentru educație" (ECDL România, 2026)
metadata.Description: Free practical guide (March 2026) with teaching scenarios and data-protection/academic-integrity guidance for AI use in schools.

summary: ECDL România’s free 2026 guide offers practical orientation for teachers, school leaders and other education stakeholders using AI in Romanian schools. It presents teaching, assessment and feedback scenarios, and guidance on pedagogically grounded and gradual adoption, human oversight, data protection, academic integrity and relevant EU and Romanian considerations. The guide also supports school-level decisions about integrating AI; students are indirect beneficiaries of the practices it promotes.
pedagogicalSummary: The accessible description presents the initiative as guidance for teachers and schools, rather than a course with a defined teaching sequence. It offers examples of AI use in teaching, assessment and feedback, alongside applicable teaching scenarios. Its stated approach is to make AI use pedagogically justified, gradual, evaluated and subject to human oversight; adoption is framed as a pedagogical and institutional decision, not merely a technical one. The guide also addresses data protection and academic integrity. The PDF’s contents page lists these themes, but the full document text could not be inspected in this review, so details of the scenarios and any further learning methods remain uncertain. Sources: https://icdl.ro/ghidaiedu-ro/ and https://icdl.ro/wp-content/uploads/2026/03/GHID_AI_PT_EDUCATIE_final.pdf
prioritySummary: The initiative principally aims to help Romanian schools integrate AI into education in a responsible, informed and pedagogically grounded way. It is explicitly offered free to schools and is aimed at teachers, school directors and other actors in the education system. The description responds to educators and pupils already using AI without clear guidance, validated competencies or shared standards; it therefore emphasizes practical orientation as well as responsible use, including privacy and academic integrity. Students may benefit through better-supported educational practice, but the accessible material presents school staff and institutions as the direct audience, rather than stating a separate student well-being or workforce objective. The detailed PDF was not fully readable in this inspection. Source: https://icdl.ro/ghidaiedu-ro/
educationalTechnologySummary: The identified learning resource is a free practical guide for schools, linked as a PDF from ICDL Romania’s page. The page characterizes it as a professional orientation tool, not a technical manual, and describes its support for educators as examples, teaching scenarios and school-level decision guidance. No named educational software, AI platform, hardware or specific AI product could be confirmed in the accessible description; the PDF’s full text was not available for detailed inspection, so it is unclear whether it names particular tools. The initiative therefore appears, from the inspected evidence, to provide guidance about using AI rather than to develop or specify a distinct educational technology. Sources: https://icdl.ro/ghidaiedu-ro/ and https://icdl.ro/wp-content/uploads/2026/03/GHID_AI_PT_EDUCATIE_final.pdf

inclusion.reason: The initiative includes clear AI literacy elements, including guidance on how AI works and should be used ethically, educational strategies, and legal frameworks. It is issued by ECDL Romania, a statutory body recognized internationally and nationally, which qualifies under the inclusion route of being formally endorsed or produced by a relevant organization with national reach.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: "Ghid de utilizare a IA în școli" (EduApps)
metadata.Description: Guide by Edu Apps Association with Romanian universities, released June 2026 as a free e-book for teachers.

summary: "Ghid de utilizare a IA în școli" is a free e-book for Romanian teachers, produced by Asociația Edu Apps with university partners as part of a broader digital-pedagogy project. It offers practical guidance for integrating AI into pre-university teaching while keeping pedagogy, teacher judgment and students’ critical thinking central. The wider project provides online teacher training, practical activities and post-course mentoring in digital competencies, including uses of AI for lesson planning, learning resources and assessment. The project reports training and certifying more than 15,200 teachers, with particular attention to educators in rural and disadvantaged areas.
pedagogicalSummary: The initiative combines practical teacher professional development with a guide that advocates keeping pedagogy and teacher judgment central when using AI. Its courses use real-school scenarios, asynchronous and live online activities, two levels, practical assessments and portfolios, with guidance from pedagogy and digital-technology trainers; the project also describes post-course mentoring. The guide proposes personalising learning, using ongoing assessment and feedback, and designing tasks where students first reason without AI and then critically review AI-assisted work. These are described as recommendations in the guide, not evidence that AI-based adaptive assessment is implemented by the initiative. The accessible pages do not detail the guide’s full learning sequence. Sources: https://pedagogiedigitala.clasaviitorului.ro/cursuri/ and https://pedagogiedigitala.clasaviitorului.ro/ghid-de-utilizare-a-inteligentei-artificiale-in-educatie-e-book-gratuit-pentru-profesori/
prioritySummary: The principal emphasis is building Romanian teachers’ digital and digital-pedagogy competencies so they can integrate technology, including AI, responsibly and effectively into pre-university teaching. The AI guide is offered free to teachers and education specialists, and the wider project reports training and certifying more than 15,200 teachers. The project also identifies teachers in rural and disadvantaged areas as a particular focus, aiming to improve their access to skills and resources. Intended benefits include better-quality teaching, time saved on preparation or repetitive work, and more responsive learning for pupils; the pages do not establish these as a ranked set of outcomes. Sources: https://pedagogiedigitala.clasaviitorului.ro/ and https://pedagogiedigitala.clasaviitorului.ro/ghid-de-utilizare-a-inteligentei-artificiale-in-educatie-e-book-gratuit-pentru-profesori/
educationalTechnologySummary: The inspected pages identify no specific AI product or platform by name. The courses teach teachers to use AI to generate text and images, lesson plans, assessment questions and educational resources, and to formulate prompts and adapt content; these are described as course activities, not as a named tool developed by the initiative. The course page also lists Google Classroom, Docs, Forms, Sites, Slides, Drive, YouTube, Earth and Maps, along with an unspecified authoring tool, as applications used in its digital-pedagogy training. The guide itself is distributed as a downloadable e-book/PDF, which is a learning resource rather than evidence of a dedicated educational-technology platform. metadata.Initiative / Programme: Rwanda National Day of AI Training for teachers
metadata.Description: Rwanda Ministry of Education, REB, Day of AI and MIT RAISE launched a national AI teacher-training programme in July 2025, reaching over 5,000 teachers in its first round.

summary: Rwanda’s Ministry of Education and Rwanda Basic Education Board, with MIT RAISE and Day of AI, are rolling out national AI-literacy training for primary and secondary teachers. In the first round, 150 master teachers were trained to cascade training to educators nationwide, reaching more than 5,000 teachers; training is intended to continue through the 2025–26 school year. The programme aims to prepare teachers and students for critical and ethical engagement with AI, drawing on Day of AI’s K–12 curriculum. Its broader materials use age-appropriate, hands-on inquiry and discussion, though the available account does not specify the methods or technologies used in Rwanda’s training sessions.
pedagogicalSummary: The Rwanda report describes a cascade model: MIT RAISE and Day of AI trained 150 master teachers, who then deliver training onward to educators nationwide. It does not detail the sessions’ teaching methods. Day of AI’s broader materials provide additional evidence of its approach: interactive professional learning, and age-graded lessons using hands-on investigations, discussion, and playful challenges; some lessons are explicitly “unplugged.” These support exploration and critical reflection rather than requiring students to use AI tools. The wider curriculum also includes structured student debate and participation in AI policymaking, though the inspected pages do not establish that these activities were part of the Rwanda training. Thus, evidence supports teacher cascade training and an inquiry- and discussion-oriented curriculum, but not a detailed account of how training was delivered in Rwanda. (https://www.mineduc.gov.rw/news-detail/in-rwanda-first-round-of-national-day-of-ai-training-reaches-5000-teachers; https://dayofai.org/professional-development; https://dayofai.org/units/grade-1-learning-from-patterns; https://dayofai.org/units/ai-student-senate-classroom-community-guides)
prioritySummary: The initiative’s central emphasis is building foundational AI literacy among Rwanda’s primary and secondary teachers at national scale, with students as the intended wider beneficiaries. The first phase reached more than 5,000 teachers, and the report says the program aims to equip all teachers; the cascade of trained master teachers is the means to extend that reach. Its stated educational purpose goes beyond learning to operate AI tools: teachers and the next generation should engage critically and ethically with AI’s role in society. The Ministry also frames AI as a way to support teachers and personalized attention for students, not replace educators. Rwanda’s national readiness and knowledge-economy ambitions are contextual goals, but the inspected account foregrounds educator capacity and student preparation. (https://www.mineduc.gov.rw/news-detail/in-rwanda-first-round-of-national-day-of-ai-training-reaches-5000-teachers; https://dayofai.org/about-us)
educationalTechnologySummary: The Rwanda announcement identifies no dedicated learning platform, software, or hardware used in the teacher training. It says MIT’s Day of AI curriculum is freely available and describes the initiative as focused on literacy, including critical and ethical engagement, rather than specifying particular AI applications. Day of AI’s broader curriculum pages identify supporting teaching materials such as slide decks, Google Slides, educator guides, and downloadable Microsoft Office resources; its professional-learning page also links to recorded sessions and webinars. These are resources associated with the wider Day of AI offering, not confirmed as tools used in Rwanda’s training. Day of AI says its student activities can be done without AI tools and its professional learning is tool-agnostic. The inspected evidence therefore supports resource-based instruction, but does not confirm the technologies used in the Rwandan delivery itself. (https://www.mineduc.gov.rw/news-detail/in-rwanda-first-round-of-national-day-of-ai-training-reaches-5000-teachers; https://dayofai.org/curriculum-resources; https://dayofai.org/units/grade-1-learning-from-patterns; https://dayofai.org/professional-development; https://dayofai.org/)

inclusion.reason: The initiative includes explicit educational content about how AI works (mechanisms, limitations, ethics), meets the AI-literacy requirement, and has evidenced system-scale adoption: used by over 30 countries with access via MIT RAISE’s national platforms. This satisfies an inclusion route under 'framework actually used by several jurisdictions' or 'non-government work with system-scale adoption'. The page URL showing adoption evidence is https://dayofai.org/curriculum-resources.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: Saudi Arabia national AI framework (SDAIA) & MoE requirements
metadata.Description: SDAIA's 2020 national data/AI strategy includes education as a priority sector; for 2025-2026, MoE/National Centre for Curriculum/SDAIA rolled out an AI curriculum to ~6 million K-12 students.

summary: Saudi Arabia’s National Strategy for Data and AI, issued by SDAIA and approved in 2020, is a government framework for developing the country’s data and AI economy and talent. It identifies education as a priority, aiming to integrate data and AI into learning and align student skills with labour-market needs. Related MoE and SDAIA implementation reportedly includes an AI curriculum for around six million K–12 students in 2025–2026; SDAIA also supports workforce development through professional training and study opportunities. The available evidence describes national goals and programmes but does not specify classroom pedagogy or learning technologies.
pedagogicalSummary: The strategy page is a national framework rather than a description of classroom teaching: it names education as a priority but does not specify a teaching method or curriculum. A related SDAIA capacity-building page describes specialized professional programs and training, plus scholarships for study at global universities in AI and data science. These establish training and formal study as ways learning is supported, but the inspected pages do not explain their instructional design, learning activities, or assessment. No specific pedagogical approach can therefore be identified from this evidence. (https://sdaia.gov.sa/en/SDAIA/SdaiaStrategies/Pages/NationalStrategyForDataAndAI.aspx; https://sdaia.gov.sa/en/Sectors/BuildingCapacity/Pages/default.aspx)
prioritySummary: The strategy principally aims to establish Saudi Arabia as a global data- and AI-driven economy, with a related priority of building national talent. Its stated education goal is to incorporate data and AI into education to align the system with labor-market requirements and improve students’ skills. The broader skills objective is to create a steady local supply of data- and AI-empowered talent, while SDAIA’s capacity-building initiatives target national talent and job-market needs through professional programs, training, and scholarships. The evidence thus points to both student skill development and workforce capacity, within a national economic and societal development agenda; it does not establish a more specific educational target group or hierarchy between these priorities. (https://sdaia.gov.sa/en/SDAIA/SdaiaStrategies/Pages/NationalStrategyForDataAndAI.aspx; https://sdaia.gov.sa/en/Sectors/BuildingCapacity/Pages/default.aspx)
educationalTechnologySummary: The inspected strategy and capacity-building pages do not identify a learning platform, educational software, hardware, or other educational technology that SDAIA develops or uses to support AI-literacy learning. The strategy refers broadly to development, creation, and adoption of data and AI technologies across the Kingdom, but that is a national technology ambition, not evidence of a learning tool. The capacity-building page names SDAIA Academy, the Information Technology Institute, an AI Scholarship Program, Cooperative Training Program, and ATHKA X; it describes training and study opportunities, but does not identify educational technologies used within them. Accordingly, no specific educational technology can be reported from the inspected pages; this is a limit of the accessible evidence, not confirmation that none exist. (https://sdaia.gov.sa/en/SDAIA/SdaiaStrategies/Pages/NationalStrategyForDataAndAI.aspx; https://sdaia.gov.sa/en/Sectors/BuildingCapacity/Pages/default.aspx)

inclusion.reason: The initiative qualifies under Inclusion Route 1 as it was approved by the Custodian of the Two Holy Mosques (the King) and issued by a national government authority (SDAIA), fulfilling the requirement for formal endorsement; while the strategy text focuses on high-level goals, the specific implementation of an AI curriculum for ~6 million students addresses the AI-literacy requirement.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: Strategy for the Development of AI in Serbia 2025–2030
metadata.Description: The Government of Serbia adopted this strategy setting goals and measures for AI development 2025-2030, continuing its 2019 predecessor strategy.

summary: The Government of Serbia’s 2025–2030 AI Development Strategy sets national priorities for AI, including education, research and innovation, infrastructure, legal frameworks, and public-sector adoption. Its education provisions span secondary and higher education and informal training; related school offerings introduce AI concepts and applications, including through work with a simple AI-enabled robot and an elective emphasizing critical, responsible use and problem-solving. The strategy also addresses AI’s effects on society and the workforce, but the available descriptions do not establish detailed teaching materials or a single pedagogy for the strategy.
pedagogicalSummary: The strategy announcement describes education investment as a policy measure, not a teaching method. Related education pages on the initiative’s site show AI learning embedded in school subjects: seventh-graders study AI’s role, everyday uses, and effects on people, while eighth-graders use constructivist modeling to assemble and operate a simple AI-enabled school robot. In high school, an elective course emphasizes critical, safe, responsible technology use, logical and algorithmic thinking, and solving problems; these objectives suggest applied and problem-centered learning. The pages do not detail lesson plans, assessment, teacher support, or a single pedagogy for the 2025–2030 strategy, so evidence is limited to these descriptions of existing school provision. Sources: https://www.ai.gov.rs/vest/sr/1503/usvojena-strategija-za-razvoj-vestacke-inteligencije-u-republici-srbiji-za-period-od-2025-do-2030-godine.php; https://www.ai.gov.rs/tekst/sr/197/ai-u-osnovnim-skolama.php; https://www.ai.gov.rs/tekst/sr/198/ai-u-srednjim-skolama.php
prioritySummary: The strategy’s central emphasis is accelerating AI development and adoption in Serbia, through continued investment in education, innovation, computing infrastructure, legal frameworks, and public-sector use. Its intended beneficiaries and users include learners and the future workforce, researchers, startups and industry, public bodies, and society more broadly. The announcement links AI deployment to national modernization and cites potential benefits such as earlier disease detection, better treatment, more efficient public services, and improved energy and agricultural production. It presents these as a range of anticipated outcomes rather than establishing one dominant social beneficiary. The inspected announcement does not give detailed measures or a ranking of priorities, so this summary reflects its high-level account. Source: https://www.ai.gov.rs/vest/sr/1503/usvojena-strategija-za-razvoj-vestacke-inteligencije-u-republici-srbiji-za-period-od-2025-do-2030-godine.php
educationalTechnologySummary: The inspected pages do not identify a dedicated learning platform, educational software, or named classroom hardware developed for AI literacy. The schools page says eighth-graders assemble and operate a simple AI-enabled school robot through modeling, but provides no robot model or associated software. The National AI Platform is a government-provided supercomputer and data-science infrastructure intended for public administration, academic research, industry, and startups; the page describes it as enabling more complex AI tasks and model development, not as a teaching tool. Thus, it is relevant AI infrastructure but should not be treated as an educational technology used for instruction based on this evidence. Specific classroom tools and the strategy’s detailed education provisions could not be established from the inspected pages. Sources: https://www.ai.gov.rs/tekst/sr/197/ai-u-osnovnim-skolama.php; https://www.ai.gov.rs/tekst/sr/189/nacionalna-vi-platforma.php

inclusion.reason: Inclusion via national government endorsement (Issued by a national government). While the initial page does not explicitly detail AI literacy content, linked pages indicate structured educational initiatives on AI in schools and universities, suggesting AI literacy components. Uncertainty remains about the depth of specific learning objectives but leans to inclusion as per guidelines.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: Digital competence framework for teachers "Teacher for the digital age"
metadata.Description: Ministry of Education framework (2019 revision) defining the digital competences expected of teachers in Serbia.

summary: “Teacher for the Digital Age” is Serbia’s 2019 revision of a national framework defining digital competencies for teachers. It covers areas including digital safety and privacy, communication and collaboration, content creation, professional development, and assistive technology; its main emphasis is broad digital competence, with AI-related concerns addressed within the framework rather than as its central focus. A related training plan targeted 3,600 primary- and secondary-school teachers and used one day of in-person training followed by online work through the Teachers’ Education Portal.
pedagogicalSummary: The initiative is a competency framework, not itself a course, and the accessible description does not specify teaching methods within the framework. Related teacher training offers evidence of a blended format: one day of in-person work followed by one day of online work on the Teachers’ Education Portal. This suggests professional learning supported through both face-to-face and online participation, but the inspected pages do not describe the activities, feedback, or assessment used, so a more specific pedagogical approach cannot be established. The framework is presented as supporting teachers’ digital competence and adapting education to an increasingly mobile and digital world. Sources: https://zuov.gov.rs/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/2019_ODK_Nastavnik-za-digitalno-doba.pdf ; https://zuov.gov.rs/raspored-obuka-zaposlenih-u-osnovnim-i-srednjim-skolama-razvoj-digitalnih-kompetencija/
prioritySummary: The main emphasis is developing digital competence among teachers in Serbia, with a specific 2019 training plan targeting 3,600 primary- and secondary-school teachers who did not have a satisfactory level of digital competence. The framework was jointly published by the education ministry and education institutes as a revision of the 2017 framework. Its stated rationale connects teachers’ capabilities with improving education through digital technologies and with the need for new approaches to teaching and learning in a more mobile, digital environment. The accessible evidence therefore points principally to teacher professional capacity, with improved educational practice as a broader intended benefit; it does not establish a separate AI-literacy priority. Sources: https://zuov.gov.rs/usvojen-novi-okvir-digitalnih-kompetencija-nastavnika/ ; https://zuov.gov.rs/raspored-obuka-zaposlenih-u-osnovnim-i-srednjim-skolama-razvoj-digitalnih-kompetencija/
educationalTechnologySummary: The training announcement identifies the Teachers’ Education Portal (Наставнички образовни портал) as the platform for the online portion of the digital-competence training: participants were to complete one day of online work there after one day of in-person training. This is evidence of a digital platform being used to support teacher professional learning, but the inspected page does not describe its features or learning materials. The framework PDF itself is a document setting out competencies, not evidence of a software or hardware product developed by the initiative. No AI-specific educational technology is identified in the accessible pages, and there is insufficient evidence to determine whether the initiative developed the portal or used other technologies. Sources: https://zuov.gov.rs/raspored-obuka-zaposlenih-u-osnovnim-i-srednjim-skolama-razvoj-digitalnih-kompetencija/ ; https://zuov.gov.rs/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/2019_ODK_Nastavnik-za-digitalno-doba.pdf

inclusion.reason: The initiative qualifies for inclusion because it is issued and mandated by a national government body (the Ministry of Education of Serbia), satisfying the 'Issued by a government' inclusion route. It includes substantive AI literacy elements: under competency domain 4 ('Digital safety'), section 2 ('Privacy') specifically addresses risks related to personal data collection, algorithmic bias, manipulation by AI, and copyright issues with AI tools; and domain 5 ('Access'), section 3 mentions the 'Digital divide,' which encompasses access barriers caused by AI technologies. The framework also covers assistive technology, relevant to inclusive AI deployment.

metadata.Description: Serbian Government adopted non-binding ethics guidelines (March 2023) for trustworthy AI, based on UNESCO's Recommendation on AI ethics.

summary: In March 2023, the Serbian Government adopted non-binding ethical guidelines for the development, application and use of trustworthy and responsible AI. Based on UNESCO’s Recommendation on AI Ethics, the guidelines set out a preventive approach that includes verifying machine-learning-based systems against ethical and security standards. They provide a national governance reference for AI policy and practice; the announcement does not specify particular user groups or describe educational activities.
pedagogicalSummary: The inspected announcement describes the Serbian Government adopting ethical guidelines, not a learning programme or teaching activity. It gives no evidence of a pedagogy, learner group, curriculum, or learning format; this is missing evidence in the inspected page, not confirmation that none exists elsewhere. The stated mechanism is preventive oversight and verification of machine-learning-based systems against ethical and security standards, which is governance rather than a described method of teaching AI literacy. Source: https://www.srbija.gov.rs/vest/en/203799/ethical-guidelines-for-development-use-of-artificial-intelligence-adopted.php
prioritySummary: The announcement presents the guidelines as a way to encourage responsible development, application, and use of AI, through a preventive mechanism and verification that machine-learning-based systems meet high ethical and security standards. Its emphasis is trustworthy and responsible AI practice, rather than a stated educational or workforce-upskilling goal. The page does not identify a particular beneficiary group or explain who will carry out verification, so any more specific account of beneficiaries would be uncertain. Source: https://www.srbija.gov.rs/vest/en/203799/ethical-guidelines-for-development-use-of-artificial-intelligence-adopted.php
educationalTechnologySummary: The inspected announcement does not identify any educational technology, learning platform, software, or hardware developed or used by the initiative. It refers to machine-learning-based systems as the subject of ethical and security verification, but does not describe them as tools for learning AI literacy. Because the page is a brief government announcement about adopting guidelines rather than an account of educational activities, the available evidence cannot establish whether educational technologies are used elsewhere in implementation. Source: https://www.srbija.gov.rs/vest/en/203799/ethical-guidelines-for-development-use-of-artificial-intelligence-adopted.php

inclusion.reason: The initiative is issued by the Government of the Republic of Serbia, a national government entity, satisfying the inclusion route for government endorsement. While the page text provided does not explicitly detail educational content or learning objectives about how AI works, the guidelines are referenced as foundational for broader responsible AI use and development in Serbia. Given the inclusive screening principle, this is treated as potentially qualifying under governmental issuance, though further review of the actual guideline documents would be needed to confirm whether they contain explicit AI literacy elements (e.g., educational components or guidance on using/understanding AI). Uncertainty remains about the presence of specific AI literacy content in the guidelines themselves, but the government endorsement qualifies for inclusion at this stage.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: ZUOV AI platform for teachers
metadata.Description: The Institute for the Improvement of Education (ZUOV) publishes guidance and tools on using AI in teaching, including lesson-prep support and tool overviews (Gemini, NotebookLM).

summary: The Institute for the Improvement of Education (ZUOV), a Serbian public education body, provides a resource hub on using AI in education. Its teacher-facing materials include introductory guidance, tutorials and examples for lesson preparation, advice on safe and pedagogically appropriate use of tools such as Gemini and NotebookLM, and ZUOV-developed AI assistants. The initiative also identifies a competency framework for AI literacy in primary and secondary education and includes resources on AI policy and strategy. The evidence supports practical, tutorial-based guidance, but does not establish a formal course or measured uptake.
pedagogicalSummary: The accessible page presents a practical, teacher-facing approach: educators are invited to study introductory material and apply AI through tutorials and examples, including using an AI assistant to prepare lessons. The materials emphasize safe, responsible, and pedagogically appropriate use rather than technology for its own sake. A competence framework is also identified for developing AI literacy in primary and secondary education, though the page does not detail its learning sequence or classroom methods. The evidence supports tutorial-based guidance and practical application, but not a specific formal instructional model, assessment design, or structured course. Source: https://zuov.gov.rs/vestacka-inteligencija/
prioritySummary: The initiative’s clearest emphasis is supporting educators in understanding and applying AI in teaching, especially through lesson-preparation assistance and guidance on safe, pedagogically appropriate use of tools. It also identifies AI-literacy competence development for primary and secondary education, indicating an intended benefit for school learners as well as teachers. The inspected page offers resources on AI basics, tool use, and education-related guidance, but does not establish a single ranked priority or provide evidence of broader workforce or individual well-being goals. The emphasis described here is limited to what the page presents. Source: https://zuov.gov.rs/vestacka-inteligencija/
educationalTechnologySummary: ZUOV states that it developed a customized AI model to generate suggested lesson plans; its page offers a work guide and links to a teaching planner through ChatGPT and Gemini. It also lists ZUOV-branded GPT pedagogical assistants concerning democratic culture, road safety, and digital citizenship. These are identified as tools for teachers to apply, although the page does not explain their technical design or evaluate their learning effects. The initiative also provides tutorials and guidance about external products, including Google Gemini and NotebookLM; these are presented as technologies to learn about or use, not as ZUOV-developed products. The inspected page does not establish further platform or hardware use. Source: https://zuov.gov.rs/vestacka-inteligencija/

inclusion.reason: The initiative qualifies under the inclusion route of being issued by a statutory/governmental body. ZUOV is explicitly identified as an institute founded by the Government Decision and operating under Serbian education law; it is not merely funded but is a public educational authority. The page provides clear AI-literacy content for teachers: explanations of how generative AI works, specific pedagogical use cases (lesson prep, feedback), tool guidance, safety policies, and prompt-engineering best practices. Therefore, the initiative satisfies both the AI-literacy requirement and the inclusion route.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: Sierra Leone Digital Transformation Project (World Bank)
metadata.Description: US$50 million World Bank/IDA-funded project (2022-2027) supporting broadband expansion, digital skills development and e-government in Sierra Leone.

summary: The Sierra Leone Digital Transformation Project (SLDTP) is a government-implemented, World Bank/IDA-funded national project (2022–2027) focused on expanding broadband, strengthening digital skills and improving digital public services. Its skills and innovation activities include a 10-day AI and blockchain bootcamp for young innovators, featuring expert instruction, practical labs, collaboration, mentorship and prototype development; reported topics and tools include LLMs, AI explainability and debugging, and development platforms. The project also reports training for public-sector ICT professionals and aims to build digital competencies among citizens, including youth, women and persons with disabilities.
pedagogicalSummary: The initiative’s main AI-specific learning example is a 10-day bootcamp structured around three tracks, combining expert-led instruction with hands-on technical sessions, practical labs, group exercises, peer collaboration and feedback, and mentorship. Participants apply ideas to real-world challenges and develop prototypes, followed by a four-week team build phase to refine or create solutions. This supports a practical, collaborative, project-based approach rather than a solely lecture-based one. A separate training example for government ICT staff describes capacity-building in digital service standards and enterprise architecture, but gives less detail about teaching methods. These are reported activities, not evidence that every digital-skills component uses the same pedagogy; the inspected pages do not provide a broader curriculum or assessment approach. Sources: https://sldtp.gov.sl/sldtp-and-mocti-conclude-transformative-10-day-ai-and-blockchain-bootcamp-for-the-big-5-ai-and-blockchain-hackathon/ and https://sldtp.gov.sl/sldtp-supports-training-of-100-ict-professionals-on-digital-service-standards-and-enterprise-architecture/
prioritySummary: SLDTP is principally a national digital-transformation project, not solely an AI-literacy initiative: its stated objectives are expanding broadband access, enhancing digital skills, and improving government capacity to deliver public services digitally. Its skills and innovation component aims to build capabilities across demographics, while the homepage particularly identifies youth, women, and persons with disabilities as groups to equip with marketable digital competencies. The AI and blockchain bootcamp gives this skills agenda a specific youth-innovation emphasis: it brought together young people to build solutions, including for public-service challenges, with stated attention to gender and disability inclusion. The site also describes training public-sector ICT professionals, reflecting an institutional capacity priority alongside citizen skills and innovation. The inspected pages present these priorities together rather than establishing a single dominant beneficiary group. Sources: https://sldtp.gov.sl/who-we-are/, https://sldtp.gov.sl/, https://sldtp.gov.sl/project-components/, and https://sldtp.gov.sl/sldtp-and-mocti-conclude-transformative-10-day-ai-and-blockchain-hackathon/
educationalTechnologySummary: The inspected bootcamp report identifies third-party software and development tools used in learning, rather than technologies developed by SLDTP. Participants in its AI track were to build AI-driven solutions using tools such as ChatGPT, Copilot, and low-code platforms; sessions also covered NotebookLM, Cursor, model-explainability tools LIME and SHAP, and hands-on AI debugging with FastAPI, Flask, and Hugging Face. It does not describe a dedicated learning platform or hardware developed by the project, nor establish that all tools were used by every participant. The broader project website mentions digital access and assistive technologies, but the inspected material does not identify those as AI-literacy teaching technologies. metadata.Initiative / Programme: Digital Coalition & Digitálna strelka (Slovakia)
metadata.Description: Ministry-led coalition promoting digital skills, incl. the "Digitálna strelka" project guiding youth (esp. girls) towards ICT.

summary: The Slovak Ministry of Investments, Regional Development and IT’s Digital Coalition brings public, private, academic and civil-society organizations together to support digital skills and readiness for digital transformation among citizens, employees, IT specialists and in education. Within this broader effort, Digitálna Strelka focuses on encouraging schoolgirls to consider digital studies and careers: its web and app resources use interest-and-strength quizzes, career and study information, and women role models, while also addressing parents and teachers as supporters. The materials emphasize self-directed career exploration and guidance rather than a documented formal curriculum; the evidence describes digital skills generally, not a specific AI-literacy programme.
pedagogicalSummary: The inspected pages describe career exploration and guidance rather than a formal teaching method or curriculum. Digitálna Strelka invites schoolgirls to reflect on their interests and strengths through quizzes, explore possible digital careers, find relevant schools and courses, and learn from women role models. Its materials also encourage parents and teachers to support and mentor girls; the teacher page suggests hands-on activities such as robotics, game programming, and app creation, but these appear as recommendations rather than documented programme delivery. The Digital Coalition’s ministry page describes coordination and commitments to improve skills, but does not specify how learning is taught. This evidence supports self-directed exploration, role-model-based inspiration, and adult guidance; it does not establish a structured pedagogy or AI-literacy teaching approach. (https://www.digitalnastrelka.sk/ziacky/; https://www.digitalnastrelka.sk/ucitelia/; https://mirri.gov.sk/sekcie/informatizacia/narodne-iniciativy/digitalna-koalicia/)
prioritySummary: The Digital Coalition’s stated emphasis is improving digital skills in Slovakia through cooperation among public, private, academic, and civil-society organizations. The ministry page identifies citizens, IT specialists, employees, and education as beneficiaries, while the coalition commits to supporting awareness and readiness for societal digital transformation. Digitálna Strelka gives this broad agenda a specific inclusion and career-orientation focus: it encourages schoolgirls to consider digital education and IT careers, with parents and teachers also addressed as supporters. Its materials frame this as both opening opportunities for girls and developing future IT talent. The inspected pages therefore indicate overlapping priorities—broad digital-skills development and greater girls’ participation in digital careers—without establishing that one supersedes the other. The evidence concerns digital skills generally, not a distinct AI-literacy priority. (https://mirri.gov.sk/sekcie/informatizacia/narodne-iniciativy/digitalna-koalicia/; https://www.digitalnastrelka.sk/)
educationalTechnologySummary: Digitálna Strelka provides a named digital resource: its web platform and associated app at digitalnastrelka.app. The accessible pages describe quizzes that help girls relate interests and strengths to digital occupations, alongside searchable information about schools, study options, careers, and media featuring role models. These tools support exploration and guidance; the pages do not establish that they teach AI or provide AI-learning functionality. The Coalition site also lists projects such as IT Fitness Test, but the inspected pages do not show whether or how it is integrated into instruction. No dedicated AI educational software, hardware, or AI-learning platform was identified in this limited inspection. The ministry page presents the coalition mainly as a partnership and commitment framework, not as a technology developer. (https://digitalnastrelka.app/; https://www.digitalnastrelka.sk/ziacky/; https://digitalnakoalicia.sk/; https://mirri.gov.sk/sekcie/informatizacia/narodne-iniciativy/digitalna-koalicia/)

inclusion.reason: The initiative qualifies for inclusion because it is issued by a national government ministry (the Slovak Ministry of Investments, Regional Development and IT), which satisfies the INCLUSION ROUTE regarding government endorsement. The page confirms it guides youth, particularly girls, towards ICT careers, indicating an educational purpose to improve digital literacy among a target demographic.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: Plan for the Responsible Use of AI (Slovak Ministry of Education)
metadata.Description: Ministry plan referenced by respondent.

summary: The Slovak Ministry of Education’s 2025–2027 Plan for the Responsible Use of AI in Education sets national priorities for AI education and responsible use in schools. It aims to build pupils’ understanding of AI and support its safe, critical and creative use, while providing guidance and professional development for teachers and promoting equitable access to AI tools. The plan envisages curriculum content, teaching materials, an information platform and AI competence centres, alongside pilots of AI-supported teaching and feedback tools. It also addresses privacy, rights and the broader social impacts of AI; many of its resources and supports are planned rather than documented as fully implemented.
pedagogicalSummary: The plan supports systematic AI education in primary and secondary schools, with teaching about AI alongside safe, critical and creative use of AI tools. It envisages curriculum content, teaching materials, school and teacher support, and AI competence centres at selected universities; school instruction is scheduled to begin in 2026–27. The document also describes personalized and interactive learning as potential uses of AI, and pilots to examine soft-skills development and generative-AI formative feedback. These indicate a mix of formal instruction, teacher-supported practice and evaluation of learning tools, but the inspected plan does not set out a detailed teaching method. metadata.Initiative / Programme: State Educational Programme – AI literacy for primary schools (2026)
metadata.Description: Ministry of Education amended the State Educational Programme making AI literacy part of primary education from March 2026.

summary: Slovakia’s amended State Educational Programme makes AI literacy part of primary and basic-school education from March 2026, with learning outcomes developed across three cycles and linked to subjects including languages, sciences, social sciences and the arts. Pupils progress from recognising AI and creating simple prompts with teacher guidance to using generative AI for learning, checking outputs and sources, and selecting tools independently. The curriculum also addresses AI principles and limitations, data, safety, privacy, ethics, and social and environmental effects. The Ministry reports initial teaching materials and plans teacher training; the programme does not prescribe specific AI applications.
pedagogicalSummary: The curriculum describes a staged, teacher-supported approach rather than prescribing a named teaching method. AI literacy develops across three learning cycles through primary school, with defined outcomes for each cycle and AI treated as a cross-curricular topic linked to subjects including languages, social sciences, science and arts. Activities progress from recognising AI in everyday life and creating simple prompts with teacher guidance, to using generative AI for learning, checking information across sources, and independently selecting tools and evaluating their outputs. Reflection on ethical, social and environmental effects, critical thinking, safety and digital balance are also included. These details come from the Ministry’s announcement; the inspected page does not specify lesson plans or classroom formats (https://www.minedu.sk/ai-gramotnost-sa-stala-sucastou-vzdelavania-na-zakladnych-skolach/).
prioritySummary: The initiative’s stated priority is to prepare primary-school pupils to understand and navigate AI’s growing role in everyday life and the future workplace, not merely to teach them to operate AI tools. The Ministry emphasizes understanding AI principles and limitations, critically assessing outputs, and using AI safely and responsibly. It also aims to support pupils’ learning while sustaining critical thought, real human relationships, privacy, and a healthy balance with technology. The curriculum includes awareness of wider social and environmental effects, suggesting a broader digital-society benefit alongside pupil learning and preparedness. The inspected announcement does not establish a single priority as more important than these stated aims (https://www.minedu.sk/ai-gramotnost-sa-stala-sucastou-vzdelavania-na-zakladnych-skolach/).
educationalTechnologySummary: The announcement names no specific platform, software product, hardware, or AI application developed by the initiative. It refers generically to AI tools: younger pupils will create simple prompts with teacher guidance, and pupils in a later cycle will use generative AI as a learning aid. Older pupils are to study large language models, AI assistants and agents, and learn to choose tools suited to tasks; these are described as learning topics or generic tools, not as technologies developed by the Ministry. The Ministry says it has made initial learning materials available, but the inspected page does not identify their format or any technology used to deliver them. The page explicitly says the curriculum does not focus on specific applications (https://www.minedu.sk/ai-gramotnost-sa-stala-sucastou-vzdelavania-na-zakladnych-skolach/).

inclusion.reason: The initiative is officially issued by the Ministry of Education of Slovakia (a sub-national government entity), which satisfies the inclusion route requiring endorsement or funding by a national or sub-national government. The page explicitly states that AI literacy has become part of the education program for primary schools, indicating the presence of educational content about AI as a subject area rather than just using AI tools to deliver content. Therefore, it qualifies under both the government issuance requirement and the AI-literacy requirement.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: Digital Slovenia 2030 strategy
metadata.Description: Slovenian Government digital transformation strategy (March 2023) covering infrastructure, digital competences, smart society and inclusion.

summary: Digital Slovenia 2030 is a Slovenian government strategy guiding the country’s digital transformation through 2030 across society, public administration and the economy. It sets out priorities including digital infrastructure, digital competences and inclusion, economic transformation, public services, cybersecurity and a “Smart Society 5.0,” which includes AI and other emerging technologies. Its competence agenda concerns learners, educators and citizens, alongside policy makers, public bodies and businesses; the available evidence describes strategic aims rather than specific learning activities or teaching methods.
pedagogicalSummary: The inspected pages identify Digital Slovenia 2030 as an umbrella strategy for Slovenia’s digital transformation and list “digital competences and inclusion” as a priority area. They do not describe lessons, learning activities, teaching methods, or a pedagogical model. The evidence therefore supports noting competence development as a strategic aim, but not identifying how learning is organised or supported. This is a gap in the accessible evidence, not confirmation that no learning activities exist elsewhere in the 74-page strategy. Source: https://www.gov.si/assets/ministrstva/MDP/Dokumenti/DSI2030-potrjena-na-Vladi-RS_marec-2023.pdf (title page and contents, pp. 1–3).
prioritySummary: Digital Slovenia 2030 is framed as an overarching strategy for the country’s digital transformation through 2030. Its contents list priorities spanning gigabit infrastructure, digital competences and inclusion, economic digital transformation, a “Smart Society 5.0,” digital public services, and cybersecurity; the smart-society section includes data, AI and new technologies, and smart cities and communities. This indicates a broad national transformation agenda rather than a clearly single-purpose AI-literacy initiative. The inspected pages do not provide enough detail to establish a hierarchy among these priorities or specify all intended beneficiary groups. Source: https://www.gov.si/assets/ministrstva/MDP/Dokumenti/DSI2030-potrjena-na-Vladi-RS_marec-2023.pdf (title page and contents, pp. 1–3).

metadata.Initiative / Programme: DBE Coding and Robotics curriculum
metadata.Description: DBE curriculum amendment introducing coding and robotics into Grades R-9, piloted in about 1,000 schools across all provinces.

summary: South Africa’s Department of Basic Education developed the Coding and Robotics curriculum for learners in Grades R–9. It covers coding, robotics, computational thinking, data management, application skills and internet communication, with a practical, problem-centred approach in which learners design and test instructions for robots. The initiative also envisaged teacher preparation and learning materials; the curriculum was piloted across provinces, with metadata reporting about 1,000 schools.
pedagogicalSummary: The article describes a planned, practical and problem-centred approach to learning coding: learners identify a task, design instructions for a robot, run the code, and observe the outcome. It also emphasizes logical, algorithmic and recursive thinking, alongside creativity, collaboration and problem solving. This supports an interpretation of learning through designing and testing solutions, rather than instruction in coding concepts alone. However, the page reports curriculum development and intended teacher preparation and piloting; it does not provide lesson plans or enough detail to establish how teaching is organized in practice. These points are based on the DBE article: https://www.education.gov.za/CodingCurriculum010419.aspx
prioritySummary: The initiative’s stated emphasis is preparing South African learners in Grades R–9 for a changing world through digital skills, coding and robotics. The article presents these skills as supporting problem solving, creativity and collaboration, and as preparation for future careers. It also describes an aspiration for learners to become inventors of new technologies and contribute to the global community. The page identifies learners as the direct beneficiaries, but does not establish a more specific workforce or societal priority, or rank these aims. It reports curriculum development and planned piloting, rather than evidence of outcomes. Source: https://www.education.gov.za/CodingCurriculum010419.aspx
educationalTechnologySummary: The article does not identify a named platform, software product, hardware model or learning technology developed by the initiative. It describes coding in general as writing instructions in a programming language and says learners would design code for a robot, send it to the robot and observe the result; it also refers to computers executing instructions. These are described as the curriculum’s learning context, not as specific tools supplied or developed by the programme. The article notes that learning materials and teacher-training activities would need to be developed, but gives no further details about them. Thus, the inspected page supports a generic role for robots and computers in learning, but not identification of particular educational technologies. Source: https://www.education.gov.za/CodingCurriculum010419.aspx

inclusion.reason: The initiative includes AI literacy through explicit definitions of coding as 'writing instructions for computation using a programming language' and focuses on computational thinking skills (logical, algorithmic, recursive thinking). It qualifies under the INCLUSION ROUTE of being issued by a national government body (the Department of Basic Education) and approved by the Council of Education Ministers. The metadata confirms it was piloted in about 1,000 schools across all provinces, indicating system-scale adoption within South Africa's school system.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: National Digital and Future Skills Strategy (South Africa, 2020)
metadata.Description: Strategy approved by Cabinet in August 2020, setting out 8 strategy elements and 28 action points to build South Africans' digital skills for the future of work.

summary: South Africa’s National Digital and Future Skills Strategy, approved by Cabinet in 2020, sets out eight strategy elements and 28 actions to develop digital and future-of-work skills nationally. It spans education and working-age learning, with schools, teachers, higher education, government and industry among its relevant stakeholders. The strategy addresses broad capabilities such as digital and data literacy, analytical skills, computational thinking and cybersecurity and privacy awareness, and considers AI as part of wider digital technology trends; available evidence does not establish a specific teaching approach or that AI literacy is a central focus.
pedagogicalSummary: The inspected government page provides the strategy as a PDF attachment but does not describe teaching or learning activities. The accessible PDF preview identifies it as the National Digital and Future Skills Strategy, but the strategy’s substantive pages could not be inspected here. Consequently, the available evidence does not establish a pedagogical approach; this is a limit of the inspection, not evidence that the strategy contains no learning activities. Source: https://www.gov.za/documents/notices/national-digital-and-future-skills-strategy-south-africa-23-sep-2020
prioritySummary: The title identifies the initiative as a national strategy focused on digital and future skills in South Africa, indicating a broad skills-development emphasis. The government page and accessible PDF preview do not provide enough detail to establish its specific intended beneficiaries, outcomes, or whether workforce preparation is its principal priority. More specific priorities remain uncertain because the substantive strategy pages were not accessible in the inspected material. Sources: https://www.gov.za/documents/notices/national-digital-and-future-skills-strategy-south-africa-23-sep-2020; https://www.gov.za/sites/default/files/gcis_document/202009/43730gen513.pdf

metadata.Initiative / Programme: Marco de Referencia de la Competencia Digital Docente (MRCDD, 2022)
metadata.Description: Spanish teacher digital competence framework (A1–C2), aligned with DigCompEdu.

summary: Spain’s Marco de Referencia de la Competencia Digital Docente (MRCDD, 2022) is a national framework for developing and recognizing teachers’ digital competence across educational stages. Aligned with DigCompEdu, it organizes competence into six areas and 23 competencies, with progression levels from A1 to C2, indicators and examples. It supports professional development and certification or accreditation through explanatory materials, including infographics, videos and practical guidance. Its emphasis is broader digital competence; the supplied evidence does not describe a dedicated AI-literacy curriculum.
pedagogicalSummary: The inspected pages present the MRCDD primarily as a professional competence framework, not as a detailed teaching course or a prescribed classroom pedagogy. Learning and development are supported by a progression model tied to phases of professional development, with indicators and examples intended to clarify what teachers should be able to do at different levels. The accompanying resources include visual infographics, videos with practical recommendations, and short informational items aligned with framework indicators. These suggest structured, self-directed support, but the pages do not establish a particular instructional method such as collaborative or project-based learning. Evidence is limited to the overview and teacher-framework pages: https://intef.es/competencia-digital-educativa/ and https://intef.es/competencia-digital-educativa/competencia-digital-docente/.
prioritySummary: The MRCDD’s clear primary emphasis is developing and recognizing the digital competence of teachers in Spain, for use across the educational stages covered by national education law. It translates the European DigCompEdu framework to Spanish educational and professional contexts, and supports this goal with competence areas, progression levels, indicators, examples, and links to certification and accreditation procedures. The page highlights participation and collaboration within schools as aspects given greater weight in the Spanish adaptation; it also includes areas such as data protection, privacy, security, and digital well-being. The broader INTEF digital-competence initiative addresses students, schools, and families too, but the inspected MRCDD page is specifically teacher-focused. Sources: https://intef.es/competencia-digital-educativa/ and https://intef.es/competencia-digital-educativa/competencia-digital-docente/.
educationalTechnologySummary: The inspected MRCDD pages do not identify a specific educational platform, software product, or hardware developed or used to deliver learning, so none can be attributed to the initiative from this evidence. The teacher page does describe supporting materials in three formats: infographics presenting framework elements, videos offering practical recommendations, and short informational resources intended to improve skills against the framework’s indicators. These are learning resources, but the page does not specify the technologies or platforms through which they are produced or accessed; the website itself is not evidence of a distinct educational technology. The framework concerns teachers’ digital competence, but that subject matter alone does not establish a technology used by the initiative. Evidence: https://intef.es/competencia-digital-educativa/competencia-digital-docente/.

inclusion.reason: This initiative includes AI literacy by defining competencies for using ICTs effectively in education, which encompasses AI tools (Level B1/C1). It meets the inclusion criteria as it is issued and mandated by Spain's Ministry of Education (via various orders listed on the page), qualifying under the national government route.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: INTEF "Guía sobre el uso de la IA en el ámbito educativo" (2024; updated)
metadata.Description: INTEF guide on ethical and pedagogical use of AI in education.

summary: INTEF, part of Spain’s Ministry of Education, provides a guide to the responsible and pedagogical use of AI in non-university education. Aimed at students, teachers, and educational centres or administrators, it introduces AI concepts and applications, offers classroom examples and recommendations, and addresses risks and ethical issues such as bias, deepfakes, and technology dependence. It is a guidance resource rather than a specific teaching model or technology platform.
pedagogicalSummary: The accessible page describes a reference guide, not a particular classroom teaching model. It organizes guidance around three groups—students, teachers, and educational centres or administrators—and provides practical examples of AI in teaching and learning, classroom implementation suggestions, and a glossary. It also recommends addressing ethical issues with students, including algorithmic bias, deepfakes, and technology dependence. These features support educators with information and examples, but the inspected page does not establish a specific instructional method or explain how learning activities are delivered. The page notes that a revised guide is available, but its contents were not inspected here. Source: https://intef.es/Noticias/guia-sobre-el-uso-de-la-inteligencia-artificial-en-el-ambito-educativo/
prioritySummary: The initiative’s stated aim is to support effective and ethical integration of AI in non-university education for the wider educational community. The guide addresses students, teachers, and educational centres or administrators, with practical applications as well as risks, limitations, preventive measures, and ethical responsibilities. The page also connects the initiative to INTEF’s commitment to educational innovation and continuing teacher training, and says AI is considered a tool for improving the quality and effectiveness of Spain’s education system. It therefore has several related emphases—educator support, student understanding of AI risks, and responsible educational integration—without specifying a single beneficiary as the exclusive priority. Source: https://intef.es/Noticias/guia-sobre-el-uso-de-la-inteligencia-artificial-en-el-ambito-educativo/

metadata.Initiative / Programme: #DigEdu – Digitalisation and Digital Competences Plan for the Education System (incl. #CompDigEdu)
metadata.Description: National plan backed by EU recovery funds to digitalise schools and develop digital competence via #EcoDigEdu and #CompDigEdu.

summary: #DigEdu is Spain’s national plan to digitalise the non-university education system and develop digital competence among students, teachers and schools. Its #EcoDigEdu and #CompDigEdu programmes support school devices, connectivity and classroom technology, teacher training and certification, school digital plans, and digital educational resources. Digital competence is integrated into the curriculum; advanced activities include computational thinking, programming, robotics and AI, alongside active methodologies, flexible learning spaces and personalized learning. AI is one element of a broader digital-education agenda, rather than the plan’s central focus.
pedagogicalSummary: The inspected pages describe several ways learning and implementation are supported, rather than one pedagogy for the whole plan. #CompDigEdu organizes school-level digital improvement through training, diagnosis, design, then implementation and evaluation; digital competence is also integrated across the student curriculum. For advanced competencies, the plan highlights active methodologies, flexible learning spaces and personalized learning. Its computational-thinking and AI initiative describes teachers developing skills while designing and implementing student activities in computational thinking, programming, robotics and AI. These approaches are described on the plan’s INTEF overview and #CompDigEdu page; the inspected pages do not specify a common lesson format or a detailed AI teaching method. Sources: https://intef.es/Noticias/plan-de-digitalizacion-y-competencias-digitales-del-sistema-educativo-plan-digedu/ and https://intef.es/competencia-digital-educativa/compdigedu/
prioritySummary: The plan principally aims to improve digital education across Spain’s non-university school system: develop students’ and teachers’ digital competence, help schools become digitally capable organizations, and integrate technology effectively into teaching and learning. It also emphasizes equitable access, including reducing students’ digital divide through devices and improving classroom provision, alongside teacher training and certification and school digital plans. AI and computational thinking appear as part of advanced digital competencies, not as the plan’s sole or central stated purpose. The pages describe benefits for students, teachers, schools and the wider educational community; they do not establish a separate priority such as workforce upskilling beyond education. Sources: http://espanadigital.gob.es/lineas-de-actuacion/plan-digedu and https://intef.es/Noticias/plan-de-digitalizacion-y-competencias-digitales-del-sistema-educativo-plan-digedu/
educationalTechnologySummary: The plan provides or supports educational technology infrastructure, including student devices, high-speed broadband connectivity and digital interactive systems for classrooms; the pages describe these as enabling digital teaching and learning and improving access. It also supports digital educational resources: INTEF’s overview says free resources are offered online and that eXeLearning, an authoring tool promoted and adapted by INTEF with regional collaboration, is used to encourage their creation. The Aula del Futuro project is described as combining flexible learning spaces, methods and digital technologies, with a kit of resources for planning activities. Although AI is included in learning activities, the inspected pages do not name a dedicated AI learning platform or AI teaching software, nor establish that the infrastructure itself is AI-specific. Sources: https://intef.es/Noticias/plan-de-digitalizacion-y-competencias-digitales-del-sistema-educativo-plan-digedu/ and https://auladelfuturo.intef.es/

inclusion.reason: The initiative qualifies for inclusion because it is a national-level plan backed by EU recovery funds and issued/endorsed by the Spanish government (Ministry of Education), satisfying the government/inclusion route requirement. It includes AI-literacy elements through its #CompDigEdu (Digital Competence) component, which covers digital literacy skills essential for understanding and using AI responsibly; the page links to documents integrating digital competencies into primary and secondary education curricula, indicating structured educational content about digital and AI-related competences. While the main page describes overall digitalization, the explicit mention of 'competencia digital' (digital competence) in a national educational framework satisfies the inclusive screening criteria for AI-literacy relevance when interpreted within the broader scope of digital competency building that includes AI awareness.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: AESIA – Spanish Agency for the Supervision of AI
metadata.Description: Spanish AI supervisory authority.

summary: AESIA is Spain’s public authority for AI supervision, with responsibilities related to implementing AI regulation and protecting fundamental rights. Alongside its oversight role, it publishes practical guides, checklists, studies, and public-awareness resources on AI governance and responsible, safe use. Its outreach includes training activities and participatory events for audiences such as students, educators, businesses, and the wider public, while its Ideas Laboratory brings together stakeholders to examine AI’s social and economic impacts and develop policy recommendations. The evidence supports a broad public-facing and professional offering, but does not describe a structured curriculum or a specific learning technology.
pedagogicalSummary: The accessible pages indicate public-facing awareness and capacity-building rather than a defined course or curriculum. AESIA says it develops training activities and events for responsible, safe AI use, and its outreach materials aim to help people understand, use, and live alongside AI. The events page describes in-person encounters and participatory activities with varied groups, including students, businesses, and members of the public. Separately, the Ideas Laboratory describes expert-informed analysis, sector-specific working groups, and participatory dialogue to develop recommendations; this is a collaborative knowledge and governance process, not necessarily instruction for learners. The inspected pages do not specify a sequence of lessons, assessment, or a consistent teaching method, so the evidence supports outreach, events, and participation but not a more detailed pedagogical model. Sources: https://aesia.digital.gob.es/es ; https://aesia.digital.gob.es/es/divulgacion ; https://aesia.digital.gob.es/es/eventos ; https://aesia.digital.gob.es/es/el-laboratorio
prioritySummary: AESIA’s principal emphasis is responsible and safe AI governance and use in Spain, including oversight of compliance and protection of privacy, equal treatment, and fundamental rights. Its AI-literacy-facing work has a broad public-benefit orientation: the agency says it seeks to build an AI culture and bring AI closer to everyone, while its awareness materials and events engage groups such as young people, families, educators, businesses, and the wider public. The Ideas Laboratory links this societal focus with evidence-informed policy, inclusive participation, and responsible innovation, and identifies topics including minors, women, disinformation, and employment. The site also refers to innovation and economic competitiveness, but the inspected material does not establish these as overriding the stated aims of rights protection, trust, and social benefit. Sources: https://aesia.digital.gob.es/es ; https://aesia.digital.gob.es/es/divulgacion ; https://aesia.digital.gob.es/es/eventos ; https://aesia.digital.gob.es/es/el-laboratorio
educationalTechnologySummary: The inspected pages do not identify an educational technology platform, software, hardware, or AI-literacy tool developed or used by AESIA. They describe guides, checklists, awareness materials, and European learning resources, including practical materials on AI regulation and AI literacy; these are informational resources, not evidence of a distinct learning technology. The agency also advertises training activities and events, but the pages do not say that these use a particular digital learning system or technology. Although the materials are presented on AESIA’s website, the evidence does not establish the website itself as an educational technology rather than a channel for publishing information. This finding is limited to the pages inspected; it does not confirm that AESIA uses or develops no such technology elsewhere. Sources: https://aesia.digital.gob.es/es/guias ; https://aesia.digital.gob.es/es/recursos ; https://aesia.digital.gob.es/es/divulgacion ; https://aesia.digital.gob.es/es

As an official supervisory authority mandated by national legislation to implement EU regulations (specifically the AI Act), AESIA qualifies under the inclusion route of being issued/endorsed by a statutory body.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: Consejo Escolar del Estado – reference framework on AI in schools (2026)
metadata.Description: Framework developed by the State and regional School Councils (Gijón, May 2026) to guide ethical, institutional use of AI in schools.

summary: A reference framework developed by Spain’s State and regional School Councils for educational communities and school councils, offering guidance on the responsible, institutional use of AI in education. It addresses human judgment and oversight in assessment, transparency, privacy and governance of AI tools, environmental impact, and the need to assess whether adoption is appropriate. Its emphasis is on policy and decision-making rather than a defined course or teaching programme.
pedagogicalSummary: The accessible cover identifies this as a reference framework for educational communities and school councils, rather than describing lessons, courses, or a teaching programme. The text available here does not establish a pedagogical approach or explain how learning is organised or supported. This is a limit of the inspected material, not confirmation that the full 23-page document contains no pedagogical recommendations. Source: https://portal.edu.gva.es/consellescolar/wp-content/uploads/sites/238/2026/06/IA_Educacion_Marco.pdf
prioritySummary: The initiative’s evident emphasis is providing a reference framework for the use of artificial intelligence in education, with educational communities and school councils named as its intended audience. This points to guidance for the school system and its communities, rather than a specific workforce-training or individual-well-being programme. The accessible cover does not reveal the framework’s detailed aims or allow a more specific priority to be established; the PDF’s full text could not be inspected here. Source: https://portal.edu.gva.es/consellescolar/wp-content/uploads/sites/238/2026/06/IA_Educacion_Marco.pdf
educationalTechnologySummary: The accessible material identifies no learning platform, software, hardware, or AI tool developed or used by the initiative. The PDF itself is a reference document about AI in education; its subject matter alone does not establish that the initiative uses AI as an educational technology. Because the document’s full text was not accessible for inspection, this is a limit of the evidence reviewed, not confirmation that no technology is mentioned elsewhere in it. Source: https://portal.edu.gva.es/consellescolar/wp-content/uploads/sites/238/2026/06/IA_Educacion_Marco.pdf

inclusion.reason: The document is issued by a national-level school council (Consejo Escolar del Estado) in Spain, satisfying the inclusion route of endorsement by a national/sub-national government body. It includes AI literacy via explicit guidance on how AI works (limits, transparency, environmental impact), how to use it responsibly in evaluation and teaching (human-in-the-loop, process over product), and decision criteria for selecting IA tools.
