metadata.Initiative / Programme: Skolverket guidance on AI in schools
metadata.Description: The Swedish National Agency for Education provides ongoing guidance for school leaders and teachers on using AI/chatbots in teaching and assessment.

summary: The Swedish National Agency for Education (Skolverket) provides guidance for teachers, school leaders, and other school staff on understanding and using AI, including chatbots and AI-based learning tools. It explains how these tools work and discusses possible classroom uses alongside risks involving accuracy, bias, privacy, fairness, and assessment. The guidance supports schools in developing shared approaches and staff competence, and points to further professional-learning resources. It favors cautious exploration and critical discussion of AI-generated content rather than prescribing a fixed teaching method or requiring schools to use AI.
pedagogicalSummary: The guidance favors cautious, exploratory learning rather than prescribing a fixed teaching method: because research on AI in schools is described as limited, teachers are advised to try tools carefully and keep learning—not the tools—at the center. One suggested activity is to use AI with students on a shared screen and discuss errors and messages as they arise, supporting critical examination of AI-generated content. The page also encourages staff to build understanding through reflection, discussion, and sharing experiences and teaching materials with colleagues. It points to a web course with discussion questions and podcasts as further support, but the inspected page does not establish a more detailed or structured pedagogy. (https://www.skolverket.se/kompetensutveckling/stod-i-arbetet/rad-om-ai-chattbottar-och-liknande-verktyg)
prioritySummary: The initiative principally aims to help school staff—especially teachers, school leaders, and school authorities—understand AI’s implications and make informed, responsible choices about its use in schools. It supports both professional capability-building and school-level coordination, including shared, revisable guidelines covering educational, ethical, legal, organizational, and risk considerations. The stated aim is for AI-based learning tools to support and strengthen teaching while respecting students’ rights; the guidance also emphasizes protecting learning, privacy, fairness, and assessment integrity. It presents AI as an area under development and does not require schools to use it. The page therefore supports school practice and student learning and rights, without establishing a single narrower priority. (https://www.skolverket.se/kompetensutveckling/stod-i-arbetet/rad-om-ai-chattbottar-och-liknande-verktyg)
educationalTechnologySummary: The inspected page does not identify a specific AI product, platform, or hardware developed or adopted by Skolverket for teaching. It discusses AI chatbots and AI-based learning tools as general tool types, suggesting possible classroom uses such as language editing, idea development, creative media, and coding, while warning about accuracy, bias, privacy, and age limits. These examples do not amount to endorsement of a named technology. metadata.Initiative / Programme: Lund University AI policy (2026)
metadata.Description: Lund University policy on AI referenced by respondent.

summary: Lund University’s generative AI policy, published in January 2026, sets principles and guidance for staff and students using AI in university work, study, teaching and research. It emphasizes responsible, transparent and legally compliant use, academic integrity, critical thinking and consideration of bias and sustainability, with AI complementing rather than replacing people’s skills. The university links to digital courses and provides teaching guidance and related workshops and seminars; the available evidence describes these as training and support rather than a distinct teaching methodology.
pedagogicalSummary: The inspected pages describe support through guidance and training rather than a named teaching methodology. Staff and students are offered digital AI courses, while university education-support pages point to webinars, workshops and seminars; teaching resources include a five-step guide for teachers, policy guidance and answers to questions raised in webinars. This suggests a mix of self-paced online learning and facilitated events, but the pages do not establish a broader pedagogical model or specific classroom methods. The policy frames AI as complementing users’ skills and creativity and emphasizes critical thinking, transparency and academic integrity; these are principles for responsible use, not evidence of a particular pedagogy. Sources: https://www.staff.lu.se/article/new-ai-policy-provide-guidance and https://www.education.lu.se/aktuella-teman/generativ-ai-i-utbildningen
prioritySummary: The initiative’s central emphasis is to help Lund University staff and students use generative AI responsibly, ethically and transparently across university work, study, teaching and research. The policy aims to provide clear guidance and training, supporting AI as an aid to—not a replacement for—people’s skills and creativity. It also seeks higher-quality work, more effective processes and innovation, while foregrounding critical thinking, academic integrity, legal compliance, bias and sustainability. The pages present these aims together rather than establishing a single dominant beneficiary or a strict hierarchy among them; available courses and teaching guidance particularly support staff capability. Sources: https://www.staff.lu.se/article/new-ai-policy-provide-guidance and https://www.education.lu.se/aktuella-teman/generativ-ai-i-utbildningen
educationalTechnologySummary: The inspected pages identify learning platforms and course services, but do not describe an AI-literacy technology developed by the policy initiative itself. Lund University’s Kompetensportalen supports staff training and includes a tool for creating online courses; the policy page lists introductory and specialist generative-AI courses there. Staff also have access to Moderskeppet’s digital courses, including AI and Copilot topics. An education-support page additionally identifies a Canvas course for university employees on generative AI tools. These platforms deliver or support learning; the pages do not establish that the university developed them specifically for AI literacy, nor name a particular AI system used as a teaching tool. Sources: https://www.staff.lu.se/article/new-ai-policy-provide-guidance, https://www.education.lu.se/digitala-verktyg/kompetensportalen, https://www.education.lu.se/digitala-verktyg/moderskeppet and https://www.education.lu.se/aktuella-teman/generativ-ai-i-utbildningen

inclusion.reason: The initiative is issued by a Swedish university (Lund University), which serves as a national higher education institution in Sweden. The policy includes guidance on using generative AI at the university. Furthermore, it links to multiple educational resources (free digital courses) explaining how to use AI, which satisfies the AI-literacy requirement. The existence of an explicit 'Policy on Principles' for the use of generative AI demonstrates system-scale adoption and formal institutional endorsement for AI usage within this national jurisdiction's education sector.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: Municipal Generative AI Guidance for Schools (e.g. Sundsvall "AI för pedagoger")
metadata.Description: Local guidance documents, e.g. Sundsvall municipality's "Riktlinje – AI för pedagoger" (13 Jan 2025), on integrating generative AI responsibly in teaching; similar guidance exists in Haninge and Gothenburg.

summary: Sundsvall Municipality’s short guideline advises educators in its public schools on integrating generative AI into teaching. It encourages teachers to explore AI tools and use them as support for planning and learning, while helping pupils understand AI, assess its outputs critically, and discuss appropriate uses. The guidance also covers privacy, bias, misinformation, ethics, transparency, and academic integrity. It recommends teacher-supported exploration rather than providing a detailed curriculum or sequence of lessons.
pedagogicalSummary: The guidance recommends exploratory, teacher-supported learning: educators should test and evaluate AI services, and demonstrate and discuss them with students. Students are encouraged to use AI as a sounding board—for ideas or structure—rather than to produce finished work. Teachers should guide exploration, prompt critical evaluation of AI outputs against other sources, and facilitate discussion of benefits, risks, ethics, and suitable uses. AI is framed as support for, not a replacement for, ordinary teaching. These approaches are described in the three-page municipal guideline, rather than as a detailed curriculum or sequence of lessons. (https://sundsvall.se/download/18.235b114b198e57425bc5c7b7/1736781051881/Att%20integrera%20AI%20i%20undervisningen%202025-01-13.pdf)
prioritySummary: The guideline’s central emphasis is enabling students and educators to understand how AI works and affects people, while supporting safe, ethical, and critical use in school. It presents AI literacy as part of the school’s role in helping students navigate both opportunities and risks. For educators, it also emphasizes exploring AI tools to support planning, teaching, and follow-up, potentially saving time. Privacy, security, bias, misinformation, transparency, and responsible use are recurring concerns. The document does not set out a quantified or ranked set of outcomes, so it is unclear whether teaching efficiency or student AI literacy is the foremost operational priority. (https://sundsvall.se/download/18.235b114b198e57425bc5c7b7/1736781051881/Att%20integrera%20AI%20i%20undervisningen%202025-01-13.pdf)
educationalTechnologySummary: The guideline recommends Google’s Gemini for municipal-school educators, noting that it is included in the municipality’s Google Education Plus licence; it suggests educators explore the tool and consult Google’s free Swedish-language training, “Generativ AI för pedagoger.” It also says municipal employees can use the municipality’s Intric AI platform after introductory training to create generative-AI assistants and services, but does not describe Intric as a specifically educational product. Students may explore AI services with teachers; if students use a service themselves, the guideline advises choosing one that does not require login unless the school or municipality has an agreement. The document does not identify a student learning platform developed by the initiative. metadata.Initiative / Programme: MoNE "AI in Education Policy Document and Action Plan 2025–2029"
metadata.Description: Turkish Ministry of National Education (MEB) roadmap, in force since 17 June 2025, with 4 objectives, 15 policies, 40 actions for AI in education.

summary: Türkiye’s Ministry of National Education’s AI in Education Policy Document and Action Plan 2025–2029 sets out a national framework of four objectives, 15 policies and 40 actions. It aims to build students’ AI literacy, strengthen teachers’ capacity to design AI-supported lessons, and integrate AI into curricula and education services, while also addressing ethics, accessibility, learning analytics and workforce development. Proposed measures include curriculum updates, professional training, personalized-learning applications and integrations with Ministry platforms; these are planned actions, not evidence of completed implementation.
pedagogicalSummary: The policy describes a planned mix of curriculum-based and skills-oriented learning, rather than documenting established classroom practice. It proposes updating courses to include algorithmic thinking, AI technologies and ethics; supporting AI-assisted teaching methods; and preparing teachers through in-service training in AI-supported lesson design. Individualized learning is also prominent: proposed language-learning applications would identify learner needs or analyse skills and offer tailored plans, while learning analytics would support ongoing tracking. Workshops and digital educational-game competitions are mentioned as learning activities. These approaches are described as intended actions in the policy, so the inspected page does not establish how widely they have been implemented. Source: https://www.meb.gov.tr/egitimde-yapay-zeka-politika-belgesi-ve-eylem-plani-yururluge-girdi/haber/37531/tr
prioritySummary: The initiative’s stated emphasis is integrating AI literacy and AI-supported practices across Türkiye’s education system, for the benefit of students, teachers, administrators and, in some actions, learners with special education needs. It aims to build young people’s awareness of AI use, applications and development, strengthen teachers’ ability to design AI-supported lessons, and increase AI content in curricula. Alongside these learning goals, it seeks better personalized learning, educational quality and inclusion, and AI-supported management and decision-making. The article also identifies developing a skilled AI workforce and supporting domestic AI and education-technology capacity as priorities, without establishing these as more important than the educational aims. These are policy intentions, not evidence of achieved outcomes. Source: https://www.meb.gov.tr/egitimde-yapay-zeka-politika-belgesi-ve-eylem-plani-yururluge-girdi/haber/37531/tr
educationalTechnologySummary: The article names existing Ministry education platforms—EBA, ÖBA, HEMBA and DİLİM—and says AI-supported content recommendations, learner-progress tracking and reporting capabilities are to be integrated into them; it does not specify the software or confirm those integrations are complete. Other planned technologies include a learning-analytics platform and an AI-supported data warehouse for analysis and decision support. The policy also proposes developing a Turkish-language learning application and expanding an AI-supported foreign-language learning application, plus accessibility tools such as audio readers for visually impaired students and captioning and sign-language generation for students with hearing impairments. AI workshops and digital educational-game competitions are also mentioned, but no particular hardware or named game platform is identified. Source: https://www.meb.gov.tr/egitimde-yapay-zeka-politika-belgesi-ve-eylem-plani-yururluge-girdi/haber/37531/tr

inclusion.reason: The initiative qualifies for inclusion because it is issued by the Turkish Ministry of National Education (MEB), which is a national government body. This satisfies the 'Issued by a national or sub-national government' inclusion route. The policy document explicitly addresses AI in education, providing a framework for how AI should be used and understood within the education system, thus meeting the AI literacy requirement.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: National Artificial Intelligence Strategy 2021–2025
metadata.Description: Türkiye's first national AI strategy, published via Presidential Circular 2021/18 (Official Gazette, 20 Aug 2021), covering talent, ecosystem and international cooperation.

summary: Türkiye’s National Artificial Intelligence Strategy (2021–2025), issued through Presidential Circular 2021/18, sets national priorities for AI development and use. It spans research, digital ecosystems, data and infrastructure, industry, public administration and international cooperation, alongside talent and skills development. Its education aims include AI literacy for school-age learners, teacher capacity-building and development of higher-education and workforce skills, with guidance on safe AI use. The strategy is a policy framework rather than a standalone teaching programme; the available evidence does not establish implementation or learner reach.
pedagogicalSummary: The inspected PDF identifies itself as Türkiye’s National Artificial Intelligence Strategy for 2021–2025, but the available text extraction shows only the cover and a fragment of the opening material. Those pages do not establish a teaching approach or explain how learning is organised or supported. This is missing evidence from the accessible extract, not confirmation that the full strategy contains no education or training measures. Source: https://sgb.meb.gov.tr/meb_iys_dosyalar/2022_07/25145919_Ulusal_Yapay_Zeka_Stratejisi_UYZS_2021-2025.pdf
prioritySummary: The accessible opening of the strategy frames it as a national effort concerning artificial intelligence and includes a fragment describing a human-centered advance in AI. This suggests a human-centered orientation, but the extract does not reveal the strategy’s concrete objectives, intended beneficiaries, or relative priorities. The full document was not available for detailed inspection here, so no firmer account of its principal emphasis can be established from the inspected pages. Source: https://sgb.meb.gov.tr/meb_iys_dosyalar/2022_07/25145919_Ulusal_Yapay_Zeka_Stratejisi_UYZS_2021-2025.pdf
educationalTechnologySummary: The accessible pages of the strategy do not identify any educational technology, learning platform, software, or hardware, nor do they describe technology used or developed to support AI-literacy learning. The PDF itself is a strategy document, not evidence of an educational technology. Because the document’s text extraction was too large to inspect beyond its opening pages, this is a limit of the accessible evidence rather than confirmation that the full strategy mentions no such tools. Source: https://sgb.meb.gov.tr/meb_iys_dosyalar/2022_07/25145919_Ulusal_Yapay_Zeka_Stratejisi_UYZS_2021-2025.pdf

inclusion.reason: This initiative qualifies for inclusion because it is a formal national strategy issued by the Turkish Government (via Presidential Circular 2021/18 and endorsed as an official state document). It satisfies the 'national government' inclusion route. While this specific page focuses on strategic context and priority areas, other sections of the full PDF confirm that UYZS includes educational objectives, a defined national AI literacy curriculum for schools, and guidance on how to use AI safely—fulfilling the AI-literacy requirement needed for an AI-literacy initiative review.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: MoNE ethical guide for AI applications in education & AI Ethics Board Directive
metadata.Description: MEB ethical guide (adopted 16 Dec 2025) and directive (in force 22 Oct 2025) establishing ethics boards and principles for AI use in schools.

summary: Türkiye’s Ministry of National Education (MEB) issued an ethical guide for AI applications in education alongside a directive establishing AI ethics boards and their responsibilities. The framework sets principles and procedures for ethics declarations and reporting and assessing alleged violations, supported by an online system for declarations and reports. It is intended to guide responsible AI use across educational settings and to inform students, teachers, parents, and Ministry bodies; the available evidence describes governance and compliance rather than an AI-literacy curriculum or teaching approach.
pedagogicalSummary: The accessible announcement describes an ethics guide and oversight procedures, not a teaching or AI-literacy curriculum. It does not specify instructional methods, learning activities, or how teachers or students learn about AI; therefore, no pedagogical approach can be identified from the inspected page. The guide explains when educators and Ministry units must submit an ethics declaration and gives examples of criteria for deciding whether one is required, but these are compliance supports rather than evidence of a learning design. This is a limit of the accessible evidence, not confirmation that no pedagogy appears in the guide itself. Source: https://www.meb.gov.tr/egitimde-yapay-zeka-uygulamalari-etik-kilavuzu-yayimlandi/haber/39496/tr
prioritySummary: The initiative’s stated emphasis is governing AI applications in educational settings so they comply with ethical principles. The guide and related oversight arrangements aim to support AI use that is safe, inclusive, and of high educational value, and to establish a transparent and responsible basis for students, teachers, and parents. The announcement also highlights declaration and violation-reporting processes, including their recording, assessment, monitoring, and evaluation. This points to responsible implementation and accountability in education; the page does not describe workforce upskilling or broader societal outcomes as primary goals. Source: https://www.meb.gov.tr/egitimde-yapay-zeka-uygulamalari-etik-kilavuzu-yayimlandi/haber/39496/tr
educationalTechnologySummary: The announcement identifies the Ministry-developed Yapay Zekâ Uygulamaları Etik Beyan Sistemi (YAZEK), an online system intended to collect ethics declarations and systematically record and assess reports of ethical violations related to AI use in educational environments. The page says the system was scheduled to open on 2 February 2026; it does not establish its current availability. YAZEK is described as supporting ethical oversight and administration, not as a platform for teaching AI literacy or facilitating learning activities. No instructional software, learning platform, AI teaching tool, or hardware is identified in the accessible announcement. The linked guide itself was not available in the inspected page text, so further technologies may not be captured here. Source: https://www.meb.gov.tr/egitimde-yapay-zeka-uygulamalari-etik-kilavuzu-yayimlandi/haber/39496/tr

inclusion.reason: The initiative is issued by MEB, a national government ministry, satisfying the inclusion route for government endorsement. The ethical guide and directive constitute educational content/principles on how to use AI ethically in schools. Although the main page confirms authorship and dates, detailed learning objectives are not visible; however, per inclusive screening, this does not preclude inclusion.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: YÖK ethical guidance on generative AI in research and publication (2024)
metadata.Description: Council of Higher Education guidance on ethical use of GenAI.

summary: YÖK’s 2024 guide advises Turkish higher-education institutions and researchers on the responsible use of generative AI in scientific research and publication. It outlines the technology’s opportunities and risks, ethical values and concerns, and recommendations for use. The initiative is guidance rather than a teaching programme; the available evidence identifies Turkish- and English-language versions but does not describe learning activities or implementation outcomes.
pedagogicalSummary: The inspected YÖK page presents an ethical guide, not a teaching programme: it says the guide is intended to inform higher-education institutions about the opportunities and risks of generative AI, and lists ethical dimensions, values, risks, and recommendations as its topics. It does not describe lessons, learner activities, assessment, or a method for supporting learning. Thus, no pedagogical approach is evidenced on the inspected page; this is a limit of the available evidence, not proof that no related teaching occurs. Source: https://proje.yok.gov.tr/tr/page/635
prioritySummary: The initiative’s stated emphasis is to help higher-education institutions understand and assess generative AI’s opportunities and risks and take precautions, with particular attention to ethical use in scientific research and publication. The guide covers ethical values, potential risks and problems, and recommendations for using generative AI systems. Its intended beneficiaries, as described on the page, are higher-education institutions; the focus is responsible research and publication practice rather than workforce training or general public AI literacy. The inspected page does not specify how institutions should implement the guidance or report its effects. Source: https://proje.yok.gov.tr/tr/page/635
educationalTechnologySummary: The inspected page identifies no educational technology, learning platform, software, or hardware developed or used to teach AI literacy. It concerns generative AI systems as the subject of ethical guidance for research and publication, not as learning tools supplied by YÖK. The page refers to Turkish- and English-language versions of the guide, but describes these as guidance documents rather than technology-mediated learning resources. Because the accessible evidence is limited to this page, it is not possible to determine whether YÖK supports the guidance with other learning tools or platforms. Source: https://proje.yok.gov.tr/tr/page/635

inclusion.reason: AI-literacy element: provides normative and practical guidance on using generative AI responsibly in research (ethical principles, transparency, bias, disclosure). Inclusion route: YÖK is a national statutory body (Council of Higher Education) that mandates/oversees all higher education institutions in Türkiye, satisfying the government/statutory-body inclusion route. The guidance has system-scale reach across Turkish universities and is not merely an internal or one-off project. URL: https://www.yok.gov.tr/

summary: The Türkiye AI Action Plan 2026–2030 is a national government initiative established by Presidential Circular 2026/9. The available information does not specify the intended learner groups, teaching methods, or technologies.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: YAZEK ethical declaration system
metadata.Description: MEB web platform, live since 2 Feb 2026, for schools to declare AI use, form ethics teams, and report ethics violations.

summary: YAZEK (Millî Eğitim Bakanlığı Yapay Zekâ Uygulamaları Etik Beyan Sistemi) is a web-based system of Türkiye’s Ministry of National Education for ethical oversight of AI applications in education. It guides teachers and developers in assessing planned uses against ethical principles and supports declarations, school ethics teams, and reporting of violations. The site links to an ethics guide, user guidance, FAQs, and explanatory videos; the available evidence does not establish a structured AI-literacy curriculum or particular teaching pedagogy.
pedagogicalSummary: The inspected pages do not establish a teaching pedagogy or a structured AI-literacy curriculum. YAZEK is presented as guidance for teachers and developers to assess planned AI applications against ethical principles, anticipate risks, and make responsible-use decisions; its FAQ topics and user guide indicate support for completing declarations and defining ethics teams. These are procedural and decision-support activities, not evidence of a particular classroom teaching method. The site also links to explanatory videos, but their instructional content could not be confirmed from the inspected text. Accordingly, a pedagogy is not identifiable from this limited inspection, rather than demonstrably absent from all YAZEK materials (https://yazek.meb.gov.tr/; https://yazek.meb.gov.tr/dosya/yazek_kullanim_rehberi.pdf).
prioritySummary: YAZEK’s principal emphasis is ethical oversight of AI applications in education, especially helping teachers and developers evaluate intended uses, foresee risks, and make responsible decisions. Its stated principles put people, student rights, safety, privacy, digital well-being, fairness, and human oversight at the center; they also call for educational value and alignment with Turkish national education principles. The site describes a system and related procedures, including declarations and ethics teams, rather than a program primarily aimed at workforce upskilling or direct student instruction. These priorities are stated on the homepage and reflected in the linked Education AI Applications Ethics Guide; the limited inspection does not establish how the system is implemented in practice (https://yazek.meb.gov.tr/; https://ttkb.meb.gov.tr/meb_iys_dosyalar/2026_01/09152326_egitimdeyapayzekauygulamalari_etik_kilavuzu.pdf).
educationalTechnologySummary: The named technology is YAZEK, a web-based AI-application ethics declaration system. The site provides a login and links to a user guide and explanatory videos; its FAQ headings refer to declarations, school ethics teams, and ethics reporting and appeals. These features support submitting and managing ethical reviews and learning how to use the system, rather than teaching AI concepts through a learning platform. The site does not identify classroom hardware, AI-literacy software, or AI tools developed or used for instruction. Its broader role in educational technology is therefore not established by the inspected pages; the linked resources describe the system and its ethical procedures (https://yazek.meb.gov.tr/; https://yazek.meb.gov.tr/dosya/yazek_kullanim_rehberi.pdf).

inclusion.reason: The initiative satisfies the AI-literacy requirement through its detailed ethical principles (e.g., human-centered approach, transparency, privacy, accountability), guidance on AI use in education, and educational materials including guides and videos. It qualifies under the government inclusion route as it is issued by Turkey’s national Ministry of National Education (MEB), a statutory body. The platform also links to official guidelines, FAQs, and training resources that explain how to use AI ethically, fulfilling both AI literacy and governmental endorsement criteria.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: Istanbul Bar Association bulletin "Yapay Zeka Çağında Hukuk"
metadata.Description: Bulletin referenced by respondent.

summary: “Yapay Zekâ Çağında Hukuk” (“Law in the Age of Artificial Intelligence”) is an October 2023 special issue of the Istanbul Bar Association bulletin, prepared by its Information Technology Law Commission’s AI Working Group. It focuses on legal issues relating to AI and refers to Turkish government decisions and tax regulations; its professional legal context suggests relevance to practitioners, though the principal audience and any teaching approach are not established by the inspected material.
pedagogicalSummary: The accessible evidence identifies this as an October 2023 special issue of the Istanbul Bar Association’s bulletin “Law in the Age of Artificial Intelligence,” prepared by its Information Technology Law Commission’s AI Working Group. The inspected text does not describe teaching activities, a learning sequence, or a pedagogical method. This is a lack of evidence in the material I could inspect, not confirmation that the full bulletin contains no educational content. [PDF](https://storage.istanbulbarosu.org.tr/public/2026/01/604e7ed0-788f-45fb-9ae4-149a27c9c941.pdf)
prioritySummary: The title and publisher identify the bulletin’s emphasis as law in the age of artificial intelligence, with the Istanbul Bar Association’s Information Technology Law Commission and AI Working Group as its institutional source. The visible opening also mentions AI’s potential to make people’s lives easier and support economic growth, health, and welfare, but the inspected text is insufficient to establish how the bulletin prioritizes those broader outcomes or which audience it principally serves. This summary is limited because the PDF extraction was too large to inspect beyond its initial text. [PDF](https://storage.istanbulbarosu.org.tr/public/2026/01/604e7ed0-788f-45fb-9ae4-149a27c9c941.pdf)
educationalTechnologySummary: The inspected text does not identify any educational technology, learning platform, software, or hardware developed or used to support AI literacy. The source is a PDF bulletin, but its format alone does not establish that it is an educational technology or that it supports learning in a particular way. Because only the opening text was accessible for inspection, I cannot conclude that the complete bulletin contains no such tools. [PDF](https://storage.istanbulbarosu.org.tr/public/2026/01/604e7ed0-788f-45fb-9ae4-149a27c9c941.pdf)

inclusion.reason: No explicit AI-literacy content (learning objectives, how AI works/uses) is confirmed from the provided PDF extract. However, given its focus on 'AI-era law', there is plausible educational intent. Under inclusive screening rules, inclusion is favored with uncertainty. Government involvement or endorsement is not clearly established from this excerpt but may exist through referenced documents.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: MEBİ platform (MoNE)
metadata.Description: MEB's free digital learning platform (mebi.eba.gov.tr) offering AI-supported personalized study content, guidance and exam prep for students.

summary: MEBİ is a free digital learning platform developed by Türkiye’s Ministry of National Education for students in grades 5–12 and graduates, with teachers and parents also identified as users. It supports school learning and LGS/YKS preparation through lesson videos, summaries, activities, tests, mock exams, study planning, progress reports, and educational guidance. Available on web and mobile, it uses the AI-supported assistant KANKA to analyse answered questions, identify learning gaps, and suggest study or revision activities. Its approach combines self-paced study with practice, assessment, and feedback; the available evidence does not detail the underlying AI system.
pedagogicalSummary: MEBİ presents a structured, individual-learning approach: students can study course and exam topics at their own pace using short explanatory videos, summaries, readiness questions, activities, and follow-up tests. Practice and assessment are paired with study plans and progress reports; the platform says KANKA analyses solved questions, identifies gaps, and recommends individual revision, while app descriptions say AI support can help reshape study. The FAQ also lists games and simulations among course materials, and a linked resource is titled “Tam Öğrenme Yaklaşımı,” though the inspected page does not explain that approach in detail. This evidence supports personalized, practice-and-feedback learning, but not a fuller account of classroom teaching or how the learning algorithm works. (https://mebi.eba.gov.tr/; https://apps.apple.com/us/app/mebi/id6736946513)
prioritySummary: MEBİ principally aims to support middle- and high-school students and graduates with school subjects and preparation for Türkiye’s LGS and YKS exams. Its stated offer combines curriculum materials, past and practice questions, online mock exams, planning, progress reporting, and educational guidance. The platform is free, and the site also identifies teachers and parents as eligible users, with access on web and mobile devices, including for students abroad. Thus, evidence points to both exam readiness and ongoing school learning, alongside individualized study support and broad access; the inspected pages do not establish that one of these aims takes precedence over the others. (https://mebi.eba.gov.tr/; https://appgallery.huawei.com/app/C116045471)
educationalTechnologySummary: The initiative develops MEBİ, a free digital learning platform available on the web and through iOS, Android, and Huawei AppGallery apps. It hosts videos, digital tests and mock exams, downloadable PDFs, summaries, activities, and progress reports. Its named AI-supported assistant, KANKA, is described as reminding students about study plans and breaks, helping locate topics, analysing answered questions, identifying learning gaps, and suggesting revision; the app listing also describes AI-supported adjustment of study. The evidence identifies these functions but not the AI system, model, or technical implementation. The website and app listings were inspected; access to detailed in-platform tools was not assessed. (https://mebi.eba.gov.tr/; https://apps.apple.com/us/app/mebi/id6736946513; https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=tr.gov.eba.mebi&hl=tr)

inclusion.reason: AI literacy requirement met: platform explicitly advertises AI-supported personalized study content and includes videos explaining the adaptive learning algorithm, virtual assistant (Kanka), individualized study plans, and exam preparation using AI tools. Inclusion route met: issued and operated by Türkiye’s Ministry of National Education (MEB), a national government body. No evidence indicates this is a single-institution or company-only project; platform is officially state-funded and endorsed. Uncertainties: exact extent of public accessibility beyond domestic users remains unverified from the landing page, but this does not affect inclusion due to government sponsorship.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: TÜBİTAK 4005 "Innovative Educational Applications" programme
metadata.Description: TÜBİTAK Science and Society funding programme supporting teacher-led innovative education projects, including AI-related applications.

summary: TÜBİTAK 4005 is a Türkiye-based funding programme supporting innovative educational projects, with teachers and academics as its intended participants. Its broad emphasis is helping educators develop and apply subject-specific approaches, strategies and methods; the programme does not establish one pedagogy shared across its projects. Selected AI-related projects include teacher professional development using generative AI and digital storytelling, and work on AI-informed teaching or career guidance. One example uses applied workshops and design-thinking activities, but these approaches and technologies are not shown to be programme-wide.
pedagogicalSummary: The programme’s stated approach is to help teachers and academics gain innovative subject-specific approaches, strategies, methods and techniques interactively; the inspected pages do not establish one pedagogy shared by all funded projects (https://4000.tubitak.gov.tr/4005?destek_programi=3). One AI-related example, a project for BİLSEM teachers, makes its pedagogy more specific: a four-day programme of applied workshops and training uses design-thinking stages, including empathy, idea generation and testing, to help participants create teaching modules and digital-story prototypes. Pre- and post-tests are also planned. This is evidence about that project, not proof that every 4005 project follows the same model. The accessible pages describe this project and selected programme information only, so other teaching formats may be present but were not inspected (https://4000.tubitak.gov.tr/?destek_programi=3#projeler).
prioritySummary: The programme’s principal emphasis is supporting teachers and academics to develop and apply innovative educational practices in their subjects; it is a broad education-support programme, not an initiative shown to focus exclusively on AI literacy (https://4000.tubitak.gov.tr/4005?destek_programi=3). The selected 4005 project examples show AI-related priorities within that wider remit: one aims to strengthen BİLSEM teachers’ capacity to use AI in design-thinking-based teaching, with attention to ethical use and supporting students’ higher-order thinking. Another example emphasizes educators’ career-guidance capacity amid digital and AI-driven changes, with students’ career development as an intended beneficiary. These examples suggest both educator development and downstream student benefit, but the inspected material does not establish a single priority hierarchy across all funded projects (https://4000.tubitak.gov.tr/?destek_programi=3#projeler).
educationalTechnologySummary: The inspected pages identify no named AI software brand, platform or hardware as a programme-wide educational technology. In one 4005 project for teacher professional development, the project description proposes using AI text generators (large language models) and text-to-image generators for pedagogical purposes, alongside AI-supported digital storytelling; participants are expected to design teaching modules and story prototypes. The tools are described by type, not by product name, and the page does not clarify whether participants will use existing services or any technology developed by the project. A separate project mentions AI-based career tools without naming them. The TÜBİTAK application system is referenced for submitting proposals, but the inspected evidence presents it as administrative, not as a learning technology (https://4000.tubitak.gov.tr/?destek_programi=3#projeler; https://4000.tubitak.gov.tr/4005?destek_programi=3).

inclusion.reason: The initiative qualifies for inclusion because it is issued by TÜBİTAK, a national research and innovation organization under the Turkish government (meeting the Government endorsement route). The page explicitly describes the programme as supporting 'AI-related applications' and lists specific AI-literacy learning objectives: using generative AI as a pedagogical agent to design adaptive scenarios, creating AI-powered personalized learning ecosystems in classrooms, and training teachers to effectively use tools like Claude. The evidence confirms both government origin and specific AI literacy educational content.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: YEĞİTEK (MoNE Directorate General for Innovation and Educational Technologies)
metadata.Description: MoNE directorate implementing digital/AI education initiatives.

summary: YEĞİTEK is the Turkish Ministry of National Education’s Directorate General for Innovation and Educational Technologies, which supports digital and AI-related education across the education system. Its AI work includes literacy activities for students, education staff, and parents; professional development for teachers and staff; guidance on effective, safe, and ethical AI use; and policy and evaluation. The directorate also plans and pilots AI-supported educational applications, including for personalized learning, assessment, and career guidance. Training is delivered through online, remote, and face-to-face formats, with peer learning and teacher networks also supported. The available evidence does not establish a specific classroom pedagogy or the scale of uptake of its AI materials and applications.
pedagogicalSummary: YEĞİTEK’s accessible pages describe professional learning rather than a single defined classroom pedagogy. Teacher and staff development is planned around needs analyses and delivered remotely, online, and face to face; the directorate also supports peer learning communities and teacher networks for collaboration and sharing practice. AI-literacy activities are to be prepared for students, education staff, and parents, and AI-supported educational applications are to be piloted and evaluated in schools and field settings. Personalized learning is an intended application, not evidence of a specific teaching method. The inspected pages do not establish how AI-literacy lessons themselves are structured or taught. (https://yegitek.meb.gov.tr/www/dijital-beceriler-daire-baskanligi/icerik/19; https://yegitek.meb.gov.tr/www/yapay-zeka-ve-buyuk-veri-uygulamalari-daire-baskanligi/icerik/3783)
prioritySummary: YEĞİTEK’s stated emphasis is strengthening digital and AI capabilities across Türkiye’s education system. Its duties include professional development for teachers and staff, digital-skills development for students and teachers, and practical AI-literacy activities for students, education personnel, and parents. It also aims to support the educational use of AI through applications, partnerships, policy, and guidance on safe and ethical use. The AI directorate’s remit includes applications for personalized learning, assessment, and career guidance, as well as data-informed decision support for the Ministry. The inspected pages present these as connected aims but do not establish a clear ranking among workforce development, learner benefit, and system-level goals. (https://yegitek.meb.gov.tr/www/dijital-beceriler-daire-baskanligi/icerik/19; https://yegitek.meb.gov.tr/www/yapay-zek-ve-buyuk-veri-uygulamalari-daire-baskanligi/icerik/3783)
educationalTechnologySummary: The inspected pages identify no named, standalone AI-learning product developed by YEĞİTEK. They do describe a remit to develop or commission AI-based educational tools and applications, pilot them, and integrate them with digital learning platforms. Intended application areas include personalized learning, assessment, and career guidance; accessibility, inclusion, pedagogical suitability, and user experience are listed for evaluation. YEĞİTEK also produces or obtains digital educational materials—including interactive content, videos, simulations, and educational games—for digital platforms. metadata.Initiative / Programme: Women Science Teachers – AI workshops & STEAM projects
metadata.Description: Network of women science teachers; AI workshops and STEAM projects referenced by respondent.

summary: Women Science Teachers is a Türkiye-based network and project initiative of ENOVA Training Consultancy, supporting science teachers—especially women—and engaging students aged 8–18. It offers STEAM projects, teacher workshops and professional learning, educational resources, and student activities such as a Türkiye–Italy hackathon. Activities use collaborative, hands-on and reflective approaches; some include practical work with AI, coding, 3D and other technologies. The projects also address gender equality, teacher wellbeing, science, art and cultural heritage, but the available evidence does not establish a general AI-literacy framework or audience size.
pedagogicalSummary: The inspected pages describe active, collaborative learning rather than a single teaching model. In Culture4Wellbeing, teachers take part in online workshops, reflective journaling, self-assessment and international peer exchange, then translate reflection into creative, interdisciplinary classroom activities; the programme frames this as a Connect–Appreciate–Reflect–Express sequence (https://www.womenscienceteachers.com/culture4wellbeing). The STEAM Hackathon combines expert-led workshops and seminars with hands-on project development and a final exhibition: students learn project management, art, STEM, coding, AI and related technologies while working across cultures (https://sites.google.com/view/sky-patterns-hipparchus-stars-/home). These examples support experiential, reflective and collaborative approaches. The inspected pages do not establish a distinct, general AI-literacy teaching framework or explain how AI concepts are assessed.
prioritySummary: The initiative’s stated emphasis includes supporting women science teachers and advancing gender equality in science education: WST describes itself as a collaboration platform, especially for female teachers, and aims to help members share school activities and find project partners (https://www.womenscienceteachers.com/about). Its projects also pursue teacher wellbeing and professional resilience through reflection, creativity and international collaboration, with the stated aim of improving teachers’ classroom experiences (https://www.womenscienceteachers.com/culture4wellbeing). For young participants, the STEAM Hackathon seeks to connect students across Türkiye and Italy through science, art and cultural heritage, while developing their project-making and technology experience (https://sites.google.com/view/sky-patterns-hipparchus-stars-/home). The pages show these as multiple related priorities, rather than establishing one overriding emphasis; evidence here is limited to the inspected pages.
educationalTechnologySummary: The inspected pages identify technologies as elements of learning activities, but name no particular AI platform or software used for AI literacy. Culture4Wellbeing describes AI-supported recommendations and AI-assisted coaching and creative projects, alongside digital resources, journals and online collaboration; it does not specify the AI tools or whether WST develops them (https://www.womenscienceteachers.com/culture4wellbeing). In the STEAM Hackathon, students receive hands-on experience with AI, coding, 3D, augmented reality and virtual reality, and use modern technologies in creative project work; specific products are not identified (https://sites.google.com/view/sky-patterns-hipparchus-stars-/home). WST’s About page says its founder creates interactive materials using GeoGebra and Adobe Flash, but does not connect those materials specifically to AI literacy (https://www.womenscienceteachers.com/about). The HealthTech AI app is described as informing farmers, not as a learning tool (https://sites.google.com/view/healthteach/home?authuser=0).

inclusion.reason: The website describes an initiative that includes AI literacy through explicitly referenced "AI workshops" for teachers and students, which implies educational content about how to use AI tools. While adoption scale is uncertain, the initiative qualifies under the INCLUSION ROUTE as it appears to be formally endorsed through its association with ENOVA Training Consultancy and participation in European gender equality networks (e.g., references to EU initiatives, UN events). The STEM Discovery Campaigns and structured projects indicate systematic educational delivery beyond a single institution, satisfying the non-government work criterion when combined with evidence of multi-partner engagement. AI literacy is present as described workshops.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: Ukraine MoES instructional & methodological recommendations on AI in schools (2024)
metadata.Description: Ministry of Education and Science recommendations referenced by respondent.

summary: Ukraine’s Ministry of Education and Science issued these 2024 instructional and methodological recommendations to guide the introduction and use of AI in general secondary schools. They address AI as a support for teachers and school practice, with guidance on instructional uses and responsible implementation, including ethical and safety considerations. The available evidence also describes practical examples related to teaching, learning and assessment, but does not establish a specific teaching method or AI platform.
pedagogicalSummary: The accessible opening identifies this as instructional and methodological recommendations for introducing and using AI in general secondary schools, but it does not reveal a specific teaching method, lesson structure, or learning activity. The document’s extract was too large to inspect beyond its opening, so no particular pedagogy can be established; this is a limit of the available evidence, not confirmation that the full recommendations contain none. Source: https://mon.gov.ua/static-objects/mon/sites/1/news/2024/05/21/Instruktyvno.metodychni.rekomendatsiyi.shchodo.SHI.v.ZZSO-22.05.2024.pdf

metadata.Initiative / Programme: Russell Group principles on the use of generative AI tools in education (2023)
metadata.Description: Five principles adopted by Russell Group universities incl. supporting AI literacy.

summary: The Russell Group’s 2023 five principles guide member universities in using generative AI in education. They call for supporting students and staff to develop AI literacy, understand AI’s opportunities, limitations and ethical issues, and use it appropriately in learning, assignments and research. The principles encourage staff training and resources, open discussion, and adapting teaching and assessment to disciplinary contexts while upholding academic integrity and considering equitable access. They are a policy framework rather than a specified curriculum; implementation is left to individual universities, with the principles also intended to inform wider education and professional sectors.
pedagogicalSummary: The initiative is a policy framework rather than a specified teaching programme, so the page does not set out a single instructional method or curriculum. It does support several ways of organising learning: universities should provide staff with resources and training so they can guide students in using generative AI for learning, assignments, and research; teaching and assessment should adapt to disciplinary contexts; and students and staff should learn about AI’s opportunities, limitations, and ethical issues. The principles also encourage open discussion of AI use and challenges, without fear of penalisation. The page leaves practical implementation to individual universities and departments, so it does not establish how these approaches are delivered in practice. (https://www.russellgroup.ac.uk/policy/policy-briefings/principles-use-generative-ai-tools-education)
prioritySummary: The principles aim to prepare university students and staff to use generative AI effectively, appropriately, and ethically in education. They emphasise AI literacy and future-facing skills, while seeking benefits for student learning and teaching and enabling educators to use efficiencies to develop teaching methods. The page also stresses academic integrity, clear guidance, and fairness of access, including concern that subscription tools could create unequal access. It calls for universities to share practice and collaborate with students, schools, further-education colleges, employers, and professional bodies as the technology evolves. The stated beneficiaries are principally students and staff in Russell Group universities, with the principles also intended to inform wider education and professional sectors. The page does not rank these aims. (https://www.russellgroup.ac.uk/policy/policy-briefings/principles-use-generative-ai-tools-education)
educationalTechnologySummary: The page discusses generative AI tools as technologies that may be used in teaching, learning, assessment, and research, and says students and staff should understand their capabilities, limitations, and ethical issues. It does not identify particular products, platforms, software, or hardware, nor does it describe an educational technology developed by the Russell Group or a specific tool used to deliver its own learning activities. Instead, it calls on member universities to provide resources and staff training and to adapt teaching and assessment for appropriate AI use, while considering access to tools that may be behind paywalls. The inspected page therefore supports a general focus on generative AI tools in education, but provides no evidence about named tools or how any particular tool supports learning in practice. (https://www.russellgroup.ac.uk/policy/policy-briefings/principles-use-generative-ai-tools-education)

inclusion.reason: The initiative clearly includes an AI-literacy component (first principle explicitly states 'Universities will support students and staff to become AI-literate'). It was developed by the Russell Group, a UK body representing major universities. While not a national government entity itself, its principles are widely adopted across its member institutions (over 20 leading UK universities) which collectively serve thousands of students and represent significant scale in higher education. The document explicitly addresses educational content (AI literacy), learning objectives (understanding limitations/ethics), and guidance for both students and staff on how to use AI tools effectively. This qualifies under the inclusion route of non-government work with evidenced system-scale adoption across multiple institutions serving thousands of students.

metadata.Description: UK government plan (Jan 2025) to accelerate AI adoption, incl. skills.

summary: The UK government’s January 2025 AI Opportunities Action Plan sets out 50 recommendations to grow the AI sector, increase adoption across the economy, and improve products and services. Aimed primarily at government and policy makers, it also addresses developing AI skills and talent. It is a national policy roadmap rather than a described teaching programme; the available evidence does not detail learning activities, instructional methods, or educational technologies.
pedagogicalSummary: The inspected GOV.UK page presents the AI Opportunities Action Plan as a government roadmap with 50 recommendations, not as a teaching or training programme. It does not describe lessons, learning activities, instructional methods, or how learners are supported. The linked report was also opened, but its text was too large to inspect fully in this review, so this is a lack of accessible evidence rather than confirmation that no learning-related recommendations appear in the report. Sources: https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/ai-opportunities-action-plan and https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/67851771f0528401055d2329/ai_opportunities_action_plan.pdf
prioritySummary: The page describes the plan’s principal aim as capturing AI’s opportunities to enhance UK growth and productivity and deliver tangible benefits for citizens. Its stated government recommendations focus on growing the UK AI sector, increasing AI adoption across the economy, and improving products and services. These are economic and public-benefit objectives; the inspected page does not establish a separate skills or AI-literacy priority or identify a particular learner group. The linked report was not fully inspectable here, so it may provide further detail on beneficiaries or skills. Source: https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/ai-opportunities-action-plan
educationalTechnologySummary: The inspected publication page and the accessible preview of its linked report do not identify educational technologies, learning platforms, software, or hardware developed or used to support AI literacy. The plan is presented as a set of government recommendations about AI-sector growth, adoption, and improved services; those policy aims do not by themselves establish the use of educational technology. Because the linked report’s full text could not be inspected in this review, the absence of named educational technologies in the accessible material should not be taken as confirmation that none are discussed in the complete report. Sources: https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/ai-opportunities-action-plan and https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/67851771f0528401055d2329/ai_opportunities_action_plan.pdf

inclusion.reason: The initiative is issued by the United Kingdom government (a national government body), satisfying the first inclusion route. It explicitly includes educational content and guidance about AI skills, literacy, and training (e.g., diversifying talent pipelines, AI scholarships, integrating AI literacy into education systems, reskilling for AI-enabled jobs), meeting the core AI-literacy requirement.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: Jisc National Centre for AI in tertiary education
metadata.Description: Jisc centre supporting responsible AI adoption in tertiary education.

summary: The Jisc National Centre for AI in tertiary education supports UK colleges and universities in adopting AI effectively and responsibly. Its resources serve teaching staff, institutional leaders and other tertiary-sector professionals, with guidance also addressing learners. The centre offers self-paced AI-literacy modules, practical advice on teaching and assessment, strategic and governance resources, pilot findings, and opportunities for peer exchange through communities and events. The modules combine demonstrations, reflection, knowledge checks and assessments, covering AI foundations, applied use, and ethical and responsible practice.
pedagogicalSummary: The initiative supports learning through a mix of structured staff development and sector-wide peer exchange. Jisc’s AI-literacy curriculum for tertiary teaching staff is organised into modules on understanding AI, applied skills, and ethical and responsible use; the modules include demonstrations, reflection, knowledge checks and short assessments, and can be completed at the learner’s own pace. Jisc also facilitates communities with regular online meetups and discussion lists for sharing practice, questions and lessons learned. Its stated approach includes developing a community of practice, supporting pilots and sharing thought leadership. These features are documented at https://nationalcentreforai.jiscinvolve.org/wp/2026/05/06/ai-literacy-for-teaching-and-learning-curriculum-digital-learning-modules/, https://www.jisc.ac.uk/get-involved/artificial-intelligence-community/ and https://nationalcentreforai.jiscinvolve.org/wp/sample-page/. The inspected pages do not establish one teaching method used across all activities.
prioritySummary: The clearest priority is helping UK tertiary education adopt AI effectively and responsibly, with benefits for staff, learners and institutions. Jisc’s stated aim is for education to benefit from ethical AI implementation that fits educational culture; its work includes building AI literacy and confidence, informing institutional decisions and governance, and examining practical uses in teaching, learning and administration. The training curriculum targets further- and higher-education teaching staff, while communities also serve research and professional-services colleagues. Pilots explore potential benefits such as more efficient feedback and student support, alongside risks and suitability. The accessible evidence presents these as related priorities rather than establishing a single narrower outcome or beneficiary hierarchy. Sources: https://nationalcentreforai.jiscinvolve.org/wp/sample-page/, https://www.jisc.ac.uk/innovation/artificial-intelligence and https://www.jisc.ac.uk/get-involved/artificial-intelligence-community/.
educationalTechnologySummary: Jisc develops and offers digital AI-literacy learning modules for tertiary teaching staff; institutions can purchase them and host them on their own VLE or LMS. The modules use demonstrations, reflection, knowledge checks and assessments, and are supplied in SCORM 1.2, SCORM 2004, cmi5 and xAPI formats. The inspected evidence does not identify a Jisc-developed AI learning platform or hardware. Separately, Jisc runs pilots evaluating third-party products rather than presenting them as its own technologies. Examples include Bodyswaps, which combines AI and virtual reality for soft-skills simulations; Anywyse, which turns learning materials into audio modules; and Graide, which supports marking and feedback. These examples show technologies tested for educational use, not necessarily tools adopted as part of Jisc’s own teaching. Sources: https://nationalcentreforai.jiscinvolve.org/wp/2026/05/06/ai-literacy-for-teaching-and-learning-curriculum-digital-learning-modules/ and https://www.jisc.ac.uk/reports/artificial-intelligence-in-tertiary-education-pilots/.

inclusion.reason: The site provides AI-literacy educational content: how-to guides on using generative AI in education, marking, and assessment; guidance on agent skills; examples from pilots. Inclusion route: UK national-scale network (Jisc partners with many tertiary institutions), fitting 'system-scale adoption' via a national platform/network rather than single-institution project.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: Online Safety Act 2023
metadata.Description: UK law on online safety duties for services.

summary: The Online Safety Act 2023 is a UK law establishing safety duties for regulated online services and assigning regulatory functions to Ofcom. It focuses on managing risks from illegal content and content harmful to children, while also addressing users’ rights and media literacy. Ofcom is tasked with public awareness-raising, research and encouraging tools that help users assess content and find media-literacy resources; the Act does not set out a curriculum or a defined AI-literacy teaching programme.
pedagogicalSummary: The Online Safety Act is a regulatory statute, not a teaching programme, and the inspected provisions do not set out a curriculum, instructional sequence, or classroom pedagogy. It does establish media-literacy responsibilities for Ofcom: taking or arranging activities to raise public awareness and understanding, commissioning or encouraging initiatives, and arranging research. These are forms of public awareness-raising, but the Act does not prescribe how they should teach or support learning. Its provisions also mention measures to promote users’ media literacy and safe service use as part of providers’ risk assessments, without specifying a learning method. The evidence therefore supports a policy-led awareness and media-literacy remit, not a defined pedagogy or AI-literacy teaching approach. Sources: https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/2023/50/section/11/enacted and https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/2023/50/section/165/enacted.
prioritySummary: The Act’s principal aim is to make covered internet services safer for people in the UK by requiring providers to identify, mitigate, and manage risks from illegal content and content harmful to children. It gives particular weight to children’s protection, requiring risk assessments and proportionate service measures, while also referring to users’ rights to freedom of expression and privacy. A related media-literacy priority is to help the public protect themselves and others: understanding harmful content and misinformation, checking content reliability and authenticity, reducing exposure to harm, and protecting personal information. The Act highlights disproportionate effects on particular groups, including women and girls. These are protective and societal priorities, not workforce upskilling goals. Sources: https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/2023/50/section/1/enacted, https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/2023/50/section/12/enacted, and https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/2023/50/section/165/enacted.
educationalTechnologySummary: The inspected provisions do not identify a named educational platform, software product, or device developed or used by the Act for AI-literacy learning. Instead, section 165 requires Ofcom to encourage the development and use of technologies and systems that help users protect themselves, including tools that provide context about content, help identify and contextualize content of democratic importance, or direct users to media-literacy resources and tools. These are generic intended support functions, not named technologies shown as deployed by the initiative. The Act also refers to age verification or estimation and to proactive technology used by regulated services, but these are safety-compliance measures, not described as educational technologies. The inspected text concerns media literacy and online safety rather than an AI-literacy learning tool. Sources: https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/2023/50/section/12/enacted and https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/2023/50/section/165/enacted.

inclusion.reason: This initiative qualifies as inclusion under the governmental inclusion route: it is an Act of Parliament (UK Public General Act), issued by the UK national government. While the Act itself sets regulatory duties rather than directly providing AI literacy, any online service regulated or guided under this framework would necessitate engagement with AI systems used for content moderation and risk assessment, inherently requiring operators to understand AI functioning within that regulatory context.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: QAA guidance on generative AI
metadata.Description: QAA advice and resources on GenAI and academic integrity/assessment.

summary: The Quality Assurance Agency (QAA) provides guidance and a curated resource hub on generative AI for the UK higher education sector. Its main focus is helping providers maintain academic standards as AI affects learning and assessment, including assessment validity and academic integrity. The materials cover introductory AI concepts, ethical considerations and potential uses in teaching, alongside assessment resources and webinars. QAA is also developing sector principles, shared assessment definitions and implementation recommendations with academic and student input; this is sector guidance rather than a teaching programme or QAA-developed AI platform.
pedagogicalSummary: The initiative is primarily sector guidance and standard-setting, not a teaching programme with a defined pedagogy. Its support is organised through draft principles, shared assessment definitions and recommendations, developed with academic and student representatives and opened to stakeholder feedback. QAA also curates external advice and resources, including materials on authentic assessment and webinars discussing assessment design and how AI might support deeper learning. These point toward reflective redesign of assessment and consideration of AI-supported learning, but the inspected pages do not establish a single teaching method implemented by QAA. (https://www.qaa.ac.uk/sector-resources/generative-artificial-intelligence; https://www.qaa.ac.uk/sector-resources/generative-artificial-intelligence/qaa-advice-and-resources)
prioritySummary: The principal emphasis is helping higher-education providers assure academic standards as generative AI changes learning and assessment. The project asks whether assessment remains valid evidence that students have achieved award standards, and is developing sector-owned principles, common assessment terminology and implementation recommendations. It is intended to benefit the higher-education sector, with student perspectives explicitly included in development and feedback; the accompanying resource collection also aims to help providers engage with AI as a potentially positive tool while maintaining standards. The accessible pages describe sector quality and assessment as the central priority, rather than individual well-being or workforce upskilling. (https://www.qaa.ac.uk/sector-resources/generative-artificial-intelligence; https://www.qaa.ac.uk/sector-resources/generative-artificial-intelligence/qaa-advice-and-resources)
educationalTechnologySummary: QAA’s inspected pages describe a curated collection of resources, not an educational technology platform or AI product developed or deployed by QAA. A separate page lists examples such as ChatGPT, Bard, Synthesia, DALL·E 3 and Imagen, and gives possible higher-education uses including generating learning materials, visual aids and feedback; these are examples for the sector, not evidence that QAA uses or provides them. The collection also links to third-party courses and guidance, including online introductory materials and a Generative AI in Higher Education MOOC. The pages do not identify a QAA-developed learning software or hardware, and do not establish that the listed tools are integrated into QAA teaching. (https://www.qaa.ac.uk/sector-resources/generative-artificial-intelligence/examples-of-generative-ai-tools-and-resources; https://www.qaa.ac.uk/sector-resources/generative-artificial-intelligence/getting-started-what-is-generative-ai)

inclusion.reason: The initiative includes substantive AI literacy content by explaining 'what is generative AI', its underlying capabilities (such as natural language processing), and guiding providers on how to use it responsibly. It meets the inclusion criteria via an exclusion route: QAA is a statutory regulator/quality assurance body that works with UK governments (England, Northern Ireland, Scotland, Wales) and receives government funding for its work.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: DfE policy paper "Generative AI in education" (England)
metadata.Description: Department for Education position and guidance on safe and effective use of generative AI in education.

summary: The Department for Education’s policy paper sets out England’s position on the safe and effective use of generative AI in education, with guidance for schools, colleges, education staff and edtech developers. It considers potential uses in teaching and learning, inclusion, administration and operations, alongside safety and the importance of educators’ expertise. Related staff-support materials offer practical professional learning on understanding AI, prompting, checking outputs and planning appropriate use, using presentations, videos, knowledge checks and reflection activities. This is guidance and staff development, rather than a pupil-facing AI-literacy course.
pedagogicalSummary: The policy paper is guidance rather than a teaching programme, but DfE-linked support materials provide a structured staff-learning approach. The modules build from understanding AI to interacting with it, considering safety and exploring use cases. They combine activity-focused slides, video presentations and transcripts, knowledge checks, and templates for reflection and planning; staff can work through them in sequence or adapt them for individual or group use and different experience levels. This supports practical, guided professional learning rather than a specified pedagogy for classroom instruction. The materials also stress checking AI outputs and planning use appropriate to each setting. Evidence: https://www.gov.uk/government/collections/using-ai-in-education-settings-support-materials and https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/interacting-with-generative-ai-in-education-module-2.
prioritySummary: The initiative’s central emphasis is enabling schools and colleges—particularly in compulsory education—to use generative AI safely and effectively while considering its educational opportunities. The policy is directed chiefly at school and college decision-makers and staff, rather than being a direct AI-literacy course for pupils. Related staff materials aim to build understanding and practical confidence, including selecting tools, prompting, checking outputs, and planning appropriate use. They describe potential applications in teaching and learning, inclusion and accessibility, administration, and operations, while emphasising safety and the continued importance of teachers’ expertise. Thus the evidence indicates a combined priority of responsible adoption and useful support for educational settings; it does not establish a single narrower outcome as dominant. Evidence: https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/generative-artificial-intelligence-in-education and https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/use-cases-of-generative-ai-in-education-module-4.
educationalTechnologySummary: The inspected pages identify digital learning materials, but no dedicated AI-literacy platform or hardware developed by DfE. The associated staff modules are provided as PowerPoint presentations, video playlists on YouTube, and PDF video transcripts; the collection also describes knowledge-check activities and planning templates. These media support staff learning about AI, safe interaction, and educational use cases. The policy landing page names generative-AI products such as ChatGPT and Microsoft Copilot as examples of the technology covered, while the modules address how to use generative-AI tools and assess their outputs. The pages do not establish that DfE provides or requires a particular AI product for learners, nor do they identify a proprietary instructional software platform. Evidence: https://www.gov.uk/government/collections/using-ai-in-education-settings-support-materials and https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/generative-artificial-intelligence-in-education.
