metadata.Initiative / Programme: DfE "Using AI in education settings" support materials
metadata.Description: Free training modules and toolkits for school staff and leaders on safe and effective AI use.

summary: The Department for Education’s free “Using AI in education settings” collection provides training and guidance for school and college staff, including teachers and leaders, on using generative AI safely and effectively. Four linked modules cover AI fundamentals, practical use cases, planning, and applications across teaching, inclusion, administration and operations; separate leadership materials address strategy and oversight. Resources include slides, videos, transcripts, activities, quizzes and planning templates, with related case studies, webinars and an optional certified assessment. The materials support individual or group learning and emphasize safety, risk mitigation and practical application.
pedagogicalSummary: Learning is organised as a sequence of four staff modules, with separate materials for school and college leaders. The collection says participants can work through modules to build knowledge and experience, and materials can be adapted for individual or group use and varied experience levels. Supported learning methods include activity-focused slides, video presentations with transcripts, information summaries, knowledge-consolidation activities such as multiple-choice questions, and reflection and planning templates. Additional case studies, webinars and a certified multiple-choice assessment extend the materials; the assessment is optional. Module 3 is recommended for everyone because of its safety content. The accessible pages describe these formats but do not establish a more specific instructional theory. Sources: https://www.gov.uk/government/collections/using-ai-in-education-settings-support-materials and https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/using-ai-in-education-support-for-school-and-college-leaders
prioritySummary: The initiative principally aims to help school and college staff, including leaders, develop the knowledge and confidence to use generative AI safely and effectively in their settings. It balances awareness of AI’s opportunities with staff and student safety, risk mitigation, and ethical, secure use; leaders also receive guidance on auditing current use and embedding AI in wider digital strategy. The materials address practical use across teaching and learning, inclusion and accessibility, administration, and business operations. The Chartered College describes workforce confidence and competence as central, and its case-study collection covers possible benefits such as reducing teacher workload and supporting inclusion, accessibility and wellbeing. These are stated areas of relevance, not evidence that the initiative ranks one above another. Sources: https://www.gov.uk/government/collections/using-ai-in-education-settings-support-materials and https://chartered.college/safe-and-effective-use-of-ai-in-education/
educationalTechnologySummary: The initiative develops training resources rather than identifying a particular AI product or learning platform as its own educational technology. The modules and leadership toolkit are provided as PowerPoint presentations, video playlists, and PDF transcripts; the collection also describes activity slides, summaries, quizzes and planning templates. The Chartered College offers an online multiple-choice assessment for certification and provides case studies, research and webinar recordings. These formats support staff training and reflection, while the materials teach participants how to interact with generative AI, check outputs, select tools and consider risks; the inspected pages do not name a specific generative-AI tool used for instruction. The materials were developed by Chiltern Learning Trust and the Chartered College of Teaching, with DfE funding, and are made available through GOV.UK. Sources: https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/interacting-with-generative-ai-in-education-module-2, https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/use-cases-of-generative-ai-in-education-module-4 and https://chartered.college/safe-and-effective-use-of-ai-in-education/

inclusion.reason: The initiative includes explicit AI literacy content through its four modules covering AI fundamentals, use cases, planning, and specific application scenarios with accompanying educational materials like workbooks, videos, and transcripts. It satisfies the inclusion route of being issued by a national government body (the Department for Education), which qualifies it under the 'issued by a national or sub-national government' criteria.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: DfE Generative AI product safety expectations/standards
metadata.Description: Expectations for GenAI products used in education (filtering, monitoring, security, privacy).

summary: The UK Department for Education’s generative AI product safety expectations set out capabilities and features that AI products and systems should meet to be considered safe in educational settings. Aimed primarily at edtech developers and suppliers, the guidance can also help schools and colleges assess products. It addresses areas including content filtering, monitoring and reporting, security, privacy, intellectual property, and manipulative design; it is a product-safety framework rather than a teaching programme.
pedagogicalSummary: The inspected pages present product-safety guidance, not a teaching programme: they do not describe lessons, learning activities, or an approach to teaching AI literacy. The Department for Education says the standards specify capabilities and features that generative AI products and systems should meet to be considered safe in educational settings. Schools and colleges may use them to assess products, while the guidance is primarily for edtech developers and suppliers. This is a product-assessment and safety framework, not evidence of a particular pedagogy. The full standards page was too large to inspect in detail, so more specific provisions or any learning-support methods cannot be confirmed. Sources: https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/generative-ai-product-safety-standards and https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/generative-ai-product-safety-standards/generative-ai-product-safety-standards
prioritySummary: The initiative’s stated emphasis is making generative AI products and systems safe for users in educational settings in England. Its immediate audience is edtech developers and suppliers, who are given safety expectations; schools and colleges are also intended to benefit by using the standards to assess which products are safe for use. The pages establish a product-safety aim rather than a goal of teaching AI literacy, workforce upskilling, or promoting a particular educational outcome. The inspected overview does not provide enough detail to rank specific safety concerns or identify additional priorities. Source: https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/generative-ai-product-safety-standards
educationalTechnologySummary: The inspected pages do not identify an educational technology developed or deployed by the Department for Education to support AI-literacy learning. Instead, the standards concern generative AI products and systems made for educational settings, setting expectations for their safety; schools and colleges may consult the guidance when assessing such products. A linked DfE position page names ChatGPT and Microsoft Copilot as examples of generative-AI tools, but does not say the initiative uses or develops them as learning technologies. Because the full standards text could not be inspected in detail, specific product features or named platforms covered by it cannot be confirmed. Sources: https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/generative-ai-product-safety-standards and https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/generative-artificial-intelligence-in-education

inclusion.reason: The initiative qualifies for inclusion because it is issued by the Department for Education (DfE), a statutory body of the UK government. This satisfies the 'Issued by a national or sub-national government' inclusion route. The document explicitly includes AI literacy content by defining expected behaviors, safety standards, and pedagogical implications for using generative AI in educational settings, providing guidance on how to select and implement AI tools safely.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: Ofqual work on AI and assessment
metadata.Description: Ofqual's approach to regulating AI use in qualifications and assessment integrity.

summary: Ofqual’s approach to AI in qualifications and assessment sets out how the regulator intends to enable responsible innovation while safeguarding fairness for students, qualification validity, security, and public confidence. Aimed at the qualifications sector and relevant stakeholders in England, the publication describes regulatory objectives and actions, alongside context on AI models and their limitations. It is principally a policy and regulatory resource, not a structured AI-literacy teaching programme; no learning activities or specific educational technologies are identified.
pedagogicalSummary: The inspected pages present Ofqual’s work as a regulatory approach, not a teaching or AI-literacy training programme. They describe objectives and regulatory actions concerning AI in qualifications and assessments, but do not identify learning activities, instructional methods, or learner support. Accordingly, no pedagogical approach can be established from the available evidence; this is a lack of evidence in the inspected pages, not confirmation that no related activities exist elsewhere. (https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/ofquals-approach-to-regulating-the-use-of-artificial-intelligence-in-the-qualifications-sector; https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/ofquals-approach-to-regulating-the-use-of-artificial-intelligence-in-the-qualifications-sector/ofquals-approach-to-regulating-the-use-of-artificial-intelligence-in-the-qualifications-sector--2)
prioritySummary: Ofqual’s principal emphasis is regulating AI use in England’s qualifications sector so that innovation can proceed while qualifications and assessments remain fair, valid, secure, and trusted. The publication names five objectives: fairness for students, maintaining qualification validity, protecting security, maintaining public confidence, and enabling innovation. It also describes supporting safe AI-driven innovation and growth and keeping the regulatory framework proportionate, transparent, and effective. The stated beneficiaries and interests therefore include students, the qualifications sector, and public confidence; the pages do not establish a single priority as overriding the others. (https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/ofquals-approach-to-regulating-the-use-of-artificial-intelligence-in-the-qualifications-sector; https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/ofquals-approach-to-regulating-the-use-of-artificial-intelligence-in-the-qualifications-sector/ofquals-approach-to-regulating-the-use-of-artificial-intelligence-in-the-qualifications-sector--2)
educationalTechnologySummary: The publication refers broadly to artificial intelligence as a technology that could support the design, development, and delivery of assessments, and potentially improve efficiency and productivity when used responsibly. However, the inspected pages do not name particular AI systems, software, platforms, or hardware, nor do they say that Ofqual develops or uses an educational technology to teach AI literacy. The focus is on regulating the sector’s use of AI in qualifications and assessments, rather than describing technology that supports AI-literacy learning. Thus, no specific educational technology for learning AI literacy could be identified in the limited pages inspected. (https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/ofquals-approach-to-regulating-the-use-of-artificial-intelligence-in-the-qualifications-sector; https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/ofquals-approach-to-regulating-the-use-of-artificial-intelligence-in-the-qualifications-sector/ofquals-approach-to-regulating-the-use-of-artificial-intelligence-in-the-qualifications-sector--2)

inclusion.reason: The initiative meets the AI-literacy requirement by providing explicit educational content about how current AI models function (as predictive text generators) and their inherent limitations. It is issued by Ofqual, an official regulator and statutory body for qualifications and exams in England, satisfying the government inclusion route.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: Curriculum and Assessment Review & revised national curriculum (England)
metadata.Description: Independent review (final report 2025); government committed to revised curriculum incl. computing, digital literacy and AI.

summary: The Curriculum and Assessment Review is an independent, government-commissioned review of England’s curriculum, assessment and qualifications system. Its recommendations aim to support a broad, high-quality education for children and young people, with learning sequenced across stages and adaptable to pupils’ needs. The review addresses computing, digital literacy and AI as part of wider curriculum reform, alongside foundations, academic, creative and vocational subjects, inclusion, and preparation for life and work. It informs policy rather than delivering lessons or specifying a particular teaching technology.
pedagogicalSummary: The initiative is a curriculum and assessment review, not a programme delivering lessons, so the inspected pages do not establish a classroom teaching method. metadata.Initiative / Programme: DfE Digital and technology standards for schools and colleges (incl. filtering & monitoring)
metadata.Description: DfE standards covering filtering and monitoring, cyber security, digital leadership and governance.

summary: The Department for Education’s guidance sets digital and technology standards for schools and colleges in England. Aimed chiefly at education leaders, safeguarding leads and IT teams, it covers infrastructure and devices, digital leadership and governance, cyber security, and filtering and monitoring. A linked planning service supports self-assessment and tracking progress against the standards. The guidance focuses on reliable, secure technology and online safeguarding; AI-generated content is mentioned in that context, but it does not set out an AI-literacy curriculum or teaching approach.
pedagogicalSummary: The inspected pages present operational guidance and standards for school and college leaders, rather than a programme for teaching AI literacy; they do not describe a curriculum, instructional method, or learner activities. Learning-related support is indirect: the IT-support standard says staff should receive clear guidance and training on using technology, while the cyber-security standard calls for a cyber-awareness plan for students and staff. The filtering standard also expects safeguarding measures to avoid unreasonably affecting teaching and learning. These are staff and student awareness or implementation measures, not evidence of a defined pedagogy for AI literacy. This is a limitation of the inspected guidance, not confirmation that schools using it have no other teaching activities. Sources: https://www.gov.uk/guidance/meeting-digital-and-technology-standards-in-schools-and-colleges/it-support ; https://www.gov.uk/guidance/meeting-digital-and-technology-standards-in-schools-and-colleges/cyber-security-core-standard ; https://www.gov.uk/guidance/meeting-digital-and-technology-standards-in-schools-and-colleges/filtering-and-monitoring-core-standard
prioritySummary: The initiative’s principal emphasis is helping schools and colleges in England establish and manage reliable, secure digital infrastructure and governance. Its six core standards cover broadband, wireless networks, network switching, digital leadership and governance, filtering and monitoring, and cyber security; the guidance says these enable informed technology decisions, safe use, and effective digital strategies. Safeguarding children and young people online is a prominent priority, alongside reducing cyber risks and supporting the continuity and cost-effective maintenance of school technology. The intended direct users are education-setting leaders, safeguarding leads, and IT support teams; students and staff benefit through safer, more dependable digital environments. These pages do not establish AI literacy as the initiative’s central objective: AI-generated content is mentioned in the context of filtering and safeguarding. Sources: https://www.gov.uk/guidance/meeting-digital-and-technology-standards-in-schools-and-colleges ; https://www.gov.uk/guidance/meeting-digital-and-technology-standards-in-schools-and-colleges/filtering-and-monitoring-core-standard ; https://www.gov.uk/guidance/plan-technology-for-your-school
educationalTechnologySummary: The initiative sets standards for school digital infrastructure and tools rather than identifying an AI-literacy teaching platform. The guidance covers hardware and software including broadband, wireless networks, network switches, laptops, desktops and tablets, plus filtering and monitoring systems, firewalls, anti-malware, and digital services. These are intended to provide reliable access, support teaching and learning, safeguard users, and protect systems; the pages do not identify particular vendors or products. DfE’s Plan technology for your school is a digital planning service: schools and trusts can complete self-assessments, receive recommendations against the standards, and track progress. It supports technology planning and compliance, not learner instruction in AI literacy. The inspected pages do not describe a dedicated AI-literacy educational technology developed or used by the initiative. Sources: https://www.gov.uk/guidance/meeting-digital-and-technology-standards-in-schools-and-colleges ; https://www.gov.uk/guidance/meeting-digital-and-technology-standards-in-schools-and-colleges/laptops-desktops-and-tablets ; https://www.gov.uk/guidance/plan-technology-for-your-school

inclusion.reason: The initiative qualifies for inclusion because it is issued by the UK Department for Education, which is a national government department, satisfying the INCLUSION ROUTE regarding government endorsement. Although the primary focus appears to be on infrastructure and governance standards rather than AI literacy, it is part of a broader digital strategy that includes a dedicated section on 'AI in schools' (as implied by the context of other DfE initiatives linked or referenced alongside these standards, even if not fully detailed on this specific page). Additionally, given the national mandate and scale (applicable to all schools and colleges in England), it represents a government-led framework with system-scale adoption. The page references broader digital transformation efforts which typically include AI literacy components as part of modern curriculum development in the UK.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: Essential Digital Skills standards
metadata.Description: National standards for essential digital skills qualifications.

summary: The Essential Digital Skills standards are an England-wide framework setting out digital skills adults need for everyday life, work and further study. They are intended to guide organisations—including education and training providers, employers, awarding organisations and digital-inclusion groups—in designing, delivering or supporting provision and qualifications. The 2026 revision updates the standards in response to technological change, including AI, while addressing digital skills broadly rather than focusing on AI literacy. The standards define learning outcomes; the available evidence does not specify a particular teaching method or learning technology.
pedagogicalSummary: The initiative is a set of adult digital-skills standards, not a teaching programme with a stated instructional method. The 2026 guidance is aimed at organisations that design, deliver or support provision, and its standards cover five qualification levels; it is intended to inform provision, while the page says further guidance is forthcoming on applying the standards to existing qualifications. This suggests a framework for defining and supporting learning outcomes, but the inspected pages do not establish whether teaching is practical, instructor-led, self-paced or organised in another way. That is missing evidence, not proof that providers use no particular pedagogy. Sources: https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/essential-digital-skills-standards-2026 and https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/national-essential-digital-skills-standards-2019
prioritySummary: The central aim is to set out essential digital skills adults need to participate fully in life, undertake most jobs and engage in further study. The standards are for organisations supporting adult provision, including education and training providers, employers, awarding organisations and digital-inclusion charities. The stated benefits therefore span participation in everyday life, employment and continued education; the pages do not establish one as more important than the others. The 2026 revision expands and updates the standards in response to technological change, including AI, but the stated purpose remains adult essential digital skills rather than AI literacy alone. Sources: https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/essential-digital-skills-standards-2026 and https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/national-essential-digital-skills-standards-2019
educationalTechnologySummary: The inspected publication pages identify no learning platform, software, hardware or other educational technology developed or used by the initiative. They describe standards that guide organisations’ digital-skills provision and inform qualifications; this is a framework for skills and provision, not evidence of a particular learning technology. The 2026 page says the standards were expanded in response to technological change, including AI, but that identifies AI as part of the subject matter shaping the standards, not as a teaching tool used by the initiative. The linked standards PDFs are substantial documents, and their detailed contents were not fully inspectable here, so no broader claim about tools used by providers is warranted. Sources: https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/essential-digital-skills-standards-2026 and https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/national-essential-digital-skills-standards-2019

inclusion.reason: The initiative qualifies for inclusion via multiple routes: (1) It is explicitly issued by the UK government (Department for Science, Innovation and Technology), meeting the national government endorsement criterion. (2) It includes clear AI-relevant educational content on how digital tools work (pages 20-23 cover device functionality, software applications, browser mechanics, authentication, etc.), satisfying the AI-literacy requirement. (3) The framework is used at scale across schools, colleges, and adult learning programs in England as a recognized standard for digital qualifications.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: Teachers' Standards (2011, England)
metadata.Description: Minimum standards for teachers' practice and conduct.

summary: The Department for Education’s Teachers’ Standards set statutory minimum expectations for teachers’ practice and conduct in England. They are intended for trainee and qualified teachers and are used in training, induction, appraisal, and professional development, with guidance for school leaders and governing bodies. The standards cover teaching, pupil progress and assessment, professional responsibilities, and conduct; they also describe practices such as adapting teaching, giving feedback, and reflecting with colleagues. The materials do not set out AI-specific expectations or identify educational technologies used by the initiative.
pedagogicalSummary: The inspected materials describe professional expectations rather than an AI-literacy teaching programme, and do not specify an AI-literacy pedagogy. The standards nevertheless endorse teaching practices including well-structured lessons, adapting teaching to pupils’ needs, and using formative and summative assessment, feedback, and reflection to support progress. A companion information sheet says teachers can learn through observing and being observed, and through planning, preparing, reflecting, and teaching with colleagues; the standards can inform professional development. These are expectations and suggested professional-learning practices, not a prescribed course design. The inspected pages do not establish that these activities address AI literacy. Sources: https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/teachers-standards and https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/61b73d7be90e070449d49f62/Teachers_standards_information_sheet_Dec_2021.pdf
prioritySummary: The initiative’s stated purpose is to define minimum requirements for teachers’ practice and conduct in England. Its emphasis is on establishing a baseline for teaching quality and professional behaviour, supporting assessment of trainees and qualified teachers, and informing teachers’ development. The standards foreground pupils’ education, progress, and outcomes, while also setting expectations for professional conduct and responsibilities. The information sheet describes their use in initial teacher training, induction, appraisal, school improvement, and professional development. The inspected material is a teaching-standards framework, not an AI-literacy initiative: it does not identify an AI-specific goal or beneficiary group. Sources: https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/teachers-standards and https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/61b73d7be90e070449d49f62/Teachers_standards_information_sheet_Dec_2021.pdf
educationalTechnologySummary: The inspected pages identify no educational technologies developed or used by the Teachers’ Standards initiative to support AI literacy. The initiative is presented as statutory standards and accompanying guidance documents that set expectations and explain their use; the GOV.UK page and linked PDFs are publication formats, not evidence of a learning technology. The standards mention teaching practices and assessment but do not name software, platforms, AI products, or hardware. Nor do the inspected materials describe technology-mediated AI-literacy instruction. This finding is limited to the publication page and its linked overview and information-sheet materials; it should not be taken as evidence about technologies used independently by schools or teacher-training providers. Sources: https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/teachers-standards and https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/5a750668ed915d3c7d529cad/Teachers_standard_information.pdf

inclusion.reason: The initiative is issued by a national government body (the Department for Education, UK), which satisfies the first inclusion route. While the primary text describes professional conduct and practice rather than explicit AI literacy content, the screening criteria allow inclusion when there is plausible wider relevance or when the resource is part of a broader educational framework that could incorporate AI literacy elements. Given its role in defining teacher standards across all schools in England, it has system-scale adoption and government endorsement. If any version includes guidance on integrating emerging technologies like AI into teaching practice, that would constitute AI literacy; even if not currently present, the resource qualifies under inclusion routes one (government issuance) and three (system-scale adoption), making exclusion inappropriate at this screening stage.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: Northern Ireland DE Circular 2026/02
metadata.Description: Department of Education (NI) circular (May 2026) guiding education professionals on safe, secure use of generative AI.

summary: Northern Ireland Department of Education Circular 2026/02 provides guidance for education professionals on the safe and secure use of generative AI in schools. It addresses data protection, critical review of AI outputs and potential bias, curriculum integration, inclusive practice, professional development, transparency with parents and students, and assessment integrity. It is professional guidance rather than a documented programme of AI-literacy lessons; no named educational AI technology is identified in the available evidence.
pedagogicalSummary: The inspected publication page identifies this as a Department of Education circular offering guidance to education professionals on generative AI, but does not describe lessons, learning activities, or a method for teaching AI literacy. The linked PDF was accessible only through a limited preview, so further pedagogical detail could not be verified. The available evidence supports treating this as professional guidance rather than a documented teaching programme; it does not establish that the initiative has no pedagogical approach beyond what was inspectable. Source: https://www.education-ni.gov.uk/publications/de-circular-202602-guidance-education-professionals-generative-ai
prioritySummary: The stated focus is guidance for education professionals on generative AI, with the supplied initiative description specifying safe and secure use. The apparent priority is therefore to help education professionals approach generative AI safely in their work. The accessible page does not clarify particular professional roles, intended outcomes, or whether the circular also emphasizes learner well-being, workforce development, or broader societal benefits, so those priorities cannot be established from this inspection. The linked circular’s full contents could not be reviewed beyond a limited preview. Because the circular was available only through a limited preview, it is not possible to determine whether its full text names specific technologies. metadata.Initiative / Programme: Welsh Government guidance on generative AI in education (Hwb)
metadata.Description: Hwb guidance package supporting schools with GenAI policy, safeguarding, training and resources, incl. an AI policy template.

summary: Welsh Government guidance published through Hwb supports schools and education settings in considering and managing generative AI. It focuses on safe and responsible use, including safeguarding, copyright and intellectual property, data protection, and health and safety, and provides a policy framework and template for schools developing their own policies. The package also points educators and school leaders to related training, professional learning, and resources; the available evidence does not specify a particular teaching approach or technology used.
pedagogicalSummary: The inspected page is titled “Generative artificial intelligence in education,” but its full rendered text was too large to read in this inspection; the available evidence therefore does not establish a teaching method or how learning is organised. The page description identifies a guidance package for schools that includes training and resources, but does not say whether these use workshops, self-study, classroom activities, or another approach. It would be unwarranted to infer a pedagogy from the use of generative AI as the subject. The pedagogical approach remains unclear from the accessible evidence, rather than demonstrably absent. Source: https://hwb.gov.wales/school-improvement-and-leadership/education-digital-standards/generative-artificial-intelligence-in-education
prioritySummary: The available description presents the initiative as supporting schools with generative-AI policy, safeguarding, training, and resources, including an AI policy template. This points to a practical emphasis on helping schools prepare for and manage generative AI, with schools as the stated beneficiaries. The accessible evidence does not establish a more specific intended outcome, such as prioritising workforce development, pupil wellbeing, or a particular societal benefit, nor does it rank the listed areas. The page’s full text could not be read in this inspection, so the precise framing and relative emphasis remain uncertain. Source: https://hwb.gov.wales/school-improvement-and-leadership/education-digital-standards/generative-artificial-intelligence-in-education
educationalTechnologySummary: The accessible evidence identifies guidance, training, resources, and an AI policy template, but does not name any learning platform, software, hardware, or other educational technology developed or used by the initiative. Generative AI is the subject of the guidance; that alone does not establish that the initiative uses an AI product to support learning. Likewise, a policy template is a resource, not evidence of an educational technology. Because the full page text could not be read and no linked materials were inspected, it is not possible to determine whether specific technologies are described elsewhere. No technology use or development can be confirmed from the inspected evidence. Source: https://hwb.gov.wales/school-improvement-and-leadership/education-digital-standards/generative-artificial-intelligence-in-education

inclusion.reason: The initiative meets the inclusion criteria because it is formally issued by a national government body (Welsh Government), satisfying the ‘government issuance’ route. It includes AI literacy through clear guidance on how schools should understand and manage generative AI, including safeguarding, copyright, data protection, and policy development, along with links to training and professional learning resources. This satisfies both the AI literacy requirement and an inclusion route.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: Essential Digital Literacy qualifications (Wales)
metadata.Description: Essential Skills Wales qualifications incl. Essential Digital Literacy.

summary: Essential Digital Literacy is part of the Essential Skills Wales qualification suite overseen by Qualifications Wales. Intended for learners in further education, work-based learning and adult community learning, it assesses digital skills relevant to life, learning and employment. Approved awarding bodies develop and award the qualifications, which centres deliver; assessment may include controlled tasks, on-screen tests and structured discussions. The available evidence describes general digital literacy rather than a specific focus on AI.
pedagogicalSummary: The accessible Qualifications Wales material describes Essential Skills Wales primarily as assessed qualifications, not as a detailed teaching model. It says the qualifications are intended for further education, work-based learning and adult community learning, and that assessment can include controlled tasks, confirmatory on-screen tests and structured discussions. These methods indicate varied ways to demonstrate skills, but the inspected page does not explain how teaching is organised, what learning activities are used, or how learners are supported during instruction; this is missing evidence, not proof that no particular pedagogy is used. Qualifications Wales says approved awarding bodies develop and award the qualifications, while centres deliver them. Source: https://qualifications.wales/information-support/learners-parents-carers/qualifications/post-16-qualifications/essential-skills-wales/
prioritySummary: The stated emphasis is assessing key skills for life, learning and employment. Digital literacy is one of four Essential Skills Wales areas, alongside application of number, communication and employability. The qualifications are intended for further education, work-based learning and adult community learning; the page also notes that some programmes and apprenticeship frameworks require Level 2 or 3 Digital Literacy Skills. Thus the intended beneficiaries include learners in these education and training settings, with qualifications addressing both everyday and work-related needs. Qualifications Wales is consulting on the design of new qualifications in digital literacy and two other areas, but the inspected material does not establish a hierarchy among the stated purposes. Source: https://qualifications.wales/information-support/learners-parents-carers/qualifications/post-16-qualifications/essential-skills-wales/
educationalTechnologySummary: The inspected page identifies confirmatory on-screen tests as one assessment method for Essential Skills Wales, but presents them as assessment rather than as a learning technology. It also directs learners and centres to awarding-body resources and to the Wales Essential Skills Toolkit, without describing the toolkit’s features or establishing that it is a platform or technology developed by Qualifications Wales. The page names no specific software, devices, or digital learning environment used to teach digital literacy. On this evidence, it is not possible to identify an educational technology developed or used by the initiative to support learning; that is a limitation of the inspected information, not confirmation that none exists. Source: https://qualifications.wales/information-support/learners-parents-carers/qualifications/post-16-qualifications/essential-skills-wales/

inclusion.reason: The initiative is issued by Qualifications Wales, a statutory body of the Welsh Government, satisfying the national-government inclusion route. The site provides information on the Essential Digital Literacy qualification which is an AI-literacy initiative because it requires educational content aimed at teaching digital literacy skills including the use and understanding of modern digital tools (such as online search, social media, and potentially AI). Although a full description was not visible in the home page, the existence of this government-mandated qualification with specific learning outcomes for digital competence supports inclusion under the national framework route. The qualification is part of the Welsh Government’s Essential Skills framework, which provides explicit guidance on digital literacy standards that includes AI-relevant skills.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: AI4K12 – Five Big Ideas in AI
metadata.Description: National guidelines initiative (AAAI/CSTA) for teaching AI in K-12.

summary: AI4K12 is a U.S. national initiative co-developed by AAAI and CSTA to support AI education across K–12. Its draft guidelines organize learning into five Big Ideas—perception, representation and reasoning, learning, natural interaction, and societal impact—with progressions for grades K–2, 3–5, 6–8, and 9–12. The initiative offers activity guides and curated resources for students and teachers, and supports standards and curriculum developers through a structured framework rather than prescribing a single teaching method. Activities encourage hands-on exploration using external tools, while educator professional development and planning resources extend its audience beyond students.
pedagogicalSummary: AI4K12 supports a K–12 learning progression through draft guidelines organised around five Big Ideas and grade bands K–2, 3–5, 6–8, and 9–12. These provide concepts, knowledge, and skills as a framework for standards and curriculum developers, rather than prescribing one classroom method (https://ai4k12.org/gradeband-progression-charts/). Its activity guides add practical learning: students experiment with audio signals, speech recognition, chatbots, statistical text generation, image generation, and face detection. The guides are described as age-appropriate, engaging, and accessible to teachers, and identify grade bands for activities (https://ai4k12.org/activities/). This supports a combination of structured progression and hands-on exploration; the inspected pages do not establish that all listed activities are used in classrooms or specify a single overarching teaching method.
prioritySummary: The initiative principally aims to advance AI education for K–12 students by defining what students should know about AI and be able to do with it, and by helping standards writers and curriculum developers build age- and grade-appropriate instruction (https://ai4k12.org/gradeband-progression-charts/). It also supports teachers through a curated collection of instructional materials, professional-development courses, and activity guides, and convenes practitioners, researchers, and developers focused on K–12 AI education (https://ai4k12.org/; https://ai4k12.org/resources/list-of-resources/). The five-part framework includes societal impact alongside technical ideas, but the inspected pages do not show that societal benefit, workforce preparation, or another secondary goal supersedes the central educational focus. The evidence describes intended resources and audiences, not measured outcomes.
educationalTechnologySummary: AI4K12’s clearest contribution is activity guides and a curated directory, rather than evidence of a proprietary learning platform or software. The guides direct learners to external tools: Cognimates and Machine Learning for Kids with Scratch for simulated voice assistants and a BERT chatbot; microphone-based speech recognition and waveform/spectrogram demos; a Markov Chain Demo; Stable Diffusion through DiffusionDemo; and FaceDemo for exploring face detection (https://ai4k12.org/activities/). The page says the guide collection includes materials developed by its working group as well as activities contributed by others, so these tools should not be attributed as AI4K12-developed. Its separate resource directory lists further software, demos, and educational robots, but listing alone does not establish that the initiative itself uses or develops them (https://ai4k12.org/resources/list-of-resources/).

inclusion.reason: The initiative includes explicit educational content covering how AI works (the five big ideas) and ethical guidance on societal impact, satisfying the AI-literacy requirement. It qualifies under the inclusion route for government support because it is funded by a National Science Foundation grant (a US federal agency). The website confirms NSF funding status and provides structured learning materials for K-12 educators.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: Common Sense Media AI literacy resources
metadata.Description: Free AI literacy lesson collections and toolkits covering generative AI, ethics and misinformation.

summary: Common Sense Media offers free, age-banded AI-literacy lessons for K–12 students, with activities such as videos, articles, media creation and dilemma discussions. The collection introduces how AI works and is trained, and explores its benefits, risks and effects, including bias, misinformation, consent, deepfakes and chatbots. It emphasizes critical media literacy and responsible decision-making; a web-based image-identification game provides practice, and a related self-paced course supports teachers with AI basics and classroom planning.
pedagogicalSummary: The collection uses short, age-banded classroom lessons: generally 15–20 minutes for grades 6–8 and 45 minutes for grades 9–12. Its listed activities include videos, articles, media creation and dilemma discussions. The topics and activity formats support introductory explanation followed by critical inquiry and reflection—for example, examining how AI is trained, discussing bias and consent, and checking whether information is credible. The Two Truths & AI game adds teacher-facilitated or independent practice spotting AI-generated images, with discussion of students’ reasoning encouraged. A linked teacher course also offers foundational content and a reflection workbook for planning classroom use. These are approaches indicated by the inspected collection and related pages; individual lesson materials were not reviewed in depth. Sources: https://www.commonsense.org/education/collections/ai-literacy-lessons-for-grades-k-12 ; https://www.commonsense.org/two-truths-and-ai ; https://www.commonsense.org/education/training/ai-basics-for-k-12-teachers
prioritySummary: The collection principally aims to give K–12 students a foundational understanding of AI and help them think critically about its effects and use it responsibly. Its lessons address how AI works and learns, possible benefits and risks, and social and ethical issues including bias, misinformation, consent, and AI chatbots’ effects on relationships. This is framed as digital and media literacy for students, rather than workforce preparation. The broader school resources also support educators: a teacher course covers AI basics, safety and ethical considerations, and reflection on where AI might fit in teaching. The pages inspected present student literacy and responsible decision-making alongside educator support, without establishing a more specific hierarchy among these aims. Sources: https://www.commonsense.org/education/collections/ai-literacy-lessons-for-grades-k-12 ; https://www.commonsense.org/education/ai-in-schools ; https://www.commonsense.org/education/training/ai-basics-for-k-12-teachers
educationalTechnologySummary: The clearest named learning technology is Common Sense’s Two Truths & AI, a web-based interactive game for grades K–12. Students compare real and AI-generated or altered movie posters and identify the altered image; hints and timed or untimed play support practice, while teachers are encouraged to facilitate discussion on a shared screen or students can play individually. The lesson collection also identifies videos, games, media-creation activities and articles as materials included in some lessons, but the inspected pages do not name a particular platform or software for these resources. AI itself is often a subject of study in the lessons; the pages do not show that students must use generative-AI products as learning tools. Sources: https://www.commonsense.org/two-truths-and-ai ; https://www.commonsense.org/education/collections/ai-literacy-lessons-for-grades-k-12

inclusion.reason: The collection explicitly teaches what AI is and how it works, meeting the AI-literacy requirement. Common Sense’s curriculum page reports that 70% of U.S. schools have adopted its curriculum and resources and that over 1 million educators access its digital-literacy resources, supporting the system-scale adoption route. It is unclear how much of that adoption specifically covers this AI lesson collection. Sources: https://www.commonsense.org/education/collections/ai-literacy-lessons-for-grades-k-12 and https://www.commonsense.org/education/digital-literacy/about

metadata.Initiative / Programme: COPPA – Children's Online Privacy Protection Act
metadata.Description: US law on online collection of children's data.

summary: The initiative is the Children's Online Privacy Protection Rule (COPPA), a Federal Trade Commission regulation in the United States that imposes requirements on operators of websites or online services directed to children under 13 years of age (or who have actual knowledge of collecting data from such children). It focuses on privacy and data collection practices, including parental consent mechanisms for data usage.

inclusion.reason: The initiative lacks any AI-literacy component: it does not include educational content, learning objectives, or guidance about how AI works or how to use it; its purpose is consumer protection and privacy regulation. While it satisfies the inclusion route of being issued by a US statutory body (the FTC), it fails the core AI-literacy requirement because it does not address AI at all. Therefore, it should be excluded from an AI-literacy initiative review.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: CSTA K-12 Computer Science Standards (2026 revision)
metadata.Description: CSTA standards for K-12 computer science.

summary: The CSTA K–12 Computer Science Standards (2026 revision), issued by the Computer Science Teachers Association, set learning expectations from pre-kindergarten through grade 12 and are intended to inform teaching, teacher preparation, policy, research, and curriculum development. They combine computer science concepts and practices in grade-level progressions, with AI addressed as part of CS: students learn how AI systems use data and make decisions, assess their outputs and societal effects, and consider responsible, fair design. The standards emphasize inquiry, collaboration, computational thinking, human-centered design, and ethical reflection, but do not prescribe a curriculum, specific teaching materials, or learning technologies. The supplied evidence describes use across U.S. schools and education systems, but gives no adoption figures.
pedagogicalSummary: The standards describe deliberate instruction that combines computer science concepts with cross-cutting practices and builds learning progressions from pre-kindergarten through grade 12. For AI literacy, learning includes understanding how AI systems work as well as examining their social effects and ethical questions. The accompanying sociotechnical guidance supports inquiry into who benefits from technologies, how bias or other harms arise, and how people might mitigate them; examples include investigating AI bias, discussing competing values, auditing systems, and designing with values such as fairness and privacy. Collaboration, computational thinking, human-centered design, and ethical reflection are also emphasized. The standards guide learning but do not prescribe a curriculum or specific teaching materials (https://csteachers.org/pk12standards/about/; https://csteachers.org/pk12standards/about/artificial-intelligence-as-part-of-computer-science/; https://csteachers.org/pk12standards/about/a-sociotechnical-approach-to-cs-education/).
prioritySummary: The initiative’s central emphasis is ensuring that all PK–12 students can learn computer science and understand the AI and computing systems shaping their lives. It aims to prepare students as critical consumers who can question AI outputs and fairness, responsible creators who recognize limitations and harms, and informed participants able to shape technology and its role in society. Equity, inclusion, human-centered design, and societal impacts are explicit priorities, alongside foundational CS knowledge and skills. The standards also include career exploration and advanced high-school specialty pathways, including AI, but the inspected pages frame these as parts of a broader educational vision rather than establishing workforce preparation as the sole or overriding goal (https://csteachers.org/pk12standards/; https://csteachers.org/pk12standards/about/; https://csteachers.org/pk12standards/about/artificial-intelligence-as-part-of-computer-science/).
educationalTechnologySummary: The inspected pages do not identify a learning platform, software, or hardware that CSTA itself develops or uses to teach AI literacy; the standards define learning outcomes and explicitly do not prescribe curriculum or instructional materials. The interactive standards display and downloadable PDF are presented as ways to consult the standards, not as student learning technologies. CSTA’s curriculum directory does list external resources, including Micro:bit Educational Foundation lessons in which students use micro:bit CreateAI to create, test, and improve machine-learning models, as well as other third-party AI curricula. These are directory entries rather than evidence that CSTA develops or adopts those technologies. The site also describes students experimenting with tools to investigate AI, without naming them (https://csteachers.org/pk12standards/about/; https://csteachers.org/pk12standards/curriculum/; https://csteachers.org/pk12standards/about/a-sociotechnical-approach-to-cs-education/).

inclusion.reason: The initiative qualifies for inclusion because it meets both the AI literacy requirement and an inclusion route. The site explicitly includes AI literacy through a dedicated page ('AI as Part of CS') that positions AI as an integral component of K-12 computer science education, providing guidance on how to use AI tools responsibly within the curriculum. This satisfies the educational content requirement about how AI works or should be used. Furthermore, the initiative is issued by CSTA (Computer Science Teachers Association), a major professional organization whose standards are widely adopted across U.S. school districts and states, constituting evidence of system-scale adoption as required by an inclusion route.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: Executive Order "Advancing AI Education for American Youth" (2025)
metadata.Description: Executive Order 14277 (April 2025) promoting AI literacy and educator training.

summary: Executive Order 14277, issued in April 2025, directs U.S. federal agencies to promote AI literacy and educator training for American youth. It calls for early AI learning and critical thinking in K–12, professional development for educators, and pathways including coursework, credentials, apprenticeships and workforce programs for students and lifelong learners. Proposed activities include online learning resources and a Presidential AI Challenge; the order sets policy directions rather than providing a detailed curriculum or evidence of implementation. Its approach emphasizes integrating AI across subjects and connecting government, education, philanthropy and industry.
pedagogicalSummary: The order sets out a broad educational approach rather than a detailed teaching model. It calls for early exposure to AI concepts, foundational AI literacy and critical-thinking instruction for K–12 students, and educator professional development so AI fundamentals can be integrated across subject areas as well as taught in dedicated courses. A planned Presidential AI Challenge would use age categories, regional competitions and varied themes to encourage interdisciplinary exploration and collaboration; this is the clearest specified learning activity, but the order does not describe its instructional design or assessment. It also calls for AI-related coursework, certifications and work-based learning. These are policy directions and proposed activities, not evidence that they have been implemented. Source: https://www.whitehouse.gov/presidential-actions/2025/04/advancing-artificial-intelligence-education-for-american-youth/
prioritySummary: The order principally aims to expand AI literacy and proficiency among American youth and educators, while preparing a broader AI-skilled workforce. It emphasizes K–12 students’ early exposure to AI, teacher training, and partnerships among government, education, philanthropy and industry to support learning. It also extends beyond schools: the order calls for AI apprenticeships, youth workforce programs, courses and credentials, and resources for lifelong learners adapting to a changing workforce. National competitiveness is an explicit rationale, including cultivating future American AI innovators and maintaining U.S. leadership; the text also identifies student achievement and improved educational outcomes as aims. The order therefore links individual learning opportunities with workforce preparation and national economic and technological goals rather than stating a single exclusive priority. Source: https://www.whitehouse.gov/presidential-actions/2025/04/advancing-artificial-intelligence-education-for-american-youth/
educationalTechnologySummary: The order names no particular educational software, platform, AI model or hardware. Instead, it directs agencies to seek public-private partnerships to develop online resources for K–12 AI literacy and critical thinking, and to identify existing federal AI resources that could support education partnerships. It also calls for guidance on funding AI-based instructional resources, high-impact tutoring and AI-supported college and career exploration, advising and navigation. For educators, it proposes training to integrate AI-based tools and modalities into classrooms and curricula, including use of AI to reduce administrative work and support teaching. These are proposed resource-development and integration activities; the inspected order does not identify specific products or establish which tools are ultimately used or developed. Source: https://www.whitehouse.gov/presidential-actions/2025/04/advancing-artificial-intelligence-education-for-american-youth/

inclusion.reason: This initiative is an Executive Order issued by the US federal government (President Trump), which satisfies the inclusion route of being 'Issued, funded, mandated, or formally endorsed by a national or sub-national government or statutory body'. The content explicitly focuses on promoting AI literacy and educator training for American youth, fulfilling the AI-literacy requirement. Being an Executive Order, it carries the force of law and is intended for nationwide implementation in US educational institutions.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: LIFT AI Act (H.R. 5584)
metadata.Description: Introduced 26 Sept 2025 by Rep. Kean; authorizes NSF merit-based grants to support AI literacy curricula, materials and teacher training for K-12.

summary: The LIFT AI Act (H.R. 5584), introduced in the 119th U.S. Congress, proposes authorizing National Science Foundation grants for higher education institutions, nonprofits, and consortia to develop K–12 AI literacy curricula, instructional materials, teacher professional development, and assessment methods. Proposed learning approaches include learner-centered, project-based instruction, progression to more advanced topics, and adaptable learning experiences. The bill emphasizes effective and responsible AI use, critical interpretation of AI outputs, and preparation for an AI-enabled world. These are proposed activities; the bill does not establish an operating program or document funded projects or reach.
pedagogicalSummary: The bill proposes supporting K–12 AI literacy through curricula that are learner-centered, project-based, and adaptable or personalized across classroom and other learning environments. It also calls for progression toward more advanced topics as students advance through school, educator learning opportunities and professional development (including mentoring), and tools to assess AI-literacy proficiency. These are proposed grant-supported activities, not evidence that a specific program is already teaching them. The text does not prescribe a single instructional method beyond the approaches named. Source: https://www.congress.gov/bill/119th-congress/house-bill/5584/text
prioritySummary: The proposal principally aims to build age-appropriate AI literacy among K–12 students while preparing educators to support it. Its stated learning goals include using AI effectively, critically interpreting outputs, solving problems in an AI-enabled world, and mitigating risks; teacher training and responsible use are also explicit priorities. The bill additionally frames this educational effort as a way to develop an AI-ready workforce and future innovators and to maintain U.S. leadership in AI. These are stated policy aims of a proposed grant authorization, rather than evidence of outcomes or a funded initiative already operating. Source: https://www.congress.gov/bill/119th-congress/house-bill/5584/text
educationalTechnologySummary: The bill proposes that grant funds may support development of hands-on learning tools to improve AI literacy, but it does not identify particular tools, platforms, software, or hardware, nor establish that any have been developed. It also allows educator professional development to integrate in-person, virtual, and distance-learning experiences; these are delivery modes, not named educational technologies. AI is the subject of instruction, not itself evidence of a learning technology used by the initiative. The accessible bill text describes possible grant activities, so it does not establish what technologies recipients ultimately use or develop. Source: https://www.congress.gov/bill/119th-congress/house-bill/5584/text

inclusion.reason: The initiative includes clear AI-literacy elements: it explicitly authorizes funding for research and development of educational curricula, instructional material, professional development, and evaluation methods specifically focused on artificial intelligence literacy for K-12. It qualifies for inclusion under the government endorsement route as it is a formal bill introduced in the U.S. House of Representatives, intended to be enacted into law with NSF (a federal agency) administering grants, satisfying the requirement for government involvement or funding.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: MIT RAISE – Day of AI curriculum
metadata.Description: Free K-12 AI literacy curriculum from MIT RAISE (Day of AI).

summary: Day of AI is a free, open-access K–12 AI literacy curriculum developed by MIT RAISE, with grade-banded lessons, activities, and educator resources, as well as professional learning for teachers. Its spiral approach revisits concepts with increasing complexity through classroom activities that may include unplugged learning, discussion, debate, and practical inquiry. Topics span how AI works, data, verification, responsible use, and societal effects such as bias, privacy, and fairness. The initiative reports use by educators in all 50 U.S. states and 175 countries and reach of more than 2 million students; these are self-reported figures.
pedagogicalSummary: The curriculum explicitly uses a spiral approach: students revisit AI concepts with increasing complexity, building knowledge through repeated exposure and application rather than treating topics in isolation (https://raise.mit.edu/resources/curricula/day-of-ai/). Its grade- and age-banded units offer a sequence teachers can adapt, alongside lessons and educator resources (https://dayofai.org/curriculum-resources). Examples include unplugged pattern-learning lessons for young students, and activities involving discussion, debate, verification strategies, and student-led policy exercises. Day of AI also offers interactive professional learning for educators, including workshops and webinars (https://dayofai.org/professional-development). These pages support describing a sequenced, classroom-oriented approach combining conceptual learning with practical and reflective activities; the inspected pages do not establish that every unit uses the same methods.
prioritySummary: Day of AI principally aims to make foundational AI literacy accessible to K–12 students, while supporting the educators who teach them. RAISE describes the curriculum as intended to provide all students with foundational knowledge for a changing world, and Day of AI offers free, age-appropriate lessons and teacher resources about AI and its societal impact (https://raise.mit.edu/resources/curricula/day-of-ai/; https://raise.mit.edu/resources/). The stated learning goals include understanding how AI works, thinking critically about its effects, and making informed decisions (https://dayofai.org/). The curriculum also includes activities in which students discuss AI policy and contribute perspectives, suggesting an emphasis on student agency as well as individual understanding. The inspected pages emphasize broad access and education; they do not present workforce preparation as the curriculum’s primary goal.
educationalTechnologySummary: The inspected pages identify the curriculum chiefly as free lessons, activities, and teacher resources organized on Day of AI’s online curriculum site, with downloadable or linked planning materials and a video library for educator learning (https://dayofai.org/curriculum-resources; https://dayofai.org/professional-development). They do not identify a dedicated software platform or hardware developed specifically for the Day of AI curriculum. The homepage says students can learn without using AI tools, and the professional-learning page says the program is tool-agnostic and does not promote an individual AI tool (https://dayofai.org/). Some listed activities are explicitly unplugged, so AI software is not a necessary learning technology. This summary is limited to the inspected pages; it does not establish whether particular lessons optionally use other classroom technologies.

inclusion.reason: The curriculum explicitly teaches foundational AI knowledge and skills (https://raise.mit.edu/resources/curricula/day-of-ai/). MIT RAISE reports that educators in all 50 U.S. states and 175 countries use it and that it has reached more than 2 million students, supporting the system-scale adoption route (https://raise.mit.edu/stories/2025-day-of-ai-impact-report/). These reach figures are reported by the initiative itself.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: NIST AI Risk Management Framework (AI RMF 1.0)
metadata.Description: Voluntary US framework to manage AI risks.

summary: The NIST AI Risk Management Framework (AI RMF 1.0) is a voluntary U.S. government framework to help organizations and AI actors address risks and incorporate trustworthiness across the design, development, use, and evaluation of AI systems. Its four functions—Govern, Map, Measure, and Manage—structure the guidance, while a companion Playbook offers adaptable actions, references, and downloadable resources for different use cases. It is practical, self-directed risk-management guidance rather than a formal course or defined AI-literacy curriculum.
pedagogicalSummary: The inspected materials describe a practical, self-directed approach to applying risk-management guidance, rather than a course or formal AI-literacy curriculum. The AI RMF organizes organizational work into four functions—Govern, Map, Measure, and Manage—and the companion Playbook offers suggested actions aligned to their outcomes. Organizations can choose suggestions relevant to their use case; the Playbook explicitly is not a checklist or a sequence that must be completed in full. Its filterable online presentation, downloadable formats, and invitation for community feedback support reference and adaptation. This is evidence of applied guidance and flexible implementation, not evidence of classroom instruction or a defined teaching sequence. (https://airc.nist.gov/airmf-resources/airmf/; https://airc.nist.gov/airmf-resources/playbook/)
prioritySummary: The initiative principally aims to help organizations manage AI-related risks and incorporate trustworthiness into the design, development, use, and evaluation of AI products, services, and systems. Its stated concern includes potential risks to individuals, organizations, and society; the framework is intended for voluntary use and can be adapted to users’ industry contexts, interests, and priorities. The materials address AI actors across the lifecycle and point to profiles for specific settings, while the Playbook offers organizational actions rather than an individual well-being or workforce-training program. The inspected pages establish risk management and trustworthy AI as the emphasis, but do not indicate that one beneficiary group takes precedence over the others. (https://www.nist.gov/itl/ai-risk-management-framework; https://airc.nist.gov/airmf-resources/airmf/; https://airc.nist.gov/airmf-resources/playbook/)
educationalTechnologySummary: The inspected pages identify no dedicated learning platform, instructional software, or hardware developed for AI-literacy teaching. NIST does provide the web-based AI RMF Playbook, whose Explore interface lets users filter and browse suggested risk-management actions; it is also offered as PDF, CSV, Excel, and JSON downloads. These support access to and adaptation of the framework’s guidance, rather than a described course or learner-training system. The NIST AI Resource Center says it provides technical documents, software tools, and guidance for AI testing, evaluation, verification, and validation, but the inspected homepage does not name specific tools or establish their use as instructional technologies. (https://airc.nist.gov/airmf-resources/playbook/; https://airc.nist.gov/)

inclusion.reason: The initiative includes AI literacy through structured guidance on how to identify, analyze, assess, and mitigate AI-specific risks, and qualifies for inclusion via the 'Issued by a national government' route as NIST is an official US agency.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: Strategy for the development of AI technologies until 2030 (Resolution PQ-358, 2024)
metadata.Description: Uzbekistan Presidential Resolution PQ-358 (14 Oct 2024) setting AI development goals including training 1 million specialists and AI use in education/healthcare.

summary: Uzbekistan’s Presidential Resolution PQ-358 (2024) approves a national strategy for developing AI technologies through 2030. Its stated goals include training AI specialists and other workers, expanding programming education in secondary schools, establishing university laboratories, and offering free online courses with foreign experts. The strategy also promotes AI applications in sectors such as education and healthcare, alongside regulatory and infrastructure development. It sets broad national priorities, but the available evidence does not detail how the learning activities are delivered or their actual reach.
pedagogicalSummary: The inspected page is a presidential resolution approving Uzbekistan’s AI development strategy, not an instructional resource. The accessible text does not establish how learning is organised or identify teaching methods such as project-based, experiential, or instructor-led learning. Although the initiative includes specialist training, that goal alone does not show how it is taught. Because the page’s full text could not be inspected, this is a lack of accessible evidence about pedagogy, not confirmation that the strategy contains no learning activities. Source: https://lex.uz/en/docs/7159258
prioritySummary: The strategy’s stated emphasis is developing AI technologies in Uzbekistan through 2030. The supplied description of the resolution identifies training one million specialists and promoting AI use in education and healthcare as goals. This points to both building AI-related skills and applying AI in public-service sectors, but the inspected material does not establish a more specific hierarchy or describe the intended beneficiaries in detail. Source: https://lex.uz/en/docs/7159258
educationalTechnologySummary: The accessible page identifies a national AI development strategy, but does not provide enough readable detail to name educational platforms, software, hardware, or learning technologies developed or used by the initiative. Its stated aim to promote AI use in education is a policy priority, not evidence by itself of a particular educational technology or how one supports learning. The page itself is a legal information page, not an identified learning tool. The full document was not available for detailed inspection, so the absence of named tools here should not be taken as confirmation that none are specified elsewhere in the strategy. Source: https://lex.uz/en/docs/7159258

inclusion.reason: The initiative includes explicit AI literacy elements through its detailed educational program targeting students and professionals. It qualifies under the inclusion route as it is issued and mandated by a national government (Uzbekistan President via Presidential Resolution PQ-358, 2024), meeting the requirement for government endorsement or mandate.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: European School Education Platform – course "Developing students' AI literacy"
metadata.Description: Online course for teachers comparing AI-literacy frameworks and showing how to integrate and assess students' AI literacy across subjects (course date 20 April 2026).

summary: The European Commission’s European School Education Platform offers a 15–20-hour self-paced online course for teachers, school leaders and teacher educators working in primary and secondary education. It explores AI literacy and compares relevant frameworks, with attention to ethical, social and emotional dimensions of AI. Participants apply these ideas to curriculum mapping, integrating AI literacy across subjects, and planning how to assess students’ learning. The course uses independent activities and self-assessment; forums and Padlet contributions are optional and unmoderated.
pedagogicalSummary: The course supports teachers through a self-paced online format, with content and activities that learners can complete independently over an estimated 15–20 hours. Its stated learning sequence includes exploring AI literacy and its connections to other literacies, comparing and analysing AI-literacy frameworks, considering ethical, social and emotional dimensions, and applying the ideas to curriculum mapping and action planning. Participants are encouraged to reflect and assess their own work against provided criteria. The current version has no live sessions, deadlines or required meetings; forums and Padlet contributions are unmoderated. The page notes that an earlier version included scheduled discussions and peer reviews, but does not describe those as part of this self-directed version. Evidence: https://school-education.ec.europa.eu/en/learn/courses/developing-students-ai-literacy
prioritySummary: The course principally aims to equip teachers, school leaders and teacher educators to develop students’ AI literacy through teaching and curriculum design. It emphasizes understanding the knowledge, skills and attitudes students need to engage meaningfully and responsibly with AI, and helping educators integrate and assess these competencies across school subjects. The page also gives explicit weight to ethical, social and emotional dimensions, including AI’s effects on learners’ experiences, wellbeing and society, and calls for responsible, human-centric teaching. These emphases are presented together; the inspected page does not establish a single priority that overrides the others. The course is aimed at primary and secondary school education. Evidence: https://school-education.ec.europa.eu/en/learn/courses/developing-students-ai-literacy
educationalTechnologySummary: The page identifies an online course delivered through the European School Education Platform, with course materials and activities for self-paced learning. It also names forum discussions and Padlet contributions as participation options in the current version, although these are unmoderated; self-assessment uses criteria provided in the course. The page does not identify a particular AI system, classroom software, or hardware used to teach AI literacy, nor does it indicate that the initiative develops an educational technology. The technologies evidenced are therefore learning-delivery and participation tools, rather than AI products being taught or practiced with. The page does not provide further technical detail about the platform or Padlet’s role in individual activities. Evidence: https://school-education.ec.europa.eu/en/learn/courses/developing-students-ai-literacy

inclusion.reason: The initiative meets the AI-literacy requirement because its core purpose is to provide educational content and learning objectives explicitly about AI literacy (definition, frameworks, ethical dimensions, integration across subjects). It qualifies for inclusion via the first inclusion route: it is issued by an intergovernmental body (the European Commission), which falls under "issued by an intergovernmental body". No exclusion criteria apply.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: Better Internet for Kids – resource directory (AI-related guides from Safer Internet Centres)
metadata.Description: EU portal collecting guides, posters and videos from national Safer Internet Centres, including AI-related items such as the German centre's brochure 'My child and AI' (2 April 2026).

summary: Better Internet for Kids’ resource directory is an EU-wide catalogue of educational materials from national Safer Internet Centres, including guides, posters, videos, toolkits and campaigns for children and young people, parents and educators. Its resources cover a range of online safety topics; AI-related examples include guidance for parents on children’s interactions with AI chatbots and companions. The directory supports resource-based learning but does not prescribe a shared teaching method, and its overall focus is broader digital safety rather than AI alone.
pedagogicalSummary: The inspected pages show a mix of self-paced and facilitated learning rather than one single method. The teacher and parent learning corners offer modules with information, suggested activities and resources for learners to use at their own pace, alongside deeper topic sessions and webinars. The teacher corner also lists MOOCs and quizzes; the children’s corner offers interactive, age-tailored materials and quizzes. The resource directory gathers guides, videos and other educational materials from national Safer Internet Centres, but does not prescribe a common teaching method. The evidence supports practical, resource-based learning and guided exploration; it does not establish how the listed AI resources are taught in practice. (https://better-internet-for-kids.europa.eu/en/learning-corner/teachers-educators; https://better-internet-for-kids.europa.eu/en/learning-corner/parents-caregivers; https://better-internet-for-kids.europa.eu/en/learning-corner/children-youth; https://better-internet-for-kids.europa.eu/en/resources/resource-directory)
prioritySummary: The initiative’s stated emphasis is helping children and young people navigate the digital world safely and develop skills to participate online, with parents, caregivers and educators supported to guide them. The portal presents online experiences in terms of both risks and opportunities, and the directory brings together resources intended to help these audiences discover the online world safely. In the AI-related evidence inspected, the German guide “My child and AI” is framed around parents accompanying children as AI becomes part of family life, including everyday and emotional contexts. The pages therefore support a child-safety and digital-literacy emphasis, with adult guidance as a complementary priority; they do not establish a separate AI workforce-upskilling goal. (https://better-internet-for-kids.europa.eu/en/learning-corner/children-youth; https://better-internet-for-kids.europa.eu/en/learning-corner/parents-caregivers; https://better-internet-for-kids.europa.eu/en/resources/resource-directory?search_api_fulltext=My%20child%20and%20AI)
educationalTechnologySummary: The inspected pages identify educational formats and one named learning game, but no dedicated AI-literacy platform, AI teaching software or hardware. BIK’s children’s corner describes interactive materials and quizzes, and names Happy Onlife as a game for learning about online safety and internet use. The teacher corner says BIK has produced MOOCs and provides quizzes, modules and webinars; the directory aggregates guides, videos, toolkits and other resources developed by Safer Internet Centres. These are learning supports, not evidence that the initiative uses AI tools to teach AI literacy. Although the directory includes AI-related resources, the inspected material does not identify a specific technology used to deliver those resources or describe an AI-specific educational technology.
