metadata.Initiative / Programme: AI2PI – Erasmus+ Teacher Academy coordinated by Humboldt-Universität zu Berlin (2025–2028)
metadata.Description: Teacher Academy (budget about €1.5m; partners incl. DFKI and the municipality of Salo) piloting with 1,000+ teachers, building open educational resources and policy recommendations; milestones include an AI literacy competency framework (Feb 2026) and piloted course modules (Mar 2027).

summary: AI2PI is a 2025–2028 Erasmus+ Teacher Academy coordinated by Humboldt-Universität zu Berlin with European partners. It supports pre-service and in-service teachers and teacher educators in developing the knowledge and judgment to assess AI tools and make informed, ethical and equitable decisions about their use in teaching. Through design-based research and practical, reflective workshops, the project is developing an AI literacy competency framework, blended training modules and open educational resources, alongside policy recommendations. Its planned work includes piloting across seven European countries with more than 1,000 teachers.
pedagogicalSummary: AI2PI describes a developing teacher-learning programme rather than a single teaching method. Accessible workshop reports show hands-on and problem-based activities: participants compare analogue and AI-supported ways of solving a task, try AI for text-related lesson preparation, and discuss the outputs’ usefulness, limitations, reliability, and ethical implications. Workshops use collective sharing and guided reflection to connect experience with professional judgment. The project also plans competence-based training modules, blended learning, and international communities of practice; its project-wide design-based research process includes piloting, but this is a development methodology rather than a classroom pedagogy. The reports provide examples, not a full account of the planned courses. (https://www2.hu-berlin.de/ai2pi/blog/ai2pi-portuguese-week-of-science; https://www2.hu-berlin.de/ai2pi/blog/digiday-tyrol-2026; https://www2.hu-berlin.de/ai2pi/; https://www2.hu-berlin.de/ai2pi/project-info)
prioritySummary: AI2PI’s central emphasis is developing educators’ capacity to engage critically and ethically with AI in teaching, rather than promoting adoption of particular AI products. It targets pre-service and in-service teachers and teacher educators, including teachers in primary and secondary education across seven European countries. The initiative aims to support informed pedagogical decisions, evaluation of AI tools and their effects, and responsible, equitable use in ways intended to benefit students as well as educators. Its stated outcomes also include teacher confidence, ongoing professional development, international communities of pedagogical practice, and resilience of the teaching profession. The inspected pages establish these linked priorities but do not indicate that one is more important than the others beyond the overarching focus on teacher capacity for critical AI engagement. (https://www2.hu-berlin.de/ai2pi/project-info; https://www2.hu-berlin.de/ai2pi/; https://www2.hu-berlin.de/ai2pi/teachers)
educationalTechnologySummary: The inspected pages do not identify a named AI product, learning platform, or hardware developed by AI2PI. Reports describe workshop participants trying generic generative AI tools for problem-solving and text-related teaching tasks, so AI tools are used as objects of practical exploration and critical evaluation; the reports do not specify which tools. One workshop used an online collaborative platform to share results, but does not name it. AI2PI says it is developing blended learning modules and an “AI2PI learning infrastructure,” and plans open educational resources, but the inspected material does not specify their technical form or platform, so these are planned learning supports rather than identifiable technologies. The teacher survey is a research instrument, not evidence of an educational technology used for instruction. (https://www2.hu-berlin.de/ai2pi/blog/ai2pi-portuguese-week-of-science; https://www2.hu-berlin.de/ai2pi/blog/digiday-tyrol-2026; https://www2.hu-berlin.de/ai2pi/project-info; https://www2.hu-berlin.de/ai2pi/teachers)

inclusion.reason: The initiative includes explicit AI literacy elements: developing an AI literacy competency framework by Feb 2026 and piloted course modules by Mar 2027 focused on teaching teachers to evaluate AI tools' quality/impact, promote reflective thinking, adapt to evolving AI roles, and ensure ethical/equitable use. It satisfies the inclusion route as it is officially funded by the European Union (Erasmus+ programme) via EACEA, with budget ~€1.5m.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: AIDEA – AI-Driven Educators Academy (Erasmus+ Teacher Academy, 2026–2028)
metadata.Description: Consortium from eight countries building a modular European training curriculum for AI in teacher education plus open resources; aims for pilots in 150+ schools and 3,000+ trained teachers, organised around teaching about AI, teaching with AI and related dimensions.

summary: AIDEA (AI-Driven Educators Academy) is an EU-funded consortium project involving partners from eight countries. It is developing a modular professional-learning programme for teachers, alongside resources for school learners and guidance for education systems. Its framework covers teaching about AI, using AI in teaching, and preparing learners for an AI-shaped future, with attention to ethical and inclusive practice. The project describes reflective, inquiry-based and collaborative approaches and plans open classroom resources and an AI-supported learning platform. Training modules remain forthcoming; stated goals include pilots in 150+ schools and training 3,000+ teachers, and a related workshop series has trained more than 220 education executives in Cyprus.
pedagogicalSummary: AIDEA describes a modular teacher-training framework that combines theory with hands-on application across teaching about AI, teaching with AI and preparing learners for an AI-shaped future. Its stated methods include reflective, inquiry-based and collaborative learning, supported by open lesson plans and classroom activities; it also emphasizes inclusive and multilingual approaches. A reported example of delivery is face-to-face workshops for education executives, while focus groups with educators informed the project’s design. These pages describe intended approaches more fully than the forthcoming training modules themselves, which are not yet available in the inspected site. Sources: https://aideaacademy.eu/ and https://aideaacademy.eu/aims-of-the-project/ and https://aideaacademy.eu/cpi-trains-ministry-of-education-executives-on-artificial-intelligence/ and https://aideaacademy.eu/mapping-ai-education-needs-across-europe-focus-group-highlights/
prioritySummary: The initiative principally aims to strengthen educators’ capacity to understand AI and integrate it responsibly and pedagogically into education. Teachers are the central intended beneficiaries, with school leaders and education systems also in scope; the framework addresses AI literacy and ethical awareness, practical classroom uses such as assessment and adaptive learning, and preparing students for an AI-mediated future. A reported national training series reached more than 220 Ministry of Education executives in Cyprus, illustrating an additional capacity-building focus beyond classroom teachers. The site also highlights inclusion, privacy and cross-cultural or multilingual needs, rather than presenting workforce preparation as its sole purpose. The training modules remain forthcoming, so the precise balance among these priorities is not yet demonstrated. Sources: https://aideaacademy.eu/aims-of-the-project/ and https://aideaacademy.eu/ and https://aideaacademy.eu/cpi-trains-ministry-of-education-executives-on-artificial-intelligence/
educationalTechnologySummary: AIDEA says it plans to develop an accessible learning platform with AI-driven functions, personalized recommendations, progress tracking and adaptive learning; the home page describes these as planned rather than as an already available learning service. It also refers to classroom resources and AI application tools, but the inspected pages do not name specific classroom software or hardware or explain how particular tools are used in lessons. AIDEA’s YouTube channel hosts an introductory project video, created with support from NotebookLM; the page presents NotebookLM as assisting production of that explanatory video, not as a learning platform used by trainees. The Learning Hub and training-module links currently lead to a “coming soon” page, so evidence about deployed educational technologies is limited. Sources: https://aideaacademy.eu/ and https://aideaacademy.eu/our-first-aidea-video-is-now-live-on-youtube/ and https://aideaacademy.eu/coming-soon/

inclusion.reason: The initiative includes clear AI literacy objectives (teaching about, with, and for AI) as stated on the Results page. It is funded by the European Union via Erasmus+, satisfying the inclusion route for intergovernmental endorsement. The project has a defined scale (150+ schools, 3,000+ teachers), moving beyond a single-institution project. Uncertainty remains only regarding the exact curriculum content as the 'Training Modules' page is currently marked as coming soon, but this does not affect the inclusion decision based on the confirmed funding and stated literacy goals.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: AI-DL – Data Literacy in the Age of AI for Education (Erasmus+, 2025–2027)
metadata.Description: Builds on AI4T to foster data literacy and critical thinking among teachers and pupils when using generative AI; teachers co-create training modules and a teacher competence framework to be piloted in schools from January 2027.

summary: AI-DL is a 2025–2027 Erasmus+ project focused on data literacy in the age of generative AI, particularly in secondary schools. Teachers, school leaders and students are involved in co-designing and testing classroom scenarios, while the project develops a teacher competence framework, training pathway and educational resources. Its collaborative, cross-curricular approach uses generative AI as a prompt for examining data, AI outputs, reliability, bias, privacy and responsible use. School-based experimentation is planned in 40 schools across seven countries, with findings also intended to inform education policy.
pedagogicalSummary: AI-DL describes a collaborative, cross-curricular and experimentation-based approach rather than a single classroom method. Teachers, school leaders and sometimes students work in school Communities of Practice to co-design and review scenarios, training content and materials; teachers are then expected to test activities with students, reflect on results and feed back into revisions. The planned pathway moves from diagnosis and content design to school-based experimentation and evaluation. Learning is intended to use meaningful classroom contexts and real-world examples, with generative AI prompting learners to examine data, outputs and assumptions. This evidence supports collaborative professional learning, practical inquiry and reflection, but does not establish a fixed lesson format. The training kit and implementation are still being developed. (https://www.aidlproject.eu/about-ai-dl/; https://www.aidlproject.eu/communities-of-practice-working-together-across-the-school/)
prioritySummary: AI-DL’s central emphasis is strengthening data literacy in secondary-school communities—especially teachers’ capacity to help students understand and critically evaluate how data and generative-AI outputs are produced and used. It aims to foster critical thinking, responsible use, ethical reflection and democratic participation, treating GenAI as an opportunity to develop these competences rather than as an end in itself. Schools, teachers and students are the direct beneficiaries: participating schools help shape the approach, and students are to learn to question AI-supported information and make informed decisions. The initiative also serves education ministries and policymakers by producing evidence, guidance and recommendations to support wider adoption. The inspected pages present these educational and civic aims together, without establishing a strict hierarchy among them. (https://www.aidlproject.eu/about-ai-dl/; https://www.aidlproject.eu/diagnosis/)
educationalTechnologySummary: The inspected pages identify generative AI as a technology used in the initiative’s educational approach: it is framed as a classroom trigger for learning about data, and planned activities will have teachers and students examine AI outputs, reliability, bias, privacy and responsible use. The pages do not name a particular GenAI product, software platform or hardware, nor do they describe AI-DL as developing an AI system or educational-technology product. Its stated outputs are instead a competence framework, teacher training modules or kit, classroom activities and teaching resources. These are educational materials, not evidence of a distinct digital technology. Although the project uses a website and LinkedIn for information and outreach, the inspected evidence does not establish them as tools used to deliver AI-literacy learning. (https://www.aidlproject.eu/about-ai-dl/; https://www.aidlproject.eu/communities-of-practice-working-together-across-the-school/; https://www.aidlproject.eu/resources/)

inclusion.reason: The initiative includes clear AI literacy elements: it teaches teachers and students how to use Generative AI as a tool for developing data literacy, critical thinking, and democratic competences. It is funded by the European Union under Erasmus+, satisfying the inclusion route of government/intergovernmental funding. The project offers educational content (training pathway, ready-to-use materials, competence framework) that explains how to use AI in education. No exclusion criteria apply.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: FLAIR – Fostering Learners' AI Readiness (Erasmus+, 2024–2026)
metadata.Description: Six-university consortium supporting teachers to convey AI literacy and developing self-learning tools for students; three work packages, running October 2024 to November 2026.

summary: FLAIR (Fostering Learners’ AI Readiness) is a 2024–2026 Erasmus+ collaboration among six universities focused on AI literacy in higher education. It supports educators in teaching AI literacy and develops learning activities and self-learning tools for students. Its framework and materials address understanding and applying AI, as well as topics including ethics, privacy, societal impacts, data and media literacy, and academic integrity. The project also publishes reports on AI competence frameworks and higher-education policies.
pedagogicalSummary: The accessible project description presents FLAIR as a six-university collaboration focused on fostering learners’ AI readiness. The initiative description indicates that it supports teachers in conveying AI literacy and develops self-learning tools for students, suggesting both teacher-supported learning and opportunities for independent study. However, the inspected material does not establish a specific teaching method, lesson structure, assessment approach, or classroom format. These broad learning arrangements should not be taken as evidence of a particular pedagogy. (https://www.wu.ac.at/en/flair/flair-erasmus-project)
prioritySummary: FLAIR’s stated emphasis is fostering learners’ AI readiness. The project description points to teachers and students as beneficiaries: teachers are supported to convey AI literacy, while students are intended to benefit from self-learning tools. The accessible evidence does not establish a further priority, such as workforce upskilling, individual well-being, or a particular societal outcome, nor does it justify ranking the teacher and student components. (https://www.wu.ac.at/en/flair/flair-erasmus-project)
educationalTechnologySummary: The project description indicates that FLAIR is developing self-learning tools for students to support AI-literacy learning. The inspected material does not identify their names, format, platform, features, or whether any particular software or hardware is used, so it is not possible to characterize them more specifically. No other educational technology is identified in the accessible evidence; AI itself is the subject of learning, not evidence of a teaching technology. (https://www.wu.ac.at/en/flair/flair-erasmus-project)

inclusion.reason: The project’s AI-readiness focus and educational materials indicate AI literacy. Its Erasmus+ project framing suggests a connection to an EU intergovernmental programme, but the page evidence available here does not establish whether the EU issued the initiative or the extent of its funding or wider adoption. metadata.Initiative / Programme: ArInLi – Artificial Intelligence Literacy as an essential digital competency (Erasmus+ KA210)
metadata.Description: School-based project in four partner schools with university partners (Sept 2024–Apr 2026) training teachers, students and families in ethical and critical AI use; outputs include a pedagogical book and a website listing recommended AI tools.

summary: ArInLi is an Erasmus+ project building AI literacy in four European secondary schools, with teachers, students and families as its audiences. It integrates ethical and critical AI use into regular teaching across Spanish, English, Philosophy and Robotics, combining hands-on workshops and university seminars with experiential and cooperative learning. A Train the Trainer approach supports teacher development, while project resources include an e-book, teacher’s guide, evaluated AI-app catalogue, podcast and videos for use by schools.
pedagogicalSummary: The initiative describes a structured, practice-oriented approach: hands-on workshops and university seminars are combined with Kolb’s Experiential Learning cycle and Johnson & Johnson’s cooperative-learning model. Students work in mandatory multinational teams, with linguistic and cultural diversity treated as a learning resource. AI is integrated into the regular curriculum across Spanish Language, English, Philosophy and Robotics, with specific assessment rubrics, rather than confined to extracurricular workshops. A Train the Trainer model extends learning through coordinators to teachers and students. The inspected page identifies these approaches but gives limited detail about individual lesson activities or how learning differs for families. (https://digital-skills-jobs.europa.eu/en/impact-shapers/good-practices/essential-digital-competency-ai-literacy)
prioritySummary: ArInLi principally aims to build AI literacy across school communities—teachers, students and families—so they can engage with AI critically and ethically. The page frames this as addressing educators’ lack of preparation, students’ use of AI without understanding its implications, and families’ limited awareness of risks and opportunities. Equity and inclusion are also explicit priorities: the project works in vulnerable urban and rural contexts and stresses access to high-quality AI education regardless of socioeconomic background. It also seeks durable adoption by integrating AI into ordinary curricula and sharing resources with other schools. The page identifies these aims but does not establish a single priority as more important than the others. (https://digital-skills-jobs.europa.eu/en/impact-shapers/good-practices/essential-digital-competency-ai-literacy)
educationalTechnologySummary: The inspected page names no specific AI software, platform or hardware used for instruction. It says the project provides a multilingual website, an 82-page e-book, a teacher’s guide, a catalogue of 153 evaluated AI apps, an AI-generated podcast and YouTube videos; these are described as freely accessible learning resources, but the page does not specify their platforms or explain how each is used in teaching. The catalogue suggests that AI apps are evaluated for schools, while the page also refers generally to students learning about AI tools and to industry examples, without naming products. Thus, the available evidence supports identifying created or shared digital resources, but not particular educational technologies used or developed beyond those descriptions. (https://digital-skills-jobs.europa.eu/en/impact-shapers/good-practices/essential-digital-competency-ai-literacy)

summary: AIware is an Erasmus+ project developing resources to help secondary schools and teachers teach about artificial intelligence. Its planned outputs include a model curriculum, learning scenarios and teaching materials, along with an “AI schools” certification scheme and policy and curriculum recommendations for education authorities. The available description does not specify teaching methods or educational technologies, or establish how widely the resources have been adopted.

The article’s broader discussion of AI in education should not be taken as evidence that AIware itself uses a particular teaching method. metadata.Initiative / Programme: MachineLearnAthon – challenge-based machine-learning learning concept and tool list (TU Dortmund and partners)
metadata.Description: Erasmus+ (KA220-HED) higher-education concept for teaching applied machine learning through challenges; the tool list recommends a no-code route (Orange Data Mining) or Python, Jupyter and Colab depending on experience. Tool list updated several times in Jan–Mar 2026.

summary: MachineLearnAthon is an Erasmus+-funded, challenge-based applied machine-learning learning concept coordinated by TU Dortmund with partner organisations. Its materials are intended to support integration into school and university curricula. The tool list offers differentiated routes for learners: visual, no-code workflows in Orange Data Mining, or programming with Python and tools such as Jupyter and Google Colab, with optional environments for larger or reproducible projects. It supports hands-on work with ML workflows, though this resource does not detail the full teaching sequence or assessment.
pedagogicalSummary: The tool list supports differentiated, hands-on learning in machine learning, offering routes for participants with different levels of coding experience. Beginners or those avoiding code can build and visualize workflows by connecting components in Orange Data Mining; learners seeking programming skills can use Python, with Jupyter described as supporting exploratory analysis and step-by-step learning. Google Colab is suggested for quick prototyping or team collaboration, while Docker is optional for more advanced work on reproducibility and production-oriented workflows. The document refers to tutorials and challenges but does not explain their structure, assessment, facilitation, or a full teaching sequence, so the precise challenge-based pedagogy cannot be established from this resource alone. (https://dss.lfo.tu-dortmund.de/wp-content/uploads/2026/03/MachineLearnAthon-Tool-List.pdf)
prioritySummary: The clearest priority in the tool list is enabling participants with varied technical backgrounds and learning goals to engage with applied machine learning, from exploring concepts without coding to developing Python skills and more advanced workflow practices. The document presents tools for preprocessing, training, evaluating, and visualizing models, and describes Python as valuable for future career development because of its use in academia and industry. It also notes industry-relevant practices such as deployment and reproducibility for advanced learners. This suggests both accessible ML learning and preparation for further technical or professional work, but the document does not establish a hierarchy among these aims or specify a broader beneficiary group beyond MachineLearnAthon participants. (https://dss.lfo.tu-dortmund.de/wp-content/uploads/2026/03/MachineLearnAthon-Tool-List.pdf)
educationalTechnologySummary: The document recommends a set of third-party tools and environments rather than identifying a proprietary learning platform developed by the initiative. Orange Data Mining provides a visual, no-code way to assemble and inspect ML workflows. For coding-based work, it recommends Python and libraries including scikit-learn, pandas, and numpy; Jupyter notebooks combine code, text, and visualizations for experimentation, while Google Colab offers browser-based Python execution and sharing for collaboration and challenge prototyping. Visual Studio Code is suggested for larger projects, and Docker is optional for isolated, reproducible workflows and production-readiness examples. The tool list describes these technologies as learning and development environments, but does not document how they are integrated into specific lessons. (https://dss.lfo.tu-dortmund.de/wp-content/uploads/2026/03/MachineLearnAthon-Tool-List.pdf)

inclusion.reason: AI-literacy requirement met: the document provides educational content about machine learning tools, explains their purposes and pros/cons, and guides users on which to choose based on experience level. Inclusion route met: the initiative is partially funded by an Erasmus+ grant (KA220-HED) from the European Union, which qualifies as intergovernmental funding per the inclusion criteria. The tool list is part of a structured higher-education concept, not a single-institution course without wider reach.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: eCraft2Learn – digital fabrication and maker learning ecosystem (H2020, GA 731345)
metadata.Description: Horizon 2020 project that researched, designed, piloted and validated a learning ecosystem for making computer-supported artefacts, for 13–17 year-olds and their teachers in formal and informal STEAM learning. Includes open resources on electronics, 3D printing and AI programming; consortium of universities, SMEs and Arduino/Ultimaker (incl. UEF, Oxford, Padua, SYNYO).

summary: eCraft2Learn was an EU-funded research project that developed and piloted an open digital-fabrication and maker-learning ecosystem for learners aged 13–17 and their teachers in formal and informal STEAM settings. Its resources and tools support electronics, programming, 3D design and printing, and AI programming, with AI presented as one part of a broader focus on making. The approach emphasizes constructivist, project-based learning through planning, iterative design, experimentation, reflection, and sharing; the ecosystem also includes teacher guides and learning analytics.
pedagogicalSummary: eCraft2Learn explicitly uses constructivist “learning by making,” linked to DIY, craft-based and project-based STEAM learning. Its described sequence starts with learners exploring an idea, then planning resources, brainstorming and making through iterative design, trial and error, and reflection, before sharing projects with an open community. The initiative also identifies communication and collaboration, teacher support, and personalised learning as parts of the ecosystem. These are pedagogical approaches, distinct from the fabrication technologies used. The inspected pages mention AI programming resources but do not describe a separate AI-literacy teaching method or its activities in detail. (https://project.ecraft2learn.eu/project-overview/; https://project.ecraft2learn.eu/)
prioritySummary: The initiative principally aims to support young people and their teachers or instructors in engaging, personalised STEAM learning through digital fabrication and making. It targets learners aged 13–17 and describes benefits including creativity, problem-solving, collaboration and broader 21st-century skills; it also connects these goals to inclusion and employability for EU youth. The site presents a wider ambition to make making technologies valuable and accessible beyond a narrow group of technically oriented or “talented” learners, and mentions teacher support and industry-academy collaboration. AI literacy appears as one resource area within this broader maker-learning initiative, not as the stated central priority. (https://project.ecraft2learn.eu/; https://project.ecraft2learn.eu/project-overview/; https://project.ecraft2learn.eu/introducing-ecraft2learn/)
educationalTechnologySummary: The project describes a developed Unified User Interface (UUI) that serves as a gateway to learning tools, resources and project stages, with a teacher-facing learning-analytics interface for viewing learner progress. The UUI lists an “A.I.” resource area, and the project site says open resources include AI programming, but the inspected pages do not identify a specific AI-learning application or explain that area’s activities. For the broader making ecosystem, the UUI integrates or links to existing tools including Tinkercad for 3D and circuit design, Beetle Blocks, Snap!, Arduino IDE and Cura, alongside Arduino and Raspberry Pi hardware. These technologies support project planning, programming, electronics and fabrication; they should not be mistaken for evidence of a particular AI tool. (https://project.ecraft2learn.eu/; https://ecraft2learn.github.io/uui/; https://ecraft2learn.github.io/learning-analytics/)

inclusion.reason: The initiative includes clear AI literacy: it offers educational resources on 'AI programming' and use cases designed to help teachers and students make computer-supported artefacts with AI tools. Crucially, the project is funded by the European Union’s Horizon 2020 programme (Grant Agreement 731345), which satisfies the inclusion route of being endorsed/funded by a national or sub-national government equivalent (EU-wide) per the screening criteria. The site confirms EU-wide scope and Horizon 2020 grant, meeting the required government involvement criterion.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: Google AI Educator Series and open-model (Gemma) tools for African educators
metadata.Description: Free Google AI Educator Series expanding to Sub-Saharan Africa, starting with South Africa (with SACE) and planned for Nigeria, Kenya and Ghana in 2027; Fab AI to lead local innovators building bespoke literacy tools on open Gemma models.

summary: Google’s initiative brings the free Google AI Educator Series to Sub-Saharan Africa, beginning in South Africa with the South African Council for Educators and with expansion to Nigeria, Kenya and Ghana planned for 2027. It offers teachers practical, responsible AI learning through virtual and in-person sessions, with micro-credentials and continued learning. In a separate planned effort, Fab AI will lead local innovators in developing Gemma-based tools for lesson planning, assessment and teacher coaching, adapted to local languages and curricula. Teachers are the main direct audience, with students expected to benefit from the tools; the announcement describes an initial target of up to 500 teachers and 15,000 students.
pedagogicalSummary: The initiative combines professional learning for teachers with development of tools intended to support classroom practice. The Google AI Educator Series is described as designed by educators for educators, delivered through virtual and in-person sessions, and focused on practical, responsible ways to use AI for lesson preparation, administrative tasks, and adapting instruction. Micro-credentials and continued learning with local partners are intended to help teachers apply skills in practice. The linked series page also describes short, flexible learning sessions and self-paced or instructor-led options. Separately, planned tools include support for curriculum-aligned lesson planning, diagnostic feedback and assessment, and practice-based teacher coaching. These details indicate practical, educator-focused learning and support, but the inspected announcement does not specify a detailed teaching method or classroom lesson sequence (https://blog.google/intl/en-africa/company-news/outreach-and-initiatives/empowering-educators-and-learners-in-sub-saharan-africa-2026/; https://edu.google.com/learning-center/google-ai-educator-series/).
prioritySummary: The stated emphasis is strengthening foundational learning by equipping teachers and supporting students, particularly in resource-constrained classrooms in Sub-Saharan Africa. The initiative plans to prepare teachers to use AI confidently and responsibly, while local innovators develop tools for lesson planning, assessment and feedback, and teacher coaching. The announcement stresses adapting tools to local languages and national curricula and making them usable on low-cost devices. It also describes equitable access, local innovation, and potential scale—from an initial phase targeting up to 500 teachers and 15,000 students to a possible future reach of over two million learners. The evidence supports both educator capacity-building and improved learning support for children; it does not establish a single priority that overrides the other (https://blog.google/intl/en-africa/company-news/outreach-and-initiatives/empowering-educators-and-learners-in-sub-saharan-africa-2026/).
educationalTechnologySummary: The announcement says local innovators, led by Fab AI, will develop bespoke educational AI tools using open Gemma models; Google DeepMind will provide compute credits and technical expertise. The planned tools are intended to assist teachers with curriculum-aligned lesson planning, diagnostic feedback and assessment, and practice-based coaching. The announcement describes small language models as suitable for low-cost devices and adaptable to local languages and curricula, but does not name specific finished tools, devices, or software platforms. The Google AI Educator Series is delivered virtually and in person; its linked page describes online learning and identifies Gemini and Gemini Notebook as tools used in practical training. The inspected material does not clarify which tools will be available in the regional delivery or whether the planned Gemma-based tools are already in use (https://blog.google/intl/en-africa/company-news/outreach-and-initiatives/empowering-educators-and-learners-in-sub-saharan-africa-2026/; https://edu.google.com/learning-center/google-ai-educator-series/).

inclusion.reason: The initiative provides AI literacy through the Google AI Educator Series, which offers educational content and guidance on how to use AI. It has formal endorsement from a statutory body, evidenced by the partnership with the South African Council for Educators (SACE), fulfilling an inclusion route related to government or statutory body support. The planned expansion across multiple countries also suggests system-scale adoption potential.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: Elements of AI (University of Helsinki & MinnaLearn)
metadata.Description: Free online introductory AI course launched in 2018; 1 million+ sign-ups from 170 countries; ~40% women participants; offered in several languages and via partners (e.g. University of Luxembourg); 2 ECTS available in Finland.

summary: Elements of AI is a free, self-paced online initiative developed by the University of Helsinki and MinnaLearn for non-experts and people seeking AI skills for work. Its courses combine explanations and interactive exercises to cover AI concepts, capabilities and limitations, practical applications, and societal and ethical issues. The introductory course requires no advanced mathematics or programming, while Building AI offers activities at different levels, including Python programming and developing an AI idea. The courses are available in several languages; the initiative reports more than one million sign-ups from 170 countries, and 2 ECTS credits are available in Finland.
pedagogicalSummary: Learning is organised as flexible, self-paced online courses that combine explanatory material with exercises. “Introduction to AI” progresses through topics from AI definitions and problem-solving to machine learning, neural networks, and societal implications, with exercises in each chapter; it is presented as accessible without advanced mathematics or programming. “Building AI” offers three difficulty levels, ranging from multiple-choice exercises to Python programming, and culminates in developing an AI idea to present to the community. The initiative therefore supports both introductory conceptual learning and more practical, graduated work. The accessible pages also point learners to an online community and student support, though they do not establish how much direct instructor-led teaching occurs. Sources: https://course.elementsofai.com/ ; https://buildingai.elementsofai.com/ ; https://www.elementsofai.com/
prioritySummary: The initiative’s central emphasis is broad public AI literacy: helping people from varied backgrounds understand what AI is, what it can and cannot do, how it is created, and how it may affect society and their lives. Its stated goal is to demystify AI and help people feel empowered rather than threatened, with free courses designed for non-experts and no advanced mathematics or programming prerequisite for the introductory course. The site also presents a distinct workplace priority: helping employees and organizations develop confident, safe and responsible AI use, including training described as mapped to the EU AI Act. The evidence supports both broad public education and workforce readiness; it does not establish that one supersedes the other across the initiative. Sources: https://www.elementsofai.com/ ; https://course.elementsofai.com/
educationalTechnologySummary: The initiative provides its learning through online course platforms for “Introduction to AI” and “Building AI,” with course chapters, sections and exercises accessible online; the site describes the courses as free and self-paced. Building AI’s exercises can range from multiple-choice work to Python programming, but Python is presented as a course activity rather than a platform developed by the initiative. An online community is also linked as a place for learners to interact and share an AI idea, and the FAQ directs learners there for interaction and support. The inspected pages do not identify particular learning-management software, hardware, or AI-powered tutoring tools. The initiative mentions services for delivering training through an LMS, but the inspected material does not specify the underlying technology. Sources: https://course.elementsofai.com/ ; https://buildingai.elementsofai.com/ ; https://community.elementsofai.com/ ; https://www.elementsofai.com/faq

inclusion.reason: The initiative includes clear AI literacy through structured educational content, learning objectives explaining how AI functions (e.g., training models, data, algorithms), and interactive exercises teaching practical AI concepts. It qualifies for inclusion via government route: it is formally supported in Finland by the University of Helsinki (a national public university) with ECTS credits offered within Finland's education system. The massive scale (>1M sign-ups from 170 countries) also supports system-scale adoption.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: Experience AI (Raspberry Pi Foundation & Google DeepMind)
metadata.Description: Free AI literacy programme with classroom resources and educator training via local partners. Resources used in 195+ countries and 22 languages; 50,000+ educators trained (RPF figures). Expansions announced for Latin America (to 2028) and Australia/Aotearoa NZ; UNESCO King Hamad Prize laureate 2025.

summary: Experience AI is a free AI literacy programme developed by the Raspberry Pi Foundation and Google DeepMind for young people, particularly secondary-school learners, and the educators who teach them. Delivered with local partners, it provides teacher-led lessons, classroom materials and educator training, alongside a free online course for teachers. Lessons combine hands-on activities and foundational learning about AI and data with critical consideration of AI’s benefits, risks, societal effects and responsible use. The programme reports resources in use across more than 195 countries and 22 languages, and more than 50,000 educators trained.
pedagogicalSummary: Experience AI supports teacher-led learning through structured, ready-to-use lessons, with educator training intended to build confidence and help teachers deliver them. The lessons include plans, slides, worksheets, videos, and hands-on activities; they use relatable AI applications and are intended for secondary classrooms, with possible use in coding clubs and other settings. Learning combines foundational understanding of how AI and data work with critical consideration of AI’s benefits, risks, social effects, and responsible use. The initiative also describes a train-the-trainer model through local partners, and offers educators a free three-week online course that includes trying AI tools and considering how to discuss them with young people. These approaches are described at https://experience-ai.org/en-US/ and https://www.raspberrypi.org/blog/bringing-ai-education-to-1-25-million-students-across-latin-america/. The inspected pages do not establish how consistently each approach is used in classrooms.
prioritySummary: The initiative’s central emphasis is making AI literacy accessible to young people globally, while equipping educators to teach it. It aims for students to understand how AI systems work, question their role and impacts, and make informed, responsible choices about using them; the programme also describes supporting young people to create AI tools. Local partnerships and translated or tailored resources are presented as ways to extend access across countries and contexts. Educator confidence is a related priority, since the programme trains teachers to deliver lessons and aims to reach millions of learners. The pages frame this as broad educational and societal benefit, not principally workforce upskilling or individual well-being. Evidence: https://experience-ai.org/en-US/ and https://www.raspberrypi.org/blog/bringing-ai-education-to-1-25-million-students-across-latin-america/.
educationalTechnologySummary: The inspected pages identify educational materials and a course, but no named dedicated learning software, platform, or hardware developed by Experience AI. The programme says it developed free AI and machine-learning lessons comprising lesson plans, slide decks, worksheets, and videos for teachers to use in classrooms and other settings. It also offers a free three-week online course for educators through the Raspberry Pi Foundation’s Training Hub; the pages do not specify the platform technology behind that course. Learners may encounter or try AI tools as lesson content, including generative AI, but the available evidence does not establish that Experience AI itself develops or deploys those tools as educational technology. Evidence: https://experience-ai.org/en-US/ and https://www.raspberrypi.org/blog/bringing-ai-education-to-1-25-million-students-across-latin-america/. These findings reflect the limited pages inspected.

inclusion.reason: The initiative qualifies for inclusion via the non-government work with evidenced system-scale adoption route (195+ countries, 22 languages, 50,000+ educators). It includes AI literacy through classroom resources designed to teach AI concepts rather than merely using AI tools. Additional support from its UNESCO King Hamad Prize laureate status in 2025 further validates its significance.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: OECD Digital Education Outlook 2023 – chapter "Emerging governance of generative AI in education"
metadata.Description: OECD review of how national/central governments are guiding generative AI use in schools; notes that guidance to date is mostly non-binding and compares approaches across countries.

summary: The OECD Digital Education Outlook 2023 chapter “Emerging governance of generative AI in education” reviews how governments and education jurisdictions are approaching generative AI in schools. Aimed primarily at policy makers, it considers guidance and guardrails for integration, including responsible and equitable use, privacy, bias, and dialogue with teaching professionals. It also highlights teachers’ role and the importance of relevant training, but is a policy analysis rather than a learner-facing curriculum or AI teaching programme.
pedagogicalSummary: The inspected material describes a policy review of how governments guide generative AI in education, not an AI-literacy teaching programme. It does not specify a learner-facing pedagogy, curriculum, or teaching activities, so no particular instructional approach can be identified. The report’s foreword says that teachers should remain a guiding force in learning and calls for dialogue between education authorities and teaching professionals, but these are governance principles rather than evidence of a teaching method. The chapter page was too large to inspect in full, so this is a limit of the accessible evidence, not confirmation that the chapter contains no further pedagogical discussion (https://www.oecd.org/en/publications/oecd-digital-education-outlook-2023_c74f03de-en/full-report/emerging-governance-of-generative-ai-in-education_3cbd6269.html; https://www.oecd.org/en/publications/oecd-digital-education-outlook-2023_c74f03de-en/full-report.html).
prioritySummary: The initiative’s evident emphasis is to help governments and education jurisdictions understand and guide generative AI’s integration into education. The report notes that few countries are prepared to guide its use and presents opportunities, guidelines, and guardrails for effective and equitable adoption. Its stated concerns include responsible and ethical use, bias, privacy, and stereotypes, alongside dialogue with teaching professionals and maintaining teachers’ role in learning. These priorities address education systems and their learners and staff, rather than a specific workforce-training or individual well-being programme. The inspected chapter page could not be read in full, so additional priorities in the chapter may not be reflected here (https://www.oecd.org/en/publications/oecd-digital-education-outlook-2023_c74f03de-en/full-report/emerging-governance-of-generative-ai-in-education_3cbd6269.html; https://www.oecd.org/en/publications/oecd-digital-education-outlook-2023_c74f03de-en/full-report.html).
educationalTechnologySummary: The accessible material does not identify an educational technology developed or used by the OECD initiative to teach AI literacy. It discusses generative AI as a technology whose use in education requires governance, and the foreword describes its potential for tailored autonomous learning; that does not establish that the OECD report itself provides or uses an AI learning tool, platform, software, or hardware. The report’s references elsewhere to digital education systems are general context, not evidence that they support this chapter’s AI-literacy learning. Because the chapter page was too large to inspect fully, the absence of an identified tool is limited to the pages accessible here (https://www.oecd.org/en/publications/oecd-digital-education-outlook-2023_c74f03de-en/full-report/emerging-governance-of-generative-ai-in-education_3cbd6269.html; https://www.oecd.org/en/publications/oecd-digital-education-outlook-2023_c74f03de-en/full-report.html).

inclusion.reason: The initiative qualifies for inclusion under the 'intergovernmental body' route (OECD). It includes AI literacy elements by explicitly promoting dedicated teacher training programmes covering technical, pedagogical, and ethical considerations of generative AI and advocating for enhanced digital literacy. The content is educational and provides guidance on how to use and govern generative AI in education.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: Google Teachable Machine
metadata.Description: Free browser tool for training image, sound and pose classifiers without code. Widely used in classrooms to show how data and training shape model behaviour and bias; recommended in K-12 AI-literacy reviews.

summary: Google Teachable Machine is a free, browser-based tool for people without coding experience to create image, sound, and pose classifiers from examples, train and test them, and export models for projects. Its hands-on approach lets learners explore how examples shape a model’s classifications. The site also links to educational activities, including external K–12 lessons on machine learning, data representation, misclassification, and bias; these extend the tool’s learning uses but do not establish a single required teaching method.
pedagogicalSummary: Teachable Machine supports hands-on, experiential learning: learners gather and group examples, train a model, test it on new examples, and can export it for a project. Its tutorials offer guided demonstrations using images, sounds, and poses. The homepage also links to lessons by other organizations; one ReadyAI lesson pairs an unplugged human classification activity with training the model, then uses misclassifications to discuss data representation and algorithmic bias. That example adds inquiry, comparison, and reflection, but is ReadyAI’s lesson rather than evidence of a required Google teaching method. The inspected pages do not establish a single formal pedagogy for all uses of the tool. Sources: https://teachablemachine.withgoogle.com/ ; https://medium.com/readyai-org/teachable-machine-course-eb925c2c370a
prioritySummary: The initiative principally makes machine-learning model creation accessible to a broad audience, including people without coding expertise, while presenting learning activities that help students understand how models are trained and used. The tool’s emphasis is on enabling users to build simple image, sound, and pose classifiers; the linked educational material extends this toward AI literacy, including classification, the role of training data, and societal impact. The ReadyAI lesson specifically targets K–12 learners, but it is an external lesson featured by Teachable Machine, not evidence that every user or use is school-focused. The inspected pages do not identify workforce upskilling as a priority or establish a hierarchy among broader public access and educational uses. Sources: https://teachablemachine.withgoogle.com/ ; https://edu.readyai.org/courses/teachable-machine/ ; https://medium.com/readyai-org/teachable-machine-course-eb925c2c370a
educationalTechnologySummary: Google’s Teachable Machine is a browser-based tool for creating machine-learning classifiers without coding. It lets learners provide image, audio, or pose examples from files or live capture, train a model, and immediately test its classifications; tutorials demonstrate simple tasks such as recognizing a ripe banana or a head tilt. The page says users can choose to keep webcam or microphone data on-device, and can download or host trained models for use in sites, apps, or projects. The models are TensorFlow.js models; the page also lists compatibility with JavaScript tools and export options for platforms such as Coral and Arduino. These are integrations and destinations for models, not technologies the page says Google developed as part of Teachable Machine. Sources: https://teachablemachine.withgoogle.com/ ; https://teachablemachine.withgoogle.com/faq#Saving-&-Exporting

inclusion.reason: The initiative includes clear AI-literacy content through its lesson plans that teach concepts of machine learning, data training, and bias. It qualifies via the inclusion route of 'evidence of system-scale adoption' because it is widely used in K-12 classrooms, recommended in AI-literacy reviews, and has a large user base with 577+ enrolled students in the ReadyAI course alone. The tool is also an official Google product designed for education.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: Microsoft Elevate (incl. Elevate for Educators)
metadata.Description: Microsoft's five-year, $4bn programme aiming to train 20 million people in AI skills through courses at several competency levels; Elevate for Educators offers free courses, live training and credentials.

summary: Microsoft Elevate is a five-year programme aiming to build AI skills among 20 million people through courses at several competency levels. Its Elevate for Educators component is a community-based professional-learning platform offering free courses, live training and credentials. The available account provides little detail about its curriculum, pedagogy, tools or assessment; much of the article’s discussion of teacher training concerns a separate Google-led partnership.
pedagogicalSummary: The accessible page gives little evidence about the pedagogy of Microsoft Elevate for Educators. It says the initiative offers free courses and live training, but does not describe lesson design, learning activities, sequencing, facilitation, or how learning is assessed. Those formats indicate learning opportunities, not a sufficiently documented teaching approach. The article’s more detailed discussion concerns a separate Google–ISTE+ASCD partnership and should not be attributed to Microsoft Elevate. Accordingly, the inspected evidence does not establish a pedagogical approach; this is a limit of the page, not evidence that the initiative has none. Source: https://www.the74million.org/article/exclusive-new-google-partnership-a-sizable-investment-in-ai-for-teachers/
prioritySummary: The page characterizes Microsoft Elevate for Educators as a community-based platform offering free courses, live training sessions, and credentials. This supports a broad emphasis on providing educators with AI-related training and recognition, but the article gives no detail about the specific skills targeted, intended outcomes, or which educator groups are prioritized. Its main reporting concerns a different, Google-led teacher-training partnership, so statements in that discussion about preparing teachers and students cannot be treated as Microsoft Elevate’s stated aims. The page therefore supports educator training as the evident priority, while leaving its precise goals and intended beneficiaries beyond educators unclear. Source: https://www.the74million.org/article/exclusive-new-google-partnership-a-sizable-investment-in-ai-for-teachers/
educationalTechnologySummary: The article identifies Microsoft Elevate for Educators as a “community-based platform” that offers free courses, live training sessions, and credentials, but does not name any specific software, learning-management system, AI tool, or hardware used or developed by Microsoft Elevate. The platform and training formats are the only technology-related details directly associated with the initiative, and the page does not explain how the platform supports learning. It separately discusses Google Gemini and NotebookLM in connection with the Google–ISTE+ASCD partnership; these should not be attributed to Microsoft Elevate. The available evidence is too limited to identify further educational technologies or their functions. Source: https://www.the74million.org/article/exclusive-new-google-partnership-a-sizable-investment-in-ai-for-teachers/

inclusion.reason: The article describes a specific educational initiative ('AI for Teachers') launched by Google that includes explicit AI literacy components: it teaches 'how to use generative AI,' covers 'responsible use' and ethics, and offers courses at multiple competency levels. Although the primary page is news reporting, the described initiative itself meets the AI-literacy requirement. For inclusion route, the metadata identifies this as part of Microsoft Elevate (a five-year, $4bn government-aligned program), and such scale/endorsement qualifies under the inclusion criteria.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: Anthropic – free AI Fluency courses for educators and students
metadata.Description: Three free courses announced for educators, including 'AI Fluency for Students' (responsible collaboration with AI on coursework while keeping independent skills) and 'Teaching AI Fluency' (for educators teaching AI literacy).

summary: Anthropic offers three free, short AI fluency courses for educators and students, focused on higher-education contexts. The courses cover integrating AI into teaching, collaborating responsibly with AI on coursework while developing independent skills, and teaching AI literacy. Each is reported to comprise four to seven videos, take about 25–35 minutes, and offer a completion certificate; detailed assessments or course activities are not described.
pedagogicalSummary: The initiative organizes learning into three short, audience-specific courses: AI Fluency for Educators, AI Fluency for Students, and Teaching AI Fluency. The reported formats include four to seven videos per course, taking about 25–35 minutes, with a completion certificate. The pedagogical emphasis is practical and responsible application: teachers consider integrating AI into materials and classroom discussions, while students learn to collaborate with AI on coursework without neglecting their own skills; educators also learn to teach AI literacy. The report additionally describes Claude Learning Mode’s guided questions as Socratic-style and collaborative, but presents those features as complementing the courses rather than specifying them as course activities. Detailed lesson plans, assessment methods, or interactive course activities are not described in the inspected pages. (https://www.zdnet.com/article/you-can-learn-ai-for-free-with-these-new-courses-from-anthropic/; https://getcoai.com/news/anthropic-launches-3-free-ai-fluency-courses-for-educators/)
prioritySummary: The initiative principally aims to build responsible AI fluency among higher-education students and educators. Its three courses address distinct needs: helping educators integrate AI into teaching, helping students collaborate responsibly on coursework while continuing to develop independent skills, and preparing educators to teach AI literacy. The coverage frames this as practical, thoughtful AI integration in university settings, not merely instruction in basic tool use. It also mentions growing employer demand for AI confidence, but this is contextual rationale rather than evidence that workforce upskilling is the courses’ sole or primary purpose. Academic integrity and student privacy appear as concerns associated with the advisory board’s guidance on education policy and products; the pages do not establish them as course outcomes. (https://www.zdnet.com/article/you-can-learn-ai-for-free-with-these-new-courses-from-anthropic/; https://getcoai.com/news/anthropic-launches-3-free-ai-fluency-courses-for-educators/)
educationalTechnologySummary: The inspected coverage identifies free AI Fluency courses, but does not name a course-delivery platform or specify what software learners use within them; it describes each course as comprising four to seven videos. Separately, it says the courses complement Anthropic’s Claude Learning Mode features in Claude.ai and Claude Code. In Claude.ai, Learning Mode uses guided questions to help learners work toward answers; in Claude Code, Explanatory mode explains reasoning and Learning Mode provides fill-in-the-blank collaborative coding exercises. These are identified as Anthropic’s features, not as the platform hosting the courses, and the report does not establish that learners must use them to complete the courses. No hardware is identified. metadata.Initiative / Programme: Raspberry Pi Foundation / Google DeepMind – "Understanding AI for educators" free online course
metadata.Description: Free online training course for educators created with Google DeepMind as part of Experience AI, to help teachers bring AI into their classrooms confidently and ethically.

summary: Understanding AI for educators is a free, three-week online professional-development course created by the Raspberry Pi Foundation with Google DeepMind as part of Experience AI. Aimed at educators with varied levels of prior experience, it develops understanding of how AI systems work and practical confidence in discussing and using AI in teaching. The course addresses generative AI tools, their social and ethical effects, and classroom applications, using the SEAME framework to structure AI discussions and the OCEAN process to guide prompting and reviewing outputs. It emphasizes adapting explanations and activities to learners rather than following a single prescribed lesson sequence.
pedagogicalSummary: The initiative supports educators through a free, three-week online course that combines conceptual learning about AI systems with practical exploration of AI tools and consideration of their social and ethical effects. The course offers structured ways to explain and discuss AI: the SEAME framework helps educators choose among social and ethical, application, model, and engine levels, while the OCEAN process guides prompting, assessing, and refining generative AI outputs. The emphasis is on building educators’ understanding and confidence so they can adapt explanations and activities to their teaching, rather than on a single prescribed lesson sequence. The inspected pages do not establish whether the course includes live teaching, peer collaboration, or assessment. Sources: https://www.raspberrypi.org/blog/free-online-course-on-understanding-ai-for-educators/ and https://experience-ai.org/en/
prioritySummary: The clearest priority is helping educators become confident, critical, and ethical guides to AI in learning settings. The course is intended for educators with varied prior experience, and the broader programme also includes people educating young people outside formal schools, such as parents and club volunteers. It aims to help them understand AI tools, weigh their risks and opportunities, and discuss their effects on education and work. A related benefit is young people’s AI literacy: the programme describes helping students understand, question, and apply AI, and widening access to relevant AI education globally. The inspected pages support these connected aims but do not establish a single priority hierarchy beyond educator learning as the course’s immediate focus. Sources: https://www.raspberrypi.org/blog/free-online-course-on-understanding-ai-for-educators/ and https://experience-ai.org/en/
educationalTechnologySummary: The identified educational technology is principally the online course itself, described as a free three-week educator course available through a Training Hub; the inspected pages do not name the course-hosting platform or specify its technical features. The course includes practical exploration of AI tools, and its OCEAN prompting guidance is presented for tools such as Gemini, Stable Diffusion, and ChatGPT. The programme’s overview says learners try out tools, but the pages do not establish that each named tool is required or provided by the course. These are AI applications used as learning objects or for practice, not evidence that Raspberry Pi Foundation or Google DeepMind developed them. The available evidence identifies no special hardware or other dedicated learning software. Sources: https://www.raspberrypi.org/blog/free-online-course-on-understanding-ai-for-educators/ and https://experience-ai.org/en/

inclusion.reason: The course includes explicit AI literacy content (how AI works, ethical use, classroom applications) and meets inclusion criteria through large-scale adoption via Google DeepMind and potential government endorsement/partnership under the Experience AI program used in multiple jurisdictions (e.g., UK schools via DfE).

metadata.Initiative / Programme: UCL-led toolkit for teaching responsible AI globally (Aug 2026)
metadata.Description: Toolkit that combines Google DeepMind's free online foundational AI courses ('AI Research Foundations') with classroom discussion, collaboration and problem-based learning; project team spans South Africa, Nigeria, Sudan and Madagascar.

summary: The UCL-led AI Research Foundations Toolkit is a free, adaptable resource for university educators and students, designed for use in classrooms worldwide. It supplements Google DeepMind’s online foundational AI courses with more than 50 hours of lesson plans, coding notebooks, slides, case studies, and classroom activities. Blending technical study of AI and machine learning with discussion, collaboration, and problem-based learning, it explores ethical, social, governance, and environmental questions alongside how AI systems work. Materials were co-designed with African educators, students, and researchers and are intended to be adapted to local contexts.
pedagogicalSummary: The toolkit uses blended, interdisciplinary learning: it connects Google DeepMind’s online foundational courses with classroom activities, including group discussion, collaboration, and problem-based learning. More than 50 hours of adaptable activities apply AI to real-world contexts and bring technical machine-learning content together with sociology, philosophy, and ethics. Activities include ethical dilemmas and environmental justice, and are intended to help learners examine AI’s purposes, impacts, governance, and limitations alongside how systems work. Its materials were co-designed with African educators, students, and researchers, and educators are encouraged to adapt lessons to their local contexts rather than follow a fixed curriculum. Evidence is from the UCL announcement: https://www.ucl.ac.uk/news/2026/aug/new-toolkit-developed-teach-responsible-ai-globally
prioritySummary: The initiative aims to widen access to AI education and prepare students to build and shape AI responsibly. It makes the toolkit freely available to educators worldwide and builds on free, globally accessible online courses, with the stated goal of democratizing access to AI education. The intended learners include university students, particularly future engineers and researchers; educators are also direct beneficiaries, receiving adaptable materials they can use in their own classrooms. The project emphasizes responsible development, including attention to social values, ethics, governance, and the communities affected by AI. Co-design with African educators and students and attention to local classroom realities are prominent, though the announcement presents the toolkit as globally adaptable. Source: https://www.ucl.ac.uk/news/2026/aug/new-toolkit-developed-teach-responsible-ai-globally
educationalTechnologySummary: The initiative develops the AI Research Foundations Toolkit, a collection of adaptable teaching resources that the announcement says includes lesson plans, coding notebooks, lecture slides, and localized case studies. It uses and augments Google DeepMind’s free online AI Research Foundations courses, which teach generative AI and large language models; these courses supply foundational technical content, while the toolkit adds classroom learning activities. The article does not identify a particular learning-management system, coding environment, software platform, or hardware, so the notebooks should not be attributed to a specific technology. It also does not establish that the toolkit itself is a software product. Source: https://www.ucl.ac.uk/news/2026/aug/new-toolkit-developed-teach-responsible-ai-globally

inclusion.reason: The UCL article describes learning about how AI systems work, alongside ethics and responsible development, so it meets the AI-literacy requirement. Its free availability to educators worldwide and adaptable classroom materials make a broader audience plausible; however, the page does not establish government endorsement or funding, system-scale adoption, or use across multiple jurisdictions. metadata.Initiative / Programme: UNICEF – Tinkering with Tech (and AI)
metadata.Description: UNICEF-led programme using design thinking and hands-on technology (micro:bit, Raspberry Pi, Arduino) to build digital and AI literacy in students and teachers, with a focus on girls and underserved communities. First cohort: Honduras, Montenegro, Maldives, Viet Nam; expanding to Lao PDR, Ukraine and Uzbekistan; next phase deepens AI literacy with Arm, Finland, micro:bit and Raspberry Pi Foundation partners.

summary: UNICEF’s Tinkering with Tech is a multi-country programme that develops students’ digital and foundational AI literacy while preparing teachers to support learner-centred technology education. Through collaborative, hands-on design challenges, students identify community problems, prototype and test solutions, and explore technology—including AI—with an emphasis on safe and responsible use. Teachers receive training and mentoring in digital pedagogy. The programme particularly seeks to engage girls and underserved learners, using tools such as micro:bit and, depending on local context, Raspberry Pi or Arduino. Its initial cohorts were in Honduras, Montenegro, Maldives and Viet Nam, with expansion described for Lao PDR, Ukraine and Uzbekistan.
pedagogicalSummary: The initiative organizes student learning around design thinking and hands-on, collaborative, experiential problem-solving. Learners explore community challenges, empathize and define problems, develop ideas, prototype and test solutions, and share their achievements; activities are intended to build agency, creativity, communication, collaboration, and computational thinking. Teachers are trained and mentored to facilitate inquiry, experimentation, and learner-centred classroom practice, with peer learning also supported through Communities of Practice. These are described teaching and learning approaches, distinct from the technologies used and from broader goals such as expanding AI literacy. The initiative’s page and implementation-research report support this account, though the inspected materials do not detail specific lesson plans: https://www.unicef.org/digitaleducation/tinkering-with-tech ; https://www.unicef.org/digitaleducation/documents/tinkering-tech-creating-pathways-future-innovators
prioritySummary: The initiative principally aims to strengthen students’ digital and foundational AI literacy, broader transferable skills, and interest in STEM/STEAM, while preparing teachers to integrate technology and learner-centred pedagogy. It emphasizes equitable access and participation, particularly for girls and underserved or underrepresented learners, and describes inclusive activities and supportive spaces intended to help address the gender digital divide. Responsible, safe, and ethical use of AI is also an explicit priority. The programme additionally seeks to support education-system capacity and scalable, context-sensitive implementation, but the inspected pages do not establish this as more important than its learner and teacher aims. Evidence: https://www.unicef.org/digitaleducation/tinkering-with-tech ; https://www.unicef.org/digitaleducation/documents/tinkering-tech-creating-pathways-future-innovators
educationalTechnologySummary: The initiative reports using micro:bit devices in its initial four-country rollout; implementation can also use Raspberry Pi devices, Arduino boards, robotic kits, or similar options, depending on local choice. The page describes students using technologies, including AI, to work on real-world challenges, but does not identify a particular AI platform or software product. Teachers also receive an introduction to UNICEF’s Superstar Teacher Toolbox, which provides self-paced digital-pedagogy professional-development materials; its Digital Pedagogy tool is available as an online course on the Learning Passport platform. The Toolbox and its course are UNICEF-developed resources, while micro:bit, Raspberry Pi, and Arduino are named hardware options rather than technologies identified as developed by this initiative. Evidence: https://www.unicef.org/digitaleducation/tinkering-with-tech ; https://www.unicef.org/digitaleducation/superstar-teacher-toolbox

inclusion.reason: This initiative qualifies for inclusion under the Inclusion Route: issued by an intergovernmental body (UNICEF). The summary confirms it focuses on building AI literacy, satisfying the primary requirement. While metadata mentions government involvement in the broader Tech4Ed programme as a partner, direct confirmation of that specific funding or endorsement is slightly ambiguous from this single view; however, inclusion is warranted due to UNICEF's intergovernmental status and the explicit focus on AI literacy.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: Machine Learning for Kids
metadata.Description: Free educational tool where students train machine-learning models (including text-based ones) and use them in their own programming projects; listed alongside Teachable Machine in K-12 AI-literacy reviews.

summary: Machine Learning for Kids is a free, web-based tool for children and students to explore machine learning through hands-on projects. Learners can train models using their own examples or experiment with pretrained models, then build interactive projects in Scratch or Python. Worksheets, stories, and a project-based book guide activities and introduce concepts such as training and test data, accuracy, bias, model limitations, and AI’s effects in everyday life. The resource is designed for schools and is also described for use by code clubs and families.
pedagogicalSummary: The initiative uses a practical, project-based approach: students collect examples, train a model, then apply it in a game or interactive project. Its worksheets provide downloadable, step-by-step instructions with explanations and screenshots, generally designed as stand-alone lesson activities. Students can also experiment more freely in Scratch, where stories describe learning through observing what models do and where they fail. Activities connect coding with concepts such as training and test data, accuracy, bias, and model limitations. The emphasis is on learning by making and experimenting, rather than instruction in AI concepts alone. The accessible pages describe this approach but do not establish how consistently teachers use the materials in practice. (https://machinelearningforkids.co.uk/#!/about; https://machinelearningforkids.co.uk/#!/worksheets; https://machinelearningforkids.co.uk/#!/stories/intro)
prioritySummary: The initiative principally aims to help children and students learn about artificial intelligence and machine learning by building things with the technology. It frames hands-on creation as a way for young people to understand how machine learning is applied, what it can do, and what its implications are. The tool extends existing efforts to teach children coding, and is designed for use in schools while also being used by code clubs and families. The accessible pages support an educational and AI-literacy emphasis; they do not present workforce preparation or individual well-being as primary goals. The site describes broad use but does not specify a particular student age range or establish a hierarchy among its school, club, and family audiences. (https://machinelearningforkids.co.uk/#!/about; https://machinelearningforkids.co.uk/#!/stories/intro)
educationalTechnologySummary: Machine Learning for Kids is a web-based learning tool developed for training machine-learning models and using them in projects; the site says it requires no installation. It provides guided model-training activities and connects models to coding environments, especially Scratch 3, where students use blocks to build games and interactive projects; worksheets also include Python projects. The platform supplies pretrained models for functions such as speech, face, pose, and hand detection, object recognition, and question answering. These are models students can use rather than models the site claims to have developed: examples include Google Chrome’s speech recognition and models based on MobileNet and BERT. It also supports using TensorFlow image classifiers, including models made with the separate Teachable Machine. (https://machinelearningforkids.co.uk/#!/about; https://machinelearningforkids.co.uk/#!/pretrained; https://machinelearningforkids.co.uk/#!/worksheets)

inclusion.reason: The initiative clearly meets the AI-literacy requirement as it provides interactive content where students learn how to train AI models (images, text, speech) and understand underlying concepts like supervised learning, decision trees, and LLMs. It includes educational worksheets, stories, and a book component specifically designed for teaching. Regarding inclusion routes, the metadata explicitly states it is 'listed alongside Teachable Machine in K-12 AI-literacy reviews,' indicating adoption or recognition in educational contexts. The tool serves a wide international audience (as seen by 23 supported languages) and is positioned as an educational resource rather than a proprietary commercial product, aligning with the scope of initiatives like Calliope mini referenced in calibration examples.
