metadata.Initiative / Programme: TeachAI – AI Guidance for Schools Toolkit
metadata.Description: Toolkit for education systems building AI guidance: seven principles (incl. promoting AI literacy), sample guidance, presentations and resources for staff and parents. Co-authored by Code.org, CoSN, Digital Promise, European EdTech Alliance and PACE; updated 2025; CC BY-NC-SA.

summary: TeachAI’s AI Guidance for Schools Toolkit helps education authorities, school leaders, and school communities develop and improve guidance for AI in primary and secondary education. It presents seven principles, including promoting AI literacy, and offers sample guidance, policy considerations, a customizable presentation, and resources for staff and parents. Its focus is responsible and equitable AI use, addressing topics such as privacy, bias, assessment, and professional learning. The toolkit supports locally adaptable organizational guidance rather than prescribing a student-facing curriculum or teaching method; it was co-authored by several education and technology organizations.
pedagogicalSummary: TeachAI’s toolkit is primarily guidance for education systems, not a prescribed classroom teaching method. It supports learning through practical resources, examples, and discussion prompts that education authorities and school communities can adapt, rather than copy verbatim. Its broader AI-literacy work describes implementation resources and the development and promotion of exemplars such as curriculum materials, assessments, and professional-development modules. The toolkit also advocates ongoing professional development, sharing educators’ experiences, gathering stakeholder input, and iteratively evaluating and improving practice. These are forms of organizational and professional learning; the inspected pages do not establish a specific student-facing pedagogy or lesson sequence. (https://www.teachai.org/toolkit; https://www.teachai.org/toolkit-framework; https://www.teachai.org/ailiteracy)
prioritySummary: The initiative’s central emphasis is helping education authorities, school leaders, and teachers develop and improve guidance for AI in primary and secondary education. It aims to help school communities realize potential benefits while understanding and mitigating risks, and to build stakeholders’ capacity to understand and use AI effectively. AI literacy is one part of this broader effort: TeachAI describes supporting learners’ knowledge and skills while providing practical resources for teachers and implementation guidance for education leaders. The toolkit also highlights equitable adoption, responsible use, privacy, and continuous improvement, without establishing one of these as the sole priority. The intended beneficiaries include students and staff, with authorities and education leaders as key users of the toolkit. (https://www.teachai.org/toolkit; https://www.teachai.org/ailiteracy; https://www.teachai.org/toolkit-framework)
educationalTechnologySummary: The inspected pages do not identify a TeachAI-developed learning platform, software product, or hardware used to teach AI literacy. TeachAI offers downloadable and adaptable learning-support materials, including a customizable AI-in-education slide presentation that can be used for professional learning or presentations about teaching with and about AI. Its AI-literacy page describes practical tools and activities and says exemplars such as curriculum materials, assessments, and professional-development modules are being developed or promoted; these are resources, not named educational technologies. The toolkit discusses types of AI tools used in schools and points to external resources, but that does not establish that TeachAI uses those tools to deliver instruction. This summary is limited to the pages inspected. (https://www.teachai.org/presentation; https://www.teachai.org/ailiteracy; https://www.teachai.org/toolkit)

inclusion.reason: The initiative includes AI literacy as a core component (one of seven principles) with practical educational content on how to use and understand AI in schools. Its toolkit and related materials help school communities develop locally adapted guidance for using AI and teaching about it responsibly. The offering is primarily policy and professional-learning support, not a defined student course or classroom pedagogy; no specific AI teaching platform is identified.

It also recommends integrating AI literacy into curriculum and educator professional development, and encourages ongoing feedback. These are directions for schools and policymakers rather than evidence of a particular student-facing pedagogy or course. The pages do not establish that TeachAI itself delivers instruction or that it uses a specific approach such as project-based learning. (https://www.teachai.org/toolkit; https://www.teachai.org/policy)
prioritySummary: TeachAI’s central emphasis is helping governments and education authorities support safe, effective, and responsible teaching with AI and teaching about AI. Its resources are directed especially to policymakers, school and system leaders, and K–12 educators, with students and school communities benefiting from clearer guidance, AI literacy, and attention to risks such as inequity and privacy. The initiative emphasizes policy development alongside building educator capacity, raising awareness, and supporting responsible adoption; the inspected pages do not establish a single priority that overrides these related aims. metadata.Initiative / Programme: IDB "AI and Education: Building the Future Through Digital Transformation" (Apr 2025) and "AI Here!" call
metadata.Description: Inter-American Development Bank report on AI in education, followed by a call (with Ceibal and Socialab) that mapped 193 real AI solutions in Latin American and Caribbean schools.

summary: The Inter-American Development Bank’s 2025 report, *AI and Education: Building the Future Through Digital Transformation*, and the related “AI Here!” call with Ceibal and Socialab examine AI’s role in education across Latin America and the Caribbean. The call mapped 193 school-related AI solutions, while the report offers policymakers a framework and practical recommendations for integrating technology, including AI, into education. The material is aimed chiefly at policymakers and education communities, addressing implementation, teacher skills, inclusion, school management, and responsible use; the available evidence does not establish a specific learner-facing pedagogy or AI-literacy curriculum.
pedagogicalSummary: The accessible pages present an article about AI in education and lessons from 193 initiatives, with sections on selected initiatives and challenges for policymakers and education communities. They do not describe how learners are taught or how learning is organized in those initiatives. The article itself is a synthesis, not evidence of a particular teaching intervention. Because the rendered pages expose only headings and not the article body, no specific pedagogy—such as tutoring, project-based learning, or teacher training—can be identified; this is missing evidence, not proof that the initiatives use no pedagogical approaches. Sources: https://www.iadb.org/en/blog/education/how-ai-transforming-education-latin-america-and-caribbean-lessons-193-solutions and https://www.iadb.org/es/blog/educacion/como-la-inteligencia-artificial-esta-transformando-la-educacion-en-america-latina-y-el-caribe
prioritySummary: The article’s stated focus is how AI is transforming education in Latin America and the Caribbean, drawing lessons from 193 solutions. Its headings point to informing policy and education communities, including discussion of implementation and challenges for policymakers and communities. This supports describing the emphasis as understanding AI’s role in regional education and informing those responsible for applying it; the accessible text does not establish a more specific beneficiary group or a ranking among priorities such as workforce development, student well-being, or equity. The article body is not available in the rendered pages, so its detailed conclusions and intended outcomes remain uncertain. Sources: https://www.iadb.org/en/blog/education/how-ai-transforming-education-latin-america-and-caribbean-lessons-193-solutions and https://www.iadb.org/es/blog/educacion/como-la-inteligencia-artificial-esta-transformando-la-educacion-en-america-latina-y-el-caribe
educationalTechnologySummary: The accessible pages identify AI in education as the subject and refer to 193 solutions, but do not name any platforms, software, hardware, or other educational technologies, nor explain how specific tools support learning. They also do not show whether the IDB develops or uses any of the solutions, as distinct from documenting them. Thus, no educational technology developed or used by the initiative can be identified from the inspected evidence; this is a limit of the accessible page content, not confirmation that the mapped initiatives use none. Sources: https://www.iadb.org/en/blog/education/how-ai-transforming-education-latin-america-and-caribbean-lessons-193-solutions and https://www.iadb.org/es/blog/educacion/como-la-inteligencia-artificial-esta-transformando-la-educacion-en-america-latina-y-el-caribe

inclusion.reason: The report provides policy-oriented guidance on integrating AI into education and identifies teacher training and skills, which plausibly supports learning how to use AI; the accessible pages do not establish a dedicated AI-literacy curriculum or framework. The IDB is an intergovernmental body, an inclusion route if the literacy connection is met. Sources: https://www.iadb.org/en/blog/education/how-ai-transforming-education-latin-america-and-caribbean-lessons-193-solutions and https://publications.iadb.org/publications/english/document/AI-and-Education-Building-the-Future-Through-Digital-Transformation.pdf. The extent of explicit AI-literacy content remains uncertain.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: TEQSA – "Gen AI strategies for Australian higher education: Emerging practice" toolkit (Nov 2024)
metadata.Description: Regulator toolkit (Process, People, Practice) built from a June 2024 request to all providers for gen-AI action plans (100% response); complemented by a research-training version (June 2025). TEQSA moves to a regulatory approach on AI and academic integrity in 2026.

summary: TEQSA’s *Gen AI strategies for Australian higher education: Emerging practice* is a toolkit for Australian higher education providers on responding to generative AI in teaching and learning. Organised around Process, People and Practice, it shares institutional ideas and experience for responsible integration while addressing assessment and award integrity. It followed TEQSA’s June 2024 request for providers’ action plans; a complementary version for research training was published in June 2025. The resource focuses on institutional strategy rather than prescribing classroom methods or specific technologies.
pedagogicalSummary: The inspected page presents an institutional strategy toolkit, not a defined teaching method. Its three dimensions—Process, People and Practice—can be read individually, in any order, or together, and are intended to share ideas and experiences for integrating generative AI into teaching and learning. The page does not describe specific classroom activities, instructional sequences, or how learners are taught, so a particular pedagogy cannot be established from this evidence; that is missing detail, not confirmation that providers use no pedagogical approaches. Source: https://www.teqsa.gov.au/guides-resources/resources/corporate-publications/gen-ai-strategies-australian-higher-education-emerging-practice
prioritySummary: The initiative principally aims to help Australian higher-education institutions respond to generative AI: integrating it effectively and ethically into teaching and learning while managing risks to assessment and award integrity. The toolkit arose from TEQSA’s request that providers submit institutional action plans addressing risks to award integrity, and is framed as sharing sector ideas and experience. The page therefore supports an emphasis on institutional capability and the integrity of higher-education awards, alongside responsible integration; it does not establish a separate priority such as workforce upskilling or individual well-being. Source: https://www.teqsa.gov.au/guides-resources/resources/corporate-publications/gen-ai-strategies-australian-higher-education-emerging-practice
educationalTechnologySummary: The inspected page identifies no educational software, learning platform, hardware, or AI product developed or used by TEQSA to support learning. Generative AI is the subject of the guidance, but the page does not identify it as a particular learning technology deployed by the initiative. The resource itself is a PDF toolkit offering institutional ideas and experiences, rather than an identified educational technology. This conclusion is limited to the inspected page; its description does not provide technical details about tools that institutions may use. Source: https://www.teqsa.gov.au/guides-resources/resources/corporate-publications/gen-ai-strategies-australian-higher-education-emerging-practice

inclusion.reason: This initiative qualifies for inclusion because it is issued by TEQSA, a statutory national body responsible for regulating higher education quality and standards in Australia, meeting the 'Issued... by a national or sub-national government or statutory body' inclusion route. The toolkit provides educational guidance on how to effectively and ethically integrate gen AI into teaching and learning, fulfilling the AI-literacy requirement. It is not merely a company product or single-institution project, but a regulatory resource with system-wide reach across Australian higher education providers (confirmed by 100% response rate from all providers).

metadata.Initiative / Programme: CSER (University of Adelaide) – free "Teaching Artificial Intelligence" courses for teachers
metadata.Description: Two free online courses designed for teachers with no technical background; CSER is also the Australian partner delivering Experience AI aligned to Australian Curriculum v9.

summary: CSER at the University of Adelaide supports Australian primary and secondary teachers, including those without a technical background, through free, self-paced courses on teaching artificial intelligence. Its wider offering includes Australian-curriculum-aligned Experience AI classroom resources, teacher workshops and classroom lending kits. The materials introduce AI and machine learning and help teachers support students to examine real-world applications, use AI responsibly, and consider its social and ethical implications.
pedagogicalSummary: CSER combines self-paced online professional learning for teachers with classroom-ready materials and live professional development. Its MOOCs are described as evidence-based and offer background knowledge, practical classroom examples, and an online community where educators can share ideas. Experience AI adds lesson plans, slides, worksheets, and videos; students encounter real-world AI applications, explore machine-learning models, and consider social and ethical implications. CSER also offers face-to-face and virtual teacher workshops. These are documented learning formats and activities; the inspected pages do not establish a more specific teaching method such as project-based learning. Sources: https://csermoocs.adelaide.edu.au/news/list/2025/05/08/teaching-artificial-intelligence ; https://csermoocs.adelaide.edu.au/available-moocs ; https://csermoocs.adelaide.edu.au/professional-learning/artificial-intelligence-in-schools
prioritySummary: The initiative principally supports Australian educators to teach AI, including teachers without a technical background, through free professional learning and resources for primary and secondary classrooms. Its stated student-facing aims include building understanding of AI, critical thinking, responsible use, and capacity to become critical consumers and responsible creators of AI systems. CSER also connects AI understanding to future problem-solving, careers, workforce needs, and society; the inspected pages present these as related reasons for the work rather than establishing a single ranked priority. Sources: https://csermoocs.adelaide.edu.au/news/list/2025/05/08/teaching-artificial-intelligence ; https://csermoocs.adelaide.edu.au/professional-learning/artificial-intelligence-in-schools
educationalTechnologySummary: The inspected pages identify online MOOCs as the delivery format for CSER’s teacher courses, but do not name the learning platform or underlying software. CSER offers Experience AI, an educational programme co-developed by the Raspberry Pi Foundation and Google DeepMind, with materials localized by CSER for the Australian curriculum; the page identifies lesson plans, slides, worksheets, and videos, not a particular AI tool students must use. CSER’s National Lending Library provides classroom kits that include AI-powered platforms and kits named DelightEx and KaiLab, supported by CSER-developed lesson plans. The pages do not clarify the specific hardware or software in these kits, or whether CSER developed the named platforms. Source: https://csermoocs.adelaide.edu.au/professional-learning/artificial-intelligence-in-schools

inclusion.reason: AI-literacy content is explicit: the courses build understanding of AI, while Experience AI includes resources for exploring machine-learning models, applications, and AI’s social and ethical implications. CSER says the Australian Government Department of Education supported the AI in Schools program and the AI courses being freely available to Australian educators, meeting the government-support inclusion route. Sources: https://csermoocs.adelaide.edu.au/news/list/2025/05/08/teaching-artificial-intelligence and https://csermoocs.adelaide.edu.au/professional-learning/artificial-intelligence-in-schools. The pages do not establish adoption levels for these specific courses.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: Alberta Government – partnership with Amii on AI learning kits and framework for schools
metadata.Description: Three-year partnership between Alberta and the Alberta Machine Intelligence Institute to develop an AI framework and learning kits for schools; Alberta School Boards Association also published AI policy guidance.

summary: The Alberta government is partnering with the Alberta Machine Intelligence Institute (Amii) on a three-year effort to develop an AI framework and learning kits for schools. The available reporting also mentions an Amii-facilitated AI competency curriculum for early-childhood teachers and AI knowledge-and-skills training for students, though the relationship of these activities to the partnership is unclear. The initiative focuses on supporting AI learning and guiding its responsible use in education; its teaching methods and the materials’ reach are not specified.
pedagogicalSummary: The inspected article reports Alberta’s three-year partnership with the Alberta Machine Intelligence Institute (Amii) to develop a framework for schools, and mentions an AI competency curriculum for early-childhood teachers facilitated by Amii. It does not explain how that curriculum teaches, how learning is organised, or what activities or instructional methods it uses. The article’s references to AI as a “thinking partner” and to fostering critical thinking describe examples from other educators, not a stated Alberta–Amii teaching approach. metadata.Initiative / Programme: BC Ministry of Education and Child Care – "Considerations for Using AI Tools in K-12 Schools" and Digital Literacy & AI resources
metadata.Description: Framework with seven categories (incl. ethical uses, needs and impacts) to help districts select and manage AI tools, plus curriculum connections for digital literacy and AI use.

summary: The British Columbia Ministry of Education and Child Care provides a framework and related K–12 resources to help school districts and educators consider, select, and manage AI tools and support students’ AI-related digital literacy. The framework covers areas including ethical use, needs and impacts, and data security and privacy; accompanying curriculum materials connect AI learning with the province’s competency-driven curriculum and encourage critical reflection on responsible use. Classroom examples include discussion, analysis of AI-generated outputs, an unplugged machine-learning activity, and guided exploration of an online tool. The materials also support education leaders developing local procedures and policies.
pedagogicalSummary: The resources connect AI learning to B.C.’s concept-based, competency-driven “Know-Do-Understand” curriculum and encourage integrating it across subject areas, with flexibility for teachers’ instructional approaches. Suggested learning includes understanding AI concepts, critically considering ethical and social effects, and reflecting on responsible use. Classroom examples show varied methods: teacher explanation and videos, whole-class discussion, examining AI-generated examples, an unplugged paired game that models machine learning, and student reflection and formative assessment. One Grade 8 example also has students explore an online application and discuss what they learn from its errors. These examples support describing the pedagogy, but do not establish that every classroom uses the same approach. (https://www2.gov.bc.ca/assets/gov/education/administration/kindergarten-to-grade-12/ai-in-education/curriculum-connections-digital-literacy-and-the-use-of-ai.pdf; https://www2.gov.bc.ca/assets/gov/education/administration/kindergarten-to-grade-12/ai-in-education/adst-3-5-teaching-and-learning-story-what-is-ai-how-can-we-use-it-and-what-should-we-look-out-for.pdf; https://www2.gov.bc.ca/assets/gov/education/administration/kindergarten-to-grade-12/ai-in-education/adst-8-teaching-and-learning-story-what-is-ai-and-the-ethical-use-of-ai.pdf)
prioritySummary: The initiative’s evident emphasis is supporting safe, responsible, and informed AI use in K–12 education, particularly by helping students build AI-related digital literacy and make considered choices. Its curriculum materials connect this learning to critical thinking, ethics, and awareness of issues such as bias and privacy. The Ministry also describes resources for boards, school and district leaders, educators, support staff, families, and students, including help with local procedures and policies and materials for learning at school and home. The stated approach is human-centered: AI may complement teaching and support student-centered activities, while teachers make classroom-use decisions based on student needs and human relationships remain fundamental. The inspected pages indicate these priorities but do not establish a ranked hierarchy among audiences or aims. (https://www2.gov.bc.ca/gov/content/education-training/k-12/administration/program-management/ai-in-education; https://www2.gov.bc.ca/assets/gov/education/administration/kindergarten-to-grade-12/ai-in-education/curriculum-connections-digital-literacy-and-the-use-of-ai.pdf)
educationalTechnologySummary: The inspected materials identify classroom examples of technology use, but do not show that the Ministry develops a dedicated educational software platform or hardware for AI-literacy teaching. In a Grade 8 teaching story, a teacher has students try Quick, Draw! to observe machine-learning image recognition and demonstrates generative AI for text and images to examine bias, errors, and ethical questions; the specific generative AI products are not named. An Apple smartwatch is used as an explanatory example of AI-system functions, not identified as a learning device. The materials also describe slide presentations, videos, and an unplugged game; these support instruction but the game is a physical simulation rather than AI software. These are examples in teacher resources, not evidence that all participating schools use these tools. (https://www2.gov.bc.ca/assets/gov/education/administration/kindergarten-to-grade-12/ai-in-education/adst-8-teaching-and-learning-story-what-is-ai-and-the-ethical-use-of-ai.pdf; https://www2.gov.bc.ca/assets/gov/education/administration/kindergarten-to-grade-12/ai-in-education/adst-3-5-teaching-and-learning-story-what-is-ai-how-can-we-use-it-and-what-should-we-look-out-for.pdf)

inclusion.reason: The initiative is issued by a provincial government body (BC Ministry of Education), which satisfies the inclusion route for government-issued documents. It explicitly contains educational content and learning objectives by providing a detailed framework on 'how to' select, manage, and integrate AI tools in schools, covering ethical considerations, curriculum alignment, pedagogical use, and data literacy. This meets both the requirement for AI literacy (guidance on using AI) and the inclusion route for government endorsement.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: Ontario Trustworthy Artificial Intelligence (AI) Framework / Responsible Use of AI Directive
metadata.Description: Provincial government-wide framework and directive that currently serve as Ontario's main AI guidance; reported in 2025–26 sector papers as the Ministry of Education not having issued separate AI guidance to boards.

summary: Ontario’s Trustworthy Artificial Intelligence Framework sets principles and guidance for responsible AI use in provincial public programmes and services. Its Responsible Use of Artificial Intelligence Directive establishes requirements for Ontario ministries and provincial agencies, including risk management, disclosure and accountability; the framework is also presented as a model for other organizations in Ontario. It emphasizes transparency, safety, democratic principles and fundamental rights, with the aim of protecting people and businesses. The initiative is a policy and governance framework, not a teaching programme; the available evidence does not describe instructional methods or learning technologies.
pedagogicalSummary: The inspected framework page describes government policy and governance, not a teaching or AI-literacy programme. It does not set out lessons, learning activities, instructional methods, or learner support. The expert working group advises government on the framework, and the page notes a public consultation; these are policy-development activities rather than evidence of pedagogy. The page says the framework will include policies, products, and guidance, but does not describe them as teaching materials or explain how they support learning. Thus, no pedagogical approach is identifiable in the pages inspected; this is a limit of the available evidence, not proof that no related learning activities exist elsewhere. (https://www.ontario.ca/page/ontarios-trustworthy-artificial-intelligence-ai-framework)
prioritySummary: The initiative’s stated emphasis is setting rules for the safe, responsible, transparent, and accountable use of AI across Ontario government ministries and provincial agencies, particularly in public programmes and services. It aims to support innovation and improve service delivery while saving time and money, and to protect people and businesses in Ontario through risk management, disclosure, accountability, and attention to democratic principles and fundamental rights. Its stated priorities include making AI use visible, defining and preventing risks so people can trust its use, and learning more about decisions made with AI. The principal beneficiaries are therefore people and businesses served by government, alongside public bodies responsible for using AI. The page describes governance priorities rather than an AI-literacy learning objective. (https://www.ontario.ca/page/ontarios-trustworthy-artificial-intelligence-ai-framework)
educationalTechnologySummary: The inspected framework page does not identify any educational technology developed or used to teach AI literacy: it names no learning platform, instructional software, courseware, or hardware, and gives no account of technology supporting learner activities. It does refer to AI systems used by government and says the framework comprises policies, products, and guidance, but these are presented as components of public-sector governance, not as educational tools. The Responsible Use of Artificial Intelligence Directive sets requirements for government AI use, including risk management and disclosure; the available page description does not identify a learning technology within it. This conclusion is limited to the pages inspected and does not establish that no such resources exist elsewhere. (https://www.ontario.ca/page/ontarios-trustworthy-artificial-intelligence-ai-framework; https://www.ontario.ca/page/responsible-use-artificial-intelligence-directive)

inclusion.reason: The Directive provides guidance on how government bodies should use AI, including principles for considering AI systems and risk-management requirements. It is formally issued by the Ontario government, meeting the sub-national government route. Sources: https://www.ontario.ca/page/ontarios-trustworthy-artificial-intelligence-ai-framework and https://www.ontario.ca/page/responsible-use-artificial-intelligence-directive. The pages describe public-sector governance guidance, not a general AI-literacy curriculum; its scope as educational AI-literacy material is therefore limited.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: Conseil de l'innovation du Québec – report on AI (2024) and Quebec AI education guidance
metadata.Description: Quebec policy work cited by Canadian teacher federation scans as a provincial step on AI, including promoting digital literacy and critical thinking about AI across education levels.

summary: The Conseil de l’innovation du Québec’s 2024 “Prêt pour l’IA” report presents recommendations to the Québec government on responsible AI development and use. Informed by expert input, public contributions and a public forum, it addresses governance and innovation alongside AI’s effects on work, democracy, the environment, culture and public services. Its intended audiences include policymakers, organizations and other stakeholders. Education-related recommendations include training workers to adapt to AI and encouraging critical evaluation of AI-generated information; the report is policy guidance, not a learner-facing teaching programme, and does not specify instructional methods or learning technologies.
pedagogicalSummary: The inspected material describes a policy and consultation process, not a teaching programme. The Council gathered expert input, public contributions and views at a public forum to develop recommendations; these are deliberative methods for shaping policy, not evidence of a learner-facing pedagogy. Although the report’s five axes include “former” (training), the pages inspected do not establish specific teaching activities, learning sequences, or instructional methods for AI literacy. This is missing evidence in the inspected pages, not confirmation that no such activities exist. Sources: https://conseilinnovation.quebec/rapport-de-recommandations-pret-pour-lia/ and https://conseilinnovation.quebec/intelligence-artificielle/reflexion-collective/.
prioritySummary: The initiative’s stated central purpose is to guide the responsible development and use of AI in Quebec through recommendations to government, balancing innovation with safeguards and public benefit. Its approach is broad and societal: the Council describes an inclusive process intended to account for diverse voices, protect citizens, and help ensure AI benefits Quebec society. The work also recognizes economic and workplace priorities: the labour-and-employment theme seeks to help organizations and workers benefit from AI and productivity gains, while supporting worker well-being and reducing disruption to jobs and communities. The inspected evidence presents these as connected concerns rather than establishing a single narrower priority. Sources: https://conseilinnovation.quebec/rapport-de-recommandations-pret-pour-lia/ and https://conseilinnovation.quebec/intelligence-artificielle/reflexion-collective/thematique-4-impacts-de-lia-sur-le-travail-et-lemploi/.
educationalTechnologySummary: The inspected pages identify no platform, software, hardware, or other educational technology developed or used by the Council to support AI-literacy learning. The 2024 “Prêt pour l’IA” report and its associated pages address AI governance, responsible development and use, and policy recommendations; mention of AI as a technology is not evidence that the initiative uses AI tools for teaching. The website provides reports and thematic materials for consultation, but the inspected evidence does not describe them as a learning platform or specify learning functions. This is a limit of the pages inspected, not proof that no related tools exist elsewhere. Sources: https://conseilinnovation.quebec/wp-content/uploads/2024/02/Rapport_IA_CIQ-1.pdf and https://conseilinnovation.quebec/intelligence-artificielle/publications-de-la-reflexion-collective/.

inclusion.reason: The initiative includes clear AI-literacy elements: it recommends a comprehensive training program for workers to develop the skills needed to adapt to new technologies; encourages critical thinking about the information generated by AI (to avoid manipulation and misinformation); promotes transparent access to data and algorithms used in decision-making; supports research and innovation in ethics, governance and regulation of AI; and proposes multi-stakeholder dialogues and educational initiatives. The report is issued/endorsed by a Quebec government statutory body (Conseil de l'innovation du Québec), satisfying the inclusion route for government-endorsed work.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: National guidelines for responsible integration of AI in schools (Danish Ministry of Children and Education, Nov 2025) and recommendations for primary/lower secondary schools (2025)
metadata.Description: National Agency for Education and Quality (STUK) recommendations on generative AI in primary and lower secondary schools, reported by Eurydice as national guidelines for responsible integration.

summary: Published in 2025 by Denmark’s National Agency for Education and Quality under the Ministry of Children and Education, the recommendations guide school leaders, teachers, pedagogues, and boards on generative AI in primary and lower secondary education. They encourage using AI when it serves educational purposes, helping pupils reflect critically on its use, building staff competence, and agreeing on appropriate classroom use. They also address school-level governance, privacy compliance, and communication with parents; they are recommendations rather than detailed national integration guidelines or a specified teaching programme.
pedagogicalSummary: The recommendations describe a broad teaching approach rather than a specific instructional model: generative AI should support learning when it suits the educational purpose, and pupils should learn to reflect critically on its use. Teachers and pedagogical staff are encouraged to discuss the technology’s opportunities and limits, build their knowledge and teaching competence, and agree with pupils on when and how AI may be used in each subject. The article does not specify lesson formats, activities, or assessment methods, so more detailed pedagogical claims are not supported by the inspected evidence. Source: https://eurydice.eacea.ec.europa.eu/news/denmark-paving-way-ai-schools-national-guidelines-responsible-integration-education
prioritySummary: The initiative’s stated emphasis is to encourage responsible use of generative AI in primary and lower secondary education in ways that support learning and help pupils critically reflect on AI use. It also aims to guide school leaders, teachers, pedagogues, and boards in discussing and managing classroom use, including attention to GDPR compliance and communication with parents. The article presents recommendations, not detailed national integration guidelines; it says each school board remains responsible for approving teaching resources. The inspected page does not establish a separate workforce or economic priority. Source: https://eurydice.eacea.ec.europa.eu/news/denmark-paving-way-ai-schools-national-guidelines-responsible-integration-education
educationalTechnologySummary: The recommendations concern generative AI as a technology that schools may use in instruction, with use advised only when it fits educational purposes and with pupils discussing when and how it is appropriate in each subject. The inspected article names no particular AI platform, software, device, or learning system, and provides no evidence that the initiative develops an educational technology. It therefore supports describing the intended technology at the general level of generative AI, but not identifying specific tools or how their features support learning. The article also notes that the recommendations do not constitute detailed national guidelines for integration. Source: https://eurydice.eacea.ec.europa.eu/news/denmark-paving-way-ai-schools-national-guidelines-responsible-integration-education

metadata.Initiative / Programme: Recommendations for the use of generative AI in teaching in youth/upper secondary education (Nov 2024)
metadata.Description: STUK recommendations for upper secondary and vocational programmes, where students already use chatbots such as ChatGPT and Copilot.

summary: Denmark’s National Agency for Teaching and Quality (STUK), with the Ministry of Children and Education, issued recommendations for the use of generative AI in upper-secondary and vocational education. Aimed at school leaders, teachers and learners, including apprentices, the guidance encourages schools to establish shared rules and plan teaching in, with and without AI. It emphasizes safe and appropriate use, developing teachers’ AI-related knowledge and didactic competence, and helping students evaluate and qualify AI-generated content. ChatGPT and Copilot are cited as examples of tools students already use; the initiative does not provide its own technology.
pedagogicalSummary: The recommendations support deliberate pedagogical planning rather than prescribe a named teaching method. They call for school leaders and teachers to plan teaching in, with, and without generative AI, and for students to learn to use it appropriately and evaluate and qualify AI-produced content. Teacher dialogue and exchange of experience, alongside development of teachers’ AI-related didactic competence, are also encouraged. The accessible page cuts off partway through the planning recommendations, so the specific practices that follow cannot be confirmed. Source: https://www.cedefop.europa.eu/en/tools/timeline-vet-policies-europe/search/49480
prioritySummary: The initiative principally aims to help schools organise appropriate use of generative AI in upper-secondary and vocational education, benefiting both learners and education professionals. It responds to students’ use of chatbots in teaching and schoolwork, sometimes without sufficient reflection, and to teachers’ difficulty navigating the technology’s effects on teaching. Recommendations therefore emphasize shared school rules and direction, safe use, teacher knowledge and skills, and using AI where it can strengthen learning and digital education. The page identifies school leaders and teachers as needing guidance and includes learners, including apprentices, among the target groups; it does not establish a narrower priority or hierarchy. Source: https://www.cedefop.europa.eu/en/tools/timeline-vet-policies-europe/search/49480
educationalTechnologySummary: The page identifies generative AI chatbots already used by students, specifically ChatGPT and Microsoft Copilot, during teaching and schoolwork. It presents recommendations for governing and planning their use, including a recommendation that school leadership choose solutions compliant with current GDPR rules. It does not say that STUK develops an educational technology, nor does it identify a learning platform, software product, or hardware provided by the initiative. The named chatbots are examples of tools in the educational context, not evidence that the initiative itself supplies or deploys them. The accessible page provides no further detail about particular learning technologies. Source: https://www.cedefop.europa.eu/en/tools/timeline-vet-policies-europe/search/49480

inclusion.reason: The initiative meets the AI-literacy requirement because it provides explicit educational objectives on evaluating and appropriately using generative AI, and satisfies an inclusion route via endorsement by a national ministry (Ministry of Children and Education) and implementation through a statutory national agency (STUK).

metadata.Initiative / Programme: Practical guide on lawful and responsible use of AI in education (Ministry of Children and Education, Jan 2026)
metadata.Description: Guide helping educational institutions use AI lawfully in teaching, administration and student support while building learners' digital skills.

summary: Published by Denmark’s Ministry of Children and Education in January 2026, this practical guide helps educational institutions use AI lawfully and responsibly in teaching, administration and student support. It addresses issues such as data protection, copyright, transparency and institutional responsibilities, and encourages clear local rules for AI use in teaching, assignments and exams. The guide also aims to support learners’ critical and responsible AI skills, including in preparation for AI-integrated workplaces; no specific course structure or teaching method is described.
pedagogicalSummary: The inspected page describes practical legal guidance, not a defined teaching method or structured course. The guide reportedly offers explanations and everyday examples for education and training institutions, and encourages local rules for AI use in assignments, exams and teaching. It frames AI integration as potentially pedagogically meaningful when transparent and governed by clear expectations, with the aim of helping learners develop critical and responsible AI competences. The page does not specify instructional sequences, learner activities, assessment methods or educator training, so evidence for a particular pedagogy is limited. Source: https://www.cedefop.europa.eu/en/news/denmark-new-guide-supports-lawful-use-ai
prioritySummary: The initiative’s stated emphasis is enabling educational institutions to use AI lawfully and responsibly in teaching, administration and student support, rather than discouraging its use. It addresses institutions’ and educators’ need to understand data protection, copyright, transparency and responsibilities, while also supporting students’ critical and responsible AI competences. The page connects this learning to digital skills and preparation for AI-integrated workplaces, particularly in vocational education and training, and notes safeguarding students’ and staff’s rights. It presents these aims together without establishing a single dominant beneficiary or priority. Source: https://www.cedefop.europa.eu/en/news/denmark-new-guide-supports-lawful-use-ai
educationalTechnologySummary: The inspected page does not identify a learning platform, software product or hardware developed by the initiative, nor does it establish that the ministry itself uses particular AI tools to teach. It names learning platforms, automated feedback tools and generative-AI assistants as examples of systems that may process personal data in educational settings; these examples illustrate legal considerations, not technologies the initiative provides. The guide is described as a practical resource for deciding when and how AI tools may be used, but the page gives no details about its format or any accompanying digital learning technology. Thus, evidence supports discussion of AI tools, but not a specific educational technology developed or deployed by the initiative. Source: https://www.cedefop.europa.eu/en/news/denmark-new-guide-supports-lawful-use-ai

inclusion.reason: The initiative is explicitly endorsed by a national government ministry (Denmark's Ministry of Children and Education), which satisfies the inclusion route for government endorsement. It includes AI literacy content by focusing on lawful and responsible AI use in education and building learners' digital skills, meeting the requirement for educational guidance about how to use AI. No exclusion criteria apply.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: Vittascience IA – AI modules, kits and teacher resources (Vittascience)
metadata.Description: French edtech platform whose AI strand lets pupils (primary to university) train and test models for image and text classification, sentiment analysis, image generation and speech synthesis, and deploy them to micro:bit, Arduino Nicla Vision or Raspberry Pi Pico boards. Offers hundreds of Creative Commons teacher resources, a micro:bit AI user guide, webinars and an embedded-AI kit (with STMicroelectronics); accessible via the national GAR system; supported by the Ministry's Édu-up scheme; the company reports 330,000+ annual users.

summary: Vittascience IA is a French educational platform for learners from preschool through higher education, with resources for teachers. Its browser-based tools let learners build, train and test image, sound, posture, text and sensor-data models, explore how models make decisions, and create text, images and speech. Learners can also use models with programming tools such as Python and Adacraft and with supported microcontrollers and kits. Tutorials, videos, webinars and teacher resources support hands-on inquiry into AI’s capabilities, workings and societal and environmental implications.
pedagogicalSummary: The accessible pages show a practical, exploratory approach: learners can supply examples, train and test image, sound, posture, hand-sign or sensor-data models, then inspect decision “influence zones” and the neural-network structure. Tutorials, videos and a webinar support use of the tools, while community resources include a mini-game activity in which learners train an image- or posture-recognition model and test it. Text- and image-generation interfaces also pair making with prompts to investigate how AI works and its environmental issues. This supports hands-on experimentation and guided inquiry, though the inspected pages do not establish a single formal teaching sequence or assessment method. Sources: https://fr.vittascience.com/ia/ ; https://fr.vittascience.com/ia/images ; https://fr.vittascience.com/ia/text ; https://fr.vittascience.com/learn/
prioritySummary: The clearest stated priority is making AI accessible for learners from kindergarten through higher education, by letting them experiment with AI models and explore how they work. The offer spans model training, programming and use of models on physical boards, as well as activities for exploring AI’s potential, challenges and environmental implications. A community resource connects AI learning to a practical health-related example—breast-cancer detection—and the “Future of IA” experience is described as exploring AI in service of public-interest missions. These indicate educational access and understanding, with some societal applications; the pages do not establish workforce upskilling or individual well-being as primary goals. Sources: https://fr.vittascience.com/ia/ ; https://fr.vittascience.com/ia/text ; https://fr.vittascience.com/learn/
educationalTechnologySummary: Vittascience presents its own browser-based AI interfaces for training classification models on images, postures, hands, sounds and sensor data, and for generating text, images and speech. The training interface supports adding categories and examples, training and visualizing models, and exporting or using them with Adacraft (described as derived from Scratch), Python or a microcontroller; sensor data can be used with micro:bit. The site also describes kits that connect trained models to micro:bit or to a Wio Lite AI board. Text generation identifies Mistral Small 3 and access to models including Mistral AI and OpenAI; image generation lists FLUX and Stable Diffusion. The pages inspected do not detail the full hardware range. Sources: https://fr.vittascience.com/ia/ ; https://fr.vittascience.com/ia/images ; https://fr.vittascience.com/ia/sensors ; https://fr.vittascience.com/ia/text ; https://fr.vittascience.com/ia/image-generate

inclusion.reason: The initiative includes clear AI literacy elements such as tutorials on neural network structure ('Réseau de neurones'), explanations of how AI makes decisions ('visualisez des zones d'interaction'), and educational content about different AI capabilities. It qualifies under the inclusion route for government endorsement/support via the Édu-up scheme from the French Ministry of National Education, which is a statutory body. The metadata confirms it's part of the national GAR system. Although adoption scale (330,000+ users) appears in metadata, this page alone provides sufficient evidence of AI literacy content and government support to warrant inclusion.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: Eduscol – shared academic work on AI teaching scenarios (Direction du numérique pour l'éducation)
metadata.Description: Multi-academy project producing classroom scenarios and training modules on AI (everyday life, identity, societal impact), including tools usable from cycle 3 to run machine-learning models on micro:bit; further academies can join and contribute.

summary: Eduscol’s Direction du numérique pour l’éducation describes a two-year, multi-academy project developing AI classroom scenarios and teacher-training resources for French schools, with participating academies including Amiens, Nice, Toulouse, Besançon, Nancy-Metz and Créteil. Aimed at pupils from cycle 3 upward, the project combines hands-on activities—such as building and using machine-learning models with tools including Teachable Machine, mBlock and micro:bit—with discussion of AI in everyday life, societal issues, bias and personal data. Its project-based approach connects AI to topics such as health and sustainable development; self-paced m@gistère training modules were planned to support teachers’ use of the resources.
pedagogicalSummary: The report describes active, project-oriented learning: classroom scenarios have students build and use machine-learning models to explore practical or societal problems, including health and sustainable development. It explicitly links using AI to address an identified need with a project approach and active pedagogy. Activities also aim to help students understand how models work and examine algorithmic bias and the handling of personal data. The initiative’s two-year structure includes academic teams first producing classroom resources and then developing teacher-training modules; the report says self-paced m@gistère courses of up to two hours were planned to support implementation. This summary is based on the inspected report, not a review of the individual scenarios or courses, so details of lesson sequences are limited. Source: https://eduscol.education.fr/document/43246/download
prioritySummary: The report’s central emphasis is to help students understand and demystify AI technologies they encounter in everyday life, while supporting digital citizenship and informed consideration of data use. It also prioritizes applying AI to current societal issues, particularly health and sustainable development, and presents technology as something that should serve the common good. A further stated aim is to give learners keys to understanding machine-learning models and potentially introduce them to future AI-related careers. Teachers are also beneficiaries: the project develops classroom resources and planned self-paced training to help them implement the scenarios. The inspected report identifies these aims but does not establish a single ranked priority among them. Source: https://eduscol.education.fr/document/43246/download
educationalTechnologySummary: The report identifies several technologies used in the classroom scenarios: mBlock 5, Teachable Machine and Adacraft for introducing AI or addressing societal problems, and VittaScience and Micropal among tools shared between academies for implementing machine-learning models. It also describes using models on micro:bit boards, with tools accessible from cycle 3, and mentions computers, tablets, smartphones, webcams and microphones as equipment selected for activities. The report describes these as tools used or shared, not as products developed by the initiative. It also says self-paced teacher courses were to be made available through m@gistère; the inspected text does not specify their technical features. Individual tool links and scenarios were not examined, so their precise learning functions are only described at the level given in the report. Source: https://eduscol.education.fr/document/43246/download

inclusion.reason: The initiative is issued by the Direction du numérique pour l'éducation (digital education direction) of the French Ministry of Education, which qualifies under the national government inclusion route. It includes educational content about how AI works (e.g., demystifying AI, understanding machine learning models), societal impact topics, and practical tools for implementation in classrooms. The project has been implemented across multiple French academies with planned training modules via m@gistère, indicating system-scale adoption within the French education system.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: KI-Campus (AI Campus) – free AI courses, videos, podcasts and tools (Stifterverband)
metadata.Description: Non-profit learning platform for AI skills; all offers free and own courses under CC BY-SA 4.0. Began as a BMBF-funded pilot in 2019 (platform live 2020); 30+ partner institutions from Germany and Luxembourg; dedicated projects for university AI competences.

summary: KI-Campus (AI Campus) is a free digital learning platform led by the German non-profit Stifterverband, offering AI courses, videos, podcasts and other learning resources. It serves learners across schools, universities, workplaces, public administration and the wider public, with material ranging from AI fundamentals to professional and discipline-specific applications, including machine learning, generative AI, ethics and legal contexts. Its practice-oriented, flexible learning offer includes assessed activities and credentials such as certificates and micro-degrees; Moodle supports course delivery and integration into university teaching.
pedagogicalSummary: AI Campus offers free, digital learning in multiple formats—online courses, videos and podcasts—intended for flexible, self-paced study and a range of prior knowledge levels. Its stated approach is practice-oriented, with offerings tailored to disciplines and professional groups; the inspected pages show examples for higher education, medicine, schools and public administration. Courses may include assessed tasks, and learners can earn participation confirmations, achievement records or micro-degrees, providing structured recognition of learning. The initiative also encourages integration of openly licensed materials into university curricula and teaching. These pages describe a varied, adaptable learning offer, but do not establish a single teaching method or provide enough detail to characterize the instructional design of individual courses. (https://ki-campus.org/en/about-us; https://ki-campus.org/en/learning-opportunities; https://ki-campus.org/en/ai-certificates; https://ki-campus.org/en/target-groups/universities)
prioritySummary: The initiative’s stated aim is to strengthen AI skills broadly through free digital learning, with the vision of an AI-competent society. It serves individuals as well as universities, companies and public administrations, and describes content for learners from foundational to specialized levels. The pages also identify concrete institutional and work-related aims: supporting employee training and practical workplace use, enabling university teaching and curricular integration, and helping public-sector staff understand legal requirements and relevant applications. A distinct higher-education priority is to embed AI competencies in study, teaching and administration across German institutions. The inspected evidence therefore supports several connected priorities—broad access, professional development and institutional uptake—without establishing that one beneficiary group takes precedence overall. (https://ki-campus.org/en/about-us; https://ki-campus.org/en/target-groups; https://ki-campus.org/en/about-us/projects)
educationalTechnologySummary: AI Campus operates a digital learning platform for its AI-literacy offer. Its About page identifies Moodle as the learning management system, operated by FernUniversität in Hagen; the university-targeted page says the Moodle environment supports integration of courses into university teaching, and the certificates page says credentials can be downloaded there. The initiative provides online courses alongside educational videos and podcasts, and its overview also refers to tools, although the inspected pages do not identify those tools or explain their learning functions. The offer includes partner-produced material; the projects page, for example, describes joint learning opportunities and IBM SkillsBuild certificates on AI Campus. The accessible evidence identifies the platform and formats, but not specific software or hardware beyond Moodle. (https://ki-campus.org/en/about-us; https://ki-campus.org/en/target-groups/universities; https://ki-campus.org/en/ai-certificates; https://ki-campus.org/en/about-us/projects)

inclusion.reason: The initiative includes clear AI literacy content through its range of educational materials covering AI fundamentals, practical applications, and related legal/ethical contexts. It qualifies under the inclusion route for government/statutory body involvement: the platform originated as a BMBF-funded pilot in 2019 (BMBF is a German federal ministry), aligns with the Stifterverband's federally supported 'Zukunftsmission Bildung' education mission, and operates within Germany's national context. Additionally, it demonstrates system-scale adoption with over 200,000 learners and partnerships across more than 30 institutions in Germany and Luxembourg.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: Calliope mini – AI (KI) teaching units and KI-Training tool (Calliope gGmbH)
metadata.Description: Non-profit behind the Calliope mini microcontroller (used in 7,000+ German schools since 2017). Its schools section includes AI teaching materials, training courses and a browser-based KI-Training tool where pupils generate data, train a model and run it on the board via Web-USB/Bluetooth.

summary: Calliope gGmbH’s AI learning resources for schools help students explore how machine learning uses data to make decisions. In the browser-based KI-Training activity, learners collect movement data, train and review a model, and use it in a MakeCode project on a Calliope mini microcontroller. The broader offering also describes an unplugged role-play activity and other web-based projects, with reflection on data quality, bias, reliability, and AI’s opportunities and limitations. Calliope also offers online sessions for educators; the available evidence does not establish how the materials are sequenced across a curriculum.
pedagogicalSummary: The initiative emphasizes hands-on, experiential learning: students record movement data, train a model, test its decisions, and apply it in a prototype using the Calliope mini. The questions about changing data, errors, bias, and prediction reliability support investigation and reflection rather than treating AI as a black box. The broader AI page also describes an unplugged role-play game in which learners act as data, algorithms, or machines, followed by discussion of AI’s opportunities and limitations. These pages support practical and inquiry-based approaches, including both digital projects and an analog activity; they do not establish how lessons are sequenced across a curriculum. (https://calliope.cc/en/school/ai/ki-training; https://calliope.cc/en/school/ai)
prioritySummary: The stated emphasis is building students’ foundational understanding of AI and machine learning through school activities. The materials focus on how data, training, and decision-making affect model behavior, including the influence of faulty, incomplete, or biased data and the reliability of predictions. The broader AI page frames this understanding as preparation for a digital future and encourages consideration of the technology’s opportunities and limitations. The pages also describe free online sessions for educators, but do not specify a workforce-upskilling goal or establish a hierarchy among broader societal benefits. The clearest evidenced beneficiaries are students, with some support also offered to educators. (https://calliope.cc/en/school/ai/ki-training; https://calliope.cc/en/school/ai)
educationalTechnologySummary: The KI-Training activity combines a browser-based tool with the Calliope mini microcontroller: students collect movement data, train and review a model, then transfer it into a MakeCode program to run on the board. The page specifies Web-USB for preparing the board and Web-Bluetooth for connecting it to the training tool, with a compatible browser required for Web-USB. The broader AI page also presents Calliope Teachable Machine as a web app for training and programming a model, HuskyLens as an intelligent camera for recognition projects, and a browser-based Face Tracking App that communicates with the board over Bluetooth. The inspected pages identify these technologies but do not clarify which are developed in-house versus provided by others. (https://calliope.cc/en/school/ai/ki-training; https://calliope.cc/en/school/ai)

inclusion.reason: The initiative includes AI literacy through direct educational content: pupils actively learn how AI works by generating data and training models, fulfilling the AI-literacy requirement. Additionally, it meets the inclusion route of 'non-government work with evidenced system-scale adoption' as the Calliope mini microcontroller is used in 7,000+ German schools since 2017, indicating large-scale adoption across an educational sector.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: App Camps – teaching materials on programming with AI
metadata.Description: German education non-profit offering free classroom units on AI, including programming simple AI applications, alongside materials on data protection and media literacy.

summary: App Camps ist eine deutsche Bildungsorganisation, die Lehrkräften und weiteren Gruppenleitungen kostenlose Unterrichtsmaterialien zu KI und maschinellem Lernen für Schüler:innen der Primar- und Sekundarstufe anbietet. Die Einheiten verbinden kurze Einführungsvideos und selbstständige, oft teamorientierte Projektarbeit mit kritischer Reflexion. Lernende erkunden unter anderem, wie KI-Modelle funktionieren, trainieren einfache Modelle und programmieren Chatbots oder andere Anwendungen mit Werkzeugen wie Scratch, App Inventor und Python. Weitere Themen sind generative KI, Bias, Ethik sowie gesellschaftliche und ökologische Auswirkungen.
pedagogicalSummary: App Camps combines theoretical introductions with practical, exploratory activities: students discuss what intelligence means, examine machine-learning concepts, experiment with generative AI, and train or program simple AI applications. The page describes each lesson as beginning with a short introductory video, followed by students working independently and at their own pace in small teams using learning cards, and ending with a video featuring practitioners. Activities include creating stories or comics with generative AI, examining bias, and building chatbots. The approach also includes critical reflection on AI’s uses and effects, alongside problem-solving and project work. These features are described on the initiative’s AI teaching-materials page: https://appcamps.de/unterrichtsmaterial/kuenstliche-intelligenz/. The inspection did not establish how consistently each format is used across all listed lessons.
prioritySummary: The initiative’s stated emphasis is to give school students practical and theoretical foundations in AI and machine learning so they can understand the technology and better assess its opportunities and risks. Materials address a broad range of learners, with recommendations spanning primary and secondary levels, and are intended for teachers as well as people running extracurricular workshops or groups. Topics and activities include AI in everyday life, creative uses, bias, ethics, environmental effects, and changes to work, so the page presents both technical understanding and critical consideration of social consequences rather than a single narrow goal. App Camps says its materials are free for teachers. Evidence for these aims and audiences appears on https://appcamps.de/unterrichtsmaterial/kuenstliche-intelligenz/; the inspected page does not specify which priority takes precedence when these aims intersect.
educationalTechnologySummary: The page identifies several technologies used in learning activities: Scratch, App Inventor, and Python for programming characters and chatbots; Teachable Machine for training an image-recognition model; and ML4Kids with Scratch for training models using students’ voices or drawings. It also mentions generative text and image AI tools, a chatbot, and Zeoob for simulating a fake social-media post. These tools support hands-on exploration and application of AI concepts. The lesson collections are linked via fobizz, while the page describes digital materials, learning cards, and start and closing videos as instructional supports. It does not identify a proprietary educational technology developed by App Camps; the extent to which any named tool is required or offered directly by App Camps is not clear from the inspected page: https://appcamps.de/unterrichtsmaterial/kuenstliche-intelligenz/.

inclusion.reason: Die Seite beschreibt konkrete KI-Lerninhalte, darunter Grundlagen des maschinellen Lernens, Funktionsweisen generativer KI, Bias, Chancen und Risiken sowie praktische Übungen. Die Materialien richten sich an Lehrkräfte und Schüler:innen und sind kostenlos; dadurch ist eine Nutzung über einzelne Einrichtungen hinaus plausibel. Die Seite belegt jedoch weder formelle staatliche Unterstützung noch eine systemweite oder zahlenmäßig belegte Adoption. Angesichts des breiten Unterrichtsziels ist dies ein plausibler, aber unsicherer Weg zur Aufnahme. Quelle: https://appcamps.de/unterrichtsmaterial/kuenstliche-intelligenz/

metadata.Initiative / Programme: Coding for Tomorrow – AI teaching materials ("So funktioniert Künstliche Intelligenz")
metadata.Description: Non-profit's free lesson concepts on how AI works, applications and potential in education, including the unit 'KI für den guten Zweck' on AI in nature conservation.

summary: Coding for Tomorrow is a German non-profit initiative offering free AI teaching resources for schools and educators, including lesson concepts and self-learning materials for students. The materials combine practical activities—such as exploring machine learning with identification apps or programming in Scratch—with discussion of AI’s everyday uses, limitations, bias, misinformation, ethics, and social and environmental effects. The listed resources span foundational AI concepts and responsible, critical use; the evidence describes a varied offering but does not establish its uptake or audience size.
pedagogicalSummary: The initiative presents AI literacy through free classroom lesson concepts that combine practical exploration with reflection. The overview describes hands-on or applied activities such as programming a face filter in Scratch, exploring how machine learning may help with waste sorting, and using animal and plant identification apps to illustrate machine learning. Other concepts ask students to reflect on their everyday AI use, assess whether chatbot responses are helpful, identify fake news and bias, and discuss ethical dilemmas. A self-learning unit is also listed. This suggests experiential learning alongside critical discussion, rather than instruction in technology alone. The accessible pages list activities but do not provide enough lesson-level detail to establish a consistent sequence or teaching method. (https://coding-for-tomorrow.de/kuenstliche-intelligenz/; https://coding-for-tomorrow.de/alle-materialien/)
prioritySummary: The AI materials aim to help school students understand AI’s fundamentals, opportunities, limitations, and challenges, and consider its role in everyday life and the future. Their emphasis includes practical AI literacy and responsible, critical use: listed topics include checking deepfakes and misinformation, examining bias, reflecting on AI companions and chatbots, and considering ethical dilemmas. The initiative also connects AI to social and environmental benefit, including a concept on AI for nature conservation and one on smart recycling. Its broader mission stresses enabling people to shape a fairer, more sustainable world, with attention to equal access, inclusion, and educational opportunity. The inspected pages do not indicate that workforce upskilling is the principal aim of these school materials. (https://coding-for-tomorrow.de/kuenstliche-intelligenz/; https://coding-for-tomorrow.de/unsere-mission/)
educationalTechnologySummary: The pages identify technologies used as learning tools or examples, but do not identify a proprietary educational technology developed by the initiative. The AI lesson overview specifically mentions programming an AI face filter in Scratch, a virtual 3D city for exploring ethical dilemmas, animal and plant identification apps, chatbots, image generators, and neural networks in a waste-sorting activity. These support programming, exploration, and examination of AI applications and their consequences. The broader materials collection also names Scratch, Delightex, and Makey Makey as digital classroom tools, although it does not establish that all are used in the AI lessons. The initiative describes its teaching resources as free OER, including concepts, explanatory videos, lesson plans, learning cards, and printables; the inspected pages do not detail the specific software or devices required for each lesson. (https://coding-for-tomorrow.de/kuenstliche-intelligenz/; https://coding-for-tomorrow.de/materialsammlungen/; https://coding-for-tomorrow.de/alle-materialien/)

metadata.Initiative / Programme: TU Dresden – AI teaching materials and tool collection for school informatics
metadata.Description: University didactics group's curated collection of AI tools and lessons: online applications (e.g. Machine Learning for Kids, TensorFlow Playground, Moral Machine, 'I AM A.I.') and programs (Orange3, Lobe, MNIST in Python), with some exercises linked to Elements of AI.

summary: TU Dresden’s EduInf initiative provides AI teaching and learning materials, tool recommendations, and workshops for school-age learners, with resources also useful to teachers. Aimed at developing informatics and AI understanding, it combines hands-on activities in which pupils train and test models with unplugged activities, games, programming exercises, and discussion of AI’s social and ethical implications. The collection recommends third-party applications and software; it also includes project-created open educational resources, such as a machine-learning museum-app activity.
pedagogicalSummary: The accessible materials point to a practical, learner-active approach: pupils experiment with AI tools, train or test models, and in some lessons build and iteratively improve their own models. For example, the EduInf “intelligent museum app” workshop follows a simplified machine-learning workflow, with learners selecting training data, testing a model, and distinguishing training from use. The collection also includes unplugged activities, games, programming exercises, and discussion-oriented resources, including activities about AI’s possibilities and desirability. These indicate varied ways to explore concepts rather than a single prescribed method; the pages do not establish how consistently each resource is taught in practice. Sources: https://tu-dresden.de/ing/informatik/smt/ddi/schulinformatik/eduinf-education_in_informatics/lehr-lern-material/kuenstliche-intelligenz/kuenstliche-intelligenz-lehr-lern-material-eduinf ; https://tu-dresden.de/ing/informatik/smt/ddi/schulinformatik/eduinf-education_in_informatics/lehr-lern-material/kuenstliche-intelligenz/copy_of_unterrichtsmaterial ; https://tu-dresden.de/ing/informatik/smt/ddi/schulinformatik/eduinf-education_in_informatics/lehr-lern-material/kuenstliche-intelligenz/copy_of_tools
prioritySummary: The clearest emphasis is supporting school-age learners’ computer-science and AI understanding through workshops and accessible teaching and learning materials. EduInf describes free workshops for school classes, generally for children and young people from grade 3 upward, intended to spark interest in computer science; its AI material page explicitly frames the resources as helping children and young people develop informatics competencies related to AI. The collection also serves teachers by making teaching resources available, including open educational materials, and some listed resources address AI’s social implications or classroom use. The inspected pages support these aims but do not establish a single ranked priority beyond school learning and engagement. Sources: https://tu-dresden.de/ing/informatik/smt/ddi/schulinformatik/eduinf-education_in_informatics ; https://tu-dresden.de/ing/informatik/smt/ddi/schulinformatik/eduinf-education_in_informatics/lehr-lern-material/kuenstliche-intelligenz/copy_of_unterrichtsmaterial ; https://tu-dresden.de/ing/informatik/smt/ddi/schulinformatik/eduinf-education_in_informatics/lehr-lern-material/kuenstliche-intelligenz/kuenstliche-intelligenz-lehr-lern-material-eduinf
educationalTechnologySummary: The initiative’s tools page is a curated collection, not evidence that TU Dresden developed each listed technology. It recommends browser-based and installed tools for learners to experiment with AI, including Teachable Machine and Machine Learning for Kids for training models, TensorFlow Playground for visualizing neural-network training, and Orange3, Lobe, and MemBrain for machine-learning or neural-network work. Other listed examples include games and simulations for reinforcement learning, classification, and image recognition, as well as Python libraries and datasets such as PyCaret and MNIST. The EduInf materials page does identify project-created open educational resources for a museum-app activity, in which pupils create, test, and apply a machine-learning model; it does not identify a developed software platform for that activity. Sources: https://tu-dresden.de/ing/informatik/smt/ddi/schulinformatik/eduinf-education_in_informatics/lehr-lern-material/kuenstliche-intelligenz/copy_of_tools ; https://tu-dresden.de/ing/informatik/smt/ddi/schulinformatik/eduinf-education_in_informatics/lehr-lern-material/kuenstliche-intelligenz/kuenstliche-intelligenz-lehr-lern-material-eduinf
