metadata.Initiative / Programme: AI Literacy Learning Framework for Primary and Secondary Schools and Guide to Using AI in Teaching (supplements to the Blueprint)
metadata.Description: Supplement 1 sets rationale, learning focuses per key stage and examples for integrating AI education; Supplement 2 guides the use of AI in teaching. EDB also offers an 'AI Literacy for Teachers' course via EdCity.

summary: Hong Kong’s Education Bureau provides an AI Literacy Learning Framework for primary and secondary schools and a companion guide to using AI in teaching, as supplements to its digital education Blueprint. The framework sets learning focuses for different school stages, offers illustrative integration scenarios and assessment recommendations, and supports schools in planning curriculum-based implementation suited to their contexts. The guide outlines principles and considerations for using AI in learning, teaching and assessment. Teacher briefings, school-sharing activities and an AI Literacy for Teachers course provide additional implementation support.
pedagogicalSummary: The accessible materials describe a curriculum-wide approach rather than a specific classroom teaching method. The AI Literacy Learning Framework sets learning focuses for different school key stages, gives illustrative application scenarios, and recommends assessment of AI literacy; schools are expected to integrate AI education into their curricula and plan implementation in light of their contexts. A companion guide sets principles for teachers’ use of AI and highlights considerations in learning, teaching, and assessment. The EDB also describes teacher briefings and school sharing as implementation support. These sources indicate staged, curriculum-integrated learning supported by guidance and assessment, but do not establish particular methods such as project-based learning or direct instruction. The framework and guide are described at https://applications.edb.gov.hk/circular/upload/EDBC/EDBC26011E.pdf and listed at https://www.edb.gov.hk/en/edu-system/primary-secondary/applicable-to-primary-secondary/it-in-edu/debp.html; the detailed supplements were not inspected here.
prioritySummary: The initiative’s central AI-literacy emphasis is comprehensive AI education for primary and secondary students: the circular explicitly frames the direction as “AI for all schools” and “AI for all students,” with the stated goal of comprehensively enhancing students’ AI literacy. It also aims to build teachers’ capacity, support school-level planning and AI-empowered learning and teaching, and improve education quality. The broader Blueprint additionally names educational equity, innovative talent development, and contribution to Hong Kong’s and the nation’s education ambitions. These are policy aims, while the materials also identify practical support for schools, including funding and teacher training. The evidence supports a student-centered system-wide priority alongside teacher and school support, rather than a single workforce or individual well-being objective. Sources: https://applications.edb.gov.hk/circular/upload/EDBC/EDBC26011E.pdf and https://www.edb.gov.hk/en/edu-system/primary-secondary/applicable-to-primary-secondary/it-in-edu/debp.html.
educationalTechnologySummary: The inspected materials do not identify a named AI product, software platform, device, or learning technology developed or adopted by the initiative. They describe AI as both a subject of education and something teachers may use in learning, teaching, and assessment; the companion guide provides principles and areas for attention, and the framework includes illustrative AI application scenarios. The EDB webpage consolidates digital-education resources for schools, but the inspected text does not specify a platform or explain a particular technology’s learning function. The circular also refers broadly to educational infrastructure and resource hubs, without naming technologies. Thus, evidence supports guidance on AI use and resource provision, but not a specific educational technology developed or used; this is a limit of the inspected pages, not confirmation that none exist. Sources: https://applications.edb.gov.hk/circular/upload/EDBC/EDBC26011E.pdf and https://www.edb.gov.hk/en/edu-system/primary-secondary/applicable-to-primary-secondary/it-in-edu/debp.html.

inclusion.reason: The initiative includes clear AI literacy components: learning objectives (learning focuses), educational content (examples for integration), and guidance on using AI in teaching. It is issued by the Education Bureau of Hong Kong SAR, a statutory government body of the HKSAR, satisfying the inclusion route for government endorsement. The metadata confirms it is a supplement to a Blueprint, further indicating formal official status.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: EdUHK AIDCEC – CoolThink curriculum Level 3 "Understanding AI" unit (PICaboo)
metadata.Description: Curriculum files hosted by The Education University of Hong Kong's AI and data-driven learning centre include a unit outline where students train an image classifier with App Inventor's Personal Image Classifier and explain the five Big Ideas of AI.

summary: PICaboo is a Level 3 unit in the CoolThink computational-thinking curriculum for primary-school students in Hong Kong. Using App Inventor’s Personal Image Classifier, students collect and label image examples, train and test a classifier, and build a Peekaboo app, while exploring image classification and the five Big Ideas of AI. The unit combines hands-on app development and computational thinking with explanations of how AI systems work. CoolThink materials have broad school-system reach, though the evidence does not establish how widely this particular unit is taught.
pedagogicalSummary: The PICaboo unit appears to combine hands-on learning with conceptual explanation: students train an image classifier and explain the five Big Ideas of AI. This suggests learning through making and examining an AI system, rather than only studying AI as a topic. The accessible evidence identifies the unit as part of CoolThink@JC’s Level 3 Computational Thinking Development materials, but does not show enough detail to establish whether activities are guided, collaborative, or assessed in a particular way. The PDF’s full text could not be inspected here, so those aspects remain unclear. (https://www.aidcec.eduhk.hk/wp-content/uploads/coolthink_curriculum/level3/L3UAI2%20PICaboo/Eng/CF3E_L3UAI2_UnitOutline.pdf)
prioritySummary: The unit’s evident emphasis is introducing AI concepts and practice to learners within a Level 3 computational-thinking education programme. Its combination of training an image classifier and explaining AI’s Big Ideas points to building students’ understanding of how AI works, alongside computational-thinking learning. The inspected material does not establish a more specific priority, such as workforce preparation or individual well-being, or identify a particular student age group. The PDF cover identifies it as CoolThink@JC Computational Thinking Development Level 3; the available unit description indicates the AI-learning focus. Further programme materials were not accessible during this inspection, so broader priorities cannot be confirmed. (https://www.aidcec.eduhk.hk/wp-content/uploads/coolthink_curriculum/level3/L3UAI2%20PICaboo/Eng/CF3E_L3UAI2_UnitOutline.pdf)
educationalTechnologySummary: The unit uses App Inventor’s Personal Image Classifier as a learning tool: students train an image classifier as part of the PICaboo activity. This gives learners a practical way to engage with an AI system while studying the unit’s AI concepts. The available evidence supports describing the classifier as a technology used in the activity; it does not establish that the initiative developed the tool. No other educational software, platforms, or hardware could be confirmed from the inspected material. The PDF is identified as a CoolThink@JC Level 3 unit outline, but its full text was not accessible for review, limiting detail on how the tool is integrated into instruction. metadata.Initiative / Programme: "Fundamentals of Artificial Intelligence" subject in VET schools (from Feb 2026) and national AI education rollout
metadata.Description: Ten-hour AI subject introduced in all vocational schools at grade 9 from the second semester of 2025/26, with an expert network supporting teachers; a government decree reportedly requires all other schools to introduce AI education by 31 Dec 2026.

summary: Hungary’s national AI education rollout introduces a standalone “Fundamentals of Artificial Intelligence” course for grade 9 students in vocational schools, expanded from a 10-hour pilot to 12 hours after student and teacher feedback. The course emphasizes practical AI knowledge and real-world applications relevant to vocational fields, with sector-specific integration described as a longer-term direction. Teacher training and an AI Ambassador Network provide methodological support and opportunities to share practice; a knowledge-sharing platform and learning materials also support the initiative. The government decree is reported to require AI education in other schools by 31 December 2026.
pedagogicalSummary: The accessible account describes a standalone “Fundamentals of Artificial Intelligence” course for grade 9 VET students, developed from a 10-hour pilot and expanded to 12 hours after student and teacher feedback. The revision is described as allowing more practice-oriented and in-depth learning; students had expressed particular interest in practical applications and real-world problem-solving. Teacher support is also part of the learning approach: an AI Ambassador Network provides methodological support, while webinars and forums facilitate sharing good practices and a working group supports knowledge sharing and learning-material development. The article does not detail specific classroom methods, assessment approaches, or lesson activities, so the pedagogy beyond this evidence is unclear. (https://www.cedefop.europa.eu/mt/news/hungary-artificial-intelligence-becomes-new-subject-vet-schools)
prioritySummary: The initiative principally aims to prepare VET students for AI-related changes in work by giving them practical, usable AI knowledge and connecting learning to vocational contexts. Its stated longer-term direction is to integrate sector-specific AI applications into different VET programmes. The initiative also emphasizes helping teachers and institutions use AI responsibly: the ambassador network provides professional and methodological support, and the programme includes teacher training and ethical and security guidance. The article frames these actions as building an AI education ecosystem in VET and supporting readiness for the future labour market. It does not establish a separate or higher priority beyond these linked aims. (https://www.cedefop.europa.eu/mt/news/hungary-artificial-intelligence-becomes-new-subject-vet-schools)
educationalTechnologySummary: The article identifies an online knowledge-sharing platform created by IKK Nonprofit Plc., intended to support the broader VET AI initiative, but does not name it or describe its features or how students use it. It also reports teacher-training programmes, webinars, and forums for sharing good practices; these support educators’ preparation and exchange, but no particular software or hardware is specified. AI itself is addressed as a subject and as a tool for responsible use in teaching and learning, rather than identified as a particular educational product developed or adopted by the initiative. The accessible account therefore supports the existence of a knowledge-sharing platform and educator-support activities, but provides insufficient detail to identify specific learning technologies, platforms, or classroom systems. (https://www.cedefop.europa.eu/mt/news/hungary-artificial-intelligence-becomes-new-subject-vet-schools)

inclusion.reason: The initiative includes explicit AI literacy: a dedicated subject titled 'Fundamentals of Artificial Intelligence' teaching the basics of AI, plus teacher support via an expert network. It qualifies under the inclusion route as it is issued/mandated by the Hungarian national government (via a ministerial decree), not merely using AI to deliver education or being a single-institution project.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: SOAR – Skilling for AI Readiness (MSDE, launched July 2025)
metadata.Description: National programme to build AI literacy for students in classes 6–12 and their teachers via the Skill India Digital Hub, with industry partners and a $14.4m skill impact bond; implemented with the Ministry of Education.

summary: SOAR (Skilling for AI Readiness) is a national Government of India programme for students in classes 6–12 and their teachers, delivered through the Skill India Digital Hub. Its three 15-hour student modules introduce AI concepts, provide practical experience with basic programming and AI tools, and address ethics, societal impacts and career pathways. A separate 45-hour AI for Educators course supports teacher preparation. The programme also emphasizes access for rural and under-resourced students and girls’ participation; adoption levels are not specified in the available evidence.
pedagogicalSummary: The reported approach is a structured, staged curriculum for students in classes 6–12: “AI to be aware” introduces AI concepts and uses; “AI to acquire” provides hands-on experience with basic programming and widely used AI tools; and “AI to aspire” addresses ethics, societal impacts, and career pathways. Each student module is described as 15 hours. A separate 45-hour “AI for Educators” training module is intended to prepare teachers to teach AI concepts. This supports describing the initiative as modular, combining introductory knowledge with practical activity and broader reflection, though the article does not explain specific teaching techniques, assessment, or how learning is delivered. (https://nenow.in/education/government-of-india-launches-soar-programme-to-teach-ai-in-schools.html)
prioritySummary: SOAR’s principal stated aim is to make students in classes 6–12 AI-literate and able to understand and apply AI in real-life situations, while preparing teachers to teach the subject. The article also reports an access and inclusion emphasis: reaching rural and under-resourced students, reducing the digital divide, and encouraging girls’ participation in STEM. Early vocational training and AI career awareness are additional aims, alongside broader digital skills and readiness for technological change. The account presents these priorities together but does not establish a clear ranking among them. (https://nenow.in/education/government-of-india-launches-soar-programme-to-teach-ai-in-schools.html)

metadata.Initiative / Programme: YUVA AI for ALL – national free AI literacy course (MeitY / IndiaAI Mission)
metadata.Description: Free self-paced 4.5-hour course (six modules, 11 languages) on FutureSkills Prime, iGOT Karmayogi and DIKSHA, with a Government of India certificate; target of 10 million learners; flagship of a National AI Literacy Programme highlighted 12 Jan 2026.

summary: Yuva AI for All is a free, self-paced 4.5-hour AI literacy course offered through FutureSkills Prime, iGOT Karmayogi and DIKSHA. Aimed at learners applying AI in study, work and everyday life, it covers AI fundamentals, hands-on use of generative AI tools, prompting, and responsible and safe practices, using practical scenarios and Indian examples. The six-module course is available in 11 languages and offers a certificate from the Government of India and nasscom.
pedagogicalSummary: The course uses a foundational, applied approach: learners are invited to practise with generative AI tools and build prompting skills, with Indian examples and practical scenarios relating to study, work, and personal tasks. Responsible and safe use is part of that practice. This supports describing the pedagogy as hands-on and context-based, rather than only conceptual. The broader FutureSkills Prime description says its foundation courses include hands-on practice, but the inspected pages do not specify this course’s lesson sequence, assessment methods, or whether learners interact with one another. Sources: https://www.futureskillsprime.in/course/yuva-ai-for-all/ and https://www.futureskillsprime.in/about-us/
prioritySummary: The stated priority is to broaden AI literacy across India so learners can understand AI, use it responsibly, and benefit from it in everyday life. The course page explicitly frames the goal as enabling every learner to apply AI in study, work, and personal tasks, so its benefits are not presented as exclusively workforce-focused. FutureSkills Prime’s wider mission also emphasizes digital skilling and employability, but the inspected course page does not establish that as the course’s sole or dominant purpose. The pages inspected do not provide evidence to rank these aims beyond the course’s explicit emphasis on broad, responsible AI adoption. Sources: https://www.futureskillsprime.in/course/yuva-ai-for-all/ and https://www.futureskillsprime.in/about-us/
educationalTechnologySummary: The course page identifies hands-on learning with generative AI tools as part of the learning experience, but it does not name those tools or specify their features. FutureSkills Prime provides the course’s online information and learner sign-up route, and the course page offers language choices; the inspected pages do not describe the learning platform’s instructional functions or establish that the initiative developed a separate educational technology. No particular software, AI product, or hardware can be identified from this inspection. The evidence therefore supports use of unspecified generative AI tools for practice, but leaves the exact tools and delivery technology unclear. Sources: https://www.futureskillsprime.in/course/yuva-ai-for-all/ and https://www.futureskillsprime.in/iDH/fsp/SignUp/?ref=https://www.futureskillsprime.in/course/yuva-ai-for-all/

inclusion.reason: The initiative clearly includes AI literacy through its curriculum covering AI basics, GenAI tool usage, responsible prompting, and ethical practices. It meets the inclusion route of being issued/endorsed by the Government of India (Ministry of Electronics & Information Technology) as confirmed on the page footer ('This Website belongs to Ministry of Electronics & Information Technology, Government of India and nasscom'). The metadata also notes it is a flagship of a National AI Literacy Programme with a target of 10 million learners, indicating system-scale adoption. All inclusion criteria for government endorsement and AI literacy are satisfied.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: Qhala – Africa AI Literacy Week (June 2025)
metadata.Description: Week of AI literacy training for nearly 700 teachers registered with national Teachers Service Commissions in Kenya, Zambia, Senegal and Togo, who then train colleagues and students in their schools.

summary: Qhala’s Africa AI Literacy Week, held over six days in June 2025, provided AI literacy activities across Kenya, Zambia, Senegal and Togo. Nearly 700 teachers registered for training, including train-the-trainer sessions intended to help them share learning with colleagues and students. The programme also featured workshops, hackathons for children and tertiary-level learners, and discussions on practical AI use and ethics in African contexts. metadata.Initiative / Programme: National AI-in-education initiative and first programme for general and vocational education (MoES / VISC, April 2026)
metadata.Description: Ministry of Education and Science with the State Education Development Agency announced a national-scale AI in education initiative on 15 April 2026.

summary: Latvia’s Ministry of Education and Science, working with the State Education Development Agency, announced a national AI-in-education initiative in April 2026, with a first multi-year programme for general and vocational education through 2030. It aims to develop students’ AI literacy and responsible use while building teachers’ and school leaders’ capacity through training, an expert community and a network of 20 AI leader schools. Planned work includes locally relevant teaching resources, guidance and curriculum revisions, with an emphasis on safe and ethical use and on choosing digital tools to serve learning goals and support students’ critical thinking. No specific classroom AI system or delivery platform is identified.
pedagogicalSummary: The initiative describes a professional-development and collaborative, practice-oriented approach: teacher and school-leader teams are to receive training, exchange experience, and work with AI experts to develop locally relevant examples and resources. It also plans teaching and methodological materials, guidance, and curriculum revisions. The stated pedagogical principle is that digital tools should serve specific learning goals and be used appropriately, supporting students’ critical thinking, judgment, and reasoning rather than being introduced for their own sake. The article does not specify training formats or classroom methods in detail, so these aspects remain unclear. (https://digital-skills-jobs.europa.eu/en/latest/news/latvia-launches-national-artificial-intelligence-program-schools)
prioritySummary: The initiative’s central aim is to build AI literacy and responsible capability across Latvian general and vocational education by 2030. Its intended beneficiaries include students, teachers, and educational institution leaders: students are to develop skills for using AI and managing its risks, while teacher professional development and educators’ ability to use AI safely and effectively are emphasized. The planned AI leader school network and national expert community are intended to support this work. The wider initiative also identifies safe and ethical use, digital leadership, and Latvian-language AI capacity as priorities; the article presents these as several pillars rather than establishing a hierarchy among them. (https://digital-skills-jobs.europa.eu/en/latest/news/latvia-launches-national-artificial-intelligence-program-schools)
educationalTechnologySummary: The inspected article does not name a particular educational platform, software product, device, or AI system developed or adopted for learning. It refers broadly to AI as a tool in pedagogical work and plans a library of resources, teaching materials, guidelines, and best-practice examples, but does not describe these as specific technologies or explain a technical delivery platform. A Latvian AI infrastructure and language-content pillar is mentioned as part of the national initiative, not as a specified classroom learning technology. Thus, the available evidence identifies intended learning resources and a broad technology focus, but is insufficient to say which educational technologies the initiative uses or develops. (https://digital-skills-jobs.europa.eu/en/latest/news/latvia-launches-national-artificial-intelligence-program-schools)

inclusion.reason: The initiative is issued by Latvia's national Ministry of Education and Science (a statutory body), includes explicit AI-literacy goals (e.g., creating an AI expert community, developing teaching materials, revising curriculum for responsible AI use), and meets the inclusion route via government issuance and support.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: JetLearn – JetAIScore AI literacy assessment (ages 6–18)
metadata.Description: Amsterdam-based edtech company launched an AI literacy assessment in US and UK schools in May 2026, positioned as a student-level benchmark; arrives while the OECD develops its own AI-literacy assessment framework.

summary: JetLearn, an Amsterdam-based edtech company, launched the JetAIScore AI literacy assessment in US and UK schools in May 2026. The initiative is a student-level benchmark designed to assess AI literacy skills across ages 6-18.

It lacks any evidence of government endorsement, funding, or mandated adoption (exclusion criteria: company product without government involvement or system-scale adoption). metadata.Initiative / Programme: Ministry of Education and NZQA guidance on generative AI in schools and on acceptable use of AI in assessment
metadata.Description: Joint guidance first issued in 2023 and since updated (incl. AI marking and NCEA authenticity); schools boards set their own policies. NZQA hosts guidance for kura and schools on when AI use is acceptable in assessment.

summary: New Zealand’s Ministry of Education and NZQA provide guidance for kura and schools on acceptable generative AI use in assessment and protecting the authenticity of student work. It covers school policies, academic integrity, source acknowledgement, and risks such as inaccurate or biased AI output. For teachers, it recommends approaches including progress check-ins, observing work, follow-up conversations, and student reflections; it also points to an online teacher module on authenticity and AI evidence. The guidance distinguishes permitted uses from external assessment, where generative AI is not allowed.
pedagogicalSummary: The inspected NZQA guidance is primarily about assessment practice and academic integrity, rather than teaching AI as a subject. It recommends that schools educate students about integrity, acknowledging and referencing sources, and the possibility that AI output may be biased or inaccurate. For teachers, it suggests supporting authentic work through progress check-ins, observing work in progress, follow-up conversations, self-reflection, and authenticity declarations. A symposium also shared ideas for assessment design that can support learning while reducing integrity concerns. These are recommendations, not evidence that every school uses them. The page identifies an online teacher-learning module on authenticity, including AI-related evidence. Evidence is limited to the guidance page; cited source: https://www2.nzqa.govt.nz/ncea/ncea-for-teachers-and-schools/managing-national-assessment-in-schools/ai-guidance/.
prioritySummary: The initiative principally aims to help kura and schools manage acceptable AI use in assessment while protecting the authenticity and academic integrity of student work. Its guidance addresses school assessment policies, teacher assessment practice, and how students should acknowledge sources and understand risks such as inaccurate or biased AI-generated information. For external assessment, it emphasizes supervised evidence collection and says generative AI, chatbots, and similar content-generating tools may not be used to produce submitted work. The intended beneficiaries are schools, teachers, and students within New Zealand assessment and qualifications settings. The inspected page does not establish a broader workforce-upskilling or individual-wellbeing priority; its stated emphasis is assessment integrity and practice. Cited source: https://www2.nzqa.govt.nz/ncea/ncea-for-teachers-and-schools/managing-national-assessment-in-schools/ai-guidance/.
educationalTechnologySummary: The page identifies Pūtake, NZQA’s learning management system, as the platform hosting “Tāku Reo, Tāku Mahi,” an online learning module for teachers on authenticity that includes strategies relating to AI evidence. This is the clearest educational technology identified as supporting learning; the page does not say that NZQA developed the platform itself. It also discusses AI checkers or detectors as possible aids to authenticity checks, but cautions teachers about false positives and against relying on them alone; it does not identify a particular product or present detectors as a learning tool. Generative AI and paraphrasing tools are discussed as assessment-use concerns, not technologies the initiative uses to teach. No AI educational software or hardware developed by the initiative is identified on the inspected page. Cited source: https://www2.nzqa.govt.nz/ncea/ncea-for-teachers-and-schools/managing-national-assessment-in-schools/ai-guidance/.

inclusion.reason: The initiative includes explicit educational content with learning objectives (e.g., referencing, bias awareness) and is issued/endorsed by national government bodies (Ministry of Education and NZQA), meeting the inclusion routes for both AI literacy and government mandate.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: Education Review Office – "Ready or not: How are schools responding to Artificial Intelligence?"
metadata.Description: ERO evaluation (16 key findings): large majorities of principals and teachers use AI; responsibility for applying guidance sits mainly with schools; recommends a national AI-in-education framework and national policies.

summary: The Education Review Office’s “Ready or not: How are schools responding to Artificial Intelligence?” is a New Zealand evaluation of how students, teachers, and school leaders are using AI in schools, including in classroom practice, assessment, and administration. It considers potential benefits alongside concerns such as accuracy, appropriate use, and effects on students’ critical thinking. The report finds that school responses can be unplanned and recommends a more consistent national approach, including AI-literacy curriculum guidance, policies for AI use, professional learning, assessment guidance, and safe tool selection. It is an evaluation and set of recommendations, not a teaching programme or course.
pedagogicalSummary: The inspected pages present an Education Review Office evaluation of how schools are responding to AI, not a learning programme delivered by ERO. They do not describe a pedagogical model, lessons, or a method for organising learner instruction. The report says schools are often responding in an unplanned way, with individual teachers determining how and when AI is used, and notes possible effects on teaching, learning, and students’ critical thinking. That evidence describes the practice being evaluated, not pedagogy adopted by the initiative. Thus, no initiative-level teaching approach could be identified in the inspected material; this is a limit of the evidence, not proof that no related guidance exists. (https://www.evidence.ero.govt.nz/documents/ready-or-not-how-are-schools-responding-to-artificial-intelligence-research-report/)
prioritySummary: The initiative’s emphasis is to understand how AI is being used in schools and support a safer, more consistent, and effective response. The ERO report considers students, teachers, and school leaders, including AI’s influence on classroom practice, assessment, and administration. It recognises potential benefits such as reducing workload and supporting teaching and learning, alongside concerns about accuracy, appropriate use, and impacts on students’ development of skills such as critical thinking. Its executive summary calls for a more coherent system-wide approach to help schools use AI in ways that enhance teaching and learning. The inspected pages do not establish workforce upskilling or individual well-being as the primary goal. (https://www.evidence.ero.govt.nz/documents/ready-or-not-how-are-schools-responding-to-artificial-intelligence-research-report/)
educationalTechnologySummary: The inspected material describes generative AI tools as technologies being used in schools and examined by the ERO evaluation, including in classroom practice, assessment, and administrative work. It does not identify particular platforms, software, or hardware, nor does it show that ERO develops or uses an educational technology to deliver AI-literacy learning. The report’s focus is evaluating school use and the need for a coherent approach, rather than describing a technology-supported course or learning resource. Accordingly, no educational technology developed or used by the initiative to support AI-literacy learning could be identified from these pages; this reflects the limits of the inspected evidence. (https://www.evidence.ero.govt.nz/documents/ready-or-not-how-are-schools-responding-to-artificial-intelligence-research-report/; https://www.evidence.ero.govt.nz/documents/ready-or-not-how-are-schools-responding-to-artificial-intelligence-summary-report/)

inclusion.reason: The initiative includes substantive AI-literacy educational content (definitions, skill frameworks, learning objectives, curriculum alignment) and is issued by ERO, a New Zealand statutory education evaluation body mandated under national law. This satisfies the inclusion route ‘issued/mandated by a national government or statutory body’ (ERO report pages 1–16). Evidence of AI literacy is explicit on pages 3–14; adoption evidence is not required because ERO’s status alone provides an inclusion route.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: TENZ / DTTA / Ministry of Education resources for teaching about AI (Years 4–13, English and te reo Māori)
metadata.Description: Classroom resources supporting teachers to teach about the technology behind AI, developed to sit alongside Ministry guidance on using AI tools.

summary: TENZ, DTTA and the New Zealand Ministry of Education developed English and te reo Māori classroom resources for kaiako teaching Years 4–13. The resources introduce AI concepts and common terms, explore potential benefits and challenges, and offer reflection prompts and suggested learning experiences to support discussion and integration into local curricula. The English version also includes a case study. They focus on understanding AI rather than guidance on using particular AI tools.
pedagogicalSummary: The resources support teacher-facilitated learning rather than prescribing a fixed teaching method. They offer reflection prompts and suggested learning experiences as a starting point for kaiako to guide discussion and integrate AI learning into local curricula, including technology and other learning areas. Content is organised around common AI terms, potential opportunities, challenges, a case study in the English resource, and suggestions for further exploration. This evidence points to discussion, reflection, and curriculum integration, but the inspected pages do not establish a more specific or mandatory pedagogy. Sources: https://newzealandcurriculum.tahurangi.education.govt.nz/introduction-to-artificial-intelligence/5637235331.p and https://kauwhatareo.tahurangi.education.govt.nz/mi/he-k-rero-whakataki-ki-te-atamai-rorohiko/5637236082.p
prioritySummary: The initiative principally aims to help teachers teach students about AI and the ideas behind the technology. The resources are intended for Years 4–13 kaiako and are presented as support for integrating AI learning into local curricula, preparing students to understand a changing technological landscape. They cover AI concepts as well as possible benefits across society and potential risks, so the emphasis includes informed understanding of both opportunities and challenges rather than simply promoting AI use. English and te reo Māori versions support different curriculum contexts. The inspected material does not identify workforce upskilling or individual well-being as primary goals. Sources: https://tenz.org.nz/an-introduction-to-artificial-intelligence/ and https://newzealandcurriculum.tahurangi.education.govt.nz/introduction-to-artificial-intelligence/5637235331.p
educationalTechnologySummary: The inspected pages identify no specific AI tool, software, hardware, or interactive educational technology developed or used to teach AI literacy. The initiative provides English and te reo Māori teacher resources: informational material organised into factsheets or sections, with reflection prompts, suggested learning experiences or activities, a case study in the English version, and further-reading links. These are available through the Tāhūrangi curriculum resource pages, which serve as access points for the materials; the pages do not describe the platform itself as a learning technology. The English resource explicitly says it does not provide guidance on individual AI tools or their use in education. This finding is limited to the pages inspected. Sources: https://newzealandcurriculum.tahurangi.education.govt.nz/introduction-to-artificial-intelligence/5637235331.p and https://kauwhatareo.tahurangi.education.govt.nz/mi/he-k-rero-whakataki-ki-te-atamai-rorohiko/5637236082.p

inclusion.reason: The initiative includes clear AI-literacy educational content focused on teaching the underlying technology of AI to school students. metadata.Initiative / Programme: National AI Policy 2025 (approved by federal cabinet, 30 July 2025)
metadata.Description: Policy targets training one million AI professionals by 2030, 3,000 annual scholarships, AI Innovation and Venture Funds, an AI Council, and inclusion of women and persons with disabilities through accessible education.

summary: Pakistan’s National AI Policy 2025 is a federal government framework for developing the country’s AI ecosystem. Its goals include training one million AI professionals by 2030, providing 3,000 annual AI scholarships, supporting research and local innovation, and promoting AI applications in public services and civic projects. The policy also emphasizes accessible education and inclusion of women and persons with disabilities, alongside measures for AI governance, cybersecurity and data security. The available report does not specify curricula, teaching methods or learning technologies.
pedagogicalSummary: The accessible report says the policy aims to train one million AI professionals by 2030, distribute 3,000 annual AI scholarships, facilitate research, and include women and people with disabilities through accessible education. It does not describe teaching activities, instructional methods, curricula, or how learning is organised, so a specific pedagogical approach cannot be established from this page. The education-related measures are stated as policy goals, not evidence of a particular pedagogy. (https://www.dawn.com/news/1927634/federal-cabinet-approves-national-ai-policy-2025)
prioritySummary: As reported, the policy seeks to build a national AI ecosystem and democratise access to AI. Its stated priorities include developing skilled professionals—especially through youth education, training, and scholarships—while widening access for women and people with disabilities. It also aims to encourage employment, private-sector innovation and local AI products, and to enhance public services and productivity. The article presents these as connected aims rather than establishing a single dominant priority. (https://www.dawn.com/news/1927634/federal-cabinet-approves-national-ai-policy-2025)
educationalTechnologySummary: The report does not identify any educational technology, learning platform, software, or hardware that the policy develops or uses to support AI-literacy learning. It mentions AI Innovation and Venture Funds, scholarships, research projects, and accessible education, but does not describe these as learning technologies or explain a technology-supported learning experience. The article is a brief account of the cabinet’s approval rather than a detailed policy text, so this is a limit of the inspected evidence, not confirmation that the wider initiative uses no educational technology. (https://www.dawn.com/news/1927634/federal-cabinet-approves-national-ai-policy-2025)

inclusion.reason: This initiative qualifies for inclusion because it is issued and mandated by a national government (Pakistan), satisfying the 'Government Issued/Endorsed' inclusion route. The metadata confirms it includes educational elements (training programs, scholarships) which satisfy the AI-literacy requirement. No uncertainty remains regarding its inclusion status based on the provided metadata.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: MOE AI literacy approach – "Four Learns" and Committee of Supply 2026 announcements
metadata.Description: MOE pillars: learn about AI, learn to use AI, learn with AI, learn beyond AI; AI literacy integrated into curriculum and co-curriculum with developmental milestones, within the EdTech Masterplan 2030.

summary: Singapore’s Ministry of Education (MOE) sets out a national AI-literacy approach within its EdTech Masterplan 2030, organized around four dimensions: learning about AI, using AI, learning with AI, and learning beyond AI. The approach is intended for school-age learners and is integrated into curriculum and co-curricular learning through developmental milestones, with self-directed learning resources also noted. It aims to build AI capabilities relevant to learning and a changing workforce; the available evidence does not detail specific teaching methods or resources.
pedagogicalSummary: The available description identifies a four-part learning framework: learning about AI, using AI, learning with AI, and learning beyond AI. It says AI literacy is integrated into curriculum and co-curriculum with developmental milestones, suggesting learning is intended to progress across school experiences rather than be confined to a standalone topic. These are the only supported details about how learning is organised; the accessible material does not describe specific classroom methods, assessment practices, or teacher-support arrangements. The source is the MOE press-release page, whose article text was not fully available for inspection: https://www.moe.gov.sg/news/press-releases/20260303-we-learn-for-life-together-building-a-we-first-society-through-education.
prioritySummary: The available evidence points to developing learners’ AI literacy across multiple dimensions—understanding AI, using it, learning with it, and learning beyond it—while situating education within the broader aim of building a “we-first society.” This indicates both learner capability and a societal aspiration, but the inspected material does not establish which is the primary priority or explain particular intended beneficiaries beyond the education context. The source description also places the approach within the EdTech Masterplan 2030, but that alone does not clarify how resources or emphasis are allocated. The press-release article text was not fully available for inspection, so finer claims about priorities are uncertain: https://www.moe.gov.sg/news/press-releases/20260303-we-learn-for-life-together-building-a-we-first-society-through-education.
educationalTechnologySummary: The accessible evidence situates the AI-literacy approach within MOE’s EdTech Masterplan 2030, but does not identify any particular platform, software, device, or hardware that the initiative develops or uses to support learning. The four learning dimensions describe educational aims, not technologies. Nor does the available material establish that an AI product is itself used as a teaching tool. Accordingly, no specific educational technology can be named on the basis of this inspection; this is a limit of the accessible evidence, not confirmation that the initiative uses none. The source page was not fully available for inspection: https://www.moe.gov.sg/news/press-releases/20260303-we-learn-for-life-together-building-a-we-first-society-through-education.

inclusion.reason: The initiative is issued by the Singapore Ministry of Education (MOE), which satisfies the inclusion route regarding a government statutory body. It explicitly includes AI literacy through its 'Four Learns' framework, providing educational content and guidance on how to use and understand AI ('Learn about', 'Learn with', 'Learn beyond') rather than just using AI tools for delivery. This aligns perfectly with the requirement of educational content or learning objectives about how AI works.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: Teacher AI Literacy Professional Learning Roadmap (MOE, Aug 2026)
metadata.Description: Roadmap setting the AI knowledge and skills teachers need; reported to make one AI module compulsory by end-2026 and a second strongly encouraged by end-2027.

summary: Singapore’s Ministry of Education’s Teacher AI Literacy Professional Learning Roadmap is a national professional-learning initiative for primary, secondary, and junior-college teachers. Reportedly, teachers must complete one online AI module by the end of 2026, with further modules encouraged and advanced subject-specific courses planned from 2027. The learning covers AI fundamentals, ethics, safety, and responsible, age-appropriate use, including how AI may affect student thinking and support deeper learning. The reported approach also includes opportunities for collegial learning; lesson examples such as verifying AI-generated information are described but are not established as required training activities.
pedagogicalSummary: The reported teacher learning combines short online modules with opportunities for collegial learning: teachers can share experience through Academy of Singapore Teachers and school-cluster sessions, and may take advanced subject-specific courses from 2027. The modules address foundational AI knowledge and responsible use, as well as deciding when AI suits different age groups, how it may affect student thinking, and how it can support deeper learning. The article also describes lesson practices teachers might use with students, such as questioning AI-generated information and checking it against trusted sources, but does not establish these as required training activities. It does not specify instructional methods within the modules beyond their online format. Evidence is from the report: https://mustsharenews.com/moe-teachers-compulsory-ai-modules/.
prioritySummary: The roadmap is principally presented as professional learning for primary, secondary, and junior-college teachers, intended to clarify the AI knowledge, skills, and ethical considerations needed as AI becomes more common in education. Its emphasis includes using AI where it can improve learning while avoiding its use as a shortcut that undermines students’ reasoning, discernment, or critical thinking. The report also describes developmentally appropriate, supervised student use and academic integrity as aims of the wider school approach, rather than priorities solely of the teacher roadmap. It identifies no separate workforce or societal priority beyond preparing educators and supporting student learning. These priorities are described in the article, not independently verified here: https://mustsharenews.com/moe-teachers-compulsory-ai-modules/.
educationalTechnologySummary: The article says the teacher modules are conducted online and take about 30–45 minutes each, but does not name the platform or identify a learning technology developed specifically for the roadmap. It separately reports that students from Primary 4 may use education-focused AI tools, particularly those in Singapore Student Learning Space (SLS), under teacher supervision, and that SLS AI features include guardrails for responsible use. This is relevant context about technologies used in school learning, but the article does not establish that SLS delivers the teacher modules or was developed by this roadmap. ChatGPT is mentioned as part of the wider context for teachers’ experimentation, not as a roadmap learning tool. Evidence and limits: https://mustsharenews.com/moe-teachers-compulsory-ai-modules/.

inclusion.reason: The initiative meets the inclusion criteria: (1) it is issued by a national government body (Singapore MOE), satisfying the 'Issued by a national or sub-national government' inclusion route; (2) it includes explicit AI literacy educational content—learning objectives such as understanding AI basics, ethical considerations, safety, and responsible use—and serves educators in Singapore's school system. The roadmap is implemented across approximately 30,000 teachers nationwide, indicating system-scale adoption. Source: https://mustsharenews.com/moe-teachers-compulsory-ai-modules/

metadata.Initiative / Programme: Code for Fun (CFF) programme – AI strand (MOE)
metadata.Description: Mandatory 10-hour programme from Primary 4 covering coding, computational thinking and an introduction to AI; to be updated to strengthen AI skills and made available to all schools in 2027.

summary: Singapore’s Ministry of Education Code for Fun (CFF) includes a mandatory 10-hour programme from Primary 4 covering coding, computational thinking and an introduction to AI. Schools may also offer two additional five-hour AI modules. MOE plans to strengthen the AI content and make the programme available to all schools in 2027. The programme sits within MOE’s broader age-calibrated approach to AI learning, which combines guided use with learning about AI’s operation, limitations and responsible use; the parliamentary reply does not specify the technologies used in CFF activities.
pedagogicalSummary: MOE describes a staged, spiral approach organised around four aims: students learn about AI, learn to use it, learn with it, and learn beyond it. Teaching is age-calibrated: Primary 1–3 students build foundational skills and learn AI basics without assigned direct AI use; from Primary 4, they use education-focused AI tools under teacher supervision. Learning combines guided hands-on practice with explicit discussion of AI’s operation, limitations, and responsible use. For example, a teacher-guided writing activity has students use prompts and personalised feedback to revise drafts, with teachers reinforcing learning habits. The mandatory Code for Fun programme also includes coding, computational thinking, and an introduction to AI. Evidence is from the inspected parliamentary reply: https://www.moe.gov.sg/news/parliamentary-replies/20260506-ai-usage-in-schools.
prioritySummary: The initiative principally aims to develop AI literacy among students in Singapore and prepare them to engage with AI in learning and everyday life. MOE emphasises equipping students to understand AI, use it purposefully, critically evaluate its outputs, and recognise risks, including errors, inappropriate use, and cognitive offloading. The stated priority is not simply exposure to AI tools: their use is to support educational objectives and students’ development, while maintaining foundational learning and academic integrity. The reply describes a calibrated approach for different ages and says students should be ready to harness AI while learning when not to use it. It also identifies future readiness as a goal. Evidence: https://www.moe.gov.sg/news/parliamentary-replies/20260506-ai-usage-in-schools.
educationalTechnologySummary: The reply identifies AI-enabled tools in the Singapore Student Learning Space (SLS), including the AI Learning Assistant (LEA), as education tools used under teacher supervision from Primary 4. In a described English composition activity, LEA responds to a student’s draft with personalised, real-time feedback to support iterative revision; it also redirects off-topic requests and requests for direct answers. MOE says SLS tools have safety guardrails, and students complete a basic module on AI and SLS-enabled features before using them. The reply does not specify the software or platforms used in Code for Fun’s coding and AI activities, nor does it clearly establish which named tools MOE developed. Evidence: https://www.moe.gov.sg/news/parliamentary-replies/20260506-ai-usage-in-schools.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: Orange Data Mining and "Introduction to Machine Learning" tutorials (University of Ljubljana, Biolab)
metadata.Description: Open-source visual, no-code data-mining and machine-learning toolkit designed for teaching, with free video tutorials and written lessons on clustering and classification (CC BY-NC-ND), plus lecture notes from 50+ workshops; used in a school teaching concept for ages 14+.

summary: An open introductory machine-learning resource from the University of Ljubljana’s Biolab, included in ARISA’s broader collection of AI learning materials. It introduces supervised and unsupervised learning through familiar comparison examples and includes written lessons and practice activities; the associated Orange Data Mining materials offer a visual, no-code approach to teaching data mining and machine learning. The resource can serve learners and educators, while the wider collection addresses professional roles in business, technology, and policymaking.
pedagogicalSummary: The accessible materials use a gentle, example-led introduction to machine learning: the Introduction to Machine Learning page frames unsupervised and supervised learning through familiar comparison questions about basketball players, tennis styles, and cheese. The collection also includes material described as interactive learning resources for professional training, organized into parts and accompanied by assignments, suggesting a combination of guided content and practice. These pages do not establish a broader teaching method or show how learners are supported beyond those materials. (https://notes.biolab.si/books/arisa/intro-ml; https://notes.biolab.si/books/arisa/AI-for-the-industry; https://notes.biolab.si/books/arisa/AI-for-the-industry/01-introduction)
prioritySummary: The Arisa collection states that it aims to build AI knowledge and skills for understanding and using AI in business and policy contexts, with attention to privacy, bias, and trust. It identifies professional roles across business leadership, technology leadership and practice, and policymaking. The inspected machine-learning materials use broadly accessible examples, but do not specify a distinct audience or a more specific priority for that book; the wider collection’s stated emphasis is professional capability in organizational and policy settings. (https://notes.biolab.si/books/arisa; https://notes.biolab.si/books/arisa/intro-ml)
educationalTechnologySummary: The inspected pages identify web-hosted learning materials, including a machine-learning book and assignment pages, and describe accompanying resources for professional training as interactive. However, the readable page text does not name a software platform, application, or hardware used or developed to support learning. In particular, the available evidence is insufficient to establish whether Orange Data Mining is used or developed by this initiative, or how it supports the lessons. (https://notes.biolab.si/books/arisa/intro-ml; https://notes.biolab.si/books/arisa/AI-for-the-industry; https://notes.biolab.si/books/arisa/AI-for-the-industry/01-introduction)

inclusion.reason: The Introduction to Machine Learning page describes learning about supervised and unsupervised machine learning, satisfying the AI-literacy requirement (https://notes.biolab.si/books/arisa/intro-ml). Orange’s teaching page explains concepts such as regression, overfitting, regularization, and clustering, and says Orange is used in schools, universities, and professional training worldwide (https://orangedatamining.com/home/teach-with-orange/; https://orangedatamining.com/). This supports a broad-reach adoption route, though the pages do not quantify adoption of these specific tutorials or establish government support.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: "AI Talent Development Plan for All" (Ministry of Education national blueprint)
metadata.Description: First national blueprint aimed at building AI capability across the lifespan; the government also plans to revise the K-12 curriculum so AI education becomes a core subject.

summary: South Korea’s Ministry of Education “AI Talent Development Plan for All” is a national blueprint for building AI capability from K–12 through higher education, research, employment, and adult learning. Its planned measures include making AI a core part of the K–12 curriculum, expanding AI-focused courses and career pathways, supporting AI degrees and research, and establishing centers to train students, parents, and teachers. The plan combines broad AI-use literacy with specialist talent development, using proposed hands-on robotics and data experiments, university and industry links, and regional facilities. The reported measures are plans; the source does not establish their implementation or uptake.
pedagogicalSummary: The blueprint describes a staged learning and training pathway, from school through higher education and adult learning, rather than a single teaching method. School activities include AI-focused courses and clubs, career programs linking schools with universities and businesses, and intelligent science labs intended for hands-on robotics and data-driven experiments. At university level, it proposes AI-focused degrees, accelerated study for high-achieving students, and joint research clusters; industry-linked degrees and company-run training extend learning into employment. Support centers are also planned to train students, parents, and teachers. These examples indicate practical, career-connected and research-oriented learning, but the article gives no detail on lesson design, assessment, or teaching practice beyond hands-on activities. Evidence is from the news report: https://asianews.network/south-korea-to-foster-ai-talent-across-all-stages-of-life/.
prioritySummary: The plan’s central emphasis is developing AI capability across the population while expanding the supply and retention of specialist talent. It aims to prepare researchers and workers for industry and academia, address a reported shortage of skilled professionals and brain drain, and support South Korea’s ambition to strengthen its global AI competitiveness. The initiative also extends beyond specialists: it includes non-STEM students and adult learners, and the education minister says the goal is for every citizen to use AI in everyday life. Regional AI universities and locally tailored programs are intended to address geographic disparities, while school and career programs broaden access. The article presents these aims together and does not establish a clear ranking among them. Evidence: https://asianews.network/south-korea-to-foster-ai-talent-across-all-stages-of-life/.
educationalTechnologySummary: The article identifies planned learning environments and computing infrastructure, but no named educational software or learning platform. Schools are to be equipped with “intelligent science labs” for hands-on robotics and data-driven experiments, and regional AI-focused colleges are to receive infrastructure including GPU computing facilities. These are described as facilities supporting practical learning and AI education, not as specific products or platforms. The plan also expands AI courses and clubs, but these are educational activities rather than technologies in themselves. The report notes that South Korea scrapped an earlier plan for AI-powered digital textbooks; it does not describe those textbooks as a technology used by this initiative. Details on lab systems, hardware specifications, software, and actual implementation are not provided in the inspected page. Evidence: https://asianews.network/south-korea-to-foster-ai-talent-across-all-stages-of-life/.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: LearningML – open-source platform for learning machine learning with Scratch (INTEF / URJC)
metadata.Description: Free, open-source web platform where learners build text and image models and use them in Scratch; created and maintained by a teacher at INTEF with URJC, with a developer guide, GitLab project, lesson plans and tutorials; developed further in the Erasmus+ FAIaS project.

summary: LearningML is a free, open-source educational platform developed in Spain for school students, particularly those aged 10–16, and the teachers who support them. Learners collect and label text, image, or other data, train classification models, and use them in Scratch projects through a modified programming editor. Its hands-on, project-oriented approach is supported by a manual, tutorials, and lesson plans; the initiative also addresses AI’s societal opportunities, risks, and ethical questions. Developed with educational and university partners and furthered through the Erasmus+ FAIaS project, it focuses on practical machine-learning learning rather than a broad range of AI topics.
pedagogicalSummary: LearningML explicitly describes “learning by doing” as its pedagogical basis. Learners collect and label their own text or image examples, train a model to classify new examples, then export or use it in a Scratch program—an applied sequence that makes the model part of a project they create. The platform’s model editor offers basic and advanced modes, described as suitable for different school stages; the advanced mode supports deeper exploration of machine-learning algorithms. The site also links a manual and mini-tutorial, though the inspected pages do not establish how consistently these supports are used in teaching. This evidence supports hands-on, project-oriented learning, but not a more specific named pedagogical framework. (https://learningml.org/lml-doc/01-intro/; https://learningml.org/lml-doc/02-descripcion/; https://learningml.org/)
prioritySummary: The initiative’s stated aim is to make practical AI and machine-learning learning possible in schools. It presents classroom projects as a way to educate conscious, critical citizens in response to AI’s opportunities, risks, and ethical questions; it also seeks to awaken young people’s interest in the field and develop students’ computational-thinking skills. The intended beneficiaries include school students and the teachers who bring these projects into educational settings. The creator’s account refers to use by teachers and students and describes research into suitability for learners aged 10–16. These pages identify connected educational and societal aims but do not establish one as more important than the others. (https://learningml.org/por-que-aprender-ml/; https://learningml.org/acerca-de-learningml-y-su-autor/)
educationalTechnologySummary: LearningML develops a web-based machine-learning model editor for building classification models, and a programming editor called LearningML Scratch: a modification of Scratch with added blocks for creating and using those models in interactive applications. The manual describes text, image, and numerical data, model training and classification blocks, and an autonomous Scratch mode that can build a model without the separate editor. The site also offers LearningML Desktop installers for Windows, macOS, and Linux, but the inspected download page does not explain how the desktop version supports learning or differs from the web platform. Scratch is the foundation for the modified editor, rather than a separate LearningML-developed product. (https://learningml.org/lml-doc/02-descripcion/; https://learningml.org/lml-doc/04-editor-programacion/; https://learningml.org/learningml-desktop-releases/)

inclusion.reason: The initiative explicitly provides AI literacy content through educational materials including lesson plans, tutorials, and guides that explain how machine learning works using Scratch. It has government support via INTEF (Spanish National Institute for Education Technology) and involvement in an Erasmus+ project (FAIaS), which qualifies it under the national/sub-national government inclusion route. The platform is supported by research studies validating its use as an educational intervention.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: "Artificial Intelligence (AI) in schools: guidelines and guardrails" (Scottish Government)
metadata.Description: First national non-statutory guidance on safe and ethical AI use in schools, co-developed with the EIS union, local government and Education Scotland; includes principles, FAQs, case studies, local authority data-controller guidance and definitions.

summary: The Scottish Government’s non-statutory guidance sets out principles and practical guardrails for safe, ethical AI use in Scottish schools. Addressed mainly to school leaders, teachers and local authorities, it also considers pupils and families. It includes explanations of AI, FAQs, classroom examples, teaching and data-protection checklists, and links to external learning resources. The guidance emphasizes children’s rights, privacy, fairness and inclusion, and positions AI as a support for learning and teaching under human oversight—not a substitute for teacher judgement or relationships. It recommends critical evaluation of AI outputs and professional learning for educators; it is guidance rather than a programme delivering classroom instruction.
pedagogicalSummary: This is non-statutory guidance rather than a programme delivering a single teaching method. It promotes human-centred teaching, with AI complementing—not replacing—teacher judgement, peer interaction and relationships. Its examples suggest active, scaffolded learning: pupils might generate practice questions, seek explanations or draft feedback, but are expected to verify outputs, reflect critically and contribute their own work; teachers can guide prompts and tailor AI-generated materials to pupils and curriculum goals. The guidance also calls for differentiated and inclusive approaches, teacher oversight of assessment uses, and professional learning so educators can make informed choices. These are recommended practices and examples, not evidence that the initiative itself runs classroom activities. The inspected pages do not establish implementation outcomes. (https://www.gov.scot/publications/scottish-guidelines-guardrails-use-artificial-intelligence-ai-schools/pages/6/; https://www.gov.scot/publications/scottish-guidelines-guardrails-use-artificial-intelligence-ai-schools/pages/8/)
prioritySummary: The initiative principally aims to help Scottish schools use AI safely, ethically and appropriately while preparing children and young people, teachers and school staff to understand, use, evaluate and critique it. It foregrounds children’s rights, privacy, safety, fairness and equitable access, and positions AI as support for learning and teaching rather than a replacement for human connection or professional judgement. It also seeks to help teachers make informed decisions and potentially tailor teaching to diverse needs or reduce routine workload. The guidance connects pupil AI learning to skills for life, learning and work, and to participation in a society where AI is widespread. It is addressed mainly to those delivering school education, with relevance to local authorities, families and others. These are overlapping aims; the inspected pages do not establish a single ranked priority. (https://www.gov.scot/publications/scottish-guidelines-guardrails-use-artificial-intelligence-ai-schools/pages/3/; https://www.gov.scot/publications/scottish-guidelines-guardrails-use-artificial-intelligence-ai-schools/pages/4/; https://www.gov.scot/publications/scottish-guidelines-guardrails-use-artificial-intelligence-ai-schools/pages/6/)
educationalTechnologySummary: The inspected pages do not identify a particular AI platform, software product or hardware that the Scottish Government guidance itself develops or deploys for teaching. Instead, the guidance sets conditions for schools’ use of AI tools and gives illustrative cases—such as tutoring for literacy, generating revision questions, differentiated resources and translation—subject to local approval, safeguards and human oversight. It links to external learning resources, including Education Scotland material, an AI Readiness Self Evaluation tool, the University of Edinburgh’s Teach AI Literacy framework and TRAILS resource archive, and a children’s rights and AI teaching pack. These are described as resources developed or provided by other organisations, not as technologies developed by this initiative. The guidance also notes that infrastructure and device access affect schools’ ability to use digital tools; the inspected pages do not specify a government-provided platform. (https://www.gov.scot/publications/scottish-guidelines-guardrails-use-artificial-intelligence-ai-schools/pages/8/; https://www.gov.scot/publications/scottish-guidelines-guardrails-use-artificial-intelligence-ai-schools/pages/12/; https://www.gov.scot/publications/scottish-guidelines-guardrails-use-artificial-intelligence-ai-schools/pages/4/)

inclusion.reason: AI-literacy requirement: The guidance includes educational content such as core principles, FAQs, a checklist, definitions of key AI terms, data protection considerations, and links to free curriculum resources and the Centre for Teaching Excellence Digital Education and AI Hub. These elements explain how AI works, ethical use, and practical guidance for teachers and students. Inclusion route: The document is issued by the Scottish Government (a sub-national government body), satisfying the inclusion criteria under national/sub-national government endorsement. Supporting pages confirm its scope to all schools in Scotland and alignment with national strategy.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: Maddie is Online – Generative AI Skills in Schools (Robert Gordon University)
metadata.Description: Cartoon-based, scenario-led resources building young people's digital resilience and critical understanding of generative AI; listed as a recommended resource in the Scottish Government guidance.

summary: Maddie is Online is a Robert Gordon University project offering digital-literacy resources for pre-teen children, with materials also intended for teachers, librarians, families, and other adults. Cartoon videos and accompanying lesson plans use everyday scenarios, co-created with young people, to prompt discussion and build digital resilience. A generative-AI series addresses critical understanding and responsible use, including issues such as bias, transparency, privacy, and safety. The resources are listed in Scottish Government guidance for schools.
pedagogicalSummary: The initiative combines scenario-based storytelling with learning activities: cartoon stories portray everyday online situations, including generative AI, and accompanying toolkits provide lesson plans and resources. Its approach is also participatory: children contribute experiences and perspectives to scripts and stories, helping make the material relevant to their lives. The project describes its model as interactive and empathetic rather than relying only on rules or warnings; it aims to support discussion, critical understanding, and emotional resilience. Teachers, librarians, families, and other adults can use the resources to facilitate learning, though the inspected pages do not specify a single required teaching sequence or assessment method. Sources: https://rgu.ac.uk/news/news-2026/maddie-is-online-project-recognised-in-new-scottish-government-guidance and https://maddiesonline.blogspot.com/p/maddie-is-online-introduction-and.html and https://maddiesonline.blogspot.com/p/co-creating-with-children-to-teach-ai.html
prioritySummary: Maddie is Online principally aims to equip pre-teen children (roughly ages 9–13) with digital and information literacy, resilience, and a critical understanding of online experiences, including generative AI. Its emphasis includes safer, ethical and responsible engagement—not simply avoiding online risks, but helping young people navigate challenges such as misinformation, privacy, bias, and cyberbullying with confidence. The materials are also intended for use by adults around children, including teachers, librarians, families, and school support staff, extending the benefit across the school community. The Scottish Government guidance recognition is described as supporting teaching practice, youth digital safety, and education-sector capacity, but the inspected evidence does not establish a workforce-first or commercial priority. Sources: https://rgu.ac.uk/news/news-2026/maddie-is-online-project-recognised-in-new-scottish-government-guidance and https://maddiesonline.blogspot.com/p/maddie-is-online-introduction-and.html
educationalTechnologySummary: The project develops cartoon video stories with voice-overs, including a generative-AI series, and accompanying resource toolkits with lesson plans and links to further resources. The videos are organized into online playlists, with the project page linking to YouTube series; these are delivery formats for the learning materials, rather than evidence that learners use a particular AI product. The RGU article describes the resources as practical and scenario-based, while the project site presents the broader cartoon series and toolkits as educational resources. A digital bookshelf is also linked from the introduction page, though its specific role in the AI materials is not detailed there. No particular generative-AI software, classroom platform, or hardware used by learners is identified in the inspected pages; this is a limit of the available evidence. Sources: https://maddiesonline.blogspot.com/p/maddie-is-online-introduction-and.html and https://rgu.ac.uk/news/news-2026/maddie-is-online-project-recognised-in-new-scottish-government-guidance

inclusion.reason: The initiative includes clear AI literacy content through its cartoon-based, scenario-led resources designed to teach young people how to engage safely and critically with generative AI. Crucially, it has been officially included as a recommended resource in the Scottish Government’s national guidance titled ‘AI in Schools: Guidelines and Guardrails’, which qualifies under the inclusion route for being formally endorsed by a sub-national government body (Scotland). This government endorsement provides the necessary systemic reach and formal recognition despite the project being originally led by an academic institution.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: US Department of Education – Dear Colleague Letter on AI (22 July 2025) and AI grant priority
metadata.Description: Guidance that federal formula and discretionary grants can fund responsible AI use, including AI literacy, teacher training and CS education; follows the April 2025 Executive Order. A supplemental grant priority was proposed in 2025 and reported finalised in April 2026.

summary: The U.S. Department of Education’s July 2025 Dear Colleague Letter clarifies how federal grants may support responsible AI use in schools, alongside a proposed supplemental priority for future grant competitions. The guidance covers potential support for AI literacy and computer science education in K–12 and higher education, educator professional development, AI-enabled instructional materials and tutoring, personalized learning, advising, and administrative tasks. It also emphasizes privacy and engagement with parents, teachers, and other stakeholders. This is a national policy and funding framework, not a defined teaching program; it does not specify a classroom model or confirm particular tools or deployments.
pedagogicalSummary: The initiative is federal guidance and a proposed grant priority, not a described teaching program, so the inspected page does not specify a complete pedagogy, lesson sequence, or classroom implementation model. It does point to learning approaches that grants may support: AI-enhanced high-impact tutoring, high-quality instructional materials, personalized learning and differentiated instruction, and integrating AI literacy and computer science fundamentals into teaching. It also calls for educator professional development and engagement with affected stakeholders, especially parents, in technology decisions; these support responsible adoption but are not themselves instructional methods. The evidence therefore indicates an emphasis on individualized instruction, tutoring, and AI/CS integration, while leaving details of how learning is organized unresolved. Source: https://www.ed.gov/about/news/press-release/us-department-of-education-issues-guidance-artificial-intelligence-use-schools-proposes-additional-supplemental-priority
prioritySummary: The initiative principally seeks to enable responsible AI use in education through federal grant funding and to expand AI and computer science education. The stated beneficiaries include students in K–12 and higher education, educators receiving professional development, and schools seeking improved learning outcomes and reduced administrative burdens. The proposed priority highlights AI literacy in teaching, AI/CS education, educator training, and AI-supported personalization and differentiated instruction; the accompanying guidance also identifies tutoring, instructional materials, and college- and career-pathway advising. The page links these efforts to preparing students with future problem-solving skills and strengthening economic competitiveness, alongside privacy and stakeholder-engagement considerations. It does not establish a single exclusive priority among these aims. Source: https://www.ed.gov/about/news/press-release/us-department-of-education-issues-guidance-artificial-intelligence-use-schools-proposes-additional-supplemental-priority
educationalTechnologySummary: The inspected page names no specific educational software, platform, AI product, or hardware, and gives no evidence that the Department develops a learning technology itself. Instead, it describes types of AI-enabled tools and uses that federal grant funds may support: AI-based instructional materials, AI-enhanced tutoring, college- and career-pathway exploration and advising, and AI for personalized or differentiated instruction. It also encourages AI technologies to improve classroom efficiency and support teacher training and evaluation. These are proposed or permitted uses, not identified products or confirmed deployments. The page mentions responsible adoption, privacy, and parent and teacher engagement, but provides no technical specifications or details about how particular technologies support learning. Source: https://www.ed.gov/about/news/press-release/us-department-of-education-issues-guidance-artificial-intelligence-use-schools-proposes-additional-supplemental-priority

inclusion.reason: AI-literacy element: The page explicitly mentions 'Integrating AI literacy into teaching practices' and 'teaching students about the appropriate use of AI' as part of the initiative. Inclusion route: This is formal guidance from the U.S. Department of Education (a national government executive department), issued as a Dear Colleague Letter and tied to federal discretionary grant priorities; this satisfies the government-endorsement/funding inclusion route. Evidence is sufficient on AI literacy content and official issuance; uncertainty remains only on whether the finalized rule after public comment modifies scope, but that does not preclude inclusion at screening.

summary: Digital Promise’s AI Literacy Framework is a guidance resource for promoting AI literacy in K–12 education. Organized around three modes of engagement—Understand, Evaluate, and Use—it emphasizes human judgment and justice and offers educators and leaders implementation “look-fors,” strategies, and case studies. The available description does not specify a teaching sequence, assessment approach, or particular delivery technology.

It highlights implementation “look-fors” for educators and leaders, plus strategies and case studies, suggesting support through examples and observable indicators. The page does not explain specific teaching activities, sequencing, or assessment methods, so these details cannot be established from the available evidence. Source: https://www.aiforeducation.io/blog/digital-promise-ai-literacy-framework
