metadata.Initiative / Programme: AFT National Academy for AI Instruction
metadata.Description: $23m programme from the American Federation of Teachers with Microsoft, OpenAI and Anthropic to train up to 400,000 K-12 educators in using and teaching AI.

summary: The AFT National Academy for AI Instruction is a U.S. professional-learning initiative developed by the American Federation of Teachers with Microsoft, OpenAI, and Anthropic. It aims to train up to 400,000 K–12 educators over five years in using and teaching AI, including its wise, ethical, and safe use in classrooms. Reported activities include hands-on workshops, with lessons intended to be shared through AFT’s Share My Lesson platform; the available evidence does not establish a detailed curriculum or specific tools used in the training.
pedagogicalSummary: The accessible reporting describes the National Academy for AI Instruction as providing hands-on workshops for teachers at a training center, with an ambition to make its lessons as open-source as possible and share them through AFT’s Share My Lesson platform. It does not explain a detailed teaching sequence, curriculum, or assessment approach. AFT’s stated aims include helping educators use AI wisely, ethically, and safely, and improve instruction and student engagement; these are goals, not evidence of a particular pedagogy. The article also reports debate over whether the training will be tool-agnostic and focused on teaching practice or will emphasize product use. Evidence is limited to reporting, not academy course materials. (https://www.the74million.org/article/will-new-ai-academy-help-teachers-or-just-improve-techs-bottom-line/)
prioritySummary: The initiative’s clearest emphasis is professional learning for K–12 educators: AFT announced a $23 million partnership with Microsoft, OpenAI, and Anthropic to establish an academy intended to train 400,000 educators over five years. AFT presents this as a way to address uneven access to AI training, support teachers in using AI wisely, ethically, and safely, and keep educators influential in decisions about classroom technology. The reported rationale also includes improving instruction and engagement, while helping students prepare to use AI effectively and safely in future work. The article includes critics’ concerns about commercial influence and whether the effort serves teachers and students, so its benefits and effects should not be treated as established outcomes. (https://www.the74million.org/article/will-new-ai-academy-help-teachers-or-just-improve-techs-bottom-line/)
educationalTechnologySummary: The reporting identifies Microsoft, OpenAI, and Anthropic as funders and partners, but does not name specific software, platforms, or hardware that the AFT academy itself develops or uses in its workshops. It reports criticism that the training could teach Microsoft tools, alongside AFT’s assurance that partners must be tool-agnostic; the inspected article does not resolve what tools will actually be used. The article about Google’s separate ISTE+ASCD partnership names Gemini and NotebookLM, but those belong to a different training initiative and should not be attributed to AFT’s academy. Thus, the available evidence establishes industry partnerships and an AI-training purpose, but not specific educational technologies deployed by AFT. (https://www.the74million.org/article/will-new-ai-academy-help-teachers-or-just-improve-techs-bottom-line/; https://www.the74million.org/article/exclusive-new-google-partnership-a-sizable-investment-in-ai-for-teachers/)

inclusion.reason: The initiative has clear AI-literacy components (training teachers in using and teaching AI) and is intended for a system-scale audience (up to 400,000 K-12 educators). It does not appear to be a single-institution project; however, the article confirms private funding and broad scope. Under inclusion rules, we lean toward inclusion when unsure about government endorsement or wide adoption evidence because the initiative is explicitly framed as national in scope and addresses AI literacy requirements.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: Google and ISTE+ASCD – free AI training for US educators (part of Google's $1bn US commitment)
metadata.Description: Three-year partnership to offer free Gemini-based AI training to all ~6 million US K-12 and higher-education faculty, within Google's $1bn, three-year US AI education commitment including the AI for Education Accelerator.

summary: A three-year Google–ISTE+ASCD partnership offering free AI professional development for K–12 teachers and higher-education faculty across the United States, with an intended audience of approximately six million educators. Training includes hands-on experience with Google Gemini and NotebookLM, certificates and digital badges, and guidance on effective, safe, and appropriate classroom use of AI. The programme emphasizes educator readiness and preparing students for an AI-influenced world; details on its curriculum, teaching methods, and assessment are not specified.
pedagogicalSummary: The accessible account describes a three-year educator training programme offered through ISTE+ASCD, with hands-on experience using Google’s Gemini and NotebookLM and certificates and digital badges. ISTE+ASCD says its role is to help educators learn effective practices for learning with AI, not merely how to operate a particular tool; the stated aims include classroom use and preparing students for a world shaped by AI. However, the article does not explain the training’s lesson sequence, teaching methods beyond hands-on experience, or how learning is assessed. The supported evidence therefore points to practical professional development and credentialing, but does not establish a more detailed pedagogical model. (https://www.route-fifty.com/artificial-intelligence/2026/02/new-google-partnership-sizable-investment-ai-teachers/411632/)
prioritySummary: The partnership principally aims to prepare US K–12 teachers and higher-education faculty for teaching in an AI-influenced environment: the article says the three-year training offer is intended to reach all six million educators. It addresses teachers’ reported lack of preparation both to use AI in classrooms and to prepare students for the world they will enter. Google also describes helping educators apply AI safely and appropriately, while its stated longer-term aspiration is to improve learning outcomes. The account presents educator readiness and student preparation as connected priorities, rather than identifying a single exclusive beneficiary or ranking these aims. The article does not establish that the programme is primarily workforce upskilling beyond educators’ professional needs. (https://www.route-fifty.com/artificial-intelligence/2026/02/new-google-partnership-sizable-investment-ai-teachers/411632/)
educationalTechnologySummary: The programme is described as using Google’s Gemini and NotebookLM for educators’ hands-on training; Google says the initiative comes with use of its products and a free access tier to help teachers get started. These are identified as technologies used in the training, not as tools developed by ISTE+ASCD. The article does not specify how either tool is integrated into instruction or provide details about course platforms, hardware, or other learning software. It also mentions ISTE+ASCD’s educator-focused AI chatbot, introduced in 2023 and built on curated, organization-approved content, but does not identify it as part of this new partnership’s training. Accordingly, the evidence supports naming the Google tools used, while the wider educational-technology setup remains unspecified. (https://www.route-fifty.com/artificial-intelligence/2026/02/new-google-partnership-sizable-investment-ai-teachers/411632/)

inclusion.reason: The initiative satisfies the AI-literacy requirement by offering 'free AI training' which implies educational content on using AI tools. It qualifies for inclusion under the non-government work with system-scale adoption route, targeting ~6 million US educators (nearly all K-12 and higher ed faculty), representing massive reach beyond a single institution. The metadata indicates a national scale partnership rather than a university-specific course.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: Private-sector pledges aligned with the April 2025 AI education executive order
metadata.Description: Company commitments including Google's $1bn, Amazon's training for 4 million learners and AI curricula for 10,000 educators by 2028, Microsoft Copilot access via Elevate, OpenAI Academy certifications and Apple free content.

summary: A collection of private-sector commitments associated with the April 2025 U.S. AI education executive order, rather than a single coordinated program. Major technology companies describe plans for AI learning and tool access for K–12 students, educators, college communities, and workers, including curricula, educator training, courses and certifications, classroom tools, learning content, funding, and student challenges. The reported approaches range from structured instruction to practical and project-based activities, with some attention to responsible AI. The commitments are broad in subject and intended audience, but the account aggregates separate pledges and does not establish how consistently they are implemented.
pedagogicalSummary: The inspected account describes a varied set of company-led learning activities, not one shared teaching model. Reported approaches include educator training and curricula, courses and certifications, classroom integration of AI, and student competitions. NVIDIA’s planned K–12 materials are described as offering hands-on experience; Intel also supports AI competitions, while Apple is working with a partner to train educators in responsible AI. These examples suggest practical and project-oriented learning alongside structured instruction, but the article gives little detail about lesson design, assessment, or how learning is delivered. The evidence is from a third-party overview of pledges, so it does not establish how consistently these approaches are implemented (https://builtin.com/artificial-intelligence/trump-big-tech-ai-education).
prioritySummary: The article presents the commitments as principally aimed at expanding AI education and skills in the United States, especially for students, educators, and workers, while supporting an “AI-ready workforce” and U.S. competitiveness in AI. Commitments include training millions of learners, preparing educators, supporting K–12 students, and offering worker certifications. Some pledges have more specific beneficiaries or aims, such as xAI’s focus on underserved youth, Google’s digital-wellbeing funding, and the Presidential AI Challenge’s emphasis on student solutions to community issues. Because the article aggregates independent company pledges, it supports multiple priorities rather than a single uniform hierarchy (https://builtin.com/artificial-intelligence/trump-big-tech-ai-education).
educationalTechnologySummary: The article reports both access to existing AI products and learning resources developed or adapted by companies and partners. Google plans to provide U.S. high schools with Gemini for Education and expand its AI for Education Accelerator; Microsoft plans broader student and teacher access to Copilot through Elevate. Anthropic describes partnerships intended to help educators and students use Claude, and NVIDIA is working with Study Fetch and CK-12 to adapt its educational content for K–12 learners. Amazon’s cloud credits are intended to connect schools and organizations to cloud and AI technologies. The article does not explain the tools’ instructional operation in detail, and some pledges concern training, funding, or content rather than educational technology itself (https://builtin.com/artificial-intelligence/trump-big-tech-ai-education).

inclusion.reason: The initiative includes significant AI literacy components (educational curricula, learner training, certifications, and specific mentions of implementing AI in schools) and is backed by the 'April 2025 AI education executive order.' This executive order route provides government endorsement and mandate, satisfying an inclusion criterion. Furthermore, the scale of commitments (e.g., 10,000 educators, millions of learners) suggests system-scale reach or platform access.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: Code.org – AI 101 for Educators and AI curricula
metadata.Description: Free self-paced foundational course for teachers (updated 2026) plus K-12 AI units such as 'How AI Makes Decisions' (one week) and 'Exploring Generative AI' (six weeks).

summary: Code.org’s free, self-paced AI 101 course provides professional learning for K–12 educators through five roughly hour-long modules. It introduces AI and large language models, supports practical classroom use through prompting and lesson planning, and addresses evaluating outputs, bias, privacy, misinformation, and academic integrity. Related student curricula span grades 3–12 and include hands-on exploration of data models and AI tools, ethical discussion, and creative projects. The evidence describes a substantial range of educator and student materials, but does not establish AI-specific audience or adoption figures.
pedagogicalSummary: AI 101 is organised as a free, self-paced professional-learning course with five roughly hour-long modules. The suggested sequence supports teachers new to AI, but modules can also be taken independently to address classroom needs. Its approach combines foundational explanations with practical application: educators learn to use and refine prompts, consider AI in planning and teaching, evaluate outputs for bias and reliability, and develop lessons and assessments. The linked student materials add evidence of hands-on and reflective learning, including making predictions with data models, exploring interactive AI widgets, discussing ethical questions, and creating projects. These are approaches described on the inspected overview pages; the full course and lesson activities were not reviewed in depth. (https://code.org/mr/professional-learning/artificial-intelligence-101; https://code.org/en-US/curriculum/how-artificial-intelligence-works; https://code.org/en-US/artificial-intelligence)
prioritySummary: The clearest emphasis is building educators’ AI and digital fluency so they can understand AI, use it deliberately, question its outputs, and teach about it with confidence and responsibility. The course is aimed at K–12 teachers, including those who have been asked to address AI without prior instruction. A related, broader priority is helping K–12 students become informed users and creators through accessible AI curricula across grade levels. The pages stress critical evaluation, bias, privacy, academic integrity, creativity, and responsible use alongside practical classroom application. They do not establish a single workforce or economic objective as the principal priority; the evidence points instead to educator readiness and student learning. (https://code.org/mr/professional-learning/artificial-intelligence-101; https://code.org/en-US/artificial-intelligence)
educationalTechnologySummary: The course is delivered through Code.org’s online Studio learning platform, where its modules are accessed; the overview describes the course as self-paced but does not expose its full interactive design in the inspected pages. Code.org also offers short “How AI Works” videos paired with classroom lessons, including hands-on widgets for exploring neural networks and image-generation models, and activities using predictive data models. These are identifiable learning technologies or media used within the linked AI education materials. The AI overview additionally names CodeAI offerings such as Web Lab, AI Tutor, and an AI Teaching Assistant, but the inspected pages do not show that they are required for AI 101. ETS Criterion Interactive, Khanmigo, and ISTE’s course are presented as external resources, not Code.org-developed technologies. (https://code.org/mr/professional-learning/artificial-intelligence-101; https://code.org/en-US/curriculum/how-artificial-intelligence-works; https://code.org/en-US/artificial-intelligence)

inclusion.reason: The initiative includes explicit AI literacy elements: educational video content explaining how AI works, demystifying AI concepts, and providing responsible use guidance. It is issued by Code.org, a non-profit organization with evidenced system-scale adoption (active in thousands of US schools and supported by major educational partnerships), satisfying the inclusion route of non-government work with evidence of system-scale adoption. The initiative also links to K-12 curricula used in school settings.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: Scale AI / UMSL / Lindbergh Schools – "Fundamentals of AI for Educators" microcredential
metadata.Description: Free 12-hour online AI fundamentals course for K-12 teachers, available nationwide through UMSL's Advanced Workforce Center; part of Scale's commitment to train 1,000 teachers and equip 500,000 students by 2029.

summary: Fundamentals of AI for Educators is a free, 12-hour online microcredential developed by Scale AI with the University of Missouri–St. Louis and Lindbergh Schools for K–12 teachers. Available nationwide, the self-paced course combines videos, readings, interactive checks, and applied assignments to build foundational AI knowledge and support ethical, effective classroom use. Participants develop a classroom-ready instructional artifact and receive a certificate and digital badge upon completion. Students are an intended downstream beneficiary as educators bring AI learning into their classrooms.
pedagogicalSummary: The course uses flexible, asynchronous, self-paced learning for K–12 educators. UMSL describes a mix of videos, readings, interactive checks, applied activities, and assignments culminating in a final artifact relevant to participants’ instructional practice. The emphasis is practical application: teachers develop classroom-ready strategies and an instructional artifact tied to a learning objective, while considering ethical use and ways AI might support instruction and student engagement. The launch article also reports that 20 Lindbergh teachers piloted the curriculum and helped shape it around educators’ practical needs. These details support a blend of independent online study, practice, and artifact-based learning; the inspected pages do not establish additional teaching methods. prioritySummary: The initiative principally aims to give K–12 teachers practical knowledge and judgment to use AI effectively and responsibly in classrooms, with the intended benefit extending to their students and school communities. The stated rationale is that teachers can pass foundational AI understanding and habits such as critical inquiry, creativity, and responsible technology use to successive groups of learners. The course is available nationwide at no cost, and it contributes to Scale’s commitment to help train 1,000 teachers and equip 500,000 students with foundational AI skills by 2029. The inspected pages foreground educator training as the means and broader student AI literacy as a desired downstream benefit; they do not present workforce upskilling as the course’s sole or primary purpose. metadata.Initiative / Programme: Penn GSE – "AI Auditing for High School" curriculum (Nov 2025)
metadata.Description: Four classroom-tested lessons (algorithmic bias, audits and inquiry, a TikTok audit, and physical-computing AI/ML with micro:bit) from Penn GSE and Penn CIS that teach students to examine AI systems critically; no coding experience required.

summary: AI Auditing for High School is a classroom-tested curriculum developed by Penn GSE with Penn’s Computer and Information Sciences department for high school students. Its four lessons use an inquiry-oriented approach to explore algorithmic bias and auditing, including a hands-on audit of TikTok and a physical-computing AI/ML activity using Microbit CreateAI. Designed for students with no coding experience, the curriculum emphasizes critically examining how AI systems work, whether they are fair, and whom they serve; educators in the Exploring Computer Science network helped pilot and shape the lessons.
pedagogicalSummary: The curriculum uses a classroom-based, inquiry-oriented approach: students learn about algorithmic bias and auditing, then conduct hands-on audits of real-world AI applications, including a TikTok audit. The release describes four classroom-tested lessons and says no coding experience is required, suggesting that critical examination and guided investigation—not programming instruction—are central. Materials are supported by research articles, classroom videos, and reports of student-led audits; educators in the Exploring Computer Science network helped pilot and shape the curriculum. The accessible overview does not provide enough detail to describe specific teaching sequences, assessment methods, or how teachers facilitate each activity. Evidence: https://www.newswise.com/articles/high-school-students-learn-to-audit-tiktok-and-other-ai-systems; lesson overview: https://docs.google.com/document/d/1_1eD0Ll185rdg20q2tbuTwnjPwK4hVo7pY277ip4Tas/edit?tab=t.0#heading=h.u4jkq3dhalqb
prioritySummary: The initiative principally aims to equip high school students to critically examine algorithmic bias and question how AI systems work, whether they work fairly, and whom they serve. Its stated benefits include developing critical thinkers and ethical technology users, with students gaining experience auditing applications they encounter in the real world. The curriculum also appears designed to be usable by computer science educators, including those whose students have no coding experience; educators contributed to piloting and shaping it. The release situates this work within Penn GSE’s broader AI-and-education activity, but the inspected evidence supports the student-facing goal of critical AI scrutiny most directly and does not establish a separate workforce or well-being priority. Evidence: https://www.newswise.com/articles/high-school-students-learn-to-audit-tiktok-and-other-ai-systems
educationalTechnologySummary: The release identifies TikTok as the subject of one lesson’s audit, and names “Microbit CreateAI” in a physical-computing AI/ML lesson. These are the only specific technologies identified in the accessible materials: TikTok is presented as an AI system students examine, while Microbit CreateAI is named as part of a lesson, though the page does not clarify what hardware or software students use or whether the curriculum supplies it. The curriculum is described as requiring no coding experience. Research articles, classroom videos, and reports of student audits support the lessons, but the inspected pages do not establish that these are interactive learning technologies developed by the initiative. The lesson document’s accessible view provides only an outline, limiting further detail. Evidence: https://www.newswise.com/articles/high-school-students-learn-to-audit-tiktok-and-other-ai-systems; https://docs.google.com/document/d/1_1eD0Ll185rdg20q2tbuTwnjPwK4hVo7pY277ip4Tas/edit?tab=t.0#heading=h.u4jkq3dhalqb

inclusion.reason: The initiative qualifies for inclusion based on the AI-literacy requirement as it is explicitly educational content teaching students 'how to examine AI systems critically' and covers concepts like algorithmic bias and physical-computing AI. It meets the inclusion route for university work (Elements of AI qualification) that has a plausible wider audience, specifically targeting high schools as evidenced by its classroom-tested nature and scaling via the PASS program. The curriculum explains how to use AI tools (like TikTok) for auditing purposes and includes learning objectives about AI systems.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: Penn GSE Living Laboratory for Human Agency and AI (and PASS programme)
metadata.Description: Penn GSE hub bringing together researchers, educators, schools and industry on AI literacy and pedagogy, trust and ethics, and co-designed tools; works with school systems through the Pioneering AI in School Systems (PASS) programme launched in 2025.

summary: Penn GSE’s Living Laboratory for Human Agency and AI is a research and collaboration hub connecting educators, researchers, schools, school systems, and industry to shape AI use in education. Its work focuses on AI literacy and pedagogy, human agency, and trustworthy, safe, and equitable use, with plans to co-design and test tools in educational settings and build evidence about their effects. The Pioneering AI in School Systems (PASS) programme supports school systems exploring AI, including questions of student outcomes, governance, and equity. Related Penn GSE examples include students investigating bias in AI and tools supporting children’s robot design and teachers’ lesson planning; the announcement does not establish that these are Living Lab projects.
pedagogicalSummary: The announcement describes practice-driven, collaborative learning and inquiry rather than a single prescribed teaching method. The Living Lab aims to co-design and test AI tools in authentic educational settings, with educators and learners helping shape designs and build evidence about their effects. Examples from Penn GSE’s broader work include young children designing humanoid robots through CORAL and high school students investigating AI bias through an algorithm-auditing project; CraftPad supports teachers’ lesson design while keeping their expertise and judgment central. These suggest hands-on design, critical investigation, and teacher-supported design practices, but the article does not specify lesson sequences or how these projects will be integrated into the new Lab. Source: https://www.newswise.com/articles/educators-are-racing-to-shape-ai-before-it-shapes-education/
prioritySummary: The initiative’s stated emphasis is to help education shape AI’s development and use, rather than leave schools reacting to technological change. It seeks AI that enhances human agency and learning, alongside attention to trust, safety, ethics, privacy, security, and learner well-being. Its intended beneficiaries and participants include students, educators, schools, and school systems; the announcement also identifies policymakers and Penn GSE and university students as audiences for related activities. Further priorities include evidence-based innovation in real educational settings, AI literacy and pedagogy, and partnerships and infrastructure to sustain work at scale. PASS is described as helping school systems explore AI in relation to student outcomes, governance, equity, and safe deployment. The article lists these priorities without establishing a hierarchy among them. Source: https://www.newswise.com/articles/educators-are-racing-to-shape-ai-before-it-shapes-education/
educationalTechnologySummary: The announcement identifies several technologies or technology-related projects in Penn GSE’s broader portfolio, but does not establish that they are products of the newly launched Living Lab itself. CORAL enables young children to design humanoid robots; CraftPad is an AI-assisted workspace for teachers’ lesson design, intended to support their work while centering their professional judgment. A separate algorithm-auditing project uses AI systems as objects of high-school students’ bias investigations, though no software or platform is named. The article mentions possible future evaluation of AI tutoring tools, not a particular tool already adopted by the initiative. It gives no hardware specifications, software platforms, or details about access and classroom deployment. The Living Lab is presented chiefly as a collaboration and research network that may translate research into practical tools. Source: https://www.newswise.com/articles/educators-are-racing-to-shape-ai-before-it-shapes-education/

inclusion.reason: The announcement explicitly identifies AI Literacy and Pedagogy as a priority and describes educational work teaching students to investigate AI bias. It reports collaboration with school systems and a three-state PASS initiative, suggesting potential reach beyond a single institution; however, it does not establish system-scale adoption. metadata.Initiative / Programme: Stanford CRAFT – Classroom-Ready Resources About AI For Teaching
metadata.Description: Free, adaptable AI-literacy resources for high school teachers in all subjects (from 15-minute activities to full lessons), co-designed with teachers by Stanford GSE with HAI; also listed on a US government information-literacy resource hub.

summary: Stanford CRAFT is a free collection of adaptable AI-literacy resources designed primarily for high-school teachers across subject areas. Co-designed with educators, it offers short activities, full lessons, and suggested multi-day sequences, alongside professional development for teachers. Materials use inquiry, discussion, and hands-on examples to help students understand AI and examine its uses, limitations, and effects, including issues such as bias, data, fairness, and creative rights.
pedagogicalSummary: CRAFT combines teacher co-design with flexible, multidisciplinary classroom instruction. Teachers contribute to resource design, and classroom implementation and discussion inform the materials; educators can adapt short activities or lessons to their students and curriculum, or use suggested multi-day sequences. Accessible examples use active learning and inquiry: students play a hiring simulation to examine algorithmic bias, investigate how AI systems work, and use discussion, debate, analysis, or creative tasks to question their effects. The initiative also supports educators through in-person or synchronous virtual professional development, including opportunities to explore and critique AI and design learning experiences. These approaches are described at https://craft.stanford.edu/ and https://craft.stanford.edu/about/co-design-fellows/, with examples at https://craft.stanford.edu/stacks/ and https://craft.stanford.edu/resource/what-is-algorithmic-bias/.
prioritySummary: CRAFT principally aims to help high-school students develop AI literacy across subject areas, while equipping teachers to teach it and make informed decisions about AI in educational practice. Its stated student-facing emphasis is on exploring, understanding, questioning, and critiquing AI, rather than simply learning to operate AI tools. The resources address AI’s benefits and limitations alongside responsibilities and harms, including bias, fairness, data use, misinformation, and environmental impacts. Professional development extends the benefit to educators, including those working across grade levels, by building their knowledge and supporting integration of AI literacy into teaching. The inspected pages present these educational goals together and do not establish a single narrower priority. See https://craft.stanford.edu/ and https://craft.stanford.edu/professional-development/.
educationalTechnologySummary: The inspected pages identify CRAFT primarily as a provider of adaptable instructional materials, including teacher guides and slides, rather than a developer of a standalone learning platform or software. Some lessons use or invite students to engage with external AI technologies: an art lesson names Adobe Firefly and has students create AI-generated artwork, while a lesson stack describes ChatGPT for narrative writing and generative AI music tools. A flood-forecasting lesson uses Market Marshes, a game-based AI Quest; the page attributes AI Quests to Google Research and the Stanford Accelerator for Learning, not to CRAFT. These examples show technologies serving as objects for exploration or hands-on learning, but the inspected pages do not establish that CRAFT itself develops these tools. See https://craft.stanford.edu/resource/how-is-ai-transforming-visual-artwork-creation/, https://craft.stanford.edu/stacks/, and https://craft.stanford.edu/resource/how-can-ai-help-a-community-prepare-for-a-flood/.

inclusion.reason: The site describes explicit AI-literacy instruction and a broad intended audience of classroom educators, with teachers from multiple US states involved in co-design. This makes reach beyond a single institution plausible, though the pages read do not establish system-scale adoption or government endorsement. The metadata’s government-hub listing was not verified. Sources: https://craft.stanford.edu/ and https://craft.stanford.edu/about/.

metadata.Description: Two-week online or residential programme for grade 9 students to explore AI through research projects, lectures and mentorship.

summary: Stanford AI4ALL is a two-week online or residential programme for students entering grade 9. Through research projects, guest lectures and mentorship from professionals, students explore AI and its applications, including in medicine and disaster response, while building confidence to pursue STEM careers.
pedagogicalSummary: The K-12 page describes Stanford AI4ALL as a two-week online or residential program for students in grade 9, combining research projects, guest lectures, and mentorship; participants also engage with professionals in the field. This indicates a mix of project-based, lecture-based, and mentored learning, with opportunities to explore real-world AI applications such as medicine and disaster response. The page does not explain the projects’ structure, how students are assessed, or how the online and residential formats differ. HAI’s broader education page describes AI4ALL as a three-week online program involving lectures, hands-on research projects, and mentoring, so the inspected pages differ on duration and format (https://hai.stanford.edu/education/k-12; https://hai.stanford.edu/education).
prioritySummary: For Stanford AI4ALL, the stated emphasis is helping grade 9 students explore artificial intelligence and supporting their confidence to pursue STEM careers. The K-12 page highlights learning from professionals and considering AI applications in areas including medicine, disaster response, and poverty alleviation. HAI’s broader education page says AI4ALL aims to increase inclusion in AI, adding an explicit field-wide inclusion goal; the inspected pages do not specify which student groups are prioritized or describe selection criteria beyond grade eligibility. The pages present these aims together but do not establish a hierarchy among them (https://hai.stanford.edu/education/k-12; https://hai.stanford.edu/education).
educationalTechnologySummary: The inspected pages identify online delivery as an option for Stanford AI4ALL, alongside a residential format, but do not name a learning platform, software, hardware, or AI tool used by participants. The K-12 page also describes CRAFT as a collection of free, co-designed AI-literacy resources for high-school teachers, intended to help students explore, understand, question, and critique AI. It does not identify specific digital technologies within those resources, and CRAFT is described as a separate teacher-resource initiative rather than a technology used by AI4ALL. Thus, the available evidence supports online delivery and classroom resources, but not any specifically named educational technology (https://hai.stanford.edu/education/k-12).

inclusion.reason: The page describes learning about AI and its applications, which supports an AI-literacy element. Stanford offers the program online to eligible students, making reach beyond a single institution plausible, though the page provides no evidence of system-scale adoption or government support; the program’s wider reach is uncertain. metadata.Initiative / Programme: MIT App Inventor – "Artificial Intelligence with MIT App Inventor" tutorials and extensions
metadata.Description: Free tutorial lessons and student project ideas for building AI-enabled mobile apps, including the Personal Image Classifier (PIC) and other machine-learning extensions; PIC is maintained by MIT under Apache 2.0 and the community forum shows 2026 activity.

summary: Artificial Intelligence with MIT App Inventor is a free collection of tutorials, project ideas, and curriculum units for learners in grades 3–12, with supporting materials for teachers. Using MIT App Inventor, students build and test AI-enabled mobile apps, including image classifiers and projects involving voice or external services such as ChatGPT. The materials combine guided, hands-on app creation with exploration of machine learning and reflection on AI’s limitations, societal effects, and ethical questions, including deepfakes.
pedagogicalSummary: The initiative explicitly describes its approach as active constructionist learning: students learn by creating programs and apps that put their own ideas into practice. Tutorials and curriculum units scaffold this work, with teacher guides, lesson plans, slides, student guides, and assessments supporting classroom use. In the image-classification unit, students first explore machine learning with Teachable Machine, then build and test an App Inventor classifier and discuss its strengths, limitations, and possible improvements. Other units add group argumentation and discussion—for example, students create a voice-changing app and consider deepfakes’ societal effects. These examples support a mix of hands-on project work, guided instruction, experimentation, and reflection, rather than a purely lecture-based model. Evidence: https://appinventor.mit.edu/explore/ai-with-mit-app-inventor ; https://appinventor.mit.edu/explore/resources/ai/image-classification-look-extension ; https://appinventor.mit.edu/explore/resources/ai/fake_voices_unit
prioritySummary: The principal emphasis is helping school-age learners understand AI and machine learning by making their own AI-related mobile applications. The initiative presents students as creators, not only users of digital technology, and aims to make app-building with AI accessible even to beginners. Its materials span elementary through high-school grades, with specific units for middle- and high-school learners. Alongside technical learning, some activities invite students to consider AI’s societal implications: the deepfakes unit asks groups to discuss possible future impacts and uses or abuses, while the image-classification unit prompts reflection on data, benefits, and limitations. The inspected pages therefore show both practical student learning and critical consideration of AI; they do not establish one as subordinate to the other. Evidence: https://appinventor.mit.edu/explore/ai-with-mit-app-inventor ; https://appinventor.mit.edu/explore/resources/ai/image-classification-look-extension ; https://appinventor.mit.edu/explore/resources/ai/fake_voices_unit
educationalTechnologySummary: MIT App Inventor is the central development environment: students use it to create mobile apps, with tutorials guiding them through app projects. The image-classification unit identifies MIT App Inventor’s LookExtension, a machine-learning extension used in an app that classifies photos taken on mobile devices; the PICaboo tutorial has students make a game using a Personal Image Classification model. The initiative also uses Teachable Machine as an introductory web-based exploration before students code their own classifier, and its teacher page describes phone or tablet testing, with a computer-based phone emulator as an alternative for classroom app testing. Tutorials also show students building apps that connect to external services such as ChatGPT, but the inspected pages do not indicate that these services are developed by MIT App Inventor. Evidence: https://appinventor.mit.edu/explore/resources/ai/image-classification-look-extension ; https://appinventor.mit.edu/explore/resources/ai/picaboo ; https://appinventor.mit.edu/explore/teach ; https://appinventor.mit.edu/explore/resources/ai/simpleChatGPT

inclusion.reason: The initiative explicitly includes AI literacy through educational content explaining how AI works (e.g., machine learning extensions, image classification) and ethical considerations (e.g., fake voices). It satisfies the inclusion route of being issued and maintained by a national institution (MIT) with active community support and open-source licensing, which aligns with the criteria for non-government work with system-scale adoption or government endorsement potential. The AI-literacy requirement is clearly met as the tutorials teach concepts and usage of AI tools.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: aiEDU – AI Readiness Framework v2.0
metadata.Description: Research-based framework in four parts: student AI literacy and readiness competencies, educator competencies, school-leader guidance and a school/district readiness rubric; first released Oct 2024 and revised; reported as cited by 13 states and 87 organisations.

summary: aiEDU’s AI Readiness Framework v2.0 is a research-based framework for preparing K–12 students to learn and thrive alongside AI, while supporting the educators and school systems who guide them. It sets out student and educator competencies, guidance for school leaders, and readiness rubrics for schools and districts, emphasizing AI literacy alongside subject knowledge and durable skills such as critical thinking and collaboration. aiEDU’s accompanying curriculum offers classroom activities, discussions, and projects, often designed for low-tech use, to help students understand AI and critically assess or direct its outputs.
pedagogicalSummary: aiEDU supports learning through short, classroom-ready activities and longer inquiry-based or scaffolded sequences. Its curriculum includes hands-on elementary activities, discussion-based activities integrated into existing subjects, projects in which students investigate a topic and create an artifact, self-paced plans, and multi-day learning journeys with practice-based assessments. The portal describes the materials as designed to foster collaboration, critical thinking, and creativity, and says teachers help shape curriculum through feedback, piloting, and co-design. Educator learning also includes a fellowship with ongoing professional learning, experimentation and reflection, and a peer network for sharing ideas. The framework describes a progression from learning AI basics to critical thinking and applying human strengths. Evidence: https://curriculum.aiedu.org/ ; https://www.aiedu.org/trailblazers-fellowship ; https://www.aiedu.org/ai-readiness-framework-new
prioritySummary: The initiative’s central aim is to prepare K–12 students to live, work, and thrive in a world where AI is pervasive. It emphasizes accessible AI literacy alongside subject knowledge and durable human skills—such as critical thinking and collaboration—so students can direct and assess AI and pursue their life and career potential. Students are the stated end beneficiaries, while educators, school leaders, and districts are supported to build that readiness. aiEDU also describes efforts to make AI-readiness work accessible across backgrounds and to support organizations serving rural and Indigenous communities. The inspected pages present these aims together rather than establishing a distinct priority hierarchy among them. Evidence: https://www.aiedu.org/impact-report-2025-ai-readiness-framework ; https://www.aiedu.org/ai-readiness-framework-new ; https://www.aiedu.org/district-programs
educationalTechnologySummary: The inspected pages identify aiEDU’s curriculum portal as the platform for browsing and previewing resources by grade, subject, or topic, creating an account, and saving or downloading materials. The materials themselves are generally described as low-tech; examples include printable activities requiring no computers and discussion starters delivered as slides without computers. The pages do not identify a particular AI application, classroom software, or hardware that aiEDU develops or requires students to use for learning. Instead, the curriculum explores AI concepts and issues through activities, discussion, and projects, including topics such as AI outputs and deepfakes. Thus, evidence supports a digital resource-access platform and downloadable materials, but not a specific AI learning tool. Evidence: https://curriculum.aiedu.org/ ; https://www.aiedu.org/impact-report-2025-ai-readiness-framework

inclusion.reason: The initiative clearly includes AI literacy through its definition of 'AI Readiness' as leveraging core content knowledge and durable skills alongside AI tools, and by outlining specific competencies for students and educators. It qualifies for inclusion under the inclusion route regarding 'evidence of system-scale adoption', as the metadata reports it is 'cited by 13 states and 87 organisations'. metadata.Initiative / Programme: aiEDU – free K-12 AI literacy curriculum, fellowships and professional learning
metadata.Description: Free standards-aligned materials (AI Snapshots five-minute warm-ups, elementary explorations, AP CSP projects), with Learning Journeys and Curriculum Companions in development for 2026–27; a Trailblazer Fellowship; a full-year grades 8–12 curriculum with Quill.org (2025–26); and Spanish-language AI Snapshots. 13,000+ registered educators.

summary: aiEDU, a US-based nonprofit, provides free AI literacy resources for K–12 students and support for educators. Its offerings include short classroom discussion activities, elementary explorations, secondary projects, a full-year grades 8–12 curriculum, educator fellowships and professional learning; some AI Snapshots are also available in Spanish. Activities use hands-on exploration, inquiry, discussion and scaffolded projects, and can be taught across existing subjects, sometimes without computers. The curriculum addresses AI concepts and use as well as ethics, social impacts, data, safety and media literacy. The initiative reports more than 13,000 registered educators.
pedagogicalSummary: The curriculum combines hands-on exploration, discussion, inquiry, and scaffolded instruction. Short elementary activities introduce foundational concepts, while secondary “Snapshots” prompt discussion within existing subject classes; longer projects ask students to investigate a topic and create a shareable artifact. Learning Journeys are described as multi-day sequences with scaffolding and practice-based assessments, and Flex Plans offer self-paced experiences. The portal emphasizes collaboration, critical thinking, creativity, student agency, and teacher co-design through feedback and piloting. It presents AI learning as adaptable across subjects rather than requiring a dedicated AI course. These are described approaches in the curriculum overview; the inspected pages do not provide detailed lesson procedures for every resource. (https://curriculum.aiedu.org/)
prioritySummary: aiEDU’s stated priority is preparing all students to understand, use, and critically evaluate AI so they can live, work, and thrive in a world where it is widespread. The curriculum portal focuses on making AI readiness usable across K–12 classrooms and existing subjects, while supporting educators with classroom materials. The broader organization describes professional development and partnerships with schools, systems, and families as part of embedding AI readiness in teaching. It also emphasizes equitable access, particularly concern that students without exposure to AI education could be left behind. Workforce preparation is one stated benefit, but the inspected pages frame the goal more broadly as student readiness for society and work. (https://curriculum.aiedu.org/; https://www.aiedu.org/about)
educationalTechnologySummary: The inspected pages identify no specific learning platform, software, or hardware that aiEDU develops or uses to deliver instruction. Instead, the curriculum is presented as downloadable teaching materials: some elementary explorations are printable and need no computers, and introductory Snapshots use slides without requiring computers or a computer-science background. The initiative describes its activities as low-tech, suggesting technology use is not necessary for at least these examples. The curriculum portal lets educators preview, save, and download resources, but the pages do not establish it as an instructional learning technology. AI systems and tools appear as topics for students to examine; the evidence does not show that students must use them as part of these activities. (https://curriculum.aiedu.org/)

inclusion.reason: The initiative includes substantive AI literacy content (curriculum materials, framework for student and educator competencies regarding AI) addressing how AI works and how to use it. It has significant scale with over 13,000 registered educators and offers fellowships and district programs. While the metadata notes it is a US initiative (not explicitly government-funded or mandated), the inclusion route of non-government work with evidenced system-scale adoption (13,000+ educators) is satisfied, making it eligible for inclusion.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: Ceibal – "Marco referencial para la enseñanza de la inteligencia artificial"
metadata.Description: Reference framework from Plan Ceibal for teaching AI, described by a regional report as a pioneering effort in Latin America aimed at forming critical citizens; sits within Ceibal's Computational Thinking and AI programme.

summary: Plan Ceibal’s “Marco referencial para la enseñanza de la inteligencia artificial” is a framework intended to guide AI education in Uruguay’s public-school context. It emphasizes helping learners understand AI and engage with it critically and ethically, within Ceibal’s broader computational-thinking and AI programme. The available evidence does not detail the framework’s specific teaching activities or how widely it has been implemented.
pedagogicalSummary: The inspected article identifies Ceibal’s framework as aiming to form citizens who can critically and ethically understand and use AI, but does not describe the framework’s specific teaching activities or implementation. The article’s broader pedagogical argument—not necessarily a description of Ceibal’s practice—is to weave AI into curricula and teaching, learning, and assessment across subjects, building students’ understanding of how AI works alongside critical, autonomous, and ethical thinking. It also emphasizes educator mediation, collaborative learning, and using AI to support rather than replace human interaction. These principles are presented as recommendations for education systems generally, so evidence about Ceibal’s actual methods remains limited. (https://www.elobservador.com.uy/opinion/sobre-vision-y-usos-la-inteligencia-artificial-ia-educacion-n6037067)
prioritySummary: The clearest stated priority for Ceibal’s “Marco referencial para la enseñanza de la inteligencia artificial” is forming a citizenry able to understand AI and engage with it critically and ethically, including its potential to transform society. The article situates this within a wider aim of democratizing learning and improving its equity and quality, with particular concern for vulnerable groups and for inclusive, cohesive democratic societies. It also presents AI literacy as relevant to education and work, but does not establish that as the framework’s leading purpose. The article reports the framework’s goal rather than detailing its beneficiaries or how its priorities are implemented. (https://www.elobservador.com.uy/opinion/sobre-vision-y-usos-la-inteligencia-artificial-ia-educacion-n6037067)
educationalTechnologySummary: The article does not identify any particular educational technology that Ceibal developed or uses to teach AI literacy; it identifies a reference framework, which is guidance rather than a technology. It discusses AI tutorials and assistants as possible supports for personalized teaching and learning, and automated test correction and AI-enabled digital textbooks as examples in broader regional or international discussion. It also mentions ChatGPT in describing an external study, not as a Ceibal learning tool. These examples therefore do not establish that Ceibal uses or develops them. On the evidence inspected, Ceibal’s educational technology provision for this initiative cannot be specified. (https://www.elobservador.com.uy/opinion/sobre-vision-y-usos-la-inteligencia-artificial-ia-educacion-n6037067)

inclusion.reason: AI-literacy element present: explicitly described as a teaching framework for forming critical citizens about AI (not just using AI to deliver education). Inclusion route satisfied: Plan Ceibal is Uruguay's national government-backed programme implemented across all public schools, indicating government involvement at scale. Uncertainties: webpage content not directly verified due to read failures; however, inclusive screening principle applies when evidence is incomplete.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: MOET Decision 3439/QD-BGDDT (15 Dec 2025) – framework for pilot AI education
metadata.Description: Pilot framework (Dec 2025–May 2026) aligned with the Informatics curriculum to avoid duplication; piloted from primary to high school before the nationwide rollout.

summary: Vietnam’s Ministry of Education and Training established a framework for piloting AI education among general-education students from primary through upper-secondary school, from December 2025 to May 2026, ahead of a planned nationwide rollout. Aligned with the Informatics curriculum to avoid duplication, it covers human-centred AI, including ethics, safety and privacy; AI techniques, data and applications; and designing and evaluating AI systems. The framework also addresses responsible use, such as verifying AI outputs, and includes programming and system-development content at higher levels. Specific teaching methods and educational technologies are not established in the available evidence.
pedagogicalSummary: The inspected page identifies a Ministry of Education and Training decision promulgating a framework for pilot AI education, but the rendered document was too large to inspect in detail. The accessible evidence therefore does not establish how learning is taught or organised—such as through projects, direct instruction, or other approaches. This is a gap in the inspected material, not evidence that the framework contains no pedagogical approach. Further detail would require examining the framework itself (https://english.luatvietnam.vn/decision-no-3439-qd-bgddt-dated-december-15-2025-of-the-ministry-of-education-and-training-promulgating-the-framework-for-pilot-artificial-intellige-421474-doc1.html).
prioritySummary: The initiative’s stated emphasis is piloting AI education for general-education students: the page identifies a decision promulgating a pilot framework, and the supplied description says the pilot covers primary through high school before a nationwide rollout. That description also says it is aligned with the Informatics curriculum to avoid duplication. These details indicate a focus on introducing AI education across school levels and preparing for wider implementation; the inspected material does not establish further priorities or their relative importance (https://english.luatvietnam.vn/decision-no-3439-qd-bgddt-dated-december-15-2025-of-the-ministry-of-education-and-training-promulgating-the-framework-for-pilot-artificial-intellige-421474-doc1.html).
educationalTechnologySummary: The accessible page identifies a framework for AI education, but the rendered document could not be inspected in detail. The available evidence does not name any learning platform, software, hardware, or other educational technology developed or used by the initiative. AI is identified as the subject of education, which alone does not establish that an AI product or tool is used to support learning. Whether the framework specifies educational technologies therefore remains unknown, rather than confirmed absent (https://english.luatvietnam.vn/decision-no-3439-qd-bgddt-dated-december-15-2025-of-the-ministry-of-education-and-training-promulgating-the-framework-for-pilot-artificial-intellige-421474-doc1.html).

inclusion.reason: This initiative qualifies for inclusion under both the AI-literacy requirement and the inclusion route for government-issued documents. The page explicitly states this is a Ministry of Education and Training (MOET) decision—a national government body—promulgating an educational framework that includes specific learning objectives about how AI works, AI ethics, and practical applications. This satisfies the core requirement of providing educational content about AI usage and functioning, rather than merely using AI tools for delivery. The document is a formal government mandate for pilot implementation across school levels.

metadata.Initiative / Programme: National Programme for Developing Artificial Intelligence Human Resources (approved Aug 2026)
metadata.Description: Government programme extending AI skills development beyond schools to vocational and higher education.

summary: Vietnam’s National Programme for Developing Artificial Intelligence Human Resources aims to build AI knowledge and skills across general, vocational and higher education, as well as support workforce training and retraining. A national AI education framework sets out 12 periods of core content per year group, to be integrated flexibly into existing lessons, projects and activities rather than initially taught as a compulsory standalone subject. School pilots and teacher preparation support planned implementation, with emphasis on responsible AI use, critical thinking and verifying AI-generated information. The programme sets 2030 participation targets, but the available evidence describes goals and early pilots rather than nationwide delivery.
pedagogicalSummary: The article describes AI learning as integrated into existing subjects and activities rather than initially taught as a compulsory standalone subject: schools may incorporate it into lessons, STEM activities, projects and extracurricular clubs. A pilot phase is used to identify implementation challenges before broader rollout, and the 2026 framework sets 12 periods of core AI content per year group while leaving schools flexibility over lesson organisation. The reported approach also emphasizes critical thinking, responsible use and checking AI-generated information against multiple sources; teacher preparation and training support delivery. These details describe intended arrangements and early pilots, not evidence of consistent classroom practice nationwide. (https://opengovasia.com/vietnam-strengthens-ai-education-across-its-school-system/)
prioritySummary: The initiative’s stated emphasis is building AI capability broadly across the education system, from general education to vocational and higher education, while also developing a skilled workforce. By 2030, targets include basic AI knowledge and skills for at least 80% of general-education students, AI-related training for at least 80% of vocational learners and all higher-education students, and training or retraining at least 50,000 university-qualified people in AI application, including 10,000 specialists. The article connects these aims to national digital transformation and innovation, while also stressing that technical ability should complement independent thought and creativity. It does not establish a single priority that overrides the others. (https://opengovasia.com/vietnam-strengthens-ai-education-across-its-school-system/)
educationalTechnologySummary: The article reports that some educational institutions use AI tools to assist teachers with preparation, including generating teaching materials, converting text to speech and creating visual content. It does not name any platforms, software or hardware, and does not specify whether these tools are supplied or developed by the initiative; no initiative-developed educational technology is identified in the inspected article. AI is also a subject of learning, but that alone does not establish use of a particular learning technology. The article notes that uneven access to digital equipment, internet connectivity and hardware limitations affect pilot delivery, without specifying equipment or systems. Thus, the available evidence identifies general-purpose AI-assisted preparation tasks but gives little detail about the technologies or their implementation. (https://opengovasia.com/vietnam-strengthens-ai-education-across-its-school-system/)

inclusion.reason: The article describes AI-literacy content and a national AI Education Content Framework, school pilots and government-approved human-resources programme, providing the government-issued/mandated inclusion route. Evidence: https://opengovasia.com/vietnam-strengthens-ai-education-across-its-school-system/. The page reports these policies but does not link to the original government documents, so their details could not be independently verified here.
